curriculumGuide.title: Before Unit 1: Hangul and sound
curriculumGuide.goal: Read Korean syllable blocks accurately before relying on romanization.
points: Know that each block is built from initial consonant, vowel, and optional final consonant.
Practice final consonants because they affect the next syllable.
Use romanization as support, then move your eyes back to Hangul and audio.
curriculumGuide.task: Read five phrases aloud, then play the audio and compare.

curriculumGuide.title: Every chapter: vocabulary, grammar, conversation
curriculumGuide.goal: Move from word to pattern to real exchange.
points: Vocabulary: learn the chunk and one sentence frame.
Grammar: learn the particle or ending that makes the sentence work.
Conversation: say the item inside a mini dialogue, then change one word.
curriculumGuide.task: Open one word card, one grammar item, and one expression before the final task.

curriculumGuide.title: Beginner functions to cover
curriculumGuide.goal: Build survival communication, not only translation.
points: Ordering food, buying items, asking price, and paying.
Asking location, transportation, classroom help, and inviting.
curriculumGuide.task: After each chapter, say one sentence you could use in Korea today.

curriculumGuide.title: Culture and politeness layer
curriculumGuide.goal: Choose Korean that fits the person and situation.
points: Default to 해요체 with adults, staff, teachers, and strangers.
Notice titles and honorific direction before casual speech.
Learn signs and staff instructions even if you do not use them often yourself.
curriculumGuide.task: For each expression, decide whether it is casual, polite everyday, or formal/service speech.

chapters.title: Hangul, Syllable Blocks, And Sound
chapters.goal: Get comfortable seeing Hangul as sound blocks, not English letters in disguise.
chapters.scenario: A first quiet study session where the learner reads one block, hears it, and repeats it back.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.en: Today we'll look at just one character. It's 한.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.ko: 한... 천천히 한 번만 더 말해 주세요.
dialogue.romanization: han... cheoncheonhi han beonman deo malhae juseyo.
dialogue.en: Han... please say it slowly one more time.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.ko: 좋아요. 한은 ㅎ, ㅏ, ㄴ이 같이 있어요.
dialogue.romanization: joayo. haneun hieut, a, nieuni gachi isseoyo.
dialogue.en: Good. 한 has ㅎ, ㅏ, and ㄴ together.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: Ah, now I'll look at the Hangul first.

chapters.guidedPractice: Break 한글 into blocks, read each block from Hangul, then check romanization only after you try.
chapters.realLifeTask: Ask someone to say one Korean word slowly, then read the Hangul before checking romanization.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend says three phrases from this chapter. Learner points to the Hangul and repeats.
chapters.review: Can you explain that 한 is ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ, read a simple block, and use romanization only as a helper?

beginnerGuide.title: What a complete beginner should notice
beginnerGuide.body: Hangul is not an alphabet written in a line like English. Korean letters are grouped into square syllable blocks, so 한 is one spoken chunk made from ㅎ, ㅏ, and ㄴ.

beginnerGuide.title: How to study this chapter
beginnerGuide.body: Look at the Hangul first, try to read it, then use romanization only to check. If you start from romanization, you will build English pronunciation habits that are hard to undo.

beginnerGuide.title: Minimum outcome
beginnerGuide.body: You do not need perfect pronunciation yet. You should be able to point to a block, name its parts, and repeat a short phrase after listening.

checkpoints: I can see 한 as ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ.
I can ask 천천히 한 번만 더 말해 주세요.
I check Hangul first and use romanization only as backup.

hook.situation: You open a Korean app and see 안녕하세요. You have no idea what any of those shapes mean. Then someone tells you: each block is one spoken syllable, and the shapes literally show you where to put your mouth. You try 한 — it's ㅎ (breath from the throat) + ㅏ (mouth open wide) + ㄴ (tongue behind teeth). Suddenly the writing system makes sense.
objectives: Read any syllable block by identifying its consonant and vowel components
Produce the basic consonants ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅅ ㅇ ㅈ ㅎ and basic vowels ㅏ ㅓ ㅗ ㅜ ㅡ ㅣ
Use romanization only as a checking tool, not as a pronunciation crutch
hook.whyItMatters: Every other chapter in this course is built on Hangul. If you skip this and rely on romanization, you will mispronounce Korean for months — romanization uses English spelling habits that do not match Korean sounds. Twenty minutes with Hangul now saves hundreds of hours of re-learning later. King Sejong designed this alphabet to be learned in a single morning, and he was right.

grammarNotes.title: 자음 (Consonants) — Ten Core Shapes
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of consonants as MOUTH BLUEPRINTS. Each shape is a rough sketch of the part of your mouth that makes the sound. ㄱ looks like the back of the throat closing (a bent shape, like the back of your tongue pressing up). ㄴ looks like the tongue tip touching the roof of the mouth. ㅁ is a closed mouth (a box). ㅂ adds lips opening from that box. ㅅ is two lines like teeth. Once you see the blueprint, the sound is no longer random — it is a diagram.
grammarNotes.formation: Consonant placed at the top-left of a syllable block (onset position) or at the bottom (coda position, called 받침)

examples.en: ㄱ with different vowels
examples.note: ㄱ makes a 'g/k' sound — the shape curves like the back of the throat closing. Same consonant, different vowels produce different syllables

examples.en: ㄴ with different vowels
examples.note: ㄴ = 'n' — the shape shows the tongue tip pressed to the ridge behind the upper teeth; this is exactly the mouth position for 'n'

examples.en: ㅁ with different vowels
examples.note: ㅁ = 'm' — literally a box representing a closed mouth; lips close for 'm', which is what the box shape shows

examples.en: ㅂ with different vowels
examples.note: ㅂ = 'b/p' — the box (ㅁ) opens at the top as lips part; the two top strokes represent the lips opening

examples.en: ㅇ as a silent placeholder — no consonant sound
examples.note: ㅇ in the onset (top) position is silent — it is a zero-sound placeholder so the syllable block can be built. When ㅇ appears at the bottom (받침), it makes an 'ng' sound

a.en: da — 'd' made with the tongue flat against the ridge

b.en: na — 'n' also made with the tongue at the same ridge

contrastPairs.explanation: ㄷ and ㄴ look similar and use the same part of the mouth. The difference: ㄴ lets air flow through the nose (nasal), while ㄷ blocks and releases air through the mouth (stop). ㄴ has a curved foot shape; ㄷ adds a top horizontal line, making it 'heavier' — visually and phonetically.

Both ㅅ and ㅈ involve the front of the mouth. ㅅ (two lines like teeth) is a light 's/sh' shape. ㅈ adds a horizontal base, increasing the pressure to produce 'j'. More strokes in Hangul often means more mouth pressure for the sound.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: Reading 이 as 'ee' (as in 'see') — exactly like English
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 이 is close to English 'ee' but shorter and unrounded — and only approximately. The real fix is to listen to a native speaker and imitate, not to map to English sounds.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers instinctively reach for their own vowel sounds when they see romanization. But Korean 이 is not English 'ee', Korean 으 has no English equivalent at all, and Korean ㄹ is not 'r' or 'l'. Romanization is a temporary scaffold — use it to check yourself, but learn the actual sounds by ear. The earlier you stop reading romanization as English, the faster your pronunciation improves.

exceptions: ㄹ is romanized as 'r' between vowels (바람 = baram) and as 'l' at the end of a syllable (달 = dal), but it is neither the English 'r' nor 'l' — it is a single Korean sound that you learn by ear
ㅇ is silent at the start of a syllable but pronounced 'ng' at the bottom (받침): 강 = gang, 방 = bang
Some consonants sound different depending on their position in the word — this is called consonant assimilation and you will learn it naturally as your listening improves

grammarNotes.title: 모음 (Vowels) — Lines, Dots, and Direction
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of vowels as a COMPASS ROSE. Every basic Korean vowel is built from three strokes: a vertical line (|), a horizontal line (—), and a short tick that points like a compass needle. The tick's direction tells you the sound. When the tick points RIGHT from a vertical line → ㅏ (open 'a'). When it points LEFT → ㅓ (deeper 'uh'). Tick ABOVE a horizontal line → ㅗ ('o'). Tick BELOW → ㅜ ('oo'). No tick on horizontal → ㅡ (flat 'eu'). Vertical line alone → ㅣ ('ee'). Once you see the compass, you never forget which way the vowel sounds.
grammarNotes.formation: Tall vowels (ㅏ ㅓ ㅣ ㅐ ㅔ) sit to the RIGHT of the consonant. Wide vowels (ㅗ ㅜ ㅡ) sit BELOW the consonant. Combined vowels are built by merging two basic vowels.

examples.en: ㅏ vs ㅓ — both tall vowels beside the consonant
examples.note: ㅏ: tick points RIGHT — mouth open, sound comes forward. ㅓ: tick points LEFT — sound pulls back in the throat. The tick is the only difference on the page and in your mouth.

examples.en: ㅗ vs ㅜ — both wide vowels below the consonant
examples.note: ㅗ: tick points UP from the horizontal line — lips round and rise. ㅜ: tick points DOWN — lips round and drop. The compass direction = the lip movement direction.

examples.en: ㅡ vs ㅣ — no tick needed
examples.note: ㅡ: just the horizontal bar — the mouth is flat and neutral, no rounding. ㅣ: just the vertical bar — teeth close, sound is 'ee'. These are the simplest vowel shapes.

examples.en: Combined vowels — ㅏ+ㅣ and ㅓ+ㅣ
examples.note: ㅐ (ㅏ+ㅣ) and ㅔ (ㅓ+ㅣ) look similar and in modern Korean are often pronounced identically as a mid-front 'e' sound. Beginners can treat them the same.

examples.en: Compound vowels starting with ㅗ/ㅜ
examples.note: ㅗ+ㅏ = ㅘ (wa), ㅜ+ㅓ = ㅝ (wo/weo), ㅜ+ㅣ = ㅟ (wi). These compound vowels are built by stacking two base vowels — you can decode them by recognizing the parts

a.en: bo — tall 'o', lips rounded, sound rises

b.en: bu — deep 'oo', lips rounded, sound drops

contrastPairs.explanation: Same consonant ㅂ, different vowels. ㅗ sits with its tick pointing UP — the vowel shape tells you the sound moves upward/forward in the mouth. ㅜ has its tick pointing DOWN — the sound descends to a deeper 'oo'. The visual and physical direction match.

ㅏ and ㅓ look almost the same but the tick faces opposite directions. ㅏ faces right (toward open space) → mouth opens. ㅓ faces left (inward) → the sound retreats to the back of the mouth. This is not coincidence — King Sejong's design mapped physical articulation to visual direction.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: Pronouncing 으 (ㅡ) as 'oo' or 'u' based on romanization 'eu'
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 으 has no English equivalent — it is a central unrounded vowel. Keep your lips flat (no rounding) and the tongue in the middle of the mouth.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: The romanization 'eu' looks like the French 'eu' or English 'uh', so beginners round their lips. But 으 is made with flat, unrounded lips — the opposite of 'oo'. To train this sound: say 'ee' (이) and keep your lips in exactly that flat position, then move your tongue back. The sound you get is 으. Practice 이 then 으 back and forth.

exceptions: ㅢ (의) is technically ㅡ+ㅣ but in natural speech it often sounds like just 이 (ee) or 에 (e) depending on position: 의사 = 'uisa' (doctor) but the particle 의 usually sounds like 에
Vowel length (long vs. short) existed in classical Korean but modern Seoul Korean has largely lost it — beginners can ignore vowel length completely
Some compound vowels like ㅙ (ㅗ+ㅐ) and ㅞ (ㅜ+ㅔ) are rare and sound very similar to ㅘ and ㅝ respectively

exampleSentence.en: Hangul is easy to learn.
exampleSentence.note: Subject marker 은 attaches to 한글 — you will learn this particle in Chapter 2

exampleSentence.en: ㄱ is a consonant.
exampleSentence.note: 이에요 means 'is/am/are' — the simplest Korean copula; perfect for labeling what something is

exampleSentence.en: ㅏ is a vowel.
exampleSentence.note: 는 is the topic marker for vowel-ending words — 모음 ends in ㅁ so it uses 은, but ㅏ alone ends in a vowel, so 는 attaches

exampleSentence.en: What is this character?
exampleSentence.note: 뭐예요 = 'what is it?' — an essential question frame for asking about unfamiliar characters

exampleSentence.en: What is the sound of this character?
exampleSentence.note: 의 is a possessive particle — '글자의 소리' = 'the sound of the character'

exampleSentence.en: 한 has the final consonant ㄴ.
exampleSentence.note: 한 = ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ. The final ㄴ is the 받침.

exampleSentence.en: The pronunciation is difficult.
exampleSentence.note: A natural comment to make as a beginner — acknowledges that pronunciation takes practice

exampleSentence.en: I read Hangul slowly.
exampleSentence.note: Focus on reading the Hangul shape before checking romanization.

exampleSentence.en: I write my name.
exampleSentence.note: 쓰다 is ㅡ-irregular: the ㅡ drops before 아/어, giving 써요 not 쓰어요

exampleSentence.en: I listen to the sound and repeat it.
exampleSentence.note: Useful first-lesson action; the irregular form 들어요 is learned later.

exampleSentence.en: I speak slowly.
exampleSentence.note: 말하다 → 말해요 in polite form; 천천히 = slowly — essential classroom vocabulary

exampleSentence.en: Please repeat after me.
exampleSentence.note: 따라 하세요 is a polite command — very common in language class settings

exampleSentence.en: Please speak slowly.
exampleSentence.note: One of the most useful phrases for a beginner — you will say this constantly in your first weeks of Korean

exampleSentence.en: I listen again.
exampleSentence.note: 다시 comes before the verb it modifies — Korean adverbs do not change form

exampleSentence.en: Yes, I understand.
exampleSentence.note: 알겠어요 literally means 'I will know it' (future-inference form of 알다) but functions as 'I get it now' — use it as a fixed phrase

extendedVocabulary.english: I don't know / I'm not sure

exampleSentence.en: I don't know this character.
exampleSentence.note: The counterpart to 알겠어요 — equally important to have in your first lesson vocabulary

exampleSentence.en: I practice Hangul every day.
exampleSentence.note: 매일 = every day; 연습하다 follows the 하다 verb pattern — 연습 (practice noun) + 하다 (to do)

extendedDialogue.setting: Jiyeon (a Korean tutor) meets Minjun (a complete beginner) for their first online lesson

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Hello! I'm Jiyeon. What's your name?
lines.grammarNote: 이름이 뭐예요? is a real first-lesson question. 뭐예요 asks 'what is it?' using the polite copula 예요.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: I'm Minjun. Hangul is new for me.
lines.grammarNote: 처음이에요 = 'it is my first time.' This sounds more natural for a beginner than asking for an abstract explanation immediately.

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 좋아요. 오늘은 글자 하나만 먼저 볼게요. 이건 '한'이에요.
lines.romanization: Joayo. Oneureun geulja hanaman meonjeo bolgeyo. Igeon 'han'ieyo.
lines.en: Good. Today let's look at just one character first. This is 한.
lines.grammarNote: 하나만 = 'only one'; 먼저 볼게요 is a teacher's gentle 'we'll look first,' not a textbook definition.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Han... please say it a little slowly.
lines.grammarNote: 조금 천천히 말해 주세요 is a natural survival request when the sound is still unfamiliar.

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 한. ㅎ, ㅏ, ㄴ이 같이 있어요.
lines.romanization: Han. Hieut, a, nieuni gachi isseoyo.
lines.en: Han. ㅎ, ㅏ, and ㄴ are together.
lines.grammarNote: 같이 있어요 keeps the syllable-block idea concrete: the letters sit together inside one block.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Then ㅎ is a consonant, and ㅏ is a vowel?
lines.grammarNote: 은/는 marks the item being identified: ㅎ은..., ㅏ는.... The learner is checking the category, not reciting a definition.

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 맞아요. 마지막 ㄴ도 자음이에요. 세 개가 모여서 한 글자가 돼요.
lines.romanization: Majayo. Majimak nieundo jaeumieyo. Se gaega moyeoseo han geuljaga dwaeyo.
lines.en: Right. The final ㄴ is also a consonant. Three pieces come together and become one character.
lines.grammarNote: 도 adds 'also'; 글자가 돼요 explains the result of combining the pieces.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 아, 한이에요. 로마자보다 한글을 먼저 볼게요.
lines.romanization: A, hanieyo. Romajaboda hangeureul meonjeo bolgeyo.
lines.en: Ah, it's 한. I'll look at the Hangul first, before the romanization.
lines.grammarNote: 보다 marks comparison: 로마자보다 한글 = Hangul rather than romanization as the main focus.

readingText.title: 민준의 첫 한글 공부 (Minjun's First Hangul Study)
readingText.body: 오늘 처음으로 한글을 공부했어요. 한글 글자는 자음과 모음으로 만들어요. 자음이 열 개 있어요: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅇ, ㅈ, ㅎ. 모음도 있어요: ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. 이 자음과 모음을 합치면 글자가 돼요. 예를 들어, ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ = 한이에요. 처음에는 어려웠지만 이제 조금 읽을 수 있어요. 내일 더 연습할 거예요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Today I studied Hangul for the first time. Hangul characters are made with consonants and vowels. There are ten consonants: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅇ, ㅈ, ㅎ. There are also vowels: ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. When you combine these consonants and vowels, you get a character. For example, ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ = 한. At first it was difficult, but now I can read a little. I will practice more tomorrow.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How many basic consonants does Minjun list in the diary?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 열 개 (ten) — ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅇ, ㅈ, ㅎ

comprehensionQuestions.question: What example does the diary give for how a syllable block is made?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ = 한 — a consonant (ㅎ) + a vowel (ㅏ) + a final consonant (ㄴ) combine into one spoken syllable block

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the 이에요/예요 copula forms in the text. Why does each one appear, and when does the ending change from 이에요 to 예요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: The true copula form in the text is 한이에요: 한 ends in the final consonant ㄴ, so it takes 이에요. 글자가 돼요 is not 이에요/예요; it is 되다, meaning 'becomes.' The reusable rule is: consonant-final words take 이에요, vowel-final words take 예요.

culturalNote.title: 한글날 — The Holiday That Celebrates an Alphabet
culturalNote.body: October 9th is 한글날 (Hangul Day), a national holiday in South Korea celebrating Hangul's proclamation. King Sejong's court created Hangul in 1443 and proclaimed it in 1446 through Hunminjeongeum. This makes Korean one of the only languages in the world with a holiday dedicated to its writing system. King Sejong commissioned Hangul because the existing Chinese characters (한자) were so difficult that ordinary people could not easily read or write. He designed Hangul specifically to be learned quickly by everyone. Historical records say it could be learned 'in a morning' by a wise person and 'in ten days' by a less clever person. Modern linguists consider it one of the most scientifically designed writing systems ever created. When you struggle with a new letter, remember: King Sejong designed it so that you would not have to struggle for long.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which vowel has a vertical stroke with a short tick pointing right?
inlineExercises.explanation: ㅏ has a vertical stroke with a short tick pointing RIGHT. ㅓ looks similar but the tick points LEFT (that is the 'uh/eo' sound). ㅗ is a horizontal stroke with a tick pointing UP (the 'o' sound). ㅣ is just a vertical bar with no tick (the 'ee' sound). The direction of the tick is the key distinguishing feature.

inlineExercises.prompt: The syllable block 한 is made of which components?
inlineExercises.explanation: Korean syllable blocks follow the order: (1) initial consonant at top-left, (2) vowel to the right or below, (3) optional final consonant at the bottom. So 한 = ㅎ (initial) + ㅏ (vowel, to the right because it is a tall vowel) + ㄴ (final, at the bottom). The other options have the order wrong or use the wrong vowel — ㅓ would give 헌, not 한.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which of these is the SILENT consonant placeholder used when a syllable starts with a vowel sound?
inlineExercises.explanation: ㅇ in the onset (initial) position makes no sound — it is a placeholder that allows vowel-initial syllables to have a proper block shape. So 아 is written as ㅇ+ㅏ, not just ㅏ floating alone. ㅎ makes an 'h' sound, ㅅ makes an 's' sound, ㄴ makes an 'n' sound. Only ㅇ is silent at the start of a syllable (though it makes 'ng' at the end).

inlineExercises.prompt: How do you say 'Please speak slowly' in Korean?
inlineExercises.explanation: 천천히 = slowly, 말해 주세요 = please speak (V + 아/어 주세요 pattern). 다시 들어요 means 'listen again', 알겠어요 means 'I understand', 모르겠어요 means 'I don't know'. The V + 아/어 주세요 pattern (pattern-015) is used for polite requests for someone to perform an action for you.

inlineExercises.prompt: A learner sees ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ. Which block should they read?
inlineExercises.explanation: ㅎ is the first consonant, ㅏ is the vowel, and ㄴ sits at the bottom as 받침. Together they form 한. This checks the Chapter 1 skill: read the block from its parts before relying on romanization.

inlineExercises.prompt: Where does a TALL vowel like ㅏ, ㅓ, or ㅣ appear in a syllable block?
options: To the right of the consonant
inlineExercises.correct: To the right of the consonant
inlineExercises.explanation: Tall vowels (ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅣ, ㅐ, ㅔ and their compounds) sit to the RIGHT of the consonant: 가 (ㄱ+ㅏ), 서 (ㅅ+ㅓ), 시 (ㅅ+ㅣ). Wide vowels (ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ) sit BELOW the consonant: 고 (ㄱ+ㅗ), 수 (ㅅ+ㅜ). This layout rule is completely regular — once you know it, you can read any block.

inlineExercises.prompt: What does 알겠어요 most naturally mean in a classroom context?
inlineExercises.explanation: 알겠어요 literally contains 알다 (to know) + 겠 (future/inference marker) + 어요, but it functions as 'I got it / I understand / Okay' in conversation. It is NOT 모르겠어요 (I don't know / I'm not sure), NOT 다시 말해 주세요 (please say it again), NOT 맞아요? (is that right?). Use 알겠어요 to signal to your teacher that you have understood what they just explained.

inlineExercises.prompt: Type the syllable block made from ㅁ + ㅏ.
inlineExercises.explanation: ㅁ gives the first sound and ㅏ sits to its right as a tall vowel. Together they form the single syllable block 마.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Please speak slowly.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 천천히 tells how to speak, and 말해 주세요 makes the polite request. This is the classroom phrase learners need when the Korean is too fast.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which block starts with a vowel sound and uses ㅇ as the silent placeholder?
inlineExercises.explanation: 아 begins with a vowel sound, so ㅇ fills the first consonant slot silently. 나 and 한 begin with real consonant sounds.

bullets: Each Hangul syllable is a BLOCK built from: initial consonant + vowel (+ optional final consonant 받침) — read left-to-right, top-to-bottom within the block

MOUTH BLUEPRINTS: consonant shapes sketch the mouth position (ㅁ = closed lips, ㄴ = tongue at ridge, ㅇ = silent/circular). COMPASS ROSE: vowel ticks point in the direction of the mouth movement (ㅏ = right/open, ㅓ = left/back, ㅗ = up, ㅜ = down)
Romanization is a CHECKING TOOL, not Korean spelling — use it to verify your reading, then cover it and practice reading Hangul directly

writingTask.prompt: Write your own first name (or a Korean word you know) in Hangul, breaking it into syllable blocks.
writingTask.hint: Build each block as 자음 + 모음 (+ 받침 if there is a bottom consonant), e.g. 한 = ㅎ+ㅏ+ㄴ.
writingTask.model: 한글: ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ → 한, ㄱ + ㅡ + ㄹ → 글. 소리: 한글.
writingTask.modelEn: Hangul: ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ → 한, ㄱ + ㅡ + ㄹ → 글. Sound: "hangeul."

canDo: Tell consonants from vowels and name the ten core 자음 shapes
See a vowel's lines and dots and read its direction (모음)
Build a syllable block from 자음 + 모음 (+ 받침)
Read a written block back as one sound, not separate letters (글자 · 소리)

chapters.title: Greetings And Self-Introduction
chapters.goal: Start a first meeting politely and say your name without freezing.
chapters.scenario: A language exchange table where two people meet for the first time.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Hello. Nice to meet you for the first time.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Hello. I'm Hana.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: I'm Minjun. Nice to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Nice to meet you too. I look forward to studying together.

chapters.guidedPractice: Replace the name in 저는 하나예요 with your own name, then add one greeting and one closing.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say hello, give your name, and close with one polite friendly line.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend asks 이름이 뭐예요? Learner answers with 저는 ___예요.
chapters.review: Can you greet, say your name, thank someone, and close the conversation politely?

beginnerGuide.title: Why greetings come before grammar
beginnerGuide.body: A beginner needs phrases that work immediately. 안녕하세요, 감사합니다, 죄송합니다, 네, and 아니요 let you participate politely before you can build long sentences.

beginnerGuide.title: Politeness first
beginnerGuide.body: Use polite everyday Korean until the other person clearly uses casual speech with you. This course treats 해요체 and polite chunks as your default safety zone.

beginnerGuide.title: Your first personal sentence
beginnerGuide.body: 저는 ___예요 is not just translation practice. It teaches 은/는 as “as for me,” which becomes the base for many later sentences.

checkpoints: I can say 안녕하세요 without looking at English.
I can say 저는 ___예요 with my own name.
I can close a first meeting with 만나서 반가워요 or 잘 부탁드려요.

curriculumTrack.description: Hangul, survival sentences, particles, polite present, and daily actions.

learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

sampleAnswer.ko: 안녕하세요. 저는 하나예요. 만나서 반가워요.
sampleAnswer.en: Hello. I'm Hana. Nice to meet you.

checklist: I can say 안녕하세요 without looking at English.
I can say 저는 ___예요 with my own name.
I can close a first meeting with 만나서 반가워요 or 잘 부탁드려요.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You walk into your first Korean language exchange. Someone smiles at you and says '안녕하세요!' You want to reply, say your name, and make a good impression — but you freeze because you're not sure whether to say '나는 마이클이에요' or '저는 마이클이에요', and you have no idea where to start. This chapter gives you the exact phrases you need from the very first second.
objectives: Greet, thank, and apologize using the five most essential Korean phrases
Introduce yourself with 저는 ___이에요 / 예요 — the pattern every Korean conversation starts with
Understand why 은/는 is the topic marker and when to use 이에요 vs 예요
hook.whyItMatters: These phrases are not 'beginner drills' — they are the exact sentences Koreans use every day in every context. Getting 저는 ___예요 right from day one sets the foundation for the entire 은/는 system, which appears in hundreds of later sentences. And using 감사합니다 vs 고마워요 correctly shows you understand Korean social register — Koreans notice that instantly.

grammarNotes.title: N은/는 — topic marker
grammarNotes.func: 은/는 marks the topic of a sentence — the thing you single out to talk about ("as for ___"). It is the backbone of introductions and of saying what something is.

examples.en: I'm Michael.
examples.note: Introducing yourself — 저 ends in a vowel, so 는.

examples.en: What's your name?
examples.note: The topic is 'the name' — 이름 ends in a consonant, so 은.

examples.en: Today I'm busy.
examples.note: Spotlighting 오늘 hints at a contrast — other days may be different.

examples.en: My friend is Korean.
examples.note: 친구 ends in a vowel → 는. Everyday topic, everyday words.

keyPoint.label: 은/는 also hints at a contrast
keyPoint.body: Besides naming the topic, 은/는 often quietly sets one thing against others. 저는 학생이에요 = 'as for me, I'm a student' (someone else might not be). 오늘은 바빠요 = 'today I'm busy' (other days, maybe not). You don't have to force this nuance — just notice that spotlighting something with 은/는 can imply a comparison.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 이름은 is pronounced [이르믄]: the final ㅁ links into the next vowel (linking, 연음).

drill.instruction: Say it about yourself — follow the model.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Don't translate "my name" word for word. 저는 ___이에요 already means "as for me, I'm ___," so there is no separate word for "name" here. Also use 저 (polite I), not 나 (casual), with people you have just met.

grammarNotes.title: N이에요/예요 — polite "to be"
grammarNotes.func: 이에요/예요 is the polite present tense of 이다 ("to be"). Attach it to a noun to say what something is: 저는 학생이에요 — "I'm a student."

examples.en: I'm a student.
examples.note: 학생 ends in a consonant → 이에요.

examples.en: I'm Hana.
examples.note: 하나 ends in a vowel → 예요.

examples.en: This person is a teacher.
examples.note: It works for other people too — 이분 = 'this person' (polite).

examples.en: This is water.
examples.note: 물 ends in a consonant → 이에요.

keyPoint.label: Polite vs formal, and the negative
keyPoint.body: 이에요/예요 is the everyday polite form — use it in class, with new acquaintances, and in shops. 입니다 (저는 학생입니다) is more formal: presentations, business, announcements. Both are correct, but 이에요/예요 is the natural default in conversation. To say what something is NOT, use N이/가 아니에요: 저는 학생이 아니에요 ("I'm not a student").

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 학생이에요 is pronounced [학쌩이에요]: ㄱ followed by ㅅ tightens the ㅅ to a tense [ㅆ].

drill.instruction: Introduce three people — follow the model.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: A consonant ending needs 이에요. 학생 ends in ㅇ (a 받침), so 학생예요 is wrong. Feel the final sound: a consonant takes 이에요, a vowel takes 예요.

exampleSentence.en: Hello. I am Jisu.
exampleSentence.note: 안녕하세요 is always the opener; then your name introduction follows naturally.

exampleSentence.en: I'll go first. Goodbye!
exampleSentence.note: Say 안녕히 계세요 when you are leaving and the other person is staying. Say 안녕히 가세요 to someone who is leaving.

exampleSentence.en: Thank you for helping me.
exampleSentence.note: 감사합니다 is the safer, more formal option — use it with strangers, in shops, and in any formal setting.

exampleSentence.en: It's a gift? Thank you so much!
exampleSentence.note: 고마워요 is warmer and more personal than 감사합니다 — great for friends and classmates.

exampleSentence.en: I'm sorry for being late.
exampleSentence.note: 죄송합니다 is the formal apology — use it when you've genuinely caused trouble or in professional/service situations.

exampleSentence.en: Sorry, I'm late.
exampleSentence.note: 미안해요 is the everyday polite apology — less heavy than 죄송합니다, appropriate for friends and classmates.

exampleSentence.en: Yes, I understand.
exampleSentence.note: 네 doesn't only mean 'yes' — it's also used as a listening signal ('I hear you') while someone is talking.

exampleSentence.en: No, I'm not a student.
exampleSentence.note: 아니요 is the polite 'no' — always softer when followed by a short explanation like 괜찮아요 or 몰라요.

exampleSentence.en: I'm Minjun. Nice to meet you!
exampleSentence.note: This is the standard 'nice to meet you' — said after exchanging names for the first time.

exampleSentence.en: One moment, please say that again.
exampleSentence.note: Use 잠시만요 any time you need a pause — at stores, classrooms, or when you haven't heard something clearly.

exampleSentence.en: I am Michael.
exampleSentence.note: 저 is the polite first-person pronoun — always use this until you're on casual terms with the other person.

exampleSentence.en: What is your name?
exampleSentence.note: 이름 ends in 'm' (consonant) → 이에요 when you predicate it: 제 이름은 ___이에요.

exampleSentence.en: I am a Korean language student.
exampleSentence.note: 학생 ends in 'ng' (consonant) → 이에요. One of the most-used identity nouns in self-introductions.

exampleSentence.en: Hello, teacher!
exampleSentence.note: 선생님 is both 'teacher' as a noun and the address form used directly — like calling someone 'Teacher' instead of their name.

exampleSentence.en: How do you do. / I'm meeting you for the first time.
exampleSentence.note: 처음 뵙겠습니다 is a very formal first-meeting phrase. In everyday language exchange settings, 만나서 반가워요 is more natural.

extendedVocabulary.english: to be glad / pleased to meet

exampleSentence.en: I'm so pleased to meet you.
exampleSentence.note: 반갑다 is an adjective meaning 'glad to see/meet someone.' In 해요 speech it becomes 반가워요 — an irregular adjective (ㅂ irregular: 반갑다 → 반가워요).

extendedVocabulary.english: am not / is not / are not

exampleSentence.en: I'm not a student. I'm a teacher.
exampleSentence.note: 아니에요 is the polite negative of 이에요/예요. Notice the pattern: N이/가 아니에요 — the noun takes 이/가 (subject marker), then 아니에요.

extendedDialogue.setting: A Korean language exchange meetup in Seoul. Minjun approaches Emma, who is joining for the first time.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Hello! Is this your first time here?
lines.grammarNote: 안녕하세요 is the all-purpose polite greeting. 오늘 처음이에요? keeps the question beginner-safe: 처음 ends in a consonant, so it takes 이에요.

lines.speaker: 엠마
lines.en: Yes, it's my first time. I'm Emma.
lines.grammarNote: 처음이에요 — 처음 ends in 'm' (consonant) → 이에요. 저는 엠마예요 — 엠마 ends in 'a' (vowel) → 예요. Two 이에요/예요 forms in one turn!

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Nice to meet you! I'm Minjun.
lines.grammarNote: 민준 ends in 'n' (consonant) → 이에요. 만나서 반가워요 is the standard 'nice to meet you' — use it immediately after learning someone's name for the first time.

lines.speaker: 엠마
lines.en: Sorry, please say your name again.
lines.grammarNote: 죄송해요 softens the request, and 다시 말해 주세요 is a survival phrase for first meetings and language class.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Sure, it is Minjun. I will say it slowly. Min-jun.
lines.grammarNote: 민준 ends in a consonant, so it takes 이에요. 천천히 is the natural adverb when repeating a name slowly.

lines.speaker: 엠마
lines.en: Ah, Minjun. Thank you.
lines.grammarNote: 씨 is a polite name suffix used after someone else's name. 감사합니다 is the safe thank-you for a new person.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: I will head out first. Goodbye.
lines.grammarNote: 안녕히 계세요 is said by the person leaving when the other person stays.

lines.speaker: 엠마
lines.ko: 네, 안녕히 가세요. 다음에 또 만나요.
lines.romanization: Ne, annyeonghi gaseyo. Daeume tto mannayo.
lines.en: Okay, goodbye. See you again next time.
lines.grammarNote: The person staying replies with 안녕히 가세요 to the person leaving. 다음에 또 만나요 is a friendly closing.

readingText.title: 첫 언어 교환 후 메시지 (Text messages after the first language exchange)
readingText.body:
민준: 엠마 씨, 오늘 만나서 반가워요.
엠마: 저도 반가워요. 이름을 다시 물어봐서 죄송해요.
민준: 괜찮아요. 한국어 공부는 처음이에요?
엠마: 네, 처음이에요. 천천히 말해 주세요.
민준: 네, 좋아요. 다음 주에 또 만나요?
엠마: 네, 감사합니다. 다음 주에 만나요!
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Minjun: Emma, nice to meet you today.
Emma: Nice to meet you too. Sorry for asking your name again.
Minjun: It's okay. Is this your first time studying Korean?
Emma: Yes, it is my first time. Please speak slowly.
Minjun: Sure, sounds good. Shall we meet again next week?
Emma: Yes, thank you. See you next week!

comprehensionQuestions.question: What does Emma apologize for in the text exchange?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: She apologizes for asking Minjun's name again: 이름을 다시 물어봐서 죄송해요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What phrase does Emma use when she needs slower Korean?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 천천히 말해 주세요 — Please speak slowly.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all instances of 이에요/예요 in the text. For each one, explain whether the noun ends in a consonant or vowel and why that determines the form used.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 처음이에요 appears twice. 처음 ends in the final consonant ㅁ, so it takes 이에요. This demonstrates the phonetic rule: consonant-final noun → 이에요, vowel-final noun → 예요.

culturalNote.title: 감사합니다 vs 고마워요 — Reading the Room
culturalNote.body: Both mean 'thank you,' but using the wrong one in the wrong setting is a social signal that Koreans pick up on immediately. 감사합니다 (formal, 입니다-style speech) is what you say to a shop assistant, a server, a stranger who helped you, your boss, or anyone you've just met — it's the safe, respectful default. 고마워요 (polite, 해요-style speech) is warmer and more personal — use it with classmates, language exchange partners, and friends you've started to get comfortable with. As a beginner, you'll never go wrong defaulting to 감사합니다. When someone uses 고마워요 with you, it's a small sign they feel at ease with you — a good thing.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 학생___ (I am a student.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 학생 ends in 'ng' — a final consonant (받침). The rule: consonant-final noun → 이에요. 학생예요 creates an awkward sound break and sounds unnatural. Check the final sound first: if you feel a consonant, attach 이에요.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 의사___ (I am a doctor.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 의사 ends in 'a' — a vowel. The rule: vowel-final noun → 예요. 의사이에요 would add an extra syllable that sounds clunky. When the noun ends in a vowel, attach 예요 directly.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '나는 마이클예요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Two errors: (1) 나는 should be 저는 in polite speech — 나 is casual and sounds rude to someone you've just met. (2) 마이클 ends in 'l' (consonant) → must use 이에요, not 예요. Always use 저 until you're on casual terms.

inlineExercises.prompt: Someone asks you 이름이 뭐예요? How do you answer if your name is 지수?
inlineExercises.explanation: Option 1 is wrong because 미국 is a country, not a name — this says 'I am America.' Option 3 is wrong because 이름 (name) is unnecessary in the answer and 나 is too casual for a first meeting. Option 2 is the natural, correct structure: topic (저는) + name + 예요. 지수 ends in a vowel, so use 예요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'Nice to meet you. I'm a Korean language teacher.'
inlineExercises.hint: 선생님 ends in 'm' (consonant) — which form of 'to be' do you use? 만나서 반가워요 is the standard 'nice to meet you' phrase.
inlineExercises.explanation: 만나서 반가워요 is the natural fixed greeting for first meetings. 저는 한국어 선생님이에요 uses 저는 for self-introduction and 이에요 after the consonant-ending noun 선생님.

inlineExercises.prompt: 이름___ 민수예요. (The name is Minsu. / My name is Minsu.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 이름 ends in 'm' — a final consonant. The 은/는 rule mirrors 이에요/예요: consonant final → 은, vowel final → 는. 이름은 spotlights 'name' as the topic of the sentence.

inlineExercises.prompt: You bump into someone accidentally and want to apologize. Which do you use in this situation?
inlineExercises.explanation: 감사합니다 means 'thank you' — not an apology. 만나서 반가워요 is 'nice to meet you' — also wrong context. 죄송합니다 is the correct formal apology for causing inconvenience to a stranger. In casual situations with friends, 미안해요 would also work, but 죄송합니다 is the safe formal choice in public.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저___ 학생이에요. (As for me, I am a student.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 저는 sets "I/me" as the topic for a polite self-introduction. With the subject marker, 저 changes form to 제가 — 저가 does not exist — and 를 would wrongly make 저 an object.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I am a student.'
inlineExercises.explanation: A simple Korean self-introduction starts with the topic 저는. 학생 ends in a consonant, so the polite “am/is” form is 이에요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'Thank you.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 감사합니다 is the safest polite thank-you for first meetings and service situations. 고마워요 is warm but a little more familiar.

bullets: 은/는 = SPOTLIGHT: attach to the topic noun to say 'as for ___' — 은 after a consonant, 는 after a vowel (학생은, 저는)
이에요/예요 = NAMEPLATE: polite 'to be' — 이에요 after a consonant, 예요 after a vowel (학생이에요, 의사예요)
감사합니다 (formal) vs 고마워요 (warm/friendly) — same meaning, different register; default to 감사합니다 until you read the room

writingTask.prompt: Write a short self-introduction (3 sentences): your name, what you do, and a polite closing.
writingTask.hint: Use 저는 ___이에요/예요 for the first two, and end with 만나서 반가워요.
writingTask.model: 안녕하세요. 저는 마이클이에요. 저는 학생이에요. 만나서 반가워요.
writingTask.modelEn: Hello. I'm Michael. I'm a student. Nice to meet you.

canDo: Greet, thank, and apologize politely (안녕하세요 · 감사합니다 · 죄송합니다)
Introduce myself with 저는 ___이에요/예요
Choose 은 or 는 correctly from the 받침
Tell 감사합니다 from 고마워요 by who I'm talking to

chapters.title: Noun Sentences: N이에요/예요 And 은/는
chapters.goal: Point at people and things around you and say what they are.
chapters.scenario: A cafe table with a menu, a notebook, and two people introducing themselves.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What is this?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: This is a menu. That is my notebook.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: I'm a student. What about you, Hana?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I'm an office worker.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make three N이에요/예요 sentences: your name, your role, and one object.
chapters.realLifeTask: Use 이건/저는 and say two noun sentences about your table or yourself.

beginnerGuide.title: The first sentence engine
beginnerGuide.body: N이에요/예요 lets you say what something is. This is the noun-sentence engine for names, jobs, objects, places, and simple identity.

beginnerGuide.title: Topic marker in plain English
beginnerGuide.body: 은/는 marks what we are talking about. In 저는 학생이에요, Korean first says “as for me,” then gives the information.

beginnerGuide.title: Do not over-translate particles
beginnerGuide.body: Particles often do not become separate English words. Learn the Korean frame and the sentence job, not a one-word English translation.

checkpoints: I can ask 이건 뭐예요?
I can choose 이에요 or 예요 from the noun ending.
I can use 저는 to set myself as the topic.

hook.situation: It's your first day at a Korean workplace or language-exchange group. Someone hands you a name card, points to a menu or book, and asks simple identity questions. You want to ask 'What is this?' and introduce your name, country, and job. You know a few Korean words — but how do you actually build a sentence that says what something IS? This chapter gives you the most useful two-word engine in Korean.
objectives: Use 이에요 after a noun ending in a consonant and 예요 after a noun ending in a vowel
Ask 이건 뭐예요? (What is this?) and answer with N이에요/예요
Use 은/는 to set the topic of a sentence, including the contrast meaning
hook.whyItMatters: N이에요/예요 is the 'is' of Korean — it builds every sentence that identifies, names, or defines something. You will use it within the first minute of any real Korean conversation. And 은/는 is not just grammar: it is how Korean tells the listener what the sentence is about. Miss this and your Korean sounds like a word list. Master it and your sentences feel complete.

grammarNotes.title: N이에요/예요 — the polite copula ("is/am/are")
grammarNotes.func: N이에요/예요 turns a noun into a polite statement of identity: "X is a/an N." It is the everyday spoken way to say what someone or something is. The negative — "X is not an N" — is N이/가 아니에요.

examples.en: I'm a student.
examples.note: 학생 ends in a consonant (받침 ㅇ) → 이에요.

examples.en: This is water.
examples.note: 물 ends in a consonant (ㄹ) → 이에요; spoken [무리에요] by linking. 이건 = 이것은 (this) shortened.

examples.en: This (person) is my friend.
examples.note: 친구 ends in a vowel → 예요, not 이에요.

examples.en: This place isn't a school.
examples.note: Negative of a vowel noun: 학교 + 가 아니에요. You attach 이/가 (never 이에요/예요) to the noun before 아니에요.

keyPoint.label: 이에요/예요 vs 입니다
keyPoint.body: Both mean "is." 이에요/예요 is the polite-conversational 해요체 you use in everyday talk. 입니다 is the formal 합니다체 used in announcements, presentations, the news, and the military. 입니다 attaches the same way regardless of 받침 — 학생입니다, 친구입니다 (no 이에요/예요 split). They mean the same thing; you choose by setting. This chapter uses 이에요/예요; 입니다 gets its own chapter.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a 받침 noun, 이에요 links onto the consonant: 물이에요 is pronounced [무리에요] and 집이 아니에요 is [지비 아니에요] (연음 — the final consonant slides onto the following vowel).

drill.instruction: Say what each thing is — follow the model, choosing 이에요 or 예요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English has one form, "is," for everything, so learners pick 이에요 or 예요 at random. In Korean the choice is automatic and depends only on the noun's last sound: 받침 → 이에요, vowel → 예요. Check the noun's ending first, then attach the matching form.

grammarNotes.title: N은/는 — the topic marker
grammarNotes.func: 은/는 attaches to a noun to mark it as the topic — the thing you single out to talk about, roughly "as for ___." It is the backbone of introductions (저는…) and of stating what something is, and it can also signal a contrast between two things.

examples.en: I'm a Korean(-language) student.
examples.note: 저 ends in a vowel → 는. The standard self-introduction frame.

examples.en: This book is a Korean book.
examples.note: 책 ends in a consonant → 은; spoken [채근] by linking.

examples.en: The teacher is Korean.
examples.note: 선생님 ends in a consonant → 은; spoken [선생니믄]. 은/는 raises 선생님 as the topic we're describing.

examples.en: I'm a student. My friend is a doctor.
examples.note: Two 는 set up a contrast — me vs. my friend — another core job of 은/는.

keyPoint.label: Topic, not subject — 은/는 vs 이/가
keyPoint.body: 은/는 marks the topic ("as for X, …") and often carries a quiet comparison; 이/가 marks the grammatical subject and points to new or specific information (누가 왔어요? — 친구가 왔어요). For now, use 은/는 for introductions and for saying what something is, and use 이/가 when answering "who/what?" The full 은/는 vs 이/가 distinction has its own chapter.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a 받침 noun, 은 links onto the consonant: 책은 is pronounced [채근] and 집은 is [지븐] (연음).

drill.instruction: Introduce each person — follow the model, choosing 은 or 는.
drill.model: (저 / 학생) → 저는 학생이에요. / (친구 / 의사) → 친구는 의사예요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English keeps the subject the same whether you add "too" or not ("I'm a student" / "I'm a student too"). In Korean, 도 ("also") replaces 은/는 rather than stacking onto it. Drop the 는 and say 저도 — never 저는도.

exampleSentence.en: I am a student.
exampleSentence.note: 저 ends in a vowel, so the topic marker is 는. Use 저 with strangers and adults; 나 is casual.

exampleSentence.en: My name is Minsu.
exampleSentence.note: 이름 ends in consonant ㅁ → topic marker 은; 민수 ends in vowel ㅜ → 예요.

exampleSentence.en: I am a university student.
exampleSentence.note: 대학생 ends in consonant 받침 ㅇ → 이에요; 대학 (university) + 학생 (student)

exampleSentence.en: I am an English teacher.
exampleSentence.note: 선생님 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요; 님 is a respectful suffix — never drop it when addressing a teacher

exampleSentence.en: My friend is a doctor.
exampleSentence.note: 의사 ends in vowel ㅏ → 예요; 제 is the possessive form of 저 (my)

exampleSentence.en: I am an office worker.
exampleSentence.note: 회사원 ends in consonant 받침 ㄴ → 이에요; 회사(company) + 원(member/worker)

exampleSentence.en: What country are you from?
exampleSentence.note: 나라 ends in vowel ㅏ → would take 예요 when used as the sentence topic; 어느 = which

exampleSentence.en: I am Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요; [country] + 사람 is the standard pattern for nationality

exampleSentence.en: What is this?
exampleSentence.note: 이건 = 이것 + 은 (contracted); 이것 = this thing, 은 = topic marker; used constantly in real speech — more natural than 이것은

exampleSentence.en: What is your name?
exampleSentence.note: 뭐 ends in vowel → 예요; 뭐 is the spoken/colloquial form of 무엇 (what)

exampleSentence.en: I am not Japanese.
exampleSentence.note: 아니에요 is the negative of 이에요/예요; the noun before it takes 이/가 (subject marker): 일본 사람이 아니에요

exampleSentence.en: My name is Minsu.
exampleSentence.note: 제 is the possessive form of 저 (polite 'I'); 내 is the possessive of 나 (casual 'I') — use 제 in formal/polite situations

exampleSentence.en: What is your job?
exampleSentence.note: 직업 ends in consonant 받침 ㅂ → if the answer uses it as topic: 직업은; as subject in the question: 직업이

exampleSentence.en: This is Korean (the language).
exampleSentence.note: 한국어 ends in vowel ㅓ → 예요. Use this when identifying a word, sentence, label, or class as Korean.

exampleSentence.en: I am an English teacher.
exampleSentence.note: 영어 describes the kind of teacher; 선생님 is the final noun, and it ends in ㅁ → 이에요.

exampleSentence.en: I'm Minjun. Nice to meet you!
exampleSentence.note: 반갑습니다 is formal; 반가워요 is slightly less formal — both are appropriate when meeting someone for the first time

exampleSentence.en: Which country are you from?
exampleSentence.note: 어느 is a modifier — it must be followed by a noun; unlike 어디 (where), 어느 modifies a noun directly

extendedDialogue.setting: Jiyeon, a Korean office worker, meets Minho, a new foreign colleague, in the break room on his first day

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Hello! I'm Jiyeon. Nice to meet you for the first time.
lines.grammarNote: 저는 — 저 ends in vowel → 는; 지연이에요 — 지연 ends in consonant ㄴ → 이에요

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: Hello! I'm Minho. I'm glad to meet you too.
lines.grammarNote: 민호예요 — 민호 ends in vowel ㅗ → 예요; 저도 — 도 means 'also/too,' not a topic marker

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Minho, what country are you from?
lines.grammarNote: 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요; the question has the same form as the statement — only intonation changes

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 저는 호주 사람이에요. 제 나라는 호주예요.
lines.romanization: Jeoneun hoju saramieyo. Je naraneun hojuyeyo.
lines.en: I'm Australian. My country is Australia.
lines.grammarNote: 호주 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요. 나라는 uses 는 because 나라 ends in a vowel, and 호주 ends in a vowel → 예요.

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Oh, really? What is your job?
lines.grammarNote: 직업이 뭐예요? — 직업 takes subject marker 이 here (not topic marker 은); 뭐 ends in vowel → 예요

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: I'm a designer. What about you, Jiyeon?
lines.grammarNote: 디자이너예요 — 디자이너 ends in vowel ㅓ → 예요; 씨는요? — 는 is the topic marker + 요 means 'and you?' — a natural way to return a question

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: I'm an office worker. This is my business card.
lines.grammarNote: 회사원이에요 — 회사원 ends in consonant ㄴ → 이에요. 이건 = 이것 + 은; 명함 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 감사합니다. 이건 제 명함이에요. 잘 부탁드려요!
lines.romanization: Gamsahamnida. Igeon je myeonghamieyo. Jal butakdeuryeoyo!
lines.en: Thank you. This is my business card. I look forward to working with you!
lines.grammarNote: 이건 제 명함이에요 repeats the chapter's object-identifying frame in a real exchange. 잘 부탁드려요 is a first-meeting set phrase.

readingText.title: 새 친구 소개 (Introducing a New Friend)
readingText.body: 엄마, 저 오늘 새 친구 생겼어요! 이름은 지수예요. 지수는 대학생이에요. 우리 학교 학생이에요. 지수 씨는 제주도 사람이에요. 저는 서울 사람이에요. 지수 씨의 꿈은 영어 선생님이에요. 정말 좋은 사람이에요!
readingText.bodyTranslation: Mom, I made a new friend today! Her name is Jisu. Jisu is a university student. She's a student at our school. Jisu is from Jeju Island. I am from Seoul. Jisu's dream is to be an English teacher. She is a really good person!

comprehensionQuestions.question: What is the new friend's name and where is she from?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 이름은 지수예요 (Her name is Jisu). 제주도 사람이에요 (She is from Jeju Island).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What is Jisu's dream job?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 꿈은 영어 선생님이에요 (Her dream is to be an English teacher). 선생님 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the 이에요/예요 forms in the text. For each one, explain why 이에요 or 예요 was chosen based on the noun it follows.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 지수예요 — 지수 ends in vowel ㅜ → 예요. 대학생이에요 — 대학생 ends in consonant 받침 ㅇ → 이에요. 학생이에요 — 학생 ends in consonant 받침 ㅇ → 이에요. 제주도 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요. 서울 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요. 영어 선생님이에요 — 선생님 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요. 좋은 사람이에요 — 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → 이에요.

culturalNote.title: 명함 (Meongham) — Business Cards and First Meetings in Korea
culturalNote.body: When meeting someone in a Korean professional or semi-formal context, business cards (명함) are exchanged with both hands or with one hand supported by the other at the wrist — never one-handed or casually tossed. You receive the card with both hands, read it, and then place it respectfully on the table in front of you (never stuff it straight into a pocket). The exchange is usually accompanied by 잘 부탁드려요, which literally means 'I humbly ask for your care' but functions like 'I look forward to working with you.' Even social introductions follow a similar rhythm: name, hometown, and job are the first three pieces of information Koreans typically share. Knowing 저는 [name]이에요/예요 and 저는 [place] 사람이에요 will carry you through the first five minutes of almost any Korean introduction.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 학생___ (I am a student.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 학생 ends in the final consonant ㅇ (받침). After a consonant, you must use 이에요 — the 이 acts as a phonetic bridge between the consonant and 에요. 예요 can only follow a vowel-ending noun, so 학생예요 is wrong.

inlineExercises.prompt: 이건 커피___ (This is coffee.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 커피 ends in the vowel ㅣ. After a vowel, 예요 attaches directly without any connector. If you chose 이에요, the 이 would create an awkward extra syllable — 커피이에요 — which sounds unnatural.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저___ 민준이에요. (I am Minjun.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 저 ends in the vowel ㅓ. After a vowel, the topic marker is 는. 은 is only used after a final consonant (받침). This is the same vowel/consonant rule as 이에요/예요 — one consistent rule governs both.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '저는 의사이에요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 의사 ends in the vowel ㅏ. After a vowel, you must use 예요, not 이에요. 의사이에요 sounds like adding an extra unnecessary syllable — 이 is only the bridge needed after a consonant. Correct: 저는 의사예요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'What is your name?'
inlineExercises.hint: 이름 (name) + subject marker 이 + 뭐 (what) + 예요 (is). 뭐 ends in a vowel — which ending does that require?
inlineExercises.explanation: 이름이 뭐예요? is the everyday way to ask someone's name. 무엇 is grammatically possible but sounds more written or formal here.

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I am not Japanese.' Which sentence is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: The careful beginner form is [noun] + 이/가 아니에요. 사람 ends in consonant ㅁ → use 이 before 아니에요. The first option says the opposite: 'I am Japanese.' The third option wrongly stacks 이에요 and 아니에요.

inlineExercises.prompt: 이___ 뭐예요? (What is this?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 이건 is the contracted form of 이것 + 은 (이것은 → 이건). This is how native speakers actually say it — 이것은 뭐예요? is grammatically correct but sounds stiff. 이는 is not a standard form. The contraction 이건 is what you will hear in real conversation every time.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저___ 민준이에요. (As for me, I am Minjun.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 저는 introduces the topic “as for me” before giving your name. 를 would mark an object, which does not fit an identity sentence.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'This is coffee.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 이건 sets “this thing” as the topic. 커피 ends in a vowel sound, so the natural copula form is 예요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '저는 학생예요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 학생 ends in a consonant sound, so it takes 이에요. 예요 is for vowel-ending nouns like 커피예요.

bullets: LABEL MAKER rule: consonant-ending noun + 이에요, vowel-ending noun + 예요 — check the very last letter of the noun
SPOTLIGHT rule: 은/는 marks what you're talking about (topic); consonant → 은, vowel → 는; 이건 (이것은) is the contraction you'll use most
Negative: [noun]이/가 아니에요 — the 이/가 before 아니에요 is required and beginners often drop it

writingTask.prompt: A new classmate points at three things and people and asks what they are; write your answers identifying each one.
writingTask.hint: Use N이에요/예요 to say what something is (이에요 after a 받침, 예요 after a vowel), and N이/가 아니에요 for one that is wrong.
writingTask.model: 저는 학생이에요. 이 사람은 선생님이에요. 이건 제 이름이에요. 의사가 아니에요.
writingTask.modelEn: I'm a student. This person is a teacher. This is my name. (I'm) not a doctor.

canDo: Say what someone or something is with N이에요/예요
Pick 이에요 or 예요 from the noun's final sound (받침 vs vowel)
Single out a topic with N은/는 (저는, 이름은)
Say what something is NOT with N이/가 아니에요

chapters.title: Existence And Possession: 있어요/없어요 And 이/가
chapters.goal: Ask what exists, say what you have, and say what is missing.
chapters.scenario: A small restaurant visit where the learner asks about seats and reservations.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Do you have a reservation?

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: No, I don't have a reservation. Is there a seat?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Yes, there is a seat by the window.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: Great. I have time too.

chapters.guidedPractice: Practice 시간이 있어요, 시간이 없어요, 예약이 있어요, 예약이 없어요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Ask whether there is a seat, bathroom, or reservation, then answer with 있어요 or 없어요.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend asks 시간이 있어요? Learner answers with 있어요 or 없어요 and one reason.
chapters.review: Can you use 이/가 with 있어요 and 없어요?

beginnerGuide.title: Existence covers more than “there is”
beginnerGuide.body: 있어요 and 없어요 also mean “I have” and “I do not have.” 시간이 있어요 can mean “there is time” or “I have time.”

beginnerGuide.title: Why 이/가 appears here
beginnerGuide.body: The thing that exists, does not exist, hurts, or appears is usually marked with 이/가: 시간이 있어요, 문제가 없어요, 머리가 아파요.

beginnerGuide.title: Survival value
beginnerGuide.body: This chapter gives you high-frequency travel and daily phrases: 예약이 있어요, 시간이 없어요, 화장실이 있어요?

checkpoints: I can ask 자리 있어요? or 화장실 있어요?
I can say 예약이 없어요 without using 을/를.
I can use 이/가 for the thing that exists or is missing.

curriculumTrack.label: A1 Foundation
curriculumTrack.description: Hangul, survival sentences, particles, polite present, and daily actions.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Ask what exists, say what you have, and say what is missing.
exitTask.prompt: Ask whether there is a seat, bathroom, or reservation, then answer with 있어요 or 없어요.

sampleAnswer.ko: 예약이 없어요. 자리 있어요?
sampleAnswer.en: I don't have a reservation. Is there a seat?

checklist: I can ask 자리 있어요? or 화장실 있어요?
I can say 예약이 없어요 without using 을/를.
I can use 이/가 for the thing that exists or is missing.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You arrive at a hotel front desk in Busan. The staff member asks '예약이 있으세요?' (Do you have a reservation?) — you freeze. You know 있어요 means something like 'there is' or 'have', but why does 예약이 have that 이 on it? And how do you say you DON'T have one? This chapter gives you the two sentences that unlock dozens of real situations.
objectives: Use 있어요 and 없어요 to express existence ('there is / there isn't') and possession ('I have / I don't have')
Attach the subject particle 이/가 correctly to the noun that exists or is possessed
Avoid the #1 beginner error: using 을/를 (object marker) instead of 이/가 with 있어요/없어요
hook.whyItMatters: 있어요 and 없어요 are two of the most-used words in Korean. They cover 'is there a bathroom?', 'do you have time?', 'no problem', 'no money' — the building blocks of travel, small talk, and daily life. The subject particle 이/가 that comes with them is equally essential: nearly every Korean sentence uses it. Master these now and half of Chapter 5 and 6 becomes review.

grammarNotes.title: 있어요/없어요 — there is / isn't, have / don't have
grammarNotes.func: 있어요 says that something exists or is present ("there is"), and also that you have it ("I have ___"). 없어요 is its opposite — "there isn't" / "I don't have ___." One pair of verbs covers both existence and possession, so it's one of the most useful things to learn early.

formTable.ex: 친구 → 친구가 있어요 · 책 → 책이 있어요

formTable.when: Something doesn't exist / you don't have it
formTable.ex: 시간 → 시간이 없어요 · 돈 → 돈이 없어요

examples.en: There is water. / I have water.
examples.note: The thing that exists takes 이/가; 물 ends in a consonant → 이.

examples.en: I don't have any friends here. / There's no friend.
examples.note: 친구 ends in a vowel → 가. 없어요 is the negative of 있어요.

examples.en: Do you have time?
examples.note: In everyday speech the 이/가 is usually dropped — 시간(이) 있어요?

examples.en: There are a lot of books at home.
examples.note: 집에 = 'at home' (location, 에); the thing that exists, 책, still takes 이/가.

keyPoint.label: 있어요 (exists / have) ≠ 이에요/예요 (is / equals)
keyPoint.body: 이에요/예요 says what something IS — its identity: 저는 학생이에요 = "I'm a student." 있어요/없어요 says something EXISTS, or that you HAVE it: 학생이 있어요 = "There's a student." English uses "there is" for both ideas, so beginners grab the wrong one. Quick test: if you can swap in "have" or "there is/exists," use 있어요; if you mean "X equals Y," use 이에요/예요. (The deeper rules of 이에요/예요 are in chapter 03.)

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 있어요 is pronounced [이써요]: the 받침 ㅆ carries over onto the next vowel (linking, 연음).

drill.instruction: Say it about your own life — fill in a noun and keep the 이/가.
drill.model: 물이 있어요. → 시간이 있어요. → 돈이 없어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 예요/이에요 means "to be (equal something)," so 저는 친구예요 says "I AM a friend," not "I have a friend." To say you have something, use 있어요: 친구가 있어요. Korean has no separate verb "to have" — possession is just existence with 있어요/없어요.

grammarNotes.title: N이/가 — the subject particle
grammarNotes.func: 이/가 marks the grammatical subject — the doer, or the thing that exists — especially when it's new information or the specific answer to a question. It's the natural partner of 있어요/없어요 (친구가 있어요) and the marker for "who/what" questions and their answers.

formTable.ex: 저 → 제가 (not 저가) · 나 → 내가 · 누구 → 누가

examples.en: A friend is coming.
examples.note: 친구 ends in a vowel → 가. Something new arriving on the scene takes 이/가.

examples.en: There's no water.
examples.note: 물 ends in a consonant → 이. With 있어요/없어요 the existing thing takes 이/가.

examples.en: Who is a student?
examples.note: 누구 + 가 contracts to 누가. 'Who?' questions take 이/가, not 은/는.

examples.en: I'm Korean. (answering 'who?')
examples.note: 저 + 가 is the irregular 제가, never 저가. Used to pin down 'who.'

keyPoint.label: 이/가 (subject / new) vs 은/는 (topic / known)
keyPoint.body: This is the contrast that confuses every learner. 은/는 sets the topic — "as for ___" — known information you want to comment on (저는 학생이에요). 이/가 spotlights the subject as NEW or SPECIFIC — it points and says "this one." The clearest test is a question: 누가 왔어요? ("Who came?") asks for new info, so the answer 친구가 왔어요 takes 이/가 — that's the new piece. Once it's established you can switch to 는: 친구가 왔어요. 그 친구는 미국 사람이에요. Note too that 있어요/없어요 almost always pairs with 이/가. (The full 은/는 vs 이/가 story is its own chapter — here just learn that answers to who/what questions and existence both take 이/가.)

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 책이 is pronounced [채기]: the 받침 ㄱ carries onto the next vowel (linking, 연음).

drill.instruction: Answer the 'who/what' question — the answer is new info, so use 이/가.
drill.model: 누가 와요? → 친구가 와요. / 뭐가 있어요? → 물이 있어요.
items: 누가 한국어를 해요? → ______ 한국어를 해요. (answer with 저 → 제가)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: When 이/가 follows 저 ("I"), the form is the irregular 제가 — never 저가. The same happens with 나 → 내가 and 누구 → 누가. Beginners regularize to 저가 because the rule says "vowel + 가," but these three pronouns are fixed exceptions you just memorize.

exampleSentence.en: Do you have time right now?
exampleSentence.note: 시간 ends in consonant ㄴ → 시간이. The presence lamp: is time available?

exampleSentence.en: Do you have a reservation?
exampleSentence.note: 예약 ends in consonant ㄱ → 예약이. Essential phrase at hotels and restaurants.

exampleSentence.en: I don't have money right now.
exampleSentence.note: 돈 ends in consonant ㄴ → 돈이. A survival phrase for daily life.

exampleSentence.en: There is no problem.
exampleSentence.note: 문제 ends in vowel 에 → 문제가. A very common reassurance phrase.

exampleSentence.en: Is there a bathroom here?
exampleSentence.note: 화장실 ends in consonant ㄹ → 화장실이. One of the most important travel questions.

exampleSentence.en: My friend is here.
exampleSentence.note: 친구 ends in vowel 구 → 친구가. Spotlight on the friend as the one who exists/is present.

exampleSentence.en: Is there a vacant room?
exampleSentence.note: 방 ends in consonant ㅇ → 방이. Essential hotel check-in phrase.

exampleSentence.en: Is there a seat available?
exampleSentence.note: 자리 ends in vowel 리 → 자리가. Used at restaurants, cafés, cinemas.

exampleSentence.en: There is no water.
exampleSentence.note: 물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 물이. Works for 'there is no water' or 'I don't have water.'

exampleSentence.en: Are you free tomorrow?
exampleSentence.note: 시간이 있다 is the go-to way to ask if someone is available — more natural than direct schedule questions.

collocations: 시간이 있을 때 (when you have time)

exampleSentence.en: There is milk in the fridge.
exampleSentence.note: 있어요 checks the presence lamp: is milk in the fridge? Yes. Note 에 for the location and 이/가 for the thing that exists.

collocations: N에 있어요 (something IS at a place)

exampleSentence.en: I don't have time today.
exampleSentence.note: 없어요 is the lamp-OFF version. 오늘은 sets the time as topic with 은/는; 시간이 is the subject of non-existence.

exampleSentence.en: There are a lot of people today.
exampleSentence.note: 사람이 많아요 uses 이/가 — the spotlight is on 사람 as the thing that is plentiful. 많다 often pairs with 이/가.

exampleSentence.en: I made a restaurant reservation.
exampleSentence.note: When 예약 is used as a verb (예약하다), the restaurant is the object → 을/를. Compare: 예약이 있어요 (the reservation exists → 이/가).

extendedVocabulary.english: to hurt / be sick / be in pain

exampleSentence.en: My stomach hurts.
exampleSentence.note: 배 ends in vowel 배 → 배가. The body part that hurts takes 이/가 — this is a core pattern for describing symptoms.

exampleSentence.en: I like coffee. / Coffee is good.
exampleSentence.note: In the 'I like X' pattern, X takes 이/가, not 을/를. The spotlight (이/가) is on the thing liked, not the object of an action.

extendedDialogue.setting: Minji and Junho are checking in at a hotel in Busan

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Welcome. Do you have a reservation?
lines.grammarNote: 예약이 있으세요? — 예약 ends in ㄱ → 이. 있으세요 is the honorific form of 있어요, used to a customer.

lines.speaker: 민지
lines.en: Yes, I have a reservation. The name is Minji.
lines.grammarNote: 예약이 있어요 — presence lamp ON for the reservation. 이름은 민지예요 reuses the noun-sentence frame from Chapter 3.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Just a moment... I'm sorry, there is no reservation.
lines.grammarNote: 예약이 없어요 — same noun + particle, opposite verb. Lamp OFF. The contrast shows how the same frame flips with 있어요/없어요.

lines.speaker: 준호
lines.ko: 어? 예약이 있어요. 이름을 다시 확인해 주세요.
lines.romanization: Eo? Yeyagi isseoyo. Ireumeul dasi hwaginhae juseyo.
lines.en: Oh? We do have a reservation. Please check the name again.
lines.grammarNote: 예약이 있어요 repeats the existence frame with a consonant-ending noun. 다시 확인해 주세요 is the natural request when the staff cannot find it.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Let me check again. Ah, there is a reservation.
lines.grammarNote: 다시 확인할게요 is a normal staff response. 예약이 있어요 confirms that the reservation exists.

lines.speaker: 민지
lines.en: That's a relief. Is there a room?
lines.grammarNote: 방이 있어요? — 방 ends in consonant ㅇ → 이. At a hotel, 방 is the natural noun for the room.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.romanization: Ne, i-cheunge bangi isseoyo. Munjega eopseoyo.
lines.en: Yes, there's a room on the 2nd floor. No problem.
lines.grammarNote: 방이 있어요 (room exists → 이/가) + 에 for location on the floor. 문제가 없어요 = classic reassurance phrase.

lines.speaker: 준호
lines.en: Thank you! Is there a bathroom here?
lines.grammarNote: 화장실이 있어요? — 화장실 ends in consonant ㄹ → 이. 여기 adds the place without changing the existence pattern.

readingText.title: 호텔 예약 문자 (Hotel Booking Text Exchange)
readingText.body:
유나: 오빠, 내일 시간이 있어요?
준서: 네, 시간이 있어요. 왜요?
유나: 부산에 같이 가요! 호텔 예약이 있어요?
준서: 아직 예약이 없어요. 지금 바로 예약할게요.
유나: 빈 방이 있어요?
준서: 네, 바다 뷰 방이 있어요. 문제가 없어요!
유나: 완전 좋아요! 돈이 있어요?
준서: 네, 돈이 있어요. 걱정하지 마세요.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Yuna: Oppa, do you have time tomorrow?
Junseo: Yes, I have time. Why?
Yuna: Let's go to Busan together! Do you have a hotel reservation?
Junseo: Not yet, there's no reservation. I'll book it right now.
Yuna: Is there a vacant room?
Junseo: Yes, there's a room with an ocean view. No problem!
Yuna: That's great! Do you have money?
Junseo: Yes, I have money. Don't worry.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Does Junseo already have a hotel reservation when the conversation starts?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: No. He says 아직 예약이 없어요 (Not yet, there is no reservation). He books one during the conversation.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What kind of room does Junseo find?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 바다 뷰 방 — a room with an ocean view.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every instance of 이/가 있어요 or 이/가 없어요 in the text. For each, identify the noun, explain why 이 or 가 was chosen, and state whether it expresses existence or possession.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 1) 시간이 있어요 (×2) — 시간 ends in ㄴ → 이; possession (I have time). 2) 예약이 있어요 — 예약 ends in ㄱ → 이; possession (has a reservation). 3) 예약이 없어요 — same noun + particle, reversed meaning; absence. 4) 방이 있어요 — 방 ends in ㅇ → 이; existence (a room exists). 5) 문제가 없어요 — 문제 ends in vowel 에 → 가; absence (no problem). 6) 돈이 있어요 — 돈 ends in ㄴ → 이; possession (has money). Pattern: every time, the particle choice follows the consonant/vowel rule — not the meaning.

culturalNote.title: 문제가 없어요 — The Korean 'No Problem'
culturalNote.body: You'll hear 문제가 없어요 constantly in Korean service situations — at hotels, restaurants, customer service lines, and repair shops. It functions just like 'no problem' or 'all good' in English, and it always brings a sense of relief. The reverse, 문제가 있어요, is softer than it sounds: Koreans tend to say it matter-of-factly rather than dramatically. A related phrase you'll encounter is 괜찮아요 (it's okay / I'm fine), which overlaps in meaning. But when a Korean staff member says 문제가 없어요 after checking something for you, you can relax — that's their professional 'everything checks out.'

inlineExercises.prompt: 시간___ 있어요? (Do you have time?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 시간 ends in consonant ㄴ → subject particle 이. You cannot use 을 (object marker) with 있어요 — that is the most common beginner mistake. 가 would be wrong here because 가 attaches after vowels only.

inlineExercises.prompt: 문제___ 없어요. (There is no problem.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 문제 ends in vowel 에 → subject particle 가. 이 would be wrong because 이 only follows consonant-final nouns. 를 (object marker) is never used with 없어요 — absence is not an action performed on an object.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '예약을 없어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 없어요 means 'does not exist / do not have' — the noun is the SUBJECT of non-existence, so it needs the subject particle 이/가, not the object marker 을/를. 예약 ends in consonant ㄱ → 예약이.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'Is there a bathroom here?'
inlineExercises.hint: 화장실 ends in a consonant. Which particle follows a consonant-final noun? The question form of 있어요 uses rising intonation — the word order stays the same.
inlineExercises.explanation: 있어요 asks whether something exists in the place you named. 여기 marks 'here,' so 여기 화장실이 있어요? asks if there is a bathroom here.

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I like coffee.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 좋아요 (to be good/to like) uses 이/가, not 을/를. The thing you like is the subject of being-good, so it takes the subject spotlight particle 이/가. 커피를 좋아요 is ungrammatical. 커피는 좋아요 is possible but shifts meaning to a general topic statement ('Coffee, in general, is good') rather than expressing personal preference.

inlineExercises.prompt: 배___ 아파요. (My stomach hurts.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 배 ends in vowel 배 → particle 가. The body part that hurts takes 이/가 in Korean — this is the same spotlight pattern as with 있어요/없어요. Never use 을 for a body part with 아프다.

inlineExercises.prompt: The hotel receptionist has found your reservation. Which sentence would they say?
inlineExercises.explanation: 예약이 있어요 — reservation exists → lamp ON → correct. 예약이 없어요 is the opposite (no reservation found). 예약을 있어요 is ungrammatical — 있어요 can never take 을/를.

inlineExercises.prompt: 예약___ 있어요? (Do you have a reservation?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 있어요 uses 이/가 for the thing that exists or is possessed. 을 would wrongly mark 예약 as an object of an action verb.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I do not have time.'
inlineExercises.explanation: The thing you do not have is marked with 이/가. 없어요 states non-existence or not having, so 시간이 없어요 is the natural chunk.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '돈을 있어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 있어요 is not an action done to money, so 돈 cannot take 을. The thing that exists or is possessed takes 이/가: 돈이 있어요.

bullets: PRESENCE LAMP: 있어요 = lamp ON (exists / have), 없어요 = lamp OFF (doesn't exist / don't have)
SPOTLIGHT particle 이/가: attaches to the noun that exists — 이 after consonant (시간이, 예약이), 가 after vowel (문제가, 친구가)
Never use 을/를 with 있어요 or 없어요 — the thing that exists is a SUBJECT, not an object

writingTask.prompt: Text a friend who is meeting you at a café: say what you have and don't have right now (time, a seat, water).
writingTask.hint: Use 있어요 for what exists/you have and 없어요 for what's missing, and mark the subject with N이/가.
writingTask.model: 지금 시간이 있어요. 자리도 있어요. 그런데 물이 없어요. 빨리 오세요!
writingTask.modelEn: I have time now. There's a seat too. But there's no water. Come quickly!

canDo: Say something exists or you have it with 있어요
Say something is missing or you don't have it with 없어요
Mark the subject or the thing that exists with N이/가
Ask and answer about availability (시간이 있어요? · 자리가 없어요)

chapters.title: Daily Actions: Present Tense And 을/를
chapters.goal: Talk about simple daily actions and the thing you do them to.
chapters.scenario: A morning check-in about breakfast, coffee, studying, and reading.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Are you eating breakfast today?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yes, I eat breakfast and drink coffee.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Are you studying Korean again today?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yes. At night I read a little.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make three present-tense sentences with 을/를, then make one negative sentence.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say two things you do today and one object you use with 을/를.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend asks 뭐 해요? Learner answers with one object sentence.
chapters.review: Can you use 먹어요, 마셔요, 공부해요, and 안 해요 naturally?

beginnerGuide.title: From words to actions
beginnerGuide.body: This chapter turns verbs into simple sentences: 밥을 먹어요, 커피를 마셔요, 한국어를 공부해요. The object marker 을/를 shows what receives the action.

beginnerGuide.title: Particle dropping comes later
beginnerGuide.body: Koreans often drop 을/를 in speech, but beginners should first understand the full frame. Once the structure is clear, natural short speech becomes easier.

beginnerGuide.title: Negatives start here
beginnerGuide.body: 안 먹어요 and 공부 안 해요 show the everyday short negative. This means “I do not do it,” not necessarily “I cannot.”

checkpoints: I can say 먹어요, 마셔요, 공부해요, and 읽어요.
I can add 을/를 when the action has an object.
I can connect two daily actions with 고.

curriculumTrack.label: A1 Foundation
curriculumTrack.description: Hangul, survival sentences, particles, polite present, and daily actions.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Talk about simple daily actions and the thing you do them to.
exitTask.prompt: Say two things you do today and one object you use with 을/를.

sampleAnswer.ko: 아침을 먹고 커피를 마셔요.
sampleAnswer.en: I eat breakfast and drink coffee.

checklist: I can say 먹어요, 마셔요, 공부해요, and 읽어요.
I can add 을/를 when the action has an object.
I can connect two daily actions with 고.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You want to tell a Korean friend 'I drink coffee every morning.' You know the word 커피, you know 마셔요 — but you're not sure what goes between them. Is it 커피가? 커피는? 커피를? One small particle changes the entire grammatical logic of the sentence.
objectives: Attach 을 or 를 correctly after the object in any present-tense sentence
Say what you eat, drink, study, read, and write every day
Use the short negative (안) to say what you don't do
hook.whyItMatters: 을/를 is the particle that tells listeners WHAT is being acted on. Without it your sentences sound like a list of disconnected words. Once this clicks, you can build an unlimited number of complete action sentences — and Koreans will immediately know you understand Korean sentence structure.

grammarNotes.title: N을/를 — the object particle
grammarNotes.func: 을/를 marks the object of a sentence — the thing the action happens to (what you eat, drink, read, watch). It attaches to the noun that receives the verb's action, so it is the partner of every action verb you learn.

formTable.ex: 밥 → 밥을 · 책 → 책을 · 물 → 물을

formTable.when: Noun ends in a vowel (no 받침)
formTable.ex: 우유 → 우유를 · 커피 → 커피를 · 친구 → 친구를

examples.en: I eat (a meal of) rice.
examples.note: 밥 ends in a consonant (ㅂ 받침) → 을. 밥 is the object of 먹다.

examples.en: I drink water.
examples.note: 물 ends in ㄹ 받침 (a consonant) → 을, not 를.

examples.en: I read a book.
examples.note: 책 ends in ㄱ 받침 → 을. 보다 here means 'read / look at'.

examples.en: I meet a friend.
examples.note: 친구 ends in a vowel (ㅜ), no 받침 → 를. 만나다 takes its object with 을/를, not 와/과.

keyPoint.label: Object 을/를 vs subject 이/가
keyPoint.body: 을/를 marks WHAT receives the action (the object); 이/가 marks WHO does it (the subject). In 친구가 밥을 먹어요 (A friend eats), 친구 is the doer → 가, and 밥 is the thing eaten → 을. Don't swap them. In casual speech Koreans often drop 을/를 (밥 먹어요), but learn to add it correctly first — the dropping comes naturally later.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 밥을 is pronounced [바블]: the final ㅂ links into the following vowel (linking, 연음). Likewise 책을 → [채글], 한국어를 → [한구거를].

drill.instruction: Add the right object particle and say the full sentence — follow the model.
drill.model: (물) 마셔요. → 물을 마셔요. · (커피) 마셔요. → 커피를 마셔요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저는 밥 먹어요 treated as the 'correct, complete' textbook form
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English has no object particle, so learners forget 을/를 and treat the bare noun as finished. The neutral, fully-formed sentence keeps the particle; dropping it is a casual-speech shortcut, not the default you should write.

grammarNotes.title: 안 + verb — the short negative
grammarNotes.func: 안 makes a verb negative — it means 'do not / does not'. You put 안 directly in front of the verb to say you don't do the action (안 먹어요 = I don't eat).

formTable.ex: 먹어요 → 안 먹어요 · 봐요 → 안 봐요 · 마셔요 → 안 마셔요

formTable.add: 안 goes between the noun and 하다
formTable.ex: 공부해요 → 공부 안 해요 · 운동해요 → 운동 안 해요

examples.en: I don't eat (the meal).
examples.note: 안 sits right before the verb 먹어요. The object 밥을 keeps its normal place.

examples.en: I don't drink water.
examples.note: Simple verb → just 안 + 마셔요.

examples.en: My friend doesn't read books.
