examples.note: 안 negates the action 보다, not the object 책을.

examples.en: Today I don't study Korean.
examples.note: With a 하다 verb, 안 splits in: 공부 안 해요, NOT 안 공부해요.

keyPoint.label: 안 (choose not to) vs 못 (can't) — preview
keyPoint.body: 안 means you simply don't / choose not to do something (안 먹어요 = I don't eat it). 못 means you're unable to even though you might want to (못 먹어요 = I can't eat it). Both go in front of the verb, but the meaning differs: 안 = won't / don't, 못 = can't. You'll practice 못 in its own chapter — for now just remember 안 is the everyday negative.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 안 + verb does not fuse: the ㄴ of 안 stays crisp and there is no tensing on the verb (안 봐요 = [안봐요], not [안뽜요]). Keep them as two clear beats.

drill.instruction: Make each sentence negative with 안 — follow the model. Watch the 하다 verb.
drill.model: 밥을 먹어요. → 밥을 안 먹어요. · 공부해요. → 공부 안 해요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English puts 'not' before the whole verb, so learners say 안 공부해요. But 공부하다 is noun(공부) + 하다, and 안 must slip between them: 공부 안 해요. This split only happens with 하다 verbs; ordinary verbs take 안 straight in front (안 먹어요).

exampleSentence.en: I eat lunch.
exampleSentence.note: 점심 ends in consonant ㅁ → 을; eating is directed at lunch

exampleSentence.en: I drink water.
exampleSentence.note: 물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 을; the drinking action hits 물

exampleSentence.en: I study Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 한국어 ends in vowel 어 → 를; can also split: 한국어 공부를 해요

exampleSentence.en: I read a book.
exampleSentence.note: 책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; reading is directed at the book

exampleSentence.en: I write a diary.
exampleSentence.note: 일기 ends in vowel 기 → 를; writing is directed at the diary

exampleSentence.en: I listen to music.
exampleSentence.note: 음악 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; listening is directed at the music

exampleSentence.en: I watch a movie.
exampleSentence.note: 영화 ends in vowel 아 → 를; watching is directed at the movie

exampleSentence.en: I exercise every day.
exampleSentence.note: 운동하다 has no object here — not everything needs 을/를; negative form: 운동 안 해요

exampleSentence.en: I'm not working today.
exampleSentence.note: Noun+하다 split negative: 일 + 안 + 해요 — the stop sign goes between noun and verb

exampleSentence.en: Are you eating? / Do you eat rice?
exampleSentence.note: 밥 ends in consonant ㅂ → 을; 밥을 먹다 is the most common eating phrase in Korean

exampleSentence.en: I drink coffee.
exampleSentence.note: 커피 ends in vowel 이 → 를; 마시다 is directed at the drink.

exampleSentence.en: I drink a lot of water.
exampleSentence.note: 물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 을; 많이 = a lot, modifying the verb

exampleSentence.en: I read a book.
exampleSentence.note: 책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; reading is directed at the book.

exampleSentence.en: I listen to music.
exampleSentence.note: 음악 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; listening is directed at the music.

exampleSentence.en: I watch a movie.
exampleSentence.note: 영화 ends in vowel 아 → 를; watching is directed at the movie.

exampleSentence.en: I drink coffee every day.
exampleSentence.note: 매일 is a time adverb — it doesn't need a particle; it modifies the entire sentence

exampleSentence.en: I drink a lot of water.
exampleSentence.note: 많이 (adverb) modifies the verb directly — no particle needed on the adverb itself

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihee (지희) and her coworker Minho (민호) are chatting over lunch about their daily habits

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.en: Minho, do you eat breakfast every day?
lines.grammarNote: 아침을 먹어요 — 아침 ends in consonant ㅁ → 을; eating (먹다) is directed at breakfast

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: No, I don't eat breakfast. I'm busy.
lines.grammarNote: 아침을 안 먹어요 — the stop-sign 안 goes directly before 먹어요 (a pure verb, not noun+하다)

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.ko: 그래요? 저는 매일 밥을 먹어요. 물을 많이 마셔요.
lines.romanization: Geuraeyo? Jeoneun maeil babeul meogeoyo. Mureul mani masyeoyo.
lines.en: Really? I eat rice every day. I drink a lot of water.
lines.grammarNote: 밥을 먹어요 and 물을 마셔요 both use 을 because 밥 and 물 end in consonants. 많이 modifies 마셔요; it does not take a particle.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: I drink coffee. That's my breakfast.
lines.grammarNote: 커피를 마셔요 — 커피 ends in vowel 이 → 를 attaches; drinking is directed at coffee

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.en: Haha, do you study Korean?
lines.grammarNote: 한국어를 공부해요 — 한국어 ends in vowel 어 → 를; this is also valid as 한국어 공부를 해요 (split form)

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 네, 매일 한국어를 공부해요. 그런데 책을 안 읽어요.
lines.romanization: Ne, maeil hangugeoreul gongbuhaeyo. Geureonde chaegeul an ilgeoyo.
lines.en: Yes, I study Korean every day. But I don't read books.
lines.grammarNote: 한국어를 공부해요 uses 를 because 한국어 ends in a vowel. 책을 안 읽어요 keeps 을 on the object and puts 안 before the pure verb 읽어요.

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.ko: 저는 책을 읽어요. 그리고 음악을 들어요.
lines.romanization: Jeoneun chaegeul ilgeoyo. Geurigo eumageul deureoyo.
lines.en: I read books. And I listen to music.
lines.grammarNote: 책을 읽어요 and 음악을 들어요 both use 을 because 책 and 음악 end in consonants. Two clean object sentences.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 좋아요. 오늘은 영화를 안 봐요. 책을 읽어요.
lines.romanization: Joayo. Oneureun yeonghwareul an bwayo. Chaegeul ilgeoyo.
lines.en: Good. Today I won't watch a movie. I'll read a book.
lines.grammarNote: 영화를 안 봐요 puts 안 before the pure verb 봐요. 책을 읽어요 keeps 을 because 책 ends in consonant ㄱ.

readingText.title: 수빈의 하루 일과 (Subin's Daily Routine)
readingText.body: 저는 매일 아침 밥을 먹어요. 커피를 마셔요. 회사에서 이메일을 써요. 보고서를 읽어요. 점심에는 동료들과 밥을 먹어요. 퇴근 후에는 음악을 들어요. 한국어를 공부해요. 드라마를 봐요. 주말에는 운동 안 해요. 그냥 책을 읽어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Every morning I eat a meal. I drink coffee. At work I write emails. I read reports. At lunch I eat with my coworkers. After work I listen to music. I study Korean. I watch dramas. On weekends I don't exercise. I just read books.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two things does Subin do in the morning?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 밥을 먹어요 (eats a meal) and 커피를 마셔요 (drinks coffee).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two things does Subin do after work?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 음악을 들어요 (listens to music) and 한국어를 공부해요 (studies Korean)

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the 을/를 in the text. For each one, explain why 을 or 를 is used — not the other form.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 밥을 (ㅂ consonant ending → 을), 커피를 (이 vowel ending → 를), 이메일을 (ㄹ consonant ending → 을), 보고서를 (어 vowel ending → 를), 밥을 (again, ㅂ → 을), 음악을 (ㄱ consonant ending → 을), 한국어를 (어 vowel ending → 를), 드라마를 (아 vowel ending → 를), 책을 (ㄱ consonant ending → 을). The rule: consonant-ending nouns take 을, vowel-ending nouns take 를.

culturalNote.title: 밥 먹었어요? — The Korean greeting that's really about food
culturalNote.body: In Korea, one of the most common informal greetings is '밥 먹었어요?' (Have you eaten?) — said instead of 'How are you?' to close friends and family. Offering food is central to Korean social bonding. Answering 'yes' (네, 먹었어요) or 'not yet' (아직요) is totally normal. Notice that in this casual greeting, the particle 을 is often dropped: '밥 먹었어요?' rather than '밥을 먹었어요?' This is the natural particle-dropping that Koreans do in fast speech — but you now know the full form with 을, which makes the shortened form easy to understand.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 아침___ 먹어요. (I eat breakfast.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 아침 ends in consonant ㅁ, so it takes 을. 를 is only used after vowel-ending nouns. 이 and 가 are subject markers, not object markers — they mark who is doing the action, not what receives it.

inlineExercises.prompt: 커피___ 마셔요. (I drink coffee.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 커피 ends in vowel 이, so it takes 를. 을 is for consonant-ending nouns. 은/는 are topic markers, not object markers — they set the topic of the sentence, which is different from marking what is being drunk.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장을 자연스럽게 고쳐보세요: '저는 안 공부해요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 공부하다 is a noun+하다 verb. In the everyday short negative, split it into 공부 + 안 + 해요. Pure verbs take 안 right before the verb (안 먹어요), but noun+하다 verbs usually split: 공부 안 해요, 운동 안 해요, 일 안 해요.

inlineExercises.prompt: 한국어___ 공부해요. (I study Korean.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 한국어 ends in vowel 어, so it takes 를. This is one of the most common sentences a Korean learner will ever say — 한국어를 공부해요 — so it's worth drilling until it's automatic.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I don't watch movies.'
inlineExercises.hint: 영화 ends in a vowel — which form of the object marker do you need? And 보다 is a pure verb, so where does 안 go?
inlineExercises.explanation: 안 goes right before the action verb to make a short negative. 영화 is the thing watched, so 영화를 stays as the object.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly says 'I don't study' using the 안 negative?
inlineExercises.explanation: 공부 안 해요 is correct — noun + stop-sign + 해요. '안 공부해요' is wrong because 안 can't go before a noun-verb compound. '공부를 않아요' is missing the -지 needed for the long negative form (공부를 하지 않아요). '안 공부를 해요' mixes up the word order in an unnatural way.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend says '책을 읽어요.' What is the role of 을 in this sentence?
options: It marks 책 as the subject doing the reading.
It marks 책 as the object receiving the action of reading.
It marks 책 as a topic being discussed.
It is a verb ending attached to 책.
inlineExercises.correct: It marks 책 as the object receiving the action of reading.
inlineExercises.explanation: 을/를 is the object marker — it marks WHAT gets acted upon. 책 is what is being read. Subject markers (이/가) mark who does the action; topic markers (은/는) set what we're talking about. 을/를 is specifically for the thing that receives the verb's action.

inlineExercises.prompt: 책___ 읽어요. (I read a book.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 읽다 is an action, and 책 is what you read, so it takes the object marker 을. 이 would mark 책 as a subject, not the thing being read.

inlineExercises.prompt: 매일 한국어를 ___ . (공부하다 → polite present)
inlineExercises.explanation: 하다 verbs become 해요 in polite present. 매일 makes this a normal present habit: 매일 한국어를 공부해요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I drink coffee every morning.'
inlineExercises.explanation: The time phrase comes before the object and verb. 커피 is what you drink, so 커피를 stays right before 마셔요.

bullets: 을/를 = ARROW from verb to object: consonant-ending noun + 을 / vowel-ending noun + 를
안 = STOP SIGN before a pure verb (안 먹어요); for noun+하다 verbs split it: noun + 안 + 해요
Key daily verbs with their objects: 밥을 먹다, 커피를 마시다, 한국어를 공부하다, 책을 읽다, 음악을 듣다, 영화를 보다

writingTask.prompt: Write 3 sentences about your daily routine: two things you do and one thing you don't do.
writingTask.hint: Mark the thing with N을/를 and use the present tense (먹어요, 마셔요); make one negative with 안 + verb.
writingTask.model: 저는 밥을 먹어요. 커피를 마셔요. 그런데 술은 안 마셔요.
writingTask.modelEn: I eat rice. I drink coffee. But I don't drink alcohol.

canDo: Mark what the action happens to with N을/를 (밥을, 커피를)
Say everyday actions in the polite present tense (먹어요, 마셔요)
Make a verb negative with 안 + verb (안 먹어요)
Choose 을 or 를 from the noun's 받침

chapters.title: Places And Time: 에 And 에서
chapters.goal: Say where you go and where something happens without mixing up 에 and 에서.
chapters.scenario: A simple plan to go to a cafe and meet a friend there.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Where are you going today?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I'm going to a cafe.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What are you doing at the cafe?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I'm meeting a friend at the cafe.

chapters.guidedPractice: Contrast 학교에 가요 with 학교에서 공부해요. Do not mix destination and action place.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say one place you go to and one thing you do there.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend asks 어디에 가요? and 어디에서 공부해요? Learner answers both.
chapters.review: Can you choose 에 vs 에서 in simple sentences?

beginnerGuide.title: The 에 / 에서 split
beginnerGuide.body: 에 points to destination, time, or where something exists. 에서 marks where an action happens. 학교에 가요 and 학교에서 공부해요 are different for a reason.

beginnerGuide.title: Movement vs action
beginnerGuide.body: If the verb is 가다 or 오다, think destination: 에. If the verb is 공부하다, 일하다, 먹다, 기다리다, or 사다, think action place: 에서.

beginnerGuide.title: Time also uses 에
beginnerGuide.body: For clock time, use 에: 7시에 일어나요. Some time words like 오늘, 내일, 지금 usually do not need 에 at beginner level.

checkpoints: I can use 에 for the destination: 카페에 가요.
I can use 에서 for the action place: 카페에서 만나요.
I can avoid 카페에서 가요 when I mean going to the cafe.

curriculumTrack.label: A1 Foundation
curriculumTrack.description: Hangul, survival sentences, particles, polite present, and daily actions.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Say where you go and where something happens without mixing up 에 and 에서.
exitTask.prompt: Say one place you go to and one thing you do there.

sampleAnswer.ko: 카페에 가요. 카페에서 친구를 만나요.
sampleAnswer.en: I'm going to a cafe. I'm meeting a friend at the cafe.

checklist: I can use 에 for the destination: 카페에 가요.
I can use 에서 for the action place: 카페에서 만나요.
I can avoid 카페에서 가요 when I mean going to the cafe.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You're texting a Korean friend to arrange where to meet. You type '카페에 만나요' — but your friend is confused. Did you mean you're going TO the café, or hanging out AT the café? In Korean, those are different sentences.
objectives: Use 에 correctly for destinations and static locations
Use 에서 correctly for places where actions happen
Avoid the #1 English-speaker mistake: mixing up 에 and 에서 with movement vs. action verbs
hook.whyItMatters: 에 and 에서 look almost identical to beginners, but Koreans hear the difference immediately. Using 에서 with 가다 (학교에서 가요) is a clear signal that you're still learning — after this chapter you won't make that mistake again.

grammarNotes.title: N에 — where you go, when it happens, where it is
grammarNotes.func: 에 attaches to a noun to mark a destination (with 가다/오다), a point in time ("at/on"), or the place where someone or something simply exists (with 있다/없다). One way to keep it straight: 에 is for going there, being there, or when — never for an action you actually do at a place.

formTable.ex: 학교 → 학교에 가요 · 집 → 집에 와요
집 → 집에 있어요 · 학교 → 학교에 없어요

formTable.when: A point in time (clock time, day, date)
formTable.ex: 세 시 → 세 시에 · 월요일 → 월요일에

formTable.when: Time words that take NO 에

examples.en: I go to school.
examples.note: 에 marks 학교 as where I'm headed — the destination of 가다.

examples.en: My friend is at home.
examples.note: With 있다, 에 marks where someone simply is. 집에 sounds like [지베].

examples.en: I meet a friend at three.
examples.note: 에 on a clock time means "at" — 세 시에 = at 3:00.

examples.en: I'm not home today.
examples.note: 집에 takes 에, but 오늘 takes none — today/tomorrow/now never use it.

keyPoint.label: 에 vs 에서 — being there vs doing there
keyPoint.body: Use 에 for where something IS or where you're GOING (있다/없다/가다/오다): 집에 있어요 (I'm at home), 학교에 가요 (I go to school). Use 에서 for where you DO something (먹다/공부하다/일하다 …): 집에서 밥을 먹어요 (I eat at home). Quick test: 있다/없다/가다/오다 → 에; any "doing" verb → 에서. The 에서 note below drills the full contrast.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a 받침 noun, 에 slides onto the final consonant (연음): 집에 → [지베]. After a vowel there's nothing to link, so 학교에 stays [학꾜에] (and note 학교 itself is [학꾜]).

drill.instruction: Say where each person goes or is, adding 에 — follow the model.
drill.model: (학교 / 가다) → 학교에 가요. · (집 / 있다) → 집에 있어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Because of "at three / on Monday," learners stick 에 onto every time word. But 에 only goes on clock times, days, and dates (세 시에, 월요일에) — the words 오늘 (today), 어제 (yesterday), 내일 (tomorrow), and 지금 (now) never take it. Just memorize that short list.

grammarNotes.title: N에서 — where you do something, and "from"
grammarNotes.func: 에서 attaches to a place noun to mark where an action happens ("at/in"): 집에서 밥을 먹어요 (I eat at home). The same 에서 also marks a starting point — where something comes "from": 한국에서 왔어요 (I'm from Korea). Same particle, two jobs: where you do something, and where it starts from.

formTable.ex: 집 → 집에서 먹어요 · 학교 → 학교에서 공부해요
한국 → 한국에서 왔어요 · 집 → 집에서 나와요

formTable.when: Same form after 받침 or vowel

examples.en: I eat at home.
examples.note: 먹다 is something you do, so the place takes 에서, not 에. Sounds like [지베서].

examples.en: I study Korean at school.
examples.note: 공부하다 is an action → 에서. Compare 학교에 가요 (going there).

examples.en: I'm from Korea.
examples.note: Here 에서 = "from," the starting point of 오다. Sounds like [한구게서].

examples.en: Where do you meet your friend?
examples.note: 만나다 is an action → 에서; 어디에서 shortens to 어디서 in everyday speech.

keyPoint.label: 에서 vs 에 — the action test
keyPoint.body: Both sit on a place noun, but the verb decides which. 에서 + a "doing" verb = where you DO something: 도서관에서 책을 읽어요 (I read at the library). 에 + 있다/없다/가다/오다 = where you ARE or GO: 도서관에 있어요 (I'm at the library), 도서관에 가요 (I go to the library). Lock in the pair: 학교에 가요 (go to school) vs 학교에서 공부해요 (study at school).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a 받침 noun, 에서 slides onto the final consonant (연음): 집에서 → [지베서], 한국에서 → [한구게서]. After a vowel there's nothing to link, so 학교에서 stays [학꾜에서].

drill.instruction: Say where each action happens, adding 에서 — follow the model.
drill.model: (집 / 밥을 먹다) → 집에서 밥을 먹어요. · (학교 / 공부하다) → 학교에서 공부해요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English uses one word, "at," for both "I'm at school" and "I study at school," so learners grab 에 for both. Korean splits them: 에 is only for existence and destination (있다/없다/가다/오다), while anything you DO at a place needs 에서. If there's a real verb of doing — eating, studying, meeting, watching — use 에서.

exampleSentence.en: I study Korean at school.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — studying is an action

exampleSentence.en: I read books at the library.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — reading is an active action

exampleSentence.en: I wait for my friend at the café.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — waiting is an active state/action

exampleSentence.en: I work at the office for 8 hours.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — working is an active action

exampleSentence.en: I eat bibimbap at the restaurant.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — eating is an active action

exampleSentence.en: I want to rest at home.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — resting is an action at a location

exampleSentence.en: I exercise at the park.
exampleSentence.note: 에서 — exercising is an action

exampleSentence.en: I go to school tomorrow.
exampleSentence.note: 가다 = movement → destination takes 에, never 에서

exampleSentence.en: Come to my place.
exampleSentence.note: 오다 = movement → destination takes 에

extendedVocabulary.english: to be / to exist / to have

exampleSentence.en: I'm at the café right now.
exampleSentence.note: 있다 = static existence → ALWAYS takes 에, never 에서

exampleSentence.en: I study at the library.
exampleSentence.note: Active verb → location takes 에서

exampleSentence.en: I do a part-time job at a café.
exampleSentence.note: Action verb → 에서

exampleSentence.en: Where shall we meet?
exampleSentence.note: Meeting is an action → 에서

exampleSentence.en: I'll wait at the café.
exampleSentence.note: Waiting = active state → 에서

exampleSentence.en: Let's eat together at the restaurant.
exampleSentence.note: Eating is an action → 에서

exampleSentence.en: What time shall we meet?
exampleSentence.note: Clock time takes 에 when you mark when something happens

exampleSentence.en: I go to school in the morning.
exampleSentence.note: 아침에 sets the time; 학교에 marks the destination

exampleSentence.en: I study at the library in the afternoon.
exampleSentence.note: 오후에 marks time; 도서관에서 marks the action place

exampleSentence.en: I come home in the evening.
exampleSentence.note: 저녁에 marks time; 집에 marks the destination of 오다

exampleSentence.en: I go to the hospital.
exampleSentence.note: 가다 is movement, so 병원 takes 에 as the destination

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihoon texts his coworker Sora to plan their lunch break

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Sora, where are you right now?
lines.grammarNote: 어디에 있어요? — 있다 is static existence, so the location takes 에, not 에서

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: I'm at the office. Why?
lines.grammarNote: 회사에 있어요 — same rule: 있다 + 에 = just existing at a place

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Let's have lunch together! Where should we eat?
lines.grammarNote: 어디에서 먹을까요? — eating is an action, so 에서 asks about the stage for that action

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.ko: 회사 근처 식당에서 먹어요. 거기 음식이 맛있어요.
lines.romanization: Hoesa geuncheo sikdangeseo meogeoyo. Geogi eumsigi massisseoyo.
lines.en: Let's eat at the restaurant near the office. The food there is good.
lines.grammarNote: 식당에서 먹어요 — 에서 marks the restaurant as the stage where eating happens

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Great! What time do we go?
lines.grammarNote: 몇 시에 — time takes 에; 가요 is movement so no location particle needed here

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: We go to the restaurant at 12.
lines.grammarNote: 12시에 (time → 에) + 식당에 가요 (destination of 가다 → 에) — two 에 in one sentence!

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 저는 지금 카페에서 일해요. 12시에 식당 앞에서 만나요.
lines.romanization: Jeoneun jigeum kapeeseo ilhaeyo. Yeoldu sie sikdang apeseo mannayo.
lines.en: I'm working at a café right now. Let's meet in front of the restaurant at 12.
lines.grammarNote: 카페에서 일해요 (action at café → 에서) + 식당 앞에서 만나요 (meeting is an action → 에서)

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: Got it! See you at twelve then.
lines.grammarNote: 12시에 봐요 — time takes 에; no location particle since 보다 (to see) doesn't specify a stage here

readingText.title: 수진의 하루 (Sujin's Day)
readingText.body: 오늘 아침 7시에 일어나요. 그리고 집에서 아침을 먹어요. 9시에 학교에 가요. 학교에서 한국어를 공부해요. 점심에 학교 식당에서 친구를 만나요. 오후에 도서관에서 숙제를 해요. 저녁 6시에 집에 와요. 집에서 쉬어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: This morning I wake up at 7. Then I eat breakfast at home. At 9 I go to school. At school I study Korean. At lunch I meet a friend at the school cafeteria. In the afternoon I do homework at the library. At 6 in the evening I come home. I rest at home.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What time did Sujin wake up?
Where did Sujin meet her friend?
Find all the 에서 in the text. Why does each one use 에서 and not 에?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 집에서 먹어요 (eating is an action), 학교에서 공부해요 (studying is an action), 식당에서 만나요 (meeting is an action), 도서관에서 해요 (doing homework is an action), 집에서 쉬어요 (resting is an action at home).

culturalNote.title: 어디에서 왔어요? — The most important question you'll hear
culturalNote.body: One of the first things Koreans ask foreigners is '어디에서 왔어요?' (Where did you come from? / Where are you from?). Notice it uses 에서 — this is the FROM meaning. The answer also uses 에서: '미국에서 왔어요' (I came from America). You'll hear this question constantly. A common beginner mistake is answering '미국에 왔어요' — that sounds like you came TO America, not FROM it. 에서 = origin/from. Get this one right and Koreans will be impressed.

inlineExercises.prompt: 학교___ 가요. (I go to school.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 가다 is a movement verb, so its destination takes 에. 학교에서 가요 would sound like the going-action happens at school, which makes no sense.

inlineExercises.prompt: 도서관___ 공부해요. (I study at the library.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 공부하다 is an action. The library is the STAGE where studying happens → 에서. If you used 에, it would sound like you're just existing at the library, not doing anything.

inlineExercises.prompt: 지금 집___ 있어요. (I'm at home right now.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 있다 always takes 에, never 에서. It describes static existence — just being somewhere, not performing an action.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '카페에서 가요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 가다 is a movement verb — its destination takes 에. 에서 with 가다 is one of the most common beginner errors. Whenever you see 가다 or 오다, the destination takes 에.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I eat at the restaurant.'
inlineExercises.hint: 먹다 (to eat) is an action. The restaurant is the stage where eating happens. Which particle marks an action stage?
inlineExercises.explanation: Eating is an action happening at a place, so the place takes 에서. 에 would fit a destination or existence sentence, not this action sentence.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend asks '어디에서 왔어요?' You want to say 'I came from England.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 에서 has a second meaning: FROM (a starting point). 영국에서 왔어요 = I came from England. If you said 영국에 왔어요, that means 'I came TO England' — the opposite!

inlineExercises.prompt: 친구를 카페___ 만나요. (I meet my friend at the café.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 만나다 (to meet) is an action. The café is the stage where the meeting happens → 에서.

inlineExercises.prompt: 카페___ 만나요. (We meet at a cafe.)
inlineExercises.explanation: Meeting is an action happening at the cafe, so use 에서. 에 would fit going to the cafe or being there, not doing the meeting action.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I go to school.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 가요 is movement toward a destination, so the place takes 에. 에서 would wrongly make 학교 the action place.

inlineExercises.prompt: 친구가 집에 ___ . (오다 → polite present)
inlineExercises.explanation: 오다 changes to 와요 in polite present. 집에 marks the place the friend comes to.

bullets: 에 = PIN DROP: destination of movement (가다/오다), time, or static location (있다/없다/살다)
에서 = STAGE: where an active verb (eat, study, work, meet, wait) happens — or FROM a starting point
The golden rule: if you're DOING something there → 에서 / if you're just GOING there or IT EXISTS there → 에

writingTask.prompt: Tell a friend your plan for today: where you're going and what you'll do there.
writingTask.hint: Use N에 for the destination with 가다/오다 and N에서 for where the action happens (학교에 가요, 도서관에서 공부해요).
writingTask.model: 오늘 학교에 가요. 도서관에서 공부해요. 그다음에 집에서 쉬어요.
writingTask.modelEn: Today I'm going to school. I study at the library. After that I rest at home.

canDo: Mark a destination or time with N에 (학교에 가요)
Mark where an action happens with N에서 (집에서 일해요)
Keep 에 and 에서 apart by going there vs doing there
Use 에서 for where you came from (한국에서 왔어요)

chapters.title: Food And Shopping
chapters.goal: Order something small and pay without overthinking the sentence.
chapters.scenario: A cafe counter where the learner orders a drink and asks about card payment.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Would you like to order?

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: One Americano, please.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Would you like it hot?

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: Yes. And is card payment okay?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Yes, card is okay.

chapters.guidedPractice: Practice N 주세요, 이것만 주세요, 이것도 주세요, 카드 돼요?, and 카드로 결제할 수 있어요?
chapters.realLifeTask: Order one drink or food item and ask if card payment is okay.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend plays staff. Learner orders, asks price, and chooses payment.
chapters.review: Can you ask for an item and use 로/으로 for payment?

beginnerGuide.title: Ordering is chunk-based
beginnerGuide.body: In a cafe or store, N 주세요 is more useful than a full English-style sentence. 아메리카노 한 잔 주세요, 빵도 하나 주세요, and 이것만 주세요 are complete practical requests.

beginnerGuide.title: Payment language
beginnerGuide.body: 카드 돼요? is a common spoken shortcut. 카드로 결제할 수 있어요? is clearer and more textbook-complete. Both are useful, but they feel different.

beginnerGuide.title: Small particles, big meaning
beginnerGuide.body: 도 means also, 만 means only, and 로/으로 can show method such as payment or transportation. These small pieces change the shopping situation.

checkpoints: I can order with N 주세요.
I can use one counter like 한 잔 or 하나.
I can ask 카드 돼요? in a simple shop situation.

curriculumTrack.label: A1 Foundation
curriculumTrack.description: Hangul, survival sentences, particles, polite present, and daily actions.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Order something small and pay without overthinking the sentence.
exitTask.prompt: Order one drink or food item and ask if card payment is okay.

sampleAnswer.ko: 아메리카노 한 잔 주세요. 카드 돼요?
sampleAnswer.romanization: amerikano han jan juseyo. kadeu dwaeyo?
sampleAnswer.en: One Americano, please. Is card payment okay?

checklist: I can order with N 주세요.
I can use one counter like 한 잔 or 하나.
I can ask 카드 돼요? in a simple shop situation.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You're at a Korean café. You want water, a croissant, and you want to pay by card. You manage to say '물 주세요' — but then you freeze. How do you add 'and the croissant too'? How do you ask if card payment is okay? You need three small but powerful particles: 도 (also), 만 (only), and 로/으로 (by means of).
objectives: Use 도 to add one more item to an order ('and this too, please')
Use 만 to set a limit ('only this, nothing else')
Use 로/으로 to express payment method, transport, or language ('by card', 'in Korean')
hook.whyItMatters: These three particles unlock real transactions. 도, 만, and 로/으로 are used in every café, restaurant, and convenience store interaction in Korea. Without them, every order is a single isolated item — with them, you can build natural, flexible requests that sound like a real customer, not a tourist reading a phrasebook.

grammarNotes.title: 도 vs 만 — also / too vs only
grammarNotes.func: 도 means "also / too" and adds this noun to others; 만 means "only" and shuts out everything else. Both attach straight to a noun and take the place of the topic/subject/object marker (은/는/이/가/을/를) instead of sitting on top of it.

formTable.ex: 저 → 저도, 물 → 물도, 친구 → 친구도
물 → 물만, 밥 → 밥만, 학생 → 학생만
밥을 → 밥도 / 밥만, 책을 → 책도 / 책만

examples.en: I'm a student too.
examples.note: 도 takes the place of 는 in 저는 — "me too," on top of the other students.

examples.en: Just water, please.
examples.note: 만 = water and nothing else; super common when you're ordering.

examples.en: My friend is coming too.
examples.note: 도 adds 친구 to the people already going; it replaces 가 in 친구가.

examples.en: I only eat rice.
examples.note: 만 stands in for the object marker 을 in 밥을 — rice and nothing else. (밥만 sounds like [밤만].)

keyPoint.label: 도 vs 만
keyPoint.body: 도 includes (this AND the rest); 만 excludes (this and NOTHING else). Quick test: if "too" fits, use 도; if "just / nothing but" fits, use 만. Either way you drop 은/는/이/가/을/를 first — 저도, never 저는도; 밥만, never 밥을만.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 만 after a 받침 nasalizes the consonant before it: 밥만 sounds like [밤만] (ㅂ → ㅁ before ㅁ).

drill.instruction: Add 도 (also) or 만 (only) to match the English. Drop any 은/는/이/가/을/를 first.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: In English you keep the subject and just bolt on "too," so learners want to hold onto 는/을 and add 도/만 after it. In Korean, 도/만 replace 은/는/이/가/을/를 — strip the old marker off completely, then add 도 or 만.

grammarNotes.title: (으)로 — by / with, and which way
grammarNotes.func: (으)로 marks how you do something — the tool, language, payment method, or transport ("by / with / in") — and also the direction you head ("toward / to"). You'll reach for it constantly when paying and ordering.

formTable.ex: 카드 → 카드로, 버스 → 버스로, 한국어 → 한국어로
손 → 손으로, 젓가락 → 젓가락으로, 현금 → 현금으로

formTable.when: Noun ends in ㄹ 받침 (special case)

formTable.ex: 집 → 집으로, 학교 → 학교로, 이쪽 → 이쪽으로

examples.en: I'll pay by card.
examples.note: 카드 ends in a vowel → 로. The exact thing you say at the register.

examples.en: Please speak in Korean.
examples.note: 한국어 ends in a vowel → 로; here 로 marks the language you're using.

examples.en: I eat with chopsticks.
examples.note: 젓가락 ends in 받침 ㄱ → 으로; marks the tool you use.

examples.en: I'm heading home.
examples.note: 집 ends in 받침 ㅂ → 으로; here 로 marks direction, not a means.

keyPoint.label: (으)로 vs 에 (direction)
keyPoint.body: For where you're going, 에 marks the destination you arrive at (집에 가요 = go home), while (으)로 stresses the direction you head (집으로 가요 = head toward home) — at this level either is fine for "go home." Mostly you'll use the "by / with" sense: 카드로, 현금으로, 한국어로. Just watch the ㄹ rule — 지하철로, not 지하철으로.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 으로 after a 받침 pulls the consonant into 으: 손으로 sounds like [소느로], 집으로 like [지브로].

drill.instruction: Add 로 or 으로. Check whether the noun ends in a vowel, a 받침, or ㄹ.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners stretch the 받침 → 으로 rule too far. Vowel-final nouns just take 로 (카드로), and ㄹ-final words are a special case that also take plain 로, not 으로 (지하철로, 연필로). Only non-ㄹ 받침 nouns get 으로.

exampleSentence.en: Two Americanos, please.
exampleSentence.note: N + 주세요 = the single most useful ordering pattern in Korea

exampleSentence.en: How much is this?
exampleSentence.note: 이거 (this) + 얼마예요 — the go-to price question in any market, convenience store, or café

exampleSentence.en: Can I pay by card?
exampleSentence.note: 카드 ends in a vowel → 로 (not 으로)

exampleSentence.en: I'll pay in cash.
exampleSentence.note: 현금 ends in a consonant (ㅁ) → 으로

exampleSentence.en: Is it okay to pay by card?
exampleSentence.note: 결제하다 is the formal word for payment processing; 내다 or 계산하다 are more casual

exampleSentence.en: Receipt, please.
exampleSentence.note: Direct N 주세요 request — no extra particles needed

exampleSentence.en: May I order now?
exampleSentence.note: 주문하다 + 아/어도 돼요? = polite permission request; 받다 (receive) is often said by staff: 주문받겠습니다

exampleSentence.en: Menu, please.
exampleSentence.note: 메뉴 is a loanword from English; in practice many Korean cafés have menus only on boards, so this is more useful than it sounds

exampleSentence.en: One Americano, please.
exampleSentence.note: Quantities in ordering use native Korean numbers (하나, 둘, 셋), not Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼)

exampleSentence.en: Some water, please.
exampleSentence.note: 좀 softens the request; 좀 주세요 sounds more polite and natural than 주세요 alone

exampleSentence.en: A little more water, please.
exampleSentence.note: 더 = more quantity; often combined with 좀 for a polite, natural request for a refill

exampleSentence.en: Is card okay?
exampleSentence.note: 카드 돼요? is a spoken shortcut — grammatically incomplete but perfectly natural in shops

exampleSentence.en: This too, please.
exampleSentence.note: 이거 is the spoken form, 이것 is written/formal; both work at a café or shop counter

exampleSentence.en: To go, please.
exampleSentence.note: 포장 (packing) = takeout in Korean. 포장이요? is how staff ask if you want it to go

exampleSentence.en: What's the recommended menu item?
exampleSentence.note: 추천 없어요? or 추천 메뉴요? are very natural ways to ask a café or restaurant what's good

exampleSentence.en: Is there a student discount?
exampleSentence.note: 할인 + 돼요? is the pattern to ask about discounts; 학생 할인, 앱 할인, 포인트 할인 all work the same way

exampleSentence.en: Please make it not spicy.
exampleSentence.note: 맵게 is the adverbial form (spicily); 안 맵게 해 주세요 = make it in a not-spicy way — practical for dietary restrictions

extendedDialogue.setting: Minjun and his coworker Yuna go to a café. Minjun orders for both of them.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Welcome! What can I get you?
lines.grammarNote: 뭐 드릴까요? — the polite 'what shall I offer you?' form staff use in Korean cafés; 드리다 is the honorific of 주다

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: One Americano, please.
lines.grammarNote: N 주세요 ordering pattern; 한 잔 = one cup using native Korean number 한 + counter 잔

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Do you need anything else?
lines.grammarNote: 더 (more/else) here asks if there's anything to add — functions like 도 in a question context

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Bread too, please.
lines.grammarNote: 빵 + 도 = adding the bread to the cart (SHOPPING CART rule); 하나 = one (native Korean number)

lines.speaker: 유나
lines.ko: 저는 물만 주세요. 커피는 안 마셔요.
lines.romanization: Jeoneun mulman juseyo. Keopineun an masyeoyo.
lines.en: Just water for me, please. I don't drink coffee.
lines.grammarNote: 물 + 만 = spotlight on water alone (SPOTLIGHT rule); this is 만 as a preference restriction

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Got it. How would you like to pay?
lines.grammarNote: 어떻게 (how) + 하시겠어요? is the polite 'how will you do X?' frame — staff asking the payment method opens the 로/으로 response

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Can I pay by card?
lines.grammarNote: 카드 + 로 = the CHANNEL SELECTOR (method particle); 카드 ends in vowel 드 → 로, not 으로. 결제해도 돼요? is the polite permission question.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Yes, card is fine. Do you need a receipt?
lines.grammarNote: 카드 됩니다 is the staff-side confirmation; 영수증 주세요 or 영수증도 주세요 is the natural follow-up if you want the receipt

readingText.title: 편의점에서 (At the Convenience Store)
readingText.body: 오늘 편의점에 가요. 과자를 하나 사요. 직원에게 '이거 얼마예요?'라고 물어요. 삼천 원이에요. 현금이 없어요. 그래서 카드로 결제해요. 영수증도 받아요. 음료는 안 사요. 이것만 사요. 다음에는 할인도 확인해요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Today I go to a convenience store. I buy one snack. I ask the staff, 'How much is this?' It is 3,000 won. I don't have cash, so I pay by card. I get a receipt too. I don't buy a drink. I buy only this. Next time I check discounts too.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How did the speaker pay, and why?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 카드로 결제해요 — they pay by card because they have no cash (현금이 없어요. 그래서...)

comprehensionQuestions.question: What does the speaker buy, and what do they not buy?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 과자를 하나 사요. 음료는 안 사요 — they buy one snack and do not buy a drink.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every 도 and 만 in the text. For each one, explain whether it is adding something or limiting something.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 영수증도 받아요 — 도 adds the receipt to the list of things that happen (CART: one more item); 이것만 사요 — 만 limits the purchase to only this item (SPOTLIGHT: nothing else); 할인도 확인해요 — 도 adds checking discounts to the plan (CART: another thing to do)

culturalNote.title: 카드 돼요? — Why Korean shops sometimes say no
culturalNote.body: In Korea, '카드 돼요?' (Is card okay?) is a completely natural counter question. In most cafés and convenience stores, card payment is normal, but at street stalls, traditional markets, or very small shops you may still hear '현금만 돼요' (cash only) or see staff point you toward a different payment method. The useful learner move is simple: ask once, then answer with 카드로 할게요 or 현금으로 할게요. Carrying a few small bills is still practical when you explore markets or small food stalls.

inlineExercises.prompt: 아메리카노 한 잔 주세요. 빵___ 하나 주세요. (One Americano, please. Bread too, please.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 도 adds the bread to the order (SHOPPING CART — one more item). If you used 만, the sentence would mean 'only bread, please' — cancelling the Americano you just ordered.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 물___ 마셔요. 다른 건 필요 없어요. (I drink only water. I don't need anything else.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 만 is the SPOTLIGHT — it limits the sentence to water and excludes everything else. 도 would mean 'I drink water too (among other things)', which contradicts '다른 건 필요 없어요'.

inlineExercises.prompt: 카드___ 결제할 수 있어요? (Can I pay by card?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 로/으로 marks the method (CHANNEL SELECTOR). 카드에 would mean 'on the card' or 'at the card' as if the card were a location, which makes no sense. The payment flows through the card channel → 카드로.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '저는도 주문할게요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 도 replaces subject and topic particles — it does not sit after them. 저는 + 도 is a double-particle error; drop 는 and say 저도. The same principle applies to 만: never 이것을만, always 이것만.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I'll pay in cash. Receipt too, please.'
inlineExercises.hint: 현금 ends in a consonant → which form? And are you adding the receipt (CART) or limiting to only the receipt (SPOTLIGHT)?
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ게요 shows the speaker's own decision, so 낼게요 fits 'I'll pay.' 도 adds 'also,' making 영수증도 주세요 natural for 'receipt too, please.'

inlineExercises.prompt: The staff asks how you want to pay. You want to ask 'Is it okay if I pay by card?' Which is the most natural?
inlineExercises.explanation: 로/으로 marks the method of payment — the card is the CHANNEL. 카드에 would mean 'at the card' (card as a location — doesn't work). 카드를 would mean 'pay the card' — as if the card itself is the thing being paid, not the payment method.

inlineExercises.prompt: 배고파요? 이거___ 드세요. 다른 건 없어요. (Are you hungry? Have just this. There's nothing else.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 만 is the SPOTLIGHT — the context confirms there's nothing else ('다른 건 없어요'), so 만 is correct. 도 would imply there are other options too, which contradicts the sentence.

inlineExercises.prompt: 카드___ 결제할게요. (I will pay by card.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 카드로 means by card or using a card as the method. 도 means also and 만 means only, so neither marks the payment method.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Water too, please.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 도 adds “too/also” to 물. 주세요 makes it a polite ordering request.

inlineExercises.prompt: 영수증도 ___ . (주다 → please do)
inlineExercises.explanation: 주다 becomes 주세요 when you politely ask someone to give something. 도 on 영수증 means “receipt too.”

bullets: 도 = SHOPPING CART: adds one more item or person to what already exists. Replaces 은/는, 이/가, 을/를 — never stacks on top of them.
만 = SPOTLIGHT: limits the sentence to exactly one thing, excluding everything else. Place it directly after the word you want to isolate.
로/으로 = CHANNEL SELECTOR: marks the method, means, or tool of an action. Use 로 after vowels or ㄹ; use 으로 after other consonants.

writingTask.prompt: Order at a café counter: ask for one item, add one more thing, and say how you'll pay.
writingTask.hint: Use N도 for 'also' and N만 for 'only', and (으)로 for the payment method (카드로); end a request with 주세요.
writingTask.model: 커피 한 잔만 주세요. 물도 주세요. 카드로 계산할게요.
writingTask.modelEn: Just one coffee, please. Water too, please. I'll pay by card.

canDo: Add one more thing with N도 and limit to one with N만
Say the payment method or means with N(으)로 (카드로, 현금으로)
Make a simple request with 주세요 (커피 하나 주세요)
Ask the price and respond (얼마예요? · 됩니다/돼요)

chapters.title: Want, Can, Cannot
chapters.goal: Say what you want, what you can do, and what you cannot do today.
chapters.scenario: Two friends trying to choose food and make a small plan.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What do you want to eat today?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I want to eat bibimbap.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Then can you go now?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 지금은 못 가요. 한 시간 후에 갈 수 있어요.
dialogue.romanization: jigeumeun mot gayo. han sigan hue gal su isseoyo.
dialogue.en: I can't go now. I can go in an hour.

chapters.guidedPractice: Transform 가다 into 가고 싶어요, 갈 수 있어요, 못 가요. Transform 먹다 into 먹고 싶어요, 먹을 수 있어요, 못 먹어요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say one thing you want to do, one thing you can do, and one thing you cannot do today.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend asks 갈 수 있어요? Learner answers with 갈 수 있어요 or 못 가요 and a reason.
chapters.review: Can you explain why 못 가해요 is wrong and say 못 가요 instead?

beginnerGuide.title: Three different meanings
beginnerGuide.body: 고 싶어요 is desire, ㄹ/을 수 있어요 is ability or possibility, and 못 + verb is inability. They are not interchangeable.

beginnerGuide.title: The 못 rule beginners need
beginnerGuide.body: For most verbs, put 못 before the normal verb: 못 가요, 못 먹어요. For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun 못 해요: 공부 못 해요. Do not make 못 가해요.

beginnerGuide.title: Why this chapter matters
beginnerGuide.body: This is the chapter that lets you explain limits politely: I want to go, I can go, I cannot go, I cannot eat spicy food.

checkpoints: I can say V고 싶어요 for something I want.
I can say Vㄹ/을 수 있어요 for something possible.
I can use 못 for a real limitation, not just preference.

curriculumTrack.label: A1 Foundation
curriculumTrack.description: Hangul, survival sentences, particles, polite present, and daily actions.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Say what you want, what you can do, and what you cannot do today.
exitTask.prompt: Say one thing you want to do, one thing you can do, and one thing you cannot do today.

sampleAnswer.ko: 비빔밥을 먹고 싶어요. 지금은 못 가요.
sampleAnswer.romanization: bibimbabeul meokgo sipeoyo. jigeumeun mot gayo.
sampleAnswer.en: I want to eat bibimbap. I can't go now.

checklist: I can say V고 싶어요 for something I want.
I can say Vㄹ/을 수 있어요 for something possible.
I can use 못 for a real limitation, not just preference.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: A Korean colleague invites you for samgyeopsal tonight. You want to go, you probably can go — but you're not sure yet. In English you'd say 'I want to go,' 'I can go,' or 'I can't go.' Korean has three distinct grammar forms for these three meanings, and mixing them up sounds strange: saying 못 가고 싶어요 (a nonsensical blend) signals confusion between wanting and being able.
objectives: Use 고 싶어요 correctly to express what you want or desire to do
Use ㄹ/을 수 있어요 to say you can do something (ability or possibility)
Use 못 + verb to say you cannot do something — and know why 못 가해요 is wrong
hook.whyItMatters: These three patterns are the engine of polite Korean conversation. Koreans use them constantly to navigate invitations, menus, schedules, and apologies. Without them you can only say what you DO — you can't express what you want, what you're capable of, or what you have to decline. Master all three and you can have real adult conversations about your life.

grammarNotes.title: -고 싶어요 — saying what you want to do ("I want to…")
grammarNotes.func: Add -고 싶어요 to a verb stem to say what you want to do. It's for your own wants; talking about what someone else wants uses -고 싶어 하다, which comes in a later chapter.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel
Verb stem ends in a consonant (받침)
Past and negative go on 싶다, not the main verb
formTable.add: …고 싶었어요 (wanted to) / …고 싶지 않아요 (don't want to)
formTable.ex: 보다 → 보고 싶었어요 / 보고 싶지 않아요

examples.en: I want to drink water.
examples.note: 마시다 ends in a vowel → 마시고 싶어요. The object keeps 을/를 (물을).

examples.en: I want to meet a friend today.
examples.note: 만나다 → 만나고 싶어요. It's your own wish, so plain -고 싶어요 is right.

examples.en: I want to watch a movie at home.
examples.note: 보다 → 보고 싶어요. The place where you do something takes 에서 (집에서).

examples.en: I wanted to study Korean more.
examples.note: Past tense goes on 싶다 (싶었어요), never on 공부하다.

keyPoint.label: Keep 을/를 on the thing you want
keyPoint.body: With -고 싶어요 the thing you want is still the object, so use 을/를: 밥을 먹고 싶어요 (I want to eat). You'll also hear 밥이 먹고 싶어요 in casual speech, but 밥을 먹고 싶어요 is the safe, standard choice for now.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 싶어요 links across the boundary and sounds like [시퍼요]; 먹고 tenses the ㄱ, so 먹고 싶어요 sounds like [먹꼬 시퍼요].

drill.instruction: Turn each verb into an "I want to…" sentence with -고 싶어요.
drill.model: 자다 → 자고 싶어요. (I want to sleep.)
items: 책을 읽다 → ____ (I want to read a book.)
집에 가다 → ____ (I want to go home.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: "I want to be happy" tempts you to stick -고 싶어요 on 행복하다. But -고 싶어요 only goes on action verbs, not on adjectives (descriptive verbs). For a state, use 행복해지다 (become happy) or the wish pattern -으면 좋겠다.

grammarNotes.title: -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 / 없어요 — can and can't
grammarNotes.func: Add -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 to a verb stem for "can / be able to," and -(으)ㄹ 수 없어요 for "can't." Putting 못 right before the verb is a shorter, more everyday way to say "can't."

formTable.ex: 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (can go) / 갈 수 없어요 (can't go)
먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요 (can eat) / 먹을 수 없어요 (can't eat)

formTable.add: stem + 수 있어요 (that ㄹ is the ending, add nothing)

formTable.ex: 먹다 → 못 먹어요 (can't eat) / 가다 → 못 가요 (can't go)

examples.ko: 저는 한국어를 조금 할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hangugeoreul jogeum hal su isseoyo.
examples.en: I can speak a little Korean.
examples.note: 하다 ends in a vowel → 할 수 있어요.

examples.en: I can't go today because I don't have time.
examples.note: 못 + 가요 is the short, natural way to say "can't" about one situation.

examples.ko: 이 책은 너무 어려워서 읽을 수 없어요.
examples.romanization: i chaegeun neomu eoryeowoseo ilgeul su eopseoyo.
examples.en: This book is too hard, so I can't read it.
examples.note: 읽다 ends in a consonant → 읽을 수 없어요.

examples.en: I can make kimchi.
examples.note: 만들다 already ends in ㄹ, so add nothing → 만들 수 있어요.

keyPoint.label: 못 (can't) vs 안 (don't / won't)
keyPoint.body: Both sit right before the verb but mean different things. 못 = can't — you're unable, even if you'd like to (시간이 없어서 못 자요, I can't sleep because I have no time). 안 = a choice not to (피곤하지만 안 자요, I'm tired but I'm not going to sleep). So "can't eat" is 못 먹어요; "don't eat (by choice)" is 안 먹어요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 수 있어요 links to [수 이써요]; 못 changes before the next sound — 못 가요 sounds like [몯까요] and 못 먹어요 like [몬머거요].

drill.instruction: Make a "can" sentence with -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요, then a "can't" sentence with 못.
drill.model: 가다 → 갈 수 있어요. / 못 가요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저는 수영을 안 할 수 있어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 저는 수영을 못 해요. / 수영을 할 수 없어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: For "I can't swim," learners try to negate 할 수 있어요 by adding 안. Korean doesn't do that — switch the whole phrase to 없어요 (할 수 없어요), or more naturally say 못 해요. Save 안 for choosing not to do something.

exampleSentence.en: I want to eat something that isn't spicy.
exampleSentence.note: 먹고 싶어요 — desire form; essential at Korean restaurants for dietary preferences

exampleSentence.en: I want to drink coffee.
exampleSentence.note: 마시 + 고 싶어요 — the stem ends in a vowel so 고 attaches cleanly

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘은 못 가요. 내일 갈 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't go today. I can go tomorrow.
exampleSentence.note: Two patterns in one sentence: 못 가요 (blocked today) vs 갈 수 있어요 (open tomorrow)

exampleSentence.en: I want to get better at Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 잘하 + 고 싶어요 — long-term aspiration; note that 못 for 하다 = 못 해요, NOT 못 하해요

exampleSentence.en: I can speak in Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 말하다 → stem 말하 + ㄹ 수 있어요 → 말할 수 있어요; often used to express language ability

extendedVocabulary.english: to be able to eat / can eat

exampleSentence.ko: 저는 매운 음식을 먹을 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can eat spicy food.
exampleSentence.note: 먹 (consonant ending stem) + 을 수 있어요 — consonant stems take 을 수, vowel stems take ㄹ 수

exampleSentence.ko: 이 음식은 너무 매워서 못 먹어요.
exampleSentence.en: This food is too spicy so I can't eat it.
exampleSentence.note: 맵다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: 매워서 (not 맵어서) — important for describing food limitations

exampleSentence.en: It's okay even if it's a little spicy.
exampleSentence.note: 괜찮아요 alone works as 'it's fine'; combined with 먹을 수 있어요 context it reassures the other person

exampleSentence.en: I know a little Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 알다 is ㄹ-irregular: 알 + 아요 = 알아요. For ability: 알 수 있어요 (stem already ends in ㄹ so no extra ㄹ added)

exampleSentence.en: Can you come to the party today?
exampleSentence.note: 오다 → stem 오 (vowel) → 올 수 있어요? A common social question — the ㄹ is added to the vowel stem

exampleSentence.en: I want to rest a bit today.
exampleSentence.note: 쉬 + 고 싶어요 — expressing the very human desire for rest; common in daily conversation

exampleSentence.en: Lately I'm busy so I can't exercise.
exampleSentence.note: 운동하다 is a 하다 verb: 못 + 해요 = 못 해요. The noun 운동 and 못 해요 can be separated: 운동 못 해요.

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘 시간이 있어요? 같이 밥 먹고 싶어요.
exampleSentence.en: Do you have time today? I want to eat together.
exampleSentence.note: 시간이 있어요 is the natural Korean way to say 'have time' — pairs perfectly with 고 싶어요 for invitations

exampleSentence.en: I'm too busy today so I can't go.
exampleSentence.note: 바쁘다 is ㅡ-irregular: 바빠서 (not 바쁘어서). Used constantly as a reason for 못 + verb

exampleSentence.en: What do you want to order?
exampleSentence.note: 주문하 + 고 싶어요 — essential restaurant phrase; 주문하다 is a 하다 verb

exampleSentence.ko: 아직 한국어를 다 이해할 수 없어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't understand all Korean yet.
exampleSentence.note: 이해하다 → 이해할 수 없어요 — a humble and accurate self-assessment for language learners

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘은 못 가요. 다음에 갈 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't go today. I can go next time.
exampleSentence.note: 못 always goes BEFORE the verb. It's not a sentence ending — it's a pre-verb blocker. 못 가요, 못 먹어요, 못 마셔요.

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihye invites her coworker Minsu to dinner at a Korean BBQ restaurant

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 민수 씨, 오늘 저녁에 삼겹살 먹고 싶어요?
lines.romanization: Minsu ssi, oneul jeonyeoge samgyeopsal meokgo sipeoyo?
lines.en: Minsu, do you want to eat samgyeopsal this evening?
lines.grammarNote: 먹고 싶어요? — direct but polite desire question. The speaker is checking whether Minsu also wants the same dinner.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 네, 먹고 싶어요! 어디에서 먹을 수 있어요?
lines.romanization: Ne, meokgo sipeoyo! Eodieseo meogeul su isseoyo?
lines.en: Yes, I want to eat it! Where can we eat it?
lines.grammarNote: 먹고 싶어요 (desire) + 먹을 수 있어요 (possibility) — two separate patterns in two sentences. 먹 ends in a consonant so 을 수 있어요.

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 회사 근처에 좋은 식당이 있어요. 7시에 갈 수 있어요?
lines.romanization: Hoesa geuncheoe joeun sikdangi isseoyo. Ilgop sie gal su isseoyo?
lines.en: There's a good restaurant near the office. Can you go at 7?
lines.grammarNote: 갈 수 있어요? — open-door question: is your door open at 7? 가다 stem 가 (vowel) → 갈 수 있어요.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 7시는 좀... 오늘 회의가 있어서 7시까지 못 가요.
lines.romanization: Ilgop sineun jom... oneul hoeuiga isseoseo ilgop sikkaji mot gayo.
lines.en: 7 o'clock is a bit... I have a meeting today so I can't get there by 7.
lines.grammarNote: 못 가요 — locked door: the meeting blocks him. 못 directly precedes the verb stem 가요. Note: NOT 못 가해요.

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.en: Then how about 8 o'clock? I can wait.
lines.grammarNote: 기다릴 수 있어요 — 기다리다 stem 기다리 (vowel) → 기다릴 수 있어요. She's reassuring him by stating her own capability to wait.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 고마워요! 그런데 저는 너무 매운 것은 못 먹어요.
lines.romanization: Gomawoyo! Geureonde jeoneun neomu maeun geoseun mot meogeoyo.
lines.en: Thank you! But I can't eat things that are too spicy.
lines.grammarNote: 못 먹어요 — locked door for spicy food: a dietary limitation. This is 못 + 먹어요 (plain verb form). Useful for communicating food restrictions.

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 괜찮아요. 거기서 맵지 않은 것도 먹을 수 있어요.
lines.romanization: Gwaenchanayo. Geogieseo maepji aneun geotdo meogeul su isseoyo.
lines.en: That's okay. You can also eat non-spicy things there.
lines.grammarNote: 먹을 수 있어요 — open door: the possibility exists. 먹 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을 수 있어요. She's reassuring with an ability/option statement.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.romanization: Wanjeon joayo! Yeodeol sie sikdang apeseo mannayo.
lines.en: Sounds perfect! Let's meet in front of the restaurant at 8.
lines.grammarNote: No grammar notes needed — 만나요 is a Chapter 6 review. Notice how want (먹고 싶어요), can (먹을 수 있어요), and can't (못 먹어요) all appeared naturally in this conversation.

readingText.title: 단체 채팅방 — 이번 주말에 뭐 할 수 있어요? (Group Chat — What can everyone do this weekend?)
readingText.body:
지은: 이번 주말에 같이 한강에 가고 싶어요. 다들 어때요?
유진: 저도 가고 싶어요! 토요일에 갈 수 있어요.
다니엘: 저는 토요일에 일이 있어서 못 가요. 일요일은 갈 수 있어요.
지은: 그럼 일요일에 가요! 자전거도 탈 수 있어요?
유진: 저는 자전거를 탈 수 있어요. 재미있겠다!
다니엘: 저는 자전거를 잘 못 타요. 천천히 가도 돼요?
지은: 물론이죠! 천천히 갈 수 있어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Jieun: I want to go to the Han River together this weekend. What does everyone think?
Yujin: I want to go too! I can go on Saturday.
Daniel: I have work on Saturday so I can't go. I can go on Sunday.
Jieun: Then let's go on Sunday! Can you also ride bikes?
Yujin: I can ride a bike. That sounds fun!
Daniel: I can't ride a bike well. Is it okay if we go slowly?
Jieun: Of course! We can go slowly.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why can't Daniel go on Saturday?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 일이 있어서 못 가요 — he has work, so something is blocking him (못 = locked door).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What does Daniel say about bike riding, and how does he express it?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 자전거를 잘 못 타요 — he can't ride a bike well. He uses 못 before 타요 (ride) to express inability. 잘 못 = 'not well' (not exactly the same as 전혀 못 = 'can't at all').

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every instance of 고 싶어요, ㄹ/을 수 있어요, and 못 in the text. For each one, identify which grammar pattern it is and explain why that specific pattern is used instead of the others.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 고 싶어요 (desire): 한강에 가고 싶어요 (Jieun wants to go — her desire), 저도 가고 싶어요 (Yujin shares the desire). | 수 있어요 (ability/possibility): 토요일에 갈 수 있어요 (Yujin: the door is open Saturday), 일요일은 갈 수 있어요 (Daniel: Sunday door is open), 자전거도 탈 수 있어요? (is the door open for biking?), 자전거를 탈 수 있어요 (Yujin: yes, open door), 천천히 갈 수 있어요 (the slow pace is possible). | 못 (inability): 토요일에 못 가요 (Daniel: work blocks Saturday — locked door), 자전거를 잘 못 타요 (Daniel: skill gap blocks him).

culturalNote.title: 못 해요 as the polite Korean refusal
culturalNote.body: In Korean social culture, saying you 'can't' do something (못 해요) is often more polite and face-saving than saying you 'don't want to' (싶지 않아요). If someone invites you somewhere you don't want to go, saying 오늘 못 가요 (I can't go today) is a softer decline than 가고 싶지 않아요 (I don't want to go), which can sound blunt or even rude. This is why Koreans sometimes use 못 해요 even when the real reason is lack of desire, not inability. When you start hearing 못 해요 in Korean conversations, know that it often carries the social function of a gentle 'no' — not necessarily a factual statement about impossibility.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 초밥을 먹___ 싶어요. (I want to eat sushi.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 고 싶어요 requires 고 between the verb stem and 싶어요. The stem of 먹다 is 먹, so: 먹고 싶어요. 을 would start the ability form (먹을 수 있어요), and 는 is a topic marker — neither makes sense here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 오늘 회의가 있어서 ___ 가요. (I can't go because I have a meeting today.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 expresses inability blocked by circumstances (the meeting). 안 가요 = 'I don't go / I won't go' (choice or habit, not inability). 고 싶지 않아요 = 'I don't want to go' (lack of desire). Only 못 captures 'I'm blocked — I can't.'

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '운동을 못 하해요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 운동하다 is a 하다 verb. The 못 inability form for 하다 verbs is 못 해요 — NOT 못 하해요, which doubles the 하다 part. The noun and 못 해요 can be split naturally: 운동 못 해요.

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I can speak a little Korean.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 한국어로 marks the language used as the means of speaking, and 말할 수 있어요 = ability/capability (open door). Option A (말하고 싶어요) = 'I want to speak Korean' — desire, not ability. Option C (못 말해요) = 'I can't speak Korean' — the opposite of what you want to say.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I want to rest today, but I can't.'
inlineExercises.correct: 오늘 쉬고 싶어요. 그런데 못 쉬어요.
inlineExercises.hint: You need two patterns: 쉬다 (to rest) with 고 싶어요 for desire, and 못 + verb for inability. The two parts contrast with 그런데 (but/however).
inlineExercises.explanation: -고 싶어요 expresses what you want to do. 못 쉬어요 says the situation blocks the action, not simply that you do not want to rest.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 매운 음식을 먹___ 수 있어요. (I can eat spicy food.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 먹다 has a consonant-ending stem (먹, ending in ㄱ). Consonant-ending stems take 을 수 있어요, not ㄹ 수 있어요. ㄹ 수 attaches to vowel-ending stems (가 → 갈 수, 오 → 올 수). 고 would start the desire form — not ability.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your Korean friend says '술 마시고 싶어요?' You can't drink alcohol. What's the most natural reply?
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 마셔요 is the most natural, socially smooth way to decline — it signals inability/circumstances rather than personal rejection, which is more polite in Korean culture. 마시고 싶지 않아요 (don't want to) sounds blunt. 마실 수 없어요 is grammatically fine but sounds formal/stiff in casual conversation. 못 마셔요 is the everyday go-to for dietary or health limitations.

inlineExercises.prompt: 한국어___ 조금 말할 수 있어요. (I can speak a little Korean.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 한국어 is what you speak, so it takes the object marker 를. 가 would make Korean the subject, which changes the sentence logic.

inlineExercises.prompt: 오늘은 집에 ___ . (가다 → want)
inlineExercises.explanation: -고 싶어요 attaches to the verb stem to express desire. 가다 loses 다, then takes 고 싶어요: 가고 싶어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I cannot eat spicy food.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 before the verb marks inability. 매운 음식 is the thing you cannot eat, so it takes 을.

bullets: MAGNET (고 싶어요): Verb stem + 고 싶어요 = desire, a pull toward an action. Always needs a verb — you can't attach it to a noun.
OPEN DOOR (ㄹ/을 수 있어요): Vowel stem + ㄹ 수 있어요 / Consonant stem + 을 수 있어요 = ability or possibility. The path is clear.
LOCKED DOOR (못 + verb): 못 goes BEFORE the regular verb form. Regular verbs use forms like 못 가요; 하다 verbs use 못 해요. Never make hybrids like 못 가해요 or 못 하해요.

writingTask.prompt: Reply to a friend planning the weekend: say one thing you want to do, one thing you can do, and one thing you can't.
writingTask.hint: Use V-고 싶어요 for wants, V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 for can, and V-(으)ㄹ 수 없어요 (or 못) for can't.
writingTask.model: 저는 영화를 보고 싶어요. 토요일에 갈 수 있어요. 그런데 일요일에는 못 가요.
writingTask.modelEn: I want to watch a movie. I can go on Saturday. But I can't go on Sunday.

canDo: Say what you want to do with V-고 싶어요 (가고 싶어요)
Say what you're able to do with V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요
Say what you can't do with V-(으)ㄹ 수 없어요 or 못 + verb
Attach -(으)ㄹ correctly after a 받침 vs a vowel stem

chapters.title: Requests, Permission, And Prohibition
chapters.goal: Ask for help, ask permission, and understand a polite no.
chapters.scenario: A museum or store where the learner wants help and asks whether photos are okay.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: Excuse me, please help me a little.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Sure, what can I help you with?

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: Is it okay to take photos here?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Sorry, but please don't take photos here.

chapters.guidedPractice: Practice 도와주세요, 앉아도 돼요?, 가지 마세요, and 가야 해요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Ask for help, ask if one action is okay, and respond politely if the answer is no.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend plays staff. Learner asks permission before taking a photo or sitting.
chapters.review: Can you separate request, permission, obligation, and prohibition?

beginnerGuide.title: Requests and permission are different
beginnerGuide.body: V아/어 주세요 asks someone to do something. V아/어도 돼요? asks if you may do something. 사진 찍어 주세요 and 사진 찍어도 돼요? are not the same.

beginnerGuide.title: Prohibition is mostly for understanding first
beginnerGuide.body: 지 마세요 appears on signs and from staff. You can use it, but it can sound like an instruction, so beginners should learn to understand it before using it broadly.

beginnerGuide.title: Make requests softer
beginnerGuide.body: 좀 often softens ordinary requests: 좀 도와주세요, 물 좀 주세요, 잠깐 기다려 주세요.

checkpoints: I can soften a request with 죄송한데.
I can ask permission with 아/어도 돼요?
I can recognize 지 마세요 as a polite prohibition.

curriculumTrack.label: A1 Foundation
curriculumTrack.description: Hangul, survival sentences, particles, polite present, and daily actions.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Ask for help, ask permission, and understand a polite no.
exitTask.prompt: Ask for help, ask if one action is okay, and respond politely if the answer is no.

sampleAnswer.ko: 죄송한데, 여기에서 사진 찍어도 돼요?
sampleAnswer.en: Excuse me, is it okay to take photos here?

checklist: I can soften a request with 죄송한데.
I can ask permission with 아/어도 돼요?
I can recognize 지 마세요 as a polite prohibition.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You're at a Korean museum and want to take a photo of an exhibit. You try to say 'May I take a photo?' but accidentally say '사진 찍어 주세요' — and the guard now thinks you're asking HIM to take your photo. The difference between asking permission and making a request is one tiny pattern.
objectives: Ask someone to do something with V아/어 주세요 (please do)
Ask for permission with V아/어도 돼요? (may I / is it okay to?)
Understand and use prohibition V지 마세요 (please do not) and obligation V아/어야 해요 (have to)
hook.whyItMatters: These four patterns cover almost every real-life rule situation: museum signs, restaurant staff, classrooms, public spaces. Miss one and you either sound rude, ask the wrong person for the wrong thing, or can't understand why someone is shaking their head at you.

grammarNotes.title: V아/어 주세요 vs V아/어도 돼요? — Asking Someone to DO vs Asking IF You May
grammarNotes.func: Use V아/어 주세요 to politely ask someone to DO something for you ('please do X'). Use V아/어도 돼요? to ask whether YOU are allowed to do something ('is it okay if I do X?'). One asks the listener to act; the other asks the listener for permission.

formTable.when: Stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ (bright)
formTable.ex: 받다 → 받아 주세요 (please take it) · 앉다 → 앉아도 돼요? (may I sit?)

formTable.when: Stem's last vowel is anything else (dark)
formTable.ex: 읽다 → 읽어 주세요 (please read it) · 먹다 → 먹어도 돼요? (may I eat?)
말하다 → 말해 주세요 (please say it) · 전화하다 → 전화해도 돼요? (may I call?)

formTable.when: Stem ends in ㅡ (the ㅡ drops)
formTable.ex: 쓰다 → 써 주세요 (please write it) · 끄다 → 꺼도 돼요? (may I turn it off?)

examples.en: Some water, please.
examples.note: 주세요 attaches straight to a NOUN (물) to ask for the thing itself — no 아/어 needed. 좀 softens it, like 'a little.'

examples.en: Please speak slowly (for me).
examples.note: 말하다 → 말해 + 주세요. The 아/어 주세요 form asks the listener to do the action for your benefit.

examples.en: Is it okay if I sit here?
examples.note: 앉다 has ㅏ, so 앉아 + 도 돼요? You're asking permission for yourself, not asking them to do anything.

examples.en: Can I take a photo?
examples.note: 찍다 has ㅣ (dark), so 찍어 + 도 돼요? Said with rising intonation, it's a real permission question.

keyPoint.label: 주세요 + noun vs 아/어 주세요 + verb
keyPoint.body: 주세요 alone follows a NOUN to ask for the thing: 물 주세요 (water, please), 메뉴 주세요 (the menu, please). To ask someone to DO an action, the verb must take its 아/어 form first: 도와주세요 (please help), 기다려 주세요 (please wait). Beginners often stick a plain dictionary verb in front of 주세요 (돕다 주세요 is wrong; 도와주세요 is right) — change the verb to its 아/어 form first.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 돼요 is one syllable, [dwae-yo] — a single glide, not two beats.

drill.instruction: Decide if it's a REQUEST (아/어 주세요) or asking PERMISSION (아/어도 돼요?), then complete the sentence.
drill.model: 창문을 (열다) → REQUEST: 창문을 열어 주세요. / PERMISSION: 창문을 열어도 돼요?
items: 이름을 (쓰다) → REQUEST: 이름을 ___ 주세요. (Please write your name → 써)
지금 (가다) → PERMISSION: 지금 ___ 돼요? (May I go now? → 가도)
문을 (닫다) → REQUEST: 문을 ___ 주세요. (Please close the door → 닫아)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 여기 앉아 주세요? (when you mean 'May I sit here?')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English uses 'can/may' for both 'please do this' and 'may I do this,' so learners mix the two Korean forms. 앉아 주세요 means 'please sit (for me)' — you're telling THEM to sit. To ask permission for yourself, add 도 돼요?: 앉아도 돼요? Remember: 아/어 주세요 = you act; 아/어도 돼요? = I'm allowed.

grammarNotes.title: V지 마세요 & V아/어야 돼요 — Telling Someone Not To, and Saying You Have To
grammarNotes.func: Use V지 마세요 to politely tell someone NOT to do something ('please don't do X'). Use V아/어야 돼요 to say something must be done ('have to do X'). Together they cover both sides of a rule: what's not allowed and what's required.

formTable.ex: 들어가다 → 들어가지 마세요 (don't go in) · 먹다 → 먹지 마세요 (don't eat it)
가다 → 가야 돼요 (have to go) · 자다 → 자야 돼요 (have to sleep)
먹다 → 먹어야 돼요 (have to eat) · 기다리다 → 기다려야 돼요 (have to wait)
공부하다 → 공부해야 돼요 (have to study) · 일하다 → 일해야 돼요 (have to work)

examples.en: Please don't smoke here.
examples.note: 피우다 → 피우 + 지 마세요. 지 마세요 attaches straight to the stem — no vowel harmony for prohibition.

examples.en: Please don't take photos.
examples.note: 찍다 → 찍 + 지 마세요. A common sign you'll see; the form is the same no matter the final consonant.

examples.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.
examples.note: 일어나다 ends in ㅏ → 일어나 + 야 돼요. 아/어야 돼요 and 아/어야 해요 mean the same thing; 돼요 is more common in everyday speech.

examples.en: I have to take the medicine.
examples.note: 먹다 (dark vowel) → 먹어 + 야 돼요. In Korean you 'eat' (먹다) medicine, not 'take' it.

keyPoint.label: 지 마세요 (don't!) vs 안 + verb (doesn't/isn't)
keyPoint.body: 지 마세요 is a COMMAND telling someone NOT to do something: 뛰지 마세요 (don't run). It is not how you say YOU don't do something — for that, use 안: 저는 안 뛰어요 (I don't run). So 지 마세요 is only for telling other people what not to do.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In 먹어야 the ㄱ links into the next vowel, so it flows as [meo-geo-ya], one smooth piece rather than 먹+어야.

drill.instruction: Turn each cue into either a PROHIBITION (지 마세요) or a 'have to' (아/어야 돼요) as marked.
drill.model: (뛰다) PROHIBITION → 뛰지 마세요. / (자다) HAVE TO → 자야 돼요.
items: (들어가다) PROHIBITION → 여기에 ___ . (Please don't go in here → 들어가지 마세요)
(공부하다) HAVE TO → 시험이 있어서 ___ . (I have to study because there's a test → 공부해야 돼요)
(기다리다) HAVE TO → 친구를 ___ . (I have to wait for my friend → 기다려야 돼요)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 먹지 않으세요 (when you mean 'please don't eat it')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners build prohibition from the negative 지 않다 ('does not'), getting 먹지 않으세요, which sounds like an odd statement, not a command. Negative commands ('don't') use the special verb 말다: 먹지 마세요. Keep 안 먹어요 / 먹지 않아요 ('I don't eat it') for plain negatives, and 지 마세요 for telling someone not to do it.

exampleSentence.en: Please help me!
exampleSentence.note: 주다 (give) fused into a request — asking someone to give you the action of helping

exampleSentence.en: May I take a photo?
exampleSentence.note: 사진 as object — permission asked using 도 돼요?

exampleSentence.en: Please do not take photos here.
exampleSentence.note: 찍지 마세요 = RED X SIGN — prohibition on the action of taking photos

exampleSentence.en: May I sit here?
exampleSentence.note: 앉아도 돼요? — vowel ending stem: 앉 + 아도 돼요?

exampleSentence.en: May I go in?
exampleSentence.note: 가 + 아도 → 가도 is absorbed into 들어가도 — entering is checked with permission form

exampleSentence.en: Please open the window a bit.
exampleSentence.note: 열다 + 어 주세요 — asking someone else to perform the opening action

exampleSentence.en: Please close the door.
exampleSentence.note: 닫다 + 아 주세요 — the ㄷ stem is regular here; asking another person to close it

exampleSentence.en: Please speak slowly.
exampleSentence.note: 말하다 + 여 주세요 → 말해 주세요 — classic classroom and daily-life request

exampleSentence.en: Please wait a moment.
exampleSentence.note: 기다리다 + 어 주세요 — 리 contracts to 려; asking someone to hold on

exampleSentence.en: Please do not run in the hallway.
exampleSentence.note: 뛰다 + 지 마세요 — common school/museum prohibition sign

exampleSentence.en: Please do not worry.
exampleSentence.note: 지 마세요 used not as a rule sign but as warm reassurance between people

exampleSentence.en: I have to go now. I'm late.
exampleSentence.note: 가다 + 아야 해요 — MUST-DO CHECKLIST: non-negotiable obligation

exampleSentence.en: Please help me (softened).
exampleSentence.note: 좀 before a request softens it — like 'kindly' or 'if you could'; almost always present in polite Korean requests

extendedVocabulary.english: I'm sorry but / I apologize but

exampleSentence.ko: 죄송하지만 여기서 음식을 드시면 안 돼요.
exampleSentence.en: I'm sorry but you cannot eat here.
exampleSentence.note: 죄송하지만 softens a refusal or prohibition — staff use this before giving bad news

exampleSentence.en: You have to show your admission ticket.
exampleSentence.note: 입장권 + 어야 해요 — obligation before entry at museums and event spaces

exampleSentence.en: Please do not eat food here.
exampleSentence.note: Common museum/gallery prohibition — 지 마세요 as RED X SIGN

exampleSentence.en: Please do not touch the exhibits.
exampleSentence.note: 만지다 + 지 마세요 — classic museum rule you will definitely encounter

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihoon visits a traditional craft museum with his friend Sora. They encounter signs and staff along the way.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 소라 씨, 저 사진 찍어도 돼요?
lines.romanization: Sora ssi, jeo sajin jjigeodo dwaeyo?
lines.en: Sora, may I take a photo?
lines.grammarNote: 사진 찍어도 돼요? — TRAFFIC LIGHT: asking if the green light is on for Jihoon's own action of taking a photo

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: I'm not sure either. Let's ask a staff member.
lines.grammarNote: 직원한테 물어봐요 — 한테 is the spoken-language form of 에게 (to/from a person): asking 'to/at the staff member'

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Excuse me! May I take photos here?
lines.grammarNote: 저기요 = 'excuse me' to get attention; 여기서 사진 찍어도 돼요? — TRAFFIC LIGHT for a specific location 여기서

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.ko: 죄송하지만 이 구역에서는 사진 찍지 마세요. 저쪽은 괜찮아요.
lines.romanization: Joesonghajiman i guyeogeseoneun sajin jjikji maseyo. Jeotjjogeun gwaenchanayo.
lines.en: I'm sorry, but please do not take photos in this section. That area over there is fine.
lines.grammarNote: 찍지 마세요 — RED X SIGN: prohibition on photo-taking in this zone; 괜찮아요 = it's okay (implicit permission for the other area)

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.ko: 알겠어요. 그리고 저 전시품 만져도 돼요?
lines.romanization: Algesseoyo. Geurigo jeo jeonsipum manjyeodo dwaeyo?
lines.en: Got it. And may I touch that exhibit?
lines.grammarNote: 만져도 돼요? — TRAFFIC LIGHT: 만지다 + 어도 돼요? asking permission to touch

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.ko: 아니요, 만지지 마세요. 그리고 음식도 안에서 드시면 안 돼요.
lines.romanization: Aniyo, manjiji maseyo. Geurigo eumsikdo aneseo deusimyeon an dwaeyo.
lines.en: No, please do not touch them. And food is also not allowed inside.
lines.grammarNote: 만지지 마세요 — another RED X SIGN; 드시면 안 돼요 = if you eat it won't be okay — a softer way to express prohibition using conditional

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 감사합니다. 소라 씨, 저기 사진 구역에서 사진 찍어 주세요!
lines.romanization: Gamsahamnida. Sora ssi, jeogi sajin guyeogeseo sajin jjigeo juseyo!
lines.en: Thank you. Sora, please take a photo of me in that photo zone!
lines.grammarNote: 사진 찍어 주세요 — HANDOFF: now asking Sora to perform the action of taking the photo for him

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.ko: 네, 찍어 줄게요! 여기 서 보세요.
lines.romanization: Ne, jjigeo julgeyo! Yeogi seo boseyo.
lines.en: Sure, I'll take it for you! Try standing here.
lines.grammarNote: 찍어 줄게요 is a natural promise between classmates/friends; 서 보세요 gently suggests a position for the photo

readingText.title: 국립 한국 문화 박물관 관람 안내 (National Korean Culture Museum Visitor Guide)
readingText.body: 박물관에 오신 것을 환영합니다. 즐거운 관람을 위해 다음 사항을 지켜 주세요. 전시실 내에서는 사진을 찍지 마세요. 전시품은 만지지 마세요. 음식이나 음료는 드시면 안 됩니다. 어린이는 보호자와 함께해야 해요. 박물관 안에서는 조용히 해 주세요. 입장 전에 가방을 검사받아야 해요. 궁금한 것이 있으면 직원한테 물어보세요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Welcome to the museum. Please observe the following for an enjoyable visit. Please do not take photos inside the exhibition hall. Please do not touch the exhibits. You may not eat food or drink beverages. Children must be accompanied by a guardian. Please be quiet inside the museum. You must have your bag inspected before entering. If you have any questions, please ask a staff member.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two things does the notice say you must NOT do with exhibits?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 사진을 찍지 마세요 (do not take photos) and 전시품은 만지지 마세요 (do not touch the exhibits)

comprehensionQuestions.question: What must children do according to the notice?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 보호자와 함께해야 해요 — children must be with a guardian (해야 해요 = must/have to)

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all 지 마세요 and 아/어야 해요 forms in the text. For each one, say whether it is a prohibition (RED X SIGN) or an obligation (MUST-DO CHECKLIST), and explain why that form is used rather than the other.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 지 마세요 forms (RED X SIGN — stopping an action): 찍지 마세요 (don't take photos — prohibition on visitor action), 만지지 마세요 (don't touch — prohibition). 아/어야 해요 forms (MUST-DO CHECKLIST — requiring an action): 함께해야 해요 (children must be with guardian — positive obligation), 검사받아야 해요 (must have bag inspected — required step). The distinction is key: 지 마세요 blocks an action the visitor might want to do; 아/어야 해요 requires an action the visitor must perform.

culturalNote.title: 좀 — the magic softener every Korean learner needs
culturalNote.body: Koreans almost always add 좀 before a request to soften it: 도와주세요 is fine, but 좀 도와주세요 sounds more polite. 물 주세요 is acceptable, but 물 좀 주세요 is what locals actually say at restaurants. 좀 doesn't mean 'a little' here — it functions like 'if you could' or 'kindly' in English. Foreigners who skip 좀 don't sound rude exactly, but they do sound slightly abrupt or robotic. In contrast, 잠깐만요 (just a moment) and 실례합니다 (excuse me, pardon) are also essential softening phrases. Watch how staff at museums and cafés use 죄송하지만 before every prohibition — Koreans soften bad news first, then deliver the rule.

inlineExercises.prompt: 사진 찍___ 돼요? (May I take a photo?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 어도 돼요? = TRAFFIC LIGHT — asking if YOU are allowed to take a photo. 지 않아도 돼요 would mean 'you don't have to take a photo' (no obligation), and 아야 해요 would mean 'you have to take a photo' (obligation). Only 어도 돼요? asks for permission.

inlineExercises.prompt: 전시품을 만지___ 마세요. (Please do not touch the exhibits.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 지 마세요 = RED X SIGN — prohibition. 어도 돼요 would turn this into a permission question. 아야 해요 would make it an obligation to touch, which is the opposite of what a museum sign says.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '사진 찍어 주세요?' (trying to ask permission to take a photo)
inlineExercises.explanation: 주세요 is a HANDOFF — it asks the OTHER person to take a photo. Adding '?' to 주세요 does not transform it into a permission question in Korean. To ask if YOU may take a photo, you need 어도 돼요? — the TRAFFIC LIGHT form.

inlineExercises.prompt: A museum staff member walks up and says something. Which sentence means 'Please do not run in the hallway'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 뛰지 마세요 = RED X SIGN — prohibition. 뛰어도 돼요? is a permission question (may I run?). 뛰어야 해요 is an obligation (you have to run). Only 지 마세요 delivers the prohibition instruction you see on signs.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'Please help me a bit.'
