inlineExercises.hint: 도와주다 = to help. Which pattern asks someone ELSE to perform an action? And which adverb softens requests?
inlineExercises.explanation: 도와주세요 is the direct polite request 'please help me.' 좀 softens the request so it sounds less blunt.

inlineExercises.prompt: 입장권을 사___ 해요. (I have to buy an admission ticket.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 아야 해요 = MUST-DO CHECKLIST — a non-negotiable obligation. 지 않아도 돼요 would mean 'you don't have to buy it' (opposite meaning). 지 마세요 would mean 'please do not buy it' — completely wrong here. Only 아야 해요 expresses the requirement.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend says '가지 마세요!' and you reply that you must go. What do you say?
inlineExercises.explanation: 가야 해요 = MUST-DO CHECKLIST — I have to go, it's an obligation. 가지 않아도 돼요 means 'I don't have to go' (no obligation), which contradicts your intention. 가지 마세요 would mean 'please don't go' — you'd be repeating your friend's prohibition back to them.

inlineExercises.prompt: 사진___ 찍어도 돼요? (May I take a photo?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 사진 is what you take, so it takes the object marker 을. 이 would make the photo the subject instead of the object.

inlineExercises.prompt: 문을 ___ . (닫다 → please do)
inlineExercises.explanation: 닫다 becomes 닫아 주세요 for a polite request. This asks someone to close the door for you.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Please do not touch this.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -지 마세요 is the polite "please do not" form. 이것 is the thing being touched, so 이것을 comes before the verb.

bullets: 주세요 = HANDOFF: V아/어 주세요 asks the OTHER person to perform the action for you
도 돼요? = TRAFFIC LIGHT: V아/어도 돼요? asks if YOU are allowed to perform the action
지 마세요 = RED X SIGN: V지 마세요 prohibits an action | 아/어야 해요 = MUST-DO CHECKLIST: V아/어야 해요 requires an action

writingTask.prompt: Leave a short note for a guest in your home: ask them to do one thing, grant one permission, and state one rule.
writingTask.hint: Use V아/어 주세요 to ask them to do something, V아/어도 돼요 for permission, and V지 마세요 / V아/어야 돼요 for the rule.
writingTask.model: 문을 닫아 주세요. 여기 앉아도 돼요. 하지만 사진은 찍지 마세요. 신발은 벗어야 돼요.
writingTask.modelEn: Please close the door. You may sit here. But please don't take photos. You have to take off your shoes.

canDo: Ask someone to do something for you with V아/어 주세요 (도와주세요)
Ask or give permission with V아/어도 돼요? (앉아도 돼요?)
Tell someone not to do something with V지 마세요 (찍지 마세요)
Say what must be done with V아/어야 돼요 (가야 돼요)

chapters.title: Travel And Classroom Help
chapters.goal: Ask for directions or repetition when you are lost or missed something.
chapters.scenario: A station or hotel lobby where the learner needs one clear answer.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: It's over there on the right.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.ko: 다시 한 번만 천천히 말해 주세요.
dialogue.romanization: dasi han beonman cheoncheonhi malhae juseyo.
dialogue.en: Please say it slowly one more time.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Sure. It's over there on the right.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.en: I understand. Thank you.

chapters.guidedPractice: Ask where something is, ask someone to repeat, and explain that you do not understand yet.
chapters.realLifeTask: Ask where something is, then ask the person to repeat slowly.
chapters.friendPractice: Friend gives a short direction. Learner asks 다시 말해 주세요 or 천천히 말해 주세요.
chapters.review: Can you ask for location and classroom help without switching to English?

beginnerGuide.title: Travel Korean needs repair phrases
beginnerGuide.body: When communication breaks down, phrases like 다시 말해 주세요, 천천히 말해 주세요, and 잘 모르겠어요 keep the conversation alive.

beginnerGuide.title: Ask short, useful questions
beginnerGuide.body: 화장실 어디예요? and 지하철역 어디예요? are natural spoken questions. Adding 이 makes them more complete, but the shorter form is common.

beginnerGuide.title: Range and route
beginnerGuide.body: 부터/까지 helps with time and route: 여기부터 역까지, 9시부터 6시까지.

checkpoints: I can begin politely with 죄송한데.
I can ask 어디예요? for a place I need.
I can ask 다시 한 번만 천천히 말해 주세요.

curriculumTrack.label: A1 Foundation
curriculumTrack.description: Hangul, survival sentences, particles, polite present, and daily actions.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Ask for directions or repetition when you are lost or missed something.
exitTask.prompt: Ask where something is, then ask the person to repeat slowly.

sampleAnswer.ko: 화장실이 어디예요? 다시 한 번만 천천히 말해 주세요.
sampleAnswer.romanization: hwajangsiri eodiyeyo? dasi han beonman cheoncheonhi malhae juseyo.
sampleAnswer.en: Where is the bathroom? Please say it slowly one more time.

checklist: I can begin politely with 죄송한데.
I can ask 어디예요? for a place I need.
I can ask 다시 한 번만 천천히 말해 주세요.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You're lost at Seoul Station. You need the bathroom urgently, but the signs are all in Korean. You try 화장실 어디예요? — and a local points down the hall, speaks three fast sentences, and walks away. You caught the direction but not the words. What do you say next?
objectives: Ask where something is using 이/가 어디예요? and 이/가 있어요?
Use 부터/까지 to describe time ranges (9시부터 6시까지) and routes (여기부터 역까지)
Deploy repair phrases — 다시 말해 주세요, 천천히 말해 주세요, 잘 모르겠어요 — to keep conversations alive
hook.whyItMatters: Travel Korean lives or dies on two skills: finding things and recovering when you get lost in a conversation. 부터/까지 turns you from someone who can only ask about single moments ('몇 시에?') into someone who can talk about ranges ('여기서 거기까지 얼마나 걸려요?'). And the repair phrases are the difference between a Korean who keeps talking to you and one who switches to mime.

grammarNotes.title: N부터 / N까지 — from … to … (ranges in time and space)
grammarNotes.func: 부터 marks where a range starts and 까지 marks where it ends — "from A to B." They work for time (아홉 시부터 여섯 시까지, from 9 to 6) and for place (집부터 학교까지, from home to school), and each can appear alone too (부터 = "starting from," 까지 = "up until / by").

formTable.when: Start point of a range (attaches to any noun)
formTable.ex: 아침 → 아침부터 · 한 시 → 한 시부터

formTable.when: End point of a range (attaches to any noun)
formTable.ex: 저녁 → 저녁까지 · 여섯 시 → 여섯 시까지
내일 → 내일까지 · 다섯 시 → 다섯 시까지

examples.en: I work from nine to six.
examples.note: Classic time range: 부터 on the start time, 까지 on the end time.

examples.en: It's far from home to school.
examples.note: Place range with 부터…까지. You'll also often hear 집에서 학교까지 — see the key point below.

examples.en: From what time is the movie?
examples.note: 부터 used alone to ask just the starting time.

examples.en: I'll read the book by tomorrow.
examples.note: 까지 alone = a deadline, "by tomorrow."

keyPoint.label: 부터 vs 에서 (both can mean "from")
keyPoint.body: For a starting point you measure a stretch from — especially time — use 부터: 아침부터 (from morning). For a physical place you set out from, native speakers usually say 에서: 집에서 학교까지 (from home to school). So time ranges lean on 부터…까지, while place ranges usually use 에서…까지. You'll still hear 집부터 학교까지, so it's not wrong — just know that 에서…까지 is the more common "place-to-place" frame. The full location particle 에서 gets its own chapter; for now just remember: time → 부터, place → often 에서, and 까지 marks the end either way.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 까지 starts with the tense consonant ㄲ, so keep it crisp — [kka-ji], not a soft [ga-ji]. After a 받침 like ㅂ/ㄱ/ㄷ, 부터 tenses a little: 집부터 sounds like [집뿌터].

drill.instruction: Make a "from … to …" sentence with 부터 and 까지, following the model.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 아홉 시까지 여섯 시부터 일해요. / 집까지 학교부터 멀어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 아홉 시부터 여섯 시까지 일해요. / 집부터 학교까지 멀어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English says "from … to …," and learners often reach for 까지 first or swap the two particles. Tie each particle to its meaning, not to word order: 부터 always sits on the START point and 까지 always sits on the END point.

grammarNotes.title: V아/어 주세요 — asking someone to do something for you
grammarNotes.func: V아/어 주세요 is the polite way to ask someone to do something for you: "please (do) … (for me)." Take the verb stem, add 아/어 by vowel harmony, then attach 주세요. It powers the survival phrases you need in class and out on the street — 다시 말해 주세요 (please say it again), 천천히 말해 주세요 (please speak slowly).

formTable.when: Stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ (bright)
formTable.ex: 받다 → 받아 주세요 · 보다 → 봐 주세요

formTable.when: Stem's last vowel is anything else (not ㅏ/ㅗ)
formTable.ex: 읽다 → 읽어 주세요 · 만들다 → 만들어 주세요
말하다 → 말해 주세요 · 일하다 → 일해 주세요
다시 → 다시 말해 주세요 · 천천히 → 천천히 써 주세요

examples.en: Please say that again.
examples.note: 말하다 is a 하다 verb → 말해. With 다시 ("again") it's the #1 classroom phrase.

examples.en: Please speak slowly.
examples.note: 천천히 ("slowly") + 말해 주세요 — use it when someone talks too fast for you.

examples.en: Please give me some water.
examples.note: With a plain noun, use 주세요 directly (no 아/어). 좀 softens it to "please / if you would."

examples.en: Please read this book (to me).
examples.note: 읽다's last vowel isn't ㅏ/ㅗ → 읽어 주세요. The 주세요 adds the "for me" nuance.

keyPoint.label: V아/어 주세요 vs N 주세요
keyPoint.body: Plain 주세요 (from 주다, "to give") means "please give me ___" and attaches straight to a noun: 물 주세요, 책 주세요. But when you want someone to DO something for you, a bare noun won't carry it — you put the verb in the 아/어 form first: 책을 읽어 주세요 (please read the book for me). So: a thing you want handed over → N 주세요; an action you want done → V아/어 주세요. The deeper 주다 "do-it-for-me" grammar comes later; for now treat V아/어 주세요 as one fixed request phrase.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In 말해 주세요 the ㄹ links into 해 — [마래 주세요]. In 읽어 주세요 the hidden ㄱ of 읽 carries onto 어 — [일거 주세요]. Keep 주세요 light and even, don't stress it.

drill.instruction: Turn each verb into a polite request with V아/어 주세요, following the model.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 다시 말하 주세요 / 천천히 말하세요 (meaning "please say it again for me")
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 다시 말해 주세요 / 천천히 말해 주세요
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Two traps. First, you have to conjugate to the 아/어 form before 주세요 — it's 말해 주세요, never the bare stem 말하 주세요. Second, plain 말하세요 is a polite command ("speak") with no "for me" warmth; adding 주세요 turns the order into a real request — exactly what you want when asking a teacher or a stranger for help.

exampleSentence.en: Where is the bathroom?
exampleSentence.note: 이 follows consonant-ending 실 — subject particle, not topic particle

exampleSentence.en: How long does it take to the subway station?
exampleSentence.note: 까지 = as far as / to — the end-point of a distance range

exampleSentence.en: Which exit number is it?
exampleSentence.note: 몇 번 = which number — essential for subway navigation

exampleSentence.en: Where is the information desk?
exampleSentence.note: A practical travel question when you need staff help, directions, or opening hours

exampleSentence.en: Where is the Line 2 boarding area?
exampleSentence.note: 타는 곳 = the place where you board; more natural than saying the line itself is an exit

exampleSentence.en: I'll study hard starting from today.
exampleSentence.note: 부터 attaches to the start-point — 오늘부터 means 'from today onward'

extendedVocabulary.english: to / until / as far as (end point)

exampleSentence.en: Until what time are you open?
exampleSentence.note: 까지 after a time = 'until' — perfect for asking business hours

exampleSentence.en: Please say it again.
exampleSentence.note: 다시 placed before the verb — it modifies the action (말하다)

exampleSentence.en: Please speak slowly.
exampleSentence.note: 천천히 before 말해 주세요 specifies the speed — add it any time you need less pace

exampleSentence.en: I'm not quite sure.
exampleSentence.note: 잘 모르겠어요 is softer and more natural than just 몰라요 — 겠 adds an element of 'I think / I guess'

exampleSentence.en: I walk from here to the station.
exampleSentence.note: 걷다 is ㄷ-irregular: 걷 + 어 → 걸어요 (ㄷ changes to ㄹ before a vowel)

exampleSentence.en: It takes 30 minutes by bus.
exampleSentence.note: 얼마나 걸려요? (How long does it take?) is a must-know travel question — 걸리다 expresses time cost

exampleSentence.en: Please help me!
exampleSentence.note: 돕다 + 아/어 주다 → 도와주다 (ㅂ-irregular): 도와주세요 is a one-word survival phrase

exampleSentence.en: I'm looking for the subway station.
exampleSentence.note: 찾고 있어요 = currently searching (ongoing action) — useful when you're lost and need help

exampleSentence.en: It's a 10-minute walk from here to the station.
exampleSentence.note: 여기부터 = starting from here — pairs naturally with 까지 for distance ranges

extendedVocabulary.english: over there (that place in the distance)

exampleSentence.en: The bathroom is over there.
exampleSentence.note: 저기 = yonder/over there (visible but farther away). 여기 = here, 거기 = there, 저기 = over there

exampleSentence.en: Go to the left.
exampleSentence.note: 으로 = direction marker (go via/toward). 왼쪽으로 가다 = go left

exampleSentence.en: There's a convenience store on the right.
exampleSentence.note: 에 있다 = something exists in that location — combine direction + 에 있다 to describe where things are

exampleSentence.en: Yes, I understand. Thank you.
exampleSentence.note: 알겠어요 is warmer and more engaged than just 네 — it shows you actually processed what was said

extendedDialogue.setting: Jimin is a foreign learner at Seoul Station. She approaches 민준 (a station employee) looking confused.

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.en: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
lines.grammarNote: 저기요 = 'hey' / 'excuse me' to get attention. 화장실이 어디예요? — 이 is the subject particle after consonant-ending 실; 어디 = where

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Go toward exit 3. It's on the right.
lines.grammarNote: 쪽으로 = toward (that direction). 오른쪽에 있어요 = exists on the right side — 있어요 + 에 for static location

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.ko: 죄송한데, 천천히 말해 주세요. 잘 이해가 안 돼요.
lines.romanization: joesonghande, cheoncheonhi malhae juseyo. jal ihaega an dwaeyo.
lines.en: Sorry, please speak slowly. I don't understand well.
lines.grammarNote: 천천히 말해 주세요 — V아/어 주세요 request pattern; 잘 이해가 안 돼요 = 'understanding doesn't work well' — natural way to say 'I don't get it'

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 아, 네! 저기 계단 보여요? 계단에서 오른쪽으로 가세요.
lines.romanization: a, ne! jeogi gyedan boyeoyo? gyedaneseo oreunjjogeuro gaseyo.
lines.en: Ah, yes! Do you see those stairs over there? From the stairs, go right.
lines.grammarNote: 계단에서 오른쪽으로 가세요 — 에서 marks the starting point of the movement (stairs → go right from there)

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.ko: 알겠어요! 감사합니다. 혹시 2호선 타는 곳은 몇 번 출구 쪽이에요?
lines.romanization: algesseoyo! gamsahamnida. hoksi i hoseon taneun goseun myeot beon chulgu jjogiyeyo?
lines.en: Got it! Thank you. Also, which exit side is the Line 2 boarding area toward?
lines.grammarNote: 2호선 타는 곳 = the place to take Line 2. 몇 번 출구 쪽이에요? asks which exit direction/side to follow.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 2호선 타는 곳은 5번 출구 쪽이에요. 여기서 5번 출구까지 걸어서 3분이에요.
lines.romanization: i hoseon taneun goseun obeon chulgu jjogiyeyo. yeogiseo obeon chulgukkaji georeoseo sambunieyo.
lines.en: The Line 2 boarding area is toward exit 5. It's a 3-minute walk from here to exit 5.
lines.grammarNote: 여기서 5번 출구까지 — 에서 marks departure point; 까지 marks arrival point; 걸어서 = 'by walking / on foot'

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.ko: 안내소는 몇 시부터 몇 시까지 열어요?
lines.romanization: annaesoneun myeot sibuteo myeot sikkaji yeoreoyo?
lines.en: From what time to what time is the information desk open?
lines.grammarNote: 몇 시부터 몇 시까지 — RULER pattern for asking time ranges; 안내소 keeps the example general instead of pretending to know a real station schedule

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.romanization: ojeon ahopsibuteo ohu yeoseot sikkaji yeoreoyo. annaesoeseo mureoboseyo.
lines.en: It's open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Please ask at the information desk.
lines.grammarNote: 오전 9시부터 오후 6시까지 — complete ruler range with both endpoints; 안내소에서 = at the information desk, the place where asking happens

readingText.title: 서울역에서 온 문자 (Text messages from Seoul Station)
readingText.body:
지민: 민아야, 지금 서울역에 있어. 근데 길을 잘 모르겠어.
민아: 어디 가려고?
지민: 2호선 타려고. 몇 번 출구 쪽인지 몰라.
민아: 14번 출구 쪽이야. 거기서 2호선 타는 곳까지 걸어서 5분이야.
지민: 아, 그리고 화장실도 찾고 있었는데.
민아: 화장실은 1번 출구 왼쪽에 있어. 출구에서 나오면 바로 보여.
지민: 알겠어! 참, 안내소는 몇 시까지 열어?
민아: 안내소는 오전 9시부터 오후 6시까지 열어.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Jimin: Mina, I'm at Seoul Station now. But I don't really know my way around.
Mina: Where are you trying to go?
Jimin: I'm trying to take Line 2. I don't know which exit side it is toward.
Mina: It's toward exit 14. From there to the Line 2 boarding area is a 5-minute walk.
Jimin: Oh, and I was also looking for the bathroom.
Mina: The bathroom is to the left of exit 1. Once you come out the exit, you'll see it right away.
Jimin: Got it! By the way, until what time is the information desk open?
Mina: The information desk is open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Which exit should Jimin use to get to Line 2?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 14번 출구 쪽 (toward exit 14). From there it's a 5-minute walk to the Line 2 boarding area.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Where is the bathroom?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 1번 출구 왼쪽에 있어 — it is to the left of exit 1, visible as soon as you exit.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every use of 부터 and 까지 in the text. Why is each one used — and why does one sentence use both?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 몇 시까지 열어? — 까지 alone marks the end-point of the opening hours (asking 'until what time'). 오전 9시부터 오후 6시까지 열어 — both 부터 and 까지 appear because Mina is giving the full range: 'from 9 AM (부터 = start) to 6 PM (까지 = end)'. The first question only needed the endpoint; the answer needed both endpoints of the ruler.

culturalNote.title: 역 문화 — Subway Station Culture in Korea
culturalNote.body: Seoul's subway is one of the world's most navigated systems, and Korean stations are built around the assumption that you might not know where you are. Every exit is numbered (1번 출구, 2번 출구…), and Koreans give directions by exit number — not left or right from the entrance. So when someone says '2호선은 5번 출구예요,' they expect you to find exit 5 on the station map and orient from there. Station staff (역무원) are trained to help and are very patient with foreigners — they will often walk you part of the way. Don't be shy about using 다시 말해 주세요 or 천천히 말해 주세요. Korean station staff hear these phrases from tourists every day, and asking for a repeat is far more respected than nodding and wandering off confused.

inlineExercises.prompt: 9시___ 6시___ 일해요. (I work from 9 to 6.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 부터 marks the start-point (9시부터 = from 9) and 까지 marks the end-point (6시까지 = to/until 6). 에 alone (9시에 / 6시에) would give two single time-points but not express a range. 에서 is for places where actions happen, not time expressions.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다시 말해 ___. (Please say it again.)
inlineExercises.explanation: The V아/어 주세요 pattern uses 주세요 (from 주다 = to give, as a favor). 말해요 alone is a statement ('you say it again'). 주어요 is not a polite request form — 주세요 is the standard polite imperative of 주다.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '여기부터 역에서 걸어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 에서 marks where an action happens (a stage), not a destination endpoint. The ending point of a range takes 까지 — '역까지' means 'all the way to the station.' 역에서 걷다 would mean 'walking at the station' (action happening there), not 'walking as far as the station.'

inlineExercises.prompt: A local just gave you fast directions. You didn't catch everything. What do you say?
inlineExercises.explanation: 천천히 말해 주세요 (Please speak slowly) is the best repair phrase when the issue is speed. 잘 모르겠어요 (I don't really know) signals confusion but doesn't ask for help. 다시 한 번 주세요 is missing the verb — it would mean 'give me one more time' (like asking for a second serving). 네, 알겠어요 would falsely signal comprehension.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'From Monday to Friday there is class.'
inlineExercises.hint: Which particle marks the start of a range? Which marks the end? What pattern says 'there is'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 부터 and 까지 mark the start and end of a range. 수업이 있어요 states that class exists or is scheduled during that range.

inlineExercises.prompt: 죄송한데, 천천히 말해 ___ . (Sorry, please speak slowly.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 말해 주세요 = the complete V아/어 주세요 request form. 말해요 alone = a statement or direct command, which would sound rude to a stranger. 주다 is the infinitive/dictionary form — you cannot end a polite sentence with a bare infinitive.

inlineExercises.prompt: 안내소는 오전 9시___ 오후 6시___ 열어요. Which pair of particles fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: This is a time range (opening hours), so you need the RULER pair: 부터 for the start (9시부터) and 까지 for the end (6시까지). 에 alone marks single moments, not ranges. 에서 is for physical locations where actions happen, not time expressions. Mixing 에서 or 에 with 까지 would be grammatically wrong here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 9시___ 6시까지 일해요. (I work from 9 to 6.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 부터 marks the starting point of a time range. 까지 already marks the endpoint, so the natural pair is 9시부터 6시까지.

inlineExercises.prompt: 천천히 ___ . (말하다 → please do)
inlineExercises.explanation: 말하다 becomes 말해 주세요 in a polite request. 천천히 tells the other person to speak slowly.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Please say it again.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 다시 means again, and 말해 주세요 is the polite request. Together they form the repair phrase you use when you missed what someone said.

bullets: 부터/까지 = the RULER: draw a line between a start (부터) and end (까지) for time ranges and routes — 9시부터 6시까지, 여기부터 역까지
V아/어 주세요 = the FAVOR TICKET: swap any verb in front of 주세요 for any polite request — 말해 주세요, 써 주세요, 찍어 주세요
Repair toolkit: 다시 말해 주세요 (again), 천천히 말해 주세요 (slowly), 잘 모르겠어요 (I'm not sure) — use these freely and Koreans will respect you for it

writingTask.prompt: Write a 3-sentence text to a friend: tell them your office hours, then ask them to speak slowly and say it again.
writingTask.hint: Use N부터 N까지 for the time range, and V아/어 주세요 for the two requests (천천히 말해 주세요, 다시 말해 주세요).
writingTask.model: 저는 아홉 시부터 여섯 시까지 일해요. 천천히 말해 주세요. 다시 말해 주세요.
writingTask.modelEn: I work from nine to six. Please speak slowly. Please say it again.

canDo: Give a time or place range with N부터 N까지 (아홉 시부터 여섯 시까지)
Ask someone to do something for me with V아/어 주세요 (말해 주세요)
Ask for repetition or a slower pace when lost (다시 · 천천히)
Ask where a place is using survival words (화장실 · 출구 · 지하철역)

chapters.title: Connecting Ideas
chapters.goal: Connect two small ideas so your Korean sounds like a real short explanation.
chapters.scenario: Two friends changing plans because one person is busy.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Why can't you come today?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I can't go because I have work.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Then if you have time, shall we meet tomorrow?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Sounds good. I'll call after I finish.

beginnerGuide.title: Longer Korean starts with connectors
beginnerGuide.body: 아서/어서, 고, and 면 let you connect simple sentences. This is how beginner Korean stops sounding like isolated flashcards.

beginnerGuide.title: Reason, sequence, condition
beginnerGuide.body: 아서/어서 gives a reason, 고 connects actions or descriptions, and 면 gives a condition. 바빠서 못 가요, 먹고 가요, 시간이 있으면 전화해 주세요.

beginnerGuide.title: Promise form
beginnerGuide.body: ㄹ/을게요 is for the speaker’s decision or promise: 제가 할게요, 기다릴게요, 전화할게요. Do not use it to predict someone else.

checkpoints: I can connect a reason with 아서/어서.
I can make a simple condition with 면.
I can promise the next action with ㄹ/을게요.

curriculumTrack.label: A1 Foundation
curriculumTrack.description: Hangul, survival sentences, particles, polite present, and daily actions.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

sampleAnswer.ko: 일이 있어서 못 가요. 끝나고 전화할게요.
sampleAnswer.romanization: iri isseoseo mot gayo. kkeunnago jeonhwahalgeyo.
sampleAnswer.en: I can't go because I have work. I'll call after I finish.

checklist: I can connect a reason with 아서/어서.
I can make a simple condition with 면.
I can promise the next action with ㄹ/을게요.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You're texting a Korean colleague to explain why you can't come to dinner. You type '바빠 못 가요' — and it works, but it sounds choppy, like two separate broken sentences. Korean has elegant connectors that glue ideas together in one breath: 바빠서 못 가요. One sentence. One smooth thought.
objectives: Use 아서/어서 to connect a reason to its result in a single sentence
Use 고 to chain two actions or descriptions without repeating the subject
Use 면 to express conditions ('if/when'), and ㄹ/을게요 to make a speaker's promise
hook.whyItMatters: Native Korean sounds like a flowing chain of connected thoughts, not isolated flashcards. Once you have 아서/어서, 고, 면, and ㄹ/을게요, you stop sounding like a beginner who pauses between every idea. These four connectors appear in virtually every real Korean conversation.

grammarNotes.title: -아서/어서 — because / so (reason and result)
grammarNotes.func: Use -아서/어서 to link a reason to its result in one sentence: the first clause is the cause, the second is what follows from it. It's the everyday way to say 'because' or 'so' when two ideas are naturally connected.

formTable.when: Verb/Adj stem with ㅏ or ㅗ as last vowel
Stem with any other last vowel
이다 (to be): after 받침 / after vowel

examples.en: I was hungry, so I ate.
examples.note: 고프다 (ㅡ drops) → 고파서; the reason (hungry) leads to the result (ate).

examples.en: I didn't have time, so I couldn't see the movie.
examples.note: 없다 → 없어서; the past tense sits only on the last verb (봤어요), never on -어서.

examples.en: I met my friend, so I was really glad.
examples.note: 만나다 → 만나서; with -아서/어서, meeting comes first and the good feeling follows from it.

examples.en: Korean is hard, so I study every day.
examples.note: 어렵다 (ㅂ irregular → 워) → 어려워서; an adjective gives the reason for an ongoing action.

keyPoint.label: -아서/어서 vs -(으)니까
keyPoint.body: Both mean 'because,' but you can't end an -아서/어서 sentence with a command or a suggestion. For 'Let's…' or 'Please…,' switch to -(으)니까: 피곤하니까 쉬세요 (You're tired, so rest), not 피곤해서 쉬세요. Also, -아서/어서 never carries past tense itself — say 늦어서 미안해요, not 늦었어서. The full -(으)니까 contrast comes later; for now just remember these two limits.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In 좋아서 the ㅎ is silent and the sounds link smoothly: [조아서]. Same with 많아서 → [마나서].

drill.instruction: Combine each pair into one sentence using -아서/어서.
drill.model: 비가 오다 / 집에 있었어요 → 비가 와서 집에 있었어요. (It rained, so I stayed home.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English puts 'was' in the reason clause ('because I WAS late'), so learners add 었 before -어서. In Korean the tense lives only on the final verb; -아서/어서 always attaches to the plain stem, no matter when it happened.

grammarNotes.title: -고 / -(으)면 / -(으)ㄹ게요 — and, if/when, I'll (a promise)
grammarNotes.func: Three small connectors for joining ideas: -고 lists or sequences two clauses ('and'), -(으)면 sets up a condition ('if/when'), and -(으)ㄹ게요 makes a promise about what the speaker will do.

formTable.when: -(으)면 after stem WITHOUT 받침 (or ㄹ 받침)

examples.en: I eat and (then) go to school.
examples.note: 먹다 → 먹고; here -고 links two actions in order, 'do A and then B.'

examples.en: If/when I have time, I watch a movie.
examples.note: 있다 (받침) → 있으면; -(으)면 states the condition before the result.

examples.en: When I get home, I'll call you.
examples.note: 가다 (no 받침) → 가면; 하다 → 할게요, a promise the speaker makes to the listener.

examples.en: I'll go get the water (for us).
examples.note: 오다 → 올게요; -(으)ㄹ게요 is first-person only — the speaker is committing to do it.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ게요 vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요
keyPoint.body: -(으)ㄹ게요 is a promise made to whoever's listening — used only with 'I/we': 제가 할게요 (I'll do it, count on me). -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is a neutral prediction or plan and can take any subject: 내일 비가 올 거예요 (It'll rain tomorrow). You can't say 비가 올게요 — rain can't make a promise. The deeper future grammar comes later; for now, promise vs. prediction is the key split.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -(으)ㄹ게요 is spelled with ㄱ but pronounced tense: 갈게요 → [갈께요], 먹을게요 → [머글께요].

drill.instruction: Fill each blank with -고, -(으)면, or -(으)ㄹ게요 as the meaning requires.
drill.model: 손을 씻___ 밥을 먹어요. → 손을 씻고 밥을 먹어요. (I wash my hands and eat.)
items: 내일 날씨가 좋___ 공원에 가요. (if it's nice) →
제가 나중에 다시 전화___. (I'll call again) →
책을 읽___ 자요. (read and then sleep) →

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English uses 'will' for both promises and predictions, so learners reach for -(으)ㄹ게요 everywhere. But -(으)ㄹ게요 is a personal promise and needs an 'I/we' subject who can actually commit. For forecasts or anything in the third person, use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 instead.

exampleSentence.en: I've been so busy lately that I want to rest.
exampleSentence.note: 아서/어서 reason → result: the busyness causes the desire to rest

exampleSentence.en: My head hurt, so I went to the hospital.
exampleSentence.note: 아서/어서 domino: the pain is the cause that pushes the result (hospital visit)

exampleSentence.en: I'm tired, so I'll go to sleep early.
exampleSentence.note: 해서 (하다 verb → 해서) + ㄹ게요 (speaker's first-person decision): double connector usage

exampleSentence.en: I'm sorry for being late.
exampleSentence.note: 늦다 (consonant-final 다 → 어서): lateness is the reason for the apology

exampleSentence.en: If it's expensive, I don't buy it.
exampleSentence.note: 면 (condition/switch): buying decision depends on the price condition being met

exampleSentence.en: This restaurant is cheap and delicious.
exampleSentence.note: 고 as coupling hook between two adjectives — just linking, no causal relationship between them

exampleSentence.en: When I arrive, I'll contact you.
exampleSentence.note: 면 (when/if condition) + 할게요 (speaker's promise): the connector and promise form working together

exampleSentence.en: When I arrive, I'll send a text.
exampleSentence.note: 하다 verb + 면 (condition): 도착하 + 면 = 도착하면; paired with ㄹ게요 promise

exampleSentence.en: If you have time, let's eat together.
exampleSentence.note: 있으면 = 있다 + 으면 (consonant-final): the condition is whether time exists

exampleSentence.en: I have a reason, so I can't go.
exampleSentence.note: 있어서 (있다 + 어서): having a reason is the domino that causes not being able to go

exampleSentence.en: I have plans, so I have to leave early.
exampleSentence.note: 있어서 reason: having plans (약속) is the cause for needing to leave early

exampleSentence.en: If it's okay with you, let's go together.
exampleSentence.note: 괜찮다 (consonant-final 다 after ㅎ drop → 괜찮 + 으면): switch track — only proceed together if condition of okayness is met

exampleSentence.en: I'll call later.
exampleSentence.note: 나중에 + ㄹ게요: a complete speaker's promise anchored in time; this exact phrase appears in the chapter dialogue

exampleSentence.en: I'll go first.
exampleSentence.note: 먼저 + 갈게요: classic speaker's promise/decision — the engineer announces departure first

extendedVocabulary.english: then / in that case / well then

exampleSentence.en: Well then, if we meet tomorrow, I'll talk about it.
exampleSentence.note: 그럼 as discourse opener + 면 condition + 게요 promise: three connective tools in one natural sentence

exampleSentence.en: If I can't call, I'll send a text.
exampleSentence.note: 못 하면 (못 + 하다 + 면): double negative condition — the inability to call triggers the text promise

exampleSentence.en: If we meet later, I'll explain it.
exampleSentence.note: 면 condition + 제가 설명할게요 (first-person promise): the engineer announces what they'll do when the switch is set

extendedDialogue.setting: Minjun texts his colleague Yuna to explain why he can't make it to their group dinner and makes promises about what he'll do instead

lines.speaker: 유나
lines.ko: 민준 씨, 오늘 같이 저녁 먹을 수 있어요?
lines.romanization: Minjun ssi, oneul gachi jeonyeok meogeul su isseoyo?
lines.en: Minjun, can you join dinner tonight?
lines.grammarNote: ㄹ 수 있어요 (ability) — 먹다 + 을 수 있어요 because 먹 is consonant-final; sets up the situation Minjun needs to respond to with connectors

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 미안해요. 오늘 너무 바빠서 못 가요.
lines.romanization: Mianhaeyo. Oneul neomu bappaseo mot gayo.
lines.en: I'm sorry. I'm too busy today, so I can't go.
lines.grammarNote: 아서/어서 domino push: 바쁘다 → 바빠서 (ㅡ drops before 어) causes the result 못 가요. The busyness is the falling domino.

lines.speaker: 유나
lines.en: Why? Is something going on?
lines.grammarNote: 있어요 = static existence without a connector; Yuna is asking for the domino (reason)

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 회사 일이 많아서 늦게까지 일해야 해요.
lines.romanization: Hoesa iri manaseo neutgekkaji ilhaeya haeyo.
lines.en: There's a lot of work, so I have to work until late.
lines.grammarNote: 많아서 (많다 → 많 + 아서, ㅏ vowel → 아서): too much work is domino 1, must-work-late is the result. Two clauses linked by one push.

lines.speaker: 유나
lines.en: Understood. Then let's eat together next time.
lines.grammarNote: 그럼 is a soft conditional ('in that case then'); suggests an alternative without a hard connector

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 고마워요! 다음 주에 시간 괜찮으면 제가 살게요.
lines.romanization: Gomawoyo! Daeum jue sigan gwaenchanheumyeon jega salgeyo.
lines.en: Thank you! If next week works, I'll treat you.
lines.grammarNote: 괜찮으면 (괜찮다 + 으면): switch track condition. 살게요 = speaker's first-person promise/decision — the speaker commits to treating.

lines.speaker: 유나
lines.ko: 와, 정말요? 그럼 제가 식당 찾아볼게요.
lines.romanization: Wa, jeongmalyo? Geureom jega sikdang chajabolgeyo.
lines.en: Wow, really? Then I'll look for a restaurant.
lines.grammarNote: 찾아볼게요 = 찾아보다 + ㄹ게요: Yuna makes her own first-person promise in response.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 일 끝나면 바로 연락할게요. 오늘 저녁 맛있게 드세요!
lines.romanization: Il kkeunnamyeon baro yeollakhalgeyo. Oneul jeonyeok masitge deuseyo!
lines.en: When I finish work, I'll contact you right away. Enjoy dinner tonight!
lines.grammarNote: 끝나면 (끝나다 + 면, vowel-final): condition 'when work ends'. 연락할게요: speaker's promise (하다 verb → 할게요). Two connectors in one message.

readingText.title: 지연 씨의 문자 대화 (Jiyeon's Text Exchange)
readingText.body:
지연: 수호 씨, 오늘 약속 괜찮아요? 저 요즘 좀 바빠서요.
수호: 아, 그래요? 많이 바빠요?
지연: 네, 이번 주에 시험이 있어서 공부해야 해요.
수호: 알겠어요. 그럼 시험 끝나면 만나요.
지연: 좋아요! 시험이 목요일이에요. 금요일에 시간 있어요?
수호: 금요일은 괜찮아요. 제가 예약할게요.
지연: 감사합니다! 시험 잘 보고 연락할게요.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Jiyeon: Suho, is our plan for today still okay? I've been a bit busy lately.
Suho: Oh, is that so? Are you very busy?
Jiyeon: Yes, I have an exam this week so I have to study.
Suho: I see. Then let's meet when the exam is over.
Jiyeon: Sounds good! The exam is Thursday. Do you have time Friday?
Suho: Friday is fine. I'll make the reservation.
Jiyeon: Thank you! I'll do well on the exam and then contact you.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why can't Jiyeon meet today?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 바빠서 — she's busy, and specifically 시험이 있어서 (because she has an exam this week so she has to study)

comprehensionQuestions.question: What does Suho promise to do?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 예약할게요 — he promises to make the reservation (a first-person speaker's decision using ㄹ/을게요)

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every connector (아서/어서, 고, 면, 게요) in the text. For each one, explain why that specific connector was chosen over the others.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 바빠서요 — 아서/어서 because being busy is the stated REASON (domino) for the uncertainty about the plan. 있어서 — 아서/어서 because having an exam CAUSES the need to study. 공부해야 해요 — no connector; standalone result clause. 끝나면 — 면 because this is a CONDITION ('when/if the exam ends') not a reason. 예약할게요 — ㄹ/을게요 because Suho is making a first-person promise/decision. 연락할게요 — ㄹ/을게요 because Jiyeon is making her own first-person promise. 잘 보고 — 고 as a simple coupling hook: do well on the exam AND THEN contact (sequence, no causal push needed).

culturalNote.title: 바빠서 못 가요 — The Korean art of the soft no
culturalNote.body: Koreans rarely say a blunt '안 가요' (I'm not going) without offering a reason. The 아서/어서 connector does vital social work: it softens a refusal by giving a cause. 바빠서 못 가요 (I'm busy, so I can't go) sounds warmer and less abrupt than just 못 가요. Similarly, making a 게요 promise — 다음에 살게요 (I'll treat you next time) — is a culturally expected gesture when you decline something. It signals that the relationship matters even if you can't make it this time. Native Korean speakers are highly attuned to whether you're giving reasons and making promises, or just flatly refusing. Learning 아서/어서 and ㄹ/을게요 together gives you the social toolkit to say no in a way that Koreans appreciate.

inlineExercises.prompt: 배가 고파___ 밥을 먹었어요. (I was hungry, so I ate.)
inlineExercises.explanation: This is a cause-result relationship: hunger caused the eating. 아서/어서 (고파서) is the domino push connector. 고 would just link the two states without showing cause ('hungry and ate' — but that doesn't explain WHY). 면 is for hypothetical conditions, not real past causes.

inlineExercises.prompt: 씻___ 자요. (I wash up and then sleep.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 씻다 ends in a consonant (ㅅ). 고 is the neutral coupling hook: wash → sleep is a simple sequence, not a causal relationship. 아서 would imply washing causes sleeping (not the intended meaning). 으면 would make it conditional ('if I wash, I sleep'), which is too hypothetical for a daily routine.

inlineExercises.prompt: 시간이 있___ 전화해 주세요. (If you have time, please call.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 있다 (consonant-final) + 으면 = 있으면. This is a condition (switch track): the call should only happen IF time exists. 어서 would state having time as a reason for calling, which works grammatically but changes the nuance to 'because you have time, please call' — less natural. 고 would link having-time and calling as sequential actions, which doesn't make logical sense here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '못 가요 바빠서.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 아서/어서 MUST come first in Korean. The reason clause with 아서/어서 always precedes the result clause — the domino must be placed before it can push. This is the opposite of English where 'because' can come at the end. Putting 바빠서 at the end is the most common error English speakers make.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'It's expensive, so I won't buy it. I'll buy a cheaper one.'
inlineExercises.correct: 비싸서 안 살게요. 더 싼 거 살게요.
inlineExercises.hint: 비싸다 → reason connector → then use the speaker's promise form for both decisions
inlineExercises.explanation: 비싸서 gives the reason before the result, 'because it's expensive.' 더 싼 거 means 'a cheaper one,' which is more natural than repeating the noun.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend says she'll treat you. You want to respond 'Then I'll choose the restaurant!' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 고르다 (to choose) → stem 고르 → ㄹ-final stem takes ㄹ게요 (not 을게요): 고를게요. This is correct ㄹ/을게요 usage — the speaker is making a first-person decision. 고릴게요 (option 2) is wrong spelling. 고를 거예요 (option 3) is grammatically fine but sounds like a neutral future plan rather than an in-the-moment promise/decision in response to your friend's offer.

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I'm tired, so I'm going to rest.' Which connector is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: Being tired is the CAUSE of the speaker's decision to rest, so 아서/어서 (해서 for 하다 verbs) is correct. 피곤하면 쉴게요 means 'if I'm tired, I'll rest,' which changes the real reason into a condition. 피곤하고 쉴게요 just links 'tired and rest' without showing that tiredness is WHY you're resting.

inlineExercises.prompt: 이유___ 있어요? (Is there a reason?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 있어요 takes 이/가 for the thing that exists. 이유를 would make 이유 an object, which does not fit 있다/있어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: 나중에 ___ . (연락하다 → promise)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ게요 is used when the speaker promises or decides what they will do. 연락하다 becomes 연락할게요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I'm busy, so I can't go.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -아서/어서 connects the reason to the result in one smooth sentence. 바빠서 gives the reason before 못 가요.

bullets: 아서/어서 = DOMINO PUSH: reason clause comes FIRST, result follows. Cannot be used before commands. (바빠서 못 가요)
고 = COUPLING HOOK: neutral link between actions or descriptions, no cause needed (먹고 가요 / 싸고 맛있어요)
면 = SWITCH TRACK: hypothetical condition before the result (시간이 있으면 전화해요) | ㄹ/을게요 = ENGINEER'S ANNOUNCEMENT: first-person speaker's promise only (전화할게요)

writingTask.prompt: Write a 3-sentence message canceling plans: give the reason you can't come, then promise to contact your friend later.
writingTask.hint: Use -아서/어서 for the reason (아파서), and -(으)ㄹ게요 for the promise (연락할게요).
writingTask.model: 오늘 너무 아파서 약속에 못 가요. 정말 미안해요. 내일 연락할게요.
writingTask.modelEn: I'm too sick today, so I can't make our plans. I'm really sorry. I'll contact you tomorrow.

canDo: Link a reason to a result with -아서/어서 (아파서 못 가요)
List or sequence two ideas with -고 (바쁘고 피곤해요)
Set up a condition with -(으)면 (시간이 있으면)
Make a promise about what I'll do with -(으)ㄹ게요 (연락할게요)

chapters.title: Opinions, Reasons & Guessing
chapters.goal: Hedge a guess or regret so it sounds socially natural.
chapters.scenario: You are not fully sure, or you wish you had done something differently.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was this movie?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Hmm, in my opinion it was a bit boring.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Really? I found it fun, you know.

chapters.realLifeTask: Make one soft guess and one small regret.
checkpoints: I can use 것 같아요 and -나 봐요 with different levels of evidence.
I can use -ㄹ걸요 for a careful prediction.
I can use -ㄹ걸 그랬어요 for regret.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Hedge a guess or regret so it sounds socially natural.
exitTask.prompt: Make one soft guess and one small regret.

sampleAnswer.ko: 오늘 사람이 많을 것 같아요. 예약할걸 그랬어요.
sampleAnswer.en: I think there will be many people today. I should have made a reservation.

checklist: I can use 것 같아요 and -나 봐요 with different levels of evidence.
I can use -ㄹ걸요 for a careful prediction.
I can use -ㄹ걸 그랬어요 for regret.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You just finished watching a Korean film with a friend. She asks '이 영화 어땠어요?' You want to say it was a bit slow — but you don't want to sound too blunt. You try '좀 느려요' and it sounds like you're stating a fact. Your friend raises an eyebrow. In Korean, the difference between 'it IS slow' and 'it SEEMS slow' is one short grammar ending — and natives use the softer version almost every time.
objectives: Use -는 것 같다 to express soft opinions and guesses without sounding arrogant
Use -잖아(요) to remind someone of something you both already know
Use -거든(요) to introduce new background information as a reason or explanation
hook.whyItMatters: At B1 level, the gap between textbook Korean and real conversation is mostly about hedging. Koreans rarely state opinions as bare facts — they soften them with -것 같다, link them to shared knowledge with -잖아, or introduce reasons with -거든. Learn these three endings and you'll immediately sound less like a robot and more like someone who understands Korean social nuance.

grammarNotes.title: -는 것 같다 — soft opinions and impressions
grammarNotes.func: Use -는 것 같다 to say 'it seems / I think / probably' instead of stating something as a flat fact. It softens your opinion so you sound less blunt and more polite, even when you're fairly sure.

formTable.ex: 오다 → 오는 것 같다 (seems to be coming); 먹다 → 먹는 것 같다
비싸다 → 비싼 것 같다 (seems expensive); 크다 → 큰 것 같다
작다 → 작은 것 같다 (seems small); 좋다 → 좋은 것 같다
가다 → 간 것 같다 (seems to have gone); 먹다 → 먹은 것 같다
오다 → 올 것 같다 (will probably come); 없다 → 없을 것 같다
학생 → 학생인 것 같다 (seems to be a student)

examples.ko: 지금 밖에 비가 오는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: jigeum bakke biga oneun geot gatayo.
examples.en: It seems to be raining outside right now.
examples.note: Action verb, present: 오는 것 같다, because the rain is happening now.

examples.ko: 이 책은 좀 어려운 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i chaegeun jom eoryeoun geot gatayo.
examples.en: This book seems a bit hard.
examples.note: Adjective 어렵다 (받침, ㅂ-irregular) → 어려운 것 같다; softer than just 어려워요.

examples.ko: 친구가 벌써 집에 간 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: chinguga beolsseo jibe gan geot gatayo.
examples.en: It seems my friend already went home.
examples.note: Past guess: 가다 → 간 것 같다 for something that already happened.

examples.en: I probably won't have time tomorrow.
examples.note: Future/guess: 없다 → 없을 것 같다; a gentle, indirect way to say no.

keyPoint.label: present 는 것 같다 vs future 을 것 같다
keyPoint.body: Use -는 것 같다 for something you can sense right now (비가 오는 것 같아요 — I can hear/see it). Use -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 for a guess about the future or when you have no direct evidence yet (비가 올 것 같아요 — the sky looks like it). For the past, use -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 (간 것 같아요). Don't worry about every irregular form yet — just get the present/past/future split right.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 것 같다 sounds like [걷 깓따]: 것 ends in a [t], which tenses the next ㄱ so 같 comes out as [깓]. In casual speech it often blurs to [거 같아요].

drill.instruction: Soften each blunt statement into a -는 것 같다 impression. Watch the tense.
drill.model: 이 영화 재미있어요. → 이 영화 재미있는 것 같아요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 나는 이 책이 어려운 것 같다고 생각해요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers tack a separate '나는 ~ 생각해요' (I think) onto -는 것 같다, but -는 것 같다 already means 'I think / it seems,' so you'd be saying it twice. Also, 것 같다 changes with tense (present 어려운, past 어려웠던, future 어려울) — English 'seems' stays the same, Korean doesn't.

grammarNotes.title: -잖아(요) vs -거든(요) — shared info vs new info
grammarNotes.func: Both end a sentence to give a reason or background, but they point in opposite directions. -잖아(요) reminds the listener of something you BOTH already know ('you know...', 'remember?'). -거든(요) gives information that's NEW to the listener, often the reason behind what you just said.

formTable.ex: 있다 → 있잖아요; 바쁘다 → 바쁘잖아요 (you know I'm busy)
가다 → 갔잖아요 (we did go, remember); 먹다 → 먹었잖아요
바쁘다 → 바쁘거든요 (the thing is, I'm busy); 좋다 → 좋거든요
가다 → 갔거든요 (the thing is, I went); 먹다 → 먹었거든요

examples.en: Let's hurry. We don't have time, you know.
examples.note: -잖아요: the listener already knows time is short; you're reminding them.

examples.ko: 어제 그 영화 같이 봤잖아요. 진짜 재미있었어요.
examples.romanization: eoje geu yeonghwa gachi bwatjanayo. jinjja jaemiisseosseoyo.
examples.en: We watched that movie together yesterday, remember? It was really fun.
examples.note: -잖아요 over a shared memory ('remember?').

examples.ko: A: 왜 안 와요? B: 지금 일이 많거든요.
examples.romanization: A: wae an wayo? B: jigeum iri mankeodeunyo.
examples.en: A: Why aren't you coming? B: The thing is, I've got a lot of work right now.
examples.note: -거든요: B's workload is NEW info that answers A's question.

examples.ko: 요즘 한국어를 공부해요. 다음 달에 한국에 가거든요.
examples.romanization: yojeum hangugeoreul gongbuhaeyo. daeum dare hanguge gageodeunyo.
examples.en: I'm studying Korean these days. It's because I'm going to Korea next month.
examples.note: -거든요 gives the new reason behind the first sentence.

keyPoint.label: -잖아요 (you know) vs -거든요 (the thing is)
keyPoint.body: Ask yourself: does the listener already know this? If YES, use -잖아요 ('you know...', 'remember?'). If NO and you're telling them for the first time, use -거든요 ('the thing is...', 'because...'). Using -잖아요 for brand-new info can sound like you're scolding them for not already knowing.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -잖아요 is pronounced [자나요]: 잖 has a silent ㅎ in its 받침, so it just links smoothly into 아요. -거든요 is simply [거든뇨], with the final 요 tucked on — no special change.

drill.instruction: Choose -잖아요 (shared knowledge) or -거든요 (new info) and finish the sentence.
drill.model: (reminding a friend you both know it's closed today) 오늘 문 닫았잖아요.
items: (reminding: we both know she's busy) 민수 씨한테 부탁하지 마세요. 그 사람 요즘 ____ .
(new reason why you can't eat it) 저는 그거 안 먹어요. 제가 채식주의자____ .
(reminding: we already paid) 또 돈 내요? 우리 아까 ____ .

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저 지금 못 가요. 일이 많잖아요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 저 지금 못 가요. 일이 많거든요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English uses one phrase, 'because / you see,' for both situations, so learners reach for -잖아요 every time. But if the listener doesn't already know your reason, -잖아요 wrongly implies 'as you obviously know,' which sounds blaming. For information you're sharing for the first time, you need -거든요.

exampleSentence.ko: 제 생각에는 이 방법이 더 좋을 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: In my opinion, I think this method is better.
exampleSentence.note: 제 생각에는 = 'in my view' — a standard phrase for introducing soft opinions in conversation

exampleSentence.en: Please share your opinion.
exampleSentence.note: More formal than 생각 — used in meetings, discussions, and written Korean

exampleSentence.en: There's a reason, you see. Let me explain.
exampleSentence.note: -거든요 introduces the fact of having a reason as new information, then promises the full explanation

exampleSentence.ko: 그 강의 진짜 지루한 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: That lecture seems really boring.
exampleSentence.note: Adjective → -(으)ㄴ 것 같다: 지루한 것 같다. Bare 지루해요 would sound like a harsh verdict

exampleSentence.en: I found it fun, actually. I rather liked it.
exampleSentence.note: -거든요: introducing a contrasting opinion the other person didn't know you held — new information to explain your reaction

exampleSentence.ko: 이 소설은 전개가 느린 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: I think this novel's pacing is slow.
exampleSentence.note: 느리다 is an adjective → 느린 것 같다. 전개 is commonly used in film and book reviews

exampleSentence.en: I think the ending was a bit disappointing.
exampleSentence.note: 아쉽다 (to feel a lack, to be slightly disappointing) → 아쉬운 것 같다. Softening a criticism with -것 같다 is natural here

exampleSentence.ko: 그 배우 연기 정말 잘하거든요. 꼭 봐 보세요.
exampleSentence.en: That actor is genuinely great at acting, you see. Definitely watch it.
exampleSentence.note: -거든요 here shares a personal assessment as new information, then follows up with a recommendation

exampleSentence.en: The acting seems natural.
exampleSentence.note: 자연스럽다 (to be natural) → irregular: 자연스러운 것 같다. The ㅂ irregular applies here

extendedVocabulary.english: to feel a slight lack, to be a (gentle) disappointment

exampleSentence.en: I think the end was a bit unsatisfying.
exampleSentence.note: ㅂ irregular adjective: 아쉽다 → 아쉬운 것 같다. This exact phrase is very common in Korean reviews and casual talk

exampleSentence.en: The protagonist seems a bit too perfect.
exampleSentence.note: 완벽하다 (to be perfect) → 완벽한 것 같다. Common critique in drama reviews

exampleSentence.ko: 그 인물한테 공감하기 어려운 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: I think it's hard to relate to that character.
exampleSentence.note: 공감하기 어렵다 = 'it's hard to empathize' — the -기 turns 공감하다 into a noun, then 어렵다 (hard) applies → 어려운 것 같다

exampleSentence.ko: 개인적으로는 이 영화가 좀 과대평가된 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: Personally, I think this movie is a bit overrated.
exampleSentence.note: 개인적으로 + -것 같다 is a double-hedging strategy very common in Korean — softens with both 'personally' and 'seems'

exampleSentence.en: To be honest, I was a bit disappointed, you see.
exampleSentence.note: -거든요 after an honest admission: the speaker is sharing the real reason/feeling the listener may not have guessed

exampleSentence.en: It seems everyone evaluates it differently.
exampleSentence.note: Verb → -는 것 같다: 평가하는 것 같다. Using this form for a general observation about people in general is very natural

extendedVocabulary.english: to expect, to look forward to

exampleSentence.en: I had high expectations, so I was a bit let down, you see.
exampleSentence.note: -거든요 again here: explaining personal background (had expectations) that the listener didn't know — this is why the disappointment makes sense

exampleSentence.ko: 이 드라마 추천할 만한 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: I think this drama is worth recommending.
exampleSentence.note: 추천할 만하다 = 'worth recommending' → 추천할 만한 것 같다. The -(으)ㄹ 만한 것 같다 construction softens a recommendation

extendedDialogue.setting: Minjun and Yujin are having coffee after watching a film at the cinema. They're comparing their reactions.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 유진 씨, 영화 어땠어요? 저는 좀 아쉬웠어요. 기대가 컸거든요.
lines.romanization: Yujin ssi, yeonghwa eottaesseoyo? Jeoneun jom aswiwosseoyo. Gidaega keotgeodeunyo.
lines.en: Yujin, how was the movie? I was a bit disappointed. My expectations were high, you see.
lines.grammarNote: -거든요: Minjun gives the background reason for his disappointment. 기대가 컸거든요 explains why 아쉬웠어요 makes sense.

lines.speaker: 유진
lines.ko: 그래요? 저는 꽤 재미있었는데요. 전개가 좀 느린 것 같긴 했지만.
lines.romanization: Geuraeyo? Jeoneun kkwae jaemiisseonneundeyo. Jeongaega jom neurin geot gatgin haetjiman.
lines.en: Really? I found it quite fun. Though I did think the pacing was a bit slow.
lines.grammarNote: -는 것 같긴 했지만: conceding a partial criticism (slow pacing) using -것 같다 in the past; 긴 했지만 = 'though it did seem that way'

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 맞아요! 전개가 너무 느리잖아요. 2시간 동안 뭔가 일어나는 게 별로 없었어요.
lines.romanization: Majayo! Jeongaega neomu neurijanayo. Du-sigan dongan mwonga ireonaneun ge byeollo eopseosseoyo.
lines.en: Right! The pacing really is too slow, you know. Not much happens in those two hours.
lines.grammarNote: -잖아요: both viewers just experienced the film, so the slow pacing is shared observable knowledge — Minjun is nudging Yujin to agree

lines.speaker: 유진
lines.ko: 음, 그래도 배우들 연기가 굉장히 좋은 것 같았어요.
lines.romanization: Eum, geuraedo baeudeul yeongiga goengjanghi joeun geot gatassoyo.
lines.en: Hmm, but I thought the acting was really good though.
lines.grammarNote: -것 같았어요: past tense of -것 같다, expressing a personal impression during and after watching

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 그건 저도 동의해요. 특히 주인공 배우가 정말 잘하거든요.
lines.romanization: Geugeon jeodo donguihaeyo. Teuki juingong baeuga jeongmal jalhageodeunyo.
lines.en: I agree on that. Especially the lead actor — they're genuinely great, you see.
lines.grammarNote: -거든요: Minjun adds this as a reason or supporting fact the listener may not have fully appreciated yet

lines.speaker: 유진
lines.ko: 맞아요, 연기가 자연스러운 것 같아요. 억지스럽지 않잖아요.
lines.romanization: Majayo, yeongiga jayeonseureoun geot gatayo. Eokjiseureopji anjanayo.
lines.en: Exactly, the acting seems natural. It's not forced, you know.
lines.grammarNote: Two different endings: 자연스러운 것 같아요 (soft impression) + 억지스럽지 않잖아요 (shared observable fact — both can see it's not forced)

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 그래서 결말이 좀 더 강했으면 좋았을 것 같아요. 솔직히 좀 아쉬웠거든요.
lines.romanization: Geuraeseo gyeolmari jom deo ganghaesseumyeon joasseul geot gatayo. Soljiki jom aswieotgeodeunyo.
lines.en: That's why I think it would've been better if the ending were stronger. Honestly, I was a bit disappointed, you see.
lines.grammarNote: -것 같아요 on a conditional (강했으면 좋았을 것 같다) softens what would otherwise sound like demanding criticism; -거든요 introduces the honest emotional reaction

lines.speaker: 유진
lines.ko: 개인적으로는 이런 열린 결말을 좋아하거든요. 생각할 거리가 많잖아요.
lines.romanization: Gaeinjeogeuro-neun ireon yeollin gyeolmareul joahageodeunyo. Saenggakhal georiga manchanayo.
lines.en: Personally, I like open endings like this, you see. There's a lot to think about, you know.
lines.grammarNote: 개인적으로는 + -거든요 = double personal-framing; then -잖아요 to invite agreement on the 'lots to think about' observation

readingText.title: 영화 보고 나서 (After the Movie)
readingText.body:
유진: 민준 씨, 아까 그 영화 어땠어요? 저는 꽤 좋았거든요.
민준: 저는 좀 아쉬웠어요. 기대가 너무 컸던 것 같아요.
유진: 아, 그래요? 전 결말이 인상적인 것 같았는데.
민준: 저는 결말이 좀 급한 것 같았어요. 그리고 스토리가 단순한 것 같기도 하고요.
유진: 음... 그래도 배우들 연기만큼은 정말 좋았잖아요.
민준: 그건 맞아요. 특히 주인공 배우가 굉장한 것 같아요. 이제 팬이 됐거든요!
유진: 저도요! 다음에 그 배우 나오는 드라마 같이 봐요.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Yujin: Minjun, how was that movie earlier? I quite liked it, you see.
Minjun: I was a bit disappointed. I think my expectations were too high.
Yujin: Oh, really? I thought the ending was impressive.
Minjun: I thought the ending felt a bit rushed. And I thought the story was kind of simple too.
Yujin: Hmm... But the acting was really good, you know.
Minjun: That's true. Especially the lead actor seems amazing. I've become a fan, you see!
Yujin: Me too! Next time let's watch the drama that actor's in together.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How does Minjun feel about the movie overall? What specific issues does he mention?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: Minjun was disappointed (아쉬웠어요). He thought his expectations were too high (기대가 너무 컸던 것 같아요), the ending felt rushed (결말이 좀 급한 것 같았어요), and the story was a bit simple (스토리가 단순한 것 같기도 하고요).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What do both Minjun and Yujin agree on?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: They both agree the acting was great, especially the lead actor (배우들 연기만큼은 정말 좋았잖아요 / 주인공 배우가 굉장한 것 같아요). They both became fans of the actor (저도요!).

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every -것 같다, -잖아요, and -거든요 in the text. For each one, explain why that ending was chosen and not one of the other two.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 1) 기대가 너무 컸던 것 같아요 — Minjun uses -것 같다 (past: -던 것 같다) to frame his high expectations as a personal impression/self-reflection, softening self-criticism. 2) 결말이 인상적인 것 같았는데 — Yujin hedges her positive reaction as a personal impression (past -것 같다), not a fact. 3) 결말이 좀 급한 것 같았어요 and 스토리가 단순한 것 같기도 하고요 — Minjun consistently uses -것 같다 to soften criticisms into impressions. 4) 배우들 연기만큼은 정말 좋았잖아요 — -잖아요 fits here because both speakers JUST WATCHED the film together — the good acting is shared, observable knowledge Yujin is reminding Minjun of. 5) 좋았거든요 (Yujin's opening) — -거든요 because Yujin is volunteering her positive reaction as NEW personal information Minjun didn't know yet. 6) 이제 팬이 됐거든요 — -거든요 because Minjun is sharing a new personal fact (becoming a fan) that Yujin didn't know.

culturalNote.title: 왜 한국인은 항상 '것 같아요'를 쓸까요? — Why Koreans always say 'it seems'
culturalNote.body: If you watch any Korean variety show or drama, you'll notice that Koreans rarely state opinions as flat facts — they're constantly hedging with -것 같아요, -것 같은데요, -것 같긴 해요. This isn't uncertainty or lack of confidence; it's a deep cultural preference for avoiding confrontational directness. Saying '이 영화 별로예요' (This movie isn't great) can come across as dismissive and final — it invites no discussion. But '이 영화가 별로인 것 같아요' opens space for the other person to disagree gracefully. This extends to professional settings too: in meetings, Koreans often frame even strong opinions as -것 같습니다 to maintain group harmony (눈치 culture). Mastering -것 같다 isn't just grammar — it's learning to speak with appropriate Korean social grace.

inlineExercises.prompt: 이 음식이 좀 짠___ 것 같아요. (I think this food is a bit salty.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 짜다 is an adjective with a vowel-ending stem (짜-), so the modifier is ㄴ: 짠 것 같아요. 는 is for present verb modifiers, and 은 is used after consonant-ending adjective stems.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저 오늘 못 가요. 약속이 있___. (I can't go today. I have plans.)
inlineExercises.explanation: -거든요 is correct because the speaker is giving the listener NEW information (the plans) as a reason. -잖아요 would only work if the listener already knew about the plans. '-는 것 같아요' expresses uncertainty — but the speaker KNOWS they have plans, so that would be odd.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '그 배우 유명하는 것 같아요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 유명하다 is an adjective (not a verb), so it takes the adjective modifier -ㄴ/-은, not the verb modifier -는. 유명하다 has a vowel-ending stem (유명하-), so the modifier is -ㄴ → 유명한 것 같아요. This is the most common -것 같다 mistake among English learners.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend says '나 왜 화났는지 알아?' You reply: '어제 네가 약속을 안 지켰___ .' Which ending fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: -잖아 is correct here. The person you're talking TO is the one who broke the promise — they KNOW they did it. You're reminding them of their own action as the reason for your anger. -거든 would mean 'just so you know you broke the promise' — but they clearly already know. -는 것 같아 would express uncertainty about whether they broke it, which is too weak for this situation.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I think it's going to rain tomorrow.'
inlineExercises.hint: Decide whether the rain is happening now, already happened, or expected later. Then choose the modifier before 것 같아요.
inlineExercises.explanation: 비가 올 것 같아요 is a softened future guess, not a firm plan. The future modifier 올 fits because the rain is expected tomorrow.

inlineExercises.prompt: At work, a colleague offers to switch to English because you look unsure. You want to say you can keep using Korean because you're actually quite good at it. Which is correct?
options: 사실 저 한국어 꽤 잘하는 것 같아요.
inlineExercises.explanation: -거든요 is correct because you're giving NEW background information as a reason to continue in Korean. -잖아요 would imply they already knew you were good at Korean. -는 것 같아요 would sound strangely uncertain — 'I seem to be good at Korean?' That doesn't convey confidence; it sounds like you're guessing about your own skill.

inlineExercises.prompt: 그 식당 오늘 문 닫___ 것 같아요. 불이 꺼져 있어요. (That restaurant seems to be closed today. The lights are off.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 닫다 (to close/be closed) is a verb, but here we're inferring a PRESENT STATE from evidence — the speaker means 'it seems closed right now.' The present state is expressed with the adjective-like -(으)ㄴ modifier: 닫은 것 같다 (seems closed). If you used 닫는 것 같다 it would mean 'seems to be in the process of closing,' and 닫을 것 같다 would mean 'seems like it will close (in the future).' The correct reading is current state: 닫은 것 같다.

inlineExercises.prompt: 약속___ 있거든요. (I have plans, you see.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 있거든요 still uses 이/가 for the thing that exists or is possessed. 을 would wrongly treat 약속 as an object of an action.

inlineExercises.prompt: 그 영화가 좀 ___ . (지루하다 → soft opinion)
inlineExercises.explanation: Adjectives use -(으)ㄴ 것 같아요 for a softened impression. 지루하다 becomes 지루한 것 같아요, not 지루하는 것 같아요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I think this movie is a little boring.'
inlineExercises.correct: 이 영화는 좀 지루한 것 같아요
inlineExercises.explanation: 좀 softens the criticism, and -한 것 같아요 makes it an impression rather than a blunt fact. This is much safer than saying 이 영화는 지루해요 directly.

bullets: -는 것 같다 = FROSTED GLASS: softens opinions/guesses into impressions; verbs use -는, adjectives use -(으)ㄴ, past uses -(으)ㄴ, future uses -(으)ㄹ
-잖아(요) = REPLAY BUTTON: reminds listener of something they already know or should know — shared information
-거든(요) = UPLOAD BUTTON: introduces new background information or a reason the listener didn't have — use this when telling someone something for the first time

writingTask.prompt: Write a short comment giving your opinion about a movie you just watched, softening it and adding a reason.
writingTask.hint: Use -는 것 같다 to soften your opinion, and use -거든요 (new info) or -잖아요 (shared info) to give a reason.
writingTask.model: 이 영화는 좀 지루한 것 같아요. 전개가 너무 느리거든요. 그래도 배우 연기는 좋잖아요.
writingTask.modelEn: I think this movie is a bit boring. The pacing is too slow (you see). But the acting is good, you know.

canDo: Soften an opinion so it sounds less blunt (-는 것 같다)
Give a reason as new information the listener didn't know (-거든요)
Remind the listener of something you both already know (-잖아요)
Talk about a movie or story using 전개 · 결말 · 연기 · 주인공

chapters.title: Society, Culture & Reported Speech
chapters.goal: Explain when an action changed, got interrupted, or ended in a new state.
chapters.scenario: You started one plan, but something happened while you were doing it.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was it?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: It was fun. But the weather was a bit cold.

chapters.realLifeTask: Describe one interrupted or changed plan using -다가 or -아/어 있다.
checkpoints: I can use -다가 when one action is interrupted or changes.
I can use -아/어 있다 for a state that remains after an action.
I can keep the before-and-after order clear.

curriculumTrack.label: A2 Builder
curriculumTrack.description: Tense, questions, numbers, modifiers, connectors, particles, counters, and repair chapters.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Explain when an action changed, got interrupted, or ended in a new state.
exitTask.prompt: Describe one interrupted or changed plan using -다가 or -아/어 있다.

sampleAnswer.ko: 공부하다가 친구 전화를 받았어요. 노트북은 아직 켜져 있어요.
sampleAnswer.en: I was studying and then got a call from a friend. The laptop is still on.

checklist: I can use -다가 when one action is interrupted or changes.
I can use -아/어 있다 for a state that remains after an action.
I can keep the before-and-after order clear.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: You're watching a Korean news program and the anchor says '전문가들은 사회가 빠르게 변한다고 했습니다.' You know most of those words — but what is 변한다고 doing? Later your Korean friend texts you '교수님이 내일 시험 있냐고 물어봤어.' Again — what is 있냐고 doing? You're bumping into reported speech, and it's everywhere in real Korean.
objectives: Report what someone said using -(ㄴ/는)다고 하다 (said that)
Report what someone asked using -(느)냐고 하다 (asked whether)
Use special honorific vocabulary — 계시다, 드리다, 잡수시다 — with the right people
hook.whyItMatters: Koreans relay other people's words constantly — in gossip, office messages, family updates, and news. If you can't use 다고 했어요 and 냐고 물어봤어요, you're stuck either quoting people with clumsy direct speech or avoiding the topic entirely. Master these two endings and you'll suddenly understand about a third of casual conversation you couldn't follow before.

grammarNotes.title: -(ㄴ/는)다고 하다 — Reporting What Someone Said
grammarNotes.func: Use this to report what someone said: "He says/said that …". Put the original verb or adjective into its plain (해라체) form and add -고 하다. It works for both "says" and "said" — 했어요 makes it past.

formTable.when: Action verb, stem ends in a vowel
Action verb, stem ends in a consonant (받침)

formTable.ex: 바쁘다 → 바쁘다고 하다 / 좋다 → 좋다고 하다
학생이다 → 학생이라고 하다 / 친구다 → 친구라고 하다
먹었다 → 먹었다고 하다 / 갔다 → 갔다고 하다

examples.en: My friend said she's going to school tomorrow.
examples.note: 가다 is a vowel-stem action verb, so it takes -ㄴ다고.

examples.en: My little brother says he's eating now.
examples.note: 먹다 has 받침, so the action-verb form is -는다고. 밥 먹다 ('eat a meal') is the everyday way to say it.

examples.en: My friend said she's really busy these days.
examples.note: 바쁘다 is an adjective, so it stays -다고 (no ㄴ/는).

examples.en: He said he's a Korean teacher.
examples.note: With a noun + 이다 you use -이라고, not -다고.

keyPoint.label: Adjectives keep -다고; action verbs split into -ㄴ다고 / -는다고
keyPoint.body: This is the one spot learners mix up. Action verbs (먹다, 가다) become 먹는다고/간다고, but adjectives (좋다, 바쁘다) and 있다/없다 just take -다고: 좋다고, 바쁘다고, 재미있다고. So 'It's fun' → 재미있다고 했어요, never 재미있는다고. (Why 있다 acts like an adjective here comes later — for now, just memorize 있다고.)

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In 먹는다고, the ㄱ before ㄴ nasalizes: [멍는다고]. 간다고 is said smoothly with no pause before 고.

drill.instruction: Report each sentence using -(ㄴ/는)다고 했어요 ("He/She said …"). Watch whether the word is an action verb or an adjective.
drill.model: 친구: "나 집에 가." → 친구가 집에 간다고 했어요.
items: 동생: "나 책 읽어." → 동생이 책을 ____ 했어요.
선생님: "이건 한국 영화예요." → 선생님이 이건 한국 영화 ____ 했어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 친구가 바쁘는다고 했어요. / 그 사람이 학생다고 했어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 친구가 바쁘다고 했어요. / 그 사람이 학생이라고 했어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English uses one pattern ('says that…') for everything, so learners over-apply -는다고. But -ㄴ다/-는다 belongs ONLY to action verbs. Adjectives take plain -다고 (바쁘다고), and nouns take -(이)라고 (학생이라고). Match the form to the word type, not to English.

grammarNotes.title: -냐고 하다 — Reporting a Question
grammarNotes.func: Use this to report a question someone asked: "He asked whether/what …". Change the original question's ending to the plain question form -냐 and add -고 하다 — though in real speech people usually say 물어보다 ('ask') instead of 하다.

examples.en: My friend asked if I had time tomorrow.
examples.note: 있다 → 있냐고; 물어봤어요 is the natural everyday verb for 'asked'.

examples.en: My little brother asked whether I'd eaten.
examples.note: Past question: 먹었다 → 먹었냐고.

examples.en: My friend asked whether that movie is fun.
examples.note: The adjective 재미있다 also just takes -냐고 in everyday speech.

examples.en: The teacher asked who the student was.
examples.note: Noun + 이다 → 이냐고; the question word 누가 just stays in place.

keyPoint.label: Statement -다고 vs. question -냐고
keyPoint.body: Both report someone's words, but the ending tells you which: a reported statement ends in -다고 (간다고 했어요 = 'said he's going'), and a reported question ends in -냐고 (가냐고 했어요 = 'asked if he's going'). Yes/no and wh-questions use the same -냐고; the question word (언제, 누가, 뭐) just stays inside the clause.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 있냐고 and 먹었냐고 nasalize across the boundary: [인냐고], [머건냐고] — the ㅆ/ㄱ before ㄴ becomes [ㄴ].

drill.instruction: Report each question using -냐고 물어봤어요 ("… asked if/what …"). Keep any question word in place.
drill.model: 친구: "시간 있어?" → 친구가 시간 있냐고 물어봤어요.
items: 친구: "이 책 재미있어?" → 친구가 이 책 ____ 물어봤어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English reports statements and questions almost the same way ('said that…' / 'asked if…'), so learners reuse -다고 for questions too. But a reported QUESTION must end in -냐고: 가냐고 / 있냐고 / 먹었냐고. If the original had a question mark, use -냐고, not -다고.

exampleSentence.en: I think our society is changing rapidly.
exampleSentence.note: 다고 생각해요 = 'I think that...' — reported-thought structure using the same 다고 pattern

exampleSentence.en: My friend said Korean culture is interesting.
exampleSentence.note: 재미있다 is 있다-type → add -다고 directly (adjective rule), not -(느)ㄴ다고

exampleSentence.ko: 이 마을은 오래된 전통을 그대로 이어 가고 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: This village is carrying on its old traditions just as they are.
exampleSentence.note: 이어 가다 = keep carrying on; present progressive 가고 있어요 emphasizes the ongoing nature

exampleSentence.ko: 선생님이 한국 역사가 아주 깊다고 하셨어요.
exampleSentence.en: The teacher said Korean history is very deep.
exampleSentence.note: 깊다 is an adjective → 깊다고 (plain adjective form + 다고). Teacher gets 하셨어요.

exampleSentence.en: The news said the economy is getting increasingly difficult.
exampleSentence.note: 어려워지다 has vowel stem 어려워지- → ㄴ다고: 어려워진다고

exampleSentence.en: My friend said he has no interest in politics.
exampleSentence.note: 없다 → add -다고 directly (없다고). 없다 is in the same category as 있다 — add -다고, not -는다고.

exampleSentence.en: Experts warned that the environment is gradually getting worse.
exampleSentence.note: 나빠지다 (vowel stem 나빠지-) → ㄴ다고: 나빠진다고. 경고했어요 = warned.

exampleSentence.ko: 부모님이 교육이 가장 중요하다고 항상 말씀하세요.
exampleSentence.en: My parents always say that education is the most important thing.
exampleSentence.note: 중요하다 is an adjective → 중요하다고. 말씀하세요 is the honorific form of 말하다 (말씀하시다), used for parents.

extendedVocabulary.english: to be (honorific for 있다 — a person's presence)

exampleSentence.en: The boss isn't at his desk right now.
exampleSentence.note: 계시다 replaces 있다 when the subject is a person you honor and you are talking about physical presence. 사장님이 있으세요 sounds awkward for the boss's location; 계세요 is the natural respectful form.

extendedVocabulary.english: to give (humble — you giving to someone senior)

exampleSentence.en: I gave my parents a gift.
exampleSentence.note: 드리다 is used when YOU give to someone above you. 주다 is the neutral form. 부모님께 uses 께 (honorific 에게).

extendedVocabulary.english: to eat (very honorific for 먹다/드시다 — for very respected elders)

exampleSentence.en: Grandma, have you finished your meal?
exampleSentence.note: 잡수시다 is higher than 드시다 — reserved for grandparents and very senior people. 진지 is the honorific word for 밥 (meal/rice).

extendedVocabulary.english: to say / to tell (humble — you speaking to someone senior)

exampleSentence.en: I explained my situation to the professor.
exampleSentence.note: 말씀드리다 = humble form of 말하다. 교수님께 uses 께 (honorific 에게). Compare: 친구한테 말했어요 (told a friend, plain).

extendedVocabulary.english: to meet / to see (humble — you meeting someone senior)

exampleSentence.en: Would it be possible to see the professor tomorrow?
exampleSentence.note: 뵙다 is the humble form of 만나다/보다 when you are meeting someone you respect. 뵈다 is the spoken short form: 뵐게요, 뵈었어요 → 봬어요.

extendedVocabulary.english: to develop / to advance / to progress

exampleSentence.en: The researchers said technology is advancing rapidly.
exampleSentence.note: 발전하다 has vowel stem (발전하-) → ㄴ다고: 발전한다고. Classic example of the 다고 pattern with a 하다 verb.

exampleSentence.en: I think traditions still exist.
exampleSentence.note: 생각해요 (I think) also uses the 다고 pattern: 존재한다고 생각해요. 생각하다 is another common reporting verb alongside 하다.

extendedVocabulary.english: to participate / to take part in

exampleSentence.en: The teacher said to be sure to participate in the event.
exampleSentence.note: This is a reported command (not statement) → -(으)라고: 참여하라고 하셨어요. Compare with 다고 (statement) and 냐고 (question).

exampleSentence.en: Even as society changes rapidly, traditions remain.
exampleSentence.note: 변해도 = even though (it) changes (-(아/어)도 concessive). 남다 (to remain) contrasts with 변하다 (to change) in this classic Chapter 36 sentence.

extendedDialogue.setting: Jiyeon missed a Korean society and culture class, so Minho relays what the professor said about the group presentation

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 민호 씨, 오늘 한국 사회 수업 어땠어요? 저는 못 갔어요.
lines.romanization: Minho ssi, oneul hanguk sahoe sueop eottaesseoyo? Jeoneun mot gasseoyo.
lines.en: Minho, how was Korean society class today? I couldn't go.
lines.grammarNote: 한국 사회 수업 keeps the scene tied to this chapter's topic; 못 갔어요 explains why Jiyeon needs reported speech.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 교수님이 다음 주에 한국 전통 발표를 한다고 하셨어요.
lines.romanization: Gyosunimi daeum jue hanguk jeontong balpyoreul handago hasyeosseoyo.
lines.en: The professor said we're doing a presentation on Korean traditions next week.
lines.grammarNote: 하다 → 한다고 for a reported statement. Professor is respected, so the reporting verb becomes 하셨어요.

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: Really? Did anyone ask what the topic is?
lines.grammarNote: 뭐냐고 relays a question. The original question was 주제가 뭐예요?, so the report uses -냐고.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 네, 소연 씨가 물어봤어요. 교수님이 현대 사회에 남아 있는 전통이라고 하셨어요.
lines.romanization: Ne, Soyeon ssiga mureobwasseoyo. Gyosunimi hyeondae sahoe-e nama inneun jeontongirago hasyeosseoyo.
lines.en: Yes, Soyeon asked. The professor said it's traditions that remain in modern society.
lines.grammarNote: 전통이라고 reports a noun phrase. Because 전통 ends in a consonant, it takes 이라고.

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: How many people did the professor say are in each team?
lines.grammarNote: 몇 명이라고 asks for a reported noun answer: 'how many people did they say it is?'

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 네 명이라고 하셨어요. 그리고 조교님이 자료는 역사와 문화 쪽으로 찾으라고 하셨어요.
lines.romanization: Ne myeongirago hasyeosseoyo. Geurigo jogyonimi jaryoneun yeoksawa munhwa jjogeuro chajeurago hasyeosseoyo.
lines.en: The professor said four people. And the teaching assistant said to look for materials on history and culture.
lines.grammarNote: 네 명이라고 reports a noun. 찾으라고 reports a command: 찾다 + 으라고.

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 그럼 교수님께 제가 참여하고 싶다고 말씀드릴게요.
lines.romanization: Geureom gyosunimkke jega chamyeohago sipdago malsseumdeurilgeyo.
lines.en: Then I'll tell the professor that I want to participate.
lines.grammarNote: 참여하고 싶다고 reports Jiyeon's own desire. 말씀드릴게요 is humble because she is speaking to the professor.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 좋아요! 교수님이 지금 연구실에 계세요. 바로 말씀드려요.
lines.romanization: Joayo! Gyosunimi jigeum yeongusire gyeseyo. Baro malsseumdeuryeoyo.
lines.en: Great! The professor is in the office right now. Tell them right away.
lines.grammarNote: 계세요 = honorific 있다 for a respected person's presence. 연구실에 계세요 is the natural professor context.

readingText.title: 단체 카톡 (Group KakaoTalk Chat)
readingText.body:
지훈: 방금 교수님이 내일 발표가 없어진다고 하셨어. 다들 들었어?

수현: 진짜? 나는 못 들었는데. 왜 없어지냐고 물어봤어?

지훈: 응, 소연이가 물어봤는데 교수님이 다음 주로 미룬다고 하셨어.

수현: 다행이다! 그럼 우리 오늘 발표 준비 안 해도 되겠다.

소연: 아, 근데 교수님이 대신 에세이 제출하라고 하셨어. 다음 주 월요일까지.

수현: 어머, 그건 물어봤을 때 왜 말 안 해줬어? ㅋㅋ

지훈: 죄송... 교수님이 한국 사회와 문화를 이해하려면 역사도 봐야 한다고 하셨어.

소연: 맞아, 교수님께서 한국 전통이 현대 사회에서 어떻게 발전하고 존재하는지 생각해 보라고도 하셨어.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Jihoon: The professor just said tomorrow's presentation is cancelled. Did everyone hear?

Suhyeon: Really? I didn't hear. Did anyone ask why it's cancelled?

Jihoon: Yeah, Soyeon asked and the professor said it's being pushed to next week.

Suhyeon: What a relief! So we don't have to prepare the presentation today.

Soyeon: Oh, but the professor said to submit an essay instead. By next Monday.

Suhyeon: Oh no, why didn't you say that when I asked? lol

Jihoon: Sorry... The professor said that to understand Korean society and culture, we need to look at history too.

Soyeon: Right, the professor also said to think about how Korean traditions develop and exist in modern society.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What did the professor say about tomorrow's presentation?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 교수님이 내일 발표가 없어진다고 하셨어 — The professor said tomorrow's presentation is cancelled (pushed to next week).
