comprehensionQuestions.question: What did Soyeon report about the essay?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 교수님이 대신 에세이 제출하라고 하셨어 — The professor said to submit an essay instead by next Monday. Note this uses -(으)라고 (reported command), not -다고 (statement).

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all instances of -다고 하다, -냐고 물어보다, and -(으)라고 하다 in the text. Why does each one use the form it uses?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 다고 하셨어 (×3): 없어진다고 (발표가 없어지다 = action verb, vowel stem → ㄴ다고), 미룬다고 (미루다 = action verb, vowel stem → ㄴ다고), 이해할 수 있다고 (있다 → 있다고, adjective/있다 rule). | 냐고 물어봤어: 없어지냐고 — relaying a question (original had a question mark) → -냐고. | 라고 하셨어 (×2): 제출하라고, 생각해 보라고 — both relay commands (imperatives) → -(으)라고. The ending matches the type of sentence being relayed: period → 다고, question mark → 냐고, command → (으)라고.

culturalNote.title: The Honorific Gap — Why Koreans Switch Vocabulary Completely
culturalNote.body: Most languages add a polite prefix or suffix to show respect. Korean does that too (-(으)시-), but for the most common, everyday verbs, Korean uses entirely different words. When your grandmother is home, she isn't 있어요 — she's 계세요. When you give something to your boss, you don't 줘요 — you 드려요. When grandpa eats, he doesn't 먹어요 — he 잡수세요. This system, called 높임말 (honorific speech), has deep roots in Korea's Confucian social hierarchy. Understanding it matters not just for politeness but for comprehension: if you only know the plain forms, you'll be lost in conversations involving elders, bosses, or customers. The safest rule for beginners: when speaking TO or ABOUT someone you must honor, mentally scan your sentence for 있다, 먹다, and 주다 — those three are the most frequently tripped-over, and swapping them to 계시다, 드시다/잡수시다, and 드리다 will immediately raise your Korean to a more respectful level.

inlineExercises.prompt: 친구가 내일 학교에 ___ 했어요. (My friend said she's going to school tomorrow.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 가다 has a vowel stem (가-). Present action verb with vowel stem → add ㄴ다고: 간다고. '가요고' is the most common mistake — you can never attach 고 to the polite -요 form for reported speech. '가다고' would only work if 가다 were an adjective, but it's an action verb.

inlineExercises.prompt: 엄마가 ___ 물어봤어요. (Mom asked whether I was tired.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 물어봤어요 means 'asked' — the clause before it must be a reported question, so use -냐고. '피곤하다고 물어봤어요' is a contradiction: 다고 reports a statement, but 물어봤어요 reports a question. Native speakers will immediately sense that something is off.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '교수님이 어디에 있으세요?'
inlineExercises.explanation: 있으세요 is acceptable for respected people's possessions or states (질문 있으세요? = Do you have a question?), but for a respected PERSON'S physical presence, 계시다 is required. 있으세요 for a person's location sounds awkward and slightly disrespectful to Korean ears — always use 계세요 when asking or saying where a respected person is.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your colleague relays this: '팀장님이 오늘 회의가 취소됐___ 하셨어요.' What ending goes in the blank?
inlineExercises.explanation: 취소됐다 is a verb in past tense — it's a statement of fact (the meeting is cancelled), not a question or a command. Statements → -다고. Past tense: 취소됐다 → 취소됐다고. '냐고' would mean the team lead asked if it was cancelled — different meaning. '(으)라고' would mean the team lead commanded someone to cancel it — again, different.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'My friend asked if I like Korean culture.'
inlineExercises.hint: 좋아하다 is an action verb (not adjective). The question is reported, so which ending do you need? Which verb means 'asked' in Korean?
inlineExercises.explanation: 좋아하냐고 물어봤어요 reports the question someone asked. The quoted question is yes/no, so -냐고 is the right reported-question shape.

inlineExercises.prompt: 할머니께 생일 선물을 ___. (I gave a birthday present to my grandmother.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 드리다 is the humble form of 주다 used when YOU give something to someone you respect. 줬어요 is perfectly grammatical but sounds flat and somewhat rude toward a grandmother. Koreans expect 드렸어요 in this context — using 줬어요 for a grandparent will strike them as unnatural, even if technically understood.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct Korean?
inlineExercises.explanation: '할아버지가 있으세요' combines the wrong subject marker (가 instead of 께서) with the wrong presence verb (있으세요 instead of 계세요). '할아버지께서 있어요' uses 께서 correctly but forgets to honor grandpa's presence with 계시다. The fully correct form uses 께서 (honorific subject marker) and 계세요 (honorific form of 있다 for a person's presence) together.

inlineExercises.prompt: 할머니___ 선물을 드렸어요. (I gave a present to my grandmother.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 께 is the respectful "to" particle for an elder, matching the humble verb 드렸어요. 에서 marks a place, and 를 would make 할머니 the object instead of the recipient.

inlineExercises.prompt: 친구가 한국 문화를 ___ . (좋아하다 → reported statement)
inlineExercises.explanation: Action verbs use -ㄴ/는다고 when you report what someone said. 좋아하다 becomes 좋아한다고 했어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'My friend said she is going to school tomorrow.'
inlineExercises.explanation: The reported content ends in 간다고 before 했어요. 내일 학교에 가요 becomes 내일 학교에 간다고 했어요 when reported.

bullets: -(ㄴ/는)다고 하다 = TELEGRAM: strip the polite -요, use plain verb form + 다고 to relay statements (verbs: 간다고, 먹는다고; adjectives: 춥다고; nouns: 학생이라고; past: 갔다고)
-(느)냐고 하다 = QUESTION BUBBLE: if the original had a question mark, use -냐고 + 물어봤어요 (가냐고, 바쁘냐고, 있냐고, 명이냐고)
Special honorific words: 있다→계시다 (person present), 주다→드리다 (you giving to someone senior), 먹다→잡수시다 (very senior eating) — memorize these swaps, they come up every day

writingTask.prompt: Write a short note telling a friend what a teacher said and what the teacher asked you.
writingTask.hint: Use -(ㄴ/는)다고 했어요 to report a statement and -냐고 했어요 (or 물어봤어요) to report a question.
writingTask.model: 선생님께서 내일 시험이 있다고 하셨어요. 그리고 저한테 공부를 다 했냐고 물어보셨어요. 저는 아직 안 했다고 말씀드렸어요.
writingTask.modelEn: The teacher said there's a test tomorrow. And she asked me whether I had finished studying. I told her I hadn't done it yet.

canDo: Report what someone said using the plain form plus -(ㄴ/는)다고 하다
Report a question someone asked (-냐고 하다 / 물어보다)
Use humble verbs when I speak to someone senior (말씀드리다 · 드리다)
Discuss a social or cultural topic with words like 사회 · 문화 · 전통 · 교육

chapters.title: Work, Money & Decisions
chapters.goal: Say a real future plan, not just a grammar example.
chapters.scenario: You are making a weekend or evening plan with someone.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What are you going to do this weekend?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I am going to meet a friend and go to a cafe.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What if it rains?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: If it rains, I am going to study at home.

chapters.realLifeTask: Answer 주말에 뭐 할 거예요? and add what you will do if the plan changes.
checkpoints: I can use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 for a plan or prediction.
I can use -면 for a simple condition.
I can tell apart 할 거예요 from 할게요.

curriculumTrack.label: A2 Builder
curriculumTrack.description: Tense, questions, numbers, modifiers, connectors, particles, counters, and repair chapters.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Say a real future plan, not just a grammar example.
exitTask.prompt: Answer 주말에 뭐 할 거예요? and add what you will do if the plan changes.

sampleAnswer.ko: 주말에는 카페에서 공부할 거예요. 비가 오면 집에서 할 거예요.
sampleAnswer.en: This weekend I am going to study at a cafe. If it rains, I will do it at home.

checklist: I can use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 for a plan or prediction.
I can use -면 for a simple condition.
I can tell apart 할 거예요 from 할게요.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You're talking to a Korean colleague about your future plans. You want to say 'I decided to start my own business' — but you accidentally say something that sounds like you're making a promise on the spot, not announcing a settled decision. Then they ask if you're worried, and you want to express 'I'm afraid it might fail' — but you use the wrong pattern and it sounds like you're asking a question. These three patterns (기로 하다, -(으)ㄹ까 봐, -게 되다) define how Koreans talk about plans, worries, and how things unfold — and mixing them up sends completely wrong signals.
objectives: Use -기로 하다 to announce a firm decision or agreed-upon plan
Use -(으)ㄹ까 봐 to express worry or fear about an unwanted outcome
Use -게 되다 to describe how a situation came about through circumstances, not pure choice
hook.whyItMatters: These three patterns appear constantly in adult Korean conversations about work, life decisions, and relationships. -기로 했어요 is how you announce plans. -(으)ㄹ까 봐 is how you express anxiety without sounding dramatic. -게 됐어요 is how Koreans modestly describe their own successes — saying 'it turned out that way' rather than 'I chose this.' Native speakers use -게 됐어요 constantly to soften good news. After this chapter you will sound like someone who actually thinks in Korean, not just translates from English.

grammarNotes.title: -기로 하다 — deciding / agreeing to do something
grammarNotes.func: Use -기로 하다 to say you've decided or agreed to do something. The verb stem + 기로 names the action and 하다 marks the act of deciding. It's usually in the past (-기로 했어요) because the decision is already made.

formTable.add: verb stem + 기로 하다 (no harmony, no stem change)
formTable.ex: 가다 → 가기로 하다, 먹다 → 먹기로 하다

formTable.when: Reporting a decision you've made (most common)
formTable.ex: 운동하다 → 운동하기로 했어요, 읽다 → 읽기로 했어요

formTable.add: 안 + verb + 기로 하다 / verb + 지 않기로 하다
formTable.ex: 안 먹기로 했어요, 먹지 않기로 했어요

examples.en: I've decided to exercise every day from tomorrow.
examples.note: Past 했어요 because the decision is already settled.

examples.en: My friend and I decided to watch a movie this weekend.
examples.note: With 친구하고 it sounds like a mutual plan, not a solo one.

examples.en: I've decided not to drink coffee from today.
examples.note: 안 goes right before the verb for a 'decide not to' meaning.

examples.ko: 우리 내년에 같이 한국어 공부하기로 해요.
examples.romanization: uri naenyeone gachi hangugeo gongbuhagiro haeyo.
examples.en: Let's make a deal to study Korean together next year.
examples.note: Present 해요 turns it into a proposal rather than a report.

keyPoint.label: -기로 했어요 vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요
keyPoint.body: Both point to the future, but -기로 했어요 reports a decision that's now fixed ('I've decided to…'), while -(으)ㄹ 거예요 just states a plan or guess ('I'm going to…'). Use -기로 하다 when the point is that a choice was made — a promise to yourself or a deal with someone. (How the 했어요 past ending works is covered separately.)

drill.instruction: Turn each plan into a decision using -기로 했어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers turn 'decided to' into 결정하다 plus a noun clause, which sounds heavy for everyday plans. Korean packs 'decide to do X' into the set phrase -기로 하다; keep 결정하다 for big, formal decisions.

grammarNotes.title: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 — doing something because you're worried ("in case / afraid that")
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)ㄹ까 봐 to give the worried 'what if' that's behind an action. It means 'because I'm afraid that…' or 'in case…', and the main clause says what you do to head that off.

formTable.when: Verb/adjective stem ends in a vowel
formTable.ex: 자다 → 잘까 봐, 오다 → 올까 봐
늦다 → 늦을까 봐, 먹다 → 먹을까 봐
멀다 → 멀까 봐, 힘들다 → 힘들까 봐

formTable.when: Worry about something that already happened
formTable.ex: 갔다 → 갔을까 봐, 잊었다 → 잊었을까 봐

examples.en: I brought an umbrella in case it rains.
examples.note: 올까 봐 is the feared event; the main clause is the precaution.

examples.en: I left early because I was afraid I'd be late for school.
examples.note: 받침 stem 늦- takes 을까 봐.

examples.en: I made some food in case my friend is hungry.
examples.note: The one you're worried about (친구) can be someone other than you.

examples.ko: 시험에서 틀릴까 봐 책을 다시 봤어요.
examples.romanization: siheomeseo teullilkka bwa chaegeul dasi bwasseoyo.
examples.en: I went over the book again because I was afraid I'd get things wrong on the test.
examples.note: 틀리다 ('get wrong') ends in a vowel, so it takes ㄹ까 봐.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 vs -(으)니까
keyPoint.body: Both give reasons, but -(으)니까 states a plain fact ('because it's raining'), while -(으)ㄹ까 봐 gives a worried 'what if' that hasn't happened ('in case it rains'). Use -(으)ㄹ까 봐 only when the reason is something you're afraid of or want to prevent, and don't put a command or suggestion in the main clause.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -(으)ㄹ까 tenses the 까: 올까 sounds like [올까], 늦을까 like [느즐까] — the 까 is always a hard, tense sound.

drill.instruction: Add the worried reason with -(으)ㄹ까 봐.
drill.model: (비가 오다) 우산을 가져왔어요 → 비가 올까 봐 우산을 가져왔어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'in case it rains, bring an umbrella' makes you want to add a command, but -(으)ㄹ까 봐 can't be followed by an order or suggestion. The main clause has to say what someone actually does or did, not what they should do.

grammarNotes.title: -게 되다 — how something ended up happening (not by your own choice)
grammarNotes.func: Use -게 되다 to show a situation came about through circumstances rather than your own decision. It's the difference between 'I do X' and 'it ended up that I do X', usually because of outside events or other people.

formTable.add: verb stem + 게 되다 (no stem change)
formTable.ex: 가다 → 가게 되다, 먹다 → 먹게 되다

formTable.when: Saying how it turned out (most common)
formTable.ex: 살다 → 살게 됐어요, 알다 → 알게 됐어요

formTable.when: Future: it'll end up that way

examples.en: I ended up living in Busan because of work.
examples.note: 되다 shows the move came from circumstances, not free choice.

examples.ko: 한국 친구를 만나서 한국어를 잘하게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: hanguk chingureul mannaseo hangugeoreul jalhage dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: After I made a Korean friend, I got good at Korean.
examples.note: A gradual change in ability — a natural result, not a decision.

examples.en: I happened to end up watching that movie.
examples.note: 우연히 ('by chance') goes well with 게 되다 for unplanned things.

examples.en: Now I've come to understand why.
examples.note: ㄹ-stem 알다 keeps its ㄹ before 게: 알게 됐어요.

keyPoint.label: -게 되다 vs plain past
keyPoint.body: Plain past (살았어요 'I lived') just states the fact. -게 됐어요 ('I ended up living') adds that it happened through circumstances or other people, not purely by your own plan. Reach for -게 되다 when you want to sound modest about a result or play down your own role in it.

drill.instruction: Say how it turned out using -게 됐어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: -기로 하다 (decide to) and -게 되다 (end up) get mixed up. If circumstances decided it for you, use -게 됐어요; -기로 했어요 means you yourself chose it. Don't blend them into 살기로 됐어요.

exampleSentence.en: I decided to start a small business.
exampleSentence.note: 기로 했어요 — a settled decision to begin the business

exampleSentence.en: I ended up starting a new project.
exampleSentence.note: 게 됐어요 — the project arose through circumstances, not purely personal choice

exampleSentence.en: I can't even sleep because I'm afraid of failing.
exampleSentence.note: 실패하다 → 실패할까 봐: feared outcome expressed with -(으)ㄹ까 봐

exampleSentence.en: As I kept working hard, I came to succeed.
exampleSentence.note: 하다 보니까 + 게 됐어요: a natural combination — persistent effort led to the circumstantial outcome

exampleSentence.ko: 걱정이 많아서 잠을 잘 못 자요.
exampleSentence.en: I have so many worries that I can't sleep well.
exampleSentence.note: 걱정이 많다 — literally 'worries are many'; Korean treats worry as a countable thing

exampleSentence.en: I've already decided. I've made up my mind.
exampleSentence.note: 결정했어요 and 기로 했어요 both express decisions, but 기로 했어요 attaches to the specific action decided upon

exampleSentence.en: I decided to give it a try.
exampleSentence.note: 도전해 보기로 했어요 — 해 보다 (try doing) + 기로 했어요: decided to at least attempt

exampleSentence.en: I decided not to give up.
exampleSentence.note: -지 않기로 하다 = decided NOT to: the negative form of 기로 하다

exampleSentence.en: I'm worried that my income might decrease.
exampleSentence.note: 줄어들다 → 줄어들까 봐: the feared outcome is shrinking income

exampleSentence.en: I decided to invest in that business.
exampleSentence.note: 기로 했어요 — a definitive financial commitment, not an on-the-spot promise

exampleSentence.en: It looks like I'll end up retiring next year.
exampleSentence.note: 게 될 것 같아요 — future form of 게 되다: circumstances will likely lead to retirement

exampleSentence.en: I'm afraid of having to take responsibility.
exampleSentence.note: 지다 → 질까 봐: ㄹ irregular — 지다 adds ㄹ before 까 봐 since the stem ends in a vowel

extendedVocabulary.english: to come to know / find out

exampleSentence.en: I found out that fact later (it came to me).
exampleSentence.note: 알다 + 게 됐어요: knowing came about through circumstances — you didn't actively seek the info, it found you

exampleSentence.en: I decided to make a 5-year plan.
exampleSentence.note: 세우다 → 세우기로 했어요: the decision is to create the plan itself

exampleSentence.en: Don't be too afraid of failure.
exampleSentence.note: 두려워하다 expresses fear about a noun; -(으)ㄹ까 봐 is used when the feared thing is an action/event

exampleSentence.en: I decided to summon my courage.
exampleSentence.note: 용기를 내다 (to gather courage) + 기로 했어요: even emotional decisions use 기로 하다

exampleSentence.ko: 일을 하다 보니까 인맥이 생기게 됐어요.
exampleSentence.en: As I worked, I ended up building a network of connections.
exampleSentence.note: 하다 보니까 + 게 됐어요: a natural growth over time through circumstances, not planned directly

extendedDialogue.setting: Jieun and her colleague Hyunwoo talk over lunch about her decision to leave the company and start a business

lines.speaker: 지은
lines.en: I've decided to quit the company this time.
lines.grammarNote: 그만두다 → 그만두기로 했어요: the contract is signed — this is a settled decision, not an on-the-spot announcement

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.en: Really? Why? It's sudden, so I'm a bit surprised.
lines.grammarNote: 갑자기라서 좀 놀랐어요 sounds more conversational than a flat 'I'm totally surprised' and keeps the reason-result feel.

lines.speaker: 지은
lines.ko: 사실 오래전부터 사업을 해 보고 싶었는데, 이번에 좋은 기회를 잡게 됐어요.
lines.romanization: sasil oraejeonbuteo saeobeul hae bogo sipeonneunde, ibeone joheun gihoereul japge dwaesseoyo.
lines.en: Actually I've wanted to try running a business for a long time, and this time I ended up getting a good opportunity.
lines.grammarNote: 잡게 됐어요 frames the opportunity as something that came about through circumstances, while still sounding like natural business talk.

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 대단하네요. 수입이 줄어들까 봐 걱정되진 않아요?
lines.romanization: daedanhaneyo. suibi jureodleulkka bwa geokjeongdoejin anayo?
lines.en: That's impressive. Aren't you worried your income might decrease?
lines.grammarNote: 줄어들다 → 줄어들까 봐: feared outcome (income drop) + 걱정되다 (feel worried) — asking if she's looking through that worst-case window

lines.speaker: 지은
lines.ko: 솔직히 실패할까 봐 두려운 건 사실이에요. 그래도 해 보기로 했어요.
lines.romanization: soljiki silpaehalkka bwa duryeoun geon sasilieyo. geuraedo hae bogiro haesseoyo.
lines.en: Honestly, I'm afraid it might fail — that's true. But I decided to try anyway.
lines.grammarNote: 실패할까 봐 — fear of failure as a worst-case window; 해 보기로 했어요 — despite the fear, the decision-contract is signed

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 용기 있네요! 저도 이 회사에 처음 오게 됐을 때 많이 떨렸어요.
lines.romanization: yongi inneyo! jeodo i hoesae cheoeum oge dwaesseul ttae mani tteollyeosseoyo.
lines.en: That takes courage! When I first ended up coming to this company, I was really nervous too.
lines.grammarNote: 오게 됐을 때: past circumstantial form — 'when it came to be that I arrived here' — Hyunwoo frames his own job as something circumstances led him into, not a pure choice

lines.speaker: 지은
lines.ko: 그 말 들으니까 위로가 되네요. 잘될지는 모르지만 일단 시작하기로 마음먹었어요.
lines.romanization: geu mal deureunikka wiroga doeneyo. jaldoeljineun moreujiman ildan sijakhagiro maeumeogeosseoyo.
lines.en: Hearing that is reassuring. I don't know if it'll go well, but I've made up my mind to start at least.
lines.grammarNote: 시작하기로 마음먹었어요: stronger form of 기로 하다 — literally 'ate the decision in my heart' — expressing firm resolve

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 응원할게요! 궁금한 것 있으면 언제든지 물어보세요.
lines.romanization: eungwonhalkkeyo! gunggeumhan geot isseumyeon eonjedeunji mureoboseyo.
lines.en: I'll cheer you on! If you have any questions, feel free to ask anytime.
lines.grammarNote: 응원할게요: -(으)ㄹ게요 — an on-the-spot promise made TO Jieun right now, in this conversation. Note the contrast with 기로 했어요 used throughout the dialogue.

readingText.title: 새로운 시작 (A New Beginning)
readingText.body: 오늘 드디어 회사에 사직서를 냈어요. 몇 달 전부터 생각해 오던 일이지만 막상 하고 나니 실감이 안 나요. 솔직히 수입이 없어질까 봐 몇 번이나 포기할 뻔했어요. 하지만 오래전부터 내 사업을 하기로 마음먹었던 게 맞는 것 같아서, 결국 사직서를 내기로 했어요. 친구 지수는 '잘 안될까 봐 걱정되지 않냐'고 물었는데, 솔직히 걱정은 돼요. 그래도 아무것도 안 하다 보면 평생 후회할 것 같아서요. 어쩌다 보니 이렇게 큰 결정을 하게 됐는데, 지금은 오히려 홀가분한 느낌이에요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Today I finally handed in my resignation at the company. It's something I'd been thinking about for months, but now that I've actually done it, it doesn't feel real. Honestly, I nearly gave up several times because I was afraid I'd lose my income. But since I'd long ago made up my mind to run my own business, I ultimately decided to hand in the resignation. My friend Jisu asked if I wasn't worried it might not go well — and honestly, I am worried. Still, I feel like if I just do nothing, I'll regret it for the rest of my life. Somehow I ended up making this big decision, and right now I actually feel strangely light.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two things was the writer afraid might happen? (Find the -(으)ㄹ까 봐 phrases.)
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 수입이 없어질까 봐 (afraid of losing income) and 잘 안될까 봐 (afraid it won't go well).

comprehensionQuestions.question: How does the writer describe making this big decision — did they plan it carefully or did it happen circumstantially? Which phrase tells you this?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 어쩌다 보니 이렇게 큰 결정을 하게 됐는데 — 'Somehow I ended up making this big decision.' 하게 됐는데 (게 되다 form) frames the decision as something that came about through circumstances, even though the writer had been thinking about it for a long time.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the -기로 하다 / 기로 마음먹다 forms in the text. What decision does each one refer to, and why is 기로 하다 (rather than -(으)ㄹ게요) used in each case?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 내 사업을 하기로 마음먹었던 게: long-ago personal resolution to run a business — settled contract, not a live promise. 사직서를 내기로 했어요: the ultimate decision to actually resign — also already made before this diary entry. Neither is an on-the-spot promise to a listener, so -(으)ㄹ게요 would be wrong in both cases.

culturalNote.title: -게 됐어요 — The Korean Art of Modest Success
culturalNote.body: Korean culture values 겸손 (humility) highly, and -게 됐어요 is one of the key grammatical tools for expressing it. When Koreans announce good news — a new job, a promotion, passing an exam, even having a baby — they often say '하게 됐어요' (it came to be that I do this) rather than '했어요' (I did it). This is not dishonesty; it's social grace. Saying '그 회사에 취직했어요' (I got that job) can sound slightly boastful. Saying '그 회사에 취직하게 됐어요' frames your success as something you were led into by fortunate circumstances, deflecting too much personal credit. Foreign learners who skip this and just use plain verbs may unintentionally come across as self-congratulatory. Pay attention to how Koreans use 게 됐어요 in news announcements, wedding speeches, and even job interviews — it signals maturity and social awareness.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저 내년에 유학 ___기로 했어요. (I decided to study abroad next year.)
inlineExercises.explanation: The pattern is [verb stem] + 기로 했어요. 가다 → 가 + 기로 했어요 = 가기로 했어요. The blank is just the verb stem 가. '가기로 하기로 했어요' would be wrong (doubled), and '갈기로 했어요' doesn't exist as a form.

inlineExercises.prompt: 비가 ___까 봐 우산을 가져왔어요. (I brought an umbrella because I was worried it might rain.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 오다 (to come/rain) has a vowel-ending stem 오-, so we add ㄹ: 올까 봐. '오를까 봐' is wrong — 를 is an object marker, not part of this pattern. '왔을까 봐' uses the past marker and would mean 'afraid that it had already rained' — different nuance, unnatural here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 고치세요: '저 그 회사에 일하기로 할게요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Two errors: (1) 기로 할게요 mixes two patterns — 기로 하다 announces a settled decision, but -(으)ㄹ게요 is an on-the-spot promise. The correct form is 기로 했어요 (past, decision already made). (2) 회사에 일하다 should be 회사에서 일하다 — working is an action, so the workplace takes 에서, not 에.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I came to understand Korean because I kept studying.'
inlineExercises.correct: 계속 공부하다 보니까 한국어를 이해하게 됐어요.
inlineExercises.hint: Use 게 됐어요 — understanding came about through the circumstance of sustained study. 하다 보니까 = 'as I kept doing...'
inlineExercises.explanation: -다 보니까 describes a result that comes from continuing or repeatedly doing something. -게 됐어요 adds the change of state: you came to understand.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly expresses 'I'm afraid I might be late for the meeting'?
inlineExercises.explanation: Option 1 (늦을까요?) asks the listener 'Do you think I'll be late?' — a question, not a worry. Option 3 (늦어서) uses a causal connector for something that already happened — but the meeting hasn't started yet. Only option 2 correctly uses -(으)ㄹ까 봐 to express a feared future outcome as the reason for worry.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your Korean friend asks why you moved to Seoul. Which answer gives a natural reason and uses -게 됐어요 well?
inlineExercises.explanation: The friend asked why, so the best answer includes a reason: 일 때문에. -게 됐어요 then frames the move as a life circumstance that came about naturally. Option 1 over-emphasizes personal choice, and option 3 only says you decided to move, without answering the why.

inlineExercises.prompt: 계속 공부하다 보니까 한국어를 이해하___ 됐어요. (As I kept studying, I came to understand Korean.)
inlineExercises.explanation: This is a gradual result that came about through repeated effort — the grammar for that is -게 됐어요. 이해하게 됐어요 = 'came to understand.' 이해하기로 했어요 would mean 'decided to understand,' which is not natural, and 이해할까 봐 would mean being afraid you might understand.

inlineExercises.prompt: 사업___ 시작하기로 했어요. (I decided to start a business.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 시작하다 is an action verb, and 사업 is what you start, so it takes 을. 이 would make 사업 the subject and break the intended meaning.

inlineExercises.prompt: 내년에 사업을 ___ . (시작하다 → decided to)
inlineExercises.explanation: -기로 했어요 states a decision or agreed plan. 시작하다 drops 다 and takes 기로 했어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I brought an umbrella because I was worried it might rain.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 gives the worry that motivated the action. The umbrella action follows because rain was the feared outcome.

bullets: 기로 했어요 = SIGNED CONTRACT: announcing a settled decision or mutual agreement — always points back to a decision already made
-(으)ㄹ까 봐 = WORST-CASE WINDOW: the feared bad outcome drives an action — 'I was afraid X would happen, so I did Y'
-게 됐어요 = CIRCUMSTANCES LED HERE: humble, natural way to describe how a situation came about — preferred in Korean for announcing life changes modestly

writingTask.prompt: Write a few sentences about a work or money decision you made, explaining a worry behind it and how things ended up.
writingTask.hint: Use -기로 했어요 for the decision, -(으)ㄹ까 봐 for the worry, and -게 됐어요 for how it turned out.
writingTask.model: 저는 작은 사업을 시작하기로 했어요. 돈을 다 잃을까 봐 조금 걱정했어요. 그래서 친구하고 같이 일하게 됐어요.
writingTask.modelEn: I decided to start a small business. I was a little worried in case I'd lose all my money. So I ended up working together with a friend.

canDo: Say I've decided or agreed to do something (-기로 하다)
Explain that I act because I'm afraid something might happen (-(으)ㄹ까 봐)
Show a situation came about by circumstance, not my own choice (-게 되다)
Talk through a work or money decision using 사업 · 결정하다 · 걱정 · 투자하다

dialogue.speaker: A

I can use 전에 and 후에 around events.

sampleAnswer.en: For the test, I will study from Monday to Friday.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: Your Korean friend tells you about a stressful day: someone at work was 'pretending not to know,' they 'almost cried' during a movie, and they're 'guessing the boss is angry.' You understand the gist but can't quite follow the grammar gluing it together. Those three reactions — faking something, narrowly avoiding something, and inferring from clues — each need their own structure in Korean.
objectives: Use -는 척하다 to say someone is pretending or faking a state or action
Use -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 to describe a close call — something that almost happened but didn't
Use -나 보다 / -(으)ㄴ가 보다 to make an evidence-based guess about someone else's situation
hook.whyItMatters: These three patterns appear constantly in Korean storytelling and conversation. Without them, you can describe facts but not the texture of human experience — the white lies, the near-misses, and the inferences you draw about the people around you. Master all three and your Korean instantly sounds more natural and more adult.

grammarNotes.title: -는 척하다 — pretend / act like
grammarNotes.func: Use -는 척하다 to say someone pretends to do or be something — putting on an act that doesn't match reality. It marks behavior that's deliberately faked.

formTable.when: Action verb, present (pretend to be doing now)
formTable.ex: 자다 → 자는 척하다 (pretend to be sleeping)

formTable.when: Action verb, past (pretend to have done)
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹은 척하다 / 보다 → 본 척하다
괜찮다 → 괜찮은 척하다 / 아프다 → 아픈 척하다
학생이다 → 학생인 척하다 (pretend to be a student)

examples.en: My friend came over, but I pretended to be asleep.
examples.note: 자다 is happening now → present -는 척하다.

examples.ko: 그 영화 안 봤는데 본 척했어요.
examples.romanization: geu yeonghwa an bwanneunde bon cheokaesseoyo.
examples.en: I hadn't seen that movie, but I pretended I had.
examples.note: 보다 done before now → past -(으)ㄴ 척하다 (본).

examples.en: I was actually sick, but I pretended I was fine.
examples.note: 괜찮다 is an adjective → -(으)ㄴ 척하다 (괜찮은).

examples.en: Don't act like you know when you don't.
examples.note: 알다 is a ㄹ-verb, present sense → 아는 척 (ㄹ drops before -는).

keyPoint.label: -는 척하다 vs -(으)ㄴ 척하다
keyPoint.body: The ending works just like a modifier (관형사형): an action happening now takes -는 (자는 척), a finished action takes -(으)ㄴ (먹은 척), and adjectives also take -(으)ㄴ (아픈 척). You can swap 척 for 체 with no change in meaning (자는 체하다), though 척 is more common in everyday speech.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 척했어요 sounds like [처캐써요] — ㄱ + ㅎ merge into the aspirated [ㅋ].

drill.instruction: Turn each cue into '(I) pretended to ~' using -는/-(으)ㄴ 척했어요.
drill.model: 안 자다 / 자다 → 안 자는데 자는 척했어요.
items: 잘 모르다 / 알다 → 잘 모르는데 잘 ___ 척했어요.
안 먹다 / 먹다 → 밥을 안 먹었는데 ___ 척했어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'pretend to be fine' makes learners reach for -는, but 괜찮다 is an adjective, so it takes the adjective modifier -(으)ㄴ → 괜찮은 척. Only action verbs happening now take -는 척.

grammarNotes.title: -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 — almost happened (a close call)
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 to say something nearly happened but didn't — a near miss. It's almost always used in the past tense (-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요) because the close call already happened.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel
Verb stem ends in a consonant (받침)
formTable.ex: 죽다 → 죽을 뻔하다 / 늦다 → 늦을 뻔하다

examples.en: I almost fell on the street.
examples.note: 넘어지다 ends in a vowel → -ㄹ 뻔하다; past 뻔했어요.

examples.en: I overslept and almost got to school late.
examples.note: 늦다 ends in 받침 ㅈ → -을 뻔하다.

examples.en: I almost cried when I heard that story.
examples.note: 울다 is a ㄹ-stem; ㄹ stays before 뻔 → 울 뻔하다.

examples.en: I spilled water and the book almost got wet.
examples.note: 젖다 ends in 받침 → -을 뻔하다; the book didn't actually get wet.

keyPoint.label: Always past tense, always 'didn't happen'
keyPoint.body: -(으)ㄹ 뻔했다 means the event did NOT happen — it only came close. So 넘어질 뻔했어요 = 'I almost fell (but didn't).' Don't put the main verb in the past too: say 넘어질 뻔했어요, never 넘어졌을 뻔했어요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 뻔했어요 sounds like [뻔해써요]; the opening ㅃ is a tense (fortis) sound — keep it hard, not a soft [ㅂ].

drill.instruction: Make a 'close call' sentence with -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요.
items: 물을 쏟다 → 컵을 건드려서 물을 ___ 뻔했어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'almost fell' is past, so learners put the main verb in the past too. But only 뻔하다 carries the past tense; the action verb stays in -(으)ㄹ form, because the fall never actually happened.

grammarNotes.title: -나 보다 / -(으)ㄴ가 보다 — guessing from evidence
grammarNotes.func: Use -나 보다 / -(으)ㄴ가 보다 to make a guess based on something you can see or hear, like English 'I guess...' or 'It seems...'. You're inferring about a situation rather than stating it as a fact.

formTable.ex: 오다 → 오나 보다 / 먹다 → 먹나 보다
가다 → 갔나 보다 / 자다 → 잤나 보다
춥다 → 추운가 보다 / 바쁘다 → 바쁜가 보다
학생이다 → 학생인가 보다 (guess: must be a student)

examples.ko: 사람들이 우산을 써요. 비가 오나 봐요.
examples.romanization: saramdeuri usaneul sseoyo. biga ona bwayo.
examples.en: People are using umbrellas. I guess it's raining.
examples.note: 오다 is an action verb, present → -나 보다.

examples.ko: 친구가 전화를 안 받아요. 자나 봐요.
examples.romanization: chinguga jeonhwareul an badayo. jana bwayo.
examples.en: My friend isn't answering the phone. I guess they're sleeping.
examples.note: 자다 action verb, present → 자나 봐요.

examples.ko: 불이 꺼져 있어요. 다들 집에 갔나 봐요.
examples.romanization: buri kkeojyeo isseoyo. dadeul jibe ganna bwayo.
examples.en: The lights are off. I guess everyone went home.
examples.note: Past inference → -았/었나 보다 (갔나).

examples.ko: 다들 두꺼운 옷을 입었어요. 추운가 봐요.
examples.romanization: dadeul dukkeoun oseul ibeosseoyo. chuunga bwayo.
examples.en: Everyone's wearing thick clothes. I guess it's cold.
examples.note: 춥다 is an adjective → -(으)ㄴ가 보다 (추운가, ㅂ-irregular).

keyPoint.label: -나 보다 vs -(으)ㄹ 것 같다
keyPoint.body: -나 보다 means you're inferring from something you observed ('I see this, so I guess that'). -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 is a softer, more general guess or impression that needs no evidence. Use -나 보다 only when you're reasoning from a clue. (The fuller contrast lives in the conjecture chapter.)

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 봐요 sounds like [봐:요], a contraction of 보아요; keep it one syllable [bwa].

drill.instruction: Given the clue, finish the guess with -나 봐요 / -(으)ㄴ가 봐요.
items: 교실에 아무도 없어요. (수업이 끝나다) → 수업이 ___ 봐요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners often attach -(으)ㄴ가 to everything, but action verbs (동사) in the present take -나 보다, while only adjectives and 이다 take -(으)ㄴ가 보다. So 오다 → 오나 봐요, but 춥다 → 추운가 봐요.

extendedVocabulary.english: deep emotion; being moved or touched

exampleSentence.ko: 그 영화 너무 감동적이어서 울 뻔했어요.
exampleSentence.en: That movie was so moving I almost cried.
exampleSentence.note: 감동적이다 = to be moving/touching; 울 뻔했어요 shows the emotional near-miss naturally

exampleSentence.ko: 그 사람 표정을 보니까 많이 두려워하나 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: From that person's expression, I guess they're really afraid.
exampleSentence.note: 두려워하다 is an action verb, so it takes -나 봐요. The visible expression is the evidence.

exampleSentence.ko: 팀장님 말투가 그러는 걸 보니까 화나신 건가 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: The way the team leader is talking, I'm guessing they're angry.
exampleSentence.note: -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 = inferring the emotion from observable evidence (their tone)

exampleSentence.ko: 합격했다는 소식을 듣고 만족스러워서 소리를 지를 뻔했어요.
exampleSentence.en: When I heard I passed, I was so satisfied I almost shouted.
exampleSentence.note: 만족스럽다 = to feel satisfied; 소리를 지르다 = to shout; 지를 뻔했어요 = almost-shouted close call

exampleSentence.ko: 그분이 모르는 척한 것 때문에 신뢰를 잃었어요.
exampleSentence.en: Because he pretended not to know, I lost trust in him.
exampleSentence.note: 모르는 척하다 (pretending not to know) combined with 신뢰를 잃다 (lose trust) — common real-life pairing

exampleSentence.ko: 그분 이야기가 나오면 다들 조용해지는 걸 보니까 많이 존경하나 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: Seeing everyone quiet down when that person comes up, I guess they respect them a lot.
exampleSentence.note: 존경하다 is an action verb, so it takes -나 봐요. The group reaction gives the clue.

exampleSentence.en: That person seems really diligent.
exampleSentence.note: 성실하다 is an adjective → 성실한 것 같다 (soft opinion); contrast with -나 보다 which implies outside evidence

exampleSentence.ko: 그 사람이 사실대로 말하는 걸 보니까 정직한 사람인가 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: Seeing that person tell the truth, I guess they're an honest person.
exampleSentence.note: 정직한 사람인가 봐요 uses noun phrase 사람인가 봐요 after the adjective modifier 정직한.

extendedVocabulary.english: to be careful; prudent; cautious in decisions

exampleSentence.ko: 그 사람 말을 잘 안 하는 걸 보니까 신중한가 봐요.
exampleSentence.en: They don't say much — I'm guessing they're the careful type.
exampleSentence.note: 신중하다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요; inferring personality from observable behavior

extendedVocabulary.english: to be coolheaded; level-headed; cold; detached

exampleSentence.en: I pretended to be coolheaded, but it was actually hard.
exampleSentence.note: 냉정한 척하다 uses the target adjective directly: acting detached even when you are shaken inside.

extendedVocabulary.english: tricky; demanding; picky; hard to satisfy

exampleSentence.ko: 심사 기준이 까다로운가 봐요. 다들 탈락했네요.
exampleSentence.en: I guess the judging criteria are strict — everyone got eliminated.
exampleSentence.note: 까다롭다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 (evidence-based inference from the result); ㅂ-irregular: 까다롭 + 은가 → 까다로운가

extendedVocabulary.english: 'I almost...'; by a narrow margin (near-miss adverb)

exampleSentence.en: I almost lost my wallet!
exampleSentence.note: 하마터면 always pairs with -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 to emphasize the narrowness of the near-miss

extendedVocabulary.english: to pick up on; to sense; to figure out (from cues)

exampleSentence.ko: 걔가 눈치챈 것 같아서 아무것도 모르는 척했어요.
exampleSentence.en: I felt like they were picking up on it, so I pretended not to know anything.
exampleSentence.note: 눈치채다 → trigger for using 척하다: when someone might catch on, you put on the ignorance mask

extendedVocabulary.english: to hide; to conceal (feelings or information)

exampleSentence.en: I pretended to be fine in an attempt to hide my feelings.
exampleSentence.note: 감추려고 (in order to hide) + 척하다 — a very natural Korean expression of masking emotions

extendedVocabulary.english: to be obvious; to show; to give away (that you're faking)

exampleSentence.en: I pretended to be asleep but I guess it was obvious.
exampleSentence.note: 티가 났나 봐요 = evidence-based guess (someone's reaction revealed it); 척하다 + 나 봐요 together in one sentence

extendedVocabulary.english: to tremble; to be shaky (with nerves or emotion)

exampleSentence.en: During my presentation, my voice almost started shaking.
exampleSentence.note: 떨리다 ends in vowel → -ㄹ 뻔했어요; common near-miss emotion verb in presentations and auditions

extendedDialogue.setting: Two coworkers, Jiyeon and Minsu, are eating lunch together and talking about a stressful morning

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 오늘 오전에 발표하다가 목소리가 떨릴 뻔했어요.
lines.romanization: oneul ojeone balpyohadaga moksoriga tteollil ppeonhaesseoyo.
lines.en: This morning during my presentation, my voice almost started shaking.
lines.grammarNote: 떨리다 = vowel-stem verb → -ㄹ 뻔했어요; the near-miss is past and already resolved

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 어, 저도 봤는데 엄청 자연스러웠어요. 몰랐어요.
lines.romanization: eo, jeodo bwanneunde eomcheong jayeonseureowosseoyo. mollasseoyo.
lines.en: Oh, I was watching and you were super natural. I couldn't tell.
lines.grammarNote: No grammar point here — a natural supportive reply that makes the 척하다 line in the next turn more impactful

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 고마워요. 사실 많이 떨렸는데 괜찮은 척했어요.
lines.romanization: gomawoyo. sasil mani tteollyeonneunde gwaenchaneun cheokaesseoyo.
lines.en: Thank you. I was actually shaking a lot, but I pretended to be fine.
lines.grammarNote: 괜찮다 is an adjective → -(으)ㄴ 척하다: 괜찮은 척했어요; confirms the mask was successfully worn

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 그래요? 팀장님도 잘 모르시는 것 같던데요.
lines.romanization: geuraeyo? timjangnimdo jal moreusineun geot gatdeondeyo.
lines.en: Really? It seemed like the team leader didn't notice either.
lines.grammarNote: -것 같던데요 = a gentle evidence-based impression recalled from the past; softer than -나 봐요 here because the speaker is recounting their own observation

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 팀장님은 지금 다른 문제로 머리가 복잡한가 봐요.
lines.romanization: timjangnimeun jigeum dareun munjero meoriga bokjapanga bwayo.
lines.en: I think the team leader's head is full of other problems right now.
lines.grammarNote: 복잡하다 = adjective → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요: 복잡한가 봐요; evidence-based inference about someone else's mental state

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 맞아요. 아침에 표정이 안 좋으시더라고요. 스트레스 많이 받으시나 봐요.
lines.romanization: majayo. achime pyojeongi an joeusideoragoyo. seuteureseu mani badeusinabwayo.
lines.en: Right. Their expression this morning didn't look good. I'm guessing they're under a lot of stress.
lines.grammarNote: 받으시나 봐요 = honorific 시 + -나 봐요. The visible evidence (bad expression) triggers the inference.

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 하마터면 제가 먼저 물어볼 뻔했는데 참았어요.
lines.romanization: hamateomyeon jega meonjeo mureobol ppeonhaenneunde chamasseoyo.
lines.en: I almost asked first, but I held back.
lines.grammarNote: 하마터면 + 물어보다 (vowel stem) → -ㄹ 뻔했는데; -는데 adds a contrastive note (almost did, but then...)

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 잘하셨어요. 지금은 모르는 척하는 게 나을 것 같아요.
lines.romanization: jalhasyeosseoyo. jigeumeun moreuneun cheokhaneun ge naeul geot gatayo.
lines.en: Good call. Right now, playing dumb is probably better.
lines.grammarNote: 모르다 = action verb → 모르는 척하다; 하는 게 나을 것 같다 = 'it's probably better to...' — 척하다 appears as a noun-modifying clause here

readingText.title: 지연의 하루 일기 (Jiyeon's Day Diary)
readingText.body: 오늘은 정말 힘든 하루였다. 아침에 중요한 발표가 있었는데, 엄청 긴장해서 울 뻔했다. 발표하는 내내 떨렸지만 괜찮은 척하면서 끝까지 버텼다. 팀장님은 좀 무표정하게 앉아 계셨는데, 뭔가 불만이 있으신가 봐서 마음이 불안했다. 나중에 동료한테 물어봤더니 "요즘 윗사람 때문에 스트레스를 많이 받으시나 봐"라고 했다. 그 말 듣고 조금 안심이 됐다. 퇴근하다가 지갑을 잃어버릴 뻔했다. 하마터면 큰일 날 뻔했는데, 다행히 가방 안쪽에 있었다. 내일은 오늘보다 나은 하루이길 바란다.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Today was a really tough day. There was an important presentation in the morning, and I was so nervous I almost cried. I was shaking the whole time but I pretended to be fine and hung in there to the end. The team leader sat there with a blank expression, and I felt uneasy thinking they seemed to have some complaint. I asked a coworker later, and they said, "It looks like the team leader is under a lot of stress because of upper management these days." Hearing that made me feel a bit relieved. On the way out of the office, I almost lost my wallet. That was almost a disaster, but thankfully it was in the inside pocket of my bag. I hope tomorrow is a better day than today.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why did Jiyeon pretend to be fine during the presentation?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: She was shaking and almost cried (울 뻔했다), but she put on a mask of composure (괜찮은 척하면서) and pushed through to the end.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How does Jiyeon learn about the team leader's stress? What Korean pattern does she use for this inference?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: She hears it from a coworker. She uses 스트레스를 많이 받으시나 봐 — the -나 봐 pattern (action verb 받다 → 받으시나 봐) because the coworker is making an evidence-based inference, not stating a confirmed fact.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every instance of 척하다, 뻔하다, and -나/-(으)ㄴ가 보다 in the text. For each one, explain WHY that particular pattern is used there.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 척하다: 괜찮은 척하면서 — she is deliberately performing composure she does not feel (adjective 괜찮다 → -(으)ㄴ 척). 뻔하다: 울 뻔했다 — she genuinely nearly cried (울다 ㄹ-stem → 울 뻔했다); 잃어버릴 뻔했다 — she genuinely almost lost her wallet (잃어버리다 vowel stem → -ㄹ 뻔했다); 큰일 날 뻔했는데 — almost a disaster (나다 vowel stem → -ㄹ 뻔했는데). -나/-(으)ㄴ가 보다: 불만이 있으신가 봐서 — 불만이 있다 + honorific 있으시다 + -ㄴ가 봐; evidence-based inference from a blank expression. 스트레스를 많이 받으시나 봐 — 받다 is an action verb → -나 봐; the coworker is inferring from workplace clues.

culturalNote.title: 척하다 and the Art of Saving Face in Korean Workplaces
culturalNote.body: Korean workplace culture places enormous value on 눈치 (the ability to read the room) and not burdening others with every private feeling. 괜찮은 척하다 (pretending to be fine) can be a way to stay professional in public, especially during a presentation or meeting. If a coworker asks how you're doing on a busy Monday and you are exhausted, the socially expected first answer may still be 괜찮아요, with details saved for a closer conversation. Similarly, 모르는 척하다 (pretending not to know) can sometimes be a face-saving move: you notice something, but you leave room for the other person to handle it. 척하다 is not always noble or dishonest; the meaning depends on the relationship, the motive, and the situation.

inlineExercises.prompt: 배가 안 고___ 척했어요. 사실 엄청 배고팠어요. (Adjective: 고프다 = to be hungry)
inlineExercises.explanation: 고프다 is an adjective, so it takes the adjective modifier -(으)ㄴ: 고픈 척했어요. If you chose -프는 척, that's the action-verb pattern (-는 척) applied to an adjective, which is the #1 척하다 mistake. Always check: adjective → -(으)ㄴ 척, verb → -는 척.

inlineExercises.prompt: 하마터면 지하철을 ___ 뻔했어요. (놓치다 = to miss a train)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 uses the future/potential modifier -(으)ㄹ, not the present continuous -는. 놓치다 has a vowel-ending stem 놓치-, so it becomes 놓칠 뻔했어요. 놓치는 뻔했어요 is ungrammatical.

inlineExercises.prompt: 답장이 없는 걸 보니까 바쁘___ 봐요. (바쁘다 = to be busy — adjective)
inlineExercises.explanation: 바쁘다 is an adjective → use -(으)ㄴ가 보다. If it were an action verb (e.g., 일하다), you'd use -나 봐요. 바쁜가 봐요 = I guess they're busy (based on the no-reply evidence). 바쁘나 봐요 is colloquially used and understood, but 바쁜가 봐요 is the textbook-correct form.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '발표할 뻔해요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Near-misses are finished events, so 뻔하다 must be in the past: 뻔했어요. 뻔해요 in the present would mean the near-miss is ongoing right now, which contradicts the logic of 뻔하다 — once you've ALMOST done something and DIDN'T, the moment is over.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I pretended not to hear.'
inlineExercises.hint: 듣다 is an action verb. But you are pretending you ALREADY didn't hear — this is a past action, so use the past action modifier -(으)ㄴ: 들은 척. Add 못 before it for 'pretended not to have heard.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 들은 척했어요 means you acted as if you did not hear. Use the past modifier 들은 before 척 because the pretended state is 'not having heard.'

inlineExercises.prompt: You notice your friend has been very quiet lately and you want to say 'I'm guessing something happened.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 있다 is a stative verb (to exist/have) → use -나 봐요 for evidence-based inference. Option 1 (척해요) means PRETENDING something happened — totally different, implying your friend is faking. Option 3 (뻔했어요) means something ALMOST happened but didn't — also wrong; you're guessing it DID happen.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly says 'She pretended to be sick'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 아프다 is an adjective. Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ in modifier position: 아프 + 은 → 아픈. Option 1 (아프는 척) wrongly uses the action-verb pattern -는. Option 3 (아팠는 척) incorrectly attaches -는 to a past tense stem — neither 아팠는 nor 척하다 work that way. The correct and only natural form is 아픈 척했어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: 친구___ 아픈가 봐요. (I guess my friend is sick.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 아프다 describes the friend, so 친구 takes the subject marker 가. 를 would make the friend an object, which does not fit an adjective sentence.

inlineExercises.prompt: 지하철을 ___ . (놓치다 → almost happened)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 means something almost happened but did not. 놓치다 becomes 놓칠 뻔했어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I pretended to be busy.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ before 척하다, so 바쁘다 becomes 바쁜 척했어요. This means you acted as if you were busy.

bullets: MASK (-는/-(으)ㄴ 척하다): put on a fake face — verb actions take -는 척, adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 척, past actions take -(으)ㄴ 척; 척하다 = deliberate pretense, not an honest impression
NEAR-MISS ALARM (-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요): something almost happened but didn't — always past tense, add 하마터면 for drama, only with action verbs
EVIDENCE GUESS (-나 봐요 / -(으)ㄴ가 봐요): action verbs → -나 봐요, adjectives/이다 → -(으)ㄴ가 봐요; used for inferring about OTHER people from visible clues, not your own obvious feelings

writingTask.prompt: Write about a moment when you hid how you really felt, almost made a mistake, and guessed how someone else was feeling.
writingTask.hint: Use -는 척했어요 to pretend, -(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 for the near miss, and -나 보다/-(으)ㄴ가 보다 to guess from evidence.
writingTask.model: 저는 안 무서운 척했어요. 그런데 너무 놀라서 소리를 지를 뻔했어요. 친구도 많이 무서웠나 봐요.
writingTask.modelEn: I pretended I wasn't scared. But I was so startled I almost screamed. My friend seems to have been very scared too.

canDo: Say someone is faking or putting on an act (-는 척하다)
Describe a close call that almost happened (-(으)ㄹ 뻔했다)
Guess about a situation from what I see or hear (-나 보다 / -(으)ㄴ가 보다)
Describe feelings and personality with 감동 · 두려움 · 성실하다 · 신중하다

hook.situation: You're telling a Korean friend why you missed a meeting. You say '비가 와서 못 왔어요' — fine, but flat. A natural Korean speaker would say '비가 오는 바람에 못 왔어요' (the rain swept in and derailed my plans) or '비가 오길래 그냥 집에 있었어요' (I noticed the rain coming, so I just stayed home). Same fact. Completely different nuance. After this chapter you'll choose the RIGHT connector, not just any connector.
objectives: Use -더니 to narrate observed patterns that led to a result
Use -길래 to explain a spontaneous reaction to something you personally noticed
Use -는 바람에 for an unexpected cause that disrupted the plan
Use -(으)ㄹ수록 for 'the more X, the more Y' proportional relationships
Use -기 위해서 to state a clear purpose
hook.whyItMatters: Beginners connect ideas with 그래서 and -아서/어서 for everything. Intermediate speakers choose from a richer toolkit: -더니 signals you WITNESSED something over time, -길래 signals you REACTED on the spot, -는 바람에 signals an unexpected disruption, -(으)ㄹ수록 signals a proportional relationship, and -기 위해서 gives a clear purpose. Using the right connector is what makes your Korean sound like a real person talking, not a grammar textbook.

grammarNotes.title: -더니 — "and then (I noticed)…"
grammarNotes.func: Links two clauses where you personally saw or noticed situation X, and then Y followed — as a result or as a contrast. The first clause is something you observed (usually about someone or something else), not a plan of your own.

formTable.when: After a verb or adjective stem
Your own past action → present result

examples.ko: 동생이 아까 울더니 지금은 자고 있어요.
examples.romanization: dongsaeng-i akka uldeoni jigeum-eun jago isseoyo.
examples.en: My little brother was crying a moment ago, and now he's sleeping.
examples.note: Plain -더니: I watched him cry, then a new state followed (contrast).

examples.ko: 친구가 열심히 공부하더니 시험을 잘 봤어요.
examples.romanization: chingu-ga yeolsimhi gongbuhadeoni siheom-eul jal bwasseoyo.
examples.en: My friend studied hard, and (sure enough) did well on the test.
examples.note: X (effort I saw) leads to Y (result); the subject is someone else.

examples.ko: 아침에는 날씨가 좋더니 오후에 비가 왔어요.
examples.romanization: achim-eneun nalssi-ga jotdeoni ohu-e bi-ga wasseoyo.
examples.en: The weather was nice in the morning, and then it rained in the afternoon.
examples.note: -더니 with an adjective (좋다), showing a contrast between two times.

examples.ko: 밥을 많이 먹었더니 배가 너무 불러요.
examples.romanization: bap-eul mani meogeotdeoni bae-ga neomu bulleoyo.
examples.en: I ate a lot, so now I'm really full.
examples.note: -았/었더니 with a first-person subject: my own past action causing a present result.

keyPoint.label: -더니 vs. -았/었더니
keyPoint.body: Use plain -더니 when you noticed someone else's situation (친구가 공부하더니… = my friend studied, and then…). Use -았/었더니 when YOU did the action and report the result now (제가 먹었더니… = I ate, so now…). Why the past form attaches the way it does is a later topic — for now, just pair plain -더니 with 'someone else' and -았/었더니 with 'I'.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 좋더니 sounds like [조터니] — the ㅎ blends with the following ㄷ into an aspirated [ㅌ].

drill.instruction: Join the two facts into one sentence with -더니 (use -았/었더니 if the subject is 저/나).
drill.model: 동생이 울다 / 지금 자다 → 동생이 울더니 지금 자요.
items: 아침에 머리가 아프다 / 약을 먹고 괜찮아지다 → ____
제가 커피를 많이 마시다 / 잠이 안 오다 → ____ (use -았/었더니)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers stick plain -더니 onto their own actions like a simple 'and then.' But plain -더니 reports something you noticed about others; for your own finished action that leads to a result, you need the past form -았/었더니.

grammarNotes.title: -길래 — "since I saw…, I…"
grammarNotes.func: Gives the reason behind your own reaction or decision: because you noticed situation X, you did Y. The first clause is an outside trigger you observed; the second is your own spontaneous response.

examples.ko: 가게에서 과일이 싸길래 좀 많이 샀어요.
examples.romanization: gage-eseo gwail-i ssagillae jom mani sasseoyo.
examples.en: The fruit was cheap at the store, so I bought quite a lot.
examples.note: X (I noticed it was cheap) triggers my reaction Y (bought a lot).

examples.en: My friend looked hungry, so I bought them a meal.
examples.note: The trigger is someone else's state; my reaction is the kind gesture.

examples.en: The weather was nice, so I went for a walk with a friend.
examples.note: -길래 with an adjective; the second clause must be the speaker's own action.

examples.en: The book was fun, so I read it all the way to the end.
examples.note: Reason (the book was fun) → my resulting action (finished reading).

keyPoint.label: -길래 vs. -아서/-니까
keyPoint.body: -아서 and -니까 give a plain reason for almost any clause, including requests and suggestions. -길래 is narrower: the reason is something you yourself noticed, and the result is your own (usually past) action — you can't say 비싸길래 사지 마세요. When telling someone else to do something, use -니까.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 맛있길래 sounds like [마싣낄래] — the ㄱ of 길 tenses to [ㄲ] after the preceding consonant.

drill.instruction: Make one sentence with -길래 (a reason you noticed + your own past reaction).
drill.model: 과일이 싸다 / 많이 사다 → 과일이 싸길래 많이 샀어요.
items: 친구가 영화를 보고 싶어 하다 / 같이 가다 → ____

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'since/because' works fine before a command, so learners attach -길래 to requests. But -길래 only leads into your own past action, never a command or suggestion. Switch to -니까 when you're telling someone else to do something.

grammarNotes.title: -는 바람에 — "because of (something unexpected)…"
grammarNotes.func: Gives a sudden, usually unwanted cause for a bad or unintended result. It signals that X threw things off and Y happened against your plans.

formTable.ex: 늦다 → 늦는 바람에 / 자다 → 자는 바람에

formTable.when: Verb stem ending in ㄹ (ㄹ drops)
formTable.ex: 울다 → 우는 바람에 / 놀다 → 노는 바람에

examples.en: I overslept, so (unfortunately) I was late to school.
examples.note: Unexpected cause (oversleeping) → unwanted result (being late).

examples.en: I missed the bus, so I was late to meet up.
examples.note: Classic disruption pattern; the result is a setback.

examples.ko: 동생이 우는 바람에 잠을 못 잤어요.
examples.romanization: dongsaeng-i uneun barame jam-eul mot jasseoyo.
examples.en: My little brother kept crying, so I couldn't sleep.
examples.note: 울다 → 우는: ㄹ drops before -는. The cause is someone else's action.

examples.ko: 비가 갑자기 오는 바람에 옷이 다 젖었어요.
examples.romanization: bi-ga gapjagi oneun barame os-i da jeojeosseoyo.
examples.en: It suddenly rained, so my clothes got all wet.
examples.note: 갑자기 (suddenly) fits the 'unexpected disruption' feel of this form.

keyPoint.label: -는 바람에 vs. -아서/-어서
keyPoint.body: -아서/-어서 states a plain cause for any kind of result, good or bad. -는 바람에 is saved for an unexpected cause that leads to a bad or unplanned result, and the second clause is normally in the past tense. You wouldn't say 열심히 공부하는 바람에 시험을 잘 봤어요 — for a good result, use -아서/-어서.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 늦는 sounds like [는는] in fast speech — the ㅈ of 늦 becomes [ㄴ] before the ㄴ of 는.

drill.instruction: Join the two facts with -는 바람에 (unexpected cause → bad result, second clause in past tense).
drill.model: 늦잠을 자다 / 학교에 늦다 → 늦잠을 자는 바람에 학교에 늦었어요.
items: 휴대폰을 잃어버리다 / 친구한테 연락 못 하다 → ____

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners use -는 바람에 for any cause, like a neutral 'because.' But -는 바람에 only fits an unexpected cause with a bad result. For a good result you brought about, use -아서/-어서 or -(은)ㄴ 덕분에 ('thanks to').

grammarNotes.title: -(으)ㄹ수록 — the more …, the more …
grammarNotes.func: -(으)ㄹ수록 attaches to a verb or adjective stem to mean "the more X happens, the more Y." It links a rising cause to a rising result, and is often paired with 점점 ("more and more").

formTable.when: Often doubled with the same verb + -(으)면

examples.en: The more I study Korean, the more fun it is.
examples.note: 공부하다 → 공부할수록 (vowel stem → ㄹ수록).

examples.en: The more I see my friend, the more I like them.
examples.note: 만나다 → 만날수록.

examples.en: The more I read this book, the harder it gets.
examples.note: 읽다 → 읽을수록 (consonant stem → 을수록).

examples.en: The more I look, the prettier it is.
examples.note: The doubled 보면 볼수록 frame is very common in speech.

keyPoint.label: Pair it with 점점
keyPoint.body: -(으)ㄹ수록 often comes with 점점 ("gradually, more and more") to stress the rising effect: 시간이 갈수록 점점 추워져요 ("as time goes on, it gets colder and colder"). The doubled V-(으)면 V-(으)ㄹ수록 form (알면 알수록) is a fixed, natural way to say "the more … the more."

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 읽을수록 is pronounced [일글쑤록]: the ㄱ links onto the following vowel and 수 tenses to [쑤].

drill.instruction: Make "the more …, the more …" sentences — follow the model.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Don't drop the (으)ㄹ. A vowel stem still needs the ㄹ (공부할수록), and a consonant stem needs 을 (먹을수록). It is never just stem + 수록.

grammarNotes.title: -기 위해서 — in order to / for the sake of
grammarNotes.func: -기 위해서 marks a purpose — the goal you do something for. Attach -기 위해서 to a verb stem ("in order to V"), or N을/를 위해서 to a noun ("for the sake of N"). The 서 is optional: 위해 = 위해서.

formTable.when: Verb stem + 기 위해서 ("in order to V")
formTable.ex: 배우다 → 배우기 위해서 · 사다 → 사기 위해서
건강 → 건강을 위해서 · 친구 → 친구를 위해서

examples.en: I came to Korea (in order) to learn Korean.
examples.note: 배우다 → 배우기 위해서. The goal comes first, the action second.

examples.en: I exercise every day for my health.
examples.note: Noun goal → 건강을 위해서.

examples.ko: 시험을 잘 보기 위해서 열심히 공부해요.
examples.romanization: si-heo-meul jal bo-gi wi-hae-seo yeol-sim-hi gong-bu-hae-yo.
examples.en: I study hard (in order) to do well on the exam.
examples.note: 보다 → 보기 위해서.

examples.en: I bought a gift for my friend.
examples.note: Noun + 를 위해서 = "for (the sake of)."

keyPoint.label: -기 위해서 vs -(으)러
keyPoint.body: Both express purpose, but -(으)러 attaches only to a verb and only pairs with going/coming verbs (가다/오다): 밥 먹으러 가요 (I go to eat). -기 위해서 is broader — any verb, any main clause, and it can also take a noun goal (건강을 위해서). Use -(으)러 for "go/come to do," and -기 위해서 for any purpose.

drill.instruction: State a purpose — follow the model.
drill.model: (한국어를 배우다 / 한국에 오다) → 한국어를 배우기 위해서 한국에 왔어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Don't forget the -기 that turns the verb into a noun-like form. It is verb-stem + 기 + 위해서 (배우기 위해서), never just verb + 위해서.

exampleSentence.en: The event got cancelled because of the rain.
exampleSentence.note: 취소되다 is passive — the subject is what was cancelled, not who cancelled it

exampleSentence.ko: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 옷이 다 젖었어요.
exampleSentence.en: My clothes got completely soaked because it suddenly started raining.
exampleSentence.note: 바람에 carries the nuance that the cause was unexpected or unwelcome, stronger than 때문에

exampleSentence.en: The more you practice, the fewer mistakes you make.
exampleSentence.note: Perfect partner for -(으)ㄹ수록: proportional improvement through practice

exampleSentence.en: The more you practice, the more your skills improve.
exampleSentence.note: 늘다 (to grow/increase) pairs naturally with 실력

exampleSentence.en: The more you use Korean, the more your skills grow.
exampleSentence.note: 늘다 is intransitive — the subject improves on its own; contrast with 늘리다 (to increase something intentionally)

exampleSentence.ko: 친구가 매일 야식을 먹더니 살이 찐 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: My friend kept eating late-night snacks, and it seems they gained weight.
exampleSentence.note: Classic -더니 scenario: you observed the habit over time → you're now noting the result

exampleSentence.en: They've been stressed lately, and they've gained weight.
exampleSentence.note: 살이 찌다 is an expression — 살 (flesh/fat) + 이 (subject marker) + 찌다 (to fatten/swell)

exampleSentence.en: It was clear, and then suddenly there was thunder.
exampleSentence.note: 갑자기 intensifies the contrast in -더니 sentences — the unexpected shift

exampleSentence.en: They kept working hard, and in the end they passed.
exampleSentence.note: 결국 often appears in the result clause of -더니 sentences, marking the endpoint of the observed sequence

exampleSentence.en: The more experience accumulates, the more confidence you gain.
exampleSentence.note: 쌓이다 is the passive of 쌓다 (to stack/pile); -ㄹ수록 pairs perfectly with gradual accumulation

exampleSentence.en: Korean food has more charm the more you know about it.
exampleSentence.note: 알다 (ㄹ-stem) drops ㄹ → 알수록. 매력이 있다 = to have charm/appeal

exampleSentence.en: The ratings were low, and in the end the drama was cancelled.
exampleSentence.note: 폐지되다 is the passive of 폐지하다 (to abolish/cancel); -더니 here: you observed the low ratings → you're reporting the outcome

exampleSentence.en: The more success experiences accumulate, the higher your self-confidence rises.
exampleSentence.note: 자신 (self/oneself) + 감 (feeling/sense) — a great -(으)ㄹ수록 vocabulary word

exampleSentence.ko: 친구가 요즘 너무 피곤하더니 결국 쓰러졌어요.
exampleSentence.en: My friend seemed so exhausted lately, and they finally collapsed.
exampleSentence.note: -더니 with an adjective: the speaker observed the state of exhaustion over time → reports the result

exampleSentence.en: The more effort you put in, the greater the sense of fulfillment you feel.
exampleSentence.note: 보람 is a uniquely Korean concept for the rewarding feeling that comes from effort well spent

exampleSentence.en: Korean seemed hard at first, and now it's gotten easier.
exampleSentence.note: -더니 with an adjective: earlier observation (it WAS hard) contrasted with a current changed state (now it's easy)

extendedVocabulary.english: to get used to / become accustomed

exampleSentence.en: The more you use it, the more accustomed you become.
exampleSentence.note: 익숙하다 (familiar/accustomed) + -아/어지다 (become) = getting used to. Perfect -(으)ㄹ수록 partner

extendedDialogue.setting: Jiyeon and her coworker Hyunwoo chat over coffee after a colleague's promotion

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 민준 씨가 몇 달 동안 매일 야근하더니 결국 팀장이 됐어요.
lines.romanization: Minjun ssiga myeot dal dongan maeil yageunhadeoni gyeolguk timjangi dwaesseoyo.
lines.en: Minjun worked late every night for months, and in the end he became team leader.
lines.grammarNote: -더니: Jiyeon personally watched the pattern of Minjun's overtime work (camera rolling) and now reports the natural outcome — his promotion

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 맞아요. 저도 봤어요. 열심히 하더니 잘 됐네요.
lines.romanization: Majayo. Jeodo bwasseoyo. Yeolsimhi hadeoni jal dwaenneyo.
lines.en: That's right. I saw it too. He worked hard and things worked out well.
lines.grammarNote: -더니 again: Hyunwoo confirming he also observed (watched) the same behavior pattern — shared camera footage, so to speak

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 사실 저도 더 노력해야겠다는 생각이 들었어요.
lines.romanization: Sasil jeodo deo noryeokhaeyagettaneun saenggagi deureosseoyo.
lines.en: Honestly, it made me think I should try harder too.
lines.grammarNote: No -더니 here — Jiyeon is talking about her own internal reaction, not an observation about another person

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 경험이 쌓일수록 기회도 많아지는 것 같아요.
lines.romanization: Gyeongheomi ssahilsurok gihoedo manajineun geot gatayo.
lines.en: It seems like the more experience piles up, the more opportunities come.
lines.grammarNote: 쌓이다 ㄹ-vowel ending → -ㄹ수록. -(으)ㄹ수록 captures the proportional scale: experience ↑ → opportunities ↑

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 맞아요. 일할수록 더 잘 알게 되는 것도 있고요.
lines.romanization: Majayo. Ilhalsurok deo jal alge doeneun geotdo itgoyo.
lines.en: True. And the more you work, the more you come to understand.
lines.grammarNote: 일하다 (consonant-free vowel stem 하) → 할수록 (contracted). Two proportional relationships in one sentence: work ↑ → understanding ↑

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 그런데 민준 씨가 처음에는 많이 힘들어하더니 이제는 여유가 생겼어요.
lines.romanization: Geureonde Minjun ssiga cheoeumeneun manhi himdeureohadeoni ijeneun yeoyuga saenggyeosseoyo.
lines.en: By the way, Minjun seemed to struggle a lot at first, and now he has breathing room.
lines.grammarNote: -더니 marks the contrast: EARLIER state (observed struggling) vs. CURRENT changed state (now relaxed) — the quintessential use of -더니 for contrast

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 저도 적응할수록 여유가 생길 거라고 믿어요.
lines.romanization: Jeodo jeogeunghalsurok yeoyuga saengil georago mideoyo.
lines.en: I believe the more I adapt, the more breathing room I'll get too.
lines.grammarNote: 적응하다 → 적응할수록. First-person -(으)ㄹ수록 expressing hope/belief about one's own proportional growth

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.ko: 물론이죠. 보면 볼수록 지연 씨도 잘하고 있는 게 보여요.
lines.romanization: Mulronijyo. Bomyeon bolsurok Jiyeon ssido jal hago inneun ge boyeoyo.
lines.en: Of course. The more I watch, the more I can see you're doing well too.
lines.grammarNote: 보면 볼수록: the emphatic -(으)면 V-(으)ㄹ수록 form — the most natural spoken pattern for 'the more X, the more Y'. 보여요 = it becomes visible/apparent

readingText.title: 성장의 기록 (A Record of Growth)
readingText.body: 처음 한국어를 시작했을 때는 발음이 너무 어렵더니 이제는 많이 익숙해졌어요. 그때는 ㄹ과 ㄴ 소리가 비슷하더니 지금은 차이가 잘 들려요. 발음을 고치기 위해서 매일 제 목소리를 녹음했고, 비가 오길래 집에서 혼자 따라 읽은 날도 많았어요. 한 번은 인터넷이 끊기는 바람에 온라인 수업을 못 들었지만, 그날도 포기하지 않고 복습했어요. 공부할수록 더 많은 것이 보이기 시작했어요. 처음에는 드라마 대사가 너무 빠르더니 요즘은 대충 내용을 이해해요. 어휘가 늘수록 한국 문화도 더 깊이 느껴지는 것 같아요. 가끔 힘들 때도 있지만, 노력할수록 보람이 커지는 게 느껴져요. 한국어는 정말 보면 볼수록 매력 있는 언어예요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: When I first started Korean, the pronunciation was so hard, but now I've gotten very accustomed to it. Back then the ㄹ and ㄴ sounds seemed similar, but now I can hear the difference clearly. To fix my pronunciation, I recorded my voice every day, and on many rainy days I noticed the rain and practiced reading aloud alone at home. Once, because the internet cut out unexpectedly, I missed an online class, but I still reviewed that day without giving up. The more I studied, the more things started to become visible. At first drama dialogue was too fast, but lately I roughly understand the content. The more my vocabulary grows, the more deeply I seem to feel Korean culture too. Sometimes it's difficult, but the more I put in effort, the more I can feel the sense of fulfillment growing. Korean really is a language that gets more charming the more you look at it.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What purpose action did the writer take to improve pronunciation?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 발음을 고치기 위해서 매일 제 목소리를 녹음했어요 — they recorded their voice every day in order to fix pronunciation. This uses -기 위해서 for a planned purpose.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two cause/reaction connectors appear in the middle of the diary?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 비가 오길래 집에서 혼자 따라 읽은 날도 많았어요 uses -길래: the writer noticed rain and reacted by practicing at home. 인터넷이 끊기는 바람에 온라인 수업을 못 들었어요 uses -는 바람에: the internet outage disrupted the online class.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all instances of -더니 and -(으)ㄹ수록 in the text. For each -더니, explain what was observed and what changed. For each -(으)ㄹ수록, identify the two proportional elements.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: -더니 instances: (1) 발음이 너무 어렵더니 — observed: pronunciation was difficult; changed: now accustomed. (2) ㄹ과 ㄴ 소리가 비슷하더니 — observed: the sounds seemed similar; changed: now the difference is clear. (3) 드라마 대사가 너무 빠르더니 — observed: drama dialogue was too fast; changed: now the writer roughly understands the content. -(으)ㄹ수록 instances: (1) 공부할수록 더 많은 것이 보이기 시작했어요 — study ↑ → visibility ↑. (2) 어휘가 늘수록 한국 문화도 더 깊이 느껴지는 것 같아요 — vocabulary ↑ → cultural feeling ↑. (3) 노력할수록 보람이 커지는 게 느껴져요 — effort ↑ → fulfillment ↑. (4) 보면 볼수록 매력 있는 언어 — exposure ↑ → charm ↑.

culturalNote.title: 보면 볼수록 — The most Korean way to express growing love for something
culturalNote.body: The phrase 보면 볼수록 (the more you look at/experience it) is a cultural formula in Korean for expressing that something deepens with time and exposure. Koreans use it constantly about food (먹을수록 맛있어 — the more you eat it, the better it tastes), people (알수록 좋은 사람이야 — the more you get to know them, the more you like them), and learning itself (한국어는 할수록 재미있어 — Korean gets more fun the more you do it). It reflects a cultural value of depth through perseverance — the appreciation that comes not at first glance, but after sustained engagement. When a Korean friend says 보면 볼수록 좋아 about something, it is one of the highest compliments possible: this thing rewards continued attention.

inlineExercises.prompt: 비가 오___ 집에서 연습했어요. (I noticed it was raining, so I practiced at home.)
inlineExercises.explanation: -길래 fits because the rain is something the speaker noticed, and practicing at home was the reaction. -기 위해서 would make the rain a purpose, which is impossible. -수록 would require a proportional 'the more...' relationship.

inlineExercises.prompt: 발표를 준비하___ 매일 연습해요. (I practice every day to prepare for the presentation.)
inlineExercises.explanation: Preparing for the presentation is the purpose of daily practice, so use -기 위해서. -는 바람에 would mean an unexpected disruption, and -더니 would report an observed sequence.

inlineExercises.prompt: 갑자기 인터넷이 끊기___ 온라인 수업을 못 들었어요. (The internet suddenly cut out, so I missed the online class.)
inlineExercises.explanation: The internet outage unexpectedly disrupted the plan, so -는 바람에 is the right connector. -기 위해서 gives purpose, and -(으)ㄹ수록 gives proportional change.

inlineExercises.prompt: 친구가 매일 운동하___ 날씬해졌어요. (My friend kept exercising and then became slimmer.)
inlineExercises.explanation: This is a CAMERA REPLAY situation: you personally watched your friend exercise over time (camera rolling) and are reporting the observed result (became slimmer). -(으)ㄹ수록 would express a proportional scale (the more they exercise, the slimmer they get) — ongoing, not a reported sequence. -길래 would mean you reacted to something yourself, which doesn't fit here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 한국어는 공부___ 더 재미있어요. (The more you study Korean, the more fun it gets.)
inlineExercises.explanation: The 'the more X, the more Y' proportional scale pattern requires -(으)ㄹ수록. 하다 has a vowel-class stem 하 → 할수록. -더니 would report an observed past change, not a proportional ongoing relationship. -해서 would give a simple cause-and-effect (I studied, so...) with no sense of proportionality.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '저는 열심히 운동하더니 건강해졌어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Plain -더니 is for observations about OTHERS. When the speaker describes the result of their OWN past action, the past tense form -았/었더니 is required. 운동하더니 with 저는 sounds like you somehow watched yourself from outside — unnatural. 운동했더니 = after I exercised (my own action), I found that I became healthier.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'The more experience you gain, the more confident you become.'
inlineExercises.hint: The stem 쌓이- ends in a vowel, so -(으)ㄹ수록 attaches as ㄹ수록: 쌓일수록. What word means 'confidence develops'?
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ수록 makes the 'the more X, the more Y' structure. 경험이 쌓이다 and 자신감이 생기다 are natural pairings for experience increasing and confidence appearing.

inlineExercises.prompt: You saw your colleague looking exhausted every day for weeks, and then they took sick leave. Which sentence is most natural?
options: 동료가 매일 피곤해 보이더니 결국 병가를 냈어요.
inlineExercises.correct: 동료가 매일 피곤해 보이더니 결국 병가를 냈어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Option B (-더니) is correct: you personally observed your colleague looking tired over multiple days (camera rolling), then report the outcome (sick leave). Option A (-ㄹ수록) would mean 'the more tired they looked, the more sick leave they took' — a proportional scale that doesn't match the scenario. Option C (-길래) would mean the tiredness prompted YOU to take an action yourself, not describing their sick leave.

inlineExercises.prompt: 서울은 살___ 더 좋아지는 것 같아요. (The longer you live in Seoul, the more you come to like it.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 살다 is an ㄹ-stem verb. ㄹ-stems drop their ㄹ and attach -(으)ㄹ수록 as -ㄹ수록: 살다 → 살 + -ㄹ수록 → 살수록. This expresses the proportional scale: time in Seoul ↑ → appreciation ↑. -더니 would report an observed change (you watched and noted a result), not a proportional relationship. -아서 is a simple cause connector.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses -(으)ㄹ수록 with the correct attachment?
inlineExercises.explanation: 읽다 ends in a consonant cluster (ㄱ final). Consonant-ending stems take -을수록: 읽 + 을수록 = 읽을수록. Option A (읽수록) skips the vowel buffer -을 needed after a consonant — this is wrong. Option C (읽어수록) confuses the polite ending 어요 with the -수록 attachment — 수록 never uses the -아/어 vowel; it attaches via -을/ㄹ.

inlineExercises.prompt: 발표___ 준비하기 위해서 매일 연습해요. (I practice every day to prepare a presentation.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 준비하다 takes the thing being prepared as an object, so 발표를 fits. 가 would make 발표 the subject, not the preparation target.

inlineExercises.prompt: 서울은 살___ 더 좋아져요. (살다 → the more)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ수록 means “the more.” 살다 has ㄹ already in the stem, so the natural form is 살수록.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'The internet suddenly cut out, so I missed class.'
inlineExercises.correct: 갑자기 인터넷이 끊기는 바람에 수업을 못 들었어요
inlineExercises.explanation: -는 바람에 frames the cause as an unexpected disruption. 못 들었어요 gives the bad result that followed.

bullets: -더니 = CAMERA REPLAY: you watched X happen (about someone else or a situation), then Y followed — use -았/었더니 for your OWN past actions
-길래 = NOTICED AND REACTED: a clue caught your attention, so you did something
-는 바람에 = DISRUPTED CAUSE: an unexpected event caused an unwanted result
-(으)ㄹ수록 = SLIDING SCALE: as one thing increases, another increases proportionally — the -면 V-ㄹ수록 form is the most natural spoken version
-기 위해서 = PURPOSE ARROW: a planned action points toward a goal

writingTask.prompt: Write a short story in one connected paragraph about how a late-night snack habit led you to a decision, joining your ideas smoothly.
writingTask.hint: Connect clauses with -더니, -길래, -는 바람에, -(으)ㄹ수록, and -기 위해서.
writingTask.model: 친구가 야식을 자주 먹더니 살이 많이 쪘어요. 저도 배가 고프길래 같이 먹었어요. 그런데 늦게 자는 바람에 다음 날 너무 피곤했어요. 야식은 먹을수록 끊기 어려워서, 건강을 지키기 위해서 이제 안 먹기로 했어요.
writingTask.modelEn: My friend kept eating late-night snacks and then gained a lot of weight. I was hungry too, so I ate with him. But because I went to bed late, I was so tired the next day. The more you eat midnight snacks the harder they are to quit, so to protect my health I've decided not to eat them anymore.

canDo: Link what I noticed to what followed (-더니)
Give the outside trigger behind my own reaction (-길래)
Blame an unexpected cause for a bad result (-는 바람에)
Express 'the more…, the more…' (-(으)ㄹ수록) and state a purpose (-기 위해서)

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: A friend asks, '어제 뭐 했어요?' If you answer in present tense — 영화 봐요, 밥 먹어요 — it sounds like you are talking about your usual routine or what you do now. For yesterday, Korean needs the polite past frame: 봤어요, 먹었어요, 갔어요, 했어요.
objectives: Build polite past-tense sentences with -았/었어요
Choose 았어요 vs 었어요 from the last vowel of the stem
Handle the first everyday contractions and irregulars: 했어요, 봤어요, 왔어요, 추웠어요
hook.whyItMatters: Past tense is the grammar that lets beginners tell real stories. You use it after class, on KakaoTalk, when explaining why you are late, and any time someone asks what happened. A clean short past sentence sounds much more natural than a long sentence with the wrong tense.

grammarNotes.title: V았/었어요 — the polite past tense
grammarNotes.func: Use V았/었어요 to say an action or state happened in the past. It is the polite, everyday way to answer questions like "What did you do yesterday?"

formTable.when: Stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ
formTable.ex: 가다 → 갔어요, 보다 → 봤어요, 살다 → 살았어요

formTable.when: Any other vowel (ㅓ, ㅜ, ㅣ, ㅡ, ㅔ …)
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹었어요, 마시다 → 마셨어요, 읽다 → 읽었어요
하다 → 했어요, 공부하다 → 공부했어요, 일하다 → 일했어요

examples.en: I met a friend yesterday.
examples.note: 만나다's stem 만나- ends in ㅏ, so -았 contracts: 만나 + 았 → 만났어요.

examples.en: I ate (a meal) in the morning.
examples.note: 먹- has the vowel ㅓ, so it takes -었어요 (no contraction).

examples.en: I studied Korean at home yesterday.
examples.note: 공부하다 is a 하다 verb, so 하다 → 했어요 → 공부했어요.

examples.en: I watched a movie over the weekend.
examples.note: 보다's stem 보- ends in ㅗ, so 보 + 았 → 봤어요.

keyPoint.label: 이다 → 였어요 / 이었어요
keyPoint.body: The copula 이다 ("to be") has its own past form. After a vowel use 였어요 (친구이다 → 친구였어요), and after a final consonant use 이었어요 (학생이다 → 학생이었어요; 책이다 → 책이었어요). For now just memorize these two endings — the full ins and outs of 이다 come in its home chapter.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 먹었어요 links across the boundary and sounds like [머거써요]; 했어요 sounds like [해써요] — the 어 is swallowed and the ㅆ is tense.

drill.instruction: Change each verb into the polite past form V았/었어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English often leans on the time word ("yesterday") and leaves the verb in its plain form. In Korean the verb itself has to carry the past tense — adding 어제 (yesterday) does not make 가요 mean "went." You have to change 가요 to 갔어요.
