readingText.title: 어제 한 일
readingText.body: 어제는 수업이 끝난 뒤에 친구를 만났어요. 같이 카페에 갔고, 저는 커피를 마셨어요. 친구는 차를 마셨어요. 그다음 영화를 봤어요. 영화는 조금 길었지만 마지막 장면이 정말 재미있었어요. 집에 올 때는 날씨가 추웠어요. 그래서 집에 오자마자 따뜻한 물을 마시고 바로 잤어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Yesterday, after class ended, I met a friend. We went to a cafe together, and I drank coffee. My friend drank tea. Then we watched a movie. The movie was a little long, but the last scene was really fun. When I came home, the weather was cold. So as soon as I got home, I drank warm water and went straight to sleep.

culturalNote.title: Short Past Answers Sound Natural
culturalNote.body: When Koreans ask 어제 뭐 했어요?, they are often opening a small everyday conversation, not asking for a long report. A natural answer can be short: 친구 만났어요, 영화 봤어요, 집에서 쉬었어요. Once the tense is clean, you can add one detail: 누구랑, 어디에서, 어땠는지. Accurate short past sentences are better than long translated sentences with the wrong ending.
culturalNote.tip: Answer in one finished event first, then add time, person, or place.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: A friend asks, '주말에 뭐 할 거예요?' You are not reporting what you usually do; you are stating a plan. Korean uses -(으)ㄹ 거예요 for that: 만날 거예요, 갈 거예요, 공부할 거예요. The same frame also works for predictions like 비가 올 거예요.
objectives: Use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 for future plans and intentions
Choose -ㄹ 거예요 after vowel stems and -을 거예요 after consonant stems
Distinguish a general future plan from a promise made to the listener with -(으)ㄹ게요
hook.whyItMatters: This is the frame learners need for weekend plans, travel plans, homework plans, weather guesses, and 'what are you going to do?' conversations. Without it, you can name activities but not place them clearly in the future.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 — saying what you'll do (plans, intentions, predictions)
grammarNotes.func: Use V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 to say what you plan or mean to do, or to guess what will happen. It's the everyday polite way to say "will" or "be going to" — perfect for weekend plans, what you'll eat, or what the weather will do.

formTable.ex: 가다 → 갈 거예요, 보다 → 볼 거예요, 하다 → 할 거예요
먹다 → 먹을 거예요, 읽다 → 읽을 거예요

formTable.add: keep ㄹ, add 거예요 (don't add 을)
formTable.ex: 살다 → 살 거예요, 만들다 → 만들 거예요

examples.en: I'm going to meet a friend tomorrow.
examples.note: 만나다 ends in a vowel, so just add ㄹ 거예요. This is a plan.

examples.en: I'm going to eat at home this evening.
examples.note: 먹다 ends in a consonant, so add 을 거예요.

examples.en: I'm going to watch a movie this weekend.
examples.note: 보다 → 볼 거예요. A simple plan with a friend-talk feel.

examples.en: It'll probably rain tomorrow.
examples.note: Here 오다 is a guess about the weather, not a personal plan — the same form covers both.

keyPoint.label: 거예요 (your plan) vs. 게요 (a promise to me)
keyPoint.body: Both look to the future. -(으)ㄹ 거예요 just states your plan or a guess: 제가 할 거예요 (I plan to do it). -(으)ㄹ게요 is something you promise the listener right now: 제가 할게요 (I'll do it / I promise). Quick tell: weather and other people can take 거예요 (비가 올 거예요), but never 게요 — rain can't promise you anything. You'll practice 게요 more later; for now, default to 거예요 for plans and guesses.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 거예요 is said like [거에요]. The ㄹ before it makes the 거 tense, so 갈 거예요 sounds like [갈 꺼예요] and 먹을 거예요 like [머글 꺼예요].

drill.instruction: Turn each verb into a future-plan sentence with V-(으)ㄹ 거예요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 제가 갈 거 있어요. / 제가 갈게 거예요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Because "I'm going to go" feels like two verbs in English, learners try to bolt on an extra 있어요 or mix in 게. But -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is already a finished sentence ending. Just attach -(으)ㄹ 거예요 straight onto the stem — nothing comes after it.

exampleSentence.note: 하다 → 할 거예요.

exampleSentence.en: It will probably rain tomorrow.
exampleSentence.note: Weather uses -(으)ㄹ 거예요 as prediction.

exampleSentence.en: I am going to travel during vacation.
exampleSentence.note: 여행을 가다 is the common phrase.

exampleSentence.en: I am going to do homework tonight.
exampleSentence.note: A practical student plan sentence.

exampleSentence.ko: 내일 약속이 있어서 일찍 나갈 거예요.
exampleSentence.en: I have plans tomorrow, so I am going to leave early.
exampleSentence.note: 약속 often means a social appointment.

exampleSentence.en: I am going to watch a movie with a friend.
exampleSentence.note: 보다 → 볼 거예요.

exampleSentence.en: I am going to go to a new cafe.
exampleSentence.note: 카페에 marks destination.

exampleSentence.en: I am going to meet up with a friend.
exampleSentence.note: 친구랑 makes the plan conversational.

extendedDialogue.setting: Two friends make weekend plans and adjust them if the weather changes.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: What are you going to do this weekend?
lines.grammarNote: 하다 → 할 거예요. This asks about a future plan.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 토요일에는 친구를 만나서 새 카페에 갈 거예요.
lines.romanization: toyoireneun chingureul mannaseo sae kape-e gal geoyeyo.
lines.en: On Saturday I am going to meet a friend and go to a new cafe.
lines.grammarNote: 가다 → 갈 거예요; 만나서 links the first planned action to the second.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: What about Sunday?
lines.grammarNote: A natural follow-up that keeps the plan conversation moving.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 비가 오면 집에서 시험공부를 할 거예요.
lines.romanization: biga omyeon jibeseo siheomgongbureul hal geoyeyo.
lines.en: If it rains, I am going to study for the exam at home.
lines.grammarNote: 오면 sets the condition; 할 거예요 gives the planned response.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 저는 영화 볼 거예요. 같이 볼래요?
lines.romanization: jeoneun yeonghwa bol geoyeyo. gachi bollaeyo?
lines.en: I am going to watch a movie. Do you want to watch together?
lines.grammarNote: 볼 거예요 is a plan. 볼래요? asks about the other person's willingness.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Sounds good. When I finish my homework, I'll contact you.
lines.grammarNote: 연락할게요 is a promise to the listener, so -ㄹ게요 is better than -ㄹ 거예요 here.

readingText.title: 이번 주말 계획
readingText.body: 이번 주말에는 조금 바쁠 거예요. 토요일 오전에는 숙제를 할 거예요. 오후에는 친구를 만나서 새 카페에 갈 거예요. 카페에서 커피를 마시고 다음 주 여행 계획을 세울 거예요. 일기예보를 보니까 일요일에는 비가 올 거예요. 그래서 집에서 영화를 보고 한국어 단어를 복습할 거예요. 시간이 있으면 저녁에 산책도 할 거예요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: This weekend will be a little busy. On Saturday morning, I am going to do homework. In the afternoon, I am going to meet a friend and go to a new cafe. At the cafe, we will drink coffee and make plans for next week's trip. According to the weather forecast, it will probably rain on Sunday. So I am going to watch a movie at home and review Korean vocabulary. If I have time, I will also take a walk in the evening.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What will the writer do on Saturday morning?
Find two future plan forms and one prediction form.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: Plans: 숙제를 할 거예요, 카페에 갈 거예요, 복습할 거예요. Prediction: 비가 올 거예요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why is 갈 거예요 used but 먹을 거예요 would use 을?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 가다 has a vowel-ending stem, so it takes ㄹ: 갈 거예요. 먹다 has a consonant-ending stem, so it takes 을: 먹을 거예요.

culturalNote.title: Plans Are Often Softened
culturalNote.body: Koreans often ask about plans with 뭐 할 거예요? or 주말에 계획 있어요? A direct answer like 친구 만날 거예요 is fine. If the plan is not fixed, soften it with 아마 or 것 같아요: 아마 집에서 쉴 거예요, 카페에 갈 것 같아요. For a promise to the listener, switch to -(으)ㄹ게요: 제가 연락할게요.
culturalNote.tip: Use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 for your plan; use -(으)ㄹ게요 when you are promising the listener.

inlineExercises.prompt: A friend asks about your weekend plan. Which answer fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: -ㄹ 거예요 presents a future plan or intention.

inlineExercises.prompt: 내일 친구를 만___ 거예요. (만나다)
inlineExercises.explanation: 만나다 has the stem 만나-. Add ㄹ 거예요: 만날 거예요.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저녁에 김밥을 ___ 거예요. (먹다)
inlineExercises.explanation: 먹다 ends in a consonant, so use -을 거예요: 먹을 거예요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence is a weather prediction, not a promise?
inlineExercises.explanation: Rain cannot make a promise, so use -ㄹ 거예요 for prediction.

inlineExercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: 제가 연락할 거예요. (You are promising the listener right now.)
inlineExercises.explanation: For a promise or offer made to the listener, -(으)ㄹ게요 is more natural than -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'If it rains, I am going to study at home.'
inlineExercises.hint: Use 오면 for 'if it rains' and 하다 → 할 거예요.
inlineExercises.explanation: -면 sets the condition, 'if it rains.' 공부할 거예요 marks the plan or future action that follows from that condition.

inlineExercises.prompt: 주말___ 친구를 만날 거예요. (I will meet a friend on the weekend.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 주말에 marks when the plan happens. 에서 would mark an action place, not the time of the plan.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저녁에 김밥을 ___ . (먹다 → future plan)
inlineExercises.explanation: Consonant-ending stems take -을 거예요 for future plans. 먹다 becomes 먹을 거예요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I'm going to travel tomorrow.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 내일 sets the future time. 여행을 가다 is the natural chunk for going on a trip, and 갈 거예요 marks the plan.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '내일 친구를 만나 거예요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Future plans use the modifier before 거예요. 만나다 becomes 만날 거예요, not 만나 거예요.

bullets: Future arrow: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 points forward to plans, intentions, or predictions.
Vowel stem → -ㄹ 거예요: 가다→갈 거예요, 보다→볼 거예요, 하다→할 거예요.
Consonant stem → -을 거예요: 먹다→먹을 거예요, 읽다→읽을 거예요.
Do not use -ㄹ게요 for weather or third-person predictions; use it for your promise to the listener.

writingTask.prompt: Write 3 sentences about your weekend plans: where you'll go, what you'll eat, and what you'll do.
writingTask.hint: Use V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 for each plan (갈 거예요, 먹을 거예요).
writingTask.model: 이번 주말에 친구를 만날 거예요. 같이 영화를 볼 거예요. 그리고 맛있는 밥을 먹을 거예요.
writingTask.modelEn: This weekend I'm going to meet a friend. We'll watch a movie together. And we'll eat a delicious meal.

canDo: Say a future plan or intention with V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 (갈 거예요)
Choose -ㄹ 거예요 vs -을 거예요 from the 받침 (볼 거예요 · 먹을 거예요)
Make a guess about what will happen (비가 올 거예요)
Talk about weekend and tomorrow plans (주말 · 내일 · 계획)

dialogue.speaker: B

dialogue.speaker: B

dialogue.speaker: B

dialogue.romanization: hanguk chingudeulgwa deo pyeonhage iyagihago sipeoseoyo.

dialogue.speaker: B

chapters.guidedPractice: Write one question each with 뭐, 어디, 언제, 왜, 어떻게, 누구, then answer three of them in Korean.
chapters.realLifeTask: Give one short route using 로/으로 for direction or transport.
chapters.friendPractice: Partner says 한국어를 배워요. Ask three follow-up questions using different question words, then listen for the answer slot.
chapters.review: Can you explain the difference between 어디에 가요? and 어디에서 공부해요?

beginnerGuide.title: Question words replace answers
beginnerGuide.body: Think from the answer first. 학교에서 공부해요 becomes 어디에서 공부해요? 친구를 만나요 becomes 누구를 만나요?

beginnerGuide.title: Particles still matter
beginnerGuide.body: Use 어디에 for destination or location, 어디에서 for the place where an action happens, 누구를 for the person you meet, and 누구랑 for the person you do something with.

beginnerGuide.title: Do not mix up 어떻게 and 어때요
beginnerGuide.body: 어떻게 asks how to do something: 어떻게 가요? 어때요 asks for an opinion or condition: 영화 어때요?

checkpoints: I can use 로/으로 for direction, route, and transport method.
I can use -(으)러 가요 for going to do something.
I can ask 몇 번 출구로 가요? when I need an exit.

learningLayers.label: Expand

sampleAnswer.ko: 지하철로 가세요. 삼 번 출구로 나가서 오른쪽으로 가세요.
sampleAnswer.en: Go by subway. Go out exit three and go to the right.

checklist: I can use 로/으로 for direction, route, and transport method.
I can use -(으)러 가요 for going to do something.
I can ask 몇 번 출구로 가요? when I need an exit.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: Asking natural follow-up questions in Korean: what, where, when, why, how, who, how many, what kind, and which one.
objectives: Choose the question word that matches the missing information.
Keep the question word in the position where the answer would normally appear.
Use particles with question words: 어디에, 어디에서, 누구를, 누구랑, 몇 시에.
hook.whyItMatters: Good follow-up questions make conversation continue. If learners only memorize isolated words like 뭐 or 어디, they often ask unclear questions. This chapter connects each question word to the sentence role it actually fills.

grammarNotes.title: Question words (누구, 뭐, 어디, 언제, 왜, 어떻게, 몇, 얼마)
grammarNotes.func: Question words ask for one missing piece of info — who, what, where, when, why, how, how many, how much. The big thing: in Korean the question word sits in the exact spot the answer would go. It does not jump to the front like English 'where' or 'what' does.

formTable.add: 누구 + 가 → 누가 (subject); 누구 + 를 (object); 누구 + 예요
formTable.ex: 누가 와요? / 누구를 만나요? / 이 사람 누구예요?

formTable.add: 뭐 + 예요; 뭐 + 를 → 뭘 (object). 무엇 is the written form, rare in speech
formTable.ex: 이거 뭐예요? / 뭘 먹어요? / 뭐 해요?

formTable.add: 어디 + 예요; 어디 + 에 (where you go / where something is); 어디 + 에서 (where you do something)
formTable.ex: 집이 어디예요? / 어디에 가요? / 어디에서 일해요?

formTable.when: when / why / how — 언제, 왜, 어떻게
formTable.add: no particle — they work like adverbs on their own
formTable.ex: 언제 와요? / 왜 안 와요? / 어떻게 가요?

formTable.when: how many / how much — 몇 + counter, 얼마
formTable.ex: 몇 개예요? / 몇 시예요? / 이거 얼마예요?

examples.en: Who is this person?
examples.note: 누구 sits right where the answer goes: 제 친구예요 (It's my friend). Same slot, just swap the word.

examples.en: What do you eat for lunch?
examples.note: 뭘 (뭐+를) stays in the object slot before the verb. Answer 밥을 먹어요 fills the very same slot.

examples.en: Where do you work?
examples.note: 어디 takes 에서 because work happens there (an action). Answer 회사에서 일해요 keeps the same 에서.

examples.en: How much is this?
examples.note: 얼마 is the normal word for asking a price. Answer 만 원이에요 drops right into the 얼마 spot.

keyPoint.label: The question word stays where the answer goes
keyPoint.body: English moves the question word up front: 'WHAT do you eat?' Korean leaves it in place, right before the verb: 뭐 먹어요? → 밥 먹어요. Look at the slot: 밥 먹어요 / 뭐 먹어요 — same spot, you just swap 밥 for 뭐. So think of the answer first, then drop the question word into its slot. (어디 still needs 에 or 에서 — that comes next.)

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 누구 + 가 squeezes down to 누가 (the 구 disappears, it doesn't just link). 뭐 + 를 squeezes to 뭘. 무엇을 links over the patchim and sounds like [무어슬].

drill.instruction: Turn each statement into a question. Swap the underlined answer for the matching question word and leave it in the same slot (keep the particle).

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: From English, people want to swing the question word to the very front of the sentence (Where do you go?). In Korean it does not move up front and it never goes after the verb — it stays in the answer's slot, right before the verb. So it's 어디 가요?, not 가요 어디? and not 어디 가요 fronted away from its slot.

exampleSentence.en: What are you doing today?
exampleSentence.note: Use 뭐 for things, actions, food, plans, or objects.

exampleSentence.en: Where are you going on the weekend?
exampleSentence.note: Pair 어디 with 에 for destination/location and 에서 for action place.

exampleSentence.en: When does class start?
exampleSentence.note: 언제 asks for time without needing a counter.

exampleSentence.en: Why do you study Korean?
exampleSentence.note: 왜 expects a reason, not a place or time answer.

exampleSentence.en: How do you memorize Korean words?
exampleSentence.note: 어떻게 asks method. For opinion, use 어때요?

exampleSentence.en: Whom are you meeting today?
exampleSentence.note: Attach the role: 누구가 becomes 누가, but 누구를 and 누구랑 stay visible.

extendedVocabulary.english: how much; how long; to what degree

exampleSentence.en: How long does it take to get to work?
exampleSentence.note: 얼마나 asks about degree, distance, time length, or frequency.

exampleSentence.en: How many people are coming to the study group?
exampleSentence.note: 몇 needs a number word or counter such as 시, 명, 개, 번.

exampleSentence.en: What kind of music do you like?
exampleSentence.note: Use 무슨 before a noun when asking the kind, name, or category.

exampleSentence.en: Which cafe shall we meet at?
exampleSentence.note: Use 어느 when choosing among options the listener can imagine.

exampleSentence.en: If you have a question, please ask now.
exampleSentence.note: 질문 pairs naturally with 하다, 있다, and 물어보다.

exampleSentence.en: Why is there no answer?
exampleSentence.note: 대답 is a spoken or written reply to a question.

exampleSentence.en: What is the reason?
exampleSentence.note: 이유 helps expand 왜 questions into clearer follow-ups.

exampleSentence.en: Is there a good way?
exampleSentence.note: 방법 helps turn 어떻게 into a fuller question about method.

lines.speaker: 민서

lines.grammarNote: 언제 asks for the time.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: I started last year.
lines.grammarNote: The answer fills the time slot.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Why do you study Korean?
lines.grammarNote: 왜 asks for a reason.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 한국 친구들과 더 편하게 이야기하고 싶어서요.
lines.romanization: hanguk chingudeulgwa deo pyeonhage iyagihago sipeoseoyo.
lines.en: Because I want to talk more comfortably with Korean friends.

readingText.title: A study-plan chat
readingText.body: 민서는 새 스터디에 들어가기 전에 지훈에게 여러 가지를 물어봤어요. 먼저 어디에서 모이는지 물었고, 지훈은 학교 앞 카페에서 만난다고 대답했어요. 민서는 몇 시에 시작하는지도 물었어요. 지훈은 토요일 두 시에 시작한다고 했어요. 민서가 왜 그 스터디를 만들었냐고 묻자, 지훈은 혼자 공부하면 자꾸 미뤄서 친구들과 같이 연습하고 싶었다고 했어요. 마지막으로 민서는 어떻게 준비하면 좋으냐고 물었고, 지훈은 짧은 자기소개와 질문 세 개를 준비하면 된다고 말했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Before joining a new study group, Minseo asked Jihoon several questions. She asked where they meet, what time they start, why he made the group, and how she should prepare. Jihoon answered each question with the missing place, time, reason, and method.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 처음에 무엇을 물어봤어요?
스터디는 몇 시에 시작해요?
민서는 마지막으로 무엇을 물어봤어요?

culturalNote.title: Follow-up questions should feel connected
culturalNote.body: In Korean conversation, a follow-up question often reuses the other person's topic instead of starting from zero. If someone says 한국어를 배워요, natural follow-ups are 어디에서요?, 언제부터요?, 왜요?, 어떻게 연습해요?, and 누구랑요?
culturalNote.tip: Short follow-ups with 요 can sound natural after the topic is already clear: 어디에서요? 왜요? 누구랑요?

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to ask where someone studies. Which form fits the action place?
inlineExercises.explanation: 공부하다 is an action, so the place of the action takes -에서.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which answer naturally responds to 왜 한국어를 공부해요?
inlineExercises.explanation: 왜 expects a reason, often answered with -아서/어서요 or -고 싶어서요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Ask 'Who are you meeting today?' in Korean.
inlineExercises.explanation: The person you meet is the object, so 누구를 is the full form.

inlineExercises.prompt: Ask 'What time does class start?' using 몇.
inlineExercises.explanation: 몇 combines with 시 to ask for clock time.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the question: 어떻게 영화였어요?
inlineExercises.explanation: Use 어땠어요 for 'How was it?' 어떻게 asks method, as in 어떻게 갔어요?

inlineExercises.prompt: 어디___ 일해요? (Where do you work?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 일하다 is an action, so the place where it happens takes 에서. 에 would fit a destination or static location, not work happening there.

inlineExercises.prompt: Ask: 'How much is this?'
inlineExercises.explanation: 얼마 asks about price. 이거 sets “this thing” as what you are asking about.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'When are you coming?'
inlineExercises.explanation: 언제 asks for time and sits before the verb. Korean keeps the question word in the answer slot rather than moving it far away.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the question: '누구가 와요?'
inlineExercises.explanation: 누구 + 가 always contracts to 누가 — 누구가 is not used in standard Korean. The correct subject question is 누가 와요?

inlineExercises.prompt: Which question asks about method or way?
inlineExercises.explanation: 어떻게 asks “how” or by what method. 언제 asks time, and 왜 asks reason.

bullets: Question words match the missing information: 뭐, 어디, 언제, 왜, 어떻게, 누구.
Particles still matter: 어디에, 어디에서, 누구를, 누구랑, 몇 시에.
몇, 무슨, and 어느 attach before nouns: 몇 명, 무슨 뜻, 어느 카페.
Best check: answer the question and see whether the answer fits the same slot.

writingTask.prompt: You just met someone new — write 3 short questions to keep the conversation going: ask where they live, what they do on weekends, and when they're free.
writingTask.hint: Put the question word in the answer's slot, with no inversion (어디 살아요? / 주말에 뭐 해요? / 언제 시간이 있어요?).
writingTask.model: 어디에 살아요? 주말에 보통 뭐 해요? 언제 시간이 있어요?
writingTask.modelEn: Where do you live? What do you usually do on weekends? When are you free?

canDo: Ask who, what, where with question words in the answer's slot (누구 · 뭐 · 어디)
Ask when and why without changing word order (언제 · 왜)
Ask how, how many, and how much (어떻게 · 몇 · 얼마나)
Ask follow-up questions that keep a conversation moving (질문 · 대답)

beginnerGuide.title: The unit chooses the number family
beginnerGuide.body: Hours and common counters use native numbers: 한 시, 두 잔, 세 명. Minutes, dates, and prices use Sino-Korean numbers: 십 분, 이월 삼일, 오천 원.

beginnerGuide.title: Native numbers change before counters
beginnerGuide.body: 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷 become 한, 두, 세, 네 before counters: 한 시, 두 잔, 세 명, 네 개.

beginnerGuide.title: Age needs politeness
beginnerGuide.body: 나이가 어떻게 되세요? is a safer polite question than 몇 살이에요? with adults or people you do not know well.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: Arranging a meeting time, counting items, reading dates, asking prices, and talking about age without mixing the two Korean number systems.
objectives: Use native Korean numbers for hours and common counters: 한 시, 두 잔, 세 명.
Use Sino-Korean numbers for minutes, dates, prices, phone-style numbers, and floors: 십 분, 이월 삼일, 오천 원.
Recognize common number questions: 몇 시, 몇 분, 몇 잔, 얼마예요, 나이가 어떻게 되세요?
hook.whyItMatters: Korean numbers are not random; the object being counted chooses the number family. Once learners know the common pairings, time, prices, dates, and simple shopping conversations become much more predictable.

grammarNotes.title: Two number systems: native (하나·둘·셋) vs. Sino-Korean (일·이·삼)
grammarNotes.func: Korean has two full sets of numbers, and which one you use depends on what you're saying — not on which you like better. Native numbers count things, people, and the o'clock hour. Sino-Korean numbers handle money, minutes, dates, and phone numbers. The clock uses both at once: native for the hour, Sino for the minute.

formTable.when: Counting things, people, or animals (with a counter)
formTable.add: Native 하나·둘·셋·넷, but 1–4 shorten before a counter → 한·두·세·네
formTable.ex: 사과 한 개 (one apple), 친구 두 명 (two friends)

formTable.add: Native number + 시 (1–4 shorten here too)
formTable.ex: 세 시 (3 o'clock), 네 시 (4 o'clock)
삼십 분 (30 minutes), 오천 원 (5,000 won)

formTable.add: Native + 살 in daily talk; Sino + 세 on official forms
formTable.ex: 스무 살 (20 years old, everyday), 이십 세 (on forms)

examples.en: One bottle of water, please.
examples.note: Counting a thing, so native — and 하나 shortens to 한 before the counter 병.

examples.en: It's 3:30 now.
examples.note: The hour 시 takes native 세, but the minute 분 takes Sino 삼십 — both systems in one time.

examples.en: This book is 5,000 won.
examples.note: Money is always Sino (오천), never 다섯천.

examples.ko: 우리 반에 학생이 열 명 있어요.
examples.romanization: uri ban-e haksaeng-i yeol myeong isseoyo.
examples.en: There are ten students in our class.
examples.note: Counting people with 명, so native 열 — and 열 keeps its shape; only 한·두·세·네 and 스무 change.

keyPoint.label: The clock uses both systems
keyPoint.body: The hour (시) is native: 한 시, 두 시, 세 시. The minute (분) is Sino: 일 분, 십 분, 삼십 분. So 3:20 is 세 시 이십 분 — native for the hour, Sino for the minute. If you can remember this one phrase, you've got the whole rule. (Which counter goes with which number is a later topic; for now just lock in hour vs. minute.)

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 여섯 개 sounds like [여섣 깨] and 일곱 시 like [일곱 씨] — the counter's first consonant tenses after the number's final consonant. Also remember the short forms before a counter: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무.

drill.instruction: Say each one out loud, picking the right number system and the right form before the counter.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: In English one set of numbers does everything, so it's tempting to grab the more familiar Sino 삼 for '3 o'clock.' But the hour is always native: 세 시. The flip side of the same habit is reaching for native 다섯 to say money (다섯천 원) instead of Sino 오천 원. Quick check before you speak: am I counting things or hours (native), or saying money, minutes, or a date (Sino)?

exampleSentence.en: Please give me one apple.
exampleSentence.note: Before many counters, 하나 becomes 한: 한 개, 한 명, 한 시.

exampleSentence.en: Please give me two cups of coffee.
exampleSentence.note: Before counters, 둘 becomes 두.

exampleSentence.en: I have class at three o'clock.
exampleSentence.note: Before counters, 셋 becomes 세.

exampleSentence.en: Please wait just one minute.
exampleSentence.note: Use 일 with minutes, dates, prices, floors, and phone-style numbers.

exampleSentence.en: I am going to Korea in February.
exampleSentence.note: Use 이 for Sino-Korean number settings such as months and prices.

exampleSentence.en: It is 3,000 won.
exampleSentence.note: Use 삼 in prices, dates, and minutes, but not for clock hour three.

exampleSentence.en: What time is it now?
exampleSentence.note: 몇 combines with a counter or number unit: 몇 시, 몇 분, 몇 명, 몇 개.

exampleSentence.en: Let's meet at two o'clock.
exampleSentence.note: Clock hours use native numbers before 시.

exampleSentence.en: Please wait just five minutes.
exampleSentence.note: Minutes use Sino-Korean numbers.

exampleSentence.en: Do you have time today?
exampleSentence.note: 시간 can mean available time or duration, so context matters.

exampleSentence.en: This is 5,000 won.
exampleSentence.note: Prices use Sino-Korean numbers before 원.

exampleSentence.en: How much is the price?
exampleSentence.note: In shops, 이거 얼마예요? is often more natural than saying 가격 every time.

exampleSentence.en: What is the reservation date?
exampleSentence.note: Dates use Sino-Korean numbers with 월 and 일.

exampleSentence.en: When is your birthday?
exampleSentence.note: 생일 questions often lead to month and day practice.

exampleSentence.en: May I ask how old you are?
exampleSentence.note: Use this polite formula with adults; actual age uses native numbers with 살.

extendedDialogue.setting: Friends arrange a meeting time and check prices before buying coffee and a birthday cake.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: What time shall we meet?
lines.grammarNote: 몇 시 asks for clock time.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 세 시 십 분에 지하철역 앞에서 만나요.
lines.romanization: se si sip bune jihacheoryeok apeseo mannayo.
lines.en: Let's meet at 3:10 in front of the subway station.
lines.grammarNote: 세 is native for the hour; 십 is Sino-Korean for the minutes.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: How many cups of coffee should we buy?
lines.grammarNote: 잔 counts cups and glasses.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 두 잔이면 돼요. 한 잔에 이천오백 원이에요.
lines.romanization: du janimyeon dwaeyo. han jane icheonobaek wonieyo.
lines.en: Two cups are enough. One cup is 2,500 won.
lines.grammarNote: 두 잔 uses a native number; 이천오백 원 uses Sino-Korean numbers.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Then two cups are 5,000 won.
lines.grammarNote: Price totals use Sino-Korean numbers before 원.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네. 생일 케이크는 만 이천 원이에요.
lines.romanization: ne. saengil keikeuneun man icheon wonieyo.
lines.en: Yes. The birthday cake is 12,000 won.
lines.grammarNote: 만 이천 원 is 10,000 + 2,000 won.

readingText.title: A birthday meet-up
readingText.body: 민서와 지훈은 토요일에 친구 생일을 준비해요. 두 사람은 세 시 십 분에 지하철역 앞에서 만나기로 했어요. 커피는 두 잔을 사고, 한 잔에 이천오백 원이라서 모두 오천 원이에요. 케이크는 만 이천 원이에요. 민서는 예약 날짜도 확인했어요. 생일은 이월 삼일이고, 케이크는 토요일 네 시 전에 찾을 수 있어요. 그래서 두 사람은 시간과 가격을 다시 확인하고 가게에 갔어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo and Jihoon prepare for a friend's birthday on Saturday. They plan to meet at 3:10, buy two coffees, check the cake price, confirm the birthday date, and pick up the cake before 4:00.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서와 지훈은 몇 시 십 분에 만나기로 했어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 세 시 십 분에 만나기로 했어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 커피 두 잔은 모두 얼마예요?
생일은 언제예요?

culturalNote.title: Age and price both need register awareness
culturalNote.body: Prices are easy to ask directly with 얼마예요? Age is more sensitive. With adults or people you do not know well, 나이가 어떻게 되세요? is safer than 몇 살이에요?, which can sound childish or too direct.
culturalNote.tip: Use 얼마예요? freely for prices, but be careful with age questions unless the situation clearly calls for it.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which time expression is natural for 3:10?
inlineExercises.explanation: Hours use native Korean numbers; minutes use Sino-Korean numbers.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which counter fits coffee?
inlineExercises.explanation: 잔 counts cups and glasses.

inlineExercises.prompt: Write 1:05 in Korean.
inlineExercises.explanation: Use native 한 for the hour and Sino-Korean 오 for the minutes.

inlineExercises.prompt: Write '3,000 won' in Korean.
inlineExercises.explanation: Prices use Sino-Korean numbers before 원.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 삼 시 십 분에 만나요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Clock hour three is 세 시, not 삼 시.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the age sentence: 저는 이십 살이에요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Age uses native Korean numbers with 살; 스물 becomes 스무 before the counter.

inlineExercises.prompt: 커피 두 잔___ 주세요. (Please give me two cups of coffee.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 두 잔 is the counted object being requested, so 을 fits when the particle is shown. In casual ordering, Koreans often drop it, but 을 is the grammatical object marker.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Let's meet at 3:10.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Hours use native Korean numbers, so 3 o’clock is 세 시. Minutes use Sino-Korean numbers, so 10 minutes is 십 분.

inlineExercises.prompt: Write 'two cups' in Korean.
inlineExercises.explanation: 잔 is a cup/glass counter and takes native Korean numbers. Two cups is 두 잔, not 이 잔.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which price expression is natural for 3,000 won?
inlineExercises.explanation: Prices use Sino-Korean numbers, so 3,000 won is 삼천 원. 세 and 셋 are native forms and do not fit this price expression.

bullets: Hours and common counters use native numbers: 한 시, 두 잔, 세 명.
Minutes, dates, and prices use Sino-Korean numbers: 십 분, 이월 삼일, 오천 원.
몇 attaches to the unit you need: 몇 시, 몇 분, 몇 잔, 몇 명.
Age is socially sensitive: use 나이가 어떻게 되세요? before jumping to 몇 살이에요?

writingTask.prompt: Write 3 sentences telling a friend the time you'll meet, the price of a coffee, and how many people are coming.
writingTask.hint: Use Sino-Korean numbers for minutes/price (세 시 삼십 분, 사천 원) and native numbers for the hour and counting people (세 시, 네 명).
writingTask.model: 우리 세 시 삼십 분에 만나요. 커피는 사천 원이에요. 친구 네 명이 와요.
writingTask.modelEn: Let's meet at 3:30. The coffee is 4,000 won. Four friends are coming.

Say minutes and prices with Sino-Korean numbers (삼십 분 · 사천 원)
Count people and things with native numbers plus a counter (네 명)
Ask "how many / how much" with 몇 and 얼마 (몇 시 · 얼마예요?)

beginnerGuide.title: Descriptions go before the noun
beginnerGuide.body: Korean does not say 가방 작은. Put the modifier first: 작은 가방, 예쁜 가방, 제가 읽는 책.

beginnerGuide.title: Adjective or verb decides the ending
beginnerGuide.body: Adjectives use ㄴ/은: 작은 가방, 조용한 카페. Verbs use 는 for present or habitual action: 찾는 모델, 읽는 책.

beginnerGuide.title: Real speech often stacks modifiers
beginnerGuide.body: 어제 본 작은 가방 has two descriptions before one noun: 본 from 보다 and 작은 from 작다.

checkpoints: I can use -지만 inside one sentence.
I can use 그런데 when the next sentence changes direction.
I can use -아/어도 when the problem does not stop the result.

sampleAnswer.en: This restaurant is a little expensive, but it is tasty. Even if there are many people, it is worth waiting.

hook.situation: Pointing out the exact item, place, food, book, or person you mean by putting a description before the noun.
objectives: Use A-ㄴ/은 N for adjective descriptions: 작은 가방, 조용한 카페.
Use V-는 N for present or habitual action descriptions: 손님이 찾는 모델, 제가 읽는 책.
Recognize completed action modifiers that appear in real shopping talk: 어제 본 가방, 새로 들어온 물건.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean descriptions come before the noun. Once learners can build 작은 가방 and 어제 본 가방, they can identify the right thing without making several short disconnected sentences.

grammarNotes.title: A-(으)ㄴ N — Adjectives describing a noun
grammarNotes.func: To put an adjective in front of a noun (a *pretty* bag, a *small* room), you can't use the plain dictionary form. You change the adjective into a modifying form with -(으)ㄴ and put it right before the noun.

formTable.when: Adjective stem ends in a vowel
Adjective stem ends in a consonant

examples.en: It's a pretty bag.
examples.note: 예쁘다 ends in a vowel, so just add ㄴ → 예쁜, right before 가방.

examples.en: I live in a small house.
examples.note: 작다 ends in a consonant, so add 은 → 작은. The adjective goes straight onto the noun — no 이/가.

examples.en: I waited for a long time.
examples.note: 길다 is a ㄹ-stem: the ㄹ drops and ㄴ is added → 긴, not 길은.

examples.en: I ate a delicious meal.
examples.note: 맛있다/맛없다 act like verbs, so they take 는, not 은 → 맛있는.

keyPoint.label: 예쁜 가방 vs 가방이 예뻐요
keyPoint.body: Korean uses an adjective in two ways. Before a noun it has to become the modifier form (예쁜 가방 = 'a pretty bag'). At the end of a sentence it stays as the predicate (가방이 예뻐요 = 'The bag is pretty'). Same adjective, two jobs — don't put the plain 예뻐요 form in front of a noun.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 좋은 is said [조은] (joeun): the ㅎ drops out between vowels and the sound links straight into the next syllable. 작은 links the same way as [자근] (jageun).

drill.instruction: Turn the adjective in parentheses into the -(으)ㄴ modifier form and attach it to the noun.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English leaves the adjective unchanged ('an expensive bag'), so learners reach for the sentence form 비싸요. But before a noun a Korean adjective needs the modifier ending: 비싸다 → 비싼 가방. The polite 비싸요 can only close a sentence (가방이 비싸요).

grammarNotes.title: V-는 N — A present/habitual action describing a noun
grammarNotes.func: To describe a noun by an action happening now or done regularly (the person who is *eating*, the book I *read* these days), add -는 to the verb stem and put it before the noun. It works like an English 'who/that' clause ('the person who eats').

examples.en: The person eating is my friend.
examples.note: 먹다 + 는 → 먹는. The whole chunk '밥을 먹는' describes 사람, and the object 밥을 stays inside it.

examples.en: It's the school I go to often.
examples.note: 가다 is a vowel stem; -는 still attaches → 가는, and 자주 ('often') gives it the habitual meaning.

examples.en: He's a student who studies Korean.
examples.note: 공부하다 → 공부하는; -는 marks an ongoing/habitual action describing 학생.

examples.en: The book I'm reading now is fun.
examples.note: 읽다 + 는 → 읽는 [잉는]; 지금 ('now') makes the in-progress meaning clear.

keyPoint.label: 먹는 사람 vs 예쁜 사람
keyPoint.body: Verbs and adjectives use different modifier endings in the present. A verb (an action) takes -는: 먹는 사람 ('the person who eats'). An adjective (a state) takes -(으)ㄴ: 예쁜 사람 ('a pretty person'). Just ask 'is this a doing-word or a describing-word?' to pick the ending.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 먹는 is said [멍는] (meongneun): a ㄱ before ㄴ turns into an [ㅇ] sound (nasal assimilation). 읽는 → [잉는] (ingneun) the same way.

drill.instruction: Make the verb into the present V-는 modifier and attach it to the noun.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 먹은 사람 (for 'the person who is eating')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'eating' is one word, so learners mix up the endings. For an action happening now or regularly, use -는 (먹는 사람). Putting -(으)ㄴ on a verb (먹은) means a *finished* action ('the person who ate') — a different time.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄴ N — A finished (past) action describing a noun
grammarNotes.func: To describe a noun by an action that's already over (the movie I *saw* yesterday, the person who *came*), add -(으)ㄴ to the verb stem and put it before the noun. It marks the action as done — the past version of the 'who/that' clause.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel
Verb stem ends in a consonant

examples.en: The movie I saw yesterday was good.
examples.note: 보다 is a vowel stem → 본; 어제 ('yesterday') shows it's finished, so we use -(으)ㄴ, not -는.

examples.en: The meal I ate earlier was delicious.
examples.note: 먹다 ends in a consonant → 먹은 [머근]; the meal is already eaten — a finished action.

examples.en: It's the food my friend made.
examples.note: 만들다 is a ㄹ-stem: drop the ㄹ, add ㄴ → 만든 (not 만들은).

examples.en: I'm listening again to the song I heard yesterday.
examples.note: 듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular: ㄷ becomes ㄹ before 은 → 들은 (not 듣은).

keyPoint.label: 본 영화 vs 보는 영화
keyPoint.body: On a verb, the ending sets the time. -(으)ㄴ = finished/past (어제 본 영화 = 'the movie I saw'). -는 = now or habitual (지금 보는 영화 = 'the movie I'm watching now'). Pick the ending by *when* the action happens compared to now.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 먹은 links as [머근] (meogeun) and 읽은 as [일근] (ilgeun): the final consonant slides into the next syllable. 만든 (from 만들다) is just [만든] (mandeun).

drill.instruction: Make the verb into the past V-(으)ㄴ modifier and attach it to the noun.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 어제 봤은 영화 / 어제 보는 영화 (for 'the movie I saw yesterday')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners either glue the past -았/었- onto the modifier (봤은 ✗) or fall back on -는. Don't add -았/었- before the noun — the 'finished' meaning is already in -(으)ㄴ by itself: 보다 → 본 영화.

exampleSentence.en: I am looking for a pretty bag.
exampleSentence.note: 예쁘다 becomes 예쁜 before a noun.

exampleSentence.en: A big bag is convenient when traveling.
exampleSentence.note: 크다 becomes 큰 before a noun.

exampleSentence.en: I am looking for a small wallet.
exampleSentence.note: 작다 becomes 작은 before a noun.

exampleSentence.en: I like the new design.
exampleSentence.note: 새롭다 becomes 새로운; 새 is also common before nouns.

exampleSentence.en: It is a good bag to carry to work.
exampleSentence.note: 좋다 becomes 좋은; do not confuse it with 좋아하는.

exampleSentence.en: I am fixing bad habits little by little.
exampleSentence.note: 나쁘다 becomes 나쁜 before a noun.

extendedVocabulary.english: that someone looks for / asks for

exampleSentence.en: It is a model customers ask for a lot.
exampleSentence.note: 찾다 becomes 찾는 before a noun.

exampleSentence.en: Do you still have the bag I saw yesterday?
exampleSentence.note: 보다 becomes 본 when it modifies a noun as a completed action.

exampleSentence.en: The neighborhood where my friend lives is quiet.
exampleSentence.note: 살다 drops ㄹ before 는.

exampleSentence.ko: 면접 때 입는 옷은 단정해야 해요.
exampleSentence.en: The clothes you wear for an interview should be neat.
exampleSentence.note: 입다 becomes 입는 before a noun.

exampleSentence.en: This is the book I am reading these days.
exampleSentence.note: 읽다 becomes 읽는; pronunciation changes to ingneun.

exampleSentence.en: The food I often eat is bibimbap.
exampleSentence.note: 먹다 becomes 먹는 before a noun.

exampleSentence.en: I want to study at a quiet cafe.
exampleSentence.note: 조용하다 becomes 조용한.

exampleSentence.ko: 바쁜 사람에게는 짧게 말하는 게 좋아요.
exampleSentence.en: It is good to speak briefly to a busy person.
exampleSentence.note: 바쁘다 becomes 바쁜 before a noun.

exampleSentence.en: A kind staff member explained it to me.
exampleSentence.note: 친절하다 becomes 친절한.

exampleSentence.en: I will buy only the things I need.
exampleSentence.note: 필요하다 becomes 필요한 before a noun.

exampleSentence.en: I put the important documents inside the bag.
exampleSentence.note: 중요하다 becomes 중요한 before a noun.

extendedDialogue.setting: A customer identifies the exact bag in a shop by using adjective and verb modifiers.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: What kind of bag are you looking for?
lines.grammarNote: 어떤 asks for a description before the noun.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 어제 본 작은 가방을 찾고 있어요.
lines.romanization: eoje bon jageun gabangeul chatgo isseoyo.
lines.en: I am looking for the small bag I saw yesterday.
lines.grammarNote: 본 and 작은 both stand before 가방.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: It is a new model that customers ask for a lot.
lines.grammarNote: 찾는 is a verb modifier; 새로운 is an adjective modifier.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Is it a good bag to carry to work?
lines.grammarNote: 좋은 modifies 가방, and the phrase explains the purpose.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Yes, many necessary things fit inside too.
lines.grammarNote: 필요한 modifies 물건.

readingText.title: Finding the right bag
readingText.body: 민서는 출근할 때 들기 좋은 가방을 찾고 있었어요. 직원에게 어제 본 작은 가방이 아직 있는지 물어봤어요. 직원은 그 가방이 손님들이 많이 찾는 새로운 모델이라고 설명했어요. 안에는 필요한 물건이 꽤 많이 들어가고, 디자인도 예뻤어요. 민서는 바쁜 아침에도 들고 다니기 편한 가방이 필요했기 때문에 그 가방을 다시 한번 확인했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo was looking for a bag that would be good to carry to work. She asked whether the small bag she saw yesterday was still available. The staff explained that it was a new model customers often ask for, and Minseo checked it again because she needed a comfortable bag for busy mornings.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 어떤 가방을 찾고 있었어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 출근할 때 들기 좋은 가방을 찾고 있었어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 직원은 그 가방을 어떤 모델이라고 설명했어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 손님들이 많이 찾는 새로운 모델이라고 설명했어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 왜 그 가방을 다시 확인했어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 바쁜 아침에도 들고 다니기 편한 가방이 필요했기 때문이에요.

culturalNote.title: Descriptions make requests sound clear and polite
culturalNote.body: In shops, offices, and meet-up situations, Korean often avoids a long chain of short sentences by placing the description before the noun. 어제 봤어요. 작은 가방이에요. 그거 찾고 있어요 can become 어제 본 작은 가방을 찾고 있어요, which is clearer and more natural.
culturalNote.tip: When the listener has several possible items in mind, build one precise noun phrase: 조용한 카페, 제가 읽는 책, 어제 본 작은 가방.

inlineExercises.prompt: In a shop, which phrase identifies the item most clearly?
inlineExercises.explanation: Korean modifiers come before the noun they describe.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which phrase uses V-는 N correctly?
inlineExercises.explanation: 찾는 modifies 모델 with an action-based description.

inlineExercises.prompt: Change 조용하다 + 카페 into a noun phrase.
inlineExercises.explanation: 하다 adjectives become 한 before a noun.

inlineExercises.prompt: Change 읽다 + 책 into 'the book I am reading.'
inlineExercises.explanation: A present or habitual verb modifier uses 는.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the phrase: 제가 읽어요 책
inlineExercises.explanation: 읽어요 is a sentence ending; 읽는 modifies 책.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the phrase: 가방 작은
inlineExercises.explanation: Adjective modifiers come before the noun.

inlineExercises.prompt: 작은 가방___ 찾고 있어요. (I am looking for a small bag.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 찾다 is an action, and 작은 가방 is what you are looking for, so it takes 을. 이 would make the bag the subject instead.

inlineExercises.prompt: ___ 가방을 찾고 있어요. (작다 → adjective modifier)
inlineExercises.explanation: Adjectives describe nouns with -(으)ㄴ. 작다 becomes 작은 before 가방.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'the book I am reading'
inlineExercises.explanation: Present action modifiers use V-는 before the noun. 읽다 becomes 읽는 when it describes 책.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which phrase means “the bag I saw yesterday”?
inlineExercises.explanation: A completed action before a noun uses V-(으)ㄴ, so 보다 becomes 본. 가방 어제 봤어요 is a full sentence, not a noun phrase.

bullets: Adjective descriptions use A-ㄴ/은 N: 예쁜 가방, 작은 지갑, 조용한 카페.
Present or habitual action descriptions use V-는 N: 찾는 모델, 읽는 책, 사는 동네.
Completed action descriptions point to a noun already affected by an action: 어제 본 가방, 새로 들어온 물건.
Best check: if the word ends like a sentence, change it before placing it in front of a noun.

writingTask.prompt: Describe a lost item to staff at an information desk in 3 sentences: name the bag you're looking for, what's inside, and where you saw it.
writingTask.hint: Use A-(으)ㄴ N for adjectives (작은 가방), V-는 N for a current action (찾는 가방), and V-(으)ㄴ N for a finished one (어제 본 가방).
writingTask.model: 저는 작은 가방을 찾아요. 제가 찾는 가방은 까만색이에요. 어제 여기에서 본 가방이에요.
writingTask.modelEn: I'm looking for a small bag. The bag I'm looking for is black. It's the bag I saw here yesterday.

canDo: Put an adjective before a noun with A-(으)ㄴ N (작은 가방 · 예쁜 옷)
Describe a noun by a current or habitual action with V-는 N (찾는 가방)
Describe a noun by a finished action with V-(으)ㄴ N (어제 본 영화)
Pick out the exact person or thing I mean from several

chapters.goal: Use 이다 forms when the sentence ends in a noun.
chapters.scenario: You explain identity, reason, contrast, or condition with noun sentences.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was it?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: It was fun. But the weather was a bit cold.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make three preference sentences and two comparisons: 커피를 좋아해요, 차보다 커피를 더 좋아해요, 생각만큼 비싸지 않아요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Make one noun sentence, one reason clause, and one condition with 이다.
chapters.friendPractice: Partner asks 커피랑 차 중에 뭐가 더 좋아요? Learner answers with N보다 N을 더 좋아해요 and one reason.
chapters.review: Can you explain why 커피를 좋아해요 and 커피가 좋아요 use different particles?

beginnerGuide.title: 좋아하다 takes 을/를
beginnerGuide.body: Say 커피를 좋아해요 and 음악을 좋아해요. 커피가 좋아해요 is wrong because 좋아하다 is a verb.

beginnerGuide.title: 보다 marks the baseline
beginnerGuide.body: 차보다 커피를 더 좋아해요 means tea is the comparison baseline and coffee is preferred. If you move 보다, the meaning changes.

beginnerGuide.title: 취향 softens preference
beginnerGuide.body: 제 취향이에요 and 제 취향에 맞아요 let you describe personal taste without sounding like the other choice is bad.

checkpoints: I can use 이에요/예요 after nouns.
I can use 이라서/라서 for because it is a noun.
I can use 이면/면 and 이고/고 with noun predicates.

curriculumTrack.description: Tense, questions, numbers, modifiers, connectors, particles, counters, and repair chapters.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Use 이다 forms when the sentence ends in a noun.
exitTask.prompt: Make one noun sentence, one reason clause, and one condition with 이다.

sampleAnswer.ko: 오늘은 휴일이라서 사람이 많아요. 학생이면 할인이 돼요.
sampleAnswer.en: There are many people because today is a holiday. If you are a student, you get a discount.

checklist: I can use 이에요/예요 after nouns.
I can use 이라서/라서 for because it is a noun.
I can use 이면/면 and 이고/고 with noun predicates.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: Choosing food, drinks, movies, music, or hobbies with a friend by saying what you like, what you like more, and what matches your taste.
objectives: Use N을/를 좋아해요 for personal preferences: 커피를 좋아해요.
Use N보다 더 to compare one option against another: 차보다 커피를 더 좋아해요.
Use N만큼 for equal degree or expectation: 생각만큼 비싸지 않아요.
hook.whyItMatters: Preference talk is where learners quickly run into Korean's particle logic. 좋아하다 takes 을/를, 좋다 takes 이/가, 보다 marks the comparison baseline, and 만큼 marks equal degree. Keeping those roles clear makes everyday choices sound natural.

grammarNotes.title: N을/를 좋아해요 — I like N
grammarNotes.func: Use 좋아하다 to say you like something or someone. It is an action verb ("to like"), not the adjective 좋다 ("to be good"), so the thing you like is the object and takes 을/를, not 이/가.

examples.en: I like coffee.
examples.note: 커피 ends in a vowel, so it takes 를.

examples.en: I like Korean food.
examples.note: 음식 ends in a 받침, so it takes 을.

examples.en: I like Korean.
examples.note: 좋아하다 takes the object with 을/를, never 이/가.

examples.en: I don't really like spicy food.
examples.note: 별로 안 softens it to "don't really like."

keyPoint.label: 좋다 vs 좋아하다
keyPoint.body: 좋다 is an adjective and takes 이/가: 커피가 좋아요 ("coffee is good to me"). 좋아하다 is a verb and takes 을/를: 커피를 좋아해요. Both can translate as "I like coffee," but the particle follows the word you actually use. For now, just lock in 을/를 with 좋아해요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 좋아해요 sounds like [조아해요] — the ㅎ in 좋 drops before the vowel, so don't say [졷아해요].

drill.instruction: Say you like each thing with N을/를 좋아해요. Pick 을 or 를 by the last sound of the noun.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English "I like X" pushes you toward the subject particle, but 좋아하다 is a verb that takes an object — use 을/를. The 가 version only works with the adjective 좋다 (커피가 좋아요).

grammarNotes.title: N보다 더 — more than N
grammarNotes.func: Attach 보다 to the thing you're comparing against (the baseline) to mean "more than N." 더 ("more") usually comes right before the adjective or verb. 더 is optional, but adding it makes the comparison clear.

formTable.when: For "less," use 덜 instead of 더

examples.en: I like coffee more than tea.
examples.note: 차 is the baseline ("than tea"); 커피 is the one I prefer.

examples.en: Today is colder than yesterday.
examples.note: 보다 attaches to 어제, the thing being compared against.

examples.ko: 이 영화가 저 영화보다 더 재미있어요.
examples.romanization: i yeong-hwa-ga jeo yeong-hwa-bo-da deo jae-mi-i-sseo-yo.
examples.en: This movie is more fun than that one.
examples.note: 보다 marks what this movie is compared against.

examples.en: The bus is slower than the subway.
examples.note: The baseline (지하철) carries 보다, no matter the word order.

keyPoint.label: 보다 marks the baseline, not the winner
keyPoint.body: In "A is more than B," 보다 goes on B — the thing you measure against — not on the one that wins: A이/가 B보다 더 ~. English speakers often want to put "than" on the smaller side, but in Korean 보다 always sits on the baseline noun. 더 is optional and just makes "more" explicit.

drill.instruction: Make a comparison with N보다 더. Put 보다 on the baseline noun.
drill.model: 차 / 커피 (좋아하다) → 저는 차보다 커피를 더 좋아해요.
items: 저 영화 / 이 영화 (재미있다) → 이 영화가 ___ 더 재미있어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저는 차보다 커피를 더 좋아해요. (said when you actually prefer tea)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners flip the nouns because English says "tea more than coffee." In Korean, 보다 sits on the baseline (the one you like less). If you like tea more, coffee is the baseline: 커피보다 차를 더.

grammarNotes.title: N만큼 — as much as N / as Adj as N
grammarNotes.func: Attach 만큼 to a noun to mean "as much as N" or "to the same degree as N." It marks an equal level in a comparison, and the adjective or verb comes after it. It's very common in "not as ... as I expected" sentences with 생각.

examples.ko: 이 카페 라떼만큼 맛있는 커피는 없어요.
examples.romanization: i ka-pe rat-te-man-keum ma-sin-neun keo-pi-neun eop-seo-yo.
examples.en: There's no coffee as tasty as this cafe's latte.
examples.note: 라떼만큼 sets the level of "tasty."

examples.en: It's not as expensive as I thought.
examples.note: 생각만큼 is a super-common chunk for "as ... as expected."

examples.en: Today is as cold as yesterday.
examples.note: 만큼 attaches to 어제, the level being matched.

examples.en: I like coffee as much as my friend does.
examples.note: 만큼 also works with verbs of degree like 좋아해요.

keyPoint.label: 만큼 (equal) vs 보다 (more)
keyPoint.body: Use 보다 for "more than" — one side wins: 친구보다 잘해요 = better than my friend. Use 만큼 for "as much as" — the two are equal: 친구만큼 잘해요 = as well as my friend. Swapping them turns "the same" into "more," so keep them apart.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 라떼만큼 is straightforward, but 책만큼 sounds like [챙만큼] — the ㄱ in 책 turns into [ㅇ] before the nasal ㅁ.

drill.instruction: Say two things are equal with N만큼. Put 만큼 on the baseline noun.
drill.model: 친구 (커피를 좋아하다) → 저는 친구만큼 커피를 좋아해요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저는 친구보다 커피를 좋아해요. (meaning "as much as," not "more than")
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English "as much as" and "more than" feel close, but Korean splits them: 만큼 = same degree, 보다 = more. Use 만큼 when the two are equal, and save 보다 for when one really beats the other.

exampleSentence.en: I like Korean food.
exampleSentence.note: 좋아하다 takes the liked item with 을/를.

exampleSentence.en: I dislike coffee that is too sweet.
exampleSentence.note: 싫어하다 follows the same object pattern as 좋아하다.

exampleSentence.en: I like coffee more than tea.
exampleSentence.note: 더 marks the stronger side of the comparison.

exampleSentence.ko: 저는 이 카페 커피를 제일 좋아해요.
exampleSentence.en: I like this cafe's coffee the most.
exampleSentence.note: Use 제일 when choosing the top option.

exampleSentence.en: It is not as expensive as I thought.
exampleSentence.note: Practiced through pattern-041, not as a fake standalone word card.

exampleSentence.en: I like coffee more than tea.
exampleSentence.note: Comparison 보다 attaches to the baseline; it is different from the verb 보다, to see.

exampleSentence.en: This cafe is my taste.
exampleSentence.note: 취향 names the personal taste behind a preference.

exampleSentence.en: What is your hobby?
exampleSentence.note: A natural topic for 좋아해요 and 비교하다.

exampleSentence.en: What food do you like the most?
exampleSentence.note: Food is one of the safest preference topics.

exampleSentence.ko: 저는 액션 영화보다 코미디 영화를 더 좋아해요.
exampleSentence.en: I like comedy movies more than action movies.
exampleSentence.note: Good for practicing 보다 더.

exampleSentence.ko: 저는 운동보다 음악 듣는 걸 더 좋아해요.
exampleSentence.en: I like listening to music more than exercising.
exampleSentence.note: Activities often become -는 걸 phrases.

exampleSentence.en: I like coffee more than tea.
exampleSentence.note: 커피 is a practical object for likes and cafe comparisons.

exampleSentence.en: Today tea sounds better than coffee.
exampleSentence.note: Use 차 as a natural comparison partner for coffee.

exampleSentence.en: I like exercise as much as my friend does.
exampleSentence.note: Useful with 만큼 and 좋아하다.

exampleSentence.en: Let's compare the price and our preferences.
exampleSentence.note: Use 비교하다 for deliberate comparison.

exampleSentence.en: I chose coffee.
exampleSentence.note: A practical verb after comparing options.

extendedDialogue.setting: Friends choose a cafe drink and compare their preferences without mixing 좋아하다, 좋다, 보다, and 만큼.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 커피랑 차 중에 뭐가 더 좋아요?
lines.romanization: keopirang cha junge mwoga deo joayo?
lines.en: Between coffee and tea, which do you like more?
lines.grammarNote: 뭐가 더 좋아요 uses 좋다 with 이/가 for a choice that feels better.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: I like coffee more than tea.
lines.grammarNote: 차보다 marks tea as the baseline; 커피를 is the object of 좋아해요.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 이 카페 라떼만큼 맛있는 커피가 또 있어요?
lines.romanization: i kape rattemankeum masinneun keopiga tto isseoyo?
lines.en: Is there another coffee as tasty as this cafe's latte?
lines.grammarNote: 라떼만큼 sets an equal-degree standard.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 아직 못 찾았어요. 여기가 제 취향에 제일 맞아요.
lines.romanization: ajik mot chajasseoyo. yeogiga je chwihyange jeil majayo.
lines.en: I have not found one yet. This place fits my taste the best.
lines.grammarNote: 취향에 맞아요 is a natural way to talk about personal taste.

readingText.title: Choosing by taste
readingText.body: 민서와 지훈은 카페에서 음료를 고르고 있었어요. 민서는 차가 깔끔해서 좋다고 했지만, 지훈은 차보다 커피를 더 좋아한다고 했어요. 특히 이 카페 라떼는 생각만큼 비싸지 않고 맛도 좋아서 지훈의 취향에 잘 맞았어요. 민서는 커피와 차를 비교해 본 뒤에 오늘은 차를 선택했어요. 두 사람은 취향이 조금 달라도 서로의 선택을 자연스럽게 이해했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo and Jihoon were choosing drinks at a cafe. Minseo liked tea because it felt clean, while Jihoon liked coffee more than tea. This cafe's latte was not as expensive as he expected and fit his taste well. After comparing coffee and tea, Minseo chose tea today.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 지훈은 차보다 무엇을 더 좋아해요?
이 카페 라떼는 생각만큼 비쌌어요?
민서는 무엇을 선택했어요?

culturalNote.title: Preference can be softened
culturalNote.body: Korean speakers often soften preferences so the other person's choice is not dismissed. Instead of 이건 싫어요, learners can say 저는 커피보다 차가 더 좋아요, 제 취향에는 조금 달아요, or 저는 별로 안 좋아해요.
culturalNote.tip: When comparing with friends, 더 좋아요 and 제 취향에는 feel smoother than bluntly saying 싫어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses 좋아하다?
inlineExercises.explanation: 좋아하다 is a verb, so the liked item takes 을/를.

inlineExercises.prompt: You like coffee more than tea. Which sentence is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 보다 attaches to the baseline, tea.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say 'It is not as expensive as I thought.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 생각만큼 is the expectation standard; 비싸지 않아요 gives the negative comparison.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say 'This cafe fits my taste.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 취향에 맞다 is the natural collocation.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 커피가 좋아해요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Use 를 with 좋아하다. 커피가 좋아요 is a different sentence with 좋다.

inlineExercises.prompt: 커피___ 좋아해요. (I like coffee.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 좋아하다 is a verb, so the thing liked takes 을/를. 커피가 좋아요 is a different adjective sentence meaning coffee is good.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 영화를 ___ . (좋아하다 → polite present)
inlineExercises.explanation: 하다 verbs become 해요 in polite present. 좋아하다 becomes 좋아해요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I like coffee more than tea.' (Start with 차보다.)
inlineExercises.explanation: N보다 sets the comparison baseline. 더 좋아해요 says the second option is preferred more.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'I like movies the most.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 제일 marks the top preference. 영화 is the thing liked, so 영화를 stays before 좋아해요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '생각만큼 비싸요 않아요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Adjectives use -지 않아요 for this negative pattern. 생각만큼 sets the comparison: not as expensive as expected.

bullets: 좋아하다 takes 을/를: 커피를 좋아해요, 음악을 좋아해요.
보다 marks the baseline: 차보다 커피를 더 좋아해요.
만큼 marks equal degree or expectation: 생각만큼 비싸지 않아요.
취향 helps soften preference talk: 제 취향이에요, 취향에 맞아요.

writingTask.prompt: Write 3 sentences comparing two foods or drinks: say what you like, which you like more, and one that isn't as good as you hoped.
writingTask.hint: Use N을/를 좋아해요 (커피를 좋아해요), N보다 더 for the comparison (차보다 더), and N만큼 for the equal/not-as comparison (커피만큼).
writingTask.model: 저는 커피를 좋아해요. 커피가 차보다 더 좋아요. 그런데 이 차는 커피만큼 맛있지 않아요.
writingTask.modelEn: I like coffee. Coffee is better than tea. But this tea isn't as tasty as coffee.

canDo: Say what I like with the object marker, N을/를 좋아해요 (음악을 좋아해요)
Compare two things with N보다 더 (커피보다 더 좋아요)
Say something is as much / not as much as another with N만큼 (커피만큼)
Say what fits my taste and what I dislike (취향 · 싫어하다 · 제일)

chapters.title: Directions and Transport
chapters.goal: Bring up background information without sounding abrupt.
chapters.scenario: A file is late, a plan changed, or you need to disagree gently.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was it?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: It was fun. But the weather was a bit cold.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make three direction sentences and two purpose sentences: 이 길로 가세요, 지하철로 가요, 친구 만나러 가요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Write a short message using 사실은 plus -는데요, -거든요, or -잖아요.
chapters.friendPractice: Partner asks 어디로 가요? Learner answers with route, transport method, and one purpose using -(으)러.
chapters.review: Can you explain the difference between 지하철역에 가요 and 지하철로 가요?

beginnerGuide.title: 로/으로 is not only 'to'
beginnerGuide.body: It can show direction, route, transport method, or transfer target: 오른쪽으로, 이 길로, 지하철로, 2호선으로.

beginnerGuide.title: 에 still marks destination
beginnerGuide.body: 지하철역에 가요 means go to the subway station. 지하철로 가요 means go by subway. You can combine them: 지하철로 학교에 가요.

beginnerGuide.title: -(으)러 gives the purpose
beginnerGuide.body: 친구 만나러 가요 and 버스 타러 정류장에 가요 explain what you are going to do there.

checkpoints: I can use -는데요 to open background softly.
I can use -거든요 for new background the listener may not know.
I can use -잖아요 only when the listener likely knows or agrees.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Bring up background information without sounding abrupt.
exitTask.prompt: Write a short message using 사실은 plus -는데요, -거든요, or -잖아요.

sampleAnswer.ko: 사실은 자료가 아직 안 끝났는데요. 어제 갑자기 일이 생겼거든요.
sampleAnswer.en: Actually, the materials are not finished yet. Something suddenly came up yesterday.

checklist: I can use -는데요 to open background softly.
I can use -거든요 for new background the listener may not know.
I can use -잖아요 only when the listener likely knows or agrees.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: Asking how to get somewhere, choosing a transport method, following exit directions, and saying the purpose of the trip.
objectives: Use N(으)로 for direction or transport method: 오른쪽으로, 지하철로.
Use V(으)러 가요 for the purpose of going: 친구 만나러 가요, 버스 타러 가요.
Connect directions with real transit vocabulary: 출구, 정류장, 환승, 갈아타다, 내리다.
hook.whyItMatters: Directions are not just place names. Korean needs the right particle for route, direction, vehicle, and purpose. This chapter makes the difference between 지하철역에 가요, 지하철로 가요, and 지하철을 타러 가요 clear.

grammarNotes.title: N(으)로 — by / toward / through (means, direction, route)
grammarNotes.func: N(으)로 marks how you travel (by bus, by subway), the direction you head (this way, toward home), or the path you go through (out that door). It points at the way you go, not the exact spot you end up.

formTable.ex: 집 → 집으로 (toward home), 오른쪽 → 오른쪽으로 (to the right)
버스 → 버스로 (by bus), 학교 → 학교로 (toward school)
지하철 → 지하철로 (by subway), 서울 → 서울로 (toward Seoul)

examples.en: I go to school by bus.
examples.note: 버스 ends in a vowel, so just 로. This is the "by what transport" use.

examples.en: Come this way.
examples.note: 이쪽 ends in a consonant, so 으로. Here 로 marks direction, not a means.

examples.en: I go home by subway.
examples.note: 지하철 ends in ㄹ, so it takes plain 로 (not 으로).

examples.en: Go out through that door.
examples.note: 문 ends in a consonant → 으로. This is the "path you go through" use.

keyPoint.label: -(으)로 vs -에 (direction vs the place you reach)
keyPoint.body: -에 names the place you arrive at: 학교에 가요 = go to school (you end up there). -(으)로 names the direction you head or the way you go: 학교로 가요 = go toward / in the direction of school. Use -(으)로 when the point is which way, and -에 when the point is the place you reach.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a noun ending in ㄹ, just add 로 with no 으, and the two ㄹ sounds run together: 지하철 + 로 → [지하철로]. Don't say 지하철으로.

drill.instruction: Add the right form of -(으)로 to each noun and say the whole sentence out loud.
drill.model: 택시 → 택시로 가요. (I go by taxi.)
items: 이 길 → ___ 가세요. (Go this way / along this road.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English says "by bus," and learners often grab -에 because they picture "on the bus." But the means of transport takes -(으)로, never -에. 버스에 would sound like "to the bus."

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)러 가요/와요 — go/come to do something
grammarNotes.func: V-(으)러 tags onto an action verb to say why you're going or coming, and it's always followed by a movement verb like 가다, 오다, or 다니다. It answers "what did you go/come to do?"

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a consonant
Verb stem ends in a vowel

examples.en: I'm going to the restaurant to eat lunch.
examples.note: 먹다 ends in a consonant → 먹으러. The thing you go to do comes first, then 가요.

examples.en: I came to school to meet a friend.
examples.note: 만나다 ends in a vowel → 만나러. Here the movement verb is 오다 (왔어요).

examples.en: I'm going to the bookstore to buy a book.
examples.note: 사다 ends in a vowel → 사러. The object 책을 stays with its own verb 사다.

examples.en: Come hang out at my place.
examples.note: 놀다 ends in ㄹ → 놀러 (not 놀으러). A super common everyday invitation.

keyPoint.label: -(으)러 vs -기 위해서 (going to do vs why in general)
keyPoint.body: -(으)러 is only for the reason you go or come, so it has to be followed by a movement verb (가다/오다/다니다): 밥을 먹으러 가요. -기 위해서 gives the reason for any action: 살을 빼려고 운동해요 sounds more natural here, but the textbook pair is -기 위해서. The simple rule: if it's about going or coming somewhere to do something, use -(으)러 가요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a stem ending in a consonant, the 으러 links right onto that consonant: 먹 + 으러 → [머그러]. No pause — the ㄱ slides into 으.

drill.instruction: Join the two verbs with -(으)러 and read the sentence aloud.
drill.model: 영화를 보다 + 가다 → 영화를 보러 가요. (I'm going to watch a movie.)
items: 돈을 찾다 + 가다 → ___ (I'm going to get some money out.)
한국어를 배우다 + 다니다 → ___ (I go to class to learn Korean.)
사진을 찍다 + 가다 → ___ (I'm going to take some photos.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 공부하기 위해서 도서관에 가요. (when you just mean "go to study")
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English "go to study" tempts learners into the heavier -기 위해서. When you're just going or coming somewhere to do something, the natural, level-right choice is -(으)러 가요. Keep -기 위해서 for reasons that aren't about going anywhere.

exampleSentence.en: Going by subway is fast.
exampleSentence.note: Use 지하철로 for 'by subway' and 지하철을 타요 for boarding.

exampleSentence.en: If you go by bus, it takes a little long.
exampleSentence.note: 버스로 marks travel method.

exampleSentence.en: If you do not have time, go by taxi.
exampleSentence.note: 택시로 means by taxi.

exampleSentence.en: Transfer to Line 2 at the station.
exampleSentence.note: The station where an action happens takes 에서.

exampleSentence.en: I go to the bus stop to take the bus.
exampleSentence.note: 정류장에 is the destination; 타러 is the purpose.

exampleSentence.en: Go out through exit three.
exampleSentence.note: 출구로 marks the route out.

exampleSentence.en: Go to the right.
exampleSentence.note: Direction nouns take 으로.

exampleSentence.en: Go left from the exit.
exampleSentence.note: 왼쪽으로 marks movement direction.

exampleSentence.en: Keep going straight on this road.
exampleSentence.note: Often used in directions with 길로.

exampleSentence.en: I transfer at City Hall Station.
exampleSentence.note: Official transit word; 갈아타다 is the everyday verb.

exampleSentence.en: Transfer to Line 2.
exampleSentence.note: The line or vehicle you transfer into takes 으로/로.

exampleSentence.en: I go to the bus stop to take the bus.
exampleSentence.note: The vehicle you board takes 을/를.

exampleSentence.en: Get off at the next bus stop.
exampleSentence.note: The place where you get off takes 에서.

exampleSentence.en: It takes ten minutes on foot to the station.
exampleSentence.note: 걸어서 is the everyday 'on foot' transport answer.

exampleSentence.en: Go straight on this road.
exampleSentence.note: 길로 marks the route.

exampleSentence.en: Is this the right direction?
exampleSentence.note: Useful when checking whether you are going the right way.

extendedDialogue.setting: A traveler asks how to reach the subway station, which exit to use, and where to transfer.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Which way do I go to get to Hongik University Station?
lines.grammarNote: 어디로 asks for direction or route.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Go straight on this road and go right.
lines.grammarNote: 길로 and 오른쪽으로 both use route/direction 로.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 지하철로 가는 게 빨라요, 버스로 가는 게 빨라요?
lines.romanization: jihacheollo ganeun ge ppallayo, beoseuro ganeun ge ppallayo?
lines.en: Is it faster to go by subway or by bus?
lines.grammarNote: 지하철로 and 버스로 mark transport method.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.romanization: jihacheollo gaseyo. sicheongnyeogeseo ihoseoneuro garatamyeon dwaeyo.
lines.en: Go by subway. You can transfer to Line 2 at City Hall Station.
lines.grammarNote: The line you transfer into takes 으로.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 친구 만나러 가는 길이라서 빨리 가야 해요.
lines.romanization: chingu mannareo ganeun giriraseo ppalli gaya haeyo.
lines.en: I am on my way to meet a friend, so I have to go quickly.
lines.grammarNote: 만나러 gives the purpose of going.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 그럼 삼 번 출구로 나가서 왼쪽으로 가세요.
lines.romanization: geureom sam beon chulguro nagaseo oenjjogeuro gaseyo.
lines.en: Then go out through exit three and go left.
lines.grammarNote: 출구로 marks the route out; 왼쪽으로 marks direction.

readingText.title: Getting to the right exit
readingText.body: 민서는 친구를 만나러 홍대입구역에 가고 있었어요. 처음에는 버스로 갈까 생각했지만, 시간이 없어서 지하철로 가기로 했어요. 시청역에서 2호선으로 갈아타고, 홍대입구역에서 삼 번 출구로 나가야 했어요. 출구에서 왼쪽으로 조금 걸으면 약속 장소가 나와요. 민서는 길을 다시 확인하고 이 길로 직진한 뒤에 왼쪽으로 갔어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo was going to Hongik University Station to meet a friend. She considered taking the bus, but because she did not have time, she decided to go by subway. She had to transfer to Line 2, go out exit three, and walk a little to the left from the exit.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 왜 홍대입구역에 가고 있었어요?
민서는 어디에서 2호선으로 갈아타요?
홍대입구역에서 몇 번 출구로 나가야 해요?

culturalNote.title: Exit numbers matter
culturalNote.body: In Korean subway directions, people often anchor the whole route around exit numbers: 몇 번 출구로 나가세요, 3번 출구 앞에서 만나요. The exit is not a tiny detail; it can decide whether you are on the correct side of a large road.
culturalNote.tip: When asking for directions, add 출구: 몇 번 출구로 나가요? 어느 출구가 가까워요?

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence gives a route or direction?
inlineExercises.explanation: -로 marks the route or direction.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'I am going to meet a friend'?
inlineExercises.explanation: -러 가요 gives the purpose of going.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say 'Go by subway.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Transport method takes 로/으로.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say 'Transfer to Line 2.'
inlineExercises.explanation: The line you transfer into takes 으로.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 버스에 가요.
inlineExercises.explanation: For 'by bus,' use 버스로.

inlineExercises.prompt: 지하철___ 가요. (I go by subway.)
inlineExercises.explanation: Transport method takes (으)로. 에 would mark a destination, not the way you travel.

inlineExercises.prompt: 친구 ___ 가요. (만나다 → go in order to)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)러 가요 gives the purpose of going. 만나다 becomes 만나러 before 가요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Please go to the right.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 오른쪽으로 gives direction toward the right. 가세요 is the polite direction/request form.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'Transfer to the bus.'
inlineExercises.explanation: The new vehicle you transfer into takes (으)로. 갈아타세요 is the transit verb for transfer.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '친구를 만나로 가요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: The purpose form is -(으)러, not -로. 만나다 becomes 만나러 because the stem ends in a vowel.

bullets: N(으)로 marks direction, route, transport method, or transfer target: 오른쪽으로, 길로, 지하철로, 2호선으로.
Destination still uses 에: 지하철로 학교에 가요.
V(으)러 가요 gives the purpose of movement: 친구 만나러 가요, 버스 타러 가요.
Exit numbers are practical anchors: 삼 번 출구로 나가세요.

writingTask.prompt: Text a friend telling them how to get to your place and what stop to get off at.
writingTask.hint: Use N(으)로 for the means/direction (지하철로, 이쪽으로) and V-(으)러 가요 to say what you're coming to do.
writingTask.model: 지하철로 오세요. 시청역에서 내려서 2번 출구로 나오세요. 저는 지금 밥 먹으러 가요. 거기에서 만나요!
writingTask.modelEn: Come by subway. Get off at City Hall Station and go out exit 2. I'm going to eat right now. Let's meet there!

canDo: Say how I travel and which way to go (지하철로, 2번 출구로)

beginnerGuide.title: Trying lowers pressure
beginnerGuide.body: 입어 보세요 means try it on before deciding. 한번 makes the suggestion even lighter: 한번 입어 보세요.

beginnerGuide.title: 주세요 makes requests polite
beginnerGuide.body: Use 추천해 주세요, 보여 주세요, 바꿔 주세요, and 도와주세요 when asking someone to do something for you.

beginnerGuide.title: ㄹ까요 checks the decision
beginnerGuide.body: 갈까요? can mean shall we go or should I go. 입어 볼까요? asks whether trying it on is a good idea.
