hook.situation: Suggesting an option, trying food or clothes before deciding, and asking for help without sounding blunt.
objectives: Use V아/어 보세요 and V아/어 볼까요? for trying an action: 입어 보세요, 먹어 볼까요?
Use V아/어 주세요 for polite requests: 추천해 주세요, 보여 주세요, 도와주세요.
Use Vㄹ/을까요? to suggest or ask what to do: 같이 갈까요?, 주문할까요?
hook.whyItMatters: Korean suggestions often soften the action before the decision. 한번 입어 보세요 feels lighter than 입으세요, and 추천해 주세요 is clearer and more polite than a blunt command.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어 보다 — try doing V (give it a go)
grammarNotes.func: Add -아/어 보다 to a verb to mean "try doing something" — do it once and see how it goes. It's the warm, everyday way to nudge someone: "go ahead and try it."

formTable.when: Stem ends in ㅏ or ㅗ
formTable.ex: 가다 → 가 보다 (try going), 오다 → 와 보다 (try coming)

formTable.when: Stem ends in any other vowel
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹어 보다 (try eating), 읽다 → 읽어 보다 (try reading)
하다 → 해 보다 (try doing), 공부하다 → 공부해 보다 (try studying)

examples.en: Try reading this book.
examples.note: 한번 ("give it a try") goes hand in hand with -아/어 보다 to soften a suggestion.

examples.en: Have you tried this food?
examples.note: Past 봤어요 asks about experience — "have you ever tried it?"

examples.en: I want to try making Korean food.
examples.note: -아/어 보다 slots right into -고 싶다 when you want to give something a try.

examples.en: Try asking your friend.
examples.note: 묻다 is a ㄷ-irregular: 묻- → 물어, then + 보세요.

keyPoint.label: V-아/어 보다 vs. plain V
keyPoint.body: 먹으세요 just says "eat it." 먹어 보세요 says "try it and see how it is" — it frames the action as something new to test out, which makes the suggestion feel friendlier and less pushy.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In 읽어 보세요, the ㄺ of 읽- links forward, so it sounds like [일거 보세요] — the ㄱ carries into the next syllable.

drill.instruction: Turn each verb into a friendly suggestion with -아/어 보세요 ("try ___-ing").
drill.model: 입다 (to wear) → 입어 보세요. (Try it on.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Here 보다 is already the main verb ("to look"), so you don't tack the helper 보다 on top of it. Doubling it — 봐 보세요 — sounds odd. Just say 보세요, or 한번 보세요 for the "give it a look" feel. The helper 보다 attaches to OTHER verbs (먹어 보세요, 읽어 보세요), not to 보다 itself.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어 주세요 — please do V (for me)
grammarNotes.func: Add -아/어 주세요 to a verb to politely ask someone to do something for you. It's the normal, warm way to make a request — softer than a bare command.

formTable.when: Stem ends in ㅏ or ㅗ
formTable.ex: 앉다 → 앉아 주세요 (please sit), 보다 → 봐 주세요 (please look)

formTable.when: Stem ends in any other vowel
formTable.ex: 열다 → 열어 주세요 (please open), 기다리다 → 기다려 주세요 (please wait)
하다 → 해 주세요 (please do), 말하다 → 말해 주세요 (please tell me)

examples.en: Please give me some water.
examples.note: With 주다 itself you just say 주세요; 좀 ("a little") softens it.

examples.en: Please open the door for me.
examples.note: 열다 → 열어 + 주세요; 좀 makes it gentler.

examples.en: Please speak slowly.
examples.note: 하다 verb: 말하다 → 말해 주세요. A really useful one for learners.

examples.en: Please wait a moment.
examples.note: 기다리다 → 기다려 주세요; the waiting is for your sake, so 주다 fits.

keyPoint.label: V-(으)세요 vs. V-아/어 주세요
keyPoint.body: 앉으세요 is a polite instruction aimed at what the listener does ("please sit"). 앉아 주세요 adds 주다 ("do it for me"), so it lands as a favor you'd be grateful for — exactly the feel of most polite English requests.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 열어 주세요 links across the ㄹ → [여러 주세요]; the ㄹ of 열- slides into the next syllable.

drill.instruction: Make a polite request with -아/어 주세요 ("please ___ for me").

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English "please" can't tell apart a plain instruction from a favor. -(으)세요 on its own can sound like an order or a general direction; adding 주다 (기다려 주세요) marks the action as done for your benefit — which is what most polite English requests really mean.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄹ까요? — shall we? / should I?
grammarNotes.func: Add -(으)ㄹ까요? to a verb to suggest doing something together ("shall we?") or to ask what the listener thinks about you doing it ("should I?"). It's the standard way to float a friendly idea.

formTable.ex: 가다 → 갈까요? (shall we go?), 마시다 → 마실까요? (shall we drink?)
먹다 → 먹을까요? (shall we eat?), 앉다 → 앉을까요? (shall we sit?)
놀다 → 놀까요? (shall we hang out?), 만들다 → 만들까요? (shall we make it?)

examples.en: Shall we eat together?
examples.note: 우리 같이 ("we, together") makes the group "shall we?" clear.

examples.en: Shall we watch a movie tomorrow?
examples.note: 보다 ends in a vowel → 볼까요?; a casual invite to do something together.

examples.en: Shall I open the window?
examples.note: 열다 ends in ㄹ, so just add -까요? → 열까요?. Here it asks the listener's opinion: "should I?"

examples.en: Where shall we meet?
examples.note: 만나다 → 만날까요?; question words like 어디 fit right in.

keyPoint.label: V-(으)ㄹ까요? vs. V-아/어요
keyPoint.body: 먹어요 states or mildly pushes ("(let's) eat"). 먹을까요? turns it into a real question that hands the decision to the listener — you propose, they answer. Reach for -(으)ㄹ까요? when you actually want their okay, not just to announce the plan.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: The 까 is always tense (ㄲ): 먹을까요? sounds like [머글까요]. The ㄱ of 먹- links forward into 을.

drill.instruction: Turn each verb into a "shall we?" suggestion with -(으)ㄹ까요?.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: After seeing 먹다 → 먹을까요?, learners often glue 을 onto ㄹ-stems too. But ㄹ-stems already end in a vowel-like ㄹ that carries the sound, so you just add -까요?: 놀다 → 놀까요?, 만들다 → 만들까요?, 열다 → 열까요?. No extra 을.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㅂ시다 — formal "let's" for groups
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)ㅂ시다 to suggest that a group do something in a formal or public setting. It sounds organized and official, so it fits meetings, announcements, campaigns, and speeches. For friends, use -자; for a softer suggestion, use -(으)ㄹ까요?

examples.en: Let's start the meeting.
examples.note: A natural meeting-room use: formal, clear, and group-directed.

examples.en: Let's get off at the next station.
examples.note: Announcement-like and organized, not a casual friend-to-friend suggestion.

examples.en: Let's all make a toast.
examples.note: Works when someone leads a group at a dinner or event.

examples.en: Let's follow the rules together.
examples.note: Campaign or public-message tone; 함께 makes the group invitation explicit.

keyPoint.label: -자 < -(으)ㄹ까요? < -(으)ㅂ시다
keyPoint.body: 가자 is casual and close. 갈까요? is softer because it asks the listener's opinion. 갑시다 is formal and group-leading — useful in meetings or public speech, but too stiff for close friends.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In 시작합시다 and 건배합시다, the ㅂ before 시다 is held clearly, and 시다 is always pronounced tense, like [씨다] — 합시다 sounds like [합씨다] at any speed, though the spelling stays 합시다. Don't turn 합시다 into 하십니다 — that is a different ending.

drill.instruction: Change each verb into a formal group suggestion with -(으)ㅂ시다.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English "let's" can sound friendly upward, but -(으)ㅂ시다 can feel like you are leading or directing the other person. With a boss, teacher, or older person one-on-one, use a respectful question such as 가시겠어요? or 가실까요? instead.

exampleSentence.note: 도와주세요 is the core polite help request.

exampleSentence.en: Please say it again slowly.

exampleSentence.en: Shall we go together?

exampleSentence.en: May I ask one small favor?

exampleSentence.en: If the size is big, please exchange it.

lines.grammarNote: 입어 볼까요 asks for an opinion before trying.

lines.ko: 네, 먼저 입어 보세요. 색이 잘 어울려요.
lines.romanization: ne, meonjeo ibeo boseyo. saegi jal eoullyeoyo.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 이 색도 괜찮은데, 다른 색도 추천해 주세요.
lines.romanization: i saekdo gwaenchaneunde, dareun saekdo chucheon hae juseyo.
lines.en: This color is okay, but please recommend another color too.
lines.grammarNote: 추천해 주세요 is a polite request.

lines.romanization: geureom i saekdo hanbeon ibeo boseyo.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 사이즈가 크면 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주세요.
lines.romanization: saijeuga keumyeon han chisu jageun geotdo boyeo juseyo.
lines.en: If the size is big, please show me one size smaller too.
lines.grammarNote: 보여 주세요 is a service request.

readingText.title: Trying before deciding
readingText.body: 민서는 옷 가게에서 재킷을 고르고 있었어요. 직원은 먼저 입어 보세요라고 말했어요. 민서는 이 색도 괜찮지만 다른 색도 보고 싶어서 추천해 달라고 했어요. 직원은 더 밝은 색을 한번 입어 보라고 했고, 민서는 그 색이 더 잘 어울린다고 느꼈어요. 사이즈가 조금 커서 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 달라고 부탁했어요. 이렇게 민서는 바로 결정하지 않고 입어 본 뒤에 선택했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo was choosing a jacket at a clothing store. The staff suggested she try it on first. Minseo asked for another color recommendation, tried a brighter color, and then asked to see one size smaller before deciding.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 직원은 민서에게 먼저 무엇을 해 보라고 했어요?
민서는 왜 추천해 달라고 했어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 다른 색도 보고 싶어서 추천해 달라고 했어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 사이즈가 커서 무엇을 부탁했어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 달라고 부탁했어요.

culturalNote.title: Trying sounds softer than deciding
culturalNote.body: In shops, restaurants, and friendly advice, Korean often uses 한번 and -아/어 보다 to lower the pressure. 한번 입어 보세요, 한번 먹어 볼까요, and 한번 가 봐요 all suggest a trial instead of forcing a decision.
culturalNote.tip: When recommending something, combine 한번 with -아/어 보세요: 한번 드셔 보세요, 한번 입어 보세요, 한번 해 보세요.

inlineExercises.prompt: A shopper wants to try on clothes. Which sentence fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어 볼까요 asks about trying an action before deciding.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which is a polite service request?
options: 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주세요.
inlineExercises.correct: 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주세요.
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어 주세요 turns the action into a polite request.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say 'Please recommend another color too.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 추천하다 becomes 추천해 주세요 in a polite request.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say 'Shall we go together?'
inlineExercises.explanation: 가다 becomes 갈까요? with ㄹ까요, and 같이 makes the suggestion shared.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 입다 보세요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Use the 아/어 form before 보다.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다른 색___ 보여 주세요. (Please show me another color.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 보여 주다 takes the thing shown as an object, so 다른 색을 fits. 이 would make the color the subject.

inlineExercises.prompt: 이 옷을 ___ . (입다 → try doing)
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어 보세요 means try doing something. 입다 becomes 입어 보세요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Shall we go together?'
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ까요? suggests or asks what to do. 같이 makes the suggestion “together.”

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'Shall we try eating it once?'
inlineExercises.explanation: 한번 softens the idea as “just to try.” 먹어 볼까요? asks whether you should try eating it.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the request: '다른 색 추천해 볼까요?'
inlineExercises.explanation: 추천해 볼까요? asks whether we should try recommending, which is not a service request. 추천해 주세요 asks the other person to recommend something for you.

bullets: V아/어 보다 means try doing: 입어 보세요, 먹어 볼까요, 해 봤어요.
한번 softens trial suggestions: 한번 입어 보세요.
V아/어 주세요 makes polite requests: 추천해 주세요, 보여 주세요, 도와주세요.
Vㄹ/을까요? asks for a shared decision or suggestion: 같이 갈까요?, 주문할까요?

writingTask.prompt: Recommend a restaurant to a friend and gently suggest going together this weekend.
writingTask.hint: Use V-아/어 보다 to nudge them to try it (가 보세요/먹어 보세요), V-아/어 주세요 for a request, and V-(으)ㄹ까요? to suggest going together.
writingTask.model: 이 식당 한번 가 보세요. 정말 맛있어요. 우리 주말에 같이 갈까요? 시간 되면 알려 주세요.
writingTask.modelEn: Try going to this restaurant once. It's really delicious. Shall we go together this weekend? If you have time, please let me know.

canDo: Nudge someone to try something with V-아/어 보다 (한번 먹어 보세요)
Make a polite request with V-아/어 주세요 (알려 주세요)
Float a friendly suggestion with V-(으)ㄹ까요? (같이 갈까요?)

chapters.title: Contrast and Concession
chapters.goal: Pass along what someone said without making it sound like your own words.
chapters.scenario: You tell a coworker, classmate, or friend what another person said or asked.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was it?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: It was fun. But the weather was a bit cold.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make three pairs: 비싸지만 맛있어요, 비싸도 갈 거예요, 비싼데도 사람이 많아요. Say what changes in the feeling each time.
chapters.realLifeTask: Report one statement and one question from someone else.
chapters.friendPractice: One person gives an obstacle such as 비싸요, 어려워요, 피곤해요. The other answers with -지만, -아/어도, or -는데도 and explains the choice.
chapters.review: Can you separate simple contrast (-지만), condition that does not change the result (-아/어도), and surprising result (-는데도)?

beginnerGuide.title: Three kinds of but
beginnerGuide.body: -지만 is the plain contrast form: 비싸지만 맛있어요. Use it when two facts pull in different directions without extra emotion.

beginnerGuide.title: Even if the plan stays
beginnerGuide.body: -아/어도 says the result does not change: 비가 와도 갈 거예요, 어려워도 해 볼게요. 괜찮아요 and 상관없어요 pair naturally with this form.

beginnerGuide.title: Even though it is surprising
beginnerGuide.body: -는데도 reacts to an actual situation where the expected result did not happen: 비가 오는데도 사람이 많아요. It sounds stronger than plain -지만.

checkpoints: I can use -다고 했어요 for reported statements.
I can use -냐고 했어요 for reported questions.
I can keep tense and speaker perspective clear.

exitTask.canDo: Pass along what someone said without making it sound like your own words.

sampleAnswer.ko: 민수 씨가 오늘 늦는다고 했어요. 몇 시에 시작하냐고도 물어봤어요.
sampleAnswer.en: Minsu said he will be late today. He also asked what time it starts.

checklist: I can use -다고 했어요 for reported statements.
I can use -냐고 했어요 for reported questions.
I can keep tense and speaker perspective clear.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: Explaining a choice that has both good and bad sides, or continuing with a plan despite a problem.
objectives: Use A/V-지만 for clean contrast: 비싸지만 맛있어요.
Use A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 when the result is surprising despite the situation: 비가 오는데도 사람이 많아요.
Use V아/어도 when the result stays the same even if the condition happens: 비가 와도 갈 거예요.
hook.whyItMatters: Learners often connect everything with 그리고 or translate every 'but' the same way. Korean separates simple contrast, surprising concession, and 'even if' conditions. This lets plans sound more precise and less flat.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-지만 — but
grammarNotes.func: Use -지만 to join two clauses that go against each other, like English "but." The first clause says one thing, and the second says something that pushes the other way.

formTable.when: Verb or adjective stem (consonant or vowel)
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹지만, 비싸다 → 비싸지만, 가다 → 가지만
먹다 → 먹었지만, 가다 → 갔지만, 공부하다 → 공부했지만

examples.en: This book is fun, but it's too long.
examples.note: 재미있- takes -지만 right on the stem; both clauses are about the same book.

examples.en: Korean is hard, but it's fun.
examples.note: The classic shape: one downside, then one upside.

examples.en: I ate, but I'm still hungry.
examples.note: Put the past tense on the first clause: 먹었- + 지만.

examples.en: My friend is a student, but works too.
examples.note: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 이지만: 학생 + 이지만.

keyPoint.label: -지만 vs. 하지만
keyPoint.body: -지만 connects two clauses inside one sentence: 비싸지만 맛있어요. 하지만 is a separate word that starts a new sentence: 비싸요. 하지만 맛있어요. Same meaning, but don't drop 하지만 in the middle of a clause — that spot belongs to -지만.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a final ㄱ or ㅈ-type sound the next syllable tightens: 먹지만 sounds like [먹찌만], 좋지만 like [조치만]. The 지만 part is never the loud part of the word.

drill.instruction: Join the two ideas into one sentence with A/V-지만. Keep any past tense on the first clause.
drill.model: 비싸다 / 사고 싶어요 → 비싸지만 사고 싶어요. (It's expensive, but I want to buy it.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: -지만 goes on the plain stem (어렵-), not on the polite -아/어요 form. Drop the 요, attach -지만 to the stem, and let the politeness show up just once at the very end.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 — even though, and still
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)ㄴ/는데도 for "even though A, B anyway," where B is surprising given A. It points out that the result happened in spite of the first clause.

formTable.when: Adjective stem ending in a vowel
Adjective stem ending in a consonant

examples.en: Even though I took medicine, I'm still sick.
examples.note: 먹었- + 는데도; the second clause is the surprising part.

examples.en: Even though this restaurant is expensive, it's packed.
examples.note: Vowel-ending adjective 비싸- takes -ㄴ데도 → 비싼데도.

examples.en: Even though I study every day, Korean is hard.
examples.note: Present verb 공부하- takes -는데도, the normal verb shape.

examples.en: Even though he has a lot of money, he barely spends it.
examples.note: Consonant-ending adjective 많- takes -은데도 → 많은데도.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄴ/는데도 vs. -지만
keyPoint.body: -지만 is a flat "but." -(으)ㄴ/는데도 adds "and still," with a sense of surprise that B happened anyway. 약을 먹었지만 아파요 just states two facts; 약을 먹었는데도 아파요 sounds more like "I took the medicine and I'm STILL sick."

grammarNotes.pronunciation: Past forms nasalize: 먹었는데도 sounds like [머건는데도], 했는데도 like [핸는데도] — the ㅅ turns into an ㄴ sound before 는. The 도 at the end gets a small push for the "and still" feeling.

drill.instruction: Combine the two clauses with A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 for "even though A, B anyway." Watch verb vs. adjective endings.
drill.model: 운동하다 / 살이 안 빠져요 → 운동하는데도 살이 안 빠져요. (Even though I work out, I don't lose weight.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners stick -는데도 on everything, but -는데도 is for verbs only. Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ데도: 비싸다 → 비싼데도, 좋다 → 좋은데도. Ask if the word is an action (verb → 는데도) or a description (adjective → ㄴ/은데도).

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어도 — even if / even though
grammarNotes.func: Use -아/어도 for "even if" or "even though." It means that no matter how the first clause turns out, the second clause still holds.

formTable.when: Stem with ㅏ or ㅗ as the last vowel
formTable.ex: 가다 → 가도, 오다 → 와도, 보다 → 봐도
먹다 → 먹어도, 읽다 → 읽어도, 마시다 → 마셔도

examples.en: Even if it rains, I go to school.
examples.note: 오다 → 와도; the going happens no matter the rain.

examples.en: No matter how much I eat, I don't get full.
examples.note: 아무리 ... -아/어도 is the set "no matter how much" frame.

examples.en: Even when I'm tired, I work out.
examples.note: 하다 adjective 피곤하- → 피곤해도.

examples.en: Even when I have no time, I still eat.
examples.note: 없- + 어도 → 없어도; the first clause is the condition you push through.

keyPoint.label: -아/어도 vs. -(으)ㄴ/는데도
keyPoint.body: Both can come out as "even though" in English, but -아/어도 covers "even IF" — it works for things that may or may not happen (비가 와도 = even if it rains, real or not). -(으)ㄴ/는데도 is for a real fact happening right now (비가 오는데도 = even though it IS raining). Use -아/어도 for conditions, -는데도 for facts.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: Watch the vowel squeeze: 오다 → 와도, 보다 → 봐도, 마시다 → 마셔도. The 도 stays quiet; the squeezed syllable carries the beat.

drill.instruction: Make a sentence with V-아/어도 for "even if / even though." Pick the right 아/어 vowel.
drill.model: 바쁘다 / 친구를 만나요 → 바빠도 친구를 만나요. (Even if I'm busy, I meet my friend.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: There's no 서 in this pattern — -아/어도 attaches straight to the 아/어 stem. And don't mix it up with -아/어서 ("because"): -아/어서 gives a reason, while -아/어도 gives a concession ("even if").

exampleSentence.en: It is good. But it is a little expensive.
exampleSentence.note: A softer pivot than 하지만.

exampleSentence.en: It is delicious. However, it is expensive.
exampleSentence.note: Use at the start of a new sentence.

exampleSentence.en: It is a little inconvenient. However, it is possible.
exampleSentence.note: A slightly fuller form of 하지만.

exampleSentence.en: It is expensive. Even so, shall we try going?
exampleSentence.note: 그래도 keeps the plan or feeling despite the previous sentence.

exampleSentence.en: It is expensive, but delicious.
exampleSentence.note: A core contrast adjective for shopping and restaurants.

exampleSentence.en: It is cheap, but the quality is good.
exampleSentence.note: Useful for positive contrast.

exampleSentence.en: It is difficult, but fun.
exampleSentence.note: ㅂ irregular appears in 어려워도.

exampleSentence.en: Even if it is easy, you can make a mistake.
exampleSentence.note: 쉽다 becomes 쉬워도.

exampleSentence.en: I will continue even if I am tired.
exampleSentence.note: Good with -아/어도 and 계속.

exampleSentence.en: I will keep going even if it is hard.
exampleSentence.note: Often appears in concession sentences.

exampleSentence.en: It is okay even if there is a problem.
exampleSentence.note: A practical concession noun.

exampleSentence.en: There are drawbacks too, but there are more advantages.
exampleSentence.note: Pairs naturally with 단점.

exampleSentence.en: Even if there is a drawback, I am okay with it.
exampleSentence.note: Useful with -아/어도.

exampleSentence.en: It is okay even if it is a little inconvenient.
exampleSentence.note: 괜찮아요 softens concession.

exampleSentence.en: It is a little inconvenient, but possible.
exampleSentence.note: A realistic planning contrast.

exampleSentence.en: It is difficult, but possible.
exampleSentence.note: Common with contrast.

exampleSentence.en: It does not matter even if it is expensive.
exampleSentence.note: A strong concession response.

extendedDialogue.setting: Friends decide whether to go to a popular restaurant despite price, crowds, and rain.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: This restaurant is expensive, but really delicious.
lines.grammarNote: -지만 gives a clean contrast.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: But there are too many people today.
lines.grammarNote: 그런데 softens the turn into a concern.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Even if there are many people, the food comes out quickly.
lines.grammarNote: -아/어도 keeps the result despite the condition.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Even though it is raining, there are many people waiting.
lines.grammarNote: -는데도 shows a surprising result.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Even so, shall we try going?
lines.grammarNote: 그래도 keeps the plan alive despite the problem.

readingText.title: A good plan with drawbacks
readingText.body: 민서는 새 식당에 가 보고 싶었어요. 그 식당은 비싸지만 음식이 맛있고 서비스도 좋다고 했어요. 지훈은 사람이 너무 많아서 걱정했지만, 민서는 사람이 많아도 음식이 빨리 나온다고 말했어요. 밖에는 비가 오는데도 기다리는 사람이 많았어요. 지훈은 조금 불편해도 괜찮다고 했고, 두 사람은 그래도 한번 가 보기로 했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo wanted to try a new restaurant. It was expensive, but people said the food was good and the service was good. Jihoon worried because there were many people, but Minseo said the food comes out quickly even when it is crowded. Even though it was raining, many people were waiting. They decided to try going anyway.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 그 식당은 비싸지만 무엇이 좋아요?
사람이 많아도 무엇이 빨리 나와요?
밖에는 비가 오는데도 무엇이 많았어요?

culturalNote.title: Softening disagreement
culturalNote.body: In Korean conversation, contrast markers can soften disagreement. 그런데 introduces a concern gently, 하지만 is clearer and firmer, and 그래도 keeps a plan or feeling alive after acknowledging the problem.
culturalNote.tip: For a friendly disagreement, start with 맞아요 or 좋아요, then add 그런데: 좋아요. 그런데 조금 비싸요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence contrasts price and quality?
inlineExercises.explanation: -지만 connects two contrasting facts.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence keeps the plan despite rain?
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어도 means even if or even though.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say 'Even though it is raining, there are many people.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -는데도 emphasizes the surprising result.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say 'It is difficult, but possible.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -지만 gives a clean contrast.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 비가 오아도 가요.
inlineExercises.explanation: 오다 contracts to 와 before 도.

inlineExercises.prompt: 비___ 와도 갈 거예요. (Even if it rains, I will go.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 비 is the subject of 오다, so it takes 가. 를 would make rain an object, which does not fit the weather verb 오다.

inlineExercises.prompt: ___ 맛있어요. (비싸다 → but)
inlineExercises.explanation: -지만 attaches directly to the stem for a clean contrast. 비싸다 becomes 비싸지만.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'It is hard, but fun.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -지만 gives a simple but contrast. The sentence balances the negative point with the positive result.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'Even though I am tired, I keep studying.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -ㄴ데도 shows a surprising result despite the situation. 피곤한데도 keeps the contrast stronger than simple 피곤하지만.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '어렵지만 할 수 없어요.' (intended: difficult but possible)
inlineExercises.explanation: The intended meaning is that it is possible, so use 할 수 있어요. 할 수 없어요 says the opposite: cannot do it.

bullets: -지만 gives clean contrast: 비싸지만 맛있어요.
-는데도 adds surprise or frustration: 비가 오는데도 사람이 많아요.
-아/어도 keeps the result despite the condition: 비가 와도 갈 거예요.
그런데, 하지만, and 그래도 differ in tone: soft concern, clear contrast, and even-so continuation.

writingTask.prompt: Write 3 sentences about something you bought or studied, noting one drawback that didn't stop you.
writingTask.hint: Use A/V-지만 for 'but' (비싸지만), A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 for 'even though' (어려운데도), and V-아/어도 for 'even if' (피곤해도).
writingTask.model: 이 가방은 비싸지만 정말 마음에 들어요. 한국어가 어려운데도 계속 공부해요. 피곤해도 매일 연습할 거예요.
writingTask.modelEn: This bag is expensive but I really like it. Even though Korean is hard, I keep studying. Even if I'm tired, I'll practice every day.

canDo: Join two opposing ideas with A/V-지만 (비싸지만 좋아요)
Say something happened in spite of A with A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 (어려운데도 공부해요)
Say a result holds no matter what with V-아/어도 (피곤해도 가요)

dialogue.en: What are you going to do this weekend?

dialogue.speaker: B

dialogue.speaker: A

dialogue.speaker: B

chapters.guidedPractice: Build three guesses from clues: 하늘이 흐려요 -> 비가 올 것 같아요; 우산을 꺼내요 -> 비가 오나 봐요; 버스가 막혀요 -> 늦을지도 몰라요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say one thing that happened because of a problem using -아서/어서 or -는 바람에.
chapters.friendPractice: One person gives a clue. The other chooses 것 같아요, 나 봐요, or ㄹ지도 몰라요 and explains how certain the guess feels.
chapters.review: Can you tell the difference between a soft prediction, an evidence-based inference, and an open possibility?

beginnerGuide.title: Soft prediction
beginnerGuide.body: Use -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 when you have an impression but not a fact: 비가 올 것 같아요, 조금 늦을 것 같아요.

beginnerGuide.title: Guess from a clue
beginnerGuide.body: Use -나 봐요 or -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 when something you see or hear supports the guess: 우산을 꺼내네요. 비가 오나 봐요.

beginnerGuide.title: Possible, not certain
beginnerGuide.body: Use -(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요 when you want to warn that something might happen: 버스가 늦을지도 몰라요.

checkpoints: I can use -아서/어서 for ordinary cause and result.
I can use -는 바람에 for an unwanted or unexpected result.
I can avoid using -아서/어서 with commands or suggestions.

sampleAnswer.ko: 비가 많이 오는 바람에 약속에 늦었어요.
sampleAnswer.en: Because it rained a lot, I was late for the appointment.

checklist: I can use -아서/어서 for ordinary cause and result.
I can use -는 바람에 for an unwanted or unexpected result.
I can avoid using -아서/어서 with commands or suggestions.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.

hook.situation: You see clues, but you are not fully sure yet: the sky is getting dark, a friend is not replying, or a bus may be late.
objectives: Use A/V-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 for a soft prediction or impression.
Use V/A-나 봐요 and -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 when a visible clue supports the guess.
Use V/A-(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요 when something is possible and the listener should be ready for it.
hook.whyItMatters: English learners often say 'I think' for everything. Korean gives you different levels of certainty: a soft guess, an evidence-based inference, and an open possibility. Choosing the right one keeps you from sounding too sure or too vague.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요
grammarNotes.func: A soft guess or gentle opinion — 'I think it'll…' or 'it looks like…'. This is the everyday, all-purpose way to make what you say sound less certain and a bit softer.

formTable.when: Stem ends in a vowel (verb or adjective)
formTable.ex: 오다 → 올 것 같아요 (it looks like it'll rain)

formTable.when: Stem ends in a consonant (verb or adjective)
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹을 것 같아요 (I think I'll eat it)

formTable.add: the ㄹ drops, then add -ㄹ 것 같아요 (so it looks unchanged)
formTable.ex: 살다 → 살 것 같아요 (it seems they'll live/stay)
가다 → 갔을 것 같아요 (I think they already left)

examples.en: I think it'll rain today.
examples.note: A classic guess from looking at the sky.

examples.en: This movie looks like it'll be fun.
examples.note: 재미있다 → 재미있을 것 같아요; a guess about something you haven't seen yet.

examples.en: I don't think my friend is home.
examples.note: 없다 → 없을 것 같아요; softens a guess about right now.

examples.en: I think I'll have time tomorrow.
examples.note: 있다 → 있을 것 같아요; a gentle 'probably yes' about your own plans.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 vs. -는/(으)ㄴ 것 같아요
keyPoint.body: Use -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 for the future or something you haven't checked yet (비가 올 것 같아요 = you're looking at the clouds). Use -는 것 같아요 / -(으)ㄴ 것 같아요 for something happening right now or already done that you can sense (비가 오는 것 같아요 = you can hear the rain). The ㄹ form is more of a hunch; the 는/ㄴ form is closer to what you're actually noticing.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 것 같아요 sounds like [걷 까타요]: the final ㅅ of 것 turns into a [t] stop, which tenses the next ㄱ into [ㄲ], so you hear 'geot-kkatayo'.

drill.instruction: Make a soft guess with A/V-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요.
drill.model: 비가 오다 → 비가 올 것 같아요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'I think' makes you want to grab 생각하다, but for a guess or impression Korean uses the set phrase -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 ('it seems like'). 생각하다 is for an opinion you actually hold, and it doesn't attach to -(으)ㄹ 것 like this.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-나 봐요 / -(으)ㄴ가 봐요
grammarNotes.func: A guess based on something you can see or hear — 'it seems like (because of what I notice)'. Unlike -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요, this one always means you're reading some clue in front of you.

formTable.ex: 오다 → 오나 봐요 (looks like someone's coming)

formTable.when: Adjective stem ending in a vowel
Adjective stem ending in a consonant

formTable.ex: 가다 → 갔나 봐요 (looks like they left)

examples.en: Looks like my friend finished eating.
examples.note: 먹었 + 나 봐요; you see the empty bowl — a guess from a clue.

examples.en: Looks like it's raining outside.
examples.note: 오다 → 오나 봐요; you hear the sound or see wet umbrellas.

examples.en: The teacher seems busy.
examples.note: 바쁘다 → 바쁜가 봐요; you can see them rushing around.

examples.ko: 이 식당 음식이 맛있나 봐요. 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: i sikdang eumsigi masinna bwayo. sarami manayo.
examples.en: The food here must be good — it's so crowded.
examples.note: 맛있다 takes -나 봐요 like a verb → 맛있나 봐요; the crowd is the clue.

keyPoint.label: -나 봐요 vs. -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요
keyPoint.body: -나 봐요 needs a real clue and is usually about other people or the world around you, not your own feelings — you wouldn't say 제가 배고프나 봐요 about yourself. -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 can be a pure hunch with no clue and can be about you too (저 배고플 것 같아요). If you can point to something you noticed, -나 봐요 sounds more natural.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: Past forms like 먹었나 봐요 blend across the seam: 먹었나 comes out as [머건나] (the ㅆ becomes [n] before 나), so you hear 'meo-geon-na bwayo'.

drill.instruction: Look at the clue and guess with V/A-나 봐요 / -(으)ㄴ가 봐요.
drill.model: (우산이 젖었어요) 비가 오다 → 비가 오나 봐요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'I guess I'm tired' tempts you to use -나 봐요 about yourself, but this pattern is for guessing about others from an outside clue — you can't 'observe' your own feeling that way. For yourself, use -(으)ㄹ/은 것 같아요 instead.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요
grammarNotes.func: Says something 'might' or 'may' happen — a real but uncertain possibility, often one you want the other person to keep in mind, like 'it might rain, so just in case…'.

formTable.when: Stem ends in a vowel (verb or adjective)
Stem ends in a consonant (verb or adjective)

formTable.add: the ㄹ drops, then add -ㄹ지도 몰라요
formTable.ex: 멀다 → 멀지도 몰라요 (it might be far)
가다 → 갔을지도 몰라요 (they might have already left)

examples.en: My friend might not come tomorrow.
examples.note: 오다 → 올지도; raises a possibility to keep in mind.

examples.en: If we go now, we might not have time.
examples.note: 없다 → 없을지도; a heads-up about a risk.

examples.ko: 그 식당은 벌써 문을 닫았을지도 몰라요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdangeun beolsseo muneul dadasseuljido mollayo.
examples.en: That restaurant might have closed already.
examples.note: 닫았 + 을지도 몰라요; a guess about something that may already be true.

examples.en: This book might be a bit hard.
examples.note: 어렵다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 어려울지도; a gentle heads-up.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요 vs. -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요
keyPoint.body: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 leans toward 'probably' — you think it's fairly likely. -(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요 means 'it's just a possibility' — less likely, often flagged as something to watch out for just in case (비가 올 것 같아요 = I expect rain; 비가 올지도 몰라요 = it might rain, so bring an umbrella to be safe).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -지도 몰라요 keeps a clear [지도]. 몰라요 comes from 모르다 (모르 + 아요 → 몰라요), said [몰라요] with a strong double ㄹ.

drill.instruction: Raise a possibility with A/V-(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요.
drill.model: 내일 비가 오다 → 내일 비가 올지도 몰라요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 몰라요 means 'don't know', so learners try to slot in a bare 모르다 ('비가 올 모르다'). But this is a fixed ending: you need -(으)ㄹ지도 right before 몰라요. And even though 몰라요 is in there, the whole thing is a statement of possibility, not a question — 비가 올지도 몰라요 means 'it might rain', not 'do you know if it'll rain?'

exampleSentence.en: I will probably be a little late.
exampleSentence.note: 아마 naturally reinforces a soft guess.

exampleSentence.en: The sky is cloudy.
exampleSentence.note: A common clue before a weather guess.

extendedVocabulary.english: to be cloudy; to be blurry

exampleSentence.ko: 하늘이 흐려서 비가 올 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: The sky is cloudy, so I think it will rain.
exampleSentence.note: Weather clue plus prediction.

exampleSentence.en: It might rain.
exampleSentence.note: 비 takes 이/가 and pairs with 오다.

exampleSentence.en: People are taking out umbrellas.
exampleSentence.note: A visible clue for 비가 오나 봐요.

exampleSentence.ko: 길이 막혀서 조금 늦을 것 같아요.
exampleSentence.en: Traffic is heavy, so I think I will be a little late.
exampleSentence.note: A high-frequency message sentence.

exampleSentence.en: There is no reply. I guess they are busy.
exampleSentence.note: Adjectives use -(으)ㄴ가 봐요.

exampleSentence.en: Their voice is quiet. I guess they are tired.
exampleSentence.note: Use for inferred tiredness in someone else.

exampleSentence.en: Since we are not sure, let's check.
exampleSentence.note: Useful when deciding how strong your guess is.

exampleSentence.en: There is a chance it will rain.
exampleSentence.note: A noun-based way to talk about probability.

exampleSentence.en: The umbrella is the clue.
exampleSentence.note: A clue supports -나 봐요.

exampleSentence.en: We can infer from the clue.
exampleSentence.note: Names the thinking process behind the grammar.

exampleSentence.en: They might be late.
exampleSentence.note: In -ㄹ지도 몰라요, 모르다 is part of a fixed possibility pattern.

exampleSentence.en: I think it will rain soon.
exampleSentence.note: Soon, from the current moment.

exampleSentence.en: The rain might stop soon.
exampleSentence.note: Often used for a short wait or quick change.

exampleSentence.en: The rain stopped.
exampleSentence.note: Weather uses 이/가 with 그치다.

extendedDialogue.setting: Two friends look at weather and message clues before meeting someone.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 하늘이 갑자기 흐려졌어요. 곧 비가 올 것 같아요.
lines.romanization: haneuri gapjagi heuryeojyeosseoyo. got biga ol geot gatayo.
lines.en: The sky suddenly got cloudy. I think it will rain soon.
lines.grammarNote: A visible clue supports a soft prediction.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 사람들이 우산을 꺼내네요. 벌써 비가 조금 오나 봐요.
lines.romanization: saramdeuri usaneul kkeonaeneyo. beolsseo biga jogeum ona bwayo.
lines.en: People are taking out umbrellas. I guess it is already raining a little.
lines.grammarNote: -나 봐요 marks evidence-based inference.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 수진 씨 답장도 없어요. 많이 바쁜가 봐요.
lines.romanization: sujin ssi dapjangdo eopseoyo. mani bappeunga bwayo.
lines.en: Su-jin is not replying either. I guess she is really busy.
lines.grammarNote: Adjective 바쁘다 becomes 바쁜가 봐요.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: If the bus is stuck too, she might be a little late.
lines.grammarNote: -ㄹ지도 몰라요 leaves the possibility open.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Since we are not sure, let's wait inside the cafe.
lines.grammarNote: A practical decision follows the uncertain guess.

readingText.title: Reading clues before a meeting
readingText.body: 민서는 약속 장소로 가는 길에 하늘이 갑자기 흐려지는 것을 봤어요. 그래서 곧 비가 올 것 같다고 생각했어요. 지하철역 앞에서는 사람들이 우산을 꺼내고 있었어요. 민서는 비가 조금 오나 봐요라고 말했어요. 그런데 친구 수진 씨는 아직 답장이 없었어요. 지훈은 수진 씨가 바쁜가 봐요, 조금 늦을지도 몰라요라고 했어요. 두 사람은 확실하지 않으니까 밖에서 기다리지 않고 카페 안으로 들어갔어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo saw the sky suddenly getting cloudy on the way to the meeting place, so she thought it would rain soon. In front of the subway station, people were taking out umbrellas, so she inferred that it was raining. Their friend Su-jin had not replied yet, so Jihoon guessed she might be busy and a little late. Since they were not sure, they waited inside a cafe instead of outside.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 무엇을 보고 비가 올 것 같다고 생각했어요?
사람들이 우산을 꺼내는 것은 어떤 단서예요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 비가 조금 오나 봐요라고 추측할 수 있는 단서예요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 두 사람은 왜 카페 안으로 들어갔어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 확실하지 않았고 밖에서 기다리기 불편해서 카페 안으로 들어갔어요.

culturalNote.title: Soft guesses in Korean conversation
culturalNote.body: Korean speakers often soften guesses with 것 같아요, 나 봐요, or -ㄹ지도 몰라요, especially when talking about another person's situation. It sounds more careful than declaring a reason you cannot fully know.
culturalNote.tip: Use direct Korean when you know the fact, but use these forms when you are reading clues: 답장이 없네요. 바쁜가 봐요.

inlineExercises.prompt: You see dark clouds and want a soft prediction. Which sentence fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: -ㄹ 것 같아요 makes a soft prediction from the clue.

inlineExercises.prompt: People are taking out umbrellas. Which form best shows inference from evidence?
inlineExercises.explanation: -나 봐요 says your guess comes from a clue you noticed.

inlineExercises.prompt: You are not sure, but the bus may be late. Which sentence fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: -ㄹ지도 몰라요 keeps the possibility open.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete: 답장이 없네요. 많이 바쁜___ 봐요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Adjective 바쁘다 becomes 바쁜가 봐요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 비가 올 모르다.
inlineExercises.explanation: The possibility pattern keeps -ㄹ지도 before 몰라요.

inlineExercises.prompt: 하늘___ 흐려요. (The sky is cloudy.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 하늘 is the subject being described, so it takes 이. 을 would make the sky an object, which does not fit 흐리다.

inlineExercises.prompt: 버스가 ___ . (늦다 → may/might)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요 marks possibility. 늦다 has a consonant-ending stem, so it becomes 늦을지도 몰라요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'There is no reply. I guess they are busy.'
inlineExercises.explanation: The missing reply is the clue. 바쁜가 봐요 gives an evidence-based guess about someone else.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'It will probably rain.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 아마 marks probability, and 올 것 같아요 softens the prediction. 비가 is the subject of the rain coming.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '친구가 피곤나 봐요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Adjectives often use -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 for evidence-based guesses. 피곤하다 becomes 피곤한가 봐요.

bullets: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 gives a soft prediction or impression: 비가 올 것 같아요.
-나 봐요 / -(으)ㄴ가 봐요 means the guess comes from a clue: 우산을 꺼내네요. 비가 오나 봐요.
-(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요 keeps a possibility open: 버스가 늦을지도 몰라요.
Do not use evidence-based inference for your own obvious feeling. Say 피곤해요, not 저는 피곤한가 봐요.

writingTask.prompt: Text a friend a careful guess about the weather and why they should bring an umbrella.
writingTask.hint: Use A/V-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 for a soft guess (올 것 같아요), V/A-나 봐요 for a guess from a clue (흐린가 봐요), and A/V-(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요 for 'might' (올지도 몰라요).
writingTask.model: 하늘이 흐린가 봐요. 오후에 비가 올 것 같아요. 비가 올지도 모르니까 우산을 가져가세요.
writingTask.modelEn: It seems cloudy out. I think it'll rain in the afternoon. It might rain, so please take an umbrella.

canDo: Make a soft guess with A/V-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 (비가 올 것 같아요)
Guess from a clue I notice with V/A-나 봐요 (흐린가 봐요)
Flag an uncertain possibility with A/V-(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요 (늦을지도 몰라요)

chapters.title: Ongoing Actions
chapters.goal: Say something almost happened, or that there is no choice but to do it.
chapters.scenario: You nearly missed a train, almost made a mistake, or have only one option.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was it?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: It was fun. But the weather was a bit cold.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make one status sentence with each frame: 공부하고 있어요, 기다리는 중이에요, 회의하는 동안 메시지를 못 봤어요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Describe one almost-happened situation and one unavoidable action.
chapters.friendPractice: One person asks 지금 뭐 하고 있어요? The other answers once with -고 있어요, once with -는 중이에요, and once with -는 동안.
chapters.review: Can you choose between broad ongoing action, in-the-middle status, and overlapping duration?

beginnerGuide.title: Action in progress
beginnerGuide.body: Use -고 있어요 for an action happening now or around now: 공부하고 있어요, 전화하고 있어요, 쉬고 있어요.

beginnerGuide.title: In the middle
beginnerGuide.body: Use -는 중이에요 or N 중이에요 for a quick current-status reply: 기다리는 중이에요, 회의 중이에요, 전화 중이에요.

beginnerGuide.title: During the span
beginnerGuide.body: Use -는 동안 when another action happens inside the same time span: 회의하는 동안 메시지를 못 봤어요.

checkpoints: I can use -ㄹ 뻔했어요 for almost happened.
I can use -ㄹ 수밖에 없어요 for no real choice.
I can use 만 to narrow the option or limit.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Say something almost happened, or that there is no choice but to do it.
exitTask.prompt: Describe one almost-happened situation and one unavoidable action.

sampleAnswer.ko: 지하철을 놓칠 뻔했어요. 그래서 택시를 탈 수밖에 없었어요.
sampleAnswer.en: I almost missed the subway. So I had no choice but to take a taxi.

checklist: I can use -ㄹ 뻔했어요 for almost happened.
I can use -ㄹ 수밖에 없어요 for no real choice.
I can use 만 to narrow the option or limit.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: You are texting someone what you are doing right now, why you did not reply, or what happened during another action.
objectives: Use V-고 있어요 for an action in progress.
Use V-는 중이에요 or N 중이에요 when you are right in the middle of something.
Use V-는 동안 to show what happens during the same time span.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean does not need a separate word like English 'am/is/are doing.' The ongoing meaning is built with endings and nouns: 공부하고 있어요, 공부하는 중이에요, 공부하는 동안. These forms make Kakao replies and daily updates much more natural.

grammarNotes.title: V-고 있다 — an action in progress
grammarNotes.func: Add -고 있다 to a verb stem to say an action is happening right now. It is the closest match to English 'be -ing' (am/is/are doing).

formTable.when: Any verb stem (vowel or consonant): drop -다, add -고 있다
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹고 있다 (eating), 보다 → 보고 있다 (watching)

examples.en: I'm eating right now.
examples.note: 지금 + -고 있어요 is the go-to pair for something happening this very moment.

examples.en: My friend is reading a book.
examples.note: Other people work the same way; just change the subject to 친구가.

examples.en: My little brother is watching a movie.
examples.note: 보다 ends in a vowel and still just takes -고 있어요 — the rule never changes.

examples.en: I was studying Korean a little while ago.
examples.note: -고 있었어요 is the past version: 'was doing.'

keyPoint.label: -고 있어요 vs. plain -아요/-어요
keyPoint.body: 먹어요 can mean 'I eat (usually)' or even 'I'll eat.' 먹고 있어요 pins it down to 'I'm eating right now.' Reach for -고 있어요 when you want to make clear the action is happening as you speak.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 있어요 runs together as [이써요], and -고 tenses to [꼬] after ㄱ, so 먹고 있어요 sounds like [먹꼬 이써요].

drill.instruction: Say what each person is doing right now with -고 있어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English can say 'I'm liking it,' but Korean feeling/state verbs like 좋아하다, 알다, 사랑하다 don't take -고 있다 for a current state. Just use the plain present. Save -고 있다 for actions you can actually watch happening.

grammarNotes.title: V-는 중이에요 / N 중이에요 — in the middle of
grammarNotes.func: 중 means 'the middle of.' Add -는 중이에요 to a verb stem, or just 중이에요 to a noun, to say you're 'in the middle of' something right now.

formTable.when: Verb stem + -는 중이에요 (vowel or consonant stem)
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹는 중이에요 (in the middle of eating)

formTable.when: ㄹ-stem verb: drop ㄹ, then add -는 중이에요
formTable.ex: 만들다 → 만드는 중이에요 (in the middle of making)
회의 → 회의 중이에요 (in a meeting), 공부 → 공부 중이에요

examples.en: I'm in the middle of eating right now.
examples.note: -는 중이에요 plays up that you're partway through it, not done.

examples.en: I'm waiting for my friend.
examples.note: 기다리다 ends in a vowel and just takes -는 중이에요.

examples.en: I'm studying right now.
examples.note: With a noun like 공부, drop the verb and say just 'noun + 중이에요' — no 을/를.

examples.en: Mom is on the phone.
examples.note: 전화 중이에요 is the set phrase for 'on the phone.'

keyPoint.label: -는 중이에요 vs. -고 있어요
keyPoint.body: Both mean 'be doing,' but -는 중이에요 means you're smack in the middle of one specific action, so it can't describe a lasting state. You can say 한국에 살고 있어요 (I'm living in Korea), but not 사는 중이에요 — 중 needs a action that starts and stops, like eating or waiting.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 먹는 → ㄱ before ㄴ turns into [ㅇ] (nasal), so 먹는 sounds like [멍는]: [멍는 중이에요].

drill.instruction: Answer '지금 뭐 해요?' saying you're right in the middle of it, with -는 중이에요 or N 중이에요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 중 is a noun, so it needs 이에요 after it: 중이에요, not 중에요. Learners drop the 이 because it goes by fast when spoken, but the full form keeps 중 + 이에요.

grammarNotes.title: V-는 동안 — while / during
grammarNotes.func: 동안 means 'the whole time of.' Add -는 동안 to a verb stem to say 'while (someone) is doing something.' The main action happens over that same stretch of time.

formTable.when: Verb stem + -는 동안 (vowel or consonant stem)
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹는 동안 (while eating), 자다 → 자는 동안 (while sleeping)

formTable.when: ㄹ-stem verb: drop ㄹ, then add -는 동안
Noun + 동안 ('for / during' a stretch of time)
formTable.ex: 한 시간 → 한 시간 동안 (for one hour), 방학 → 방학 동안 (during vacation)

examples.en: While I cooked, my friend cleaned.
examples.note: Two people, same time: I cook, my friend cleans.

examples.ko: 동생이 자는 동안 저는 책을 읽었어요.
examples.romanization: dongsaengi janeun dongan jeoneun chaegeul ilgeosseoyo.
examples.en: While my little brother was sleeping, I read a book.
examples.note: 자다 → 자는 동안. The main verb (past) tells you when it all happened.

examples.en: I watched a movie while I ate.
examples.note: One person doing both at once is fine too.

examples.en: I'll study Korean during the vacation.
examples.note: With a noun like 방학, use just 'noun + 동안' for 'during / for' that time.

keyPoint.label: -는 동안 (always 는) vs. -(으)ㄹ 때
keyPoint.body: -는 동안 always keeps -는, no matter the tense, because it marks a whole stretch of time. 때 ('when') points at one moment or occasion; 동안 covers the full length. Use 동안 when one action runs the whole time another is going on.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 먹는 동안 → 먹는 nasalizes to [멍는] (ㄱ+ㄴ → ㅇ+ㄴ), so it's [멍는 동안].

drill.instruction: Join the two halves with -는 동안 to mean 'while ___, ___.'
drill.model: 제가 자다 / 엄마가 요리하다 → 제가 자는 동안 엄마가 요리했어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English puts 'while' on a past verb ('while I ate'), so learners add 었 before 동안. In Korean, -는 동안 stays in the -는 form no matter the tense — only the main clause shows past.

exampleSentence.en: I am in a meeting.

exampleSentence.en: I read a book while waiting.
exampleSentence.note: 동안 marks the overlapping time span.

exampleSentence.note: A basic V-고 있어요 example.

exampleSentence.en: I am waiting for a friend.
exampleSentence.note: Waiting is a natural ongoing action.

exampleSentence.en: I am on a call right now.
exampleSentence.note: 전화 중이에요 is also common.

exampleSentence.en: I could not see the message during the meeting.
exampleSentence.note: A common reason for a delayed reply.

exampleSentence.en: I did not see the message.

exampleSentence.en: I am still in a meeting.

exampleSentence.en: Is it already finished?

exampleSentence.en: I am still studying / I keep studying.
exampleSentence.note: 계속 emphasizes the action continues.

exampleSentence.en: I am resting for a moment.
exampleSentence.note: Useful for short status updates.

exampleSentence.en: I am working right now.
exampleSentence.note: Natural quick reply to why you cannot talk.

exampleSentence.en: I am resting for a moment.
exampleSentence.note: A simple ongoing action.

exampleSentence.en: I am eating right now.
exampleSentence.note: 먹다 becomes 먹는 before 중.

exampleSentence.en: I am making presentation materials.

readingText.title: Why the reply was late
readingText.body: 지훈은 도서관에서 한국어를 공부하고 있었어요. 민서가 메시지를 보냈지만 지훈은 바로 답장하지 못했어요. 그때 지훈은 회의하는 동안 휴대폰을 보지 못했고, 회의가 끝난 뒤에도 발표 자료를 만드는 중이었어요. 민서는 카페에서 친구를 기다리는 중이라 시간이 조금 있었어요. 그래서 두 사람은 지훈이 끝나면 잠깐 전화하기로 했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Jihoon was studying Korean at the library. Minseo sent a message, but Jihoon could not reply right away. During the meeting he could not check his phone, and after the meeting he was still making presentation materials. Minseo had a little time because she was waiting for a friend at a cafe, so they decided to call briefly when Jihoon finished.

culturalNote.title: Short status replies
culturalNote.body: In Korean messaging, short status replies like 회의 중이에요, 가는 중이에요, and 지금 공부하고 있어요 are common and polite. They explain availability without over-explaining.
culturalNote.tip: Use N 중이에요 for quick status, and V-고 있어요 when you want to state the actual action.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence describes an action in progress?
inlineExercises.explanation: -고 있어요 marks an ongoing action.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence is the best short status reply?

bullets: V-고 있어요 marks an action in progress: 한국어를 공부하고 있어요.
V-는 중이에요 and N 중이에요 focus on being in the middle of something: 회의 중이에요.
V-는 동안 marks an overlapping time span: 회의하는 동안 메시지를 못 봤어요.
Do not use -고 있어요 with adjectives like 바쁘다 or 피곤하다.

writingTask.prompt: Reply to a friend's message saying what you're doing right now and asking them to wait a moment.

Say I'm in the middle of something with V-는 중이에요 (회의 중이에요)
Set one action against a stretch of time with V-는 동안 (기다리는 동안)

beginnerGuide.title: Completed first
beginnerGuide.body: Use -고 나서 when the first action is finished before the next one starts: 손을 씻고 나서 밥을 먹어요.

beginnerGuide.title: No gap
beginnerGuide.body: Use -자마자 when the second action happens immediately: 도착하자마자 전화해 주세요.

beginnerGuide.title: Timeline words
beginnerGuide.body: 먼저, 그다음, 바로, 방금, and 이미 make the order and completion status clear.

I can give a reason with -거든요 or -아서/어서.
I can use 것 같아요 when I want the opinion to feel less direct.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: You need to explain a routine, a travel step, or a small mistake in the exact order it happened.
objectives: Use V-고 나서 when one action is finished before the next starts.
Use V-자마자 when the second action happens immediately after the first.
Use sequence words like 먼저, 그다음, 바로, 이미, and 방금 to make the timeline easy to follow.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean sequence is not only 'and then.' Plain -고 can list actions, but -고 나서 highlights completion, and -자마자 highlights no gap. This matters in real messages like 'after I arrive, I will call' versus 'the moment I arrive, I will call.'

grammarNotes.title: V-고 나서 — after finishing, then
grammarNotes.func: V-고 나서 means "after doing V (and finishing it)." It tells the listener that the first action is done before the next one starts. Usually the same person does both actions.

formTable.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel
formTable.ex: 보다 → 보고 나서, 자다 → 자고 나서

formTable.when: Verb stem ending in a consonant
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹고 나서, 씻다 → 씻고 나서
놀다 → 놀고 나서, 만들다 → 만들고 나서

formTable.when: Never put past tense on this verb
formTable.add: keep the stem plain — 나서 already means "after"

examples.en: After I eat, I brush my teeth.
examples.note: Eating finishes first, then the next thing starts.

examples.en: After I did my homework, I met a friend.
examples.note: The past tense goes only on the last verb (만났어요), not on 하다.

examples.en: After I wash my hands, I eat.
examples.note: Same person does both — the usual case for -고 나서.

examples.ko: 이 책을 읽고 나서 영화를 볼 거예요.
examples.romanization: i chaek-eul ilkko naseo yeonghwa-reul bol geoyeyo.
examples.en: After I finish this book, I'm going to watch a movie.
examples.note: Works for plans too. 읽고 sounds like [일꼬]. The reading has to finish first.

keyPoint.label: -고 나서 vs. plain -고
keyPoint.body: Plain -고 just links two actions like "and": 밥을 먹고 이를 닦아요 (I eat and brush my teeth). Adding 나서 puts the spotlight on finishing the first one before starting the next. Reach for -고 나서 when you want "after I'm done with this, then that."

grammarNotes.pronunciation: You hear it as [고 나서]. Note that 고 tenses after a stem ending in a stop sound: 먹고 나서 sounds like [먹꼬 나서], 받고 나서 like [받꼬 나서]. After a vowel (보고 나서) it stays soft. Keep 나서 light so it links right on.

drill.instruction: Join the two actions into one sentence with V-고 나서, in the 해요 form.
drill.model: 손을 씻다 + 밥을 먹다 → 손을 씻고 나서 밥을 먹어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: "After I ate" feels past in English, so people add -었- to the first verb. But 나서 already carries "after finishing," so the first verb stays a plain stem. Only the last verb shows the real tense.

grammarNotes.title: V-자마자 — as soon as
grammarNotes.func: V-자마자 means "as soon as / the moment V happens." The second thing comes right after the first, with no time in between. The two halves can have the same person or different ones.

formTable.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel
Verb stem ending in a consonant
Never put past tense on this verb
formTable.add: keep the stem plain — tense goes on the second half only

examples.en: As soon as I get home, I wash my hands.
examples.note: No gap — the washing happens the instant you walk in.

examples.en: As soon as the movie ended, I went home.
examples.note: Here the two halves have different subjects (the movie / I).

examples.en: As soon as I got to school, I called my friend.
examples.note: Past tense shows up only on the second verb (전화했어요).

examples.en: As soon as I lay down, I fell asleep.
examples.note: An immediate, almost automatic reaction with no delay.

keyPoint.label: -자마자 vs. -고 나서
keyPoint.body: Both put one action before another, but the timing is different. -고 나서 is "after finishing," and a pause is fine: 밥을 먹고 나서 좀 쉬었어요 (I ate, then rested a bit). -자마자 is "the very moment," no gap at all: 집에 오자마자 잤어요 (got home and went straight to sleep). Use -자마자 only when there's truly no time in between.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: You hear it as [자마자], three even, light beats. After a stem ending in a stop sound it tenses a little: 듣자마자 sounds like [듣짜마자], 눕자마자 like [눕짜마자]. After a vowel (오자마자) it stays soft. No pause before it.

drill.instruction: Join the two actions into one sentence with V-자마자.
drill.model: 집에 오다 + 손을 씻다 → 집에 오자마자 손을 씻어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: "As soon as I came home" is past in English, so people add -았/었- to the first verb. In Korean, 자마자 sticks to the plain stem (오-), never a past form. Put the past tense only on the second verb (씻었어요).

exampleSentence.en: After getting ready, I left right away.

extendedDialogue.setting: A friend asks about a morning mistake and the steps that followed.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: What order did you get ready in this morning?
lines.grammarNote: 순서 sets up a step-by-step explanation.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 먼저 손을 씻고 나서 아침을 먹었어요.
lines.romanization: meonjeo soneul ssitgo naseo achimeul meogeosseoyo.

lines.grammarNote: -고 나서 marks the completed first step.

lines.speaker: 민서

lines.speaker: 지훈

readingText.title: A small morning mistake
readingText.body: 지훈은 아침에 먼저 손을 씻고 나서 아침을 먹었어요. 그다음 불을 끄고 문을 닫고 집에서 나왔어요. 그런데 엘리베이터 앞에 도착하자마자 지갑을 두고 온 걸 알았어요. 그래서 다시 집에 올라갔어요. 지갑을 챙기고 나서 다시 출발했고, 역에 도착하자마자 친구에게 전화했어요. 친구는 이미 예약을 확인하고 기다리고 있었어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: In the morning, Jihoon first washed his hands and ate breakfast. Then he turned off the light, closed the door, and came out. But as soon as he reached the elevator, he realized he had left his wallet behind. So he went back up. After grabbing his wallet, he left again, and as soon as he arrived at the station, he called his friend. His friend had already checked the reservation and was waiting.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 지훈은 아침을 먹기 전에 무엇을 했어요?
지훈은 언제 지갑을 두고 온 걸 알았어요?
지훈은 지갑을 챙기고 나서 무엇을 했어요?

culturalNote.title: Clear order in practical messages
culturalNote.body: Korean sequence markers are useful for quick explanations: 먼저, 그다음, -고 나서, and -자마자 let the listener follow the order without guessing.
culturalNote.tip: Use -고 나서 for completed steps and -자마자 for immediate next actions, especially in travel, errands, and appointment updates.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'as soon as I arrived'?

inlineExercises.prompt: 집에 ___ 전화했어요. (도착하다 → as soon as)
inlineExercises.explanation: -자마자 means as soon as the first action happens. 도착하다 becomes 도착하자마자.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'After washing up, I slept.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -고 나서 makes the first action clearly finished before the second starts. 씻고 나서 comes before 잤어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'First get ready, then depart.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 먼저 and 그다음 make the timeline explicit. 준비하고 links the first step before 출발해요.

inlineExercises.explanation: -자마자 attaches to the verb stem, not the past form. 끝나다 becomes 끝나자마자.

bullets: V-고 나서 means after finishing the first action: 손을 씻고 나서 밥을 먹어요.
V-자마자 means as soon as, with almost no gap: 도착하자마자 전화했어요.
먼저, 그다음, 바로, 방금, and 이미 help the timeline feel clear.
Do not put tense on the first verb: 도착하자마자, not 도착했자마자.

writingTask.prompt: Describe your morning routine in order: what you do first, then next, and what you do as soon as you arrive.

writingTask.model: 먼저 씻고 나서 밥을 먹어요. 그다음에 준비하고 나서 출발해요. 회사에 도착하자마자 메일을 확인해요.

beginnerGuide.title: Interrupted action
beginnerGuide.body: Use -다가 when the first action is underway and then something changes: 학교에 가다가 전화를 받았어요.

beginnerGuide.title: Changed plan words
beginnerGuide.body: 중간에, 계획, 바꾸다, 취소하다, 문자, and 갑자기 help explain why the original action changed.

beginnerGuide.title: Result state
beginnerGuide.body: Use -아/어 있어요 for the state that remains: 앉아 있어요, 문이 열려 있어요, 불이 켜져 있어요.

hook.situation: A plan changes while you are on the way, eating, watching something, or already seated somewhere.
objectives: Use V-다가 when an action is interrupted, paused, or changed mid-way.
Use V-아/어 있다 for a state that remains after an action or change.
Explain changed plans with practical words like 중간에, 바꾸다, 취소하다, 문자, and 갑자기.
hook.whyItMatters: English 'while' can hide the difference between two actions happening together and one action being interrupted. Korean -다가 clearly says the first action was in progress and then something changed. V-아/어 있다 then lets you describe the state after the change.

grammarNotes.title: V-다가 — break off one action to do another
grammarNotes.func: V-다가 says you were in the middle of one action when you stopped partway and switched to (or got interrupted by) a second one. The first action does not finish — you break off from it. The same person does both actions.

formTable.when: Add straight to the plain verb stem (no vowel change, same after vowel or consonant)
formTable.ex: 가다 → 가다가, 먹다 → 먹다가, 자다 → 자다가

formTable.when: Often cut to just -다 in everyday speech
Past stem -았/었다가 = first action was finished, then undone or reversed

examples.en: I was on my way to school and ran into a friend.
examples.note: The going gets cut off partway by something you didn't plan.

examples.en: I was doing my homework and fell asleep.
examples.note: You stop the homework because the second thing happens to you.

examples.en: I was eating and then took a phone call.
examples.note: Same person breaks off from eating to do the next thing.

examples.en: I bought this book and then returned it.
examples.note: -았다가 shows the buying was finished, then reversed.

keyPoint.label: V-다가 vs. V-고 나서
keyPoint.body: V-고 나서 means you finish the first thing all the way, then do the next (밥을 먹고 나서 = after you're done eating). V-다가 means the first thing gets cut off in the middle and you switch (밥을 먹다가 = you were still eating and then stopped to...). 다가 = broke off; 고 나서 = finished.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 다가 is said plainly as [다가]. In -았다가/-었다가 the ㅆ makes the ㄷ tense, so 샀다가 sounds like [삳따가].

drill.instruction: Join the two actions into one sentence with V-다가, so the first action gets interrupted by the second.
drill.model: 집에 가다 / 친구를 만나다 → 집에 가다가 친구를 만났어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 숙제를 하고 잠이 들었어요. (meant: I fell asleep WHILE doing homework)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English "and then" hides whether action 1 finished. -고 just lists things in order and sounds like you finished the homework. To say you broke off in the middle of it, you need -다가.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어 있다 — a state that stays after the action
grammarNotes.func: V-아/어 있다 describes the state that is left over after an action is done. The action already happened, and the subject stays in that result (앉아 있다 = is sitting, having sat down). It goes with verbs that leave a state behind, like 앉다, 서다, 오다, 열리다.

formTable.when: Stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ
formTable.ex: 앉다 → 앉아 있다, 오다 → 와 있다
서다 → 서 있다, 열리다 → 열려 있다

formTable.when: Passive / result verbs work too (the door opens, the light comes on)
formTable.ex: 켜지다 → 켜져 있다, 쓰이다 → 쓰여 있다

examples.en: My friend is sitting on the chair.
examples.note: They sat down earlier and are still in the seated state now.

examples.en: The door is open.
examples.note: Someone opened it before and it stays open — a lasting result. Note 열리다 (opens), not 열다 (open it).

examples.en: A name is written on the board.
examples.note: Someone wrote it earlier; the result (the name being there) stays. Use the passive 쓰이다 → 쓰여 있다.

examples.en: My younger sibling is still at school (went and is there).
examples.note: 가 있다 = went and is staying there, not the act of going.

keyPoint.label: V-아/어 있다 vs. V-고 있다
keyPoint.body: V-고 있다 = an action happening right now (앉고 있어요 = is in the middle of sitting down). V-아/어 있다 = the state after it's done (앉아 있어요 = is already seated and staying that way). Use -아/어 있다 for the leftover result, -고 있다 for the action in progress.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 앉아 있어요 links across the words — the ㅈ carries over, so it sounds like [안자 이써요]. 열려 있어요 sounds like [열려 이써요].

drill.instruction: Answer that the subject is right now in the result state, using V-아/어 있다.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 문이 열고 있어요. (meant: The door is open)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English "is open" looks like a -ing form, which tempts -고 있다. But -고 있다 means the action is happening now. A door just staying open is a result state, so you need -아/어 있다 — and with the intransitive 열리다 (opens), not 열다 (open it).

exampleSentence.en: I got a call while going to school.
exampleSentence.note: 가다가 is the core movement interruption frame.

exampleSentence.en: A call came while I was eating.
exampleSentence.note: The meal is not the completed first step.

exampleSentence.en: I fell asleep while watching the movie.
exampleSentence.note: A common unintended switch.

exampleSentence.en: I changed the plan midway.
exampleSentence.note: A direct plan-change phrase.

exampleSentence.en: I changed the plan.
exampleSentence.note: The object being changed takes 을/를.

exampleSentence.en: The class was canceled.
exampleSentence.note: A common reason a plan changes mid-way.

exampleSentence.en: I got a class cancellation text.
exampleSentence.note: The message interrupts the original plan.

exampleSentence.en: I got a text while riding the subway.
exampleSentence.note: -고 있다가 makes the ongoing ride explicit.

exampleSentence.en: I got a phone call.
exampleSentence.note: The incoming call can interrupt an action.

exampleSentence.en: I am sitting at the cafe.
exampleSentence.note: 앉아 있다 is a result-state phrase.

exampleSentence.en: People are standing in line.
exampleSentence.note: 서 있다 describes a continuing posture or line state.

exampleSentence.en: The door is open.
exampleSentence.note: The open state remains.

extendedVocabulary.english: to turn on; to be on

exampleSentence.en: The light is on.
exampleSentence.note: The on-state remains.

exampleSentence.en: The door is in an open state.
exampleSentence.note: Names the state directly.

exampleSentence.en: I suddenly got a text while going.
exampleSentence.note: Signals the interruption was unexpected.

exampleSentence.en: I will rest a little and then go again.
exampleSentence.note: A temporary pause before resuming.

extendedDialogue.setting: A class is canceled while someone is already on the way.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Why did you come back while going to school?
lines.grammarNote: -다가 shows the original movement was interrupted.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 지하철을 타고 있다가 수업 취소 문자를 받았어요.
lines.romanization: jihacheoreul tago itdaga sueop chwiso munjareul badasseoyo.
lines.en: While I was riding the subway, I got a class cancellation text.
lines.grammarNote: -고 있다가 makes the ongoing action very clear.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: So did you change the plan midway?
lines.grammarNote: 중간에 and 바꾸다 name the plan change.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Yes, now I am sitting at a cafe.
lines.grammarNote: 앉아 있어요 describes the current seated state.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Is the cafe door open?
lines.grammarNote: 열려 있어요 is a result-state question.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네, 불도 켜져 있어요. 조금 쉬다가 다시 갈 거예요.
lines.romanization: ne, buldo kyeojyeo isseoyo. jogeum swidaga dasi gal geoyeyo.
lines.en: Yes, the light is on too. I will rest a little and then go again.
lines.grammarNote: 켜져 있어요 is result state; 쉬다가 shows a temporary pause.

readingText.title: A plan changes on the way
readingText.body: 지훈은 학교에 가다가 수업 취소 문자를 받았어요. 처음에는 그냥 학교까지 가려고 했지만, 지하철을 타고 있다가 문자를 보고 중간에 계획을 바꿨어요. 그래서 근처 카페로 갔어요. 카페 문이 열려 있었고 불도 켜져 있었어요. 지훈은 창가 자리에 앉아 있었어요. 조금 쉬다가 다시 집에 돌아가기로 했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Jihoon got a class cancellation text while going to school. At first he planned to keep going, but while riding the subway he saw the text and changed the plan midway. So he went to a nearby cafe. The cafe door was open and the light was on. Jihoon was sitting by the window. After resting a bit, he decided to go back home.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 지훈은 무엇을 하다가 문자를 받았어요?
지훈은 왜 계획을 바꿨어요?
카페는 어떤 상태였어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 문이 열려 있었고 불도 켜져 있었어요.

culturalNote.title: Explaining changed plans
culturalNote.body: When Korean speakers explain a changed plan, -다가 is very useful because it shows the original action was already underway. It sounds more natural than simply listing two past actions.
culturalNote.tip: Use -다가 for the interrupted action, then give the new result: 학교에 가다가 문자를 받고 카페로 갔어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence shows a mid-action interruption?
inlineExercises.explanation: -다가 shows the phone call happened while the first action was underway.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence describes the continuing state after sitting?
inlineExercises.explanation: 앉아 있어요 means the person is seated. The place takes 에.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means the door is already open?
inlineExercises.explanation: Result state uses the thing as subject: 문이.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete: 밥을 먹___ 전화가 왔어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: 먹다가 shows the call interrupted the meal.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 불을 켜져 있어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: For result state, the light is the subject with 이/가.

inlineExercises.prompt: 문자___ 받다가 전화를 했어요. (I got a text, then switched to calling.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 문자를 받다 is the action phrase “receive a text.” 받다가 shows that action was interrupted or shifted.

inlineExercises.prompt: 지금 자리에 ___ . (앉다 → remaining state)
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어 있어요 describes a state that remains after an action. 앉다 becomes 앉아 있어요 for the state of being seated.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I was going, then changed plans midway.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -다가 shows the original action was interrupted. 중간에 makes the mid-way change explicit.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'The door is open.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 열려 있어요 describes the resulting open state of the door. It is not about someone opening it right now.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '문이 열고 있어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 문이 열고 있어요 makes the door sound like it is actively opening something. For the open state, use 열려 있어요.

bullets: V-다가 shows an action was interrupted or changed mid-way: 학교에 가다가 전화를 받았어요.
V-아/어 있어요 describes a continuing result state: 카페에 앉아 있어요, 문이 열려 있어요.
Use -다가, not -고 나서, when the first action did not simply finish before the second.
Result-state sentences usually make the thing or person in the state the subject: 문이, 불이, 사람이.

writingTask.prompt: Text a friend explaining that you were on your way but something interrupted, and describe where you're waiting now.
writingTask.hint: Use V-다가 to break off one action for another (가다가), and V-아/어 있다 for the leftover state (앉아 있어요).
writingTask.model: 버스를 타고 가다가 문자를 받았어요. 그래서 중간에 내렸어요. 지금 카페에 앉아 있어요. 문도 열려 있어요.
writingTask.modelEn: I was going by bus when I got a text. So I got off midway. I'm sitting in a cafe now. The door is open too.

canDo: Break off one action to switch to another with V-다가 (가다가 받았어요)
Describe a state left after an action with V-아/어 있다 (앉아 있어요, 열려 있어요)
Explain a mid-action change with everyday words (중간에, 바꾸다, 취소하다)

chapters.title: Cause and Unexpected Result
chapters.goal: Talk through a work or money decision in a realistic, cautious way.
chapters.scenario: A friend is deciding whether to start a job, buy something, or try a side project.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was it?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: It was fun. But the weather was a bit cold.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make one sentence with each cause shape: 길이 막혀서 늦었어요, 버스가 고장 나는 바람에 늦었어요, 비 때문에 취소했어요. Then change the cause word.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say one decision you made and one worry you still have.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner asks 왜 늦었어요? or 왜 취소됐어요? Answer once with -아서/어서, once with -는 바람에, and once with N 때문에.
chapters.review: Can you choose between neutral cause, unexpected-disruption cause, and noun cause without saying 비가 때문에?

beginnerGuide.title: Three cause shapes
beginnerGuide.body: Use -아서/어서 for ordinary reason-result, -는 바람에 for an unexpected event that caused trouble, and N 때문에 when the cause is a noun.

beginnerGuide.title: Use real situation words
beginnerGuide.body: 비, 길, 버스, 택시, 약속, 모임, 막히다, 고장나다, 놓치다, 늦다, and 취소하다 all belong to the same late-or-canceled-plan scene.

beginnerGuide.title: Watch the tone
beginnerGuide.body: 바람에 can sound like an excuse because it points to something that disrupted the plan. If someone waited for you, add 죄송해요 or 미안해요.

checkpoints: I can use -기로 했어요 for a decision.
I can use -ㄹ까 봐 걱정돼요 for a worry.
I can add 그래도 when I will try anyway.

sampleAnswer.en: I decided to save a little money this month. Still, I plan to continue Korean class.

I can use -ㄹ까 봐 걱정돼요 for a worry.
I can add 그래도 when I will try anyway.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
