naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: A plan was canceled, someone was late, or transport failed. You need to explain the cause without making every sentence sound the same.
objectives: Use V/A-아서/어서 for ordinary reason-result sentences.
Use V-는 바람에 when an unexpected event disrupted the plan.
Use N 때문에 when a noun is the cause, without adding a subject particle before 때문에.
hook.whyItMatters: English uses one broad word, 'because', for many situations. Korean asks you to choose the shape of the cause: a neutral clause, an unwanted event, or a noun cause. That choice changes the tone from a simple explanation to an excuse-like disruption.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-아서/어서 — because, so
grammarNotes.func: Use -아서/어서 to link a reason to its result: the first part is the cause, the second is what comes from it. It's the everyday, neutral way to say "because" or "so."

formTable.when: Stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ

examples.en: I was hungry, so I ate.
examples.note: 고프다 (hungry) is the cause; eating is the result.

examples.en: I had no time, so I couldn't go.
examples.note: A reason for not doing something — a very common pattern.

examples.en: I met my friend and (we) watched a movie.
examples.note: Here -아서 instead links two connected actions in order, not cause and result. Same form, different job.

examples.en: Korean is fun, so I study it every day.
examples.note: An adjective as the reason; the result is a habit.

keyPoint.label: Tense goes on the last verb only
keyPoint.body: Don't put past tense before -아서/어서. Say 고파서 먹었어요 (not 고팠어서). The part before -아서/어서 stays plain, and when something happened is shown only on the final verb.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 없어서 is read [업써서]: the ㅄ batchim links over, so ㅅ moves to the next syllable and tenses to [써].

drill.instruction: Join the two ideas with -아서/어서 to show reason → result.
drill.model: 비가 오다 / 집에 있었어요 → 비가 와서 집에 있었어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English puts past tense on the "because" part ("because I was busy"), but Korean doesn't add past tense before -아서/어서. The tense shows up once, on the final verb.

grammarNotes.title: V-는 바람에 — because of (something unexpected)
grammarNotes.func: Use -는 바람에 when an unplanned or unwanted event causes a result — usually a bad one. It carries the feeling of "and because of that, things went wrong."

formTable.ex: 늦다 → 늦는 바람에, 오다 → 오는 바람에

formTable.when: Stem ending in ㄹ (drop the ㄹ)
formTable.ex: 울다 → 우는 바람에, 놀다 → 노는 바람에

examples.en: I overslept, so I was late for school.
examples.note: Oversleeping is an unintended event with a bad result.

examples.ko: 비가 오는 바람에 옷이 다 젖었어요.
examples.romanization: bi-ga o-neun ba-ram-e o-si da jeo-jeo-sseo-yo.
examples.en: It started raining, so my clothes got all wet.
examples.note: Sudden rain disrupts things — a classic 바람에 use.

examples.ko: 친구가 전화하는 바람에 잠을 못 잤어요.
examples.romanization: chin-gu-ga jeon-hwa-ha-neun ba-ram-e ja-meul mot ja-sseo-yo.
examples.en: My friend called, so I couldn't sleep.
examples.note: Someone else's action disrupts the speaker; the result is negative.

examples.en: I missed the bus, so I was late for the meet-up.
examples.note: Unexpected cause + unwanted result, both verbs.

keyPoint.label: -는 바람에 vs -아서/어서
keyPoint.body: -아서/어서 is neutral and works for any reason. -는 바람에 adds the feeling "and this unexpected thing messed things up," so the result is almost always bad and in the past. Don't use 바람에 for a planned action or a good outcome: say 열심히 공부해서 합격했어요 (not 공부하는 바람에).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 늦는 is read [난는]: the ㅈ batchim sounds like [ㄷ], then turns into [ㄴ] before the ㄴ of 는. So read 늦는 바람에 as [난는 바라메].

drill.instruction: Connect the unexpected cause to its bad result with -는 바람에.
drill.model: 길이 막히다 / 약속에 늦었어요 → 길이 막히는 바람에 약속에 늦었어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 열심히 공부하는 바람에 시험을 잘 봤어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: -는 바람에 is only for unwanted disruptions, so it clashes with a good result like doing well on a test. For an intended cause and a good outcome, use -아서/어서.

grammarNotes.title: N 때문에 — because of (a noun)
grammarNotes.func: Use a noun + 때문에 to point to a person, thing, or situation as the cause. It means "because of ~" and is followed by a result.

formTable.ex: 비 → 비 때문에, 일 → 일 때문에
친구 → 친구 때문에, 돈 → 돈 때문에

examples.en: Because of the rain, I couldn't go to school.
examples.note: 비 (a noun) is the cause; 때문에 attaches straight to it.

examples.en: Because of work, I couldn't meet my friend.
examples.note: An everyday noun cause with a negative result.

examples.en: I got mad because of my little brother.
examples.note: A person as the cause — often blame or trouble.

examples.en: Because of money, I can't go on a trip.
examples.note: 때문에 takes a bare noun, with no verb on the cause.

keyPoint.label: 때문에 vs 아서/어서
keyPoint.body: 때문에 follows a NOUN (비 때문에), while -아서/어서 follows a VERB or ADJECTIVE (비가 와서). Same meaning, just attached to a different kind of word. So if you have a noun, reach for 때문에; if you have a verb or adjective, use -아서/어서.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 때 starts with the tense consonant ㄸ — say it hard and tight, not as a soft [대].

drill.instruction: Use N + 때문에 to give the reason for each result.
drill.model: (눈) 길이 미끄러웠어요 → 눈 때문에 길이 미끄러웠어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 비 때문에 못 갔어요. / 비가 와서 못 갔어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 때문에 attaches to a noun, not a verb. Use the bare noun (비 때문에), or switch to the verb form with -아서/어서 (비가 와서). Don't stick a verb directly in front of 때문에.

exampleSentence.en: The road was jammed. So I was a little late.
exampleSentence.note: Use 그래서 after the cause has already been stated.

exampleSentence.en: I canceled the appointment because of the rain.
exampleSentence.note: A clean N 때문에 sentence.

exampleSentence.en: The road is jammed because it is rush hour.
exampleSentence.note: In Korean, the road is the subject of 막히다.

exampleSentence.en: The bus broke down, so I ended up late.
exampleSentence.note: A transport noun that naturally pairs with 바람에.

exampleSentence.en: Because of the rain, I could not take a taxi.
exampleSentence.note: Keeps 때문에 attached to a real noun.

extendedVocabulary.english: to be blocked; to be jammed

exampleSentence.en: The road was jammed, so I was late to the appointment.
exampleSentence.note: The subject is 길 or 차, not the late person.

exampleSentence.ko: 버스가 고장 나는 바람에 오래 기다렸어요.
exampleSentence.en: The bus broke down, so I waited for a long time.
exampleSentence.note: A strong 바람에 cause because the problem was not planned.

exampleSentence.en: I missed the bus, so I was late to class.
exampleSentence.note: 놓치다 often creates an unwanted result.

exampleSentence.en: I am sorry I am late.
exampleSentence.note: The simplest apology frame uses -어서.

exampleSentence.en: We canceled the gathering because of the rain.
exampleSentence.note: The thing canceled takes 을/를.

exampleSentence.en: Sorry I am late to the appointment.
exampleSentence.note: 약속 is the real-life event affected by the cause.

exampleSentence.en: We moved the gathering to next week.
exampleSentence.note: A natural result when everyone is late or the weather is bad.

exampleSentence.en: I explained the reason I was late.
exampleSentence.note: Useful when someone asks 왜.

exampleSentence.en: A problem came up because of a mistake.
exampleSentence.note: A result noun that often follows 때문에.

exampleSentence.en: The road was jammed because of an accident.
exampleSentence.note: A concrete noun cause for N 때문에.

exampleSentence.ko: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 약속을 취소했어요.
exampleSentence.en: It suddenly rained, so we canceled the appointment.
exampleSentence.note: 갑자기 makes the unexpected cause clearer.

extendedDialogue.setting: Two friends explain why a rainy-day gathering was canceled.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Why was the appointment canceled?
lines.grammarNote: 왜 asks for the reason, so this chapter's connectors become useful immediately.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 갑자기 비가 많이 오는 바람에 길이 막혔어요.
lines.romanization: gapjagi biga mani oneun barame giri makhyeosseoyo.
lines.en: It suddenly rained a lot, so the roads got jammed.
lines.grammarNote: -는 바람에 frames the rain as an unexpected disruption.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Because of the rain, you could not take a taxi either?
lines.grammarNote: 비 때문에 names the noun cause directly.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네. 버스까지 고장 나는 바람에 다들 늦었어요.
lines.romanization: ne. beoseukkaji gojang naneun barame dadeul neujeosseoyo.
lines.en: Right. Even the bus broke down, so everyone was late.
lines.grammarNote: 고장 나는 바람에 is a very natural unwanted-event cause.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: So you moved the gathering to next week.
lines.grammarNote: 그래서 connects the already stated causes to the final decision.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Yes. I also said I was sorry for being late.
lines.grammarNote: An apology softens the excuse-like tone of 바람에.

readingText.title: Why the gathering moved
readingText.body: 토요일에 민서와 지훈은 카페에서 만나기로 했어요. 그런데 갑자기 비가 많이 와서 길이 막혔어요. 지훈은 버스를 탔지만, 버스가 고장 나는 바람에 한 정류장에서 오래 기다렸어요. 비 때문에 택시도 타기 어려웠어요. 결국 두 사람은 약속을 취소하고 모임을 다음 주로 바꿨어요. 지훈은 길이 막혀서 늦었다고 설명했고, 버스가 고장 나는 바람에 더 늦었다고 말했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: On Saturday, Minseo and Jihoon planned to meet at a cafe. But it suddenly rained a lot, so the roads got jammed. Jihoon took a bus, but the bus broke down and he waited at one stop for a long time. Because of the rain, it was hard to take a taxi too. In the end, the two canceled the appointment and moved the gathering to next week. Jihoon explained that he was late because the roads were jammed, and said he was even later because the bus broke down.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 길은 왜 막혔어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 갑자기 비가 많이 와서 길이 막혔어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 지훈은 왜 오래 기다렸어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 버스가 고장 나는 바람에 오래 기다렸어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 두 사람은 모임을 언제로 바꿨어요?

culturalNote.title: Reasons can sound like excuses
culturalNote.body: When you use 바람에, Korean listeners often hear that something unexpected caused trouble. That is useful, but in real conversation it can also sound like you are defending yourself. If the listener was inconvenienced, add an apology or responsibility after the reason.
culturalNote.tip: A balanced message sounds like this: 길이 막히는 바람에 늦었어요. 죄송해요. 다음에는 더 일찍 나갈게요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence gives a neutral reason-result explanation?
inlineExercises.explanation: -아서/어서 connects a reason and result neutrally.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence sounds like an unexpected problem disrupted the plan?
inlineExercises.explanation: -는 바람에 is for an unwanted or disruptive event.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses N 때문에 correctly?
inlineExercises.explanation: Put the noun directly before 때문에. Do not add 가 or 를.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete: 버스를 놓치___ 수업에 늦었어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: 놓치는 바람에 shows the missed bus caused an unwanted result.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 비가 때문에 약속을 취소했어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Use N 때문에 with the noun alone, or make a full clause with -아서/어서.
inlineExercises.correct: 비 때문에 약속을 취소했어요. / 비가 와서 약속을 취소했어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 추운 바람에 못 갔어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Plain adjectives take -아서/어서. 바람에 works better with an event or change.
inlineExercises.correct: 추워서 못 갔어요. / 갑자기 추워지는 바람에 못 갔어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: 비___ 약속을 취소했어요. (I canceled because of rain.)
inlineExercises.explanation: N 때문에 follows the noun directly. 비가 때문에 adds an unnecessary subject marker before 때문에.

inlineExercises.prompt: 길이 ___ 늦었어요. (막히다 → unexpected disruption)
inlineExercises.explanation: -는 바람에 frames the cause as an unexpected disruption. 막히다 becomes 막히는 바람에.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I was late because I missed the bus.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -아서/어서 gives a neutral reason-result connection. 놓치다 becomes 놓쳐서 before the result 늦었어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'I couldn't go because the bus broke down.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 고장나는 바람에 makes the broken bus feel like an unexpected cause. 못 갔어요 gives the disrupted result.

bullets: Use V/A-아서/어서 for ordinary cause and result.
Use V-는 바람에 when an unexpected event created an unwanted result.
Use N 때문에 for noun causes like 비, 일, 실수, 사고, and 문제.
Never say 비가 때문에. Say 비 때문에 or 비가 와서.
If 바람에 sounds like an excuse, add apology or responsibility.

writingTask.prompt: Text a friend to apologize for being late, explaining the cause and the unexpected thing that went wrong.
writingTask.hint: Use V/A-아서/어서 for 'because, so' (늦어서), V-는 바람에 for an unexpected cause (버스가 고장 나는 바람에), and N 때문에 for 'because of' a noun (비 때문에).
writingTask.model: 비 때문에 길이 많이 막혔어요. 버스가 고장 나는 바람에 약속에 늦었어요. 정말 늦어서 미안해요.
writingTask.modelEn: Because of the rain, the roads were very jammed. The bus broke down, so I was late for our appointment. I'm really sorry for being late.

canDo: Link a cause to its result with V/A-아서/어서 (늦어서 미안해요)
Blame an unexpected mishap with V-는 바람에 (고장 나는 바람에 늦었어요)
Point to a noun cause with N 때문에 (비 때문에 막혔어요)

chapters.title: Purpose and Duration
chapters.goal: Use counters in the places where Koreans expect them.
chapters.scenario: You buy drinks, count people, book tickets, or ask for quantity.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What are you going to do this weekend?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I am going to meet a friend and go to a cafe.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What if it rains?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: If it rains, I am going to study at home.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make two purpose sentences and two duration sentences: 배우기 위해서 왔어요, 취업을 위해서 연습해요, 세 달 동안 머물 거예요, 한국에 있는 동안 공부할 거예요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say three real quantities using counters like 잔, 명, 개, 번, or 장.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner asks 왜 왔어요? and 얼마 동안 있을 거예요? Answer with -기 위해서, N을/를 위해서, N 동안, and V-는 동안.
chapters.review: Can you keep purpose 'for' and duration 'for' separate in Korean?

beginnerGuide.title: Two kinds of for
beginnerGuide.body: English uses 'for' in 취업을 위해서 and 세 달 동안, but Korean separates purpose from duration. 위해서 gives the goal; 동안 gives the time span.

beginnerGuide.title: Purpose needs the right shape
beginnerGuide.body: Use V-기 위해서 for verb goals like 배우기 위해서 and 합격하기 위해서. Use N을/를 위해서 for noun goals like 취업을 위해서 and 건강을 위해서.

beginnerGuide.title: Duration is a span
beginnerGuide.body: Use 세 달 동안, 방학 동안, and 한국에 있는 동안 to show the time period. Do not say 세 달에 동안 or 방학에 동안.

checkpoints: I can pair native numbers with common counters.
I can choose 잔, 명/분, 개, 장, 번, and 시간.
I can avoid translating English plurals directly.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.prompt: Say three real quantities using counters like 잔, 명, 개, 번, or 장.

sampleAnswer.ko: 커피 두 잔하고 티켓 세 장 주세요.
sampleAnswer.en: Please give me two cups of coffee and three tickets.

checklist: I can pair native numbers with common counters.
I can choose 잔, 명/분, 개, 장, 번, and 시간.
I can avoid translating English plurals directly.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You explain why you came to Korea, what goal you are working toward, and how long the plan will last.
objectives: Use V-기 위해서 and N을/를 위해서 for deliberate goals.
Use N 동안 for a time span like 세 달 동안 or 방학 동안.
Use V-는 동안 when one action or situation continues while something else happens.
hook.whyItMatters: Learners often translate English 'for' in two different ways: for a purpose and for a duration. Korean keeps those separate. 취업을 위해서 means 'for the purpose of employment', while 세 달 동안 means 'for three months'. Mixing them makes the sentence hard to understand.

grammarNotes.title: V-기 위해서 / N을 위해서 — in order to, for the sake of
grammarNotes.func: Shows purpose. The goal comes first, then the action you take to reach it. Use V-기 위해서 with a verb ("in order to do X") and N을/를 위해서 with a noun ("for N").

formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹기 위해서 / 사다 → 사기 위해서

examples.en: I came to Korea to learn Korean.
examples.note: -기 위해서 goes on the verb 배우다 to give the reason for coming.

examples.en: I work a part-time job to save money.
examples.note: The goal (saving money) comes first, the action (working) second.

examples.en: I work hard every day for my family.
examples.note: 가족 is a noun, so it takes 을 위해서, not 기 위해서.

examples.en: I drink a lot of water for my health.
examples.note: 건강 ends in a consonant, so it takes 을 위해서.

keyPoint.label: Verb goal vs. noun goal
keyPoint.body: For a verb goal, use V-기 위해서 (배우기 위해서 = in order to learn). For a noun goal, use N을/를 위해서 (가족을 위해서 = for my family). Keep the particle 을/를 before 위해서 with a noun — don't drop it. Later you'll meet V-(으)려고, a more casual "in order to" that only works with verbs.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 위해서 is often shortened to 위해 in writing and quick speech; both sound natural. 모으기 keeps each syllable clear: [모으기].

drill.instruction: Join the goal and the action into one sentence using V-기 위해서 or N을 위해서.
drill.model: 한국 친구를 사귀다 + 한국어를 공부해요 → 한국 친구를 사귀기 위해서 한국어를 공부해요.
items: 시험을 잘 보다 + 매일 공부해요 → 시험을 잘 보___ ___ 매일 공부해요.
부모님 + 선물을 샀어요 → 부모님___ ___ 선물을 샀어요.
살을 빼다 + 운동을 시작했어요 → 살을 빼___ ___ 운동을 시작했어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 가족 위해서 일해요 / 건강 배우기 위해서
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English uses "for" with both nouns and the "-ing" form, so learners mix them up. Korean splits them: a verb takes -기 위해서, a noun takes 을/를 위해서. Keep the particle 을/를 before 위해서 with a noun, and never put -기 on a noun.

grammarNotes.title: N 동안 — for / during N (a length of time)
grammarNotes.func: Goes right onto a time-span noun to mean "for" or "during" that period. It tells you how long something lasts.

formTable.ex: 방학 → 방학 동안 / 일주일 → 일주일 동안

examples.en: I studied for three hours.
examples.note: 동안 goes straight onto the duration 세 시간 with no extra particle.

examples.en: I stayed at my parents' house during the vacation.
examples.note: 방학 is a period, so N 동안 means "during" the whole break.

examples.en: I learned Korean for one week.
examples.note: 일주일 (one week) is a span, so 동안 gives its length.

examples.en: How long did you live in Korea?
examples.note: 얼마 동안 asks about length of time, not a clock time.

keyPoint.label: 동안 vs. 에 vs. 까지
keyPoint.body: N 동안 = how long something lasts (세 시간 동안 = for three hours). N 에 = a point in time (세 시에 = at three). N 까지 = a deadline (세 시까지 = by three). Use 동안 only for a stretch of time, never a single moment.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 동안 [동안]. In 일주일 동안 the final ㄹ links smoothly into the next word: [일쭈일 똥안].

drill.instruction: Add the time noun + 동안 to finish each sentence.
drill.model: (한 시간) ___ 친구를 기다렸어요. → 한 시간 동안 친구를 기다렸어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 세 시간에 공부했어요 / 세 시간을 공부했어요
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English says "for" with durations, but learners often reach for 에 or 을/를 out of habit. For "how long," use 동안 with no particle on the time span. Save 에 for a clock time (세 시에 = at 3:00).

grammarNotes.title: V-는 동안 — while V is happening
grammarNotes.func: Goes on a verb to mean "while (someone) is doing X." It marks a stretch of time set by one ongoing action, during which something else happens.

formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹는 동안 / 자다 → 자는 동안
살다 → 사는 동안 / 만들다 → 만드는 동안

examples.en: While I cooked, my friend cleaned.
examples.note: -는 동안 on 요리하다 sets the time frame; the two subjects (제가 / 친구가) are different.

examples.en: While the baby was sleeping, I read a book.
examples.note: 자다 → 자는 동안; one action (sleeping) frames the other (reading).

examples.ko: 제가 한국에 사는 동안 친구를 많이 사귀었어요.
examples.romanization: jega hanguge saneun dongan chingureul mani sagwieosseoyo.
examples.en: While I lived in Korea, I made a lot of friends.
examples.note: 살다 drops ㄹ before -는: 살다 → 사는 동안.

examples.en: While I ate, I watched TV.
examples.note: Same subject is fine too; 먹다 → 먹는 동안 frames both actions in one time span.

keyPoint.label: V-는 동안 vs. N 동안
keyPoint.body: Same word 동안, two ways to attach it. N 동안 takes a time noun (방학 동안 = during vacation). V-는 동안 takes a verb in the -는 form (밥을 먹는 동안 = while eating). If a verb names the time span, you must use -는 동안 — never put 동안 onto the dictionary form.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 먹는 동안 → [멍는 동안] (ㄱ before ㄴ turns into ㅇ). 사는 동안 has no cluster and stays smooth.

drill.instruction: Change the verb to V-는 동안 and finish the sentence.
drill.model: (제가 샤워하다) ___ 전화가 왔어요. → 제가 샤워하는 동안 전화가 왔어요.
items: (아기가 자다) ___ 책을 읽었어요. → 아기가 ___ 책을 읽었어요.
(엄마가 요리하다) ___ 저는 상을 차렸어요. → 엄마가 ___ 저는 상을 차렸어요.
(제가 한국에 살다) ___ 한국어를 배웠어요. → 제가 한국에 ___ 한국어를 배웠어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 먹다 동안 / 먹었는 동안 텔레비전을 봤어요
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: "While" describes an ongoing action, so Korean uses the present -는 form even about the past — the past tense stays on the final verb only. Don't put 동안 on the dictionary form (먹다 동안), and don't make the 동안 clause past (먹었는 동안).

exampleSentence.en: I came to Korea in order to learn Korean.
exampleSentence.note: The language is the goal of the stay.

exampleSentence.en: I came in order to learn Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 배우기 위해서 is the purpose frame.

exampleSentence.en: I study in order to pass the exam.
exampleSentence.note: A deliberate goal with 위해서.

exampleSentence.ko: 세 달 동안 매일 연습할 거예요.
exampleSentence.en: I will practice every day for three months.
exampleSentence.note: A repeated action over a duration.

exampleSentence.en: I practice Korean in order to get a job.
exampleSentence.note: Noun plus 을 위해서.

exampleSentence.en: I prepare in order to pass the exam.
exampleSentence.note: 합격하다 becomes 합격하기.

exampleSentence.ko: 시험을 위해서 한 달 동안 준비했어요.
exampleSentence.en: I prepared for the exam for one month.
exampleSentence.note: A noun goal plus a duration.

exampleSentence.ko: 방학 동안 취업 준비를 할 거예요.
exampleSentence.en: I will prepare for employment during vacation.
exampleSentence.note: 준비하다 links naturally to both purpose and duration.

exampleSentence.en: I studied every day during the preparation period.
exampleSentence.note: 기간 names the period; 동안 marks what happens through it.

exampleSentence.ko: 세 달 동안 한국에 머물 거예요.
exampleSentence.en: I will stay in Korea for three months.
exampleSentence.note: 동안 marks the time span.

exampleSentence.ko: 한국에 머무는 동안 많이 연습할 거예요.
exampleSentence.en: While I stay in Korea, I will practice a lot.
exampleSentence.note: 머무는 동안 uses the verb modifier form.

exampleSentence.en: I will travel during vacation.
exampleSentence.note: A common period noun before 동안.

exampleSentence.ko: 한국에 있는 동안 여행도 하고 싶어요.
exampleSentence.en: While I am in Korea, I also want to travel.
exampleSentence.note: A natural extra plan during a stay.

exampleSentence.en: I exercise for my health.
exampleSentence.note: Noun plus 을 위해서.

exampleSentence.en: I exercised for one week for my health.
exampleSentence.note: Purpose and duration can appear in one sentence.

exampleSentence.en: The purpose of coming to Korea is study.
exampleSentence.note: Names the idea behind 위해서 sentences.

extendedDialogue.setting: A learner explains a Korea stay, study goal, and study period.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Why did you come to Korea?
lines.grammarNote: 왜 opens a purpose explanation.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 한국어를 배우기 위해서 왔어요. 세 달 동안 머물 거예요.
lines.romanization: hangugeoreul baeugi wihaeseo wasseoyo. se dal dongan meomul geoyeyo.
lines.en: I came in order to learn Korean. I will stay for three months.
lines.grammarNote: -기 위해서 gives purpose; N 동안 gives duration.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 한국에 있는 동안 뭐 할 거예요?
lines.romanization: hanguge inneun dongan mwo hal geoyeyo?
lines.en: What will you do while you are in Korea?
lines.grammarNote: 있는 동안 frames the stay as a time span.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 취업을 위해서 매일 한국어를 연습할 거예요.
lines.romanization: chwieobeul wihaeseo maeil hangugeoreul yeonseupal geoyeyo.
lines.en: I will practice Korean every day in order to get a job.
lines.grammarNote: 취업 is a noun, so it takes 을 위해서.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Are you preparing for an exam too?
lines.grammarNote: 시험 준비 is a natural study-goal phrase.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네, 합격하기 위해서 방학 동안 계속 공부할 거예요.
lines.romanization: ne, hapgyeokagi wihaeseo banghak dongan gyesok gongbuhal geoyeyo.
lines.en: Yes, I will keep studying during vacation in order to pass.
lines.grammarNote: A verb goal and a duration period can appear together.

readingText.title: A three-month study plan
readingText.body: 지훈은 한국어를 배우기 위해서 한국에 왔어요. 세 달 동안 서울에 머물 거예요. 한국에 있는 동안 매일 한국어를 연습하고, 주말에는 짧게 여행도 할 거예요. 지훈의 큰 목표는 취업이에요. 그래서 취업을 위해서 시험 준비도 하고 있어요. 방학 동안은 합격하기 위해서 더 오래 공부할 계획이에요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Jihoon came to Korea in order to learn Korean. He will stay in Seoul for three months. While he is in Korea, he will practice Korean every day and take short trips on weekends. His big goal is employment. So he is also preparing for an exam in order to get a job. During vacation, he plans to study longer in order to pass.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 지훈은 왜 한국에 왔어요?
지훈은 얼마 동안 한국에 머물 거예요?
지훈은 방학 동안 왜 더 오래 공부할 거예요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 합격하기 위해서 더 오래 공부할 거예요.

culturalNote.title: Goal language sounds deliberate
culturalNote.body: -기 위해서 is clear and useful, but it can sound a little formal or earnest. It works well for interviews, plans, introductions, and serious goals. With close friends, -(으)려고 often sounds lighter.
culturalNote.tip: Use 위해서 when the goal matters: 취업을 위해서, 건강을 위해서, 합격하기 위해서.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence gives a deliberate purpose?
inlineExercises.explanation: Use the -기 form before 위해서.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which phrase gives a duration?
inlineExercises.explanation: 동안 attaches directly to the time span.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'while I am in Korea'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 있다 becomes 있는 before 동안.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete: 취업___ 위해서 한국어를 연습해요.
inlineExercises.explanation: 취업 is a noun goal, so use 취업을 위해서.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 공부하다 위해서 한국에 왔어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: A verb must become the -기 form before 위해서.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 방학에 동안 여행할 거예요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Do not put 에 between the period noun and 동안.

inlineExercises.prompt: 취업___ 위해서 한국어를 연습해요. (I practice Korean for employment.)
inlineExercises.explanation: N을 위해서 marks the purpose or goal you are working for. 취업이 위해서 is not the purpose pattern.

inlineExercises.prompt: 한국어를 ___ 한국에 왔어요. (배우다 → in order to)
inlineExercises.explanation: V-기 위해서 turns the verb into a deliberate purpose. 배우다 becomes 배우기 위해서.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I studied for three months.'
inlineExercises.explanation: N 동안 marks the time span. 세 달 동안 tells how long the studying continued.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'While I was preparing for the exam, I practiced every day.'
inlineExercises.explanation: V-는 동안 marks what continued during another action. 준비하다 becomes 준비하는 동안 before the main action.

bullets: Use V-기 위해서 for verb goals: 배우기 위해서, 합격하기 위해서.
Use N을/를 위해서 for noun goals: 취업을 위해서, 건강을 위해서.
Use N 동안 for duration: 세 달 동안, 방학 동안.
Use V-는 동안 for overlapping time: 한국에 있는 동안.
Do not confuse purpose 'for' with duration 'for'.

writingTask.prompt: Write 3 sentences explaining why you are studying Korean and for how long you plan to stay or study.
writingTask.hint: Use V-기 위해서 or N을/를 위해서 for the purpose, N 동안 for the time span, and V-는 동안 for 'while doing'.
writingTask.model: 저는 취업을 위해서 한국어를 공부해요. 시험에 합격하기 위해서 6개월 동안 준비할 거예요. 그리고 공부하는 동안 한국 친구도 사귈 거예요.
writingTask.modelEn: I study Korean in order to get a job. I'll prepare for six months to pass the exam. And while I'm studying, I'll also make Korean friends.

canDo: State a purpose before the action (V-기 위해서 · N을/를 위해서)
Say how long something lasts with a time-span noun (6개월 동안 · 방학 동안)
Mark 'while something is happening' on a verb (공부하는 동안)

chapters.title: Decisions and Changes
chapters.goal: Make one longer sentence that still feels easy to follow.
chapters.scenario: You explain why you practiced, what your purpose was, and what changed after that.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was it?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: It was fun. But the weather was a bit cold.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make one sentence for each change type: 운동하기로 했어요, 일찍 자게 됐어요, 건강이 좋아졌어요. Then change the verb or state.
chapters.realLifeTask: Connect cause, purpose, and result in two short Korean sentences.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner asks 뭐가 달라졌어요? Answer with -기로 했어요, -게 됐어요, and -아/어졌어요.
chapters.review: Can you tell the difference between a decision, a situation you ended up in, and a changed state?

beginnerGuide.title: Agency comes first
beginnerGuide.body: Use -기로 했어요 when you made the decision. Use -게 됐어요 when circumstances led to the result. Use -아/어졌어요 when the state itself changed.

beginnerGuide.title: Use change words together
beginnerGuide.body: 결정하다, 시작하다, 바뀌다, 달라지다, 좋아지다, 늘다, and 줄다 help explain what changed in a real routine or study plan.

beginnerGuide.title: Do not hide decisions
beginnerGuide.body: If you simply chose something, say 운동하기로 했어요. Use 운동하게 됐어요 only when the situation led you there.

checkpoints: I can use -길래 for a reason I reacted to.
I can use -기 위해서 for purpose.
I can use -ㄹ수록 when something changes more and more.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Make one longer sentence that still feels easy to follow.
exitTask.prompt: Connect cause, purpose, and result in two short Korean sentences.

sampleAnswer.ko: 발표가 있어서 집에서 연습했어요. 연습할수록 조금 더 자연스러워져요.
sampleAnswer.en: I practiced at home because I had a presentation. The more I practice, the more natural it gets.

checklist: I can use -길래 for a reason I reacted to.
I can use -기 위해서 for purpose.
I can use -ㄹ수록 when something changes more and more.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: You explain a decision you made, a situation you ended up in, or a change you can now feel in your body, schedule, or skill.
objectives: Use V-기로 했어요 for decisions that are already settled.
Use V-게 됐어요 for changes that came about through circumstances.
Use A/V-아/어지다 for state changes like 좋아지다, 편해지다, and 가벼워지다.
hook.whyItMatters: English often says 'I started', 'I decided', or 'I became' loosely. Korean separates agency. 운동하기로 했어요 says you decided. 운동하게 됐어요 says circumstances led you there. 몸이 가벼워졌어요 says the state changed.

grammarNotes.title: V-기로 했어요 — decided to V
grammarNotes.func: Used to say you have decided or made up your mind to do something. Often the decision was made after thinking it over or agreeing with other people.

formTable.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel
Verb stem ending in a consonant

formTable.add: 안 + V-기로 했어요 (or stem + 지 않기로 했어요)
formTable.ex: 마시다 → 안 마시기로 했어요 (decided not to drink)

examples.en: I decided to study Korean starting tomorrow.
examples.note: 공부하다 → 공부하기로 했어요; an everyday verb plus a personal decision.

examples.en: My friend and I decided to watch a movie together.
examples.note: 보다 → 보기로 했어요; a decision made together with someone (친구하고).

examples.en: I decided to drink a lot of water from today.
examples.note: 마시다 → 마시기로 했어요; a simple self-improvement plan.

examples.en: I decided not to eat dinner.
examples.note: Negative: 안 먹기로 했어요, for deciding NOT to do something.

keyPoint.label: -기로 했어요 (a decision) vs. -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (a plan)
keyPoint.body: -기로 했어요 stresses that you reached a decision, often after thinking or agreeing with others. -(으)ㄹ 거예요 just says what you are going to do. 했어요 is past because the deciding already happened, even though the action itself is still coming up. (The negative -지 않기로 했어요 comes later.)

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 먹기로 sounds like [먹끼로] (meok-kkiro): after the ㄱ at the end of 먹, the next ㄱ becomes a tense [ㄲ].

drill.instruction: Turn each cue into a sentence saying you decided to do it, using V-기로 했어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: The decision was already made, so 하다 stays past (했어요), not present (해요). English 'I decided' is past, and Korean keeps it past too.

grammarNotes.title: V-게 됐어요 — ended up V-ing / came to V
grammarNotes.func: Used when something happens because of circumstances rather than your own choice. It shows a change or a result that came about, often through other people or how things worked out.

formTable.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel
Verb stem ending in a consonant

formTable.ex: 먹다 → 못 먹게 됐어요 (ended up not being able to eat)

examples.en: I ended up living in Korea because of work.
examples.note: 살다 → 살게 됐어요; 일 때문에 shows an outside reason, not a personal choice.

examples.ko: 친구 덕분에 한국 영화를 좋아하게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: chingu deokbune hanguk yeonghwa-reul joahage dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Thanks to my friend, I came to like Korean movies.
examples.note: 좋아하다 → 좋아하게 됐어요; a feeling that changed because of someone else.

examples.ko: 시간이 없어서 밥을 못 먹게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: sigani eopseoseo bab-eul mot meokge dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: I ended up not being able to eat because I had no time.
examples.note: 못 먹다 → 못 먹게 됐어요; the situation (시간이 없어서) caused the result.

examples.en: I ended up going to that school.
examples.note: 다니다 → 다니게 됐어요; announces a new situation that came about, often happy news.

keyPoint.label: -기로 했어요 (my choice) vs. -게 됐어요 (not my choice)
keyPoint.body: -기로 했어요 means 'I decided' — the will is yours. -게 됐어요 means 'it came about' — the result is from circumstances or other people. Koreans often use -게 됐어요 to sound modest, even with good news (for example, 결혼하게 됐어요, 'I'm getting married').

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 좋아하게 sounds like [조아하게] (jo-a-ha-ge): the ㅎ in 좋 goes silent before the vowel, so 좋아 links smoothly.

drill.instruction: Rewrite each cue to say it came about by circumstances, using V-게 됐어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Don't mix up 되다 (to become / come about) with 하다. For 'I ended up living,' use 되다 → 됐어요. 살게 해요 means 'make someone live' — a different grammar point.

grammarNotes.title: A-아/어졌어요 — became / got (a change of state)
grammarNotes.func: Added to adjectives to say a state changed — something 'became' or 'got' a certain way. It turns a description (is ~) into a change (became ~).

formTable.when: Stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ

formTable.ex: 많다 → 많아졌어요 (became more); 크다 → 커졌어요 (got bigger)

examples.en: Studying Korean has gradually gotten fun.
examples.note: 재미있다 → 재미있어졌어요; 점점 (gradually) goes naturally with a change of state.

examples.en: The weather has gotten warm.
examples.note: 따뜻하다 (a 하다 adjective) → 따뜻해졌어요; the change has already happened (past).

examples.en: I have more friends now.
examples.note: 많다 → 많아졌어요; the ㅏ stem takes 아졌어요, showing things increased.

examples.en: I exercised, so I got healthier.
examples.note: 건강하다 → 건강해졌어요; the change comes from a cause (운동을 해서).

keyPoint.label: 좋다 (a state) vs. 좋아졌어요 (a change of state)
keyPoint.body: 좋다 means 'is good' — it just describes. 좋아졌어요 means 'got/became good' — it shows a change. Use -아/어졌어요 whenever English would say 'became,' 'got,' or 'grew' plus an adjective. (For ㅡ-vowel stems like 크다, the ㅡ drops: 크 → 커졌어요 — more on those later.)

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 많아졌어요 sounds like [마나져써요] (ma-na-jyeo-sseo-yo): the ㅎ in 많 is silent and the ㄴ links to the next vowel.

drill.instruction: Change each adjective into a 'became/got' statement using A-아/어졌어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 따뜻했어요 just means 'it was warm' — a past state, no change. To say it CHANGED and 'became' warm, add -아/어지다 → 따뜻해졌어요. English 'got warm' means it changed, so keep the 졌어요.

exampleSentence.en: I decided to exercise starting next month.
exampleSentence.note: A direct verb for decision-making.

exampleSentence.en: I decided to exercise every morning.
exampleSentence.note: A natural new-habit decision.

exampleSentence.ko: 건강이 안 좋아져서 운동을 시작하기로 했어요.
exampleSentence.en: My health got worse, so I decided to start exercising.
exampleSentence.note: The new action begins because of a change.

exampleSentence.en: The plan changed.
exampleSentence.note: A common changed-schedule sentence.

exampleSentence.en: As I exercised, my habits changed.
exampleSentence.note: The noun that names the lifestyle change.

exampleSentence.en: My health got better.
exampleSentence.note: A core state-change sentence.

exampleSentence.en: My Korean ability improved.
exampleSentence.note: 좋다 plus -아지다.

exampleSentence.en: The meeting time changed to three.
exampleSentence.note: Useful for schedules and plans.

exampleSentence.en: After starting exercise, my day became different.
exampleSentence.note: Emphasizes that the whole feel is different now.

exampleSentence.en: The more I practice, the more my skill improves.
exampleSentence.note: 실력 pairs naturally with 늘다 and 좋아지다.

exampleSentence.en: Because I use Korean every day, my skill improved.
exampleSentence.note: Intransitive improvement: 실력이 늘다.

exampleSentence.en: After I started exercising, my stress decreased.
exampleSentence.note: A natural result-change verb.

exampleSentence.ko: 회사 일 때문에 한국에 살게 됐어요.
exampleSentence.en: Because of work, I ended up living in Korea.
exampleSentence.note: A classic circumstantial 게 되다 sentence.

exampleSentence.en: Because of work, I suddenly ended up moving.
exampleSentence.note: A change caused by circumstances.

extendedVocabulary.english: to take charge of; to be assigned

exampleSentence.en: I ended up taking charge of a new task.
exampleSentence.note: Good for work or school responsibilities.

exampleSentence.en: These days I have come to sleep earlier.
exampleSentence.note: A practical new-habit sentence.

exampleSentence.en: I decided to sleep early starting today.
exampleSentence.note: 자다 becomes 자기로 in the decision pattern.

exampleSentence.en: After exercising, my body felt lighter.
exampleSentence.note: 몸 is the subject of the changed state.

exampleSentence.en: My body felt lighter.
exampleSentence.note: 가볍다 becomes 가벼워지다.

extendedDialogue.setting: A friend explains a new health decision and the changes that followed.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: What will be different starting next month?
lines.grammarNote: 달라지다 is a practical change verb.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: I decided to exercise every morning.
lines.grammarNote: -기로 했어요 reports a settled decision.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Did you decide that yourself?
lines.grammarNote: 결정하다 checks agency.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네, 건강이 안 좋아져서 시작하기로 했어요.
lines.romanization: ne, geongangi an joajyeoseo sijakagiro haesseoyo.
lines.en: Yes, my health got worse, so I decided to start.
lines.grammarNote: 좋아지다 in the negative gives a state-change reason.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Have your habits already changed?
lines.grammarNote: 바뀌다 is a real-life change verb.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네. 일찍 자게 되고 몸도 가벼워졌어요.
lines.romanization: ne. iljjik jage doego momdo gabyeowojyeosseoyo.
lines.en: Yes. I came to sleep earlier, and my body feels lighter too.
lines.grammarNote: 자게 되다 shows a new habit that came about; 가벼워지다 shows state change.

readingText.title: A habit that changed the day
readingText.body: 지훈은 건강이 안 좋아져서 아침마다 운동하기로 했어요. 처음에는 직접 결정한 일이었지만, 운동을 시작하고 나서 하루가 조금씩 달라졌어요. 밤에는 일찍 자게 됐고, 아침에는 몸이 가벼워졌어요. 한 달 후에는 습관도 많이 바뀌었어요. 지훈은 한국어도 매일 연습하기로 했고, 연습할수록 실력이 늘어서 더 자신감이 생겼어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Jihoon decided to exercise every morning because his health had gotten worse. At first it was a decision he made himself, but after he started exercising, his day gradually became different. At night he came to sleep earlier, and in the morning his body felt lighter. After one month, his habits changed a lot too. Jihoon also decided to practice Korean every day, and as he practiced, his ability improved and he gained more confidence.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 지훈은 왜 운동하기로 했어요?
지훈은 밤에 어떻게 자게 됐어요?
한국어를 연습할수록 무엇이 늘었어요?

culturalNote.title: Agency matters
culturalNote.body: Korean often cares whether you chose something, it happened through circumstances, or the state simply changed. 기로 했어요 sounds responsible and deliberate. 게 됐어요 can sound softer or more modest. 아/어졌어요 focuses on the result you can observe.
culturalNote.tip: Ask yourself: Did I decide it? Use 기로 했어요. Did circumstances lead there? Use 게 됐어요. Did the state change? Use 아/어졌어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence states a settled decision?
inlineExercises.explanation: -기로 했어요 reports a decision that has already been made.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence sounds like the situation came about through circumstances?
inlineExercises.explanation: -게 됐어요 shows how the situation came to be.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence describes a state change?
inlineExercises.explanation: 가볍다 becomes 가벼워지다 for a change of state.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete: 오늘부터 일찍 자___ 했어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: 자다 becomes 자기로 in the decision frame.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 운동하기로 할 거예요. (The decision is already made.)
inlineExercises.explanation: Use 했어요 when reporting a decision that has already been made.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 건강이 좋게 됐어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: For a simple state improvement, use 좋아지다.

inlineExercises.prompt: 건강___ 좋아졌어요. (My health got better.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 좋아지다 describes a subject changing state, so 건강 takes 이. 을 would make health the object of an action.

inlineExercises.prompt: 오늘부터 운동을 ___ . (시작하다 → decided to)
inlineExercises.explanation: V-기로 했어요 states a settled decision. 시작하다 becomes 시작하기로 했어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'My habit changed.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 바뀌다 describes something changing, so 습관이 is the subject. The past form 바뀌었어요 reports the completed change.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'I ended up exercising every morning.'
inlineExercises.explanation: V-게 됐어요 sounds like the situation developed that way. It is less like a sudden promise and more like a change in routine.

bullets: Use V-기로 했어요 for a decision you made: 운동하기로 했어요.
Use V-게 됐어요 when circumstances led to a new situation: 살게 됐어요.
Use A/V-아/어지다 for state change: 좋아졌어요, 가벼워졌어요.
Use real change words too: 바뀌다, 달라지다, 늘다, 줄다.
Do not use 게 되다 to hide a simple decision unless the situation really led you there.

writingTask.prompt: Write a short note about a decision you made and a change that has happened since, like starting a new habit.
writingTask.hint: Use V-기로 했어요 for the decision, V-게 됐어요 for what came about, and A-아/어졌어요 for how something became.
writingTask.model: 저는 매일 운동하기로 했어요. 그래서 아침에 일찍 일어나게 됐어요. 요즘 건강이 좋아졌어요.
writingTask.modelEn: I decided to exercise every day. So I ended up getting up early in the morning. These days my health has gotten better.

canDo: Announce a decision you made (운동하기로 했어요)
Describe a change that came about from circumstances (-게 됐어요)
Say how a state changed over time (좋아졌어요 · 달라졌어요)

beginnerGuide.title: Setting changes the ending
beginnerGuide.body: Use 합쇼체 in formal public settings like 발표 and 면접. Use 해요체 for ordinary polite conversation with classmates, teachers, and people you just met.

beginnerGuide.title: Polite is not one style
beginnerGuide.body: 존댓말 is the broad polite category. 해요체 and 합쇼체 are both polite, but 합쇼체 sounds more formal and public.

beginnerGuide.title: Use 반말 carefully
beginnerGuide.body: 반말 is natural with close friends, but it can sound rude with teachers, staff, strangers, or people who have not agreed to speak casually.

checkpoints: I can use 안 for not doing by choice or fact.
I can use 못 for cannot because of ability or situation.
I can use 아니에요 and -지 않아요 where short negation is not natural.

hook.situation: You give a short presentation, answer a formal question, and then talk normally with a classmate afterward.
objectives: Use formal polite endings like -습니다, -ㅂ니다, and -습니까 in public or formal settings.
Choose between 해요체, 합쇼체, 존댓말, and 반말 based on relationship and setting.
Avoid using the stiffest style everywhere just because it feels safer.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean speech level is not decoration. The same idea can sound natural, stiff, friendly, distant, or rude depending on the ending and the relationship. A learner who says correct grammar in the wrong speech level can still sound socially off.

grammarNotes.title: V-(스)ㅂ니다 — the formal polite ending (합니다체)
grammarNotes.func: This is the formal polite ending for statements. It sounds more formal than the everyday -아요/-어요 (해요체) ending, so you hear it in announcements, at work, in the news, and when you first meet someone.

formTable.when: Stem ends in a vowel (no 받침)
formTable.ex: 가다 → 갑니다 / 오다 → 옵니다 / 크다 → 큽니다

formTable.when: Stem ends in a consonant (has 받침)
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹습니다 / 읽다 → 읽습니다 / 작다 → 작습니다

formTable.when: Stem ends in ㄹ (the ㄹ drops)
formTable.ex: 살다 → 삽니다 / 만들다 → 만듭니다 / 알다 → 압니다

examples.en: I'm a student.
examples.note: 이다 attaches to the noun 학생 as 입니다 — the standard way to introduce yourself.

examples.en: I eat every morning.
examples.note: 먹다 has a 받침 (ㄱ), so it takes 습니다 → 먹습니다. 밥을 먹다 just means "to eat (a meal)".

examples.en: I'm going to school now.
examples.note: 가다 ends in a vowel, so it takes ㅂ니다 → 갑니다.

examples.en: Do you live in Busan?
examples.note: 살다 ends in ㄹ, which drops before ㅂ; the question ending -ㅂ니까? makes it 삽니까?

keyPoint.label: 받침 decides ㅂ니다 vs 습니다
keyPoint.body: No 받침 → add ㅂ니다 (가 → 갑니다). Has 받침 → add 습니다 (먹 → 먹습니다). The one exception is ㄹ stems: the ㄹ drops and you use ㅂ니다 (살 → 삽니다), so they act like vowel stems.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: The ㅂ in -ㅂ니다 sounds like [m] before ㄴ: 갑니다 sounds like [감니다], 입니다 like [임니다], and 습니다 like [슴니다].

drill.instruction: Change each dictionary-form verb into the formal 합니다체 statement (V-(스)ㅂ니다).

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: The ending depends on the last letter of the stem, not the meaning. A stem ending in a consonant like 먹 takes 습니다 (not ㅂ니다), and a stem ending in a vowel like 가 takes ㅂ니다 (not 습니다). Check the stem's last letter first.

grammarNotes.title: Choosing the style — 해요체 vs 합니다체 vs 반말
grammarNotes.func: Korean changes the verb ending depending on who you're talking to. The three everyday styles are 해요체 (polite, all-purpose), 합니다체 (formal polite), and 반말 (casual, no -요). The listener and the situation pick the ending — not the meaning of the sentence — so the wrong choice can sound rude or oddly stiff.

formTable.when: 해요체 — polite, the default for daily life
formTable.ex: 가다 → 가요 / 먹다 → 먹어요 / 공부하다 → 공부해요

formTable.when: 합니다체 — formal polite (work, announcements, first meeting)
반말 — casual (close friends, younger people, family)
formTable.ex: 가요 → 가 / 먹어요 → 먹어 / 공부해요 → 공부해
all mean "(I) eat", from most formal to most casual

examples.en: Hello. I'm Korean.
examples.note: 해요체 — the safe, friendly default for people you don't know well.

examples.en: Hello. Nice to meet you.
examples.note: 합니다체 — a formal first greeting; you'd hear this in business and formal settings.

examples.en: Hey, where are you going right now?
examples.note: 반말 — 가요 drops 요 to become 가; used with a close friend the same age. 너 (you) also marks 반말.

examples.en: Mom, I'm hungry.
examples.note: 반말 — used at home with family; 배고파요 drops 요 to 배고파, and 나 (casual "I") fits the casual style.

keyPoint.label: The listener, not the meaning, picks the ending
keyPoint.body: 합니다체 = formal/distant (work, strangers, announcements). 해요체 = polite all-purpose (the safe everyday choice). 반말 = casual, only with close friends, younger people, or family. When unsure, use 해요체 — it's polite and never rude.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In 반말 questions, the rising pitch alone marks the question: 가? rises at the end, while the statement 가. falls. There's no -까? ending and no spelling change.

drill.instruction: Rewrite each 해요체 sentence in the style named in brackets (합니다체 = formal, 반말 = casual).

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English has one neutral register, so learners drop 요 to sound casual and friendly — but 반말 can be disrespectful to someone older or senior. Default to 해요체 with anyone you aren't clearly close to, and switch to 반말 only once the relationship plainly allows it.

grammarNotes.title: 반말 4형 — casual statements, questions, commands, and let's
grammarNotes.func: 반말 is the casual style used with close friends, younger people, and some family members. For many everyday statements and questions, you can start from the 해요체 form and remove 요: 먹어요 → 먹어. Commands use the same -아/어 shape, while casual "let's" uses -자.

formTable.ex: 먹어요 → 먹어. / 먹어?; 가요 → 가. / 가?

examples.en: I'm going home now.
examples.note: Statement: 가요 loses 요 → 가. 나 also matches the casual style.

examples.en: Did you eat?
examples.note: Question: 먹었어요 loses 요 → 먹었어? The rising pitch makes it a question.

examples.en: Come here for a second.
examples.note: Command: 오다 becomes 와. This is only safe when 반말 is already okay.

examples.en: Jimin, let's go together.
examples.note: Name + 아 calls someone with 받침; 가자 is the casual let's form.

keyPoint.label: 요-drop is grammar; permission is social
keyPoint.body: The form is simple: remove 요 for many statements and questions, use -자 for "let's," and use 야/이야 after nouns. The hard part is social timing. Switch to 반말 only after the relationship allows it, often after someone asks 말 놔도 돼요? or suggests 우리 말 놓을까요?

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In 반말 questions, spelling often stays the same as the statement and pitch does the work: 먹어. falls, 먹어? rises. With names, 지민아 flows as [지미나] because the final ㄴ links to 아.

drill.instruction: Change each polite sentence into natural 반말 for a close friend.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 반말 is just Korean slang, so it is okay with anyone if I sound friendly.
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 반말 is a relationship signal. Use it only with close people, younger people, or when both sides have agreed.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: The form itself is not rude; the mismatch is rude. A perfect 먹어? can be warm to a close friend and very disrespectful to a teacher or stranger. Decide the relationship first, then choose the ending.

readingText.title: One topic, two speech levels
readingText.body: 민서는 내일 수업에서 발표를 해요. 발표는 격식 있는 자리라서 처음에는 “지금부터 발표를 시작하겠습니다”라고 말할 거예요. 발표가 끝난 뒤에는 “질문 있으십니까?”라고 물을 수 있어요. 하지만 발표 후에 친구와 이야기할 때는 합쇼체를 계속 쓰지 않아요. 친구에게는 “발표 끝났어요”처럼 해요체가 더 자연스러워요. 친한 친구라면 반말도 가능하지만, 처음 만난 사람에게는 존댓말이 안전해요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo has a class presentation tomorrow. Since a presentation is a formal setting, she will begin by saying, 'I will begin the presentation now.' After the presentation, she can ask, 'Do you have any questions?' But when talking to a friend after the presentation, she does not keep using formal style. With a friend, haeyo style like 'The presentation is over' sounds more natural. Casual speech is possible with a close friend, but with someone you just met, polite speech is safe.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 발표 처음에 뭐라고 말할 거예요?
친구에게는 어떤 말투가 더 자연스러워요?
처음 만난 사람에게는 무엇이 안전해요?

culturalNote.title: The most formal style is not always the most natural
culturalNote.body: Learners sometimes use 합쇼체 everywhere because it feels safest. Korean speakers may understand it, but with classmates or friendly staff it can sound stiff, distant, or scripted. Good Korean is not only polite; it fits the relationship.
culturalNote.tip: When unsure, start with 해요체. Move to 합쇼체 for formal public settings, and use 반말 only when the relationship allows it.

inlineExercises.explanation: With a classmate after the formal setting, 해요체 sounds more natural.

inlineExercises.prompt: 선생님___ 질문이 있어요. (I have a question for the teacher.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 께 marks the respected recipient of the question. 께서 marks a respected subject doing an action, and 를 would wrongly mark the teacher as an object.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 한국어를 ___ . (공부하다 → formal polite)
inlineExercises.explanation: Formal polite statements use -ㅂ니다/습니다. 하다 verbs become 합니다, so 공부하다 becomes 공부합니다.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build a formal sentence: 'I study Korean.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 합니다체 is appropriate for presentations and interviews. 한국어를 stays as the object before the formal verb.

inlineExercises.prompt: After class, you speak casually with a close friend. Which ending fits best?
inlineExercises.explanation: With a close friend, 반말 can be natural. The other two are much more formal and would sound distant after class.

bullets: Use 합쇼체 for formal public settings: 발표를 시작하겠습니다.
Use 해요체 for ordinary polite conversation: 발표 끝났어요.
Use 반말 only when the relationship allows it.
존댓말 is the broad polite category; 해요체 and 합쇼체 are both polite styles.
Good Korean matches grammar, relationship, and setting together.

beginnerGuide.title: Respect has direction
beginnerGuide.body: -(으)시- and 께서 honor the subject. 께 and 드리다 honor the person who receives your action.

beginnerGuide.title: Use special verbs
beginnerGuide.body: 계시다, 드시다, 주무시다, and 말씀하시다 are not random alternatives; they are common honorific verbs for respected subjects.

beginnerGuide.title: Do not honor yourself
beginnerGuide.body: Do not add -(으)시- to your own action. Say 제가 가요, not 제가 가세요. Use 드리다 only when your action goes toward someone respected.

Use 께서 for a respected subject and 께 for a respected recipient.
Use special honorific verbs like 계시다, 드시다, 주무시다, 말씀하시다, and 드리다.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean honorifics are not just 'being polite'. 해요체 can be polite to the listener, but honorific grammar often honors the person you are talking about. 선생님께서 오세요 honors the teacher as the subject; 선생님께 말씀드려요 honors the teacher as the recipient.

grammarNotes.title: -(으)시- — the subject honorific suffix
grammarNotes.func: You add -(으)시- to a verb or adjective stem to show respect toward the person doing the action or being described — usually someone older or higher than you. It raises the SUBJECT of the sentence, not the listener.

examples.en: The teacher is reading a book.
examples.note: The subject 선생님 is honored, so 읽다 takes the -으시- form (consonant stem) → 읽으세요.

examples.en: Grandmother is sleeping right now.
examples.note: 주무세요 already has -시- inside it (from the special honorific 주무시다); the honored subject is 할머니.

examples.en: Dad exercises every morning.
examples.note: 하다 ends in a vowel, so it just adds -시- → 하세요; the honored subject is 아버지.

examples.en: Are you in a good mood today?
examples.note: Adjectives take -(으)시- too when they describe an honored person: 좋다 (consonant stem) → 좋으세요.

keyPoint.label: -(으)시- vs. -아/어요
keyPoint.body: -아/어요 is polite toward the LISTENER; -(으)시- raises the SUBJECT of the sentence. You can be polite to a friend (친구가 와요) without -시-, but to honor a teacher you add it (선생님이 오세요). Never use -시- about yourself: say 저는 가요, never 저는 가세요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 읽으세요 is pronounced [일그세요] (ilgeuseyo) — the ㄱ of 읽 moves over to fill the 으 syllable.

drill.instruction: Make each sentence honorific by adding -(으)시- (use the -(으)세요 form).
drill.model: 선생님이 책을 읽어요. → 선생님이 책을 읽으세요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English has no grammar that raises the subject, so learners over-use -시- and end up honoring themselves. -(으)시- is only for someone you respect — never 저/나. For yourself, use the plain polite form.

grammarNotes.title: N께서 V-(으)시- — 께서 and the special honorific verbs
grammarNotes.func: When the subject deserves respect, the subject particle 이/가 changes to 께서, and the verb takes -(으)시-. A few very common verbs have their own honorific forms you just have to memorize, instead of adding -시-.

formTable.when: 있다 (to be / stay somewhere) → special form

examples.en: Grandfather is in the room.
examples.note: 있다 (existence) becomes the special honorific 계시다 → 계세요, and the subject takes 께서 instead of 가.

examples.en: The teacher is eating lunch.
examples.note: 먹다 → 드시다 (everyday honorific); 잡수시다 is the more formal version. The subject takes 께서.

examples.en: My parents watch a movie on the weekend.
examples.note: 보다 has no special form, so it just adds -시- → 보세요, but the honored subject 부모님 still takes 께서.

examples.en: Grandmother goes to sleep early.
examples.note: 자다 → 주무시다, which already has -시- built in; pair it with 께서 for the honored subject.

keyPoint.label: 있다: 있으세요 vs. 계세요
keyPoint.body: When 있다 means existence/being somewhere ('to be there'), the honorific is 계세요 (할아버지께서 집에 계세요). When 있다 means possession ('to have'), use 있으세요, NOT 계세요 (선생님께서 시간이 있으세요). 계세요 is only for a person being present, never for having things.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 계세요 is usually said [게세요] (geseyo) in everyday speech — the ㅖ softens to ㅔ after ㄱ.

drill.instruction: Rewrite each sentence with 께서 and the correct honorific verb (use the special form where one exists).
drill.model: 할아버지가 집에 있어요. → 할아버지께서 집에 계세요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners add -으시- to 있다 and get 있으세요, but for a respected person who is present somewhere, Korean swaps in the special verb 계시다 → 계세요. 있으세요 is only for possession ('have').

grammarNotes.title: N께 V-아/어 드리다 — honoring the person you do something for
grammarNotes.func: While -(으)시- honors the subject, 드리다 honors the RECIPIENT — the person you do something FOR. 주다 ('give / do for someone') becomes 드리다, and the recipient particle 에게/한테 becomes 께.

formTable.ex: 도와주다 → 도와 드리다 / 읽어 주다 → 읽어 드리다

formTable.when: ㅏ/ㅗ stem → -아 드리다; other vowels → -어 드리다
formTable.ex: 사다 → 사 드려요 / 만들다 → 만들어 드려요

examples.en: I gave Grandmother a present.
examples.note: The recipient 할머니 is honored, so 주다 → 드리다 and 에게/한테 → 께.

examples.en: I bought my parents a meal.
examples.note: 사 주다 ('buy for someone') → 사 드리다 because the recipient 부모님 deserves respect.

examples.en: I'll read the book for the teacher.
examples.note: 읽어 주다 → 읽어 드리다; the action is done FOR the honored recipient 선생님.

examples.en: I showed Grandfather the way.
examples.note: 가르쳐 주다 → 가르쳐 드리다, with 께 marking the honored recipient 할아버지.

keyPoint.label: -(으)시- vs. -아/어 드리다
keyPoint.body: -(으)시- raises the person DOING the action (subject); 드리다 raises the person RECEIVING it (recipient). 선생님께서 가르치세요 = the teacher (subject) teaches; 선생님께 가르쳐 드려요 = I teach FOR the teacher. The 드리다 sentence usually has 저/제가 as the (humble) subject.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 읽어 드려요 is pronounced [일거 드려요] (ilgeo deuryeoyo) — the ㄹㄱ of 읽 links into the next syllable.

drill.instruction: Rewrite with 께 and 드리다 (or -아/어 드리다) to honor the recipient.
drill.model: 친구에게 선물을 줬어요. → 부모님께 선물을 드렸어요.
items: 동생한테 책을 사 줬어요. → 할머니____ 책을 사 ____.
친구에게 밥을 만들어 줬어요. → 부모님____ 밥을 만들어 ____.
동생한테 길을 가르쳐 줬어요. → 선생님____ 길을 가르쳐 ____.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 할머니께 선물을 주세요. (meaning 'I gave Grandmother a gift')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners reach for 주다 with -시- (주세요) to sound polite, but -(으)시- honors the subject (the giver), not the recipient. To honor the person RECEIVING, you change the verb itself to 드리다. (주세요 only works as a request: 'please give.')

exampleSentence.ko: 선생님에 대해 말할 때는 높임말을 써요.
exampleSentence.en: When talking about a teacher, I use honorific language.
exampleSentence.note: The honored person can be the person being discussed.

exampleSentence.en: The teacher is coming.
exampleSentence.note: The teacher is the respected subject.

exampleSentence.en: I contact my parents.
exampleSentence.note: Parents are the respected recipient.

exampleSentence.en: The boss is not here right now.
exampleSentence.note: Honorific form of 있다 for a respected person.

exampleSentence.en: The teacher drinks coffee.
exampleSentence.note: Honors the person eating or drinking.

exampleSentence.en: My parents sleep early.
exampleSentence.note: Special honorific form of 자다.

exampleSentence.en: The teacher spoke.
exampleSentence.note: Honors the teacher as speaker.

extendedVocabulary.english: to give or do for a respected person

exampleSentence.en: I told the teacher.
exampleSentence.note: Humbly describes your action toward a respected recipient.

exampleSentence.en: The teacher is coming soon.
exampleSentence.note: Common respected subject.

exampleSentence.en: I will contact my parents first.
exampleSentence.note: Common respected recipient.

exampleSentence.en: The boss is not here right now.
exampleSentence.note: Common workplace honorific noun.

exampleSentence.en: I will guide the customer again.
exampleSentence.note: Service-register honorific noun.

extendedDialogue.setting: A learner talks about a teacher and parents respectfully.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: When is the teacher coming?
lines.grammarNote: 께서 marks 선생님 as the respected subject.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: They will come soon and speak first.
lines.grammarNote: 오시다 and 말씀하시다 honor the teacher as subject.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Did you contact your parents too?
lines.grammarNote: 께 plus 드리다 honors the recipient.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Yes, I told my mother first.
lines.grammarNote: 말씀드리다 humbly describes speaking to a respected person.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Is the boss here now?
lines.grammarNote: 계시다 honors the person who is present.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Yes, they are in the meeting room.
lines.grammarNote: 계세요 is the polite present form of 계시다.

readingText.title: Who receives the respect?
readingText.body: 민서는 선생님에 대해 말할 때 높임말을 써요. 선생님이 주어일 때는 “선생님께서 오세요”라고 말해요. 선생님이 말하는 사람일 때는 “선생님께서 말씀하셨어요”라고 해요. 하지만 민서가 선생님에게 말한 일을 설명할 때는 “선생님께 말씀드렸어요”라고 해요. 께서는 주어를 높이고, 께는 받는 사람을 높여요. 그래서 높임말을 쓸 때는 먼저 누가 행동하는지, 그 행동이 누구에게 가는지 봐야 해요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo uses honorific language when talking about her teacher. When the teacher is the subject, she says, 'The teacher is coming.' When the teacher is the speaker, she says, 'The teacher spoke.' But when Minseo explains that she told something to the teacher, she says, 'I told the teacher.' 께서 honors the subject, and 께 honors the recipient. So when using honorifics, first check who is doing the action and who receives the action.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 께서는 누구를 높여요?
께는 누구를 높여요?
선생님이 말한 경우에는 어떻게 말해요?

culturalNote.title: Respect has direction
culturalNote.body: Honorific Korean asks where respect is pointing. Sometimes it points to the subject with -(으)시- or 께서. Sometimes it points to the recipient with 께 and 드리다. Overusing honorifics on yourself sounds wrong, not extra polite.
culturalNote.tip: Before adding -시-, ask: who is the subject? Before using 드리다, ask: who receives my action?

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence honors the teacher as subject?
inlineExercises.explanation: 께서 marks the respected subject, and 오세요 honors that subject.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence honors the teacher as recipient?
inlineExercises.explanation: 께 marks the respected recipient, and 드리다 humbly describes your action.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses 계시다 correctly?
inlineExercises.explanation: 계시다 is for respected people, not objects or yourself.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete: 어머니___ 먼저 말씀하셨어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: 어머니 is the respected subject who spoke.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 제가 선생님께서 말씀드렸어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: The teacher is the recipient, so use 께, not 께서.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: 가방이 책상 위에 계세요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Objects use 있다, not 계시다.

inlineExercises.prompt: 선생님___ 오셨어요. (The teacher came.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 께서 marks a respected subject. 께 marks a respected recipient, not the person doing the action.

inlineExercises.prompt: 할머니가 아침을 ___ . (드시다 → polite past)
inlineExercises.explanation: 드시다 is the honorific verb for eating or drinking. In polite past it becomes 드셨어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I gave it to my parents.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 께 honors the recipient, and 드리다 is humble for giving upward. This combination respects 부모님.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'My mother is at home.'
inlineExercises.explanation: A respected person as subject takes 께서, and 있다 becomes 계세요. Use 있어요 for objects or non-honorific subjects.

bullets: -(으)시- honors the subject: 선생님이 오세요.
께서 marks a respected subject: 선생님께서 오세요.
께 marks a respected recipient: 선생님께 말씀드려요.
Special honorific verbs matter: 계시다, 드시다, 주무시다, 말씀하시다.
Do not use honorifics on yourself or on objects.

writingTask.prompt: Write a few sentences about your day with a respected elder (e.g. your grandmother), honoring her actions and something you did for her.
writingTask.hint: Use 께서 + -(으)시- and special honorific verbs (계시다·드시다·주무시다), and -아/어 드리다 with 께 for what you did for her.
writingTask.model: 할머니께서는 지금 집에 계세요. 아침을 맛있게 드셨어요. 그리고 제가 할머니께 커피를 만들어 드렸어요.
writingTask.modelEn: My grandmother is at home now. She ate breakfast well. And I made coffee for her.

canDo: Raise the subject with the honorific suffix (-(으)시-)
Use 께서 and special honorific verbs (계시다 · 드시다 · 주무시다)
Honor the person I do something for (N께 V-아/어 드리다)
Show respect to elders and seniors naturally (선생님 · 부모님 · 사장님)

chapters.title: Discourse Markers
chapters.goal: Talk about family and older relatives with the right respect.
chapters.scenario: You introduce family members or ask about someone else's family politely.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 사실은 오늘 자료가 아직 다 안 끝났는데요.
dialogue.romanization: sasireun oneul jaryoga ajik da an kkeunnanneundeyo.
dialogue.en: Actually, today's materials are not finished yet.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 그러니까 먼저 회의를 시작해도 된다는 말이죠?
dialogue.romanization: geureonikka meonjeo hoeuireul sijakaedo doendaneun marijyo?
dialogue.en: So you mean we can start the meeting first, right?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Yes. Something suddenly came up yesterday, you see.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 알겠어요. 그런데 발표 전에 자료는 보내 줄 수 있어요?
dialogue.romanization: algesseoyo. geureonde balpyo jeone jaryoneun bonae jul su isseoyo?
dialogue.en: I understand. But can you send the materials before the presentation?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 네, 그건 가능해요. 회의 시간이 짧잖아요.
dialogue.romanization: ne, geugeon ganeunghaeyo. hoeui sigani jjaljanhayo.
dialogue.en: Yes, that is possible. The meeting time is short, you know.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Then I will explain the background first.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make three meeting-message lines: one with 사실은 ...는데요, one with ...거든요 for new background, and one with ...잖아요 for shared information.
chapters.realLifeTask: Introduce one family member and say one respectful sentence about them.
chapters.friendPractice: One person gives a problem in a meeting or study group. The other brings it up softly, then explains whether the reason is new information or shared information.
chapters.review: Can you choose 거든요 for new background and 잖아요 for shared information without making the listener feel blamed?

beginnerGuide.title: Open the topic softly
beginnerGuide.body: 사실은 and -는데요 let you start a sensitive topic without sounding like you are dropping bad news too suddenly.

beginnerGuide.title: Separate new and shared information
beginnerGuide.body: Use -거든요 when the listener does not know the background yet. Use -잖아요 when the listener already knows or can see the reason.

beginnerGuide.title: Soften disagreement
beginnerGuide.body: 그런데, 근데, and -는데요 can make pushback feel conversational, but the sentence still needs a clear point.

I can use honorific forms when talking about older or respected family members.
I can avoid overusing casual family terms in polite situations.

sampleAnswer.en: My mother lives in Busan.

I can use honorific forms when talking about older or respected family members.
