Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: Your meeting is starting, but your materials are not ready. You need to bring it up, give background, and push the conversation forward without sounding abrupt or defensive.
objectives: Open a sensitive topic with 사실은 and sentence-final -는데요.
Separate new background with -거든요 from shared information with -잖아요.
Use 그런데/근데 to shift or push back while keeping the conversation cooperative.
hook.whyItMatters: A direct translation of 'but' or 'because' often sounds too flat in Korean. These markers show whether the listener already knows the reason, whether you are adding new context, and how much room you are leaving for the other person to respond.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-(으)ㄴ/는데 — Giving Background Before Your Point
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)ㄴ/는데 to give a piece of background first, then say what you really mean (a question, a suggestion, or a request) in the next clause. It loosely links two ideas, a bit like English "so..." or "and...".

formTable.when: Adjective stem ending in a vowel/ㄹ
Adjective stem ending in a consonant

examples.en: We don't have time, so should we take a taxi?
examples.note: The background (no time) sets up the suggestion that follows.

examples.ko: 이 책이 좀 어려운데 같이 읽어요.
examples.romanization: i chaegi jom eoryeounde gachi ilgeoyo.
examples.en: This book is a bit hard, so let's read it together.
examples.note: 어렵다 has an irregular ㅂ, so it becomes 어려운데, not 어렵은데.

examples.en: I'm eating right now, so I'll call you later.
examples.note: Action verb 먹다 takes -는데 no matter the final sound.

examples.ko: 제 친구가 학생인데 한국어를 정말 잘해요.
examples.romanization: je chinguga haksaeginde hangugeoreul jeongmal jalhaeyo.
examples.en: My friend is a student, and she speaks Korean really well.
examples.note: Noun + 이다 becomes 인데; here it just adds info, not contrast.

keyPoint.label: -는데 vs. -아서/어서
keyPoint.body: -아서/어서 ties a clause as a tight cause ('because A, B'). -(으)ㄴ/는데 just sets the scene ('A, and now...') and feels softer. Only -는데 can lead naturally into a -ㄹ까요? or -ㄹ래요? question. The full contrast use of -는데 comes later.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 는데 sounds like [는데] with no change, but after a ㄷ/ㅅ/ㅈ-final stem like 받다, 받는데 becomes [반는데] (the ㄷ turns into ㄴ before 는).

drill.instruction: Attach -(으)ㄴ/는데 to the cue verb to give background, then read the whole sentence aloud.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers grab -아서/어서 ('because') to lead into a suggestion, but -아서/어서 can't come before a -ㄹ까요?/-ㄹ래요? ending. Use -는데 to set up the background first.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-잖아요 — Reminding Someone of What You Both Know
grammarNotes.func: Use -잖아요 to remind the listener of something you both already know, or to point out something obvious as your reason. It carries the feeling of "you know..." or "remember...".

examples.ko: 그 식당은 비싸잖아요. 다른 데 가요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdangeun bissajanayo. dareun de gayo.
examples.en: That restaurant is expensive, you know. Let's go somewhere else.
examples.note: Reminds the listener of a shared fact (it's expensive) as the reason.

examples.en: It's Sunday today, remember? We don't have school.
examples.note: Noun + 이다 → 일요일이잖아요; pointing out an obvious fact.

examples.ko: 어제 같이 밥 먹었잖아요. 벌써 잊었어요?
examples.romanization: eoje gachi bap meogeotjanayo. beolsseo ijeosseoyo?
examples.en: We ate together yesterday, remember? Did you forget already?
examples.note: Past tense -었잖아요 brings back a shared experience.

examples.ko: 민수 씨가 한국어 잘하잖아요. 민수 씨한테 물어봐요.
examples.romanization: minsu ssiga hangugeo jalhajanayo. minsu ssihante mureobwayo.
examples.en: Minsu is good at Korean, you know. Ask him.
examples.note: Uses a known fact about Minsu to back up the suggestion.

keyPoint.label: -잖아요 vs. -거든요
keyPoint.body: -잖아요 points to OLD information the listener already knows ('you know that...'). -거든요 gives NEW information they don't know yet. Using -잖아요 for brand-new facts sounds odd, like 'you should have known this already'.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 잖아요 links across the syllable and sounds like [자나요], with the ㅈ and ㅇ flowing together. Don't break it into [잗-아요].

drill.instruction: Turn each known fact into a reminder with -잖아요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저 처음 보죠? 제 이름은 민수잖아요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 저 처음 보죠? 제 이름은 민수거든요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Don't use -잖아요 for information that's new to the listener — it sounds like you're saying they should already know it, which can feel like a scolding. For brand-new info, use -거든요.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-지요/죠 — Checking Shared Understanding
grammarNotes.func: Use -지요? or its spoken contraction -죠? when you think you already know the answer and want the listener to confirm or agree. It is softer than a plain information question because it sounds like "right?" or "you know, don't you?" In everyday speech, -죠 is more common than the full -지요.

examples.en: It's really hot today, isn't it?
examples.note: Weather small talk: the speaker expects agreement, not new information.

examples.en: Minsu is a student, right?
examples.note: Noun + 이다 becomes 학생이지요; the speaker is confirming something they think is true.

examples.en: Korean is fun, you know.
examples.note: As a statement, -죠 invites agreement and creates a shared feeling.

examples.en: The test is tomorrow, right? That's right, isn't it?
examples.note: A gentle self-check; 맞죠? is a common quick confirmation.

keyPoint.label: -아요? asks; -지요?/죠? confirms
keyPoint.body: Use -아요? when you do not know and need information. Use -지요?/죠? when you already have an idea and want confirmation, agreement, or shared footing. If you truly have no idea, plain -아요? is safer.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: The contracted 죠 is one quick syllable. After a stop consonant like the ㅂ in 덥죠, the ㅈ is always pronounced tense, so 덥죠 sounds like [덥쬬] at any speed — but keep the spelling 덥죠, not 덥쬬.

drill.instruction: Change each plain question into a confirmation question with -죠?

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 이름이 뭐죠? (when you truly do not know and are asking a stranger)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English tag questions are flexible, so learners overuse -죠 for ordinary questions. But -죠 suggests you expected or half-knew the answer. For new information, use a normal question; save -죠 for confirmation or shared facts.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-거든요 — Adding a Reason They Didn't Know
grammarNotes.func: Use -거든요 to give the listener new information — usually a reason or background fact they didn't know — often answering a spoken or silent "why?". It feels like "...you see" at the end.

examples.ko: 오늘은 못 만나요. 할 일이 많거든요.
examples.romanization: oneureun mot mannayo. hal iri mankeodeunyo.
examples.en: I can't meet today. I have a lot to do, you see.
examples.note: Gives a reason the listener didn't know.

examples.ko: 저 요즘 한국어 배워요. 한국 친구가 많거든요.
examples.romanization: jeo yojeum hangugeo baewoyo. hanguk chinguga mankeodeunyo.
examples.en: I'm learning Korean these days. I have a lot of Korean friends, you see.
examples.note: Adds fresh background that explains the first sentence.

examples.en: I went to bed early yesterday. I was so tired, you see.
examples.note: Past tense -었거든요 gives the reason for a past action.

examples.ko: 오늘 우산 가져왔어요. 비가 온다고 했거든요.
examples.romanization: oneul usan gajyeowasseoyo. biga ondago haetgeodeunyo.
examples.en: I brought an umbrella today. They said it would rain, you see.
examples.note: Introduces a new fact that explains the action.

keyPoint.label: -거든요 vs. -아서/어서
keyPoint.body: Both can give a reason, but -아서/어서 joins two clauses inside one sentence ('A여서 B'). -거든요 ends the sentence and tacks the reason on afterward as a fresh follow-up — it signals 'here's something you didn't know'. -아서/어서 doesn't carry that 'news' feeling.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 거든요 keeps each syllable clear: [거든뇨] in fast speech as the ㄴ and ㅛ glide together. Don't soften it to [거더요].

drill.instruction: Add a reason the listener doesn't know yet, using -거든요.
drill.model: (못 만나요 / 할 일이 많다) → 못 만나요. 할 일이 많거든요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: -거든요 goes at the END of a sentence, not in the middle like English 'because'. Say your main point first, then add the reason as a separate sentence ending in -거든요.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-는데요 — A Soft, Trailing Ending
grammarNotes.func: Use sentence-final -는데요 to leave your statement gently open, inviting the other person to react or softening a reply. It often hints at an unspoken 'but...', which makes answers and mild objections sound polite instead of blunt.

examples.en: I'm a little busy right now... (so maybe later?)
examples.note: Trails off softly instead of a flat 'no', leaving room for the other person.

examples.en: Hmm, I don't really know that...
examples.note: A gentle way to admit you don't know, softer than 몰라요.

examples.en: But I already finished eating...
examples.note: Past tense -었는데요 here carries a mild 'but', a soft pushback.

examples.en: Um, someone's sitting here...
examples.note: Softly tells someone a seat is taken without sounding harsh.

keyPoint.label: -는데 vs. -는데요
keyPoint.body: -는데 in the middle of a sentence sets up background for a following clause. -는데요 stands at the very END as a soft, open finish. Same shape, but here it's a complete reply that trails off, not a connector. The honorific 요 is what makes it a polite stand-alone ending.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 는데요 sounds like [는데요]; after a ㄷ/ㅅ/ㅈ-final stem the ㄴ-change still applies (먹었는데요 → [머건는데요]). Let the final 요 drift up slightly to keep the soft, open feel.

drill.instruction: Answer each prompt with a soft, trailing -는데요 ending.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 지금 바빠요. (flat, can sound blunt when declining)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers end a refusal with a plain -아요/어요, which can land too direct in Korean. Adding -는데요 leaves the sentence softly open, so a 'no' feels gentler and more polite.

exampleSentence.ko: 사실은 오늘 자료가 아직 안 끝났는데요.
exampleSentence.en: Actually, today's materials are not finished yet.
exampleSentence.note: Opens a sensitive update softly.

exampleSentence.ko: 알겠어요. 그런데 발표 전에 자료는 보내 줄 수 있어요?
exampleSentence.en: I understand. But can you send the materials before the presentation?
exampleSentence.note: Shifts from accepting the situation to asking for the next action.

exampleSentence.en: But that is a little difficult, though.
exampleSentence.note: Casual version of 그런데 for spoken conversation.

exampleSentence.ko: 그러니까 먼저 회의를 시작해도 된다는 말이죠?
exampleSentence.en: So you mean we can start the meeting first, right?
exampleSentence.note: Checks the implied meaning before moving on.

exampleSentence.en: The meeting time is short, you know.
exampleSentence.note: Use when the listener already knows the reason.

exampleSentence.en: Something suddenly came up yesterday, you see.
exampleSentence.note: Use when the listener does not know the background yet.

exampleSentence.en: The materials are not finished yet, though.
exampleSentence.note: Leaves space for the listener to respond.

exampleSentence.en: I will send the materials before the meeting.
exampleSentence.note: The actual file, handout, slide deck, or reference material.

exampleSentence.en: I will explain the background first.
exampleSentence.note: Context that helps the listener understand the situation.

exampleSentence.ko: 상대방이 모르는 내용이면 거든요가 더 자연스러워요.
exampleSentence.en: If the other person does not know it, 거든요 is more natural.
exampleSentence.note: The listener's knowledge decides the marker.

exampleSentence.ko: 그 의견에는 부드럽게 반대하는 게 좋아요.
exampleSentence.en: It is better to disagree with that opinion gently.
exampleSentence.note: Names the tone this chapter is practicing.

exampleSentence.ko: 자료가 늦어진 이야기는 제가 먼저 말을 꺼낼게요.
exampleSentence.en: I will bring up the delayed materials first.
exampleSentence.note: 말 means words or speech here.

exampleSentence.en: I will explain the background.
exampleSentence.note: A practical verb for giving context.

exampleSentence.en: I agree with that opinion too.
exampleSentence.note: Pairs with 의견 and polite discussion.

exampleSentence.en: I disagree with that opinion a little, though.
exampleSentence.note: Use -는데요 to make disagreement less abrupt.

exampleSentence.en: If you say it like that, the mood becomes a little stiff.
exampleSentence.note: Discourse markers affect the mood of a conversation.

exampleSentence.ko: 상황을 먼저 설명하면 상대방이 이해하기 쉬워요.
exampleSentence.en: If you explain the situation first, it is easier for the other person to understand.
exampleSentence.note: The larger situation tells you which marker fits.

exampleSentence.en: That opinion is good too, but we are short on time.
exampleSentence.note: Natural noun for agreeing, disagreeing, or softening pushback.

extendedDialogue.setting: A team member brings up unfinished materials before a meeting starts.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 사실은 오늘 자료가 아직 다 안 끝났는데요.
lines.romanization: sasireun oneul jaryoga ajik da an kkeunnanneundeyo.
lines.en: Actually, today's materials are not finished yet.
lines.grammarNote: 사실은 plus -는데요 opens bad news without sounding too sudden.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 그러니까 먼저 회의를 시작해도 된다는 말이죠?
lines.romanization: geureonikka meonjeo hoeuireul sijakaedo doendaneun marijyo?
lines.en: So you mean we can start the meeting first, right?
lines.grammarNote: 그러니까 checks the implied meaning instead of assuming.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Yes. Something suddenly came up yesterday, you see.
lines.grammarNote: -거든요 gives new background the listener did not have.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 알겠어요. 그런데 발표 전에 자료는 보내 줄 수 있어요?
lines.romanization: algesseoyo. geureonde balpyo jeone jaryoneun bonae jul su isseoyo?
lines.en: I understand. But can you send the materials before the presentation?
lines.grammarNote: 그런데 shifts to the next practical concern.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 네, 그건 가능해요. 회의 시간이 짧잖아요.
lines.romanization: ne, geugeon ganeunghaeyo. hoeui sigani jjaljanhayo.
lines.en: Yes, that is possible. The meeting time is short, you know.
lines.grammarNote: -잖아요 treats the short meeting time as shared information.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Then I will explain the background first.
lines.grammarNote: 배경 keeps the reason organized instead of sounding like an excuse.

readingText.title: 자료가 아직 안 끝났는데요
readingText.body: 팀 회의에서 자료가 늦어졌다면 바로 '못 했어요'라고만 말하면 조금 딱딱하게 들릴 수 있어요. 먼저 '사실은'으로 말을 꺼내고, '자료가 아직 안 끝났는데요'처럼 상황을 부드럽게 열어 주세요. 상대방이 모르는 이유를 설명할 때는 '어제 갑자기 일이 생겼거든요'가 자연스럽고, 이미 같이 아는 사실을 다시 짚을 때는 '회의 시간이 짧잖아요'가 자연스러워요. 그다음에는 '그런데 발표 전에 자료는 보내 줄 수 있어요?'처럼 다음 행동을 확인하면 대화가 멈추지 않아요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: If the materials are late in a team meeting, simply saying 'I did not do it' can sound stiff. Open the topic with 사실은, soften the situation with -는데요, use -거든요 for new background, and use -잖아요 for shared information. Then move the conversation to the next action.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 자료가 늦어졌을 때 먼저 어떤 표현으로 말을 꺼낼 수 있어요?
상대방이 모르는 이유를 설명할 때 어떤 표현이 자연스러워요?
이미 같이 아는 사실을 다시 짚을 때는 어떤 표현이 자연스러워요?

culturalNote.title: Soft does not mean unclear
culturalNote.body: In Korean, softening a sentence often means preparing the listener for the point, not avoiding the point. A good update still says what happened, why it happened, and what can happen next.
culturalNote.tip: Before choosing 잖아요 or 거든요, ask one question: does the listener already know this reason?

inlineExercises.prompt: The listener does not know why the materials are late. Which ending fits best?
inlineExercises.explanation: Use -거든요 for new background the listener does not know yet.

inlineExercises.prompt: Everyone knows the meeting time is short. Which sentence uses that shared fact naturally?
inlineExercises.explanation: Use -잖아요 when the reason is shared, visible, or already mentioned.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence brings up bad news most softly?
inlineExercises.explanation: 사실은 opens the topic and -는데요 leaves room for the next step.

inlineExercises.prompt: 자료___ 아직 안 왔거든요. (The thing is, the materials have not arrived yet.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 자료 is the subject of not arriving, so it takes 가. 거든요 adds new background the listener may not know.

inlineExercises.prompt: 자료가 아직 안 ___ . (오다 → soft trailing background)
inlineExercises.explanation: -는데요 opens background and leaves room for the listener to respond. 오다 in past becomes 왔는데요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Actually, the materials are late, you see.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 사실은 prepares the listener for sensitive background. -거든요 explains new information rather than reminding them of something shared.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'We do not have much time, you know.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -잖아요 reminds the listener of shared information. It fits when both people already know time is short.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence if the listener already knows: '시간이 별로 없거든요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: If the listener already knows the fact, 잖아요 is more natural. 거든요 presents it as new background.

inlineExercises.prompt: You need to bring up bad news softly. Which opener is best?
inlineExercises.explanation: 사실은 and -는데요 soften the approach. The shorter alternatives can sound abrupt in a sensitive conversation.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'But I have one question.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 근데 shifts the conversation without sounding too formal. 질문이 하나 있어요 is a natural way to bring in one question.

bullets: 사실은 + -는데요 is useful for opening a sensitive update softly.
-거든요 gives new background; -잖아요 points to shared information.
그런데 and 근데 shift the conversation, but 근데 is more casual.
A soft marker should still lead to a clear next action.

writingTask.prompt: Text a coworker to ask if you can borrow their notes, but first explain the background (you were absent yesterday) before you make the request.
writingTask.hint: Open with background using -(으)ㄴ/는데 (어제 못 왔는데), give a reason the other person didn't know with -거든요 (감기에 걸렸거든요), and remind them of a shared fact with -잖아요 (내일 시험이 있잖아요).
writingTask.model: 어제 학교에 못 왔는데, 혹시 자료 좀 빌려줄 수 있어요? 사실은 감기에 걸렸거든요. 내일 시험이 있잖아요. 그래서 좀 부탁드려요.
writingTask.modelEn: I couldn't come to school yesterday, so could you maybe lend me your materials? Actually, the thing is I caught a cold. We have the exam tomorrow, you know. So I'd appreciate it.

canDo: Lead with background before my real point using -(으)ㄴ/는데 (어제 못 왔는데...)
Remind someone of something we both know with -잖아요 (시험이 있잖아요)
Add a reason they didn't know with -거든요 (감기에 걸렸거든요)
Soften a reply and leave room to react with trailing -는데요

chapters.title: Observation and Retrospection
chapters.goal: Suggest trying something without sounding pushy.
chapters.scenario: You suggest food, clothing, an app, or a study method to a friend.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was it?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: It was fun. But the weather was a bit cold.

chapters.guidedPractice: Describe one place you visited with 가 보니까 ...더라고요, then add one change sentence with 처음에는 ...더니 ...졌어요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Make one gentle suggestion with 한번 -아/어 보세요 or -아/어 볼까요?
chapters.friendPractice: One person asks about a place or event. The other gives one firsthand observation and one observed change over time.
chapters.review: Can you tell the difference between a plain past fact and a firsthand observation with -더라고요?

beginnerGuide.title: Firsthand evidence
beginnerGuide.body: -더라고요 means you saw, tried, felt, or realized something yourself. It is not for information you only heard from someone else.

beginnerGuide.title: Observed change
beginnerGuide.body: -더니 links an earlier thing you observed to the change or result that followed: 처음에는 조용하더니 금방 붐볐어요.

beginnerGuide.title: Your own result
beginnerGuide.body: For your own action causing a result, use -았/었더니: 많이 먹었더니 졸렸어요. Plain -더니 usually watches someone or something else change.

checkpoints: I can use -아/어 보다 for trying an action.
I can use -아/어 보세요 as a gentle suggestion.
I can use -ㄹ까요? when deciding together.

curriculumTrack.label: A2 Builder
curriculumTrack.description: Tense, questions, numbers, modifiers, connectors, particles, counters, and repair chapters.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Suggest trying something without sounding pushy.
exitTask.prompt: Make one gentle suggestion with 한번 -아/어 보세요 or -아/어 볼까요?

sampleAnswer.ko: 이 앱 한번 써 보세요. 단어 복습하기 좋아요.
sampleAnswer.en: Try this app once. It is good for reviewing vocabulary.

checklist: I can use -아/어 보다 for trying an action.
I can use -아/어 보세요 as a gentle suggestion.
I can use -ㄹ까요? when deciding together.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: You tried a new restaurant, class, cafe, or event and want to tell a friend what you noticed. The point is not just that something happened, but that you personally saw the result or watched it change.
objectives: Use 가 보니까 and -더라고요 to report firsthand observations.
Use -더니 to connect an observed earlier state to a later change.
Keep -더니 separate from -았/었더니, which is used for your own action leading to a result.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean often marks the source of your information. -더라고요 tells the listener, 'I noticed this myself,' while -더니 tells a small before-and-after story that you watched unfold.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-더라고요 — reporting what I noticed firsthand
grammarNotes.func: Use -더라고요 to report something you personally saw, heard, or felt in the past, usually with a touch of mild surprise or fresh discovery. It means "I noticed / it turned out that..." — the information comes from your own direct experience, not from what someone else told you.

examples.en: That movie was really fun (I saw for myself).
examples.note: You watched it yourself, so you report your own impression with -더라고요.

examples.en: I went outside yesterday, and it was colder than I thought.
examples.note: -더라고요 carries the 'I felt it firsthand' nuance — perfect for weather you experienced.

examples.en: Minsu speaks Korean really well (I noticed).
examples.note: You observed his ability directly, so the slight surprise is built in.

examples.ko: 그 식당에 가 봤는데 사람이 정말 많더라고요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdange ga bwanneunde sarami jeongmal mandeoragoyo.
examples.en: I tried that restaurant, and there were a lot of people.
examples.note: Reporting a scene you saw with your own eyes — a classic -더라고요 use.

keyPoint.label: -더라고요 vs. plain -았/었어요
keyPoint.body: Both talk about the past, but -았/었어요 just states a fact, while -더라고요 frames it as something YOU personally witnessed and are now reporting, often with mild surprise. '비가 왔어요' = it rained (fact); '비가 오더라고요' = I saw that it was raining.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In casual speech -더라고요 is often said as -더라구요, but -더라고요 is the standard spelling. 많더라고요 sounds like [만더라고요].

drill.instruction: Report something you personally noticed, using -더라고요.
drill.model: 그 카페 / 조용하다 → 그 카페가 조용하더라고요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 제가 어제 피곤했어요. / (친구를 보고) 친구가 피곤해 보이더라고요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: -더라고요 usually reports what you observe about OTHER people or the outside world, not your own feeling as you have it. For your own past feelings, use plain -았/었어요. (Your own feelings take -더라고요 only when you look back and 'notice' them as a discovery.)

grammarNotes.title: V/A-더니 — I saw X happen, and then Y followed
grammarNotes.func: Use -더니 to link two things you personally watched: 'I noticed X (in the past), and then Y happened.' The second part is often a change, a result, or a contrast that grows out of the first. The subject of the first part is usually someone else, not you.

formTable.when: After a completed first action (-았/었-), often I-subject

examples.ko: 동생이 아까 울더니 지금은 잘 놀아요.
examples.romanization: dongsaengi akka uldeoni jigeumeun jal norayo.
examples.en: My little brother was crying earlier, and now he's playing happily.
examples.note: You watched the change yourself; -더니 links 'was crying' to the new state 'now playing.'

examples.ko: 아침에는 비가 오더니 오후에는 날씨가 좋아요.
examples.romanization: achimeneun biga odeoni ohueneun nalssiga joayo.
examples.en: It was raining in the morning, but in the afternoon the weather is nice.
examples.note: Here -더니 marks a contrast between two states you saw one after the other.

examples.ko: 친구가 밥을 너무 많이 먹더니 배가 아프대요.
examples.romanization: chinguga babeul neomu mani meokdeoni baega apeudaeyo.
examples.en: My friend ate way too much, and now says his stomach hurts.
examples.note: The watched first part causes the second — a natural cause and effect with -더니.

examples.ko: 동생이 열심히 공부하더니 시험을 잘 봤어요.
examples.romanization: dongsaengi yeolsimhi gongbuhadeoni siheomeul jal bwasseoyo.
examples.en: My brother studied hard, and so he did well on the test.
examples.note: -더니 shows the result naturally following the effort you witnessed.

keyPoint.label: -더니 vs. -았/었더니
keyPoint.body: Plain -더니 reports what you watched someone else (or the world) do, then a follow-up. -았/었더니 usually has 'I' as the subject who finished an action, leading to a result you then found: '제가 밥을 먹었더니 졸려요' (I ate, and now I'm sleepy). Rule of thumb: 더니 → 'they...', 았/었더니 → 'I did..., and then...'.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In -더니 the 더 is said clearly as [더], with no blending into the next part. With past -었더니, 었더 sounds like [얻떠] with a light tense ㄷ.

drill.instruction: Link a first event you watched to its result, using -더니.
drill.model: 비가 오다 / 길이 막히다 → 비가 오더니 길이 막혀요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 제가 친구를 만났더니 기분이 좋았어요. / 친구가 저를 만나더니 반가워했어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: When 'I' am the one who finished the first action, use -았/었더니, not plain -더니. Plain -더니 is for watching someone else (or the world), so its first subject is usually NOT 'I.'

exampleSentence.en: When I tried going, it was better than I expected.
exampleSentence.note: Experience leads into a firsthand observation.

exampleSentence.en: There were more people than I expected, I noticed.
exampleSentence.note: Reports what the speaker personally saw.

exampleSentence.en: The food came out faster than expected, I noticed.

lines.romanization: eoje sae sikdange ga bonikka eottaesseoyo?

lines.grammarNote: 가 보니까 asks for a report based on actual experience.

lines.speaker: 지훈

lines.grammarNote: -더니 connects the observed first state to the later change.

lines.speaker: 민서

lines.grammarNote: The question invites another observation.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: It came out faster than expected, and the taste was good too.

readingText.title: 가 보니까 생각보다 괜찮더라고요
readingText.body: 새 식당이나 카페에 다녀온 뒤에는 그냥 '좋았어요'라고 말할 수도 있지만, 직접 보고 느낀 느낌을 살리려면 '-더라고요'가 훨씬 자연스러워요. '가 보니까 생각보다 조용하더라고요'라고 하면 내가 직접 가서 알게 된 정보라는 느낌이 들어요. 시간이 지나면서 변한 모습을 말할 때는 '-더니'가 좋아요. 예를 들어 '처음에는 조용하더니 금방 붐비더라고요'라고 하면 처음 상태와 나중 상태가 한 장면처럼 이어져요. 하지만 내 행동 때문에 생긴 결과라면 '많이 먹었더니 졸렸어요'처럼 '-았/었더니'를 써야 해요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: After visiting a restaurant or cafe, -더라고요 lets you report what you personally noticed. -더니 links an observed first state to a later change. For the result of your own action, use -았/었더니 instead.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 직접 보고 느낀 내용을 말할 때 어떤 표현이 자연스러워요?
처음 상태와 나중 상태를 이어 말할 때 어떤 표현이 좋아요?
내 행동 때문에 생긴 결과에는 어떤 형태를 써야 해요?

culturalNote.title: Korean marks how you know
culturalNote.body: A Korean review often hints at the evidence source. -더라고요 tells the listener this came from your own experience, not just a rumor or general fact.
culturalNote.tip: Before using -더라고요, ask: did I personally see, hear, feel, try, or realize this?

inlineExercises.prompt: You visited the restaurant yourself and noticed it was crowded. Which sentence fits best?
inlineExercises.explanation: -더라고요 reports a firsthand observation.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence shows an observed change over time?
inlineExercises.explanation: -더니 connects the observed first state with the later change.

inlineExercises.prompt: You ate a lot, so you became sleepy. Which form is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: Use -았/었더니 for your own action leading to a result.

inlineExercises.prompt: 그 식당___ 가 보니까 생각보다 조용하더라고요. (When I tried going to that restaurant...)
inlineExercises.explanation: 가 보다 is movement/trying a place, so the destination takes 에. 에서 would mark an action happening at the place.

inlineExercises.prompt: 그 카페가 많이 ___ . (붐비다 → firsthand notice)
inlineExercises.explanation: -더라고요 reports what you personally noticed. 붐비다 becomes 붐비더라고요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'When I tried going there, it was quieter than expected.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 가 보니까 sets up what you learned by trying it yourself. -더라고요 reports the firsthand observation.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'At first it was quiet, and then it quickly got crowded.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -더니 connects an observed earlier state to a later change. 금방 makes the change feel quick.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence about your own action result: '제가 많이 먹더니 졸렸어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: For your own action leading to a result, use -았/었더니. Plain -더니 is better for something you observed in others or outside yourself.

inlineExercises.prompt: You saw a shop get crowded over time. Which sentence fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: -더니 fits the observed change from quiet to crowded. The other choices either misuse the subject or switch to a different grammar.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'These days it turned out to be crowded.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 요즘은 sets the current period. -더라고요 makes it sound like something you noticed yourself.

bullets: -더라고요 reports what you personally noticed or realized.
-더니 connects an observed earlier state/action with a later change.
가 보니까, 생각보다, 처음에는, 예전에는, and 요즘은 make the observation scene clearer.
Use -았/었더니, not plain -더니, for your own action causing a result.

writingTask.prompt: Tell a friend about a cafe you went to recently: report what you noticed when you got there, and how it had changed from before.
writingTask.hint: Report what you saw firsthand with -더라고요 (조용하더라고요), and link 'I noticed X, and then Y' with -더니 (사람이 늘더니 붐비더라고요). Use 예전에는 / 요즘은 for the before-and-after.
writingTask.model: 어제 그 카페에 가 봤는데, 생각보다 사람이 많더라고요. 예전에는 조용했는데 요즘은 손님이 늘더니 정말 붐비더라고요. 그래도 커피는 맛있더라고요.
writingTask.modelEn: I went to that cafe yesterday, and there were more people than I expected. It used to be quiet, but these days the customers increased and then it got really crowded. Still, the coffee was good (I found).

canDo: Report something I personally saw or felt, with mild surprise, using -더라고요 (붐비더라고요)
Link 'I noticed X, and then Y followed' with -더니 (늘더니 붐비더라고요)
Contrast before and after with 예전에는 / 요즘은
Describe a place changing over time (조용하다 → 붐비다, 달라지다)

chapters.title: Reported Speech
chapters.goal: Talk about a cultural or social topic and report what someone said.

chapters.guidedPractice: Report three things from class: one statement with -다고 했어요, one question with -냐고 물어봤어요, and one embedded question with -는지.
chapters.realLifeTask: Report one thing you heard, read, or learned using -다고 해요 or -라고 해요.
chapters.friendPractice: One person plays the teacher or friend and says a statement, question, or instruction. The other reports it accurately.
chapters.review: Can you match the reported ending to the original sentence type: statement, question, or instruction?

beginnerGuide.title: Match the source sentence
beginnerGuide.body: Statements use -다고 했어요, questions use -냐고 물어봤어요, and instructions use -(으)라고 했어요.

beginnerGuide.title: Embed questions with -는지
beginnerGuide.body: Use -는지 when the question becomes part of another sentence: 시험이 언제인지 알아요?, 몇 시에 만나는지 확인해 주세요.

beginnerGuide.title: Do not translate English word order
beginnerGuide.body: English uses 'said that' and 'asked if,' but Korean changes the inner ending. The ending shows whether the original was a statement or a question.

checkpoints: I can report a noun sentence with -이라고/라고 해요.
I can report an adjective or verb sentence with -다고 해요.
I can keep my own opinion separate from what someone else said.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand

hook.situation: After class, a friend asks what the teacher said. You need to pass along a statement, a question, and an instruction without mixing the endings.
objectives: Report statements with -다고 했어요 and recognize the spoken contraction -대요.
Report questions with -냐고 물어봤어요.
Use -는지 when a question is embedded inside 알다, 모르다, 확인하다, or 궁금하다.
hook.whyItMatters: Reported speech is not one pattern. Korean changes the ending depending on what the original sentence was: a statement, a question, or an instruction.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-다고 했어요 — Reporting what someone said
grammarNotes.func: Use -다고 했어요 to report a statement someone made, like English "said that …". You report the meaning, not the exact words, so you drop the original ending (요/-어) and attach -다고 to the plain stem.

formTable.when: Action verb, present — stem ends in a vowel
Action verb, present — stem ends in a 받침

formTable.ex: 바쁘다 → 바쁘다고 했어요 / 좋다 → 좋다고 했어요
먹었다 → 먹었다고 했어요 / 갔다 → 갔다고 했어요
학생 → 학생이라고 했어요 / 친구 → 친구라고 했어요

examples.ko: 친구가 내일 학교에 안 온다고 했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga naeil hakgyoe an ondago haesseoyo.
examples.en: My friend said he won't come to school tomorrow.
examples.note: 오다 is an action verb, so present is 온다고, not 오다고.

examples.en: Mom said she finished eating.
examples.note: Past tense: keep 먹었- and add -다고. The past never takes -ㄴ다고/-는다고.

examples.en: The teacher said Korean isn't hard.
examples.note: 어렵다 is an adjective, so just -다고 — no -ㄴ-/-는-.

examples.en: He said he's my friend.
examples.note: Noun + 이다 becomes (이)라고. 친구 ends in a vowel, so 친구라고.

keyPoint.label: Verbs vs. adjectives in the present
keyPoint.body: Only action verbs add -ㄴ다고/-는다고 (간다고, 먹는다고). Adjectives, and all past forms, just add -다고 (바쁘다고, 먹었다고). The common slips are 먹다고 (should be 먹는다고) and 바쁜다고 (should be 바쁘다고).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In 먹는다고 the ㄱ before ㄴ turns into an ㅇ sound, so it comes out [멍는다고].

drill.instruction: Report what each person said using -다고 했어요. Watch verb vs. adjective and tense.
drill.model: 민수: "시간이 없어요." → 민수가 시간이 없다고 했어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: In English you just add "that," so it's tempting to glue -다고 onto the dictionary form 오다. But present-tense action verbs need -ㄴ다고/-는다고: 오다 → 온다고.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-냐고 물어봤어요 — Reporting a question
grammarNotes.func: Use -냐고 물어봤어요 (or 물었어요) to report a question someone asked — "someone asked whether/what …". The reported part ends in -냐고 no matter how polite the original question was.

examples.en: My friend asked me whether I'd eaten.
examples.note: Past yes/no question → -었냐고. 한테 marks the person who was asked.

examples.en: The teacher asked the students whether they had time.
examples.note: 있다 → 있냐고. A yes/no question with no question word.

examples.en: Mom asked where I was going.
examples.note: The question word 어디 stays where it is — Korean doesn't move it to the front.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 제가 한국 사람이냐고 물어봤어요.
examples.romanization: geu sarami jega hanguk saraminyago mureobwasseoyo.
examples.en: That person asked whether I was Korean.
examples.note: Noun + 이다 → 이냐고. The subject inside the quote takes 가/이 (제가), not 는.

keyPoint.label: -다고 vs. -냐고
keyPoint.body: Statements use -다고 했어요; questions use -냐고 물어봤어요. The following verb is your clue: 했어요/말했어요 (said) for statements, 물어봤어요/물었어요 (asked) for questions.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In 먹었냐고 the ㅆ받침 before ㄴ becomes an ㄴ sound, so it links as [머건냐고].

drill.instruction: Report each question with -냐고 물어봤어요. Keep any question word in place.
drill.model: 엄마: "숙제 다 했어?" → 엄마가 숙제 다 했냐고 물어봤어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners reuse the statement ending -다고 with 물어봤어요. But a reported question has to end in -냐고; -다고 only goes with 했어요/말했어요.

grammarNotes.title: V-는지 / A-(으)ㄴ지 / N인지 — "whether / what / where …" inside a sentence
grammarNotes.func: Use -는지/-(으)ㄴ지/-인지 to tuck a question inside a bigger sentence — "I don't know whether/what/where …", "Do you know if …?". It turns the question into a clause that then connects to verbs like 알다, 모르다, 궁금하다.

examples.en: I don't know where my friend lives.
examples.note: 살다 drops the ㄹ before -는지 → 사는지. 어디 stays inside the clause.

examples.en: I wonder whether this movie is good.
examples.note: 재미있다 takes -는지 (not -(으)ㄴ지) because of the 있다 part.

examples.en: I'm not sure whether he finished eating.
examples.note: Past → -었는지. 모르겠어요 sounds softer than 몰라요, more like "I'm not sure."

examples.en: Do you know who that person is?
examples.note: 누구 + 이다 → 누구인지. It pairs naturally with 알다/아세요.

keyPoint.label: Adjective -(으)ㄴ지 vs. verb -는지
keyPoint.body: In the present, adjectives take -(으)ㄴ지 (좋은지, 바쁜지) and action verbs take -는지 (가는지, 먹는지). In the past, both use -았/었는지 (좋았는지, 갔는지), so the split only matters in the present.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 먹는지 comes out [멍는지] (ㄱ → ㅇ before ㄴ); in 좋은지 the ㅎ drops, so it sounds like [조은지].

drill.instruction: Finish each sentence with -는지/-(으)ㄴ지/-인지. Watch verb vs. adjective and tense.
drill.model: (친구가 오다) 친구가 ___ 모르겠어요. → 친구가 오는지 모르겠어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 재미있다/맛있다/없다 look like adjectives, but the 있/없 part acts like a verb and takes -는지, not -(으)ㄴ지. So it's 재미있는지, 맛있는지, 없는지.

readingText.title: 선생님이 뭐라고 하셨어요?
readingText.body: 수업이 끝난 뒤 친구에게 내용을 전할 때는 원래 문장이 어떤 종류였는지 먼저 봐야 해요. 선생님이 '금요일에 시험을 봐요'라고 말한 내용은 '금요일에 본다고 하셨어요'로 전할 수 있어요. 질문을 전할 때는 '-냐고'를 써요. 그래서 '몇 시에 만나요?'는 '몇 시에 만나냐고 물어봤어요'가 돼요. 하지만 누가 질문한 것이 아니라 내가 답을 알고 싶은 상황이면 '-는지'가 자연스러워요. '시험이 언제인지 알아요?'처럼 큰 문장 안에 질문을 넣는 거예요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: When passing along class information, first identify the original sentence type. Statements use -다고 했어요, questions use -냐고 물어봤어요, and embedded questions use -는지 inside verbs like know, not know, or check.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 원래 문장이 statement이면 어떤 표현을 써요?
질문을 전할 때는 어떤 표현을 써요?
큰 문장 안에 질문을 넣을 때는 어떤 표현을 써요?

culturalNote.title: The ending carries the original sentence type
culturalNote.body: In Korean, the listener can often tell whether the original was a statement, question, or instruction from the reported ending itself. That is why choosing -다고, -냐고, or -(으)라고 matters.
culturalNote.tip: Before reporting someone else's words, label the source sentence: statement, question, or instruction.

inlineExercises.prompt: The teacher said, '금요일에 시험을 봐요.' Which report is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: The original is a statement, so use -다고 하셨어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend asked, '몇 시에 만나요?' Which report is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: The original is a question, so use -냐고 물어봤어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Choose the embedded question form.
inlineExercises.explanation: 알다 takes the embedded question form -는지/-인지.

inlineExercises.prompt: 선생님___ 숙제를 제출하라고 하셨어요. (The teacher told us to submit homework.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 선생님 is the respected subject who gave the instruction, so use 께서. 께 would mark a recipient instead.

inlineExercises.prompt: 친구가 영화를 ___ . (보다 → reported statement)
inlineExercises.explanation: Action verbs use -ㄴ/는다고 for reported statements. 보다 becomes 본다고 했어요 in this sentence.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'My friend asked what time we meet.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Reported questions use -냐고 물어봤어요. The embedded question keeps 몇 시에 inside the reported content.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'Please check whether there is homework.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -는지 embeds the question inside 확인하다. 숙제가 있는지 means whether homework exists.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the report: '친구가 몇 시에 만나다고 물어봤어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: A reported question needs -냐고, not -다고. -다고 reports a statement.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which is the spoken short form of 선생님이 내일 시험이 있다고 했어요?
inlineExercises.explanation: -대요 is the common spoken contraction for “they say that.” 있냐고요 would report or repeat a question.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'I don't know whether there is an exam.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -는지 works inside 모르다 for an embedded question. 시험이 있는지 means whether there is an exam.

bullets: Statements: -다고 했어요 / -대요.
Questions: -냐고 물어봤어요.
Instructions: -(으)라고 했어요.
Embedded questions: -는지 with 알다, 모르다, 확인하다, 궁금하다.

writingTask.prompt: Message a classmate to relay what the teacher announced today: what the teacher said about the homework, and what a classmate asked you about it.
writingTask.hint: Report a statement with -다고 했어요 (제출하라고 했어요 / 어렵다고 했어요), report a question with -냐고 물어봤어요, and embed a question with -는지 (언제까지인지 몰라서).
writingTask.model: 선생님이 오늘 숙제를 금요일까지 제출하라고 했어요. 그리고 시험이 어렵다고 했어요. 민수 씨가 저한테 숙제가 언제까지냐고 물어봤는데, 저도 정확히 언제까지인지 몰라서 다시 확인했어요.
writingTask.modelEn: The teacher said today to submit the homework by Friday. And said the exam is hard. Minsu asked me when the homework is due, but I didn't know exactly when it was due either, so I checked again.

canDo: Pass along what someone said with -다고 했어요 (어렵다고 했어요)
Relay an order with -(으)라고 하다 (제출하라고 했어요)
Report a question someone asked with -냐고 물어봤어요
Tuck a question inside a sentence with -는지/-(으)ㄴ지 (언제까지인지 몰라요)

chapters.title: Advanced Noun Modification and Passive
chapters.goal: Make a careful guess from what you can see or hear.
chapters.scenario: You infer why someone is late, tired, busy, or quiet.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was it?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: It was fun. But the weather was a bit cold.

chapters.guidedPractice: Take one long notice sentence and underline the final noun first: 공지, 일정, 문장, 내용, or 보고서. Then unpack the phrase before it.
chapters.realLifeTask: Look at one situation and make a soft guess using -나 봐요 or 것 같아요.
chapters.friendPractice: One person gives a short notice sentence. The other says the final noun first, then explains what modifier or passive verb describes it.
chapters.review: Can you read 변경된 일정 or 어제 올라온 공지 as one noun phrase instead of separate beginner sentences?

beginnerGuide.title: Find the final noun
beginnerGuide.body: In long Korean noun phrases, the important noun comes at the end: 올라온 공지, 변경된 일정, 제출할 보고서.

beginnerGuide.title: Passive focuses the result
beginnerGuide.body: 잡히다, 닫히다, 팔리다, and 보이다 make the schedule, door, product, or visible thing the subject.

beginnerGuide.title: Causative adds a controller
beginnerGuide.body: 먹이다, 앉히다, and 입히다 add someone who causes another person to eat, sit, or wear something.

checkpoints: I can use -나 봐요 when I infer from a clue.
I can use 것 같아요 for a softer guess or opinion.
I can avoid using a guess form when I already know the fact.

curriculumTrack.label: A2 Builder
curriculumTrack.description: Tense, questions, numbers, modifiers, connectors, particles, counters, and repair chapters.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Make a careful guess from what you can see or hear.
exitTask.prompt: Look at one situation and make a soft guess using -나 봐요 or 것 같아요.

sampleAnswer.ko: 비가 많이 와서 길이 막히나 봐요. 조금 늦을 것 같아요.
sampleAnswer.en: It looks like traffic is bad because it is raining a lot. I think I will be a little late.

checklist: I can use -나 봐요 when I infer from a clue.
I can use 것 같아요 for a softer guess or opinion.
I can avoid using a guess form when I already know the fact.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: You are reading a notice, product description, or short news paragraph where Korean packs actions into noun phrases and often hides the actor with passive forms.
objectives: Unpack long noun phrases such as 어제 올라온 공지 and 변경된 일정.
Recognize when Korean emphasizes the result with passive verbs such as 닫히다, 팔리다, 잡히다, and 보이다.
Compare base, passive, and causative verb pairs without translating word-for-word from English.
hook.whyItMatters: Real Korean notices and articles rarely stay at short beginner sentences. This chapter teaches learners to read compressed information: what was posted, what was changed, what was sold out, and who was made to do something.

grammarNotes.title: Stacked Noun Modifiers: Packing a Clause Before a Noun
grammarNotes.func: In Korean a whole clause can describe a noun, but it always comes BEFORE the noun, and the verb changes into a modifier form ending in -ㄴ/-은/-는/-(으)ㄹ. So "the book my friend gave me yesterday" becomes 어제 친구가 준 책 — everything piles up in front of 책.

examples.ko: 어제 친구가 준 책을 다 읽었어요.
examples.romanization: eoje chinguga jun chaegeul da ilgeosseoyo.
examples.en: I finished reading the book my friend gave me yesterday.
examples.note: 준 (past modifier of 주다) packs "my friend gave" in front of 책.

examples.ko: 제가 자주 가는 카페가 문을 닫았어요.
examples.romanization: jega jaju ganeun kapega muneul dadasseoyo.
examples.en: The cafe I often go to closed down.
examples.note: 가는 (present modifier of 가다) shows an ongoing, habitual action before 카페. 문을 닫다 = to close down.

examples.en: I called the person I'm going to meet tomorrow.
examples.note: 만날 (future modifier of 만나다) marks an action that hasn't happened yet.

examples.en: There are a lot of students who study Korean.
examples.note: 배우는 (present modifier of 배우다) turns a whole clause into one big descriptor for 학생.

keyPoint.label: Past vs. present vs. future modifier
keyPoint.body: The modifier ending carries the TIME, so the final verb of the sentence can stay simple: 친구가 준 책 (already gave), 친구가 주는 책 (is giving), 친구가 줄 책 (will give). Pick the wrong one and the meaning of the whole noun phrase changes.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 읽은 sounds like [일근] — the ㄺ cluster splits and ㄱ links to 은. 많아요 sounds like [마나요], with the ㅎ in ㄶ dropping out.

drill.instruction: Combine the two ideas into one noun phrase using the correct past/present/future modifier, then finish the sentence.
drill.model: 친구가 책을 줬어요 + 그 책 → 친구가 준 책을 읽었어요.
items: 제가 영화를 봐요 + 그 영화 → 제가 ___ 영화가 재미있어요.
어제 밥을 먹었어요 + 그 식당 → 어제 ___ 식당이 좋았어요.
내일 학교에 가요 + 그 친구 → 내일 학교에서 ___ 친구를 만나요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English puts the describing clause AFTER the noun ("the book that my friend gave"), so learners often leave 책 first. In Korean the whole clause comes before the noun, and the verb must take a modifier ending — never a sentence-ending form like 줬어요 right in front of the noun.

grammarNotes.title: Passive Verbs (이/히/리/기): Focusing on What Happens, Not the Doer
grammarNotes.func: Passive verbs describe what HAPPENS to something without saying who did it — the focus moves to the result or the affected thing. You build them by adding -이-, -히-, -리-, or -기- inside certain action verbs: 열다 (to open) → 열리다 (to be opened / to open on its own).

formTable.ex: 산이 보여요. (You can see the mountain.)
전화가 끊겼어요. (The call got cut off.)

examples.en: The door suddenly closed.
examples.note: 닫히다 (passive of 닫다) — nobody is named as the one closing it; we just see the result.

examples.en: You can see the sea well from here.
examples.note: 보이다 (passive of 보다) means "is visible," focusing on what shows up, not who looks.

examples.en: I can hear music from the next room.
examples.note: 들리다 (passive of 듣다) = "is heard"; the sound reaches you on its own.

examples.en: This book is selling a lot these days.
examples.note: 팔리다 (passive of 팔다) puts the book, not the seller, in the subject spot.

keyPoint.label: Active vs. passive subject marking
keyPoint.body: In an active sentence the doer takes 이/가 and the thing takes 을/를: 제가 문을 열었어요. In the passive, the affected thing becomes the 이/가 subject and the doer usually drops out: 문이 열렸어요. If you do keep the doer, it takes 에 or 한테/에게: 문이 바람에 열렸어요 (The door opened from the wind).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 닫히다 sounds like [다치다] — ㄷ and ㅎ blend into ㅊ. 막히다 sounds like [마키다], where ㄱ and ㅎ blend into ㅋ.

drill.instruction: Rewrite each active sentence as a passive one: drop the doer and move the thing into subject position.
items: 사람들이 그 책을 많이 사요. → 그 책이 많이 ___.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English has one passive ("be + past participle"), so learners reach for -아/어지다 every time. But verbs in the 이/히/리/기 group already have their own passive form, and that is the natural choice. Save -아/어지다 mainly for verbs that don't have such a form.

grammarNotes.title: Causative Verbs (이/히/리/기/우): Making or Helping Someone Do Something
grammarNotes.func: Causative verbs say that the subject CAUSES another person or thing to do or undergo the action. You build them by adding -이-, -히-, -리-, -기-, or -우- inside the verb: 먹다 (to eat) → 먹이다 (to feed = make someone eat).

formTable.ex: 아기에게 밥을 먹여요. (I feed the baby rice.)
아이에게 옷을 입혀요. (I dress the child.)
동생을 울렸어요. (I made my sibling cry.)
아기를 재웠어요. (I put the baby to sleep.)

examples.en: The mom feeds the baby rice.
examples.note: 먹이다 (causative of 먹다) = make the baby eat; the eater takes 에게/한테.

examples.en: I dressed the child in warm clothes.
examples.note: 입히다 (causative of 입다) — the parent makes the child wear the clothes.

examples.en: I made my little brother cry, so Mom scolded me.
examples.note: 울리다 (causative of 울다) = make cry; the one crying becomes the 을/를 object.

examples.en: I put the baby to sleep early.
examples.note: 재우다 (causative of 자다, with -우-) = make sleep; very common in daily life.

keyPoint.label: Causative vs. plain verb — who acts
keyPoint.body: Plain 자다 means the subject sleeps (아기가 자요 = the baby sleeps). Causative 재우다 means the subject makes someone else sleep (엄마가 아기를 재워요 = Mom puts the baby to sleep). The original doer (the baby) moves from the 이/가 subject to a 을/를 (or 에게) slot — the new subject is the cause.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 입히다 sounds like [이피다] — ㅂ and ㅎ blend into ㅍ. 읽히다 sounds like [일키다], where the ㄱ in the ㄺ cluster joins ㅎ to make ㅋ.

drill.instruction: Turn the plain action into a causative — "someone makes the subject do it" — and complete the sentence.
items: 아기가 밥을 먹어요. (엄마) → 엄마가 아기에게 밥을 ___.
아이가 옷을 입어요. (아빠) → 아빠가 아이에게 옷을 ___.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 엄마가 아기를 먹게 해요 (always using -게 하다)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English forces "make/let someone do" with a separate verb, so learners default to -게 하다 for everything. When a verb HAS a built-in causative (먹이다, 입히다, 재우다), that one-word form sounds far more natural for concrete, physical actions like feeding, dressing, and putting to sleep.

exampleSentence.en: I checked the notice that was posted yesterday.
exampleSentence.note: A compact noun phrase: 올라온 tells you which 공지.

exampleSentence.en: The changed schedule appeared in the notice.
exampleSentence.note: 변경된 focuses on the resulting state.

exampleSentence.en: I reviewed the report I will submit tomorrow.
exampleSentence.note: 제출할 marks a future action attached to 보고서.

extendedVocabulary.english: to be read / to make someone read

exampleSentence.ko: 이 책은 초급 수업에서 자주 읽혀요.
exampleSentence.en: This book is often read in beginner classes.
exampleSentence.note: Passive reading: the book is the subject.

extendedVocabulary.english: to be seen / to be visible

exampleSentence.en: The sea is visible from far away.
exampleSentence.note: The thing visible becomes the subject.

exampleSentence.ko: 인기 상품이 하루 만에 다 팔렸어요.
exampleSentence.en: The popular item sold out in one day.
exampleSentence.note: The product is the subject; the seller is not important.

extendedVocabulary.english: to be caught / to be set

exampleSentence.en: The meeting schedule was set for next week.
exampleSentence.note: For schedules, 잡히다 means it has been fixed/set.

exampleSentence.en: The door closed automatically.
exampleSentence.note: The door is the subject; the closing result is highlighted.

exampleSentence.en: The mother made the child take medicine.
exampleSentence.note: Causative: someone causes another person to eat/take something.

exampleSentence.en: The employee seated the guest by the window.
exampleSentence.note: Causative: someone makes/lets another person sit.

extendedVocabulary.english: to dress someone / put clothes on someone

exampleSentence.en: The father put a coat on the baby.
exampleSentence.note: Causative pair with 입다.

exampleSentence.ko: 안내 문자가 변경 사항을 알려 줬어요.
exampleSentence.en: The 안내 text message informed me of the changes.
exampleSentence.note: Causative-like lexical verb: make information known.

exampleSentence.ko: 긴 문장은 먼저 명사구를 찾아서 읽어요.
exampleSentence.en: For long sentences, first find the noun phrases.
exampleSentence.note: This chapter is about unpacking compressed sentence structure.

exampleSentence.ko: 기사에는 변경된 일정과 새 규칙이 함께 나왔어요.
exampleSentence.en: The article included the changed schedule and the new rule together.
exampleSentence.note: News prose often uses noun modification and passive/result forms.

extendedDialogue.setting: Minseo reads a school portal notice and explains the changed presentation schedule to Jihoon.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Did you see the notice posted yesterday?
lines.grammarNote: 올라온 공지 is a compressed noun phrase describing which notice.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네, 발표 시간이 다음 주로 잡혔더라고요.
lines.romanization: ne, balpyo sigani daeum juro japhyeotdeoragoyo.
lines.en: Yes, the presentation time was set for next week.
lines.grammarNote: 잡히다 focuses on the schedule being set, not on who set it.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 변경된 일정이 표 아래에 작게 쓰여 있었어요.
lines.romanization: byeongyeongdoen iljeongi pyo araee jakge sseuyeo isseosseoyo.
lines.en: The changed schedule was written in small print below the table.
lines.grammarNote: 변경된 일정 is a result-state noun phrase.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 저는 그 문장이 처음에 잘 안 읽혔어요.
lines.romanization: jeoneun geu munjangi cheoeume jal an ilkhyeosseoyo.
lines.en: At first, that sentence did not read clearly to me.
lines.grammarNote: 읽히다 can describe how a text is read or understood.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 담당자가 학생들을 앞자리에 앉힌다는 내용도 있었어요.
lines.romanization: damdangjaga haksaengdeureul apjarie anjhindaneun naeyongdo isseosseoyo.
lines.en: It also said the staff would seat students in the front rows.
lines.grammarNote: 앉히다 adds a causer who makes someone sit.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 이런 공지는 누가 했는지보다 뭐가 바뀌었는지가 중요하네요.
lines.romanization: ireon gongjineun nuga haenneunjiboda mwoga bakkwieonneunjiga jungyohaneyo.
lines.en: For notices like this, what changed matters more than who did it.
lines.grammarNote: This is why passive and result forms are common in notices.

readingText.title: 어제 올라온 공지에서 변경된 일정 보기
readingText.body: 학교나 회사 공지는 짧아 보여도 정보가 압축되어 있는 경우가 많아요. '어제 올라온 공지'는 '공지가 어제 올라왔어요'라는 문장을 명사 앞에 붙인 표현이고, '변경된 일정'은 이미 바뀐 결과를 일정 앞에 붙인 표현이에요. 이런 문장을 읽을 때는 끝에 있는 명사를 먼저 찾으세요. 공지인지, 일정인지, 문장인지, 내용인지 확인한 다음 앞에 붙은 말을 풀어 보면 훨씬 잘 읽혀요. 또 '발표 시간이 다음 주로 잡혔어요'처럼 피동형이 쓰이면 누가 정했는지보다 결과가 중요하다는 뜻으로 읽으면 됩니다.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Notices often compress information into noun phrases. First find the final noun, then unpack the words before it. Passive/result forms like 잡히다 focus on the result, not on who caused it.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 긴 명사구를 읽을 때 무엇을 먼저 찾아야 해요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 끝에 있는 명사를 먼저 찾아야 해요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 변경된 일정은 어떤 뜻이에요?
잡혔어요 같은 피동형은 무엇을 더 강조해요?

culturalNote.title: Notices prefer result-focused wording
culturalNote.body: Korean notices often care more about what changed than who changed it. That is why forms like 변경된 일정, 시간이 잡혔어요, and 문이 닫힙니다 feel natural in official or informational writing.
culturalNote.tip: When a sentence feels dense, ask: what is the final noun, and what result is being emphasized?

inlineExercises.prompt: Which phrase means “the notice posted yesterday”?
inlineExercises.explanation: 올라온 is a completed-action modifier attached to 공지.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence focuses on the schedule being set, not who set it?
inlineExercises.explanation: 잡히다 makes the schedule the subject and highlights the result.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses a causative verb naturally?
inlineExercises.explanation: 앉히다 means someone causes another person to sit.

inlineExercises.prompt: 공지___ 올라왔어요. (The notice was posted.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 올라오다 describes the notice appearing or being posted, so 공지 is the subject. 를 would make it an object of someone else’s action.

inlineExercises.prompt: ___ 일정이 있어요. (변경되다 → noun modifier)
inlineExercises.explanation: A completed passive/change before a noun uses -ㄴ/은. 변경되다 becomes 변경된 before 일정.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'the schedule changed today' as a noun phrase
inlineExercises.explanation: Korean packs the description before the noun. 변경된 comes before 일정 to make one noun phrase.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'The door is closed.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 닫혀 있어요 focuses on the resulting closed state. It does not need to mention who closed the door.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the passive sentence: '일정을 잡혔어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 잡히다 is passive, so 일정 is the subject and takes 이. 일정을 would fit an active verb like 잡았어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses a causative verb naturally?
inlineExercises.explanation: 앉히다 means to seat someone or make/help someone sit. 손님 is the person being seated.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'the report to submit'
inlineExercises.explanation: 제출할 is the future/required action modifier before 보고서. It means the report that is to be submitted.

bullets: Find the final noun first: 공지, 일정, 보고서, 문장, 내용.
Read modifiers before the noun as compressed information: 어제 올라온 공지, 변경된 일정, 제출할 보고서.
Passive/result verbs like 잡히다, 닫히다, 팔리다, 보이다 focus on the result or visible state.
Causatives like 먹이다, 앉히다, 입히다 add someone who causes another person to act or enter a state.

writingTask.prompt: Write a short note to a roommate about a club notice: describe the notice using a clause before the noun, and mention what got changed and what you have to do.
writingTask.hint: Stack a modifying clause before a noun (어제 올라온 공지), use a passive verb (일정이 바뀌었어요 / 변경됐어요, 문이 닫혔어요), and a causative if it fits (사람들에게 알리다 → 알렸어요).
writingTask.model: 어제 게시판에 올라온 공지를 봤는데, 모임 일정이 바뀌었어요. 변경된 시간은 토요일 2시예요. 그래서 친구들한테도 그 소식을 알렸어요. 그날은 일찍 문이 닫히니까 늦지 마세요.
writingTask.modelEn: I saw the notice that was posted on the board yesterday, and the meeting schedule changed. The changed time is Saturday at 2. So I let our friends know the news too. The door closes early that day, so don't be late.

canDo: Pack a whole clause before a noun to describe it (어제 올라온 공지, 변경된 일정)
Describe what happens to something with passive verbs (바뀌다, 닫히다, 팔리다)
Say someone makes/lets another do something with causatives (알리다, 먹이다)
Build longer, more precise noun phrases for notices and schedules

chapters.goal: Describe feelings with a little more honesty and nuance.
chapters.scenario: After a presentation, test, date, or awkward message, you tell a friend how it felt.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What are you going to do this weekend?

dialogue.speaker: B

dialogue.speaker: A

dialogue.speaker: B

chapters.guidedPractice: Write one deadline sentence with -ㄹ 수밖에 없다, one strong denial with -ㄹ 리가 없다, and one only-option sentence with -뿐이다.
chapters.realLifeTask: Describe one feeling, then add what you pretended or almost did.
chapters.friendPractice: One person gives a constraint such as 마감, 규칙, 품절, or 시간이 부족하다. The other explains the only option and rejects one impossible misunderstanding.
chapters.review: Can you separate no choice (-ㄹ 수밖에 없다), strong impossibility (-ㄹ 리가 없다), and only/nothing more (-뿐이다)?

beginnerGuide.title: No choice is not cannot
beginnerGuide.body: 할 수 없어요 means you cannot do it. 할 수밖에 없어요 means you must do it because there is no other option.

beginnerGuide.title: 리가 없다 is strong disbelief
beginnerGuide.body: 포기할 리가 없어요 means the speaker strongly rejects that possibility. It is stronger than 아마 포기하지 않을 거예요.

beginnerGuide.title: 뿐이다 closes the scope
beginnerGuide.body: 이 방법뿐이에요 means only this method remains. It differs from 뿐만 아니라, which adds another point.

checkpoints: I can use -는 척했어요 when I acted differently from how I felt.
I can use -ㄹ 뻔했어요 for something that almost happened.
I can soften emotional sentences with 좀 or 사실.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Describe feelings with a little more honesty and nuance.
exitTask.prompt: Describe one feeling, then add what you pretended or almost did.

sampleAnswer.ko: 사실 좀 떨렸는데 괜찮은 척했어요.
sampleAnswer.en: Honestly, I was a little nervous, but I pretended I was okay.

checklist: I can use -는 척했어요 when I acted differently from how I felt.
I can use -ㄹ 뻔했어요 for something that almost happened.
I can soften emotional sentences with 좀 or 사실.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: Your team has a deadline today. You cannot cancel, you do not believe anyone will give up, and only one realistic method remains.
objectives: Use -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 for a no-choice situation.
Use -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 to strongly reject a possibility.
Use -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 or N뿐이다 to limit the situation to only one action or option.
hook.whyItMatters: English learners often say 'I can't' when they mean 'I have no choice but to.' Korean separates inability, inevitability, disbelief, and only-option nuance very clearly.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 — to have no choice but to
grammarNotes.func: Use this to say there's no other option, so you end up doing the action whether you want to or not. It often sounds a little reluctant: "There's nothing else I can do, so I just do this."

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a consonant (받침 O)
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹을 수밖에 없다 (have no choice but to eat)

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel (받침 X)
formTable.ex: 가다 → 갈 수밖에 없다 (have no choice but to go)

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in ㄹ (ㄹ stays, just add 수밖에 없다)
formTable.ex: 살다 → 살 수밖에 없다 (have no choice but to live)

formTable.when: Adjectives work too (= it can only be / it's bound to be)
formTable.ex: 비싸다 → 비쌀 수밖에 없다 (it's bound to be expensive)

examples.en: There was no bus, so I had no choice but to walk.
examples.note: A reason clause (없어서) plus this pattern is the most common shape: cause, then forced result.

examples.ko: 시간이 없어서 택시를 탈 수밖에 없어요.
examples.romanization: sigani eopseoseo taeksi-reul tal su-bakke eopseoyo.
examples.en: I don't have time, so I have no choice but to take a taxi.
examples.note: 탈 from 타다 (vowel stem) just adds -ㄹ. Shows the everyday 'I'm forced into it' feeling.

examples.ko: 친구가 약속을 안 지켜서 화가 날 수밖에 없었어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga yaksogeul an jikyeoseo hwaga nal su-bakke eopseosseoyo.
examples.en: My friend broke our plans, so I couldn't help getting angry.
examples.note: With feelings it means 'can't help but'. Getting angry was the only natural reaction.

examples.ko: 이 식당은 음식이 맛있어서 사람이 많을 수밖에 없어요.
examples.romanization: i sikdangeun eumsigi masisseoseo sarami manheul su-bakke eopseoyo.
examples.en: This place's food is so good, of course it's packed.
examples.note: With an adjective (많다) it means 'it's bound to be'. A natural, can't-be-otherwise conclusion.

keyPoint.label: 수밖에 없다 vs. -아/어야 하다
keyPoint.body: -아/어야 하다 means you 'have to / should' do something (a duty, but other choices might still exist). V-(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 means every other option is gone, so you do it even if you'd rather not. '공부해야 해요' = I should study; '공부할 수밖에 없어요' = I've got no other choice but to study. (You'll meet -아/어야 하다 in its own lesson.)

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 수밖에 sounds like [수바께]: the ㄲ of 밖 links into 에 and stays tense. So 수밖에 없다 comes out as [수바께 업따].

drill.instruction: Because of the reason, only one thing is left to do. Answer with V-(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없어요.
drill.model: 비가 와요. (집에 있다) → 비가 와서 집에 있을 수밖에 없어요.
items: 돈이 없어요. (집에서 밥을 먹다) → 돈이 없어서 집에서 밥을 ____.
길이 막혀요. (지하철을 타다) → 길이 막혀서 지하철을 ____.
숙제가 많아요. (집에 늦게까지 있다) → 숙제가 많아서 집에 늦게까지 ____.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 밖에 ('other than / except') always pairs with a negative, so the ending is always 없다, never 있다. 'There's nothing other than walking' = 없다. Saying 있어요 here flips the meaning and just sounds broken to a Korean ear.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 — there's no way that's true
grammarNotes.func: Use this to say you really don't believe something: you're sure it can't be the case because it makes no sense. It's the Korean way of saying "There's no way…" or "It can't possibly be that…"

formTable.when: Verb/Adjective stem ends in a consonant (받침 O)
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹을 리가 없다 (there's no way he'd eat it)

formTable.when: Verb/Adjective stem ends in a vowel (받침 X)
formTable.ex: 오다 → 올 리가 없다 (there's no way it'll come / he'll come)
가다 → 갔을 리가 없다 (there's no way he went)
학생 → 학생일 리가 없다 (there's no way he's a student)

examples.ko: 그 친구가 거짓말을 했을 리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: geu chinguga geojinmareul haesseul liga eopseoyo.
examples.en: There's no way that friend lied.
examples.note: Past form 했을 리가 없다 rejects that a past action happened. Very common with 거짓말.

examples.ko: 지금 밤 12시인데 학생들이 학교에 있을 리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: jigeum bam yeoldu-si-inde haksaengdeuri hakgyo-e isseul liga eopseoyo.
examples.en: It's midnight now, so there's no way the students are at school.
examples.note: A known fact (it's the middle of the night) makes the idea impossible. The typical 'fact + 리가 없다' shape.

examples.ko: 한국어를 배운 지 일주일밖에 안 됐는데 잘할 리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeo-reul baeun ji iljuilbakke an dwaenneunde jalhal liga eopseoyo.
examples.en: He's only been learning Korean for a week, so there's no way he's good at it.
examples.note: Often follows a reason clause with -는데. Uses 잘하다, an everyday verb.

examples.ko: 이 책이 만 원이라고요? 그렇게 쌀 리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: i chaegi man wonira-goyo? geureoke ssal liga eopseoyo.
examples.en: This book is 10,000 won? There's no way it's that cheap.
examples.note: Adjective 싸다 works too. The speaker rejects the claim as impossible, not just unlikely.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 vs. -(으)ㄹ 수 없다
keyPoint.body: -(으)ㄹ 수 없다 is about real ability: 'can't do it' (갈 수 없어요 = I'm not able to go). -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 is about your certainty that a claim is false: 'there's no way that's true' (갔을 리가 없어요 = no way he went). The first is about being able; the second is about believing.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 없어요 sounds like [업써요]: the ㅅ of the 없- cluster slides onto the next syllable and goes tense, while ㅂ stays as a stop. So 리가 없어요 comes out as [리가 업써요].

drill.instruction: You don't believe the statement. Reject it with V-(으)ㄹ 리가 없어요.
drill.model: 민수가 시험에 떨어졌어요. → 민수가 시험에 떨어졌을 리가 없어요.
items: 저 사람이 한국 사람이에요. → 저 사람이 한국 사람일 리가 ____.
동생이 벌써 집에 갔어요. → 동생이 벌써 집에 ____ 리가 없어요.
이 영화가 재미없어요. → 이 영화가 재미____ 리가 없어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저는 오늘 갈 리가 없어요. (meaning: I can't go today)
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 저는 오늘 못 가요. / 갈 수 없어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'there's no way' covers both 'I'm unable to' and 'I don't believe it.' But 리가 없다 only means disbelief about a fact, and it sounds odd about your own plans. For 'I can't go,' use 못 가요 or 갈 수 없어요. Save 갈 리가 없어요 for 'there's no way he'd go.'

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 / N뿐이다 — only, nothing more
grammarNotes.func: Use this to limit things to just one: 'that's all there is, nothing else.' With verbs/adjectives it means 'only does / is only'; attached straight to a noun, 뿐이다 means 'only that, and nothing else.'

formTable.ex: 믿다 → 믿을 뿐이다 (I just believe it, that's all)
하다 → 했을 뿐이다 (I just did it, nothing more)

formTable.when: Noun (no -(으)ㄹ; 뿐 attaches straight to the noun)

examples.en: I only told the truth, that's all.
examples.note: Past 말했을 뿐이다 is the classic 'I just did X, so don't blame me' use.

examples.en: I was just joking, nothing more. Don't be mad.
examples.note: 그냥 ('just') goes naturally with 뿐이다 to play an action down.

examples.en: Right now there's only water in the fridge.
examples.note: Noun case: 뿐 attaches straight to 물 (no -(으)ㄹ). Means 'water and nothing else.'

examples.en: In this neighborhood, Minsu is my only friend.
examples.note: N뿐이다 with a person noun (민수) = 'only him, no one else.' Very common in speech.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 vs. N뿐이다 (and 만)
keyPoint.body: After a verb or adjective, use the -(으)ㄹ form: 기다릴 뿐이에요. After a noun, drop -(으)ㄹ and stick 뿐 right on: 물뿐이에요. Compare 만 ('only'): 만 picks one out of several options (물만 마셔요 = I drink only water), while N뿐이다 says that noun is all there is (물뿐이에요 = water is all there is).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 뿐이에요 links smoothly as [뿌니에요]: the ㄴ of 뿐 slides onto 이. With a noun like 물, 물뿐이에요 sounds like [물뿌니에요].

drill.instruction: Say it's only this, nothing more. Answer with -(으)ㄹ 뿐이에요 for verbs/adjectives, or N뿐이에요 for nouns.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: After a noun, 뿐 attaches directly with no -(으)ㄹ: 물뿐이에요, 저뿐이에요. The -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 form is only for verbs and adjectives (기다릴 뿐이에요). English speakers tend to glue an extra ending on before 뿐 with nouns, but the noun just takes 뿐 by itself.

extendedVocabulary.english: to have no choice but to

exampleSentence.en: The deadline is today, so we have no choice but to work late.
exampleSentence.note: No-choice situation caused by a real constraint.

exampleSentence.en: There is no way we would give up now.
exampleSentence.note: Strong disbelief, not a soft guess.

exampleSentence.en: The only thing left is this method.
exampleSentence.note: Limits the situation to one option.

exampleSentence.en: If the deadline is today, it cannot be helped.
exampleSentence.note: Accepts the constraint.

exampleSentence.en: The deadline is today, so there are not many choices.
exampleSentence.note: The pressure that creates the no-choice frame.

exampleSentence.en: Today I have no choice but to work late.
exampleSentence.note: A common work-life no-choice sentence.

exampleSentence.en: There is no way we would give up now.
exampleSentence.note: Natural with -ㄹ 리가 없다.

exampleSentence.en: The only thing left is this method.
exampleSentence.note: Pairs naturally with 뿐이다.

exampleSentence.en: Is it possible within today?
exampleSentence.note: Plain possibility, not no-choice.

exampleSentence.en: With the current method, it is almost impossible.
exampleSentence.note: Useful contrast with -ㄹ 리가 없다.

exampleSentence.ko: 이런 상황에서는 다시 확인할 수밖에 없어요.
exampleSentence.en: In this situation, we have no choice but to check again.
exampleSentence.note: The noun that explains why there is no other option.

exampleSentence.en: There is no way the data is wrong.
exampleSentence.note: Work/study content that can be checked or revised.

exampleSentence.en: We have no choice but to rewrite the explanation.
exampleSentence.note: A realistic repair action under a deadline.

extendedDialogue.setting: A team handles a deadline where there is no realistic choice left.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: The deadline is today, so we have no choice but to work late.
lines.grammarNote: -ㄹ 수밖에 없다 shows the situation leaves no other option.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Still, there is no way we would give up now.
lines.grammarNote: -ㄹ 리가 없다 strongly rejects a possibility.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 자료는 맞지만 설명은 다시 쓸 수밖에 없어요.
lines.romanization: jaryoneun matjiman seolmyeongeun dasi sseul subakke eopseoyo.
lines.en: The data is right, but we have no choice but to rewrite the explanation.
lines.grammarNote: The no-choice frame fits a specific next action.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: In the end, this method is the only thing left.
lines.grammarNote: N뿐이다 limits the remaining option to one thing.

readingText.title: 마감이라서 할 수밖에 없어요
readingText.body: 마감이 가까우면 선택지가 줄어들어요. 이때 '할 수 없어요'라고 말하면 능력이 없거나 불가능하다는 뜻이 되지만, '할 수밖에 없어요'라고 말하면 하기 싫어도 그 방법밖에 없다는 뜻이 돼요. 반대로 '포기할 리가 없어요'는 포기할 가능성을 강하게 부정하는 말이에요. 그리고 '남은 건 이 방법뿐이에요'는 다른 선택이 없고 이 방법만 남았다는 뜻이에요. 세 표현은 모두 한계와 관련이 있지만, 각각 no choice, no way, only one이라는 다른 느낌을 가지고 있어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: When a deadline is close, choices shrink. 할 수밖에 없어요 means there is no choice but to do it, not that you cannot do it. 리가 없어요 strongly rejects a possibility, and 뿐이에요 limits the situation to only one remaining option.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 할 수 없어요와 할 수밖에 없어요는 어떻게 달라요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 할 수 없어요는 불가능, 할 수밖에 없어요는 다른 선택이 없다는 뜻이에요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 포기할 리가 없어요는 어떤 느낌이에요?
이 방법뿐이에요는 무엇을 뜻해요?

culturalNote.title: No Choice, No Way, Only
culturalNote.body: Korean often separates the speaker's attitude from the facts of the situation. 수밖에 없다 sounds resigned to a constraint, 리가 없다 sounds confident or emotionally certain, and 뿐이다 sounds limiting or modest.
culturalNote.tip: Before choosing the pattern, label the meaning in English: no choice, no way, or only.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means “I have no choice but to work late”?
inlineExercises.explanation: 수밖에 없다 means the situation leaves no other option.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence strongly rejects a possibility?
inlineExercises.explanation: -ㄹ 리가 없다 means there is no way that possibility is true.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means only one method remains?
options: 남은 건 이 방법일 리가 없어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: N뿐이다 limits the situation to only that noun.

inlineExercises.prompt: 마감___ 있어서 야근할 수밖에 없어요. (Because there is a deadline...)
inlineExercises.explanation: 있다 takes 이/가 for the thing that exists. 마감이 있어서 gives the reason before the no-choice result.

inlineExercises.prompt: 오늘은 ___ . (야근하다 → no choice)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없어요 means there is no choice but to do it. 야근하다 becomes 야근할 수밖에 없어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'There is no way that person will give up.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ 리가 없어요 strongly rejects a possibility. 포기할 리가 없어요 means giving up is not plausible.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'This is the only method.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 뿐이에요 limits the situation to only one thing. 방법은 sets the topic as the available method.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '그 사람이 포기할 리가 있어요.' (intended: no way)
inlineExercises.explanation: The “no way” pattern needs 리가 없어요. 리가 있어요 does not express strong rejection.

inlineExercises.prompt: Only one realistic option remains. Which sentence fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: 뿐이에요 means only this and nothing more. The other options compare or guess rather than limit the options.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'It cannot be helped.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 어쩔 수 없죠 is the fixed phrase for accepting a no-choice situation. It fits when the speaker cannot change the circumstances.

bullets: -ㄹ 수밖에 없다 = no choice but to do it.
-ㄹ 리가 없다 = there is no way that is true.
-뿐이다 = only this action, role, or option.
Do not confuse 할 수 없어요 with 할 수밖에 없어요.

writingTask.prompt: Reply to a friend who invited you out tonight: explain that you have no choice but to work late, and that there's no way you'll finish early.
writingTask.hint: Use -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 for 'no choice but to' (야근할 수밖에 없어요), -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 for 'no way' (일찍 끝날 리가 없어요), and -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 / N뿐이다 for 'only' (방법이 이것뿐이에요).
writingTask.model: 미안해요, 오늘은 마감이라서 야근할 수밖에 없어요. 일이 너무 많아서 일찍 끝날 리가 없어요. 지금은 그냥 열심히 하는 수밖에 없죠. 방법이 이것뿐이에요.
writingTask.modelEn: Sorry, today is the deadline, so I have no choice but to work late. There's so much work that there's no way it'll finish early. For now I just have no choice but to work hard. This is the only way.

canDo: Say I have no other option with -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 (야근할 수밖에 없어요)
Reject something as impossible with -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 (끝날 리가 없어요)
Limit things to just one with -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 / N뿐이다 (이것뿐이에요)
Sound resigned about a fixed situation (어쩔 수 없죠, 마감)

chapters.title: Nuance and Hedging
chapters.goal: Describe decisions and changes that happened over time.
chapters.scenario: You decided to start a habit, changed a plan, or something became easier.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What are you going to do this weekend?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I am going to meet a friend and go to a cafe.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What if it rains?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: If it rains, I am going to study at home.

chapters.guidedPractice: Turn three blunt statements into careful Korean: one with -ㄹ걸요, one with -다면, and one with -는 것 같아요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say one decision and one change using -기로 했어요 and -게 됐어요.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner gives you an uncertain workplace or group-chat situation; answer with a guess, a hypothetical, and a gentle suggestion.
chapters.review: Can you choose between -ㄹ걸요, -다면, -겠-, 좋겠어요, and 것 같아요 instead of using one vague 'I think' for everything?

beginnerGuide.title: Guess without overclaiming
beginnerGuide.body: -ㄹ걸요 gives a soft but fairly confident guess: 아직 회의 중일걸요. Use it when you have a hunch, not when you are simply unsure.

beginnerGuide.title: Open a careful possibility
beginnerGuide.body: -다면 sets up a what-if frame: 이미 나갔다면. It lets you discuss the next step without pretending you know the fact.

beginnerGuide.title: Soften the opinion itself
beginnerGuide.body: 것 같아요 softens a whole impression or opinion. Do not treat it as 같다 meaning 'same'; here it means 'it seems / I think.'

checkpoints: I can use -기로 했어요 for a decision.
I can use -게 됐어요 for a change that came to happen.
I can use -아/어지다 for becoming a new state.
