sampleAnswer.ko: 매일 십 분씩 듣기로 했어요. 그래서 조금 익숙해졌어요.
sampleAnswer.en: I decided to listen for ten minutes every day. So I became a little more used to it.

checklist: I can use -기로 했어요 for a decision.
I can use -게 됐어요 for a change that came to happen.
I can use -아/어지다 for becoming a new state.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: A teammate is not sure whether a manager is still in a meeting, already left work, or can still reply. The goal is not to sound vague; it is to say your guess, condition, hope, or opinion at the right strength.
objectives: Use -ㄹ걸요 for a soft but fairly confident guess.
Use -다면 to open a hypothetical path before giving the next step.
Use 좋겠어요 and 것 같아요 to make wishes, suggestions, and opinions less blunt.
hook.whyItMatters: English learners often use one all-purpose 'I think...' for every uncertain sentence. Korean splits that work across several endings, so the listener can feel whether you are guessing, imagining a condition, hoping for an outcome, or politely softening your own opinion.

grammarNotes.title: -(으)ㄹ걸요 — A Soft but Confident Guess
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)ㄹ걸요 when you make a guess you're fairly sure about, but want to sound gentle instead of flat-out telling someone. It feels like "I'd say..." or "probably..." based on what you know.

formTable.when: Verb/adjective stem ends in a vowel
Verb/adjective stem ends in a consonant

examples.en: My friend is probably home right now.
examples.note: A guess you're fairly sure of, softened so it doesn't sound like a flat claim.

examples.en: That movie's probably good.
examples.note: 있다 ends in a consonant, so it takes -을걸요.

examples.en: This book's probably a bit pricey.
examples.note: 비싸- ends in a vowel, so it takes -ㄹ걸요.

examples.en: My parents are probably asleep already.
examples.note: Uses the honorific 주무시다 (to sleep) for parents, while still keeping the guessing feel.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ걸요 vs. -(으)ㄹ 거예요
keyPoint.body: Both say something is likely. -(으)ㄹ 거예요 sounds like a plain prediction; -(으)ㄹ걸요 adds a softer "I'd guess" feeling, often when the other person might be thinking otherwise. Save the finer back-vowel rules for later — just match vowel vs. consonant stems for now.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 걸요 sounds like [거료], so 갈걸요 comes out [갈꺼료] — the ㄱ tenses and the ㄹ links smoothly into 요.

drill.instruction: Answer each question with a soft guess using -(으)ㄹ걸요.
drill.model: 친구 지금 뭐 해요? → 아마 자고 있을걸요.
items: 그 식당 지금 문 열었어요? → 아마 ___.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers stack "probably" on top of another guess word. -(으)ㄹ걸요 already means "probably," so don't combine it with -(으)ㄹ 것 같다. Attach it straight to the plain stem: 올걸요.

grammarNotes.title: -(으)면 좋겠어요 — A Hope or Gentle Wish
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)면 좋겠어요 to say "I hope..." or "I wish...". It literally means "it'd be nice if...," and it's the everyday way to say what you'd like to happen.

formTable.ex: 오다 → 오면 좋겠어요; 싸다 → 싸면 좋겠어요
먹다 → 먹으면 좋겠어요; 많다 → 많으면 좋겠어요

formTable.when: Wish about now / something not true
formTable.ex: 오다 → 왔으면 좋겠어요; 있다 → 있었으면 좋겠어요

examples.en: I hope the weather's nice tomorrow.
examples.note: A simple hope about the future; 좋다 ends in a consonant, so -으면.

examples.en: I wish I had a little more time.
examples.note: Everyday wish; 있다 takes -으면 좋겠어요.

examples.en: I hope this test is easy.
examples.note: The -었으면 form here makes the hope feel stronger, even though the test hasn't happened yet.

examples.en: I wish our place were closer to school.
examples.note: A wish about how things are now; 가깝다 is ㅂ-irregular, so 가까웠으면.

keyPoint.label: -(으)면 좋겠어요 vs. -고 싶어요
keyPoint.body: -고 싶어요 means "I want to (do it myself)." -(으)면 좋겠어요 means "I hope (it happens)," so it can be about other people, the weather, or things you don't control. The contrary-to-fact nuance of the -았/었으면 form gets fuller treatment in a later chapter.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 좋겠어요 sounds like [조케써요]: ㅎ + ㄱ blend into an aspirated [ㅋ], and 겠 tenses the next ㅅ into [써].

drill.instruction: Turn each situation into a wish using -(으)면 좋겠어요.
drill.model: 비가 와요. (싫어요) → 비가 안 오면 좋겠어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Don't slip 싶다 in. "I hope I go to Korea" is just 가면 좋겠어요. Adding 싶다 doubles the wanting and sounds off. Keep 가고 싶어요 for a plain "I want to go."

grammarNotes.title: -겠- — Intention, a Good Guess, or a Set Polite Phrase
grammarNotes.func: -겠- does three everyday jobs: stating your own plan ("I'll..."), making a guess about a situation ("that must be..."), and forming a few set polite phrases. You read which one it is from the context and the subject.

formTable.ex: 알겠어요 (got it); 모르겠어요 (I don't know); 잘 먹겠습니다

examples.en: I'll come back tomorrow.
examples.note: Your own plan; -겠습니다 sounds firm and polite, common when serving someone or in formal speech.

examples.en: This food looks so good!
examples.note: A guess from what you see — you haven't tasted it yet, but you can tell it must be good.

examples.en: That must have been rough with so much homework.
examples.note: -었겠어요 guesses about someone else's past and shows you feel for them.

examples.en: I don't really get what you mean.
examples.note: 모르겠어요 is a set, softened way to say it; plain 몰라요 can sound more blunt.

keyPoint.label: Intention -겠- vs. Guess -겠-
keyPoint.body: With "I" as the subject and an action verb, -겠- usually means a plan ("I'll"). With someone else, or with an adjective describing a situation, it means a guess ("must be / looks like"). The subject and the kind of verb tell you which. The polite "future" feel of -겠- in set phrases comes later.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -겠- tenses the next consonant: 먹겠어요 → [먹께써요], 맛있겠어요 → [마싣께써요].

drill.instruction: Decide if it's a plan or a guess, then finish it with -겠-.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 그 사람 학생이에요? — said as 그 사람 학생이겠어요?
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Don't use -겠- for a plain yes/no question. -겠- adds "must be / I'm guessing," so 학생이겠어요? asks "I suppose he's a student?" To simply ask whether someone is a student, use 학생이에요?

grammarNotes.title: -다면 / N(이)라면 — If That Were the Case
grammarNotes.func: Use -다면 / N(이)라면 to set up a "what if" — an imagined or supposed situation, often one you don't really expect or that isn't true right now: "if (let's say)...".

examples.ko: 돈이 많다면 큰 집을 사고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: doni mantamyeon keun jibeul sago sipeoyo.
examples.en: If I had a lot of money, I'd want to buy a big house.
examples.note: A "what if" the speaker doesn't really expect; 많다 is an adjective, so -다면.

examples.ko: 내가 너라면 그 사람한테 전화할 거예요.
examples.romanization: naega neoramyeon geu saramhante jeonhwahal geoyeyo.
examples.en: If I were you, I'd call him.
examples.note: Noun + 라면 sets up an imagined "if I were" situation.

examples.en: If you happen to have time, let's catch a movie.
examples.note: 있다 takes -다면; here it frames a supposed condition before a suggestion.

examples.ko: 그때 일찍 출발했다면 안 늦었을 거예요.
examples.romanization: geuttae iljjik chulbalhaetdamyeon an neujeosseul geoyeyo.
examples.en: If we'd left early back then, we wouldn't have been late.
examples.note: -았/었다면 looks back at something that didn't happen — a regret about the past.

keyPoint.label: -다면 vs. -(으)면
keyPoint.body: -(으)면 is the all-purpose "if/when," fine for real, likely things (밥 먹으면 = when/if I eat). -다면 puts more weight on "just supposing," so it suits imagined or unlikely cases. For everyday real conditions, -(으)면 is still your default. The full -았/었다면 "would have" pattern is explored more later.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 많다면 sounds like [만타면]: the ㅎ in 많 blends with the following ㄷ into an aspirated [ㅌ].

drill.instruction: Make a "what if" sentence using -다면 / N(이)라면.
drill.model: (복권 당첨) 복권에 당첨된다면 여행을 갈 거예요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: After a noun, you can't just add -다면. Nouns use (이)라면: 학생이라면 (if you're a student), 부자라면 (if you're rich). Only verb and adjective stems take -다면 directly.

grammarNotes.title: -(으)ㄴ/는데요 — Softening and Leaving Room
grammarNotes.func: Ending a sentence with -(으)ㄴ/는데요 softens it. Instead of a hard statement, it sets something up and leaves the door open — for the other person to react, for a "but...," or for a gentle pushback. It's one of the most common ways Koreans avoid sounding too direct.

examples.en: I'm kind of busy right now... (so maybe later?)
examples.note: A soft "no" — it states the situation and lets the other person draw the conclusion, instead of flatly refusing.

examples.en: Um, this is my seat... (could you move?)
examples.note: Noun + 인데요 makes a gentle correction without sounding harsh.

examples.ko: 저는 매운 거 잘 못 먹는데요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun maeun geo jal mot meongneundeyo.
examples.en: I'm not so good with spicy food, actually...
examples.note: -는데요 softly raises a concern and leaves room for the other person to respond.

examples.en: It rained yesterday, though...
examples.note: Past -았/었는데요 gently offers a fact, often hinting at a "but" the listener can pick up on.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄴ/는데요 vs. a plain -아/어요 ending
keyPoint.body: 좀 바빠요 just states "I'm busy." 좀 바쁜데요 says the same thing but trails off, inviting the other person to fill in the rest — softer and less final. Use it to hedge, hint, or set up a contrast. Its longer use for connecting two clauses ("~는데, …") comes in a separate point.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In 먹는데요, the ㄱ before ㄴ turns nasal: it sounds like [멍는데요]. 좋은데요 sounds like [조은데요], with the ㅎ dropping out.

drill.instruction: Soften each blunt sentence by re-ending it with -(으)ㄴ/는데요.
items: 저는 그 영화 별로예요. → 저는 그 영화 ___.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저 지금 바쁜데요 그래서 못 가요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 저 지금 바쁜데요. (and let the meaning land on its own)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers spell out the whole "so I can't go." The point of -(으)ㄴ/는데요 is to leave that part unsaid and let the listener get it. Tacking on the blunt conclusion undoes the softening the ending is there to create.

extendedDialogue.setting: Two coworkers need to contact someone, but they are not sure whether that person is still available.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: They are probably still in a meeting.
lines.grammarNote: -ㄹ걸요 gives a soft but fairly confident guess.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Hmm, they may have already left work.
lines.grammarNote: 글쎄요 and 수도 있어요 keep the uncertainty open.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 혹시 이미 나갔다면 메시지를 남겨 두면 좋겠어요.
lines.romanization: hoksi imi nagatdamyeon mesijireul namgyeo dumyeon jokesseoyo.
lines.en: If they already left, it would be good to leave a message.
lines.grammarNote: -다면 opens the hypothetical; -으면 좋겠어요 gives a gentle next step.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Yes, since I am not sure, I will ask carefully.
lines.grammarNote: 조심스럽게 controls tone, not just grammar.

readingText.title: 확실하지 않을 때 말하는 법
readingText.body: 회사 단톡방에서 누가 아직 회의 중인지, 이미 퇴근했는지 모를 때가 있어요. 이때 한국어는 한 가지 'I think'만 쓰지 않아요. 기억이나 상황을 보고 짐작하면 '아직 회의 중일걸요'라고 말할 수 있고, 가능성을 열어 두고 싶으면 '이미 나갔다면 메시지를 남겨 두면 좋겠어요'처럼 말해요. 내 의견을 조심스럽게 말할 때는 '제 생각에는 먼저 물어보는 게 좋을 것 같아요'가 자연스러워요. 중요한 건 약하게 말하는 것이 아니라, 내가 아는 정도에 맞게 문장을 고르는 거예요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: In a work chat, you may not know whether someone is still in a meeting or already left work. Korean does not use one single 'I think' for every case. Use -ㄹ걸요 for a hunch, -다면 for a hypothetical, 좋겠어요 for a hoped-for or gentle next step, and 것 같아요 to soften your own opinion. The point is not to be weak; it is to match the sentence to how much you actually know.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 회의 중인지 확실하지 않을 때 어떤 표현을 쓸 수 있어요?
이미 나갔을 가능성을 열어 둘 때 어떤 연결을 썼어요?
내 의견을 조심스럽게 말할 때 왜 것 같아요를 써요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 의견을 너무 단정적으로 들리지 않게 부드럽게 만들기 위해서예요.

culturalNote.title: Soft does not mean unclear
culturalNote.body: Korean hedging is often about social accuracy. If you are guessing, your ending should sound like a guess. If you are giving advice, the sentence should leave room for the listener. This is why 아마, 글쎄요, 혹시, 제 생각에는, -ㄹ걸요, -다면, 좋겠어요, and 것 같아요 often appear together in workplace chats, group projects, and polite disagreement.
culturalNote.tip: Before speaking, ask: am I guessing, imagining a condition, hoping for a result, or giving an opinion? Then choose the ending that matches that job.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence gives a soft but fairly confident guess?
inlineExercises.explanation: -ㄹ걸요 marks a careful guess based on what the speaker thinks.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence opens a hypothetical before suggesting the next step?
options: 이미 나갔다면 메시지를 남겨 두면 좋겠어요.
이미 나간 것 같아요 회의 중이에요.
inlineExercises.correct: 이미 나갔다면 메시지를 남겨 두면 좋겠어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: -다면 sets up the condition, and -으면 좋겠어요 gives a gentle suggestion.

inlineExercises.prompt: Soften this opinion: 제 생각에는 먼저 물어보는 게 좋을 ____.
inlineExercises.explanation: 좋을 것 같아요 softens the whole opinion. 같아요 alone would not attach correctly here.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses 겠 as a fixed polite response?
inlineExercises.explanation: 알겠어요 is a set response meaning 'I understand / okay.'

inlineExercises.prompt: 제 생각___ 먼저 물어보는 게 좋아요. (In my opinion...)
inlineExercises.explanation: 제 생각에는 frames the statement as your opinion. 을 and 에서 do not make the opinion-frame expression.

inlineExercises.prompt: 회의 자료는 아직 회의실에 ___ . (있다 → soft confident guess)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ걸요 gives a soft but fairly confident guess. 있다 becomes 있을걸요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'If that is the case, let's ask first.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 그렇다면 opens a hypothetical path from the previous idea. 먼저 물어봐요 gives the suggested next step.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'I hope it goes well.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -면 좋겠어요 expresses a hope or gentle wish. 잘되면 sets the hoped-for condition.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence if you mean a wish: '잘될걸요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 잘될걸요 is a guess that it will probably go well. 잘되면 좋겠어요 is the wish: I hope it goes well.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which response is the cautious “Hmm, I am not sure”?
inlineExercises.explanation: 글쎄요 is the natural cautious hesitation. 좋겠어요 is a wish, and 그렇다면요 depends on a hypothetical.

bullets: -ㄹ걸요: a hunch or careful guess, as in 아직 회의 중일걸요.
-다면: a hypothetical condition, as in 이미 나갔다면.
좋겠어요: a hoped-for result or gentle suggestion, as in 메시지를 남겨 두면 좋겠어요.
것 같아요: a softened impression or opinion, not 같다 meaning 'same.'
-겠-: context decides the meaning: 알겠어요, 물어보겠습니다, 피곤하시겠어요.

writingTask.prompt: Answer a coworker who asks whether the boss will approve the plan: give a soft, confident guess, then add what you'd personally hope happens.
writingTask.hint: Make a gentle guess with -(으)ㄹ걸요 (괜찮을걸요) and -겠- or 것 같아요, express a wish with -(으)면 좋겠어요 (괜찮으면 좋겠어요), and soften the whole reply with trailing -(으)ㄴ/는데요.
writingTask.model: 글쎄요, 아마 부장님이 괜찮다고 하실걸요. 제 생각에는 큰 문제는 없을 것 같은데요. 그래도 다들 부담 없이 받아들이면 좋겠어요. 내일이면 확실히 알 수 있겠죠.
writingTask.modelEn: Hmm, the manager will probably say it's fine, I'd guess. In my opinion there shouldn't be a big problem, though. Still, I hope everyone takes it without feeling pressured. By tomorrow we'll surely know for sure.

canDo: Offer a soft but confident guess with -(으)ㄹ걸요 (괜찮을걸요)
Express a hope or wish with -(으)면 좋겠어요 (괜찮으면 좋겠어요)
Read -겠- as intention, a guess, or a set phrase (알 수 있겠죠)
Hedge and leave room with trailing -(으)ㄴ/는데요 and 아마 / 글쎄요

beginnerGuide.title: Change before vowel endings
beginnerGuide.body: Most changes happen when a vowel-starting ending arrives: 춥다 + 어요 becomes 추워요, 듣다 + 어요 becomes 들어요, and 모르다 + 아요 becomes 몰라요.

beginnerGuide.title: Learn useful pairs
beginnerGuide.body: Do not memorize rules alone. Memorize pairs you will actually say: 덥다/더워요, 어렵다/어려워요, 듣다/들어요, 걷다/걸어요, 모르다/몰라요, 어떻다/어때요.

beginnerGuide.title: Watch regular lookalikes
beginnerGuide.body: Not every final consonant changes. 듣다 becomes 들어요, but 닫다 stays 닫아요. 낫다 becomes 나아요, but 웃다 stays 웃어요.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: A learner can read dictionary forms like 춥다, 듣다, 모르다, and 빨갛다, but the real spoken forms are 추워요, 들어요, 몰라요, and 빨개요. This chapter turns those shape changes into usable habits.
objectives: Match high-frequency dictionary forms with their real polite forms.
Separate true irregular stems from regular lookalikes such as 닫다 and 웃다.
Use irregular forms inside natural sentences about weather, food, health, walking, listening, knowing, and colors.
hook.whyItMatters: If a learner says 춥어요 or 듣어요, the meaning may be understandable, but the sentence immediately sounds broken. Irregulars are not rare grammar trivia; they appear in the first hundred everyday sentences a learner wants to say.

grammarNotes.title: ㅂ Irregular: 춥다 → 추워요
grammarNotes.func: A lot of describing words (and a few action words) whose stem ends in ㅂ change that ㅂ to 우 when a vowel ending comes next. That's why 춥다 (to be cold) becomes 추워요, not 춥어요.

formTable.when: Stem ends in ㅂ, before a vowel ending (-아/어요, -았/었-, -으니까)
formTable.add: ㅂ → 우, then add 어요 (우+어 = 워)

formTable.when: Stem ends in ㅂ, before a consonant ending (-고, -지만, -습니다)

examples.en: The weather is so cold today.
examples.note: 춥다 + 아/어요: ㅂ turns to 우, then 우+어 joins into 워.

examples.en: This bag is really light.
examples.note: 가볍다 follows the same ㅂ → 우 → 워 pattern.

examples.en: My friend helped me with my work.
examples.note: 돕다 is special: ㅂ → 오, so 도+오+아 = 도와요/도와줬어요.

examples.en: Studying Korean is hard but fun.
examples.note: Before a consonant ending (-지만), ㅂ does NOT change: 어렵지만.

keyPoint.label: Vowel ending vs consonant ending
keyPoint.body: The ㅂ only changes before a vowel: 춥다 → 추워요 (vowel) but 춥다 → 춥고 (consonant). Almost all ㅂ-irregular words use 우; only 돕다 and 곱다 use 오. For now, just learn 추워요 as a set phrase and you'll see the pattern.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 추워요 is said smoothly as [추워요]. The 우+어 → 워 is a real spelling change, not just a sound, so you actually write 워.

drill.instruction: Change each ㅂ-irregular dictionary form to the polite -아/어요 form.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: It feels natural to just add the ending and say 춥어요, but ㅂ-irregular stems change the ㅂ to 우 before a vowel, giving 추워요.

grammarNotes.title: ㄷ Irregular: 듣다 → 들어요
grammarNotes.func: A small group of action words whose stem ends in ㄷ change that ㄷ to ㄹ when a vowel ending follows. So 듣다 (to hear/listen) becomes 들어요, not 듣어요.

examples.en: I listen to music a lot.
examples.note: 듣다 + 아/어요: ㄷ becomes ㄹ before the vowel, so 들어요.

examples.en: I walk to school every day.
examples.note: 걷다 (to walk) is ㄷ-irregular: 걷 → 걸 → 걸어요.

examples.en: I asked the teacher a question.
examples.note: 묻다 (to ask) → 물어봤어요; ㄷ → ㄹ before the past-tense vowel.

examples.en: I got a present from my friend.
examples.note: 받다 is a REGULAR ㄷ verb, so ㄷ stays: 받았어요, never 발았어요.

keyPoint.label: Not every ㄷ verb is irregular
keyPoint.body: Only a few verbs change (듣다, 걷다, 묻다 'ask', 싣다 'load'). Everyday verbs like 받다 (get), 닫다 (close), 믿다 (believe) keep their ㄷ: 받아요, 닫아요, 믿어요. You just have to remember which ones are irregular.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 들어요 links as [드러요] — the ㄹ slides into the next syllable. Don't worry about the rule mid-conversation; learn 들어요 as a chunk.

drill.instruction: Conjugate these ㄷ-irregular verbs into the -아/어요 form.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: It's tempting to keep the ㄷ and say 듣어요, but ㄷ-irregular verbs change ㄷ to ㄹ before a vowel ending, giving 들어요.

grammarNotes.title: ㅅ Irregular: 낫다 → 나아요
grammarNotes.func: Some action/describing words whose stem ends in ㅅ drop the ㅅ before a vowel ending — but unlike ㄷ and ㅂ, the two vowels do NOT join up. So 낫다 (to get better) becomes 나아요, keeping both vowels.

formTable.add: ㅅ drops; vowels stay separate (no joining)

examples.en: My cold is all better now.
examples.note: 낫다 → 나았어요; ㅅ drops but 나+았 stays as two parts, no joining.

examples.en: This restaurant is better than that one.
examples.note: 낫다 'be better' → 나아요; the two ㅏ's stay separate, written 나아.

examples.en: Please pour the water into the cup.
examples.note: 붓다 (to pour) → 부어 주세요; ㅅ drops, vowels do not merge.

examples.en: The child laughs loudly.
examples.note: 웃다 is a REGULAR ㅅ verb, so ㅅ stays: 웃어요, never 우어요.

keyPoint.label: ㅅ drops but the vowels stay apart
keyPoint.body: Unlike 추워요 or 들어요, the ㅅ-irregular leaves the two vowels apart: 낫다 → 나아요 (not 나요). Compare regular 웃다 → 웃어요, where the ㅅ stays. The irregular ones to know: 낫다, 붓다, 젓다, 짓다.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 나아요 keeps two clear ㅏ sounds [나아요]; don't shorten it to [나요]. That held, two-beat vowel is the giveaway of the ㅅ-irregular.

drill.instruction: Conjugate these ㅅ-irregular verbs into the -아/어요 form (keep the vowels separate).

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners drop the ㅅ and then wrongly squeeze the vowels into 나요. The ㅅ-irregular keeps both vowels: present 나아요, past 나았어요.

grammarNotes.title: 르 Irregular: 모르다 → 몰라요
grammarNotes.func: Words ending in 르 add an extra ㄹ to the syllable before 르 and drop the ㅡ before -아/어. So 모르다 (to not know) becomes 몰라요, with a doubled ㄹ.

formTable.when: 르 stem + vowel ending, when the syllable before 르 has ㅏ or ㅗ
formTable.add: drop ㅡ, add ㄹ to the syllable before, then 라

formTable.when: 르 stem + vowel ending, when the syllable before 르 has any other vowel
formTable.add: drop ㅡ, add ㄹ to the syllable before, then 러

examples.en: I don't really know that person's name.
examples.note: 모르다 → 몰라요; 모 before 르 has ㅗ, so the ending is 라.

examples.en: My friend sang a song.
examples.note: 부르다 → 불렀어요; 부 has ㅜ (not ㅏ/ㅗ), so the ending is 러/렀.

examples.en: Please call a taxi quickly.
examples.note: 부르다 'call' → 불러; same doubled-ㄹ rule with 러.

examples.en: Time goes by so fast.
examples.note: 빠르다 → 빨라요; 빠 has ㅏ, so it takes 라.

keyPoint.label: 라 vs 러 depends on the vowel before 르
keyPoint.body: If the syllable before 르 has ㅏ or ㅗ, use 라 (모르다 → 몰라요, 빠르다 → 빨라요). Otherwise use 러 (부르다 → 불러요, 누르다 → 눌러요). It's the same ㅏ/ㅗ vs everything-else choice as -아요/-어요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 몰라요 has a strong doubled ㄹ [몰라요] — the first ㄹ closes 몰 and the second opens 라.

drill.instruction: Conjugate these 르-irregular words into the -아/어요 form (watch 라 vs 러).

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners try to add the ending straight onto 모르 and get 모르아요. The 르-irregular drops the ㅡ and doubles the ㄹ, so it's 몰라요.

grammarNotes.title: ㅡ Irregular: 바쁘다 → 바빠요
grammarNotes.func: When a stem ends in ㅡ (like 쓰다, 바쁘다), the ㅡ drops out before -아/어. Then the syllable before it decides whether you add 아 or 어. So 바쁘다 (to be busy) becomes 바빠요.

formTable.when: ㅡ stem + vowel ending, when the syllable before ㅡ has ㅏ or ㅗ
ㅡ stem + vowel ending, other vowel (or no syllable before, like 쓰다)

examples.en: I'm so busy these days.
examples.note: 바쁘다 → 바빠요; 바 has ㅏ, so the dropped ㅡ takes 아 → 빠.

examples.en: I'm writing a letter right now.
examples.note: 쓰다 → 써요; nothing before ㅡ, so it defaults to 어 → 써.

examples.en: My younger sibling is really pretty.
examples.note: 예쁘다 → 예뻐요; 예 is not ㅏ/ㅗ, so it takes 어 → 뻐.

examples.en: My head hurts a little.
examples.note: 아프다 → 아파요; 아 has ㅏ, so the dropped ㅡ takes 아 → 파.

keyPoint.label: Drop the ㅡ, then pick 아 or 어
keyPoint.body: The ㅡ always disappears before -아/어. To choose, look at the syllable before it: ㅏ/ㅗ → 아 (바빠요, 아파요), anything else (or nothing) → 어 (써요, 예뻐요). This is the same vowel-harmony idea as regular -아요/-어요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 바빠요 has a tense ㅃ [바빠요], and 써요 starts with a tense ㅆ [써요]. The dropped ㅡ leaves a strong, double consonant sound.

drill.instruction: Conjugate these ㅡ-irregular words into the -아/어요 form (watch 아 vs 어).

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: It feels natural to keep the ㅡ and add the ending, giving 바쁘어요. But ㅡ-stems drop the ㅡ first, so it's 바빠요 (and 쓰다 → 써요, not 쓰어요).

grammarNotes.title: ㅎ Irregular: 빨갛다 → 빨개요
grammarNotes.func: Most color words and a few pointing words (그렇다, 어떻다) end in ㅎ. Before -아/어, the ㅎ drops AND the vowel changes to ㅐ. So 빨갛다 (to be red) becomes 빨개요. Note: 좋다 is regular — 좋아요.

formTable.add: drop ㅎ, vowel becomes ㅐ, add 요

examples.en: The apple is really red.
examples.note: 빨갛다 → 빨개요; ㅎ drops and the vowel turns into ㅐ.

examples.en: The sky is so blue.
examples.note: 파랗다 → 파래요; same ㅎ-drop with the vowel becoming ㅐ.

examples.en: Me too / Same here.
examples.note: 그렇다 → 그래요; a super common one to just memorize.

examples.en: How's the weather?
examples.note: 어떻다 → 어때요; you'll hear 어때요 constantly, so learn it as a set phrase.

keyPoint.label: ㅎ drops and the vowel turns into ㅐ
keyPoint.body: With ㅎ-irregulars, two things happen at once before -아/어: the ㅎ disappears and the vowel becomes ㅐ (빨갛다 → 빨개요, 그렇다 → 그래요). Watch out: 좋다 (be good) is NOT irregular — it's just 좋아요. Learn 그래요 and 어때요 as ready-made phrases first.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 빨개요 is said [빨개요] with the ㅐ vowel; 그래요 is [그래요]. Don't try to keep the ㅎ sound — it's gone before the ending.

drill.instruction: Conjugate these ㅎ-irregular words into the -아/어요 form (ㅎ drops, vowel → ㅐ).

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: It seems logical to keep the ㅎ and add 아요, giving 빨갛아요. But ㅎ-irregulars drop the ㅎ and change the vowel to ㅐ, so it's 빨개요. (And don't overcorrect 좋다 — that one really is 좋아요.)

extendedDialogue.setting: A learner asks why common words change shape in polite speech.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 오늘 너무 추워요. 그런데 왜 '춥어요'가 아니에요?
lines.romanization: oneul neomu chuwoyo. geureonde wae 'chupeoyo'ga anieyo?
lines.en: It is so cold today. But why isn't it '춥어요'?
lines.grammarNote: 춥다 follows the ㅂ irregular, so the natural form is 추워요.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 춥다처럼 ㅂ으로 끝나는 말은 추워요, 더워요처럼 바뀌어요.
lines.romanization: chupdacheoreom bieubeuro kkeutnaneun mareun chuwoyo, deowoyo-cheoreom bakkwieoyo.
lines.en: Words ending in ㅂ, like 춥다, change to forms like 추워요 and 더워요.
lines.grammarNote: The pair is more useful than the label: 춥다/추워요, 덥다/더워요.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 그럼 듣다는 들어요, 걷다는 걸어요가 맞죠?
lines.romanization: geureom deutdaneun deureoyo, geotdaneun georeoyoga matjyo?
lines.en: Then 듣다 becomes 들어요, and 걷다 becomes 걸어요, right?
lines.grammarNote: ㄷ changes to ㄹ in common verbs like 듣다 and 걷다.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 맞아요. 모르다는 몰라요, 빨갛다는 빨개요처럼 익히면 돼요.
lines.romanization: majayo. moreudaneun mollayo, ppalgataneun ppalgaeyo-cheoreom ikhimyeon dwaeyo.
lines.en: Right. Learn them as pairs, like 모르다 to 몰라요 and 빨갛다 to 빨개요.
lines.grammarNote: 르 and ㅎ irregulars are easier when memorized through common pairs.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Got it. I will memorize the high-frequency words first.
lines.grammarNote: 알다 keeps ㄹ in 알아요, but drops it in forms like 아세요 and 압니다.

readingText.title: 사전형과 말할 때의 모양
readingText.body: 한국어 사전에는 춥다, 듣다, 모르다처럼 기본형이 나오지만, 실제 대화에서는 추워요, 들어요, 몰라요처럼 바뀐 모양을 더 자주 들어요. 그래서 불규칙 활용은 시험용 표가 아니라 일상 발음과 문장을 바로잡는 도구예요. '오늘 추워요', '음악을 들어요', '저는 잘 몰라요', '이 방법은 어때요?' 같은 문장을 먼저 익히면 규칙 이름도 자연스럽게 따라와요. 단, 비슷하게 생겼다고 모두 바뀌지는 않아요. 듣다는 들어요지만 닫다는 닫아요이고, 낫다는 나아요지만 웃다는 웃어요예요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Korean dictionaries show base forms such as 춥다, 듣다, and 모르다, but real conversation uses changed forms such as 추워요, 들어요, and 몰라요. Irregular conjugation is not just a test table; it repairs everyday pronunciation and sentences. Learn useful sentences first, then attach the rule names. Also remember that lookalikes are not always irregular: 듣다 changes to 들어요, but 닫다 stays 닫아요; 낫다 changes to 나아요, but 웃다 stays 웃어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 사전에는 어떤 모양이 나오지만 실제 대화에서는 어떤 모양을 더 자주 들어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 사전에는 춥다, 듣다, 모르다 같은 기본형이 나오지만 실제 대화에서는 추워요, 들어요, 몰라요 같은 활용형을 더 자주 들어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 듣다와 닫다는 어떻게 달라요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 듣다는 들어요로 바뀌지만 닫다는 닫아요로 그대로 활용해요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 불규칙 활용은 왜 일상 대화에 중요해요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 추워요, 들어요, 몰라요 같은 매우 자주 쓰는 문장에 바로 들어가기 때문이에요.

culturalNote.title: Learn the spoken form, not only the dictionary form
culturalNote.body: Korean learners often study dictionary forms first because that is how apps and dictionaries organize words. Native conversation, however, usually gives you the conjugated shape. If you only memorize 춥다 and 듣다, you may hesitate when you need 추워요 and 들어요. Treat each high-frequency irregular as a pair: dictionary form plus the first sentence you would actually say.
culturalNote.tip: For each new irregular, memorize one real chunk: 추워요, 들어요, 나았어요, 몰라요, 어때요, 아세요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which form correctly conjugates 춥다 in polite present speech?
inlineExercises.explanation: 춥다 follows the ㅂ irregular: ㅂ changes to 우 before 어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which pair shows the ㄷ irregular?
inlineExercises.explanation: 듣다 changes ㄷ to ㄹ. 닫다 and 받다 are regular.

inlineExercises.prompt: 낫다 + 았어요 = 감기가 다 ____.
inlineExercises.explanation: ㅅ drops in 낫다 before a vowel-starting ending.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses 르 irregular correctly?
inlineExercises.explanation: 모르다 becomes 몰라요: ㄹ doubles onto the previous syllable.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which form is natural for 어떻다?
inlineExercises.explanation: 어떻다 is a ㅎ irregular adjective: 어떻다 + 어요 → 어때요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence shows ㄹ deletion before -세요?
inlineExercises.explanation: 알다 keeps ㄹ in 알아요 but drops ㄹ before -세요: 아세요.

inlineExercises.prompt: 날씨___ 추워요. (The weather is cold.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 춥다 describes the weather, so 날씨 takes 가. 를 would make weather an object, which does not fit an adjective sentence.

inlineExercises.prompt: 오늘은 많이 ___ . (춥다 → polite present)
inlineExercises.explanation: 춥다 is a ㅂ irregular, so ㅂ changes to 워 before 어요. The natural spoken form is 추워요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I don't know well.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 모르다 is a 르 irregular and becomes 몰라요. 잘 softens it to “I do not know well.”

inlineExercises.prompt: 걷다 + 어요 = ___
inlineExercises.explanation: 걷다 is a ㄷ irregular, so ㄷ changes to ㄹ before 어요. 닫다 is a regular lookalike, but 걷다 becomes 걸어요.

bullets: ㅂ irregular: 춥다→추워요, 덥다→더워요, 어렵다→어려워요.
ㄷ irregular: 듣다→들어요, 걷다→걸어요, but 닫다→닫아요.
ㅅ irregular: 낫다→나아요, 짓다→지어요, but 웃다→웃어요.
르 irregular: 모르다→몰라요, 다르다→달라요, 부르다→불러요.
ㅎ irregular: 빨갛다→빨개요, 어떻다→어때요, but 좋다→좋아요.
ㄹ deletion: 알다→알아요, but 아세요/압니다/아는.

writingTask.prompt: Write 3-4 sentences about today's weather and how you feel, using describing words that are irregular verbs.
writingTask.hint: Conjugate irregulars into 해요체: ㅂ (춥다→추워요, 덥다→더워요, 맵다→매워요), ㄷ (듣다→들어요), ㅡ (바쁘다→바빠요), 르 (모르다→몰라요, 다르다→달라요).
writingTask.model: 오늘은 날씨가 추워요. 요즘 저는 너무 바빠요. 그래서 음악을 들어요. 한국어가 어려워도 답을 몰라도 괜찮아요.
writingTask.modelEn: Today the weather is cold. These days I'm very busy. So I listen to music. Even if Korean is hard and I don't know the answer, it's okay.

canDo: Conjugate ㅂ-irregular adjectives correctly (춥다→추워요 · 어렵다→어려워요)
Conjugate ㄷ-irregular verbs correctly (듣다→들어요 · 걷다→걸어요)
Conjugate 르-irregular and ㅡ-irregular words (모르다→몰라요 · 바쁘다→바빠요)

chapters.title: Particle Expansion
chapters.goal: Show respect without making every sentence overly formal.
chapters.scenario: You talk about a teacher, boss, parent, or older customer.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Are you also going to see a movie with a friend this weekend?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 아니요, 시험 문제가 세 개나 남아서 공부밖에 못 해요.
dialogue.romanization: aniyo, siheom munjega se gaena namaseo gongbubakke mot haeyo.
dialogue.en: No, as many as three exam questions are left, so I can only study.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Then do you want to at least drink coffee? Just one hour.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 좋아요. 선생님께 이메일도 보내드리고, 친구의 책도 돌려줘야 해요.
dialogue.romanization: joayo. seonsaengnimkke imeildo bonaedeurigo, chinguui chaekdo dollyeojwoya haeyo.
dialogue.en: Sounds good. I also need to send the teacher an email and return my friend's book.

chapters.guidedPractice: Rewrite the same noun with three particles: 친구에게, 친구랑, 친구도; then contrast 공부만 해요 with 공부밖에 못 해요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Make one sentence about a respected person using -(으)시- and one honorific word.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner gives a noun like 친구, 선생님, 커피, 시간, or 공부; answer with a sentence using 도, 만, 밖에, 이라도, or 에게/께.
chapters.review: Can you choose the right particle for also, only, receiver, possession, with, as many as, and at least without mixing their jobs?

beginnerGuide.title: Particles change the job
beginnerGuide.body: 친구 can become 친구에게 (to a friend), 친구랑 (with a friend), 친구도 (a friend too), 친구만 (only a friend), or 친구의 (a friend's). The noun is the same; the relationship changes.

beginnerGuide.title: 만 and 밖에 are not twins
beginnerGuide.body: 공부만 해요 is neutral: I only study. 공부밖에 못 해요 needs a negative predicate and feels limited: I can do nothing but study.

beginnerGuide.title: 이라도 gives a minimum option
beginnerGuide.body: 커피라도 마실래요? means coffee is not the full plan, but it is at least something possible. It is different from 커피만 and 커피도.

checkpoints: I can add -(으)시- when the subject deserves respect.
I can use words like 드시다, 계시다, 말씀하시다, and 댁.
I can separate subject honorifics from listener politeness.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Show respect without making every sentence overly formal.
exitTask.prompt: Make one sentence about a respected person using -(으)시- and one honorific word.

sampleAnswer.ko: 선생님께서 지금 사무실에 계세요.
sampleAnswer.en: The teacher is in the office now.

checklist: I can add -(으)시- when the subject deserves respect.
I can use words like 드시다, 계시다, 말씀하시다, and 댁.
I can separate subject honorifics from listener politeness.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: A weekend plan keeps changing: you may go with a friend, you also need to email a teacher, you only have one hour, and you can do nothing but study. The nouns are simple; the particles decide the relationships.
objectives: Choose the right particle for receiver, companion, possession, also, only, scarcity, surprising amount, and minimum option.
Contrast similar particles such as 만 vs 밖에 and 도 vs 이라도.
Build real weekend-plan sentences instead of memorizing particle labels.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean particles are small, but they carry the grammar that English often puts in word order or prepositions. 친구, 친구에게, 친구랑, 친구도, 친구만, and 친구의 all start from the same noun but tell different stories.

grammarNotes.title: 에게 / 한테 / 께 — to a person (께 = honorific)
grammarNotes.func: Marks the person who receives or is the target of an action: giving, sending, asking, telling, lending. English uses 'to (a person)'.

formTable.when: Neutral or written, after any person noun
Casual spoken, after any person noun

formTable.ex: 친구한테서 들었어요 (I heard it from a friend)

examples.en: I gave a gift to a friend.
examples.note: 친구 is the receiver of 주다, so the person-target 에게 fits.

examples.en: I lent a book to my younger sibling.
examples.note: 한테 is the everyday spoken choice in casual talk.

examples.en: I sent an email to the teacher.
examples.note: 께 raises the receiver and pairs naturally with the humble verb 드리다.

examples.en: I sent an email to the company.
examples.note: A place or organization takes 에, not 에게 — 에게 is only for people (and animals).

keyPoint.label: 에게/한테 vs 께
keyPoint.body: 에게 and 한테 mean the same thing (한테 just sounds more casual). 께 is the honorific version for a respected person and usually rides with humble verbs like 드리다 and 여쭤보다.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 께 is a tense [kk] sound, like the kk in 'bookkeeper' — 선생님께 is [seon-saeng-nim-kke], never a plain [g].

drill.instruction: Fill the blank with 에게/한테 or 께, then read the whole sentence aloud.
drill.model: 친구___ 선물을 줬어요. → 친구에게 선물을 줬어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'gave to the gift' is obviously wrong, but learners attach 에게 to whatever follows 'to'. 에게 marks only the person receiver; the thing given takes the object particle 을/를.

grammarNotes.title: 와/과 · 하고 · (이)랑 — and / with
grammarNotes.func: Links two nouns ('A and B') or marks the companion you do something with ('with A'). All three mean the same; they differ only in register.

formTable.ex: 책 → 책과 가방 (a book and a bag)

examples.en: I watch a movie with a friend.
examples.note: 친구 ends in a vowel, so 랑; casual speech prefers (이)랑.

examples.en: I went together with Minsu.
examples.note: 하고 plus 같이 makes the 'with / together' reading unmistakable.

examples.en: I bought coffee and water.
examples.note: 커피 ends in a vowel → 와; this sounds tidy and slightly written.

examples.en: I brought only a book and a bag.
examples.note: 책 ends in a consonant → 과; the linker comes before the next particle 만.

keyPoint.label: 와/과 vs 하고 vs (이)랑
keyPoint.body: Meaning is identical; register differs. 와/과 = neutral-to-written, 하고 = neutral spoken, (이)랑 = casual spoken. Add 같이 when you want 'with' to be clear over 'and'.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 과 after a consonant tenses: 책과 sounds like [chaek-kkwa]; 와 after a vowel stays light, 커피와 [keo-pi-wa].

drill.instruction: Choose 와/과 or (이)랑 to match the final sound, then read it aloud.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 와/과·하고·(이)랑 connect nouns, not actions. To join two verbs ('watch and eat'), use the connective -고, not these particles.

grammarNotes.title: 밖에 + negative — nothing but / only (and it's not enough)
grammarNotes.func: Marks a limit that always needs a negative predicate. It frames the amount as scarce or insufficient: 'nothing but X', 'only X (and that's all there is)'.

formTable.ex: 한 시간밖에 없어요 (I only have one hour)
물밖에 못 마셔요 (I can drink nothing but water)
공부밖에 안 해요 (I do nothing but study)

examples.en: I can do nothing but study.
examples.note: 못 supplies the required negative; 밖에 alone can't stand with a positive verb.

examples.en: I only have one hour.
examples.note: 없어요 carries the negative and signals the time feels too short.

examples.en: There's no way except this one.
examples.note: 밖에 plus 없어요 = a forced, no-other-choice frame.

examples.en: I can only drink water.
examples.note: 물 takes 밖에 with no extra particle, paired with 못.

keyPoint.label: 밖에 vs 만
keyPoint.body: Both translate as 'only', but 밖에 demands a negative predicate and feels scarce/insufficient (공부밖에 못 해요), while 만 is neutral and takes a positive verb (공부만 해요). If you see a positive verb, you need 만, not 밖에.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 밖에 links across the ㄲ: [ba-kke], so 공부밖에 is [gong-bu-ba-kke] and 한 시간밖에 is [han si-gan-ba-kke].

drill.instruction: Complete each sentence so the predicate is negative (못/안/없어요).

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Because English 'only' goes with positive verbs, learners drop the negative. 밖에 grammatically requires 못/안/없어요. If you want a plain positive 'only', switch to 만.

grammarNotes.title: (이)나 — as many as / or
grammarNotes.func: After a number or amount it adds 'surprisingly much' (as many as); between two nouns it offers a loose choice ('A or B'). This chapter centers on the 'as many as' use.

formTable.ex: 다섯 잔 → 다섯 잔이나 (as many as 5 cups)
세 개 → 세 개나 (as many as 3)
물이나 마실까요? (shall we just drink water or something?)

examples.en: As many as three questions are left.
examples.note: 개 ends in a vowel → 나; the speaker feels three is a lot.

examples.en: I drank as many as five cups of coffee.
examples.note: 잔 ends in a consonant → 이나; emphasizes the surprisingly high count.

examples.en: I waited a whole hour.
examples.note: 시간 ends in a consonant → 이나; the wait felt long.

examples.en: Give me coffee or water (either is fine).
examples.note: Here (이)나 means a loose 'or' between two acceptable options.

keyPoint.label: (이)나 vs 밖에
keyPoint.body: Both attach to amounts but pull opposite ways. 다섯 잔이나 = the amount feels big (more than expected); 다섯 잔밖에 못 마셨어요 = the amount feels small (less than wanted). 나 says 'wow, that much'; 밖에 says 'only that little'.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 이나/나 trigger no special tensing; just match the final sound: 개나 [gae-na], 잔이나 [jan-i-na].

drill.instruction: Add 이나 or 나 to the number to mean 'as many as'.
drill.model: 세 개 ___ 남았어요. → 세 개나 남았어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 세 개나 남았어요. / 세 개밖에 안 남았어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners blend the two because both attach to numbers. Pick one stance: 나 = surprisingly many (positive verb), 밖에 = surprisingly few (negative verb). They cannot stack.

grammarNotes.title: (이)라도 — at least; even if only
grammarNotes.func: Offers a minimum or fallback option when the ideal one isn't available: 'at least X', 'even if only X', 'X if nothing else'.

formTable.ex: 물이라도 마실까요? (shall we at least drink some water?)
잠깐이라도 쉬세요 (rest, even for a moment)

examples.en: If you don't have time, at least drink some water.
examples.note: 물 is consonant-final → 이라도; water is the fallback when there's no time for more.

examples.en: Shall we at least grab a coffee?
examples.note: 커피 is vowel-final → 라도; offers coffee as a modest plan.

examples.en: Rest, even for just a moment.
examples.note: 잠깐 is consonant-final → 이라도; 'even a little' time is better than none.

examples.en: Let's at least take the bus (go by bus).
examples.note: 버스 is vowel-final → 라도; the bus is the second-best option.

keyPoint.label: (이)라도 vs 만
keyPoint.body: 만 picks X as the exclusive choice ('only X'); (이)라도 picks X as a settling-for second choice ('X if nothing better'). 물만 마셔요 = I drink only water (by choice); 물이라도 마셔요 = at least drink water (since there's nothing else).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: (이)라도 is light with no tensing; just link smoothly: 물이라도 [mu-ri-ra-do], 커피라도 [keo-pi-ra-do].

drill.instruction: Add 라도 or 이라도 to the noun to mean 'at least / if nothing else'.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: (이)라도 and 만 express opposite attitudes (settling vs. exclusive), so they don't stack. Choose 이라도 for 'at least, if nothing else' or 만 for 'only, by choice'.

grammarNotes.title: 의 — 's / of (noun-to-noun link)
grammarNotes.func: 의 links two nouns to show possession or relationship, like English "'s" or "of": 친구의 가방 (a friend's bag). In speech it is usually dropped (친구 가방), and 저의/나의 contract to 제/내.

formTable.ex: 친구의 책 (a friend's book) · 한국의 음식 (Korea's food)

examples.en: This is my friend's book.
examples.note: 친구 + 의 + 책 — the first noun owns the second.

examples.en: Where is my bag?
examples.note: 저의 contracts to 제 — the everyday way to say "my."

examples.en: I like Korean food.
examples.note: 의 links 한국 to 음식 ("of Korea").

examples.en: My sibling's room is really big.
examples.note: In speech the 의 is dropped — 동생 방 = 동생의 방.

keyPoint.label: Drop 의 in speech; contract 저의 → 제
keyPoint.body: Written Korean keeps 의 (친구의 책), but spoken Korean usually drops it (친구 책). The one place it survives is the contractions 제 (저의), 내 (나의), 네 (너의) — always say 제 책, not 저의 책 in conversation.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 의 as a particle is pronounced [에]: 친구의 → [친구에]. (의 keeps its [의] sound only at the start of a word, like 의자.)

drill.instruction: Link the two nouns with 의 (or its contraction).
drill.model: (친구 / 책) → 친구의 책 · (저 / 가방) → 제 가방

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: In speech, 저의 always shrinks to 제. Say 제 가방 (my bag), not 저의 가방 — the full form sounds stiff and written.

grammarNotes.title: (으)로 — by means of / toward (direction)
grammarNotes.func: Marks how you do something (tool, means, transport) or which direction you head: 'by/with X', 'toward X'.

examples.en: I go to school by bus.
examples.note: 버스 is vowel-final → 로; (으)로 marks the means of transport.

examples.en: I ate with my hands.
examples.note: 손 is consonant-final → 으로; the hand is the means/tool.

examples.en: I transferred to the subway.
examples.note: 지하철 ends in ㄹ, so just 로 (no 으); pronounced [ji-ha-cheol-lo].

examples.en: Come this way.
examples.note: 이쪽 is consonant-final → 으로; here it marks direction, not means.

keyPoint.label: (으)로 vs 에 (destination)
keyPoint.body: 에 marks the exact destination you arrive at (학교에 가요 = go to school); (으)로 marks the direction you face or the means you use (학교로 가요 = head toward school; 버스로 가요 = go by bus). For transport and tools, always (으)로, never 에.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After ㄹ the 로 doubles the ㄹ: 지하철로 is [ji-ha-cheol-lo], not [ji-ha-cheol-ro].

drill.instruction: Add 로 or 으로 to match the final sound, then read it aloud.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English uses 'by bus' / 'to school' with no particle clash, but in Korean the means takes (으)로 and the destination takes 에. Don't put 에 on the transport — 버스에 가요 would mean 'go onto the bus'.

grammarNotes.title: 마다 — every / each
grammarNotes.func: Attaches to a noun to mean 'every X' or 'each X', often for repeated times or all members of a group: 'every morning', 'each person'.

formTable.ex: 세 시간 → 세 시간마다 (every three hours)

examples.en: I drink coffee every morning.
examples.note: 아침 + 마다 = 'every morning'; no extra time particle is needed.

examples.en: I meet my friends every weekend.
examples.note: 마다 attaches straight to 주말; it already means 'every', so don't add 에.

examples.en: Each person thinks differently.
examples.note: 사람마다 = 'each/every person'; great for talking about variation.

examples.en: I take medicine every three hours.
examples.note: 마다 after a counted unit gives regular intervals.

keyPoint.label: 마다 vs 매-
keyPoint.body: 마다 is a particle stuck onto a noun (아침마다, 날마다). 매 is a prefix glued in front (매일 = every day, 매주 = every week). Both mean 'every', but 매 forms set words while 마다 attaches freely to almost any noun.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 마다 is plain and light: 아침마다 [a-chim-ma-da], 주말마다 [ju-mal-ma-da]. No tensing or linking surprises.

drill.instruction: Add 마다 to the noun to mean 'every / each'.
drill.model: 아침 ___ 커피를 마셔요. → 아침마다 커피를 마셔요.
items: 세 시간 ___ 약을 먹어요. (every three hours)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 마다 already carries the 'at every' meaning, so adding the time particle 에 is redundant and wrong. Use 마다 alone — never 마다에.

extendedDialogue.setting: Two friends negotiate a weekend plan while one person has study obligations.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Are you also going to see a movie with a friend this weekend?
lines.grammarNote: 친구랑 marks companionship; 영화도 adds another activity.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 아니요, 시험 문제가 세 개나 남아서 공부밖에 못 해요.
lines.romanization: aniyo, siheom munjega se gaena namaseo gongbubakke mot haeyo.
lines.en: No, as many as three exam questions are left, so I can only study.
lines.grammarNote: 세 개나 shows the amount feels large; 밖에 pairs with 못 해요.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Then do you want to at least drink coffee? Just one hour.
lines.grammarNote: 라도 offers a minimum option; 만 limits the time.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 좋아요. 선생님께 이메일도 보내드리고, 친구의 책도 돌려줘야 해요.
lines.romanization: joayo. seonsaengnimkke imeildo bonaedeurigo, chinguui chaekdo dollyeojwoya haeyo.
lines.en: Sounds good. I also need to send the teacher an email and return my friend's book.
lines.grammarNote: 께 marks the respected receiver; 의 marks possession; 도 adds tasks.

readingText.title: 주말 계획을 입자로 정리하기
readingText.body: 주말 계획을 말할 때는 명사보다 입자가 더 많은 정보를 줄 때가 있어요. 친구랑 영화를 보면 함께 가는 사람을 말하는 것이고, 영화도 본다고 하면 다른 일에 영화를 추가하는 거예요. 시험 문제가 세 개나 남았다고 하면 양이 많게 느껴지고, 공부밖에 못 한다고 하면 선택지가 거의 없다는 뜻이에요. 그래도 커피라도 마시자고 하면 완전한 약속은 아니지만 최소한 가능한 제안을 하는 거예요. 마지막으로 선생님께 이메일을 보내드리고 친구의 책을 돌려줘야 한다면, 께는 받는 사람의 높임, 의는 소유 관계를 보여 줘요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: When talking about weekend plans, particles often carry more information than the noun itself. 친구랑 tells who you go with, 영화도 adds a movie to other plans, 세 개나 shows the amount feels large, 공부밖에 못 해요 means the options are limited, 커피라도 offers a minimum plan, 께 marks a respected receiver, and 의 marks possession.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 친구랑 영화 보면 어떤 의미예요?
공부밖에 못 해요에서 왜 못 해요가 필요해요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 밖에가 부정 표현과 함께 쓰여서 선택지가 제한된다는 뜻을 만들기 때문이에요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 커피라도 마실래요?는 어떤 느낌이에요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 완전한 계획은 아니지만 최소한 커피라도 마시자는 제안이에요.

culturalNote.title: A small particle can change the social meaning
culturalNote.body: 선생님에게 이메일을 보냈어요 is grammatically possible, but 선생님께 이메일을 드렸어요 sounds more respectful because 께 and 드리다 work together. In everyday speech, Korean speakers also drop 의 often, but they keep particles like 께, 밖에, 만, and 도 when those particles carry important social or logical meaning.
culturalNote.tip: When a sentence feels wrong, do not only change the noun. Ask what relationship the particle is trying to mark: receiver, companion, possession, addition, limit, scarcity, large amount, or minimum option.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly marks the teacher as a respected receiver?
inlineExercises.explanation: 께 marks a respected person receiving the action, and 드리다 matches the respectful tone.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses 밖에 correctly?
inlineExercises.explanation: 밖에 needs a negative idea such as 못, 안, or 없어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'as many as three exam questions are left'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 이나/나 after a number shows the amount feels large or surprising.

inlineExercises.prompt: At least coffee: 커피____ 마실래요?
inlineExercises.explanation: 라도 offers a minimum or fallback option.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which pair shows the difference between 만 and 밖에?
inlineExercises.explanation: 만 works with a positive predicate; 밖에 needs a negative predicate.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence naturally marks possession?
inlineExercises.explanation: 의 links 친구 to 책: the friend's book.

inlineExercises.prompt: 선생님___ 이메일을 보냈어요. (I sent an email to the teacher.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 께 respectfully marks the receiver of the email. 께서 would mark the teacher as a respected subject, and 를 would make the teacher a direct object.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I have only one hour, and it is not enough.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 밖에 must pair with a negative like 없어요. It sounds like the amount is limited or insufficient.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'Would you like at least coffee?'
inlineExercises.explanation: (이)라도 offers a minimum acceptable option. 커피라도 sounds like coffee would be okay even if it is not ideal.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means “I only drink coffee” without the scarcity feeling?
inlineExercises.explanation: 만 simply limits the choice to coffee. 밖에 plus negative adds a stronger “nothing except” feeling.

bullets: 에게/한테/께 marks a person receiving an action: 친구에게 선물을 줬어요, 선생님께 이메일을 드렸어요.
와/과/하고/(이)랑 links nouns or marks companionship: 친구랑 영화 봐요.
밖에 needs a negative predicate: 공부밖에 못 해요, 한 시간밖에 없어요.
이나/나 after a number shows a surprisingly large amount: 세 개나, 다섯 잔이나.
이라도/라도 offers a minimum option: 커피라도, 잠깐이라도.
의 marks possession or noun-to-noun relation, while 도 and 만 add or limit focus.

writingTask.prompt: Write a short message about giving something to a friend and what you do each week, using several particles.
writingTask.hint: Use 에게/한테 (to a person), 하고/(이)랑 (with/and), 밖에 + negative (only), 마다 (every), and (으)로 (by means of).
writingTask.model: 저는 친구한테 선물을 줬어요. 주말마다 친구하고 커피를 마셔요. 그런데 오늘은 시간이 한 시간밖에 없어요. 그래서 버스로 빨리 가요.
writingTask.modelEn: I gave a gift to my friend. Every weekend I drink coffee with my friend. But today I only have one hour. So I go quickly by bus.

canDo: Mark the person who receives an action (친구한테 · 선생님께)
Link nouns or a companion with 'and/with' (친구하고 · 친구랑)
Use 밖에 + negative for 'only', and 마다 for 'every' (한 시간밖에 없어요 · 주말마다)
Show means or direction with (으)로 (버스로 가요)

chapters.goal: Ask better follow-up questions so the conversation does not stop.
chapters.scenario: You are getting to know a classmate, tutor, or language partner.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: How was it?

chapters.guidedPractice: Make one sentence each with 명, 개, 마리, 잔, 권, 장, 벌, 대, and 번, then check whether the number should be native or Sino-Korean.
chapters.realLifeTask: Ask three follow-up questions using 어디, 언제, 왜, 어떻게, or 누구.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner gives you a noun like 학생, 커피, 책, 종이, 옷, 사진, or 강아지; answer with the correct counter and a full sentence.
chapters.review: Can you choose the counter first, then pick the correct number shape: 한/두/세/네/스무 vs 일/이/삼?

beginnerGuide.title: Noun + number + counter
beginnerGuide.body: Most everyday counting uses the noun first, then number plus counter: 학생 세 명, 커피 두 잔, 책 두 권, 종이 열 장.

beginnerGuide.title: Native number changes
beginnerGuide.body: Before counters, 하나/둘/셋/넷/스물 become 한/두/세/네/스무: 한 개, 두 잔, 세 명, 네 장, 스무 명.

beginnerGuide.title: Not every counter uses native numbers
beginnerGuide.body: Everyday object counters use native numbers, but some units use Sino-Korean numbers, especially 번 for sequence or repeated actions in many contexts: 세 번, 일 번.

I can keep the question word in the Korean answer slot.
I can ask a short follow-up like 왜요? or 언제부터요?

Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: A class event needs chairs, drinks, guide books, paper, and even a dog coming with a student. In Korean, each of those quantities needs the right counter.
objectives: Use noun + number + counter order confidently.
Pick the common counter for people, animals, things, cups, books, sheets, clothing sets, machines, and occurrences.
Use the changed native number forms 한, 두, 세, 네, and 스무 before counters.
hook.whyItMatters: English can say 'three students, two coffees, ten papers' with almost no classifier changes. Korean asks what kind of thing you are counting: people take 명, animals take 마리, drinks take 잔, books take 권, and flat sheets take 장.

grammarNotes.title: Counting Word Order: Noun + Number + Counter
grammarNotes.func: To count things in Korean, you name the thing first, then say how many. The pattern is NOUN + NUMBER + COUNTER, with no particle between the number and the counter. English says 'three apples'; Korean says 'apple three (units)' — 사과 세 개.

formTable.ex: 사과 세 개 = three apples (apple / three / units)

formTable.when: Add a verb after the count
formTable.add: keep noun + number + counter, then verb
formTable.ex: 커피 두 잔 주세요 = please give me two coffees

formTable.when: Mark the counted noun as object
formTable.add: the object particle 을/를 goes on the NOUN, not on the counter
formTable.ex: 빵을 네 개 샀어요 = I bought four pieces of bread

examples.en: Please give me three apples.
examples.note: Order is noun (사과) → number (세) → counter (개); no particle joins 세 and 개.

examples.en: There are two cats.
examples.note: The subject particle 가 attaches to the counter 마리 at the end of the count phrase, not to 고양이.

examples.en: I'll buy one bottle of water.
examples.note: 한 (from 하나) sits before the counter 병; the noun 물 comes first as always.

examples.en: I bought two tickets.
examples.note: The object particle 를 stays on the noun 표; the count 두 장 follows it directly.

keyPoint.label: Korean reverses the English order
keyPoint.body: English: number + noun ('three apples'). Korean: noun + number + counter (사과 세 개). The counter is a required 'unit word' — you cannot say 사과 셋 to mean 'three apples'; you need the counter 개.

drill.instruction: Put the words in the correct Korean counting order: noun + number + counter. Say the full phrase out loud.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers copy 'three apples' and put the number first with no counter. Korean needs the noun first and a counter word after the number: 사과 세 개.

grammarNotes.title: Native-Number Contractions Before a Counter
grammarNotes.func: Korean native numbers 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷 and 스물 change shape when a counter follows them. They drop their final part: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무. Use the contracted form only when a counter comes right after.

formTable.ex: 한 개 = one item (NOT 하나 개)

examples.en: I drank one cup of coffee.
examples.note: 하나 contracts to 한 before the counter 잔; saying 하나 잔 is wrong.

examples.en: Please lend me two pencils.
examples.note: 둘 becomes 두 before 자루, the counter for pencils and pen-shaped things.

examples.en: Four friends came.
examples.note: 넷 contracts to 네 before 명; 넷 명 would be incorrect.

examples.en: My older brother is twenty years old.
examples.note: 스물 drops its ㄹ to become 스무 before the age counter 살.

keyPoint.label: Contract only before a counter
keyPoint.body: 하나/둘/셋/넷/스물 keep their full form when counting alone ('하나, 둘, 셋…') but contract to 한/두/세/네/스무 the moment a counter follows. Compare: 사과가 하나 있어요 (one apple, no counter) vs. 사과 한 개 있어요 (one apple, with counter 개).

drill.instruction: Contract the native number to its pre-counter form and read the phrase aloud.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 하나 개, 둘 잔, 넷 마리
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 한 개, 두 잔, 네 마리
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners memorize 하나/둘/셋/넷 and use them unchanged. Before any counter they MUST contract to 한/두/세/네. This is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

grammarNotes.title: Counting People and Animals: 명 / 분 / 마리
grammarNotes.func: People are counted with 명 (plain) or 분 (honorific, for people you respect). Animals — pets, fish, birds, insects — are all counted with 마리.

examples.en: There are five students in the classroom.
examples.note: 명 is the neutral counter for people: classmates, friends, ordinary people.

examples.en: Two grandmothers came.
examples.note: 분 is the honorific counter, right for elders; the verb is also honorific 오셨어요.

examples.ko: 우리 집에 강아지 세 마리가 있어요.
examples.romanization: uri jib-e gangaji se mari-ga isseoyo.
examples.en: We have three puppies at home.
examples.note: 마리 counts animals of any kind, including pets like puppies.

examples.en: There are four fish in the tank.
examples.note: Even fish use 마리 — it covers all animals, not just four-legged ones.

keyPoint.label: 명 vs. 분 = respect level
keyPoint.body: 명 and 분 both count people; the difference is politeness. Use 분 for guests, elders, teachers, and customers; use 명 for friends, kids, or a general headcount. Never use 분 for yourself. Animals always take 마리, never 명.

drill.instruction: Choose the right person/animal counter (명, 분, or 마리) and complete the phrase.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 손님 두 명이 왔어요 (said to a customer's face)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English has no built-in 'respect counter,' so learners default to 명 for everyone. For guests, elders, and customers, use the honorific 분 to sound polite.

grammarNotes.title: Counting Objects, Drinks, Books, and Sheets: 개 / 잔 / 권 / 장
grammarNotes.func: Different kinds of things take different counters. 개 = general objects, 잔 = cups/glasses of a drink, 권 = books and notebooks, 장 = flat sheets (paper, tickets, photos).

formTable.when: A drink served in a cup or glass
formTable.ex: 물 한 잔 = one glass of water
종이 네 장 = four sheets of paper

examples.en: Please give me just two erasers.
examples.note: 개 is the all-purpose counter for everyday objects like erasers.

examples.en: One more cup of green tea, please.
examples.note: 잔 counts drinks served in a cup or glass — tea, coffee, water, juice.

examples.ko: 이번 달에 책 두 권을 읽었어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon dar-e chaek du gwon-eul ilgeosseoyo.
examples.en: I read two books this month.
examples.note: 권 is the counter for books and notebooks.

examples.en: I printed five photos.
examples.note: 장 counts flat, thin things: photos, paper, tickets.

keyPoint.label: 개 is the safe default
keyPoint.body: When you don't know the right counter, 개 usually works for objects. But the specific counters are expected for their categories: drinks → 잔, books → 권, flat sheets → 장. Saying 책 세 개 is understandable but sounds like a learner; 책 세 권 is correct.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 권 ends in a clear final ㄴ; before 을 it links as 권을 [궈늘 / gwo-neul]. 장을 links as [장을 / jang-eul] with the ㅇ carrying over.

drill.instruction: Pick the correct counter (개, 잔, 권, or 장) for each noun and complete the phrase.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 책 세 개, 커피 두 개
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 책 세 권, 커피 두 잔
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English uses 'three books / two coffees' with no special unit, so learners overuse 개. Match the counter to the category: 권 for books, 잔 for cups of a drink.

grammarNotes.title: Counting Clothes and Machines: 벌 / 대
grammarNotes.func: 벌 counts sets of clothing — an outfit, a suit, pajamas. 대 counts machines and vehicles — cars, phones, computers, TVs, anything mechanical.

formTable.when: A set or suit of clothes
formTable.ex: 옷 한 벌 = one set of clothes

examples.en: I bought one new set of clothes.
examples.note: 벌 counts a full outfit, not single garments; 한 from 하나 before the counter.

examples.en: I need two suits.
examples.note: 벌 also counts suits and other matched sets of clothing.

examples.ko: 우리 집에 차가 한 대 있어요.
examples.romanization: uri jib-e cha-ga han dae isseoyo.
examples.en: We have one car at home.
examples.note: 대 is the counter for vehicles; 가 attaches after the counter phrase.

examples.en: There are three computers in the classroom.
examples.note: 대 counts machines and appliances — computers, phones, washing machines.

keyPoint.label: 벌 = clothing sets, 대 = machines
keyPoint.body: Use 벌 for clothes you wear as a set (옷 한 벌, 양복 두 벌) and 대 for anything mechanical (차 한 대, 핸드폰 두 대, 세탁기 한 대). Don't reach for 개 here — 차 한 개 or 옷 한 개 sounds clearly wrong to native ears.

drill.instruction: Pick the correct counter (벌 or 대) for each noun and complete the phrase.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 차 한 개, 옷 두 개
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 차 한 대, 옷 두 벌
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners fall back on the all-purpose 개, but vehicles and machines need 대 and sets of clothing need 벌. 차 한 개 and 옷 한 개 sound clearly wrong to native speakers.

grammarNotes.title: Counting Time and Frequency: 번 / 시간 / 살
grammarNotes.func: 번 counts the number of times something happens (once, twice). 시간 counts hours of duration. 살 counts years of age. All three take native numbers, contracted before the counter.

formTable.ex: 세 번 봤어요 = I saw it three times

examples.en: I watched that movie twice.
examples.note: 번 counts how many times; 둘 contracts to 두 before it.

examples.en: I take medicine three times a day.
examples.note: 번 with a native number gives the frequency of an action.

examples.en: I slept five hours yesterday.
examples.note: 시간 counts a span of hours; it is different from 시 (clock o'clock).

examples.en: My daughter is seven years old.
examples.note: 살 is the everyday counter for age, always with native numbers.

keyPoint.label: 시간 (duration) vs. 시 (o'clock)
keyPoint.body: 세 시간 means 'three hours' (how long), but 세 시 means 'three o'clock' (what time). Both use native numbers but answer different questions. 번 counts occurrences (한 번 = once), and 살 counts age (열 살 = ten years old).

drill.instruction: Choose the right counter (번, 시간, or 살) and complete the phrase.

englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 세 시에 (at three o'clock) vs. 세 시간 (for three hours)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'three hours' and 'three o'clock' look alike, so learners mix up 시간 and 시. Use 시간 for how long something lasts and 시 for the time on the clock.

readingText.title: 몇 개가 아니라 무엇을 세는지 먼저 보기
readingText.body: 한국어에서 수량을 말할 때는 숫자만 맞으면 끝이 아니에요. 무엇을 세는지 먼저 봐야 해요. 학생은 세 명, 강아지는 한 마리, 커피는 네 잔, 책은 두 권, 종이는 열 장처럼 명사에 맞는 단위가 달라져요. 처음에는 개를 모든 물건에 붙이고 싶지만, 책 두 개보다 책 두 권이 자연스럽고, 사진 세 개보다 사진 세 장이 자연스러워요. 또 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷은 단위명사 앞에서 한, 두, 세, 네로 줄어들어요. 그래서 하나 명이 아니라 한 명, 둘 잔이 아니라 두 잔이라고 말해요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: In Korean, counting is not only about choosing the right number. You first look at what kind of thing you are counting. Students are counted with 명, animals with 마리, cups of coffee with 잔, books with 권, and sheets of paper or photos with 장. The first few native Korean numbers also contract before counters: 하나 becomes 한, 둘 becomes 두, 셋 becomes 세, and 넷 becomes 네.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 학생을 셀 때 어떤 단위명사를 써요?
책 두 개보다 어떤 표현이 더 자연스러워요?
하나, 둘, 셋, 넷은 단위명사 앞에서 어떻게 바뀌어요?

culturalNote.title: Using 개 for everything sounds beginner-like
culturalNote.body: 개 is useful and often understood, but Korean speakers use more specific counters whenever they are common. 책 두 개, 사진 세 개, 커피 두 개 may be understood, but 책 두 권, 사진 세 장, 커피 두 잔 sound much more natural. In service settings, using the right counter also makes requests clearer.
culturalNote.tip: When you learn a new noun, learn one counting chunk with it: 책 한 권, 커피 한 잔, 사진 한 장, 강아지 한 마리.

bullets: Basic order: noun + number + counter, as in 학생 세 명 and 커피 두 잔.
Native number contractions: 한, 두, 세, 네, 스무 before counters.
People and animals: 명/분 for people, 마리 for animals.
Objects and formats: 개 for general things, 잔 for drinks, 권 for books, 장 for flat sheets.
Sets and machines: 벌 for clothing sets, 대 for vehicles and machines.
번 can mean times or number labels: 세 번 vs 삼 번.

writingTask.prompt: Write 3-4 sentences counting different things around you: people, drinks, books, and animals.
writingTask.hint: Use NOUN + NUMBER + COUNTER with contracted native numbers (한/두/세/네) and the right counter: 명 (people), 마리 (animals), 잔 (cups), 권 (books), 개 (things).
writingTask.model: 교실에 학생이 세 명 있어요. 저는 커피 두 잔을 마셨어요. 책을 네 권 샀어요. 우리 집에 강아지가 한 마리 있어요.
writingTask.modelEn: There are three students in the classroom. I drank two cups of coffee. I bought four books. We have one puppy at home.

canDo: Order a count as NOUN + NUMBER + COUNTER (학생이 세 명)
Contract native numbers before a counter (하나→한 · 둘→두 · 셋→세 · 넷→네)
Pick the right counter for people, animals, and objects (명 · 마리 · 잔 · 권 · 개)

beginnerGuide.title: Hangul is regular, speech is connected
beginnerGuide.body: Korean spelling is reliable, but spoken Korean connects blocks: 먹어요 is read closer to [머거요], and 한국어 is read closer to [한구거].

beginnerGuide.title: Blocked sounds can push the next sound
beginnerGuide.body: After a final consonant, the next plain sound can become tense: 학교 [학꾜], 국밥 [국빱], 먹고 [먹꼬].

beginnerGuide.title: Nasals and ㅎ change neighbors
beginnerGuide.body: Before ㄴ/ㅁ, stops often become nasal: 국민 [궁민]. When ㅎ meets a stop, it often makes an aspirated sound: 좋다 [조타], 입학 [이팍].

checkpoints: I can use -더라고요 for something I personally observed.
I can use -더니 when one observed situation led to a change.
I can avoid using plain -더니 for my own neutral actions.

hook.situation: A learner can read Hangul blocks, but native speech connects and changes the sounds: 먹어요 sounds like [머거요], 학교 like [학꾜], 국민 like [궁민], and 좋다 like [조타].
objectives: Map written Korean to spoken Korean using four high-frequency rules.
Practice each rule with everyday words instead of isolated sound names.
Explain why a block-by-block reading can sound unnatural even when the spelling is correct.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean spelling is systematic, but actual pronunciation is connected. Learners who pronounce every block separately often sound choppy and may be hard to understand. These rules help the ear catch what native speakers are already doing automatically.

grammarNotes.title: 연음 (Linking): A Final Consonant Slides onto the Next Vowel
grammarNotes.func: When a syllable ends in a 받침 (final consonant) and the next syllable starts with ㅇ (a silent placeholder before a vowel), the 받침 jumps over and is pronounced as the first sound of that next syllable. The spelling never changes — only the sound. This is why 한국어 is said [한구거]: the ㄱ of 국 links onto the 어.

formTable.when: 받침 + a vowel starting with ㅇ
formTable.add: the 받침 moves into the empty ㅇ slot

formTable.when: a single 받침 (ㄱ/ㄴ/ㄹ/ㅁ/ㅂ/ㅅ etc.) before a vowel
formTable.add: that consonant becomes the next syllable's onset

formTable.when: a double 받침 (겹받침) before a vowel
formTable.add: the first consonant stays, the second links over
no linking; ㅇ [ŋ] stays where it is

examples.en: Korean pronunciation is hard.
examples.note: 한국어 → [한구거] (국's ㄱ links to 어); 발음이 → [바르미] (음's ㅁ links to 이).

examples.en: Try reading this word.
examples.note: 단어 → [다너] (단's ㄴ links to 어); 읽어 → [일거] (겹받침 ㄺ splits: ㄹ stays, ㄱ links).

examples.en: What is my name? (lit.)
examples.note: 이름이 → [이르미]: 름's ㅁ links onto 이. Compare 이름 alone, said [이름].

examples.en: The clothes are really pretty.
examples.note: 옷이 → [오시]: the ㅅ 받침 links onto 이 and is pronounced as a clear ㅅ, not [옫이].

keyPoint.label: Spelling vs. sound
keyPoint.body: Linking changes only the sound, never the spelling. You always write 한국어, but you say [한구거]. Reading each syllable as written (han-guk-eo) sounds robotic; native speakers link automatically.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 한국어 is [한구거], not [한국어]. Listen for the 받침 sliding right: 옷이 [오시], 꽃이 [꼬치], 밥을 [바블].

drill.instruction: Say each phrase aloud, then write the linked pronunciation in brackets.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: han-guk · eo (a hard stop between the syllables)
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: han-gu-geo (the ㄱ glides into the next syllable)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers tend to pronounce every syllable as written and insert a small gap before a vowel. In Korean the 받침 must flow onto the following vowel with no break, so 한국어 sounds like [한구거].

grammarNotes.title: 경음화 (Tensing): A Plain Consonant Tenses After a Stop
grammarNotes.func: When a 받침 pronounced as a stop [ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ] is immediately followed by a plain consonant ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ, or ㅈ, that following consonant becomes its tense (된소리) version: ㄱ→ㄲ, ㄷ→ㄸ, ㅂ→ㅃ, ㅅ→ㅆ, ㅈ→ㅉ. This is why 학교 is said [학꾜].

formTable.when: [ㄷ] 받침 (ㄷ,ㅅ,ㅈ,ㅊ,ㅌ all sound [ㄷ]) + a plain consonant

formTable.add: usually NO tensing (those are not stops)

examples.en: I learn Korean at school.
examples.note: 학교 → [학꾜]: the [ㄱ] of 학 tenses the following ㄱ into ㄲ.

examples.en: There is a book on the desk.
examples.note: 책상 → [책쌍]: the [ㄱ] 받침 tenses ㅅ to ㅆ. (책이 → [채기] is linking, a separate rule.)

examples.en: Let's eat together at the restaurant.
examples.note: 식당 → [식땅]: the [ㄱ] 받침 tenses ㄷ to ㄸ.

examples.en: I couldn't catch this pronunciation.
examples.note: 잡지 → [잡찌]: the [ㅂ] 받침 tenses ㅈ to ㅉ.

keyPoint.label: Tense only after a stop
keyPoint.body: Tensing happens after the three stop sounds [ㄱ][ㄷ][ㅂ], not after the sonorants ㄴ/ㄹ/ㅁ/ㅇ. Compare 학교 [학꾜] (tensing) with 안경 [안경] (no tensing) — the 받침 in 안경 is ㄴ, which is not a stop.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 학교 is [학꾜], not [학교]. The ㄲ is the same tense sound as in 꼬리/꽃 — tighten the throat, no puff of air.

drill.instruction: Read each word and write the tensed pronunciation in brackets.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: hak-gyo (a soft, voiced 'g' after the k)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers often voice the consonant after a stop, turning ㄱ into a soft 'g'. Korean does the opposite: the consonant tenses to ㄲ. So 학교 is [학꾜], with a tight, unaspirated ㄲ, never a relaxed 'g'.

grammarNotes.title: 비음화 (Nasalization): A Stop Becomes Nasal Before ㄴ/ㅁ
grammarNotes.func: When a 받침 pronounced as a stop [ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ] is followed by the nasal consonant ㄴ or ㅁ, the stop changes into the matching nasal: ㄱ→ㅇ[ŋ], ㄷ→ㄴ, ㅂ→ㅁ. The mouth assimilates to the nasal that follows. This is why 한국말 is said [한궁말].

examples.en: Your Korean pronunciation is natural.
examples.note: 한국말 → [한궁말]: the [ㄱ] of 국 becomes ㅇ before ㅁ.

examples.en: Thank you.
examples.note: 합니다 → [함니다]: the [ㅂ] of 합 becomes ㅁ before ㄴ — the single most common nasalization learners hear.

examples.en: I am a student.
examples.note: 입니다 → [임니다]: [ㅂ] → ㅁ before ㄴ; this is how every formal '-입니다' ending is actually said. (학생 → [학쌩] is tensing.)

examples.en: I'm listening to a song right now.
examples.note: 듣는 → [든는]: the [ㄷ] of 듣 becomes ㄴ before ㄴ.

keyPoint.label: -입니다 / -습니다
keyPoint.body: The polite formal endings -ㅂ니다 / -습니다 are ALWAYS nasalized in speech: 입니다 [임니다], 습니다 [슴니다]. Saying [입니다] with a real ㅂ sounds unnatural — the ㅂ always becomes ㅁ before the ㄴ.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 한국말 is [한궁말]: the ㄱ disappears into a nasal ㅇ. Hum it — the air should go through your nose on the 궁.

drill.instruction: Read each word and write its nasalized pronunciation in brackets.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English keeps the stop and nasal separate ('hap-nip'). Korean blends them: a stop before ㄴ/ㅁ assimilates into the matching nasal. So 합니다 is [함니다] and 한국말 is [한궁말], never with the original stop intact.

grammarNotes.title: 격음화 (Aspiration): ㅎ Merges with a Plain Stop into an Aspirate
grammarNotes.func: When ㅎ meets a plain consonant ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, or ㅈ (in either order — ㅎ before the consonant, or a [ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ] 받침 before ㅎ), the two merge into a single aspirated consonant: ㄱ→ㅋ, ㄷ→ㅌ, ㅂ→ㅍ, ㅈ→ㅊ. This is why 좋다 is said [조타].

examples.en: I heard your pronunciation is good.
examples.note: 좋다 → [조타]: ㅎ 받침 + ㄷ merge into the aspirate ㅌ.

examples.en: Congratulations on starting school!
examples.note: 입학 → [이팍]: [ㅂ] + ㅎ → ㅍ; 축하 → [추카]: [ㄱ] + ㅎ → ㅋ. Two aspirations in one sentence.

examples.en: How do you read this word?
examples.note: 어떻게 → [어떠케]: ㅎ 받침 + ㄱ → ㅋ. (읽어요 → [일거요] is separate linking.)

examples.en: The pronunciation is really good and natural.
examples.note: 좋고 → [조코]: ㅎ 받침 + ㄱ merge into the aspirate ㅋ.

keyPoint.label: Aspiration vs. tensing
keyPoint.body: Both reshape a plain stop, but the trigger differs. ㅎ + ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ gives an ASPIRATED consonant (ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ, with a puff of air): 좋다 [조타]. A stop + plain consonant gives a TENSE consonant (ㄲ/ㄸ/ㅃ, no air): 학교 [학꾜]. Hold your hand to your mouth — aspiration puffs, tensing doesn't.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 좋다 is [조타], not [졷다] or [조따]. The ㅌ is aspirated like the ㅌ in 타요 — release a clear puff of air, not a tense ㄸ.

drill.instruction: Read each word and write the aspirated pronunciation in brackets.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: jot-da (keeping the ㅎ and ㄷ as two separate hard sounds)
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: jo-ta (the ㅎ and ㄷ merge into one aspirated ㅌ)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers try to pronounce both the ㅎ and the following stop, or drop the ㅎ entirely as a tense [조따]. In Korean the two fuse into a single aspirated consonant with a puff of air, so 좋다 is [조타] and 축하 is [추카].
