extendedDialogue.setting: A learner compares written Hangul with actual pronunciation.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: 먹어요 is not [meok-eo-yo]; it links and sounds like [머거요].
lines.grammarNote: 연음 links the final ㄱ to the following vowel.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Why do 학교 and 국밥 sound like [학꾜] and [국빱]?
lines.grammarNote: 경음화 makes the next consonant tense after certain final consonants.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: It is because a tense sound appears after the final consonant.
lines.grammarNote: This explains the tense consonant in 학교 and 국밥.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Then 국민 sounds like [궁민], and 먹는 sounds like [멍는], right?
lines.grammarNote: 비음화 changes stop sounds before ㄴ or ㅁ.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 맞아요. 좋다와 입학은 [조타], [이팍]처럼 ㅎ 때문에 세게 나요.
lines.romanization: majayo. jotdawa iphak-eun [jota], [ipak]cheoreom hieut ttaemune sege nayo.
lines.en: Right. 좋다 and 입학 become stronger sounds like [조타] and [이팍] because of ㅎ.
lines.grammarNote: 격음화 creates aspirated sounds like ㅌ and ㅍ.

readingText.title: 글자대로 읽는 것과 실제로 들리는 소리
readingText.body: 한글은 규칙적인 문자지만, 실제 말소리는 글자 블록을 하나씩 끊어 읽지 않아요. 먹어요는 [먹-어-요]가 아니라 [머거요]처럼 이어지고, 한국어도 [한구거]처럼 들려요. 반대로 학교와 국밥은 뒤 음절이 세져서 [학꾜], [국빱]처럼 들려요. 또 국민과 먹는처럼 ㄴ이나 ㅁ 앞에서는 받침 소리가 코소리로 바뀌고, 좋다와 입학처럼 ㅎ을 만나면 [조타], [이팍]처럼 거센소리가 나요. 철자는 그대로 외우되, 말할 때는 실제 소리 지도를 함께 익혀야 자연스럽게 들립니다.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Hangul spelling is regular, but speech does not read each block separately. 먹어요 links to [머거요], 한국어 sounds like [한구거], 학교 and 국밥 gain tense sounds, 국민 and 먹는 nasalize before ㄴ or ㅁ, and 좋다 and 입학 aspirate because of ㅎ. Keep the spelling, but learn the spoken map too.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 먹어요는 실제로 어떻게 이어져 들려요?
학교와 국밥에서 어떤 변화가 일어나요?
좋다와 입학은 왜 [조타], [이팍]처럼 들려요?

culturalNote.title: Do not rewrite the spelling as the sound
culturalNote.body: Native speakers hear [머거요] when they read 먹어요, but they still write 먹어요. Korean pronunciation rules are not alternate spellings; they are the bridge between correct spelling and natural speech. For learners, the best practice is to keep the written word in Hangul and add the spoken form in brackets during practice.
culturalNote.tip: Practice in pairs: write 먹어요, say [머거요]; write 학교, say [학꾜]; write 국민, say [궁민]; write 좋다, say [조타].

inlineExercises.prompt: 먹어요 is naturally pronounced closer to:
inlineExercises.explanation: 연음 links ㄱ into the following vowel.

inlineExercises.prompt: 학교 often sounds like [학꾜] because of:
inlineExercises.explanation: The following ㄱ becomes tense after the final consonant.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which word shows nasalization?
inlineExercises.explanation: ㄱ becomes ㅇ before ㅁ.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which pair shows aspiration caused by ㅎ?
inlineExercises.explanation: ㅂ and ㅎ combine into ㅍ in speech.

inlineExercises.prompt: 한국어 is heard closer to ____.
inlineExercises.explanation: The ㄱ links into the following vowel.

inlineExercises.prompt: 먹어요 is heard closer to ___.
inlineExercises.explanation: With 연음, the final ㄱ slides onto the following vowel. So 먹어요 is heard closer to 머거요.

inlineExercises.prompt: 국민 is naturally heard closer to:
inlineExercises.explanation: Before ㄴ or ㅁ, a stop sound can nasalize. ㄱ before ㅁ is heard closer to ㅇ, giving 궁민.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the pronunciation note: '좋다 sounds like [조다].'
inlineExercises.explanation: ㅎ combines with ㄷ and makes the aspirated ㅌ sound. That is why 좋다 is heard as [조타].

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Read Korean slowly.'
inlineExercises.explanation: This sentence keeps pronunciation practice inside a real action phrase. 한국어를 is the object and 천천히 tells how to read.

inlineExercises.prompt: 학교___ 가요. (I go to school.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 가요 takes 에 for the destination. 에서 marks an action place, and 가 would make 학교 the subject of going. The pronunciation of 학교 may tense in speech, but the written particle is still 에.

bullets: 연음: final consonant links to a following vowel, as in 먹어요 [머거요].
경음화: a following plain consonant becomes tense, as in 학교 [학꾜] and 국밥 [국빱].
비음화: ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ become nasal before ㄴ or ㅁ, as in 국민 [궁민].
격음화: ㅎ creates aspirated sounds, as in 좋다 [조타] and 입학 [이팍].
Do not rewrite spelling as sound. Keep 먹어요, but practice saying [머거요].

writingTask.prompt: Write 3-4 short sentences using everyday words whose spelling and sound differ, and note in English how one of them is pronounced.
writingTask.hint: Use words with sound changes: 연음 (한국어 → [한구거]), 경음화 (학교 → [학꾜]), 비음화 (국민 → [궁민]), 격음화 (좋다 → [조타]). Write the words normally; spelling stays the same.
writingTask.model: 저는 한국어를 공부해요. 학교에서 밥을 먹어요. 김치는 좋아요. 그런데 한국어를 잘 못해요.
writingTask.modelEn: I study Korean. I eat at school. Kimchi is good. But I'm not good at Korean. (한국어 is written han-gug-eo but pronounced [han-gu-geo]: the final ㄱ links onto the next vowel.)

canDo: Read a 받침 linking onto the next vowel (한국어 → [한구거], 연음)
Hear a plain consonant tense after a stop (학교 → [학꾜], 경음화)
Recognize nasalization and aspiration in speech (국민 → [궁민]; 좋다 → [조타])

beginnerGuide.title: Choice or blocked situation
beginnerGuide.body: 안 가요 can sound like a choice. 못 가요 says something blocks you: time, ability, rules, schedule, or health.

beginnerGuide.title: No thing, no time, no option
beginnerGuide.body: N이/가 없어요 is not just a vocabulary phrase. It is a negation strategy for absence: 시간이 없어요, 돈이 없어요, 방법이 없어요.

beginnerGuide.title: Careful or written negation
beginnerGuide.body: -지 않아요 sounds more careful than short 안. It is useful for clarification: 싫지 않아요, 어렵지 않아요, 먹지 않아요.

naturalWhy.title: Why past tense sounds natural here
naturalWhy.todayScene: Someone asks 어제 뭐 했어요? The time word 어제 already tells the listener the event is finished.
naturalWhy.why: 어제 points to a finished time, so Korean expects the verb ending to match that finished feeling. 봐요 sounds like now, usually, or a future plan. 봤어요 closes the event and matches 어제.
koreanSense: 오늘 봐요 feels present or scheduled.
어제 봤어요 feels finished and easy to understand.
내일 볼 거예요 points forward, so it should not use past tense.

hook.situation: A friend says they cannot come, cannot eat meat, or do not want something. Korean needs different negative forms depending on whether the issue is choice, ability, absence, or careful clarification.
objectives: Choose 안 for simple choice or ordinary negation.
Choose 못 when something blocks the action: schedule, ability, rule, or health.
Use 없다 for absence and -지 않아요 for careful or more formal negation.
hook.whyItMatters: English 'not' hides several different Korean meanings. 안 가요 can sound like you are choosing not to go, while 못 가요 says you cannot go because something blocks you. That difference matters when declining invitations or explaining food restrictions.

grammarNotes.title: 안 + verb/adjective — simple negation
grammarNotes.func: Put 안 directly in front of a verb or adjective to make it negative. This is the everyday spoken negation: "I don't / it isn't." It states a choice or a plain fact, with no sense of being blocked or unable.

formTable.add: 안 in front of the word
안 splits IN: noun + 안 + 해요

examples.en: I don't drink alcohol.
examples.note: 안 sits right before 마셔요; a stated habit, not an inability. Pronounced [an ma.syeo.yo], no tensing.

examples.en: I'm not going to school today.
examples.note: A simple choice or plan; 안 negates 가요 directly.

examples.en: This movie isn't scary.
examples.note: 안 also negates adjectives (무섭다 = scary), describing a plain quality.

examples.en: I don't exercise.
examples.note: With 운동하다, 안 goes BETWEEN the noun and 해요: 운동 안 해요, not 안 운동해요.

keyPoint.label: 안 vs 못
keyPoint.body: 안 = don't or won't, by choice or as a plain fact (안 가요, I'm not going). 못 = can't, blocked by an outside obstacle (못 가요, I can't go). If you simply chose not to, use 안; if something stops you, use 못.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 안 is pronounced [an] and, unlike 못, it does NOT tense the next sound. 안 가요 stays [an ga.yo], 안 봐요 stays [an bwa.yo]. Before a verb starting with ㅁ/ㄴ the nasal flows smoothly: 안 마셔요 → [an ma.syeo.yo]. No double-consonant tensing anywhere.

drill.instruction: Make each sentence negative using 안. Watch the 하다 verbs, where 안 goes between the noun and 해요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers treat 공부하다 as one block and put 안 in front of the whole thing. But noun + 하다 verbs split: the noun stays, then 안, then 해요. So it's 공부 안 해요, 운동 안 해요, 요리 안 해요.

grammarNotes.title: 못 + verb — cannot, because something blocks you
grammarNotes.func: Put 못 in front of a verb to say you CANNOT do it — not because you don't want to, but because something blocks or prevents you (no time, no skill, no permission, an obstacle). 못 is used with action verbs, not with descriptive adjectives.

formTable.add: 못 in front of the verb
못 splits IN: noun + 못 + 해요

examples.en: I can't go today because I'm too busy.
examples.note: 못 = blocked by an outside reason (being busy), not a choice. Pronounced [몯 까요].

examples.en: I can't eat spicy food.
examples.note: My body can't handle it — an inability, so 못, not 안.

examples.en: I can't swim.
examples.note: 하다 verb: 못 goes between 수영 and 해요. It's a lack of skill, hence 못.

examples.en: I couldn't sleep because it was noisy.
examples.note: An external obstacle (noise) prevented the action — a classic 못 situation, here in the past.

keyPoint.label: 못 + verb only (never adjectives)
keyPoint.body: 못 means 'unable to DO an action,' so it attaches to action verbs (못 가요, 못 먹어요). You can't be 'unable to be tall' or 'unable to be busy' — for adjectives use 안 (안 커요, 안 바빠요). 못 바빠요 is wrong.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 못 is written with final ㅅ but pronounced [몯]. Before a vowel it links: 못 와요 → [모 돠요]. Before ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ it TENSES the next sound: 못 가요 → [몯 까요], 못 봐요 → [몯 빠요]. That tensing is the audible signal of 못 — and the clearest way to tell it apart from 안.

drill.instruction: Rewrite using 못 to mean 'cannot.' For 하다 verbs, put 못 between the noun and 해요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저는 안 수영해요 (when you mean you literally can't swim)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'I don't swim' and 'I can't swim' look similar, so learners default to 안. But when an ability or obstacle is involved, Korean wants 못. 안 수영해요 means you choose not to; 수영 못 해요 means you're unable.

grammarNotes.title: -지 않아요 — the longer / written negation
grammarNotes.func: Attach -지 않아요 to a verb or adjective stem for the 'long form' of negation. It means the same as 안, but is a little more formal and is common in writing, careful speech, and longer sentences. It works smoothly with every verb and adjective, including 하다 verbs (no splitting).

examples.en: I don't eat meat.
examples.note: 먹다 → 먹지 않아요; same meaning as 안 먹어요 but sounds a touch more formal or written.

examples.en: That shop isn't expensive.
examples.note: Works with adjectives too: 비싸다 → 비싸지 않아요 (= 안 비싸요).

examples.en: I don't smoke.
examples.note: A clean way to state a habit you don't do; common on forms and in polite explanations.

examples.en: I don't exercise these days.
examples.note: With 하다 verbs there is NO split: 운동하 + 지 않아요. Compare the spoken 운동 안 해요.

keyPoint.label: 안 vs -지 않아요
keyPoint.body: They mean the same thing. 안 먹어요 = 먹지 않아요 (I don't eat). 안 is short and spoken; -지 않아요 is longer and slightly more formal or written. Bonus: 하다 verbs DON'T split with -지 않아요 (운동하지 않아요), unlike 운동 안 해요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 않아요 is pronounced [아나요] — the ㅎ in 않 is silent and the ㄴ links into the following vowel: 가지 않아요 → [가지 아나요]. The ㅎ never makes its own sound here.

drill.instruction: Convert each verb or adjective to the long negative with -지 않아요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Two errors are common: splitting 안 out as a separate word, and misspelling the ending. The fixed ending is one unit, -지 않아요 [지 아나요]. Don't insert 안 separately, and don't write 않어요.

grammarNotes.title: N이/가 없어요 — absence / "don't have"
grammarNotes.func: 없어요 is the verb for 'there isn't / I don't have.' It is the opposite of 있어요 (there is / have). The noun takes the subject marker 이/가, and 없어요 covers both 'don't possess' and 'isn't present / doesn't exist.'

examples.en: I don't have time right now.
examples.note: 시간 ends in a consonant, so 시간이; 없어요 = don't have. Pronounced [시가니 업써요].

examples.en: I don't have a car.
examples.note: 차 ends in a vowel, so the marker is 가. 없어요 here means 'don't possess.'

examples.en: There's no milk in the fridge.
examples.note: Same 없어요 also means 'isn't there / doesn't exist' — the absence of a thing in a place. 우유 ends in a vowel → 우유가.

examples.en: I don't have any plans today.
examples.note: 없어요 negates having something (약속 = plans/an appointment); 약속 ends in a consonant → 약속이.

keyPoint.label: 없어요 vs 안 + verb
keyPoint.body: For NOT HAVING or NOT EXISTING, use 없어요, never 안 있어요. 안 있어요 is wrong. So 'no time' = 시간이 없어요 (○), not 시간이 안 있어요 (✗). 안 negates actions and qualities; 없어요 negates existence and possession.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 없어요 is pronounced [업써요]: the ㅂㅅ cluster keeps the ㅂ [p] sound, and the ㅅ links to the next vowel as a tense [ss]. So 시간이 없어요 → [시가니 업써요].

drill.instruction: Say you don't have each thing using 이/가 없어요. Choose the right marker by the noun's last sound.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'I don't have time' tempts learners to negate 있어요 with 안. Korean has a dedicated negative verb 없어요 for this; 안 있어요 sounds wrong to native ears. Memorize 있어요 ↔ 없어요 as a pair.

grammarNotes.title: Boundary check — 안 vs 못 vs 아니에요 vs 싫어요
grammarNotes.func: Korean splits the English word 'not' across several forms, and choosing the wrong one sounds off. This note sorts them: 안 = don't/won't (choice or fact), 못 = can't (blocked), 아니에요 = 'it's not [a noun]' (identity), 싫어요 = 'I don't like it / I don't want to' (dislike or refusal). Match the form to the meaning, not to the English word.

formTable.when: Choice / plain fact about an action or quality

examples.en: I'm not going today.
examples.note: A choice or plan — plain negation of the action, so 안.

examples.en: I can't go today because I'm busy.
examples.note: Something blocks the action (being busy), so 못, not 안.

examples.en: This isn't my bag.
examples.note: Saying a noun is NOT something uses 아니에요, never 안 — 안 가방이에요 is wrong.

examples.en: I don't like spicy food.
examples.note: Dislike, not inability: 싫어요. (못 먹어요 would mean 'I can't eat it.')

keyPoint.label: One English 'not,' four Korean choices
keyPoint.body: Ask what kind of 'not' it is. Action by choice → 안. Action blocked → 못. 'It's not [a noun]' → 아니에요. 'I don't like / don't want' → 싫어요. Picking by feeling, not by the English word, is the whole skill of this chapter.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 아니에요 → [아니에요], four clear syllables, no linking trick. 싫어요 → [시러요]: the ㅎ in 싫 is silent and the ㄹ links into the vowel, so it sounds like [시러요], not [실허요].

drill.instruction: Choose 안, 못, 아니에요, or 싫어요 for each meaning.
items: 'I'm not going today (I just won't)' → 오늘은 ____ 가요
'This isn't my phone' → 이건 제 폰이 ____

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 이건 제 가방 안 이에요 / 저는 그게 안 좋아요 (meaning 'I hate it')
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 이건 제 가방이 아니에요 / 저는 그게 싫어요
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Two traps: (1) you can't negate 이에요/예요 with 안 — to say a noun is NOT something, use 아니에요. (2) For strong dislike or refusal, 싫어요 is the natural word; 안 좋아요 just means 'not good,' which is milder and can sound evasive.

extendedDialogue.setting: A friend clarifies whether a refusal is about choice, schedule, or a real restriction.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 오늘 모임에는 못 가요. 시간이 없어요.
lines.romanization: oneul moimeneun mot gayo. sigani eopseoyo.
lines.en: I cannot go to the gathering today. I do not have time.
lines.grammarNote: 못 marks the blocked action; 시간이 없어요 gives the absent resource.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 안 가는 거예요, 아니면 정말 못 가는 거예요?
lines.romanization: an ganeun geoyeyo, animyeon jeongmal mot ganeun geoyeyo?
lines.en: Are you choosing not to go, or are you really unable to go?
lines.grammarNote: This line directly contrasts 안 and 못.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 가기 싫은 건 아니에요. 야근 때문에 못 가요.
lines.romanization: gagi silheun geon anieyo. yageun ttaemune mot gayo.
lines.en: It is not that I do not want to go. I cannot go because of overtime.
lines.grammarNote: 아니에요 rejects the claim; 못 gives the real reason.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Then at the company dinner, do you not eat meat?
lines.grammarNote: 안 먹어요 asks about habit, choice, or preference.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 싫어서 안 먹는 게 아니라 알레르기가 있어서 못 먹어요.
lines.romanization: silheoseo an meongneun ge anira allereugiga isseoseo mot meogeoyo.
lines.en: It is not that I avoid it because I dislike it; I cannot eat it because I have an allergy.
lines.grammarNote: 알레르기 makes 못 the right choice.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 그럼 어렵지 않게 다른 메뉴로 예약할게요.
lines.romanization: geureom eoryeopji anke dareun menyuro yeyakhalgeyo.
lines.en: Then I will reserve a different menu so it is not difficult.
lines.grammarNote: -지 않게 gives a careful adjective negation.

readingText.title: 안 가요와 못 가요는 같은 말이 아니에요
readingText.body: 친구의 초대를 거절할 때 '안 가요'와 '못 가요'는 느낌이 달라요. '안 가요'는 내가 가지 않기로 한 선택처럼 들릴 수 있고, '못 가요'는 시간, 일, 건강 같은 이유 때문에 갈 수 없다는 뜻이에요. 그래서 '시간이 없어서 못 가요'라고 말하면 오해가 줄어요. 음식도 마찬가지예요. '고기는 안 먹어요'는 취향이나 습관처럼 들릴 수 있지만, '알레르기가 있어서 못 먹어요'는 몸의 제한을 설명해요. 더 조심스럽게 말하고 싶을 때는 '싫지 않아요', '어렵지 않아요', '먹지 않아요'처럼 -지 않아요를 쓸 수 있어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: When declining an invitation, 안 가요 and 못 가요 do not feel the same. 안 가요 can sound like a choice, while 못 가요 says you cannot go because of time, work, health, or another limit. Food works similarly: 고기는 안 먹어요 may sound like preference or habit, but 알레르기가 있어서 못 먹어요 explains a physical restriction. For careful clarification, use -지 않아요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 안 가요는 어떤 느낌으로 들릴 수 있어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 내가 가지 않기로 한 선택처럼 들릴 수 있어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 알레르기가 있을 때 왜 못 먹어요가 자연스러워요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 취향이 아니라 몸의 제한 때문에 먹을 수 없다는 뜻이기 때문이에요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 조심스럽게 부정하거나 설명할 때 어떤 형태를 쓸 수 있어요?

culturalNote.title: Soft refusals often hide the exact negative
culturalNote.body: Korean speakers often soften refusals with phrases like 오늘은 좀 어려울 것 같아요 instead of a blunt 안 가요 or 못 가요. That phrase may mean 'I cannot make it' without naming the full reason. Still, when you do give a reason, choosing 안, 못, 없다, or -지 않다 correctly prevents misunderstanding.
culturalNote.tip: If the listener might think you simply do not want to, add the reason: 시간이 없어서 못 가요, 알레르기가 있어서 못 먹어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence says circumstances make it impossible to go?
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 marks inability or a blocked situation.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence best explains a medical food restriction?
inlineExercises.explanation: 알레르기 is an outside restriction, so 못 먹어요 is natural.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses absence as the reason?
inlineExercises.explanation: 없어요 negates the existence/possession of time.

inlineExercises.prompt: Careful adjective negation: 이 일은 어렵____ 않아요.
inlineExercises.explanation: Adjective stem + -지 않아요: 어렵지 않아요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which pair correctly contrasts choice and inability?
inlineExercises.explanation: 안 often marks not doing or choosing not to; 못 marks inability or blocked action.

inlineExercises.prompt: 시간___ 없어요. (I do not have time.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 없어요 uses 이/가 for the thing that is absent. 시간 is not an object of an action here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 오늘은 회의가 있어서 ___ . (가다 → cannot)
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 marks that something blocks the action. A meeting is the blocker, so 못 가요 is more natural than 안 가요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I cannot eat meat because of an allergy.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 때문에 gives the medical reason, and 못 marks inability. 고기 is what cannot be eaten, so 고기를 is the object.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say carefully: 'This work is not difficult.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -지 않아요 is the longer, careful negative. It often sounds more measured than a short 안 negative.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '고기가 못 먹어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: The meat is the thing you cannot eat, so it takes 를. 가 would make meat the subject, which changes the structure.

bullets: 안: simple negative or choice, as in 오늘은 안 가요.
못: blocked action or inability, as in 시간이 없어서 못 가요.
-지 않아요: careful or written negation, as in 어렵지 않아요.
없어요: absence or not having, as in 시간이 없어요.
Do not translate every English 'not' the same way. Decide what is being denied.

writingTask.prompt: Write a short reply explaining why you can't join an outing today, using different negatives correctly.
writingTask.hint: Use 안 (don't/won't, a choice), 못 (can't, blocked), -지 않아요 (longer negation), and N이/가 없어요 (don't have): e.g. 시간이 없어요, 못 가요.
writingTask.model: 오늘은 시간이 없어요. 그래서 못 가요. 저는 고기를 안 먹어요. 운동도 별로 좋아하지 않아요.
writingTask.modelEn: I don't have time today. So I can't go. I don't eat meat. I don't really like exercise either.

canDo: Negate by choice or fact with 안 (안 먹어요)
Say you can't because something blocks you with 못 (시간이 없어서 못 가요)
Use the longer written negation -지 않아요 (좋아하지 않아요)
Express absence or 'don't have' with N이/가 없어요 (시간이 없어요)

chapters.title: 이다 Deep Dive
chapters.goal: Build longer noun phrases and describe passive situations clearly.
chapters.scenario: A door is closed, a file was uploaded, or a thing you found needs description.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What are you going to do this weekend?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: I am going to meet a friend and go to a cafe.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: What if it rains?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: If it rains, I am going to study at home.

chapters.guidedPractice: Choose one role noun and one time noun, then make five sentences: past identity, background, reason with 라서, reason with 니까, and a fallback with 라도.
chapters.realLifeTask: Describe one object with a modifier and one passive result.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner asks about your role or schedule; answer with 학생이었어요, 회사원인데요, 주말이라서, 주말이니까, or 한 시간이라도.
chapters.review: Can you explain why 학생, 회사원, 주말, 평일, 아침, and 시간 fit this chapter better than random nouns?

beginnerGuide.title: 이다 changes nouns into sentence material
beginnerGuide.body: This chapter should start from nouns that naturally become identity or schedule explanations: 학생이었어요, 회사원인데요, 주말이라서, 평일이니까.

beginnerGuide.title: 라서 explains; 니까 often leads to action
beginnerGuide.body: 회사원이라서 한국어가 필요해요 simply explains the cause. 주말이니까 공부해요 sounds more like a reason for a decision or suggestion.

beginnerGuide.title: 라도 is the fallback marker
beginnerGuide.body: 한 시간이라도 공부해요 means one hour is not ideal, but it is still worth doing. That is why 시간 is a useful core noun here.

checkpoints: I can make a noun phrase before the noun.
I can use passive forms when the subject receives the action.
I can avoid mixing passive and causative meanings.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Build longer noun phrases and describe passive situations clearly.
exitTask.prompt: Describe one object with a modifier and one passive result.

sampleAnswer.ko: 어제 받은 파일이 열리지 않아요.
sampleAnswer.en: The file I received yesterday will not open.

checklist: I can make a noun phrase before the noun.
I can use passive forms when the subject receives the action.
I can avoid mixing passive and causative meanings.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You are explaining who you were, who you are now, and why your schedule works the way it does. This is where 이다 stops being only 이에요/예요 and becomes a tool for identity, reason, contrast, and fallback options.
objectives: Turn role nouns into past identity: 학생이었어요, 회사원이었어요.
Use noun background and contrast with 인데/인데도.
Choose 라서, 니까, and 라도 based on explanation, decision, or minimum acceptable option.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean often explains a situation through what something is: 학생이라서, 회사원이니까, 주말이라서. If the vocabulary is random, the grammar feels random too. This chapter uses role nouns and time nouns because they naturally carry the 이다 forms.

grammarNotes.title: N이었어요 / N였어요 — "It was an N" (past of 이다)
grammarNotes.func: Says what something was in the past — an identity, role, or category that was true before now: "It was my birthday," "She was a student," "Yesterday was the weekend." It is just 이다 put into the past polite form.

formTable.ex: 주말이었어 / 친구였어 (was the weekend / was a friend)

examples.en: Yesterday was my birthday.
examples.note: 생일 ends in a consonant (ㄹ), so it takes the full 이었어요.

examples.en: That person was my friend.
examples.note: 친구 ends in a vowel, so 이었어요 shortens to 였어요.

examples.en: Last year I was a student too.
examples.note: 학생 ends in a consonant → 이었어요; 작년 (last year) sets the past time.

examples.en: That wasn't my umbrella.
examples.note: Past negative uses 아니다 → 아니었어요, never 였어요.

keyPoint.label: 이었어요 vs 였어요 — just a sound rule
keyPoint.body: Both are the same past form of 이다. After a consonant, keep the full 이었어요 (학생이었어요). After a vowel, 이었어요 shrinks to 였어요 (친구였어요). The meaning is identical — only the spelling and sound change, based on the noun's final letter.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 학생이었어요 links across the boundary and sounds like [학쌩이어써요]; 친구였어요 sounds like [친구여써요].

drill.instruction: Add the correct past form (이었어요 or 였어요) to each noun.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners grab 였어요 because it is shorter, but 였어요 only attaches to vowel-final nouns. 학생 ends in a consonant, so it needs the full 이었어요. Choose the ending by the noun's last letter, not by what is easier to say.

grammarNotes.title: N인데 / N인데도 — "it's N, and… / even though it's N"
grammarNotes.func: Attaches to a noun to set the scene before the main clause: "It's the weekend, so…/and…" (인데), or to mark a mild contrast "even though it's N" (인데도). 인데 softens a statement and leads into the rest; 인데도 adds "despite that."

formTable.ex: 여기 제 자리인데요. (Um, this is my seat…)

examples.en: It's the weekend today, so where shall we go?
examples.note: 인데 gives the noun (주말) as background leading into a suggestion.

examples.en: It's my first time, so please be kind to me.
examples.note: 처음 (first time) + 인데 sets up the polite request.

examples.en: Even though it's the weekend, I go to work.
examples.note: 인데도 = 인데 + 도, marking contrast: "despite it being the weekend."

examples.en: We're in the same class, but I don't know their name.
examples.note: 인데 here leans contrastive — "it's the case that…, yet…"

keyPoint.label: 인데 vs 인데도
keyPoint.body: 인데 is neutral: it just hands you a noun-fact as a lead-in, and context decides whether it means "so" or "but." 인데도 is clearly concessive — it always means "even though it's N," and the next clause is something surprising. Add 도 only when you want the firm "despite" feeling.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 인데 sounds like [인데] with no change; 인데도 sounds like [인데도], the 도 stays plain.

drill.instruction: Turn each noun into a background clause with 인데, then say the 인데도 version.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 인데 comes from 이다, so a noun needs the 이 (학생 + 이 + ㄴ데 → 학생인데). Learners drop the 인 and stick 는데 straight onto the noun as if it were a verb. 는데 is for verbs and adjectives; 인데 is the noun version.

grammarNotes.title: N이라서 / 라서 — "because it is N"
grammarNotes.func: Gives a reason that is a noun fact: "Because it's the weekend, the shop is closed," "Because I'm a beginner, it's hard." It is the 이다 version of the reason ending -아서/어서.

examples.en: Because it's the weekend today, the shop is closed.
examples.note: 주말 ends in a consonant → 이라서.

examples.en: Because I'm a beginner, I'll go slowly.
examples.note: 초보 ends in a vowel → 라서.

examples.en: Because it's a weekday, there's nobody around.
examples.note: 평일 (consonant-final) + 이라서 gives the reason.

examples.en: Because I'm not family, I can't go in.
examples.note: Noun negative reason: 아니다 → 아니라서.

keyPoint.label: 이라서 vs verb -아서/어서
keyPoint.body: For verbs and adjectives you say -아서/어서 (먹어서, 좋아서). For nouns you must run the reason through 이다 → 이라서/라서. So "because it's a student" is 학생이라서, never 학생어서. Reach for the noun form whenever the reason is a noun.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 학생이라서 sounds like [학쌩이라서]. The [쌩] is just how 학생 is always said — the ㄱ받침 of 학 tenses the 생; 이라서 itself adds no new tensing.

drill.instruction: Give the reason form (이라서 or 라서) for each noun.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 이어서/여서 is correct grammar but sounds formal or bookish in speech. In everyday conversation Koreans overwhelmingly say 이라서/라서. Both are right; pick 이라서/라서 to sound natural when you're talking.

grammarNotes.title: N이니까 / 니까 — "since it is N, so…"
grammarNotes.func: Gives a reason with a "since you know this, therefore let's…" feel — strong for backing up a command, suggestion, or decision: "Since it's the weekend, let's study," "Since it's my birthday, I'll treat you." It is the 이다 version of -(으)니까.

formTable.ex: 주말이니까 같이 공부해요 (it's the weekend, so let's study together)
애기가 아니니까 (since you're not a baby)

examples.en: Since it's the weekend today, let's study together.
examples.note: 주말 (consonant-final) + 이니까 backs up the suggestion.

examples.en: Since we're friends, it's okay.
examples.note: 친구 ends in a vowel → 니까.

examples.en: Since it's my birthday today, I'll treat you.
examples.note: 이니까 supports the speaker's decision (제가 살게요).

examples.en: Since it's a weekday, please go to bed early.
examples.note: 이니까 + command 자세요 — a natural pairing that 이라서 avoids.

keyPoint.label: 이니까 vs 이라서
keyPoint.body: Both mean "because it's N," but 이니까 is the one you use before commands and suggestions (조용히 하세요, 같이 공부해요) and when the reason is shared or obvious. 이라서 is more about plain cause and sounds off before a command. Rule of thumb: order or invite → 이니까; just explain → 이라서.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 주말이니까 sounds like [주마리니까]; 까 is written with ㄲ, so it is always tense.

drill.instruction: Make a "since it's N, so…" clause using 이니까 / 니까.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Before a suggestion (같이 공부해요) or command (하세요), Koreans use 이니까, not 이라서. 이라서 is for plainly stating a cause; it sounds unnatural right before "let's…" or an order. When your sentence ends in a suggestion or command, switch the noun reason to 이니까/니까.

grammarNotes.title: N이라도 / 라도 — "even just an N / at least N"
grammarNotes.func: Marks a noun as a not-ideal-but-acceptable fallback: "Let's study even just one hour," "Have at least some water." It says "this isn't the best option, but it'll do." It is the 이다 form behind the 라도 fallback marker.

formTable.ex: 물이라도 드세요 (at least have some water)
주말이라도 (even on the weekend, at least)

examples.en: Since it's the weekend, let's study together even if just for one hour.
examples.note: 시간 ends in a consonant → 이라도; one hour isn't much, but it's still worth it.

examples.en: If you're busy, let's at least grab a coffee.
examples.note: 커피 ends in a vowel → 라도; coffee as a quick fallback plan.

examples.en: If you're hungry, at least have some bread.
examples.note: 빵 (consonant-final) + 이라도 offers a fallback food.

examples.en: If you have no time, do a little even just in the morning.
examples.note: 아침에 + 라도 — "even at/in the morning" as a fallback time.

keyPoint.label: 라도 = "not the best, but okay"
keyPoint.body: 이라도/라도 picks a noun that isn't your first choice but is good enough: 한 시간이라도 (even just one hour), 커피라도 (at least a coffee). Use 이라도 after a consonant and 라도 after a vowel — the same sound split you see in 이라서/라서 and 이니까/니까.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 한 시간이라도 sounds like [한 시가니라도]; 커피라도 sounds like [커피라도], no special change.

drill.instruction: Add the fallback form (이라도 or 라도) to each noun.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 시간 ends in a consonant (ㄴ), so it needs 이라도, not 라도. Learners default to the shorter 라도 everywhere, but 라도 only goes on vowel-final nouns (커피라도). Check the noun's last letter first, just like with 이라서 and 이니까.

exampleSentence.en: I was a student last year.
exampleSentence.note: Core role noun for N이었어요/였어요, N이라서, and N이니까.

exampleSentence.en: Even though I am an office worker now, I keep studying.
exampleSentence.note: Better fit than a random job word because it explains a busy adult schedule.

exampleSentence.en: I am an employee, but I am not the person in charge.
exampleSentence.note: Useful for soft background with 인데요.

exampleSentence.en: I was a student last year.
exampleSentence.note: Time anchor for past identity.

exampleSentence.en: This year I am an office worker.
exampleSentence.note: Pairs naturally with 작년 when comparing past and present identity.

exampleSentence.en: Since it is the weekend, let's study even if just for one hour.
exampleSentence.note: Time noun that naturally supports 니까 and 라도 practice.

exampleSentence.en: Because it is a weekday, I cannot do it for long.
exampleSentence.note: Useful contrast with 주말 for schedule-based reasons.

exampleSentence.en: Would even morning be okay?
exampleSentence.note: Works as a fallback time when the better time is unavailable.

exampleSentence.en: Let's study even if it is just one hour.
exampleSentence.note: A high-value noun for 라도 because learners often negotiate minimum time.

exampleSentence.en: Try asking at least one question.
exampleSentence.note: A small action that fits the minimum-option meaning of 라도.

exampleSentence.en: Because I am a student, I can get a discount.
exampleSentence.note: Shows why 학생 is not just an identity word but a real reason in daily life.

extendedDialogue.setting: Two learners are scheduling study time while explaining role and time with 이다 forms.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Were you a student last year?
lines.grammarNote: 학생이었어요 is past identity: noun + 이었어요.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Yes, even though I am an office worker now, I keep studying.
lines.grammarNote: 회사원인데도 gives role-based contrast.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Because you are an office worker, do you need Korean more?
lines.grammarNote: 회사원이라서 explains the cause through the role.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네. 평일에는 바쁘니까 아침에만 조금 해요.
lines.romanization: ne. pyeongireneun bappeunikka achimenman jogeum haeyo.
lines.en: Yes. Since weekdays are busy, I only do a little in the morning.
lines.grammarNote: The sentence uses 평일 as the schedule frame; the next line uses 주말이니까 for an 이다-based reason.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 그럼 주말이니까 한 시간이라도 같이 공부해요.
lines.romanization: geureom jumarinikka han siganirado gachi gongbuhaeyo.
lines.en: Then since it is the weekend, let's study together even if just for one hour.
lines.grammarNote: 주말이니까 gives the reason; 한 시간이라도 marks a minimum acceptable amount.

readingText.title: 회사원인데도 계속 공부해요
readingText.body: 지훈은 작년에는 학생이었어요. 올해는 회사원인데도 한국어를 계속 공부해요. 회사원이라서 회의와 이메일에서 한국어가 더 필요해요. 평일은 바쁘니까 아침에만 조금 공부하고, 주말이니까 한 시간이라도 친구와 같이 공부해요. 시간이 많지 않아도 역할 명사와 시간 명사를 잘 고르면 이다 표현을 자연스럽게 쓸 수 있어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Jihun was a student last year. This year, even though he is an office worker, he keeps studying Korean. Because he is an office worker, he needs Korean more in meetings and email. Weekdays are busy, so he studies only a little in the morning, and since it is the weekend, he studies with a friend even if just for one hour. Even without much time, choosing role nouns and time nouns well makes the 이다 forms feel natural.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 지훈은 작년에 무엇이었어요?
지훈은 왜 한국어가 더 필요해요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 회사원이라서 회의와 이메일에서 한국어가 더 필요해요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 주말에는 얼마나 공부해요?

culturalNote.title: Roles often become reasons
culturalNote.body: In Korean, a role noun can explain a lot with very few words. 학생이라서요 can explain a discount, a question, or limited knowledge. 회사원이라서요 can explain why business Korean matters. The important point is not memorizing random nouns; it is choosing nouns that naturally justify the next sentence.
culturalNote.tip: When choosing between 라서 and 니까, ask what the next sentence does. If it simply explains, 라서 is often enough. If it leads to a decision, suggestion, or permission, 니까 often sounds clearer.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly says 'I was a student last year'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 학생 ends in a consonant, so the past copula is 학생이었어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Choose the soft explanation: 'Because I am an office worker, I need Korean.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 이라서 gives a cause based on what someone is. 라도 means fallback, and 인데도 means contrast.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses 니까 as a reason for a decision?
inlineExercises.explanation: 주말이니까 gives the reason, and 한 시간이라도 gives the minimum study amount.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence marks a minimum acceptable option?
inlineExercises.explanation: 이라도 means 'even if only / at least'. 만 means only, and 이라서 gives a cause.

inlineExercises.prompt: 작년___ 학생이었어요. (Last year, I was a student.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 작년에 marks the time when the identity was true. 에서 would mark an action place, not a year.

inlineExercises.prompt: 작년에 ___ . (학생 → past identity)
inlineExercises.explanation: N이었어요/였어요 is the past of 이다. 학생 ends in a consonant, so it becomes 학생이었어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Since it is the weekend, let's meet in the morning.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -니까 gives a reason that supports the next decision. 주말이니까 sounds like “since it is the weekend.”

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'Even a question is okay.'
inlineExercises.explanation: N이라도 offers a minimum acceptable option. 질문이라도 means even just a question would be okay.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '학생였어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Consonant-ending nouns take 이었어요. 였어요 is for vowel-ending nouns.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence gives a soft noun background?
inlineExercises.explanation: N인데 gives background before the main point. 이라도 and 뿐 do not fit this explanation.

bullets: Past identity: 학생이었어요, 회사원이었어요, 휴가였어요.
Background or contrast: 회사원인데 계속 공부해요, 회사원인데도 계속 공부해요.
Reason: 회사원이라서 explains softly; 주말이니까 can support a decision or suggestion.
Fallback: 한 시간이라도 means one hour is not ideal, but it is enough to act.
Vocabulary fit: roles and time nouns belong here because 이다 forms attach directly to nouns.

writingTask.prompt: Write 3-4 sentences about what your job was last year and what plans you have for the weekend, ending sentences in nouns.
writingTask.hint: Use 이다 forms: N이었어요/였어요 (was), N인데 (it's N, and/so), N이라서/라서 (because it's N), N이니까/니까 (since it's N, so), N이라도/라도 (even just N).
writingTask.model: 작년에 저는 학생이었어요. 올해는 회사원인데 일이 많아요. 내일은 주말이라서 회사에 안 가요. 주말이니까 친구하고 커피라도 마실까요?
writingTask.modelEn: Last year I was a student. This year I'm an office worker, and there's a lot of work. Tomorrow is the weekend, so I won't go to the office. Since it's the weekend, shall we at least grab a coffee with a friend?

canDo: Say what something was in the past (학생이었어요 · 주말이었어요)
Set the scene or mark mild contrast on a noun (회사원인데 · 주말인데도)
Give a noun-based reason (주말이라서 · 주말이니까)
Offer a fallback option with N이라도/라도 (커피라도 마셔요)

beginnerGuide.title: Count people with 명, not 개
beginnerGuide.body: 가족이 몇 명이에요? and 저희 가족은 네 명이에요 are the base sentences. People take 명, and the number before 명 is native Korean: 한, 두, 세, 네, 다섯.

beginnerGuide.title: Sibling terms depend on the speaker
beginnerGuide.body: A male speaker says 형 for an older brother and 누나 for an older sister. A female speaker says 오빠 and 언니. 동생 works for a younger sibling.

beginnerGuide.title: Honor the subject with 께서 and -(으)시-
beginnerGuide.body: 부모님께서 오세요 and 어머니께서 오셨어요 honor the person doing the action. 께서 is for the subject; 께 without 서 marks a respected receiver.

hook.situation: You are introducing your family to someone outside the family and then talking about parents, grandparents, and siblings without sounding too blunt or using the wrong sibling word.
objectives: Describe family size with 저희 가족은 ~ 명이에요.
Choose 형, 오빠, 누나, and 언니 from the speaker's point of view.
Use 께서 with honorific verb forms when parents, grandparents, teachers, or elders are the subject.
hook.whyItMatters: Family vocabulary in Korean is not just a list of relatives. The word you choose tells the listener your relationship, your gendered point of view, and your level of respect. That is why the vocabulary must be tied to real family-introduction scenes.

grammarNotes.title: 저희 가족은 ~ 명이에요 — Saying How Many People Are in Your Family
grammarNotes.func: To tell someone how big your family is, politely. 저희 is the humble form of 우리 ("our"), used to be modest in front of a listener, and 명 is the counter for people. You name the group (저희 가족은 = "my family"), then give the count with a native-Korean number + 명 + 이에요.

formTable.when: Counting people, use a native-Korean number + 명
formTable.ex: 네 명 (four people), 다섯 명 (five people)

formTable.when: Numbers 1–4 change shape right before a counter
formTable.ex: 두 명, 세 명, 네 명 (NOT 둘 명 / 셋 명)

formTable.add: 명 + 이에요 (명 ends in a consonant, so 이에요)

examples.en: There are four people in my family.
examples.note: 저희 (humble "our") + 명 is the standard polite way to give family size; the native number 네 is used before 명.

examples.ko: 저희 가족은 다섯 명이에요. 부모님, 형, 누나, 그리고 저요.
examples.romanization: jeohui gajogeun daseot myeong-ieyo. bumonim, hyeong, nuna, geurigo jeoyo.
examples.en: There are five people in my family: my parents, older brother, older sister, and me.
examples.note: Shows how to break the number down into members; 저요 ("and me") naturally closes the list.

examples.en: There are three people in my family.
examples.note: 우리 (plain "our") is fine with friends; 저희 is the more polite choice with strangers or elders.

examples.en: How many people are in your family?
examples.note: 몇 명 ("how many people?") is the question your answer responds to.

keyPoint.label: 명 vs. 분 for counting people
keyPoint.body: 명 is the neutral people-counter and is correct for your own family: 저희 가족은 네 명이에요. When you respectfully count other people (elders, guests), use 분 instead: 손님 세 분 (three guests). You always count your OWN family with 명, never 분, because you don't elevate your own in-group when speaking to others.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 가족은 links across the 받침: 가족 + 은 → [가조근]. The same happens in 가족이 → [가조기]. The final ㄱ of 가족 slides onto the following vowel.

drill.instruction: Say your family size. Fill in the native number that matches the count in parentheses, keeping 명이에요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Native numbers 1–4 take a special shortened shape before a counter: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네. English speakers tend to keep the standalone form (넷) and say 넷 명, but before 명 it must become 네 명.

grammarNotes.title: 형 / 오빠 / 누나 / 언니 — Older-Sibling Words That Depend on YOUR Gender
grammarNotes.func: To name an older brother or older sister. Korean has no single word for "older brother" or "older sister" — the word you pick depends on whether YOU (the speaker) are male or female. A man and a woman use completely different words for the very same person.

examples.en: (male speaker) My older brother works at a company.
examples.note: A boy calls his older brother 형; 오빠 would be wrong here for a male speaker.

examples.en: (female speaker) My older brother is tall.
examples.note: A girl calls her older brother 오빠 — same person, different word from a boy's 형.

examples.en: (male speaker) I have two older sisters.
examples.note: A boy's older sister is 누나; the counter 명 is used, with 두 (not 둘) before it.

examples.en: (female speaker) I live with my older sister.
examples.note: A girl's older sister is 언니; ~랑 ("with") is common in casual talk about family.

keyPoint.label: The word encodes the SPEAKER's gender, not the sibling's
keyPoint.body: Picture a 2×2 grid. Older brother: 형 (said by a male) vs. 오빠 (said by a female). Older sister: 누나 (said by a male) vs. 언니 (said by a female). The same older brother is 형 to his younger brother and 오빠 to his younger sister at the same time. Younger siblings have no gendered split — they are just 동생 (남동생 = younger brother, 여동생 = younger sister).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 오빠's ㅃ is a tense, slightly held stop. 언니 → [언니] keeps both ㄴ sounds clear. 형은 → [형은], with the ㅇ (ng) carrying over softly; no tensing here.

drill.instruction: Choose the correct older-sibling word for the speaker's gender given in parentheses.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: (a male speaker) 우리 오빠는 키가 커요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: (a male speaker) 우리 형은 키가 커요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English has one word, "older brother," so learners grab whichever Korean word they heard first — often 오빠 from K-pop. But 오빠 is only for FEMALE speakers. A male speaker must say 형. Always ask first: who is talking, a man or a woman?

grammarNotes.title: 부모님 / 아버지 / 어머니 — Respectful Words for Parents
grammarNotes.func: To talk about your parents respectfully. These are the polite nouns for family elders. 부모님 = "parents" (with the honorific suffix ~님), 아버지 = "father," 어머니 = "mother." They contrast with the casual 아빠 (dad) and 엄마 (mom) that children use at home.

examples.en: My parents live in Busan.
examples.note: 부모님 + the honorific verb 사세요 (from 살다) elevate the parents — the natural pairing for elders.

examples.en: My father is a teacher.
examples.note: 아버지 (not 아빠) is the respectful choice when speaking to people outside the family; ~세요 honors him.

examples.en: My mother makes kimchi.
examples.note: 어머니 pairs naturally with the honorific subject marker 께서 and 만드세요 (from 만들다).

examples.en: Dad, where are we going?
examples.note: A child speaking straight to their own father at home uses casual 아빠 — natural in-family address, unlike the formal 아버지.

keyPoint.label: 아버지/어머니 (respectful) vs. 아빠/엄마 (casual)
keyPoint.body: Use 아버지/어머니 when you describe your parents TO other people, in writing, or in any polite setting — they show respect. Use 아빠/엄마 to ADDRESS your own parents at home or among close family, like English "Dad/Mom" vs. "father/mother." 부모님 always carries ~님 and has no casual short form.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 부모님은 links the 받침: 부모님 + 은 → [부모니믄], the ㅁ carrying onto 은. 선생님이세요 → [선생니미세요] in the same way.

drill.instruction: Replace the casual word with the respectful word to make each sentence polite for outsiders.
drill.model: 우리 아빠는 회사원이에요. → 저희 아버지는 회사원이세요.
items: 우리 아빠는 운동을 좋아해요. → 저희 ___는 운동을 좋아하세요.
우리 엄마 아빠는 집에 있어요. → 저희 ___은 집에 계세요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저희 엄마는 의사예요. (in a polite self-introduction)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English uses "my mom" comfortably even in semi-formal speech, so learners say 엄마 everywhere. In Korean, 엄마/아빠 sound childish when you introduce your family to strangers or elders. Switch to 어머니/아버지 (and 부모님 with ~님) to be polite.

grammarNotes.title: N께서 V-(으)시- — Honoring a Family Elder Who Does the Action
grammarNotes.func: To honor the person doing the action — usually a family elder like a parent or grandparent. Two pieces work together: 께서 replaces the subject marker 이/가 (or 은/는) to lift up the subject, and the verb takes the honorific infix ~(으)시~, which surfaces as ~세요/~으세요 in polite speech.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel + honorific
Verb stem ends in a consonant + honorific

examples.en: My grandfather reads the newspaper.
examples.note: 할아버지께서 marks the honored subject; 읽다 (consonant stem) → 읽으세요 with the ~으세요 form.

examples.en: My mother is in the room.
examples.note: 있다 has the special honorific 계시다, not 있으세요 — use 계세요 for an elder's location/presence.

examples.en: My father is eating dinner.
examples.note: 먹다 becomes the honorific 드시다 → 드세요; you never say 먹으세요 about an elder.

examples.en: My grandmother goes to bed early.
examples.note: 자다 becomes the honorific 주무시다 → 주무세요; a fully irregular special form to memorize.

keyPoint.label: 께서 and the honorific verb travel together
keyPoint.body: Honoring is a two-part move: 께서 lifts the subject AND the verb takes ~(으)시~. Marking only one feels incomplete — 아버지께서 가요 (no honorific on the verb) sounds broken. Also, you can be humble about yourself with 저희 while still honoring your elders: 저희 어머니께서 만드세요 is natural. Just never apply 께서/~세요 to yourself — you don't honor your own actions.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 읽으세요 → [일그세요]: the ㄺ cluster splits, ㄱ moving onto the 으. 계세요 → [게세요] in casual speech (the ㅖ often flattens to ㅔ). 께서 keeps its tense ㄲ at the start.

drill.instruction: Rewrite each plain sentence to honor the elder: change 이/가 to 께서 and put the verb in the honorific ~(으)세요 form (watch for special verbs).
drill.model: 아버지가 신문을 읽어요. → 아버지께서 신문을 읽으세요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners remember to add 께서 but then forget to honor the VERB, leaving a plain form like 먹어요 or 있어요. Honoring must reach the verb too — and some verbs have special honorific forms (먹다→드시다, 있다→계시다, 자다→주무시다) that you cannot build with ~으세요. So it's 드세요, not 먹으세요.

exampleSentence.en: There are four people in my family.
exampleSentence.note: Core word for polite family introductions.

exampleSentence.en: How many people are in your family?
exampleSentence.note: Pairs with 명 for family size.

exampleSentence.en: There are five people in my family.
exampleSentence.note: People take 명, not 개.

exampleSentence.en: My parents are coming to the wedding too.
exampleSentence.note: Respected family noun plus 께서.

exampleSentence.en: My father is coming too.
exampleSentence.note: Use 아버지 in polite introductions.

exampleSentence.en: My mother came.
exampleSentence.note: Use 어머니 in polite introductions.

exampleSentence.en: I have one older brother.
exampleSentence.note: Used by a male speaker.

exampleSentence.en: I have one older brother.
exampleSentence.note: Used by a female speaker.

exampleSentence.en: I have one older sister.
exampleSentence.note: Used by a male speaker.

exampleSentence.en: I have one older sister.
exampleSentence.note: Used by a female speaker.

exampleSentence.en: I have one younger sibling.
exampleSentence.note: Works regardless of the speaker's gender.

exampleSentence.en: My grandfather is coming.
exampleSentence.note: Good noun for practicing 께서.

exampleSentence.en: Please send my regards to your grandmother.
exampleSentence.note: 께 marks a respected receiver; 께서 marks a respected subject.

exampleSentence.en: My parents are coming to the wedding too.
exampleSentence.note: A natural event where family members are introduced politely.

exampleSentence.en: My mother came.
exampleSentence.note: 오다 becomes 오세요/오셨어요 when honoring the subject.

exampleSentence.en: I often call my parents.
exampleSentence.note: Useful family-contact verb; 전화드려요 is the more respectful version.

extendedDialogue.setting: A learner introduces family and checks sibling terms before a friend's wedding.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: How many people are in your family?
lines.grammarNote: 몇 명 asks about people, not objects.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 저희 가족은 다섯 명이에요. 부모님하고 형, 동생이 있어요.
lines.romanization: jeohui gajogeun daseot myeongieyo. bumonimhago hyeong, dongsaengi isseoyo.
lines.en: There are five people in my family. I have my parents, an older brother, and a younger sibling.
lines.grammarNote: 저희 sounds polite because 민서 is outside the family group.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Hyeong is the word a male speaker uses, right?
lines.grammarNote: 형 is chosen from the speaker's perspective.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네. 여자가 부르면 오빠라고 해요. 누나와 언니도 달라요.
lines.romanization: ne. yeojaga bureumyeon opparago haeyo. nuna-wa eonnido dallayo.
lines.en: Yes. If a female speaker says it, she says oppa. Nuna and eonni are different too.
lines.grammarNote: 오빠/형 and 언니/누나 divide by speaker gender.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Are your parents coming to the wedding too?
lines.grammarNote: 께서도 honors the parents as subject and adds also.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Yes, my mother is coming, and my father is coming too.
lines.grammarNote: 오시고/오세요 are honorific forms of 오다.

readingText.title: 저희 가족은 다섯 명이에요
readingText.body: 지훈은 회사 동료에게 가족을 소개했어요. '저희 가족은 다섯 명이에요. 부모님하고 형, 동생이 있어요.'라고 말했어요. 지훈은 남자라서 자기보다 나이 많은 남자 형제를 형이라고 불러요. 여자가 같은 사람을 부르면 오빠가 돼요. 나이 많은 여자 형제도 남자가 말하면 누나, 여자가 말하면 언니예요. 친구 결혼식 이야기를 할 때는 '어머니께서 오시고 아버지께서도 오세요'라고 말했어요. 가족 이야기는 단어 선택과 높임 선택이 같이 가야 자연스러워요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Jihun introduced his family to a coworker: 'There are five people in my family. I have my parents, an older brother, and a younger sibling.' Because Jihun is male, he calls an older male sibling hyeong. If a female speaker refers to the same person, the word becomes oppa. For an older female sibling, a male speaker says nuna and a female speaker says eonni. When talking about a friend's wedding, he says, 'My mother is coming, and my father is coming too' with honorific subject language. Family talk sounds natural when word choice and respect level work together.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 지훈의 가족은 몇 명이에요?
남자가 나이 많은 남자 형제를 부를 때 어떤 말을 써요?
지훈은 부모님에 대해 어떤 높임 표현을 썼어요?

culturalNote.title: Family words are social words
culturalNote.body: Korean family terms often travel outside the literal family. 형, 오빠, 누나, and 언니 can be friendly terms for slightly older people, but they are not automatic. In a class, workplace, or first meeting, use names, titles, or neutral polite speech until the relationship is clear.
culturalNote.tip: For polite introductions, start with 저희 가족 and 부모님. Save 엄마, 아빠, 형, 오빠, 누나, and 언니 for contexts where the relationship is close enough.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence describes family size naturally?
inlineExercises.explanation: 명 counts people. 개 counts things, and 잔 counts cups or glasses.

inlineExercises.prompt: A male speaker is talking about his older brother. Which word fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: A male speaker calls an older brother 형. A female speaker calls an older brother 오빠.

inlineExercises.prompt: A female speaker is talking about her older sister. Which word fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: A female speaker calls an older sister 언니. A male speaker calls an older sister 누나.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence honors the mother as the subject?
inlineExercises.explanation: 께서 marks the respected subject, and 오셨어요 is the honorific past of 오다.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses 께 as a respected receiver, not a subject?
inlineExercises.explanation: 께 means to a respected person. 께서 means the respected person is the subject.

inlineExercises.prompt: 어머니___ 오셨어요. (My mother came.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 어머니 is the respected subject, so use 께서. 께 marks a respected receiver instead.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'My family has four people.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 저희 가족은 politely sets the family as the topic. People are counted with 명, and four before a counter is 네.

inlineExercises.prompt: A female speaker says “older sister”: ___.
inlineExercises.explanation: A female speaker calls an older sister 언니. 누나 is used by a male speaker.

inlineExercises.prompt: A male speaker is talking about his older sister. Which word fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: Male speakers use 누나 for older sister. 언니 is from a female speaker’s point of view.

inlineExercises.prompt: 아버지가 지금 ___ . (주무시다 → polite present)
inlineExercises.explanation: 주무시다 is the honorific verb for sleep. In polite present it becomes 주무세요.

bullets: Family size: 저희 가족은 네 명이에요. Use 명 for people, not 개.
Polite self-side: 저희 가족 and 저희 부모님 are natural when speaking to someone outside the family.
Sibling terms: male speaker uses 형/누나; female speaker uses 오빠/언니.
Honorific subject: 부모님께서 오세요, 어머니께서 오셨어요.
Particle boundary: 께서 is subject; 께 is receiver.

writingTask.prompt: Write a short message to a new classmate introducing your family (how many people, an older sibling, and one thing a parent does).
writingTask.hint: Use 저희 가족은 ~ 명이에요 for the size, the right older-sibling word (형/오빠/누나/언니) for your gender, and N께서 V-(으)시- to honor a parent.
writingTask.model: 저희 가족은 네 명이에요. 저는 누나가 한 명 있어요. 아버지께서는 요리를 잘하세요.
writingTask.modelEn: There are four people in my family. I have one older sister. My father cooks well.

canDo: Say how big my family is politely (저희 가족은 ~ 명이에요)
Pick the right older-sibling word for my own gender (형 · 오빠 · 누나 · 언니)
Refer to my parents respectfully (부모님 · 아버지 · 어머니)
Honor a family elder who does the action (아버지께서 ~하세요)

chapters.title: Health and Body
chapters.goal: Explain symptoms and ask for help in a clinic or pharmacy.
chapters.scenario: You have a headache, stomachache, cold, or injury and need simple help.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Where does it hurt? What brings you in?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 아침부터 열이 나고 목이 아파요. 기침도 나요.
dialogue.romanization: achimbuteo yeori nago mogi apayo. gichimdo nayo.
dialogue.en: Since this morning I have had a fever and a sore throat. I also have a cough.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 감기 때문에 그런 것 같아요. 약은 식후에 하루 세 번 드셔야 해요.
dialogue.romanization: gamgi ttaemune geureon geot gatayo. yageun sikhue haru se beon deusyeoya haeyo.
dialogue.en: It seems to be because of a cold. You have to take the medicine three times a day after meals.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 기침 때문에 잠을 못 자면 다시 와야 하나요?
dialogue.romanization: gichim ttaemune jameul mot jamyeon dasi waya hanayo?
dialogue.en: If I cannot sleep because of the cough, should I come back?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 네. 열이 계속 나니까 물을 많이 마시고 쉬세요.
dialogue.romanization: ne. yeori gyesok nanikka mureul mani masigo swiseyo.
dialogue.en: Yes. Since the fever is continuing, drink a lot of water and rest.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make one clinic line for each step: symptom, cause, instruction, warning sign, and pharmacy direction.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say where it hurts, since when, and what you need.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner gives a symptom card; answer with a clinic sentence and one medicine instruction using 식후 or 하루 세 번.
chapters.review: Can you connect symptoms, causes, and instructions without mixing up 열이 나다, 기침이 나다, 아프다, 때문에, and 식후?

beginnerGuide.title: Symptoms often use 이/가
beginnerGuide.body: 목이 아파요, 배가 아파요, 열이 나요, 기침이 나요. The body part or symptom usually becomes the subject.

beginnerGuide.title: Clinic and pharmacy words belong together
beginnerGuide.body: 병원에서 의사에게 증상을 말하고 처방전을 받아요. 약국에서는 약사에게 약 먹는 시간과 식후 지시를 확인해요.

beginnerGuide.title: Instructions need clear timing
beginnerGuide.body: 약은 식후에 하루 세 번 드셔야 해요 means after meals, three times a day. 식후 is not a random health word; it is the timing word on medicine labels.

checkpoints: I can use 아파요 with body parts.
I can use -부터 for when the symptom started.
I can make a polite request at a clinic or pharmacy.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Explain symptoms and ask for help in a clinic or pharmacy.
exitTask.prompt: Say where it hurts, since when, and what you need.

sampleAnswer.ko: 어제부터 목이 아파요. 감기약이 필요해요.
sampleAnswer.en: My throat has hurt since yesterday. I need cold medicine.

checklist: I can use 아파요 with body parts.
I can use -부터 for when the symptom started.
I can make a polite request at a clinic or pharmacy.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You are at a clinic or pharmacy and need to say symptoms clearly, explain what changed your day, and understand medicine instructions before you leave.
objectives: Describe symptoms with body part or symptom + 이/가 + 아프다/나다.
Explain causes with 아파서, 때문에, 니까, or 는 바람에 without mixing their tones.
Understand pharmacy directions like 식후에, 하루 세 번, and 드셔야 해요.
hook.whyItMatters: Health Korean is practical under pressure. A learner does not need random body words here; they need symptom phrases, clinic nouns, pharmacy nouns, and instruction patterns that can be used immediately.

grammarNotes.title: Symptom frame — body part + 이/가 아프다
grammarNotes.func: Say what hurts at the clinic. Korean makes the body part the grammatical subject, marked with 이/가, and 아프다 (to hurt / be sore) describes its state. This is your answer when the doctor asks 어디가 아파요? (Where does it hurt?).

formTable.when: Body part ends in a consonant (받침)
Body part ends in a vowel

formTable.ex: 어제부터 배가 아팠어요 (my stomach has hurt since yesterday)

examples.en: My head hurts.
examples.note: 머리 ends in a vowel, so it takes 가; 아프 + 아요 → 아파요.

examples.en: My throat hurts and I also have a fever.
examples.note: 목 has a 받침, so it takes 이; 열이 나다 is the natural way to say 'have a fever.'

examples.en: Where does it hurt?
examples.note: The doctor's standard question; 어디 + 가 makes the sore spot the subject.

examples.en: My stomach hurts so much that I came in.
examples.note: 배 + 가; 너무 (so / too much) intensifies the pain.

keyPoint.label: The body part is the SUBJECT, not the object
keyPoint.body: Use 아프다 for physical body pain (머리가 아파요). Korean makes the body part the subject with 이/가 — it 'hurts' by itself. There is no 'I have a pain' verb that takes the body part as an object, so never mark it with 을/를 here.

drill.instruction: Make a sentence saying this body part hurts. Choose 이 or 가 by the final sound.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English says 'I hurt my head' with the head as object (를). In Korean the body part is the SUBJECT (가), and 아프다 describes its state. Never mark the body part with 를 here.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어야 해요 — must / have to (medical instruction)
grammarNotes.func: Give or receive a medical instruction: something you must do. The doctor uses it for what's necessary (약을 먹어야 해요 — you have to take the medicine), and you use it for what you must do (쉬어야 해요 — I have to rest).

formTable.ex: 받다 → 받아야 해요 (have to get / receive)
먹다 → 먹어야 해요 (have to take / eat)
검사하다 → 검사해야 해요 (have to get tested)

examples.ko: 이 약을 하루에 세 번 먹어야 해요.
examples.romanization: i yageul harue se beon meogeoya haeyo.
examples.en: You have to take this medicine three times a day.
examples.note: 먹다 → 먹어야 해요; the doctor's dosage instruction (하루에 세 번 = three times a day).

examples.en: You have to rest well.
examples.note: 쉬다 → 쉬어야 해요; 푹 is the set adverb that pairs with resting.

examples.en: Do I have to come back tomorrow?
examples.note: 오다 → 와야 해요; a yes/no question about a required visit.

examples.en: You have to get a blood test.
examples.note: 받다 has ㅏ, so 받아야 해요; 피 검사 = blood test.

keyPoint.label: 해요 vs 돼요
keyPoint.body: -아/어야 해요 and -아/어야 돼요 both mean 'must / have to.' 돼요 is a touch more conversational and very common in speech; 해요 feels slightly more standard. In a clinic you will hear both.

drill.instruction: Turn the verb into a 'have to ___' medical instruction with -아/어야 해요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners drop the 야. The obligation meaning lives entirely in -야; without it the sentence is broken. Always keep -아/어 + 야 + 해요/돼요 together.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-아서/어서 — symptom causing a result
grammarNotes.func: Link a symptom to its consequence: 'because X, Y happened.' This is your go-to for explaining the visit: 배가 아파서 왔어요 (my stomach hurt, so I came). The 아서/어서 clause is the cause; the second clause is the result.

formTable.ex: 열이 나서 (because I have a fever)

examples.en: My stomach hurt, so I came to the clinic.
examples.note: 아프다 → 아파서; the classic reason-for-visit sentence.

examples.en: I had a fever, so I couldn't go to school.
examples.note: 열이 나다 → 나서; a symptom leading to an inability.

examples.en: My cough was bad, so I couldn't sleep.
examples.note: 심하다 → 심해서; severity causing a result.

examples.en: I have a runny nose, so I need tissues.
examples.note: 콧물이 나다 → 나서; an everyday cold symptom.

keyPoint.label: 아서/어서 vs 때문에
keyPoint.body: Both mean 'because.' Use V-아서/어서 to chain a state or action straight into its result in one flowing clause. Use N 때문에 when the cause is a NOUN. With 아서/어서 you cannot put a command or suggestion in the result clause — for that use -(으)니까.

drill.instruction: Join the symptom and result with -아서/어서.
drill.model: 배가 아프다 / 병원에 오다 → 배가 아파서 병원에 왔어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: You can't end an 아서/어서 result clause with a command or suggestion. 'You have a fever, so take medicine' needs -(으)니까, not 아서/어서.

grammarNotes.title: N 때문에 — because of (a symptom / illness)
grammarNotes.func: State a NOUN cause: 'because of my cold / fever / headache.' When the reason is a noun — a named symptom or illness — use N 때문에: 감기 때문에 일을 못 했어요 (I couldn't work because of a cold).

formTable.ex: 감기 → 감기 때문에 (because of a cold)

examples.en: My throat hurts because of a cold.
examples.note: 감기 is a noun, so 때문에 fits perfectly.

examples.en: I couldn't sleep because of the fever.
examples.note: 열 (fever) as a noun cause of a result.

examples.en: I couldn't work because of a headache.
examples.note: 두통 (headache) noun + 때문에.

examples.en: I can't sleep because of the cough.
examples.note: 기침 (cough) noun + 때문에; a line straight from the clinic.

keyPoint.label: 때문에 (negative cause) vs 덕분에 (positive cause)
keyPoint.body: Both attach to a noun. 때문에 marks a cause, usually neutral or negative (감기 때문에 — because of a cold). 덕분에 means 'thanks to' and is positive (약 덕분에 나았어요 — I got better thanks to the medicine).

drill.instruction: Make a 'because of N' sentence with N 때문에.
drill.model: 감기 / 목이 아프다 → 감기 때문에 목이 아파요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 아파서 병원에 왔어요. / 통증 때문에 병원에 왔어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 때문에 attaches to a NOUN only. You cannot stack a verb-form (아파서) in front of 때문에. Either use 아파서 alone, or put a noun like 통증 (pain) before 때문에.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-(으)니까 — since this is so, do this (advice)
grammarNotes.func: Give advice or instruction grounded in a fact: 'since X is the case, do / let's do Y.' Unlike 아서/어서, the second clause CAN be a command or suggestion — perfect for a doctor's advice: 열이 나니까 약을 드세요 (since you have a fever, take the medicine).

formTable.ex: 열이 나니까 (since you have a fever)

examples.ko: 열이 계속 나니까 물을 많이 마시세요.
examples.romanization: yeori gyesok nanikka mureul mani masiseyo.
examples.en: Since the fever keeps up, drink a lot of water.
examples.note: 나다 → 나니까; result clause is a command (마시세요) — only 니까 allows this.

examples.en: Since your throat hurts, drink warm water.
examples.note: 아프다 → 아프니까; advice based on a stated fact.

examples.en: Since you've taken the medicine, get some rest.
examples.note: Past tense + 으니까 → 먹었으니까; the result is a suggestion.

examples.ko: 오늘은 병원이 문을 닫았으니까 내일 가요.
examples.romanization: oneureun byeongwoni muneul dadasseunikka naeil gayo.
examples.en: Since the clinic is closed today, let's go tomorrow.
examples.note: 닫다 → 닫았으니까; result is a suggestion (가요), which 니까 permits.

keyPoint.label: 니까 lets you give a command; 아서/어서 doesn't
keyPoint.body: The big difference from 아서/어서 is the second clause. With -(으)니까 the result can be a command (-세요), a suggestion (-아요/-(으)ㅂ시다), or a request. So whenever a doctor's 'because…, do this' sentence ends in an instruction, you must use 니까, not 아서/어서.

drill.instruction: Join the fact and the advice with -(으)니까, keeping the command in the second clause.
drill.model: 열이 나다 / 약을 먹다 → 열이 나니까 약을 드세요.
items: 목이 아프다 / 말을 많이 하지 않다 → ___

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Both 아서/어서 and 니까 mean 'because,' so learners reach for 아서/어서 by habit. But when the result is a command or suggestion (약을 드세요), only -(으)니까 is grammatical.

grammarNotes.title: 열이 나다 / 기침이 나다 — symptom 'comes out' with 나다
grammarNotes.func: Describe symptoms that 'come out' of the body — fever, cough, runny nose — with the symptom noun + 이/가 + 나다. You don't 'have' these in Korean; they 나다 ('arise / come out'). This is the most common way to list cold symptoms at the clinic.

formTable.when: Symptom noun ends in a consonant
formTable.ex: 열 → 열이 나요 (I have a fever)

formTable.when: Symptom noun ends in a vowel
formTable.ex: 콧물 → 콧물이 나요 (note: 콧물 ends in ㄹ → 이)
어제 열이 났어요 (I had a fever yesterday)

examples.en: I've had a fever since this morning.
examples.note: 열 + 이 나다; 아침부터 (since this morning) sets the start time.

examples.en: I have a cough and a runny nose too.
examples.note: 기침이 나다 + 콧물이 나다 chained with -고; the classic cold combo.

examples.en: I have a fever and my throat also hurts.
examples.note: 나다 for fever, but 아프다 for the throat — different verbs.

examples.en: I had a high fever yesterday.
examples.note: 나다 → 났어요 (past); 많이 = a lot / high.

keyPoint.label: 나다 symptoms vs 아프다 pain
keyPoint.body: Symptoms that 'come out' — 열(fever), 기침(cough), 콧물(runny nose) — use 이/가 나다. A body part that aches — 머리, 목, 배 — uses 이/가 아프다. Mixing them up (열이 아파요 ✗, 머리가 나요 ✗) is the giveaway, so memorize which noun pairs with which verb.

drill.instruction: Pick the right verb: symptom that 'comes out' → 나요, body part that aches → 아파요.
drill.model: 열 → 열이 나요. / 머리 → 머리가 아파요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'I have a fever' tempts you into 열이 있어요 ('a fever exists'), which sounds off for an active symptom. Koreans say 열이 나요 — the fever 'comes out.' Use 나다, not 있다, for fever, cough, and runny nose.

grammarNotes.title: 못 + V — can't do it (symptom blocking an action)
grammarNotes.func: Say you were unable to do something because of a symptom: 'I couldn't ___.' Put 못 right before the verb: 잠을 못 자요 (I can't sleep), 학교에 못 갔어요 (I couldn't go to school). This is how you describe what the illness stopped you from doing.

examples.en: I can't sleep because of the cough.
examples.note: 못 sits right before 자요; 잠을 자다 → 잠을 못 자요.

examples.en: I had a fever, so I couldn't go to school.
examples.note: Past: 가다 → 못 갔어요.

examples.en: My throat hurts, so I can't eat.
examples.note: 못 + 먹어요; a common reason given at the clinic.

examples.en: I couldn't work yesterday.
examples.note: 일하다 splits: 일을 못 했어요 — 못 goes before 하다.

keyPoint.label: 못 = couldn't (blocked); 안 = didn't (chose not to)
keyPoint.body: 못 means you were UNABLE — something (a symptom) prevented you: 못 잤어요 (couldn't sleep). 안 means you simply didn't / chose not to: 안 잤어요 (didn't sleep). At the clinic you almost always want 못, because the illness is what stopped you.

drill.instruction: Say you couldn't do this because of a symptom, using 못 + verb.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Don't stack 못 and 안 together — pick one. Use 못 for 'unable to' (a symptom blocked you). Also keep 못 directly before the verb (못 자요), and for 하다 verbs split the noun off: 일을 못 해요, not 못 일해요.

exampleSentence.en: When did the symptoms start?
exampleSentence.note: Clinic intake word.

exampleSentence.en: My stomach hurts, so I came to the clinic.
exampleSentence.note: In Korean, 병원 often covers neighborhood clinics too.

exampleSentence.en: I take the prescription to the pharmacy.
exampleSentence.note: Clinic-to-pharmacy flow.

exampleSentence.en: My throat hurts.
exampleSentence.note: In symptom talk, 목 often means throat.

exampleSentence.en: My stomach hurts.
exampleSentence.note: Most natural first sentence for stomach pain.

exampleSentence.en: I have had a fever since this morning.
exampleSentence.note: Use 열이 나다 for having a fever.

exampleSentence.en: I could not sleep because of the cough.
exampleSentence.note: Good noun for 때문에.

exampleSentence.en: I came to the clinic because of a cold.
exampleSentence.note: Common named cause in clinic talk.

exampleSentence.en: You have to take the medicine after meals.
exampleSentence.note: Core pharmacy noun.

exampleSentence.en: I got a prescription at the clinic.
exampleSentence.note: Bridge between clinic and pharmacy.

exampleSentence.en: Take it three times a day after meals.
exampleSentence.note: Medicine timing word.

exampleSentence.en: Take it three times a day.
exampleSentence.note: Frequency word for medicine instructions.

exampleSentence.en: I told the doctor my symptoms.

extendedDialogue.setting: A clinic visit moves from symptoms to medicine instructions and follow-up advice.

lines.speaker: 의사
lines.en: Where does it hurt? What brings you in?
lines.grammarNote: 아파서 connects the symptom to the clinic visit.

lines.speaker: 환자
lines.ko: 아침부터 열이 나고 목이 아파요. 기침도 나요.
lines.romanization: achimbuteo yeori nago mogi apayo. gichimdo nayo.
lines.en: Since this morning I have had a fever and a sore throat. I also have a cough.
lines.grammarNote: 열이 나다, 목이 아프다, and 기침이 나다 are symptom phrases.

lines.speaker: 의사
lines.ko: 감기 때문에 그런 것 같아요. 약은 식후에 하루 세 번 드셔야 해요.
lines.romanization: gamgi ttaemune geureon geot gatayo. yageun sikhue haru se beon deusyeoya haeyo.
lines.en: It seems to be because of a cold. You have to take the medicine three times a day after meals.
lines.grammarNote: 때문에 names the cause; 드셔야 해요 gives an instruction.

lines.speaker: 환자
lines.ko: 기침 때문에 잠을 못 자면 다시 와야 하나요?
lines.romanization: gichim ttaemune jameul mot jamyeon dasi waya hanayo?
lines.en: If I cannot sleep because of the cough, should I come back?
lines.grammarNote: 기침 때문에 explains the blocked action.

lines.speaker: 의사
lines.ko: 네. 열이 계속 나니까 물을 많이 마시고 쉬세요.
lines.romanization: ne. yeori gyesok nanikka mureul mani masigo swiseyo.
lines.en: Yes. Since the fever is continuing, drink a lot of water and rest.
lines.grammarNote: 니까 gives the reason for advice.

lines.speaker: 환자
lines.ko: 네. 처방전을 받고 약국에 가서 약을 기다릴게요.
lines.romanization: ne. cheobangjeoneul batgo yakguge gaseo yageul gidarilgeyo.
lines.en: Okay. I will take the prescription, go to the pharmacy, and wait for the medicine.
lines.grammarNote: The patient repeats the practical next steps after hearing the instructions.

readingText.title: 약은 식후에 하루 세 번 드세요
readingText.body: 민수는 아침부터 열이 나고 목이 아파서 동네 병원에 갔어요. 의사 선생님은 감기 때문에 그런 것 같다고 말했어요. 기침이 심해지는 바람에 어젯밤에는 잠도 거의 못 잤어요. 민수는 처방전을 받아서 약국에 갔고, 약사에게 복약 방법을 들었어요. 약은 식후에 하루 세 번 먹어야 하고, 열이 계속 나니까 물을 많이 마시고 쉬어야 해요. 증상이 나아지지 않으면 다시 병원에 와야 해요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minsu had a fever and sore throat from the morning, so he went to a neighborhood clinic. The doctor said it seemed to be because of a cold. Because his cough got worse, he barely slept the night before. Minsu got a prescription and went to the pharmacy, where he heard the medicine instructions from the pharmacist. He has to take the medicine three times a day after meals, and since the fever is continuing, he has to drink a lot of water and rest. If the symptoms do not improve, he has to go back to the clinic.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민수는 왜 병원에 갔어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 열이 나고 목이 아파서 병원에 갔어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 기침이 심해지는 바람에 무엇을 못 했어요?
약은 언제, 얼마나 먹어야 해요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 식후에 하루 세 번 먹어야 해요.

culturalNote.title: Clinic and pharmacy flow
culturalNote.body: In Korea, many neighborhood clinics are paired with nearby pharmacies. The clinic gives a 처방전, and the pharmacy prepares medicine by dose. That is why phrases like 하루 세 번, 식후, 식전, 자기 전, and 며칠분 are practical, not optional.
culturalNote.tip: At the clinic, lead with symptoms and time: 아침부터, 어제부터, 열이 나요, 목이 아파요. At the pharmacy, confirm timing and frequency: 식후에요? 하루 몇 번이에요?

inlineExercises.prompt: Which symptom phrase is natural?
inlineExercises.explanation: 열이 나다 and 목이 아프다 are natural symptom frames.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence names a symptom as the cause?
inlineExercises.explanation: N 때문에 attaches directly to the noun.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which instruction means 'You have to take the medicine after meals'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 식후에 gives timing; 드셔야 해요 gives a necessary instruction.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses 는 바람에 for an unwanted disruption?
options: 기침이 심해지는 바람에 잠을 못 잤어요.
기침이 심해지는 덕분에 잠을 못 잤어요.
기침이 심해지는 중에 잠을 못 자야 해요.
inlineExercises.correct: 기침이 심해지는 바람에 잠을 못 잤어요.
inlineExercises.explanation: 는 바람에 fits an unwanted cause that disrupted sleep.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence reports a current pharmacy action?
inlineExercises.explanation: V-는 중이에요 reports an action in progress.

inlineExercises.prompt: 목___ 아파요. (My throat hurts.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 아프다 describes the body part that hurts, so 목 takes 이. 목을 아파요 is a common learner error.

inlineExercises.prompt: 식후에 약을 ___ . (먹다 → must)
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어야 해요 gives a must/have-to instruction. 먹다 becomes 먹어야 해요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I have a fever and a cough.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Korean uses 나다 for fever and cough symptoms. -고 links the two symptoms naturally.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'You have to take the medicine after meals.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 식후에 means after meals. 드셔야 해요 is the respectful instruction form for taking medicine.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '배를 아파요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: The hurting body part is the subject of 아프다, so use 배가. 를 would mark it as an object.

bullets: Symptom frames: 목이 아파요, 배가 아파요, 열이 나요, 기침이 나요.
Clinic flow: 병원에서 증상을 말하고 처방전을 받아요.
Pharmacy flow: 약국에서 약을 받고 식후/하루 세 번을 확인해요.
Cause choices: 아파서 is neutral, 때문에 names the problem, 니까 leads to advice, 는 바람에 implies disruption.
Instruction frame: 약은 식후에 드셔야 해요.

writingTask.prompt: At the clinic, explain your symptoms to the doctor: say what hurts, what symptom came out, why you came, and what you couldn't do.
writingTask.hint: Use body part + 이/가 아프다 (목이 아파요), symptom + 이/가 나다 (열이 나요), -아서/어서 for cause-result (아파서 왔어요), and 못 + V for what you couldn't do (잠을 못 잤어요).
writingTask.model: 어제부터 목이 아프고 열이 나요. 감기 때문에 머리도 아파요. 너무 아파서 병원에 왔어요. 어젯밤에는 기침 때문에 잠을 못 잤어요.
writingTask.modelEn: Since yesterday my throat hurts and I have a fever. Because of a cold my head hurts too. It hurt so much that I came to the hospital. Last night I couldn't sleep because of the cough.

canDo: Say what hurts with body part + 이/가 아프다 (목이 아파요)
Describe a symptom 'coming out' with 이/가 나다 (열이 나요, 기침이 나요)
Explain the visit with cause-result -아서/어서 and N 때문에 (아파서 왔어요, 감기 때문에)
Say what a symptom kept me from doing with 못 + V (잠을 못 잤어요)

dialogue.ko: 이사하기 전에 계약서를 확인해 두면 되죠?
dialogue.romanization: isahagi jeone gyeyakseoreul hwaginhae dumyeon doejyo?

dialogue.speaker: B

dialogue.romanization: ne. maeume deulmyeon oneul gyeyakal su isseoyo.
