chapters.guidedPractice: Make five real-estate sentences: layout, deposit/monthly rent, separate fees, included utilities, and contract preparation.
chapters.realLifeTask: Describe one housing problem and ask someone to check or fix it.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner plays the agent; ask about 보증금, 월세, 관리비, 포함 여부, and 계약서.
chapters.review: Can you explain why 원룸, 부동산, 보증금, 월세, 관리비, 포함되다, 따로, and 계약서 belong together in one housing task?

beginnerGuide.title: Housing price has more than one number
beginnerGuide.body: A Korean listing often gives 보증금 and 월세 together. 월세만 물어보면 실제 비용을 놓칠 수 있어요.

beginnerGuide.title: 관리비 changes the real monthly cost
beginnerGuide.body: 관리비는 따로예요? 인터넷도 포함돼 있어요? 공과금이나 인터넷이 포함되는지에 따라 실제 월 비용이 달라져요.

beginnerGuide.title: Prepare before signing
beginnerGuide.body: 이사하기 전에 계약서를 확인해 두세요. -아/어 두다 fits this chapter because it means doing a task in advance and leaving it ready.

checkpoints: I can name common home items and rooms.
I can use 고장 났어요, 안 돼요, and 필요해요.
I can ask politely for checking, repair, or help.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Talk about home problems and daily living needs.
exitTask.prompt: Describe one housing problem and ask someone to check or fix it.

sampleAnswer.ko: 방에 불이 안 켜져요. 한번 확인해 주실 수 있어요?
sampleAnswer.en: The light in my room will not turn on. Could you check it once?

checklist: I can name common home items and rooms.
I can use 고장 났어요, 안 돼요, and 필요해요.
I can ask politely for checking, repair, or help.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You are viewing a studio through a real-estate office and need to ask the questions that change the real cost: deposit, monthly rent, maintenance fee, included utilities, options, and contract details.
objectives: Ask about 보증금, 월세, 관리비, and what is included.
Describe the room and layout with housing nouns and adjective modifiers.
Use 조건, 가능, 목적, and 준비 patterns for real housing decisions.
hook.whyItMatters: Housing Korean is full of words that come as a set. 원룸 without 보증금, 월세, 관리비, 포함되다, and 계약서 is not enough for the real task.

grammarNotes.title: N이/가 있어요 — saying what a home has
grammarNotes.func: Use 있어요 to say a room or feature exists in a home. It is the everyday way to describe what an apartment or house comes with: a balcony, an elevator, parking, and so on.

formTable.ex: 방 → 방이 있어요 (there is a room)
엘리베이터 → 엘리베이터가 있어요 (there is an elevator)

examples.ko: 이 집에 방이 세 개 있어요.
examples.romanization: i jibe bangi se gae isseoyo.
examples.en: This house has three rooms.
examples.note: 방 ends in a consonant, so it takes 이; 있어요 says the rooms exist.

examples.en: Our apartment has an elevator.
examples.note: 엘리베이터 ends in a vowel, so it takes 가.

examples.en: There is a big supermarket near the house.
examples.note: 있어요 also covers 'there is X nearby,' a common housing detail.

examples.en: Is there a balcony?
examples.note: A rising tone turns the statement into a yes/no question renters actually ask.

keyPoint.label: 있어요 vs 이에요/예요
keyPoint.body: 있어요 means 'there is / it has' (existence). 이에요/예요 means 'it is' (identity). 방이 있어요 = 'there is a room'; 방이에요 = 'it is a room.' For listing what a home has, you almost always want 있어요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 있어요 links the 받침 ㅆ into the next vowel: [이써요]. So 방이 있어요 runs together as [방이 이써요].

drill.instruction: Add 이 or 가 to the noun and finish with 있어요 to say the home has it.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English drops the subject marker ('the house has rooms'), but Korean normally needs 이/가 on the thing that exists. Don't omit the particle before 있어요 in careful speech.

grammarNotes.title: N이/가 없어요 — saying a home lacks something
grammarNotes.func: 없어요 is the negative of 있어요: it says a feature does NOT exist. In housing talk it covers a missing room, no parking, no elevator, or 'there is no extra fee.'

formTable.ex: 창문 → 창문이 없어요 (there is no window)
엘리베이터 → 엘리베이터가 없어요 (there is no elevator)

examples.en: This room has no window.
examples.note: 창문 ends in a consonant → 이 없어요; says the feature is absent.

examples.en: This building has no elevator.
examples.note: 엘리베이터 ends in a vowel → 가 없어요.

examples.en: There's no extra cost besides the deposit.
examples.note: A reassuring rental phrase: 없어요 = 'there is no (extra fee).'

examples.en: There are no empty rooms right now.
examples.note: 빈방 'empty room' + 이 없어요 = a common reply from a landlord.

keyPoint.label: 있어요 ↔ 없어요
keyPoint.body: These are a fixed pair, not 있어요 + 안. To say a home lacks something, use 없어요, never 안 있어요. 방이 있어요 (has a room) ↔ 방이 없어요 (has no room).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 없어요 links the cluster ㅄ so only ㅅ carries over: [업써요]. So 창문이 없어요 sounds like [창무니 업써요].

drill.instruction: Use 이/가 없어요 to say the home lacks the feature.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: There is no '안 있어요.' The negative of 있어요 is the separate word 없어요. Reach for 없어요 directly instead of negating 있어요 with 안.

grammarNotes.title: A-(으)ㄴ N — describing a home (넓은 방)
grammarNotes.func: Turn a descriptive adjective into a word that modifies a noun, like 'a spacious room' or 'a clean house.' This is how you describe homes: 넓은 방, 깨끗한 집, 조용한 동네.

formTable.when: Adjective stem ends in a consonant (받침)
Adjective stem ends in a vowel

examples.en: I'm looking for a spacious room.
examples.note: 넓다 (consonant stem) → 넓은 modifies 방; the adjective comes before the noun.

examples.en: I like a clean house.
examples.note: 하다-adjective 깨끗하다 → 깨끗한 (drop the vowel-ending 하, add ㄴ).

examples.en: I want to live in a quiet neighborhood.
examples.note: 조용하다 → 조용한; describes the kind of 동네 (neighborhood).

examples.en: I'm looking for a house close to work.
examples.note: 가깝다 is ㅂ-irregular → 가까운 집; a very common housing criterion.

keyPoint.label: 넓은 방 vs 방이 넓어요
keyPoint.body: Modifier form goes BEFORE the noun: 넓은 방 ('a spacious room' — naming a thing). Predicate form ends the sentence: 방이 넓어요 ('the room is spacious' — stating a fact). Use 넓은 방 when the adjective is labeling the noun.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 넓다 is pronounced [널따], and 넓은 links the ㄼ cluster as [널븐]. 가까운 and 깨끗한 link smoothly.

drill.instruction: Make the adjective modify the noun with -(으)ㄴ.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Don't put a sentence-ending form in the modifier slot. 넓어요 ends a sentence; to attach it to 방 you must change it to the modifier form 넓은. English uses 'wide' in both spots, but Korean changes the ending.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-(으)면 — stating a housing condition
grammarNotes.func: -(으)면 means 'if / when.' Use it to set a condition about a home: 'if it's too expensive...', 'if I like the place...', 'when I sign the contract...'

examples.ko: 방이 너무 비싸면 다른 집을 볼게요.
examples.romanization: bangi neomu bissamyeon dareun jibeul bolgeyo.
examples.en: If the room is too expensive, I'll look at another place.
examples.note: 비싸다 (vowel stem) → 비싸면; sets the condition before the result clause.

examples.en: It'd be nice if it's close to the subway station.
examples.note: 가깝다 → 가까우면 (ㅂ-irregular); '(으)면 좋아요' = 'it'd be nice if.'

examples.en: When you sign the contract, you pay the deposit.
examples.note: 계약하다 → 계약하면; here -(으)면 means 'when/once' for a routine step.

examples.en: If I like the house, I'll sign the contract.
examples.note: 들다 is ㄹ-final → 마음에 들면 (keep ㄹ, add 면); 마음에 들다 = 'to like.'

keyPoint.label: -(으)면 vs -아/어서
keyPoint.body: -(으)면 is a hypothetical 'if/when' — the result depends on the condition. -아/어서 gives an actual reason that already holds. 비싸면 안 사요 = 'if it's expensive, I won't buy.' 비싸서 안 사요 = 'I'm not buying because it's (actually) expensive.'

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a 받침, 으면 links: 좋으면 sounds like [조으면] (ㅎ weakens between vowels). The ㄹ-stem 들면 is simply [들면].

drill.instruction: Attach -(으)면 to make the housing condition.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: ㄹ-final stems do NOT add 으; they keep ㄹ and add 면 directly: 들다 → 들면. Learners over-apply 으면 to every consonant ending, but ㄹ is special here.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 — what's possible/allowed at home
grammarNotes.func: Express that something is possible or allowed in a home: you can park, you can keep a pet, you can move in next week. The opposite, 'cannot,' is V-(으)ㄹ 수 없어요.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a consonant (받침)
Verb stem ends in a vowel

formTable.ex: 키우다 → 키울 수 없어요 (cannot keep a pet)

examples.en: Can I park here?
examples.note: 주차하다 (vowel stem) → 주차할 수 있어요; a yes/no question about what's allowed.

examples.ko: 이 집에서 강아지를 키울 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: i jibeseo gangajireul kiul su isseoyo.
examples.en: You can keep a dog in this house.
examples.note: 키우다 (vowel stem) → 키울 수 있어요; asking about pets is a common rental question.

examples.en: I can move in next week.
examples.note: 이사하다 → 이사할 수 있어요; states a possible move-in time.

examples.en: You can't keep pets here.
examples.note: The negative uses 없어요: 키울 수 없어요 = 'cannot keep.'

keyPoint.label: 있어요 → 없어요 for 'cannot'
keyPoint.body: To make V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 negative, swap 있어요 for 없어요, not 안: 살 수 있어요 (can live) → 살 수 없어요 (cannot live). The 수 (way/possibility) stays; only the existence verb flips.

drill.instruction: Make 'can do' with V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 수 있어요 is pronounced [수 이써요], and the ㄹ before 수 stays light: 살 수 → [살 쑤] (the ㅅ tenses to ㅆ after the ㄹ).

drill.instruction: Make 'can do' with V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 여기에서 주차 안 할 수 있어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: To say 'cannot park,' don't insert 안 into the can-phrase. The negative of (으)ㄹ 수 있어요 is (으)ㄹ 수 없어요. 안 주차하다 would mean 'choose not to park,' which is different from 'not allowed/able to park.'

grammarNotes.title: N에 살아요 — saying where you live
grammarNotes.func: Use 에 + 살아요 to say where you live: in a city, a neighborhood, an apartment, or on a particular floor. 에 marks the place of residence.

formTable.ex: 아파트에 살아요 (I live in an apartment)

examples.en: I live in Busan.
examples.note: 부산 (place) + 에 살아요; 에 marks where you live.

examples.en: I live in a studio apartment right now.
examples.note: 원룸 'one-room/studio' is a very common type of home in Korea.

examples.en: I live on the 5th floor.
examples.note: 층 'floor' + 에 살아요; 5층 is read 오층.

examples.en: Which neighborhood do you live in?
examples.note: 어느 'which' + 동네 + 에 살아요? — a natural getting-to-know-you question.

keyPoint.label: 에 살아요 vs 에서 + action
keyPoint.body: For living (a state), use 에: 서울에 살아요. For an action that happens at a place, use 에서: 집에서 일해요 ('I work at home'). With 살다 specifically, Korean uses 에, not 에서.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 살아요 links the ㄹ into the next vowel: [사라요]. 부산에 살아요 runs together as [부사네 사라요].

drill.instruction: Add 에 살아요 to say where you live.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: With 살다 (to live/reside), the standard particle is 에, not 에서. English 'live in/at' tempts learners toward 에서, but residence as a state takes 에.

grammarNotes.title: N(으)로 이사 가요/와요 — moving house
grammarNotes.func: Use (으)로 to mark the destination you move TO when changing homes: 이사 가다 'to move (away to)' and 이사 오다 'to move (here to).' (으)로 means 'to / toward.'

formTable.ex: 서울 → 서울로 이사 가요 (ㄹ받침: just 로)

formTable.when: Place ends in a vowel or ㄹ
formTable.ex: 부산 → 부산으로… / 학교 앞 → 학교 앞으로
새집으로 이사 와요 (move into a new house)

examples.en: I'm moving to a new house next month.
examples.note: 새집 'new house' + 으로 (받침 ㅂ) + 이사 가요; (으)로 marks the destination.

examples.en: I'm going to move to Busan.
examples.note: 부산 ends in ㄴ → 으로; 이사 갈 거예요 = future 'will move.'

examples.ko: 우리 옆집에 새 이웃이 이사 왔어요.
examples.romanization: uri yeopjibe sae iusi isa wasseoyo.
examples.en: A new neighbor moved in next door.
examples.note: 이사 오다 → 이사 왔어요 (past); 옆집 'next-door house,' 이웃 'neighbor.'

examples.en: When are you moving out?
examples.note: 언제 'when' + 이사 가요? — a natural question to a friend who's moving.

keyPoint.label: 이사 가요 vs 이사 와요
keyPoint.body: 이사 가다 = move away (the speaker is not at the destination). 이사 오다 = move here (toward the speaker's location). 서울로 이사 가요 = 'I'm moving to Seoul'; 여기로 이사 왔어요 = 'I moved here.'

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 이사 가요 is [이사 가요]; 으로 links its ㄹ into 이사: 새집으로 → [새지브로]. 이사 왔어요 sounds like [이사 와써요].

drill.instruction: Add (으)로 이사 가요 to say where you're moving to.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: For the destination of a move, Korean prefers (으)로 ('toward/to') with 이사 가다, not 에. English 'move to a new house' suggests 에, but the directional (으)로 is the natural choice here.

exampleSentence.en: How much is the deposit for this studio?
exampleSentence.note: Core real-estate viewing noun.

exampleSentence.note: In daily speech, 부동산 often means the office.

exampleSentence.en: The monthly rent is 700,000 won.

exampleSentence.en: I am looking for a monthly-rent studio rather than jeonse.
exampleSentence.note: Lease type contrast.

exampleSentence.en: Is the maintenance fee separate?
exampleSentence.note: Core cost question.

exampleSentence.en: Is the maintenance fee separate?
exampleSentence.note: Small word that changes total cost.

exampleSentence.en: Internet is included in the maintenance fee.

exampleSentence.en: Check the contract before moving.

extendedDialogue.setting: A tenant checks rent, deposit, utilities, and contract preparation at a real-estate office.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: How much is the deposit for this studio?
lines.grammarNote: 원룸 and 보증금 belong together in listing questions.

lines.speaker: 중개사
lines.en: The deposit is 5 million won and the monthly rent is 700,000 won.
lines.grammarNote: 은/는 separates the two money topics clearly.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Is the maintenance fee separate? Is internet included too?
lines.grammarNote: 따로 and 포함되다 are the key fee-boundary words.

lines.speaker: 중개사
lines.en: The maintenance fee is 70,000 won, and internet is included.
lines.grammarNote: 인터넷 is the subject of 포함돼 있어요.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.ko: 이사하기 전에 계약서를 확인해 두면 되죠?
lines.romanization: isahagi jeone gyeyakseoreul hwaginhae dumyeon doejyo?
lines.en: I should check the contract before moving, right?
lines.grammarNote: 확인해 두다 means check it in advance and keep it ready.

lines.speaker: 중개사
lines.ko: 네. 마음에 들면 오늘 계약할 수 있어요.
lines.romanization: ne. maeume deulmyeon oneul gyeyakal su isseoyo.
lines.en: Yes. If you like it, you can sign the contract today.
lines.grammarNote: 면 sets the condition; ㄹ 수 있어요 gives possibility.

readingText.title: 관리비에 인터넷이 포함돼 있어요?
readingText.body: 하나는 이사하기 위해 부동산에 갔어요. 공인중개사는 넓은 원룸 하나를 보여 줬어요. 보증금은 500만 원이고 월세는 70만 원이었어요. 하나는 관리비가 따로인지, 인터넷이 관리비에 포함돼 있는지 물어봤어요. 베란다는 없었지만 부엌에 냉장고와 세탁기가 있었고 화장실도 깨끗했어요. 마음에 들면 오늘 계약할 수 있다고 해서, 하나는 계약하기 전에 계약서를 다시 확인해 두었어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Hana went to a real-estate office to move. The licensed agent showed her a spacious studio. The deposit was 5 million won and the monthly rent was 700,000 won. Hana asked whether the maintenance fee was separate and whether internet was included in the fee. There was no balcony, but there was a refrigerator and washing machine in the kitchen, and the bathroom was clean. Since she could sign the contract that day if she liked it, Hana checked the contract again before signing.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 하나는 왜 부동산에 갔어요?
하나가 확인한 비용 두 가지는 뭐예요?
계약하기 전에 무엇을 확인해 두었어요?

culturalNote.title: The real cost is not only 월세
culturalNote.body: In Korean rentals, 월세 is only one part of the monthly burden. 보증금 is paid up front, 관리비 may be separate, and utilities such as internet, water, gas, or electricity may or may not be included. A good housing conversation checks all of these before 계약하다.
culturalNote.tip: Ask in this order: 보증금이 얼마예요? 월세가 얼마예요? 관리비는 따로예요? 뭐가 포함돼 있어요? 계약서 먼저 확인해도 돼요?

inlineExercises.prompt: At a real-estate office, which pair belongs together?
options: 포크 세 개 / 커피 두 잔
inlineExercises.explanation: 보증금 and 월세 are core housing price terms.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which question checks whether a fee is separate?
inlineExercises.explanation: 따로 means separately and is essential for fee questions.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence asks whether internet is included?
inlineExercises.explanation: The included item is the subject, and 관리비 takes 에.

inlineExercises.prompt: Before moving, the prepared-action sentence is:
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어 두세요 means do it in advance and leave it prepared.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses possibility naturally?
inlineExercises.explanation: Vㄹ/을 수 있어요 expresses practical possibility.

inlineExercises.prompt: 관리비___ 포함돼요? (Is the maintenance fee included?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 포함되다 is passive/included, so 관리비 is the subject and takes 가. 를 would fit an active verb like 포함하다.

inlineExercises.prompt: 인터넷이 관리비에 ___ ? (포함되다 → polite question)
inlineExercises.explanation: 포함되다 becomes 포함돼요 in polite speech. As a question, rising intonation or the question mark makes it “is it included?”

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Is internet included?'
inlineExercises.explanation: 인터넷이 is the subject of being included. 포함돼요? is the natural real-estate question.

inlineExercises.prompt: Ask: 'How much is the deposit?'
inlineExercises.explanation: 보증금은 sets the deposit as the topic. 얼마예요 asks for the amount or price.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '월세가 매달 내요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 내다 is an active verb, so 월세 is its object and takes 를. 가 would make the rent the subject, which does not fit paying.

bullets: Cost set: 보증금, 월세, 관리비, 따로, 포함되다.
Housing nouns: 원룸, 거실, 부엌, 화장실, 베란다, 현관.
Listing descriptions: 넓은 원룸, 밝은 방, 조용한 동네, 깨끗한 화장실.
Decision patterns: 마음에 들면, 계약할 수 있어요, 집을 구하기 위해, 확인해 두세요.
Contract habit: check 계약서 before 계약하다.

writingTask.prompt: Message a friend about a studio apartment you saw at the real-estate office: describe what it has and lacks, say where it is, and add a condition about whether you'll take it.
writingTask.hint: Use N이/가 있어요/없어요 (거실은 있는데 주차장은 없어요), an adjective + noun (넓은 방), N에 살아요 for location, and -(으)면 for the condition (월세가 싸면 계약할 거예요).
writingTask.model: 오늘 부동산에서 원룸을 봤는데, 넓은 방하고 깨끗한 부엌이 있어요. 그런데 주차장은 없어요. 조용한 동네에 있어서 마음에 들어요. 월세가 너무 비싸지 않으면 다음 달에 이사 가려고 해요.
writingTask.modelEn: I saw a studio at the real-estate office today, and it has a spacious room and a clean kitchen. But there's no parking lot. It's in a quiet neighborhood, so I like it. If the monthly rent isn't too expensive, I'm planning to move in next month.

canDo: Say what a home has or lacks with N이/가 있어요/없어요 (주차장이 없어요)
Describe a home with adjective + noun (넓은 방, 깨끗한 집, 조용한 동네)
State a housing condition with -(으)면 (싸면 계약할 거예요)
Say where I live and where I'm moving with N에 살아요 / N(으)로 이사 가요

chapters.title: Weather and Seasons
chapters.goal: Talk about weather in a way that connects to plans.
chapters.scenario: The weather changes what you wear, where you go, or whether you meet.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Did you see the weekend forecast?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 태풍이 올 것 같아서 비행기가 늦을 수도 있어요.
dialogue.romanization: taepungi ol geot gataseo bihaenggiga neujeul sudo isseoyo.
dialogue.en: It looks like a typhoon may come, so the plane might be late.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 미세먼지가 심하면 일정은 취소하는 게 좋겠어요.
dialogue.romanization: misemeonjiga simhamyeon iljeongeun chwisohaneun ge jotgesseoyo.
dialogue.en: If the fine dust is bad, it would be better to cancel the plan.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Let's book again when the weather clears.

chapters.guidedPractice: Make five forecast-plan sentences: prediction, concern, condition, cause, and timing.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say today's weather and how it changes your plan.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner gives a forecast; decide whether to bring an umbrella, cancel, delay, or rebook.
chapters.review: Can you connect 일기예보, 태풍, 미세먼지, 비/눈, 우산, 일정, 취소하다, and 다시 예약하다 in one real plan?

beginnerGuide.title: Forecast language changes plans
beginnerGuide.body: 일기예보를 보고 비가 올 것 같아요, 태풍이 올 텐데요, 미세먼지 때문에 취소해요처럼 계획을 조정해요.

beginnerGuide.title: 비 and 눈 both use 오다
beginnerGuide.body: 비가 와요 and 눈이 와요 use the same everyday verb 오다. 날씨의 눈은 eye가 아니라 snow예요.

beginnerGuide.title: 미세먼지 is plan vocabulary
beginnerGuide.body: Korean daily plans often change because of 미세먼지, 황사, 태풍, 장마, or 소나기. Weather words should connect to 일정 and 취소하다.

checkpoints: I can describe weather with 덥다, 춥다, 흐리다, 비가 오다, and 눈이 오다.
I can connect weather to a result with -아서/어서 or -면.
I can use 것 같아요 for weather predictions.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Talk about weather in a way that connects to plans.
exitTask.prompt: Say today's weather and how it changes your plan.

sampleAnswer.ko: 오늘은 비가 올 것 같아요. 그래서 우산을 가져갈 거예요.
sampleAnswer.en: I think it will rain today. So I will bring an umbrella.

checklist: I can describe weather with 덥다, 춥다, 흐리다, 비가 오다, and 눈이 오다.
I can connect weather to a result with -아서/어서 or -면.
I can use 것 같아요 for weather predictions.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You check the weekend forecast before a trip, see typhoon and fine-dust warnings, and need to decide whether to bring an umbrella, cancel the schedule, or book again later.
objectives: Use 날씨, 일기예보, 비, 눈, 태풍, 미세먼지, and 우산 in forecast-based plan talk.
Connect weather words to real decisions with -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요, -(으)ㄹ 텐데, V면, N 때문에, and V(으)ㄹ 때.
Write a short message that delays, cancels, or rebooks a plan because of weather.
hook.whyItMatters: Weather words are not just description words. In daily Korean, they often explain why a plan changes: 비 때문에 못 가요, 미세먼지가 심하면 취소해요, 날씨가 맑아질 때 다시 예약해요.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 — "I think it'll..." (a soft guess about the weather)
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 to make a soft prediction about the weather from signs you can see — clouds, a dark sky, a dropping temperature. It is the everyday way to say "I think it's going to rain / snow / be cold." Because it is a guess, not a fact, it sounds careful and polite rather than absolute.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel (오다)
formTable.ex: 오다 → 올 것 같아요 (it looks like it'll rain)

formTable.when: Verb/adjective stem ends in a consonant (맑다, 좋다)
formTable.ex: 맑다 → 맑을 것 같아요 (I think it'll be clear)
춥다 → 추울 것 같아요 (I think it'll be cold)

formTable.when: ㄹ-final stem (얼다, 불다) — ㄹ stays, no extra 으
formTable.ex: 불다 → 불 것 같아요 (it looks like the wind will blow)

examples.ko: 오늘 오후에 비가 올 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: oneul ohue biga ol geot gatayo.
examples.en: I think it's going to rain this afternoon.
examples.note: 오다 is a vowel-stem, so just -ㄹ; the model weather-guess sentence.

examples.ko: 하늘을 보니까 눈이 올 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: haneureul bonikka nuni ol geot gatayo.
examples.en: Looking at the sky, I think it's going to snow.
examples.note: Pairs the guess with visible evidence (하늘을 보니까), the natural reason for a forecast.

examples.en: I think it'll be a bit cold tomorrow.
examples.note: 춥다 is ㅂ-irregular → 추우- + ㄹ; 좀 softens the guess even more.

examples.en: I think the weather will be clear this weekend.
examples.note: 맑다 ends in a consonant, so it takes -을; everyday seasons vocabulary.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 vs. -아/어요
keyPoint.body: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 is a guess about something not yet certain (비가 올 것 같아요 = I think it'll rain), while plain 비가 와요 states it as a present fact (it's raining). Reach for 것 같아요 when you're reading the signs, not reporting what's already true.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 것 같아요 is pronounced [걷 까타요]: the final ㅅ of 것 becomes a [t] stop, and the following ㄱ tenses to [ㄲ], so it sounds like "geot kkatayo."

drill.instruction: Make a soft weather guess with -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요. Follow the model.
drill.model: 비가 오다 → 비가 올 것 같아요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers try to glue "will" (-ㄹ 거예요) onto "seems" (같아요). In Korean the single chunk is -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 — the noun 것, not the sentence-ending 거예요, attaches before 같아요.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-(으)ㄹ 텐데 — "it'll probably... so" (a likely situation plus concern)
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)ㄹ 텐데 to predict a likely situation and then add worry, advice, or a suggestion about it. It is the warm "it'll probably rain, so (take an umbrella)" pattern — you forecast something and immediately care about its effect on the listener. The 텐데 part leaves the sentence half-open, inviting a follow-up clause.

formTable.ex: 오다 → 올 텐데 (it'll probably rain, so...)
많다 → 많을 텐데 (there'll probably be a lot, so...)
춥다 → 추울 텐데 (it'll probably be cold, so...)
얼다 → 얼었을 텐데 (it must have frozen, so...)

examples.en: It'll probably be cold outside, so please wear a coat.
examples.note: 춥다 → 추우- + ㄹ 텐데; forecast (cold) + caring advice (wear a coat), the core use.

examples.ko: 오후에 비가 올 텐데 우산을 가져가세요.
examples.romanization: ohue biga ol tende usaneul gajyeogaseyo.
examples.en: It'll probably rain in the afternoon, so take an umbrella.
examples.note: The everyday "take an umbrella" sentence; 올 텐데 sets up the practical suggestion.

examples.ko: 눈이 많이 올 텐데 운전 조심하세요.
examples.romanization: nuni mani ol tende unjeon josimhaseyo.
examples.en: It'll probably snow a lot, so drive carefully.
examples.note: Shows 텐데 carrying genuine concern (조심하세요) about a weather outcome.

examples.ko: 내일은 더울 텐데 물을 많이 드세요.
examples.romanization: naeireun deoul tende mureul mani deuseyo.
examples.en: It'll probably be hot tomorrow, so drink a lot of water.
examples.note: 덥다 → 더우- + ㄹ 텐데; summer-heat advice, everyday seasonal vocabulary.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ 텐데 vs. -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요
keyPoint.body: Both predict, but -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 just states the guess and stops (비가 올 것 같아요 = I think it'll rain). -(으)ㄹ 텐데 predicts and then leans into a consequence — concern or advice — so it almost always has a second clause: 비가 올 텐데 우산을 가져가세요 (it'll rain, so take an umbrella).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 올 텐데 links smoothly into one breath group — "ol-ten-de," no pause — so the forecast flows straight into the advice. 텐데 itself is read [텐데] as written.

drill.instruction: Predict the weather and add caring advice with -(으)ㄹ 텐데. Follow the model.
drill.model: 비가 오다 / 우산을 가져가세요 → 비가 올 텐데 우산을 가져가세요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers treat -(으)ㄹ 텐데 as a complete sentence ("it'll probably rain."). But 텐데 ends in -ㄴ데, which dangles — it expects a following clause. Left alone it sounds unfinished, as if you trailed off.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-(으)면 — "if / when the weather is like this" (condition)
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)면 to set up a weather condition and its result: "if it rains, I'll stay home," "when spring comes, flowers bloom." It covers both English "if" (a possibility) and "when" (a regular trigger) — exactly how Koreans talk about weather shaping everyday decisions.

formTable.when: Stem ends in a vowel (오다, 따뜻하다)
Stem ends in a consonant (좋다, 많다)
formTable.ex: 좋다 → 좋으면 (if the weather is good)
그치다 → 그쳤으면 (if the rain/snow has stopped)

examples.en: If it rains, I'll stay home.
examples.note: 오다 vowel-stem → 오면; the model "if it rains" sentence with a plan as the result.

examples.en: When spring comes, flowers bloom.
examples.note: Here -면 = "when" for a regular seasonal pattern, not a one-time "if."

examples.en: When it's hot, I turn on the air conditioner.
examples.note: 덥다 → 더우- + 면; a habitual weather-triggered action.

examples.ko: 눈이 많이 오면 학교에 안 가요.
examples.romanization: nuni mani omyeon hakgyoe an gayo.
examples.en: If it snows a lot, we don't go to school.
examples.note: Shows a weather condition deciding an everyday outcome (no school).

keyPoint.label: -(으)면 vs. -(으)니까
keyPoint.body: -(으)면 introduces a condition that may or may not happen (비가 오면 = if/when it rains — uncertain). -(으)니까 gives a reason that is already true (비가 오니까 = since it's raining — a fact right now). Use -면 for forecasts and rules, -니까 for what's actually happening.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 좋으면 is pronounced [조으면]: the ㅎ of 좋 goes silent (ㅎ-탈락) before the vowel 으, so it's "jo-eu-myeon," not "joh-eu-myeon."

drill.instruction: Join the weather condition to its result with -(으)면. Follow the model.
drill.model: 비가 오다 / 집에 있어요 → 비가 오면 집에 있어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 비가 올 거면 집에 있을 거예요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers add a future marker inside the if-clause ("if it WILL rain"). Korean keeps the -(으)면 clause plain present — 비가 오면, not 비가 올 거면. Only the result clause carries the future (있을 거예요).

grammarNotes.title: N 때문에 — "because of..." (a weather cause)
grammarNotes.func: Use N 때문에 to name a noun — usually a weather event — as the cause of something, especially something inconvenient: "because of the rain," "because of the heat." It attaches straight to a noun and is the everyday way to blame the weather for a delay, a cancellation, or how you feel.

formTable.when: Noun ending in a vowel (비, 더위)
formTable.ex: 비 → 비 때문에 (because of the rain)

formTable.when: Noun ending in a consonant (태풍, 눈)
formTable.ex: 태풍 → 태풍 때문에 (because of the typhoon)

examples.en: The picnic was cancelled because of the rain.
examples.note: 비 + 때문에; the classic "weather ruined the plan" sentence.

examples.en: I couldn't sleep because of the heat.
examples.note: 더위 (the heat) as a cause of how you feel — very common in summer.

examples.en: The plane is late because of the typhoon.
examples.note: 태풍 ends in a consonant; 때문에 attaches with no change.

examples.en: The roads are really backed up because of the snow.
examples.note: Everyday winter complaint; 눈 (snow) named as the cause of traffic.

keyPoint.label: N 때문에 vs. N 덕분에
keyPoint.body: 때문에 is neutral-to-negative — you usually blame it for trouble (비 때문에 취소됐어요 = cancelled because of the rain). For a good outcome, Koreans switch to 덕분에 "thanks to" (좋은 날씨 덕분에 = thanks to the nice weather). Don't use 때문에 to thank the weather.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 때문에 is pronounced [때무네]: the ㄴ of 문 links into the following 에 (연음), so it sounds like "ttae-mu-ne," run together as one word after the noun.

drill.instruction: Name the weather cause with N 때문에. Follow the model.
drill.model: 비 / 소풍이 취소됐어요 → 비 때문에 소풍이 취소됐어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English "because of" is neutral, so learners use 때문에 for good things too. But 때문에 carries a blaming nuance; for a positive cause Korean uses 덕분에 (thanks to). Saving 때문에 for problems keeps you natural.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-(으)ㄹ 때 — when (a time or situation)
grammarNotes.func: -(으)ㄹ 때 marks the time or situation when something happens: "when it rains," "when it's cold." Attach it to a verb or adjective stem; for a past time, use -았/었을 때.

examples.en: When it rains, I use an umbrella.
examples.note: 오다 → 올 때. The 때 clause sets the time for the main action.

examples.en: When the weather is cold, I stay home.
examples.note: 춥다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 추울 때.

examples.en: When it's hot, I drink a lot of water.
examples.note: 덥다 → 더울 때.

examples.en: When it snowed, I took photos.
examples.note: Past time → 왔을 때 (오다 + 았을 때).

keyPoint.label: 때 is a noun, so use the -(으)ㄹ modifier
keyPoint.body: 때 means "time," so the verb in front must be in the noun-modifying -(으)ㄹ form: 올 때, 추울 때 — never 와 때 or 춥어 때. For a finished past time, use -았/었을 때 (왔을 때).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 때 begins with the tense consonant ㄸ — say it hard: 올 때 is [올 때], not a soft [대].

drill.instruction: Make a "when …" clause with -(으)ㄹ 때.
drill.model: (비가 오다) → 비가 올 때 · (춥다) → 추울 때

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 비가 와 때 / 비가 오을 때
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 때 needs the -(으)ㄹ modifier form. 오다 ends in a vowel, so it's 올 때 (not 와 때, not 오을 때). A consonant stem takes -을 때 (추울 때).

extendedDialogue.setting: Two friends check the forecast before a weekend trip and decide what to do with their plan.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Did you see the weekend forecast?
lines.grammarNote: 일기예보를 보다 is the natural first action before changing plans.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 태풍이 올 것 같아서 비행기가 늦을 수도 있어요.
lines.romanization: taepungi ol geot gataseo bihaenggiga neujeul sudo isseoyo.
lines.en: It looks like a typhoon may come, so the plane might be late.
lines.grammarNote: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아서 links the forecast to the travel problem.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 미세먼지가 심하면 일정은 취소하는 게 좋겠어요.
lines.romanization: misemeonjiga simhamyeon iljeongeun chwisohaneun ge jotgesseoyo.
lines.en: If the fine dust is bad, it would be better to cancel the plan.
lines.grammarNote: V/A면 sets the condition, and 취소하는 게 좋겠어요 gives a soft recommendation.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Let's book again when the weather clears.
lines.grammarNote: V(으)ㄹ 때 marks the timing for rebooking.

readingText.title: 태풍이 올 것 같아서 일정을 바꿔요
readingText.body: 민서는 주말 일기예보를 봤어요. 태풍이 올 것 같아서 비행기가 늦을 수도 있었어요. 또 미세먼지가 심하면 밖에서 오래 있기 어려워요. 그래서 친구에게 '미세먼지가 심하면 일정은 취소하는 게 좋겠어요'라고 보냈어요. 친구는 날씨가 맑아질 때 다시 예약하자고 했어요. 이처럼 날씨 표현은 단순히 하늘을 설명하는 말이 아니라, 약속과 여행 계획을 바꾸는 말로 자주 쓰여요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo checked the weekend forecast. A typhoon might come, so the plane could be late. If fine dust is bad, it is hard to stay outside for long. Minseo texted that it would be better to cancel the plan if the fine dust was bad. The friend suggested booking again when the weather clears. Weather expressions often change appointments and travel plans.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 무엇을 봤어요?
태풍이 오면 무엇이 늦을 수도 있어요?
언제 다시 예약하기로 했어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 날씨가 맑아질 때 다시 예약하기로 했어요.

culturalNote.title: Weather talk often means plan talk
culturalNote.body: In Korean daily conversation, weather is often the reason for a practical decision. People may mention 일기예보 before travel, 태풍 before flights, 미세먼지 before outdoor plans, and 장마 before bringing an umbrella. The natural Korean move is usually cause plus action: 비 때문에 못 가요, 미세먼지가 심하면 취소해요, 날씨가 맑아질 때 다시 예약해요.
culturalNote.tip: For weather words, learn the verb that normally goes with the noun: 비가 오다, 눈이 오다, 안개가 끼다, 미세먼지가 심하다, 기온이 떨어지다.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence gives a cautious weather forecast?
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 makes a cautious guess, and 비 uses the subject particle 가.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses 눈 as weather?
inlineExercises.explanation: In this chapter, 눈 is snow. 눈이 오다 means 'it snows.'

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence names fine dust as the cause of canceling?
inlineExercises.explanation: Use noun plus 때문에 without adding 가 or 를.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete: 날씨가 맑아질 ___ 다시 예약해요. (Let's book again when the weather clears up.)
inlineExercises.explanation: V(으)ㄹ 때 marks the time when the weather clears.

inlineExercises.prompt: 비___ 오면 우산을 가져가요. (If it rains, take an umbrella.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 비 is the subject of 오다, so it takes 가. 를 would make rain an object.

inlineExercises.prompt: 내일 비가 ___ 우산을 가져가세요. (오다 → likely situation/concern)
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ 텐데 gives a likely situation plus concern. 오다 becomes 올 텐데.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Because of fine dust, I canceled the plan.'
inlineExercises.explanation: N 때문에 names the weather or pollution cause. 일정을 취소했어요 gives the concrete decision.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'I think it will rain.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 softens the weather prediction. 비가 is the subject of the rain coming.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '눈을 오면 운전하지 마세요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Snow as weather takes 이/가 with 오다. 눈을 would make snow an object, which is wrong here.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence delays a plan because the weather may clear later?
inlineExercises.explanation: -ㄹ 때 marks the situation/time when the weather clears. The other options mix the weather word with the wrong particles or endings.

bullets: Core use: weather words explain real plan changes.
비, 눈, and 태풍 commonly pair with 오다; 안개 pairs with 끼다; 미세먼지 and 황사 often pair with 심하다.
-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 gives a cautious forecast, while -(으)ㄹ 텐데 adds concern or a soft warning.
N 때문에 explains a weather cause, and V/A면 sets the condition for what to do next.

writingTask.prompt: Text a friend a quick weather update and one piece of advice for tomorrow's outing.
writingTask.hint: Use -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 to guess the weather, -(으)ㄹ 텐데 to add concern, and N 때문에 for the cause.
writingTask.model: 내일은 비가 올 것 같아요. 비 때문에 추울 텐데 우산하고 따뜻한 옷을 가져오세요. 비가 오면 우리 집에서 만나요.
writingTask.modelEn: I think it'll rain tomorrow. It'll probably be cold because of the rain, so bring an umbrella and warm clothes. If it rains, let's meet at my place.

canDo: Make a soft weather guess from what I see (비가 올 것 같아요)
Forecast a likely situation and add advice (추울 텐데 우산을 가져오세요)
Set up a weather condition and its result (비가 오면 집에 있어요)
Name a weather event as the cause (비 때문에, 황사 때문에)
Point to a time or situation when something happens (추울 때)

chapters.title: Clothing and Appearance
chapters.goal: Describe clothes and appearance without sounding too blunt.
chapters.scenario: You choose clothes, compliment a friend, or explain what someone is wearing.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: May I try on this shirt?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.en: Yes, the fitting room is on the right.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 조금 커 보여요. 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
dialogue.romanization: jogeum keo boyeoyo. han chisu jageun geotdo boyeo jusigesseoyo?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 네. 면접에는 이 셔츠보다 남색 셔츠가 더 단정해 보여요.
dialogue.romanization: ne. myeonjeobeneun i syeocheuboda namsaek syeocheuga deo danjeonghae boyeoyo.
dialogue.en: Sure. For an interview, the navy shirt looks neater than this shirt.

dialogue.ko: 그럼 이걸로 할게요. 교환이나 환불도 돼요?
dialogue.romanization: geureom igeollo halgeyo. gyohwanina hwanbuldo dwaeyo?
dialogue.en: Then I'll take this one. Can I exchange or refund it too?

chapters.guidedPractice: Build five shop sentences: try on, ask another size, describe fit, compare interview options, and ask exchange/refund policy.
chapters.realLifeTask: Describe one outfit and add one soft opinion or compliment.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner chooses an outfit situation; answer with 잘 어울려요, 커 보여요, 단정해 보여요, or 교환돼요?
chapters.review: Can you separate size fit (맞다/크다/작다), appearance (어울리다/보이다), and store policy (교환/환불)?

beginnerGuide.title: Fit and style are different
beginnerGuide.body: 사이즈가 맞아요 means the size fits. 잘 어울려요 means it suits the person. 커 보여요 or 작아 보여요 describes how it looks.

beginnerGuide.title: Store requests need soft endings
beginnerGuide.body: 입어 봐도 돼요? asks permission to try on. 보여 주시겠어요? is a polite staff request for another size or color.

beginnerGuide.title: Interview clothing uses 단정하다
beginnerGuide.body: For interviews or work, 단정해 보여요 is often more useful than 예뻐요 because it means neat, presentable, and appropriate.

checkpoints: I can use 입다, 신다, 쓰다, and 끼다 with the right item.
I can describe color, size, and fit before the noun.
I can soften appearance comments with 잘 어울려요 or 괜찮은 것 같아요.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Describe clothes and appearance without sounding too blunt.
exitTask.prompt: Describe one outfit and add one soft opinion or compliment.

sampleAnswer.ko: 오늘 입은 셔츠가 잘 어울려요. 색도 깔끔한 것 같아요.
sampleAnswer.en: The shirt you are wearing today suits you well. I think the color is clean too.

checklist: I can use 입다, 신다, 쓰다, and 끼다 with the right item.
I can describe color, size, and fit before the noun.
I can soften appearance comments with 잘 어울려요 or 괜찮은 것 같아요.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You are in a clothing store, want to try on a shirt, ask for a different size, choose something neat for an interview, and check whether exchange or refund is possible.
objectives: Use clothing words with 입다, 신다, 사이즈가 맞다, and 잘 어울리다.
Ask store staff politely with 입어 봐도 돼요? and 보여 주시겠어요?
Describe appearance and interview appropriateness with 커 보여요, 단정해 보여요, and N보다 더 A.
hook.whyItMatters: This chapter should not be a random clothing list. The vocabulary has to serve one real flow: try on clothes, judge fit and style, compare options, and confirm store policy before buying.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어 보세요 — Try doing it
grammarNotes.func: Suggest that the listener try an action to see how it goes — perfect for inviting someone to try a piece of clothing on, try a color, or give a style a go. It softens a plain command into friendly encouragement: go ahead and try it.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in ㅏ or ㅗ
Verb stem ends in any other vowel or a consonant
formTable.ex: 입다 → 입어 보세요 (try wearing it), 신다 → 신어 보세요 (try them on)
착용하다 → 착용해 보세요 (try wearing it on)

examples.en: Try this dress on.
examples.note: 한번 (once / give it a go) commonly pairs with -아/어 보세요 to mean a light, no-pressure try.

examples.en: Try this hat on too.
examples.note: 쓰다 (to wear on the head) is a ㅡ-irregular: ㅡ drops before -어, giving 써 보세요.

examples.en: Try these shoes on.
examples.note: 신다 = to wear on the feet. Each clothing verb is different, but all combine the same way with 보세요.

examples.en: Try picking the red one.
examples.note: 고르다 is a 르-irregular, so 고르 → 골라 before -아; you are inviting them to try choosing.

keyPoint.label: -(으)세요 vs -아/어 보세요
keyPoint.body: 입으세요 = Put it on (a plain polite command). 입어 보세요 = Try it on (and see) — it adds the nuance of testing or experiencing, which is why a shop clerk says 입어 보세요, not 입으세요.

drill.instruction: Invite the customer to try each item, using V-아/어 보세요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English try on makes learners reach for a word meaning try/attempt (시도하다). In Korean you keep the real clothing verb (입다/신다/쓰다) and just attach 보세요; the try meaning comes entirely from 보세요.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어 주시겠어요? — Could you please do it for me?
grammarNotes.func: A very polite request asking someone to do something for your benefit. In a shop or fitting room it is how you ask the clerk to bring another size, show you a color, or give you a hand. -주다 adds for me, and -시겠어요? makes it gentle and respectful.

formTable.ex: 찾다 → 찾아 주시겠어요? (could you find it for me?)

formTable.when: Stem ends in another vowel or consonant
formTable.ex: 보이다 → 보여 주시겠어요? (could you show me?)
추천하다 → 추천해 주시겠어요? (could you recommend one?)

examples.en: Could you bring me a bigger size?
examples.note: 가져다주다 (bring for someone) is the go-to fitting-room request; -주시겠어요? keeps it polite to the clerk.

examples.en: Could you show me another color too?
examples.note: 보이다 → 보여; 보여 주다 literally show for me, the natural way to ask to be shown an item.

examples.en: Could you find this shirt for me?
examples.note: 좀 softens the request even more — a near-obligatory politeness word in spoken requests.

examples.ko: 이 바지 잘 어울리는지 봐 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: i baji jal eoullineunji bwa jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you check whether these pants suit me?
examples.note: 보다 → 봐; asking someone to look or check for your benefit, a common appearance question to a friend or clerk.

keyPoint.label: -아/어 주세요 vs -아/어 주시겠어요?
keyPoint.body: 가져다 주세요 = Please bring it (polite request). 가져다 주시겠어요? = Could you bring it? — the -시겠어요? question form is one step more deferential and indirect, the safest choice with a stranger or staff.

drill.instruction: Make each request polite using V-아/어 주시겠어요?
items: 작은 사이즈 / 찾다 (write: 작은 사이즈 찾아 주시겠어요?)
이 옷 / 추천하다 (write: 이 옷 추천해 주시겠어요?)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 더 큰 사이즈로 가져다 주시겠어요 나를 위해?
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners add for me as a separate phrase (나를 위해) by analogy with English. The benefit is already built into 주다, so adding 나를 위해 is redundant and unnatural — just use 주시겠어요?.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-아/어 보이다 — It looks / appears
grammarNotes.func: Describe how something or someone appears to the observer. Attached to an adjective it means looks (pretty/big/expensive); it is the everyday way to compliment an outfit or comment on how clothes look on someone.

formTable.when: Stem ends in another vowel or consonant

examples.en: That dress really looks pretty.
examples.note: 예쁘다 → 예뻐 (ㅡ drops before -어); the headline example for this pattern.

examples.en: This coat looks a bit expensive.
examples.note: 비싸다 ends in ㅏ, so the -아 merges in: 비싸 보여요; commenting on apparent price.

examples.en: That color looks like it suits you well.
examples.note: 어울리다 → 어울려; pairing 잘 어울리다 with 보이다 is the standard it looks good on you comment.

examples.ko: 이 신발을 신으니까 키가 커 보여요.
examples.romanization: i sinbareul sineunikka kiga keo boyeoyo.
examples.en: With these shoes on, you look taller.
examples.note: 크다 → 커; appearance changes caused by clothing are exactly what -아/어 보이다 expresses.

keyPoint.label: 예뻐요 vs 예뻐 보여요
keyPoint.body: 예뻐요 = It is pretty (your judgment of the thing itself). 예뻐 보여요 = It looks pretty (how it appears, possibly more than it really is). Use 보이다 when you are describing an impression or the effect an outfit gives.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 보여요 is pronounced with a smooth y-glide [bo-yeo-yo]; learners often clip it to [bo-eo-yo] — keep the ㅕ. In 좋아 보여요, ㅎ is silent before a vowel, so 좋아 links as [jo-a].

drill.instruction: Say how each looks using A-아/어 보여요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English looks like it is pretty tempts learners to build a heavy ~것처럼 보이다 clause. For a simple adjective impression, Korean just fuses the adjective with 보이다: 예뻐 보여요.

grammarNotes.title: A-(으)ㄴ N — An adjective before a noun
grammarNotes.func: Turn a descriptive adjective into a modifier that sits directly in front of a noun — the basic way to say a pretty dress, a long skirt, black shoes. Essential for describing clothing and appearance with detail.

formTable.when: Adjective stem ends in a vowel
Adjective stem ends in a consonant

examples.en: I like long skirts.
examples.note: 길다 is a ㄹ-irregular: ㄹ drops and -ㄴ attaches → 긴. A classic irregular to flag for clothing length.

examples.en: I wore black dress shoes.
examples.note: 검다 → 검은; consonant-final stems take -은. 검은색 (black color) is everyday clothing vocabulary.

examples.en: This is a small hat.
examples.note: 작다 → 작은; the modifier comes directly before the noun with no extra particle — unlike English, no is needed.

examples.en: I bought new sneakers.
examples.note: 새 (new) is a determiner that takes no ending at all — a common exception worth memorizing alongside the rule.

keyPoint.label: 치마가 길어요 vs 긴 치마
keyPoint.body: 치마가 길어요 = The skirt is long (adjective as predicate, sentence-final). 긴 치마 = a long skirt (adjective modifying the noun, mid-sentence). The same adjective takes -아/어요 to end a sentence but -(으)ㄴ to sit before a noun.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 작은 links as [ja-geun] — the final ㄱ of 작 moves onto the -은 (resyllabification). Likewise 검은 → [geo-meun], 좋은 → [jo-eun] (ㅎ silent).

drill.instruction: Combine the adjective and noun into A-(으)ㄴ N.
items: 하얗다 + 셔츠 (write: 하얀 셔츠 — ㅎ-irregular: ㅎ drops)
멋있다 + 코트 (write: 멋있는 코트 — 있다 type takes -는)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: With ㄹ-irregular adjectives like 길다, learners try to add -은 to a stem that already kept ㄹ. Instead the ㄹ drops and only -ㄴ attaches: 길다 → 긴 치마, not 길은/긴은 치마.

grammarNotes.title: N보다 (더) — More ... than N
grammarNotes.func: Compare two things: mark the standard of comparison (the thing you measure against) with 보다, and add 더 (more) for emphasis. Ideal for clothing and appearance — saying one skirt is longer than another, or one coat is more expensive than another.

formTable.when: After any noun (the thing compared against)
formTable.ex: 이 치마가 저 치마보다 길어요 (this skirt is longer than that one)

formTable.when: Add 더 before the adjective for emphasis
formTable.ex: 이 코트가 저 코트보다 더 비싸요 (this coat is more expensive than that one)
이 신발이 저 신발보다 덜 편해요 (these shoes are less comfortable than those)

examples.en: This dress is prettier than that one.
examples.note: 보다 attaches to 저 원피스, the thing being compared against — no separate word for than is needed.

examples.ko: 검은색 구두가 흰색보다 더 잘 어울려요.
examples.romanization: geomeunsaek guduga huinsaekboda deo jal eoullyeoyo.
examples.en: Black shoes suit you better than white ones.
examples.note: 더 (more) plus 잘 어울리다 is the natural way to say something suits you better.

examples.en: These pants are shorter than those.
examples.note: 짧다 → 짧아요; comparing length is a very common clothing comment.

examples.ko: 이 모자가 저 모자보다 더 커요.
examples.romanization: i mojaga jeo mojaboda deo keoyo.
examples.en: This hat is bigger than that one.
examples.note: 크다 → 커요; 더 reinforces the comparison but the sentence is already comparative thanks to 보다.

keyPoint.label: Where 보다 attaches
keyPoint.body: 보다 attaches to the standard (the thing you measure against), not the subject. 이 치마가 저 치마보다 길어요 = this skirt is longer than that skirt. The 가-marked noun is the winner; the 보다-marked noun is what it beats.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 보다 is always pronounced [bo-da] and attaches directly with no space in writing: 저 치마보다. 더 [deo] is a separate word with a clear ㅓ vowel — do not reduce it to [deu].

drill.instruction: Make a comparison with N보다 (더) using the cue.
drill.model: 이 치마 / 저 치마 / 길다 → 이 치마가 저 치마보다 길어요.
items: 이 코트 / 저 코트 / 비싸다 (write: 이 코트가 저 코트보다 비싸요.)
이 신발 / 저 신발 / 더 편하다 (write: 이 신발이 저 신발보다 더 편해요.)
빨간색 / 파란색 / 잘 어울리다 (write: 빨간색이 파란색보다 잘 어울려요.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English puts than that one at the end, so learners tack 저 치마보다 on after the adjective. In Korean the 보다 phrase must come before the adjective: subject + 보다-phrase + 더 + adjective.

extendedDialogue.setting: A shopper tries on a shirt, asks for another size, and chooses an interview outfit.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: May I try on this shirt?
lines.grammarNote: -아/어 봐도 돼요 asks permission to try an action.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Yes, the fitting room is on the right.
lines.grammarNote: 피팅룸 is the store-location word connected to trying on.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.ko: 조금 커 보여요. 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
lines.romanization: jogeum keo boyeoyo. han chisu jageun geotdo boyeo jusigesseoyo?
lines.en: It looks a little big. Could you show me one size smaller too?
lines.grammarNote: 커 보여요 is appearance; 한 치수 작은 거 is the size request.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.ko: 네. 면접에는 이 셔츠보다 남색 셔츠가 더 단정해 보여요.
lines.romanization: ne. myeonjeobeneun i syeocheuboda namsaek syeocheuga deo danjeonghae boyeoyo.
lines.en: Sure. For an interview, the navy shirt looks neater than this shirt.
lines.grammarNote: 이 셔츠보다 gives the comparison baseline, and 더 단정해 보여요 describes the appearance.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.ko: 그럼 이걸로 할게요. 교환이나 환불도 돼요?
lines.romanization: geureom igeollo halgeyo. gyohwanina hwanbuldo dwaeyo?
lines.en: Then I'll take this one. Can I exchange or refund it too?
lines.grammarNote: 교환/환불이 되다 asks about store policy.

readingText.title: 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
readingText.body: 민서는 면접에 입을 셔츠를 사러 갔어요. 먼저 직원에게 '이 셔츠 입어 봐도 돼요?'라고 물었어요. 피팅룸에서 입어 보니 사이즈가 조금 커 보였어요. 그래서 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 달라고 했어요. 직원은 면접에는 이 셔츠보다 남색 셔츠가 더 단정해 보인다고 말했어요. 민서는 그 셔츠가 잘 어울리고 사이즈도 맞아서 샀어요. 마지막으로 교환이나 환불이 되는지도 확인했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo went to buy a shirt for an interview. First, Minseo asked a staff member if trying on the shirt was allowed. After trying it on in the fitting room, the size looked a little big, so Minseo asked to see one size smaller. The staff member said a navy shirt looked neater for an interview. It suited Minseo and the size fit, so Minseo bought it. Finally, Minseo checked whether exchange or refund was possible.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 무엇을 사러 갔어요?
셔츠는 어떻게 보였어요?
마지막으로 무엇을 확인했어요?

culturalNote.title: Fit, style, and policy are separate questions
culturalNote.body: In a Korean clothing store, keep three questions separate. First, size: 사이즈가 맞아요? 한 치수 작은 거 있어요? Second, style: 잘 어울려요? 단정해 보여요? Third, policy: 교환돼요? 환불돼요? Learners often mix these because English can say 'it works' for all three, but Korean uses different verbs.
culturalNote.tip: For clothes, 입다 is for clothing and 신다 is for shoes. For compliments, the clothing or color is the subject: 이 옷이 잘 어울려요, not 이 옷을 잘 어울려요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence asks permission to try on a shirt?
inlineExercises.explanation: 입다 is for clothing, and -아/어 봐도 돼요? asks permission.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence asks for one size smaller politely?
options: 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
한 치수 작은 것도 먹어 보세요?
한 치수 작은 것도 잘 어울려요?
inlineExercises.correct: 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
inlineExercises.explanation: 보여 주시겠어요? is a polite request to staff.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence is about style, not size?
inlineExercises.explanation: 어울리다 describes whether something suits someone. 맞다 is about fit.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete: 면접에는 남색 셔츠가 더 단정해 ___.
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어 보이다 describes how it appears.

inlineExercises.prompt: 셔츠___ 입어 봐도 돼요? (May I try on the shirt?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 입다 takes the clothing item as an object, so 셔츠를 fits. 가 would make the shirt the subject.

inlineExercises.prompt: 이 셔츠를 ___ ? (입다 → try with permission)
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어 봐도 돼요? asks whether it is okay to try doing something. 입다 becomes 입어 봐도 돼요?

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Could you show me a smaller size?'
inlineExercises.correct: 한 사이즈 작은 거 보여 주시겠어요?
inlineExercises.explanation: 작은 거 describes the smaller item you want. -주시겠어요? is a polite staff-facing request.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'It suits you well.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 잘 어울려요 comments on style or fit with the person. It is not about the physical size being correct.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '운동화를 입어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: Shoes use 신다, not 입다. 입다 is for clothes worn on the body like shirts or coats.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means “It looks too big”?
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어 보이다 describes how something appears. 커 보여요 is the natural “looks big.”

bullets: Core flow: try on clothing, ask for another size, compare appearance, then check exchange/refund.
Use 입다 for clothes and 신다 for shoes.
맞다 is size fit, 어울리다 is style harmony, and 단정해 보이다 is presentable appearance.
Use 보여 주시겠어요? for polite staff requests and N보다 더 A for comparing options.

writingTask.prompt: Write a short message to a shop clerk while trying on clothes: compliment a color, ask for another size, and compare two items.
writingTask.hint: Use A/V-아/어 보이다 to say how it looks, A-(으)ㄴ N for the adjective+noun, N보다 (더) to compare, and V-아/어 주시겠어요? to ask politely.
writingTask.model: 이 남색 코트가 정말 따뜻해 보여요. 이 코트가 저 코트보다 더 예뻐요. 한 사이즈 작은 옷을 보여 주시겠어요?
writingTask.modelEn: This navy coat looks really warm. This coat is prettier than that coat. Could you show me a size smaller?

canDo: Invite someone to try something on (한번 입어 보세요)
Ask a clerk politely for help (다른 사이즈를 보여 주시겠어요?)
Say how clothes or a person look (따뜻해 보여요, 예뻐 보여요)
Put a descriptive adjective before a noun (예쁜 치마, 긴 바지)
Compare two items (이 옷이 저 옷보다 더 좋아요)

beginnerGuide.title: 인분 counts servings, not people
beginnerGuide.body: 삼겹살 두 인분 is two servings of pork belly. 두 명 is two people, so do not use 명 when ordering portions.

beginnerGuide.title: Grilling has action and result words
beginnerGuide.body: 굽다 is the action of grilling. 익다 is the result: 고기가 익었어요. When it is cooked, you can say 잘라 주세요.

beginnerGuide.title: Requests split into item and action
beginnerGuide.body: N 주세요 orders an item: 공기밥 주세요. V아/어 주세요 asks for an action: 잘라 주세요, 포장해 주세요.

checkpoints: I can ask if a food is spicy or contains an ingredient.
I can describe taste with 맵다, 짜다, 달다, 싱겁다, and 고소하다.
I can use 덜 or 빼 주세요 when ordering.

I can describe taste with 맵다, 짜다, 달다, 싱겁다, and 고소하다.

hook.situation: You sit down at a 삼겹살 restaurant with coworkers, order by servings, ask for side dishes and rice, grill meat at the table, cut it when it is cooked, and pack leftovers.
objectives: Order Korean barbecue with 인분, 공기밥, 밑반찬, and N 주세요.
Talk about table grilling with 굽다, 익다, 자르다, and V아/어 주세요.
Describe taste and reasons with 맵다, 짜다, 신선하다, -아서/어서, and -(으)니까.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean food culture is not just food names. At many meals, you order shared portions, cook at the table, ask for refills, and explain taste or cooking stage before making a request.

grammarNotes.title: N 주세요 — Ordering an Item
grammarNotes.func: Use N 주세요 to ask someone to give you a thing. In a restaurant or café this is your basic ordering phrase: name the item, optionally with a number, then add 주세요 ("please give me"). It is polite and works with any server.

formTable.ex: 커피 두 잔 → 커피 두 잔 주세요 (Two coffees, please.)
물 → 물 좀 주세요 (Some water, please.)

examples.en: One kimchi stew here, please.
examples.note: 여기 ("here") flags you're ordering for this table; 하나 is the casual way to count one dish.

examples.en: Some water, please.
examples.note: 좀 softens the request and is almost automatic with 물 in a restaurant.

examples.en: This one, please.
examples.note: 이거 ("this thing") lets you point at the menu without knowing the dish name.

examples.en: Two colas, please.
examples.note: 개 is the all-purpose counter for canned/bottled drinks; 잔 is for glasses you pour.

keyPoint.label: 주세요 vs. 주문할게요
keyPoint.body: 주세요 literally means "give me," so you attach it to the THING (커피 주세요). If you want to say "I'll order," that's the verb 주문하다 → 주문할게요. Beginners only need N 주세요 to order; save 주문할게요 for flagging the server that you're ready.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 주세요 is read [주세요], no special linking. Watch the counter 한 개: say 한 / 개 as two clear beats — learners squash it into 항개. Keep the ㄴ of 한 crisp before 개.

drill.instruction: You are at a restaurant. Order each item by putting it into the N (수량) 주세요 frame.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers add "I" (저는) out of habit, but 주세요 already means "give ME," so 저는 is redundant and sounds odd. Just name the item + 주세요.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어 주세요 — Asking for an Action
grammarNotes.func: Use V-아/어 주세요 to ask someone to DO something for you, not just hand you a thing. Take a verb stem, add the 아/어 connector, then 주세요. In a restaurant this is how you ask the server to bring, change, cut, or wrap something.

formTable.ex: 계산하다 → 계산해 주세요 (Please ring it up.)

examples.en: Could you bring more side dishes, please.
examples.note: 갖다 주세요 ("bring and give") is the set phrase for asking a server to fetch something; 좀 더 = a bit more.

examples.en: Please cut the meat for us.
examples.note: At a Korean BBQ you ask staff to cut the meat; 자르다 → 잘라 (르 irregular).

examples.en: Please wrap this to go.
examples.note: 포장하다 ("to pack") → 포장해 주세요 is the standard way to ask for takeout.

examples.en: Please make it less spicy.
examples.note: 하다 → 해 주세요; 덜 맵게 ("less spicily") tells the kitchen how to cook it.

keyPoint.label: N 주세요 vs. V-아/어 주세요
keyPoint.body: N 주세요 asks for a THING (물 주세요 = give me water). V-아/어 주세요 asks for an ACTION (포장해 주세요 = pack it). If the English word is a noun ("water," "the menu"), use N 주세요; if it's a verb ("cut it," "wrap it," "bring it"), use V-아/어 주세요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a stem ending in ㄹ like 만들다, the form is 만들어 주세요 [만드러 주세요] — the ㄹ links into the next syllable. Say it smoothly as 만드러, not 만들-어.

drill.instruction: Turn each verb into a polite request with V-아/어 주세요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners attach 주세요 to the bare stem (포장하-), but you must first conjugate with 아/어: 하다 → 해. The connector vowel is not optional — 하 주세요 is ungrammatical; it must be 해 주세요.

grammarNotes.title: V-고 — Linking Food Actions in Order
grammarNotes.func: Use V-고 to chain two verbs done by the same person, usually in sequence: "do A and (then) B." Attach 고 directly to the verb stem — no vowel changes, no tense on the first verb. It's the everyday way to describe eating-and-doing routines.

formTable.when: Tense goes on the LAST verb only

examples.en: I eat a meal and (then) drink coffee.
examples.note: Classic sequence; tense (present) appears only on the final verb 마셔요.

examples.en: I wash my hands and eat.
examples.note: Natural order-of-events use; 씻고 stays plain even though the action is habitual.

examples.en: I cooked ramyeon and took out the kimchi.
examples.note: Past tense 꺼냈어요 sits only on the last verb; 끓이고 carries no -었-.

examples.en: We grill the meat and wrap it in lettuce to eat.
examples.note: Describes the two-step BBQ routine; 굽고 links the grilling to the eating.

keyPoint.label: V-고 vs. V-아서/어서 (sequence)
keyPoint.body: Both can mean "and then," but 고 just lists separate actions in order (먹고 마셔요 = eat, then drink — different objects). 아서/어서 is used when action B builds on A with the same object (사서 먹어요 = buy it and eat it). For loosely sequenced food steps, 고 is the safe default.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a stem ending in ㄱ, like 먹다, 먹고 is pronounced [먹꼬] — the 고 tenses to 꼬. Likewise 씻고 [씯꼬]. The 고 itself never changes spelling.

drill.instruction: Join the two actions with V-고. Keep tense on the second verb only.
drill.model: 손을 씻다 / 밥을 먹다 → 손을 씻고 밥을 먹어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English marks tense on both verbs ("ate and drank"), so learners add -었- to the first verb. In Korean, tense appears ONLY on the final verb; the first stays plain (먹고).

grammarNotes.title: A/V-아서/어서 — Reason and Result
grammarNotes.func: Use A/V-아서/어서 to give a reason: "because A, B." The first clause is the cause, the second is the result. Attach the 아/어 connector + 서 to the stem. With food you use it to explain why you can or can't eat something, or why you like a dish.

examples.en: It's so spicy that I can't eat it.
examples.note: 맵다 → 매워서 (ㅂ irregular); the spiciness is the reason for not eating.

examples.ko: 이 집 김치찌개가 맛있어서 자주 와요.
examples.romanization: i jip gimchijjigaega masisseoseo jaju wayo.
examples.en: This place's kimchi stew is delicious, so I come often.
examples.note: 맛있어서 explains the reason for the result 자주 와요 (come often).

examples.en: I was hungry, so I made ramyeon.
examples.note: 고프다 → 고파서; even though the result is past, the reason clause stays plain (no 고팠어서).

examples.ko: 커피를 많이 마셔서 잠이 안 와요.
examples.romanization: keopireul mani masyeoseo jami an wayo.
examples.en: I drank a lot of coffee, so I can't sleep.
examples.note: 마시다 → 마셔서; everyday cause-and-result about a drink.

keyPoint.label: -아서/어서 vs. -(으)니까 (reason)
keyPoint.body: Both mean "because," but -아서/어서 cannot be followed by a command or suggestion, and never takes past/future tense in the reason clause. Use -아서/어서 for a plain reason → result (매워서 못 먹어요). When you want to follow with a command or suggestion ("It's spicy, so order something else"), switch to -(으)니까.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 맛있어서 is pronounced [마시써서] — the ㅅ of 맛 links forward and the double ㅆ stays tense. Say it as one smooth 마시써서, not 맛-있-어-서.

drill.instruction: Combine the two clauses with -아서/어서. Keep the reason clause plain (no past tense on it).
drill.model: 맛있다 / 자주 와요 → 맛있어서 자주 와요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English puts past tense on both clauses ("was hungry, so ate"), so learners write 고팠어서. The -아서/어서 reason clause never carries -었-; the tense lives only in the result clause (먹었어요).

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄹ게요 — Saying What You'll Have
grammarNotes.func: Use V-(으)ㄹ게요 to announce a decision you're making on the spot — "I'll have / I'll do ___." At the table it's how you tell the server or your friends what you've chosen, with a nuance of committing to it right now. Add -ㄹ게요 to a vowel-ending stem, -을게요 to a consonant-ending stem.

examples.en: I'll have bibimbap.
examples.note: Announcing your own choice at the table; 저는 marks "as for me" when each person picks a dish.

examples.en: Excuse me, we're ready to order.
examples.note: 저기요 calls the server; 주문할게요 signals you've decided and want to order now.

examples.en: Then I'll order naengmyeon.
examples.note: 시키다 ("to order/make happen") → 시킬게요; 그럼 ("then") reacts to what others chose.

examples.en: I'll pay.
examples.note: Offering to pay the bill; -ㄹ게요 carries the "I'll take care of it" promise to the listener.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ게요 vs. -(으)ㄹ래요
keyPoint.body: -(으)ㄹ게요 is you committing to do something, often for the listener's sake (저는 비빔밥 먹을게요 = I've decided, I'll have bibimbap). -(으)ㄹ래요 is more about your wish/preference and can sound like you're asking or stating want (비빔밥 먹을래요 = I want bibimbap / shall I?). To simply state your order, -(으)ㄹ게요 is the smoother choice.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -ㄹ게요 is pronounced [ㄹ께요] — the ㄱ tenses to ㄲ. So 먹을게요 is [머글께요] and 갈게요 is [갈께요]. The spelling stays 게, but you say 께.

drill.instruction: Say what you'll have using V-(으)ㄹ게요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 states a future plan as information ("I'm going to eat bibimbap") and sounds detached when ordering. -(으)ㄹ게요 directs the decision at the listener — the server or your friends — which is what ordering needs. For "I'll have ___" at the table, use -(으)ㄹ게요.

readingText.title: 삼겹살 두 인분 주세요
readingText.body: 민서는 회사 사람들과 삼겹살집에 갔어요. 먼저 삼겹살 두 인분하고 공기밥 하나를 주문했어요. 밑반찬이 부족해서 직원에게 밑반찬도 좀 더 달라고 했어요. 고기를 굽고 마늘도 같이 구웠어요. 고기가 익었으니까 먹기 좋게 잘라 달라고 했어요. 양념이 조금 매워서 공기밥을 같이 먹었고, 쌈장은 짜니까 조금만 넣었어요. 마지막에는 남은 음식을 포장해 달라고 했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo went to a samgyeopsal restaurant with coworkers. First, Minseo ordered two servings of samgyeopsal and one bowl of rice. Because the side dishes were not enough, Minseo asked the staff for more. They grilled the meat and garlic together. When the meat was cooked, Minseo asked someone to cut it into easy-to-eat pieces. The seasoning was a little spicy, so they ate it with rice, and since the ssamjang was salty, they added only a little. At the end, they asked to pack the leftovers.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 무엇을 주문했어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 삼겹살 두 인분하고 공기밥 하나를 주문했어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 고기가 익었을 때 무엇을 부탁했어요?
왜 공기밥을 같이 먹었어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 양념이 조금 매워서 공기밥을 같이 먹었어요.

culturalNote.title: Shared food, shared actions
culturalNote.body: At many Korean barbecue restaurants, the meal is shared at the table. People order meat by 인분, grill it together, ask for 밑반찬 refills, and often eat meat with 상추, 마늘, and 쌈장. The language follows the workflow: N 주세요 for items, V아/어 주세요 for actions, and -(으)니까 when a reason leads to a request.
culturalNote.tip: Keep 굽다 and 익다 separate: 사람이 고기를 구워요, but 고기가 익어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which counter fits restaurant servings?
inlineExercises.explanation: 인분 counts food servings. 명 counts people.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly separates cooking action and result?
inlineExercises.explanation: 굽다 takes the meat as object; 익다 uses the food as subject.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence gives a reason before a request?
inlineExercises.explanation: -(으)니까 naturally supports a following request.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete: 남은 건 ___ 주세요. (use 포장하다)
inlineExercises.explanation: 포장해 주세요 asks the restaurant to pack leftovers to go.

inlineExercises.prompt: 삼겹살 2인분___ 주세요. (Two servings of pork belly, please.)
inlineExercises.explanation: The ordered amount is the object of 주세요, so 을 is grammatical when the particle is shown. In restaurant speech, this particle is often dropped.

inlineExercises.prompt: 고기를 좀 ___ . (굽다 → please do)
inlineExercises.explanation: 굽다 is a ㅂ irregular in this form, becoming 구워. 구워 주세요 asks someone to grill it for you.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'When the meat is cooked, please cut it.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -으면 sets the condition. 익으면 means when it is cooked, and 잘라 주세요 is the request.

inlineExercises.prompt: Order: 'One bowl of rice, please.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 공깃밥 is ordered by item, and 하나 is the native number one. 주세요 makes it a polite restaurant order.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '고기를 익어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 익다 means the meat becomes cooked, so the meat is the subject and takes 가. If a person cooks it, use 굽다 or 익히다 instead.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which counter fits Korean barbecue servings?
inlineExercises.explanation: Restaurant servings use 인분. 잔 counts cups, and 권 counts books.

bullets: Core flow: order by 인분, add 공기밥, ask for 밑반찬, grill meat, cut it when cooked, and pack leftovers.
굽다 is the cooking action; 익다 is the food becoming cooked.
N 주세요 orders an item; V아/어 주세요 requests an action.
-아서/어서 explains a plain result, while -(으)니까 works well before a request or suggestion.

writingTask.prompt: Write what you say at a Korean BBQ restaurant: order food, ask the server to do one thing, and announce what you'll have.
writingTask.hint: Use N 주세요 to order, V-아/어 주세요 to ask for an action, V-고 to chain actions, A/V-아서/어서 for a reason, and V-(으)ㄹ게요 to announce your choice.
writingTask.model: 여기 삼겹살 이 인분 주세요. 고기를 다 굽고 먹기 좋게 잘라 주세요. 저는 배가 고파서 먼저 먹을게요.
writingTask.modelEn: Two servings of pork belly here, please. Please grill the meat fully and cut it into bite-size pieces. I'm hungry, so I'll start eating first.

canDo: Order an item with a quantity (삼겹살 이 인분 주세요)
Ask the server to do something (잘라 주세요, 바꿔 주세요)
Chain food actions in order (고기를 굽고 자르고)
Give a food reason and result (매워서 물을 마셔요)
Announce what you'll have on the spot (저는 비빔밥을 먹을게요)

beginnerGuide.title: Drama talk starts with experience
beginnerGuide.body: 이 드라마 본 적 있어요? asks whether someone has watched it before. Use 봤어요 for a specific past time, but 본 적 있어요 for experience.

beginnerGuide.title: Digital reactions are short
beginnerGuide.body: 댓글이 재미있어요, 대박, 헐, ㅋㅋ, 좋아요 눌렀어요 are real chat pieces. They should connect to the content, not float as random slang.

beginnerGuide.title: Streaming problems use 끊기다
beginnerGuide.body: 영상이 끊겨요 or 와이파이가 끊겼어요 describes buffering or disconnection. 끊다 is active; 끊기다 is the problem happening.
