hook.situation: You recommend a drama in KakaoTalk, react to comments, report what a friend said about subtitles, share a video, and troubleshoot a stream that keeps cutting out.
objectives: Ask about watching experience with V(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요.
React naturally to dramas, comments, idols, and shared videos.
Explain streaming problems with 영상이 끊기다 and suggest reconnecting Wi-Fi.
hook.whyItMatters: Entertainment talk in Korean is fast, casual, and full of short reactions. Digital-life Korean also needs practical verbs like 공유하다, 누르다, 끊기다, and 연결하다.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 — Have you ever…? (past experience)
grammarNotes.func: Says you have had the experience of doing something at least once. The negative, V-(으)ㄴ 적이 없어요, means you have never done it. It is about whether something has ever happened, not about one specific past event.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a consonant
formTable.ex: 듣다 → 들은 적이 있어요 (have heard it before)

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel
formTable.ex: 보다 → 본 적이 있어요 (have seen it before)
가다 → 간 적이 없어요 (have never gone)

examples.ko: 저는 그 드라마를 본 적이 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun geu deuramareul bon jeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: I have seen that drama before.
examples.note: 보다 ends in a vowel, so just -ㄴ 적이 있어요 — talking about a past viewing experience.

examples.ko: 그 가수 콘서트에 간 적이 있어요?
examples.romanization: geu gasu konseoteue gan jeogi isseoyo?
examples.en: Have you ever been to that singer's concert?
examples.note: As a question it asks about life experience, not one specific event you both know about.

examples.ko: 이 게임은 한 번도 해 본 적이 없어요.
examples.romanization: i geimeun han beondo hae bon jeogi eopseoyo.
examples.en: I have never played this game even once.
examples.note: 없어요 makes it the 'never' negative; 한 번도 reinforces 'not even once.'

examples.en: I have uploaded a video to YouTube before.
examples.note: 올리다 ends in a vowel → 올린; the experience of having uploaded at some point.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 vs. plain past -았/었어요
keyPoint.body: Plain past 봤어요 reports one specific event ('I watched it yesterday'). 본 적이 있어요 reports the experience itself ('I have watched it at some point'). Use -(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 when the time doesn't matter, only whether it has ever happened.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 적이 is pronounced [저기] (jeogi): the final ㄱ of 적 links onto the 이 of the next syllable.

drill.instruction: Turn each verb into a 'have you ever…?' question using -(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요.
drill.model: 라이브 방송을 보다 → 라이브 방송을 본 적이 있어요?

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저는 그 영화를 봤은 적이 있어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 저는 그 영화를 본 적이 있어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers add 었 because the meaning feels 'past.' But -(으)ㄴ already carries the past sense; attach it straight to the plain stem (보 → 본), never to the -았/었 form.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-는 것 같아요 — I think… / It seems… (soft impression)
grammarNotes.func: Softens a statement into an impression or guess: 'it seems,' 'I think,' 'probably.' It makes you sound less blunt and more polite, which is why Korean speakers use it constantly even when fairly sure.

formTable.ex: 보다 → 보는 것 같아요 (seems to be watching)
재미있다 → 재미있는 것 같아요 / 좋다 → 좋은 것 같아요 (seems good)
끝나다 → 끝난 것 같아요 (seems to have ended)
재미있다 → 재미있을 것 같아요 (looks like it'll be fun)

examples.ko: 이 드라마가 요즘 제일 인기 있는 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i deuramaga yojeum jeil ingi inneun geot gatayo.
examples.en: I think this drama is the most popular these days.
examples.note: 있다 takes the verb-style -는 것 같아요; softens a strong claim into an opinion.

examples.ko: 새 앨범이 정말 좋은 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: sae aelbeomi jeongmal joeun geot gatayo.
examples.en: I think the new album is really good.
examples.note: 좋다 is an adjective → -은 것 같아요; gives a gentle personal opinion.

examples.ko: 댓글을 보니까 사람들이 화난 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: daetgeureul bonikka saramdeuri hwanan geot gatayo.
examples.en: Judging by the comments, people seem to be angry.
examples.note: 화나다 here is a completed state → past -ㄴ 것 같아요 ('have gotten angry').

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 영화관이 붐빌 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: ibeon jumare yeonghwagwani bumbil geot gatayo.
examples.en: The movie theater will probably be crowded this weekend.
examples.note: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 is a guess about the future you can't see yet.

keyPoint.label: Present -는 것 같아요 vs. future -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요
keyPoint.body: Use -는 것 같아요 for something happening or true now ('seems to be ~ing'). Use -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 for a prediction about something not yet visible ('will probably ~'). Same softener, different time: 보는 것 같아요 = 'seems to be watching it'; 볼 것 같아요 = 'will probably watch it.'

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 것 같아요 is pronounced [걷 가타요] → naturally [걷까타요]: the final ㅅ becomes [t] and tenses the following ㄱ to [ㄲ].

drill.instruction: Make each statement softer with the correct form of -는 것 같아요.
drill.model: 이 노래가 좋다 → 이 노래가 좋은 것 같아요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 재미있다 and 맛있다 look like adjectives but contain 있다, so they pattern as verbs here: use -는 것 같아요, not the adjective -은 것 같아요.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-다고 했어요 — They said that… (reported speech)
grammarNotes.func: Reports what someone else said (or what you read or heard). It quotes a statement indirectly: 'He said that it's fun.' Used constantly for relaying news, comments, and messages.

formTable.ex: 보다 → 본다고 했어요 / 먹다 → 먹는다고 했어요 (said they watch/eat)
가수 → 가수라고 했어요 (said they're a singer)

examples.ko: 친구가 그 영화 진짜 재미있다고 했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga geu yeonghwa jinjja jaemiitdago haesseoyo.
examples.en: My friend said that movie is really fun.
examples.note: 재미있다 is an adjective, so plain -다고 했어요 with no 는.

examples.en: My younger sibling said they're going to play a new game.
examples.note: 하다 is a verb ending in a vowel → -ㄴ다고 했어요 (한다고).

examples.en: The news said that singer made a comeback.
examples.note: Past tense 했 + -다고 했어요; the source (뉴스에서) is marked with 에서.

examples.en: They said that person is a popular YouTuber.
examples.note: 유튜버 is a noun → -(이)라고 했어요; ends in a vowel so 라고, not 이라고.

keyPoint.label: Verb -ㄴ/는다고 vs. adjective -다고
keyPoint.body: The trap is the present tense. Verbs insert 는/ㄴ: 먹는다고, 본다고. Adjectives do NOT: 좋다고, 재미있다고. Past tense erases the difference — both verbs and adjectives use -았/었다고 (봤다고, 좋았다고).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -다고 했어요: 했어요 is said [해써요], and the whole reporting tail comes out quickly and flatly, lower in pitch than the quoted part.

drill.instruction: Report each sentence with -다고 했어요.
items: "저는 매일 웹툰을 봐요" → ___ (said they watch every day)
"제 친구는 게이머예요" → ___ (said their friend is a gamer)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 친구가 영화를 본다고 말했어요 라고 했어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'said that' makes learners reach for an extra verb. In Korean, -다고 했어요 already contains 'said.' Don't double it up; just attach -다고 to the quoted clause and end with 했어요.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-지만 — but / although (clean contrast)
grammarNotes.func: Joins two clauses in a straightforward 'A, but B' contrast. Neutral and clear, it works in both speech and writing, much like English 'but' or 'although.'

examples.en: This drama is long, but it's really fun.
examples.note: 길다 + 지만; clean contrast between 'long' and 'fun.'

examples.en: I like that game, but I don't have time.
examples.note: 좋아하다 (verb) + 지만; one clause for liking, one for the obstacle.

examples.en: I booked the ticket, but I couldn't go.
examples.note: Past -했 + 지만 contrasts a completed action with the result.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 유명한 가수지만 저는 노래를 몰라요.
examples.romanization: geu sarameun yumyeonghan gasujiman jeoneun noraereul mollayo.
examples.en: That person is a famous singer, but I don't know their songs.
examples.note: Noun 가수 + 지만; contrasts fame with the speaker's unfamiliarity.

keyPoint.label: -지만 (one sentence) vs. 하지만 (sentence-starter)
keyPoint.body: -지만 is a connector glued onto a verb or adjective inside one sentence: 좋지만 비싸요. 하지만 is a standalone conjunction that starts a new sentence: 좋아요. 하지만 비싸요. Same meaning 'but,' different position — don't put -지만 at the start of a sentence or 하지만 in the middle of one.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -지만 is said evenly as [지만]; in 봤지만 the ㅅ tenses the ㅈ, giving [봗찌만].

drill.instruction: Join the two ideas into one sentence with -지만.
drill.model: 이 영화 / 무섭다 + 재미있다 → 이 영화는 무섭지만 재미있어요.
items: 표를 사다(past) + 시간이 없어서 못 가다 → ___
그 배우 / 유명한 사람이다 + 저는 잘 모르다 → ___

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners attach -지만 to the full polite form (길어요지만). -지만 goes on the plain stem instead: 길다 → 길지만. For past, use 봤지만, not 봤어요지만.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄹ게요 — I'll do it (promise / casual intention)
grammarNotes.func: States what the speaker will do, often as a light promise or a response to the listener: 'I'll watch it,' 'I'll send it to you.' It is speaker-only (you can't use it for someone else) and signals you're deciding in reaction to the situation. Extremely common in texting and chatting.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel
Verb stem ends in a consonant

examples.en: I'll watch that drama tonight.
examples.note: 보다 ends in a vowel → 볼게요; a personal decision about what I'll do.

examples.en: I'll send you the link.
examples.note: Very common in chat; 보내 주다 → 보내 줄게요, promising to do it for the listener.

examples.en: I'll edit the video.
examples.note: 하다 → 할게요; offering to take on the task yourself.

examples.en: I'll check the comments and reply.
examples.note: Two actions chained with -고, then -ㄹ게요 for the promise to reply.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ게요 vs. -(으)ㄹ 거예요
keyPoint.body: -(으)ㄹ게요 is a promise made to the listener, decided on the spot ('okay, I'll do it'). -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is a plain statement of plan or prediction and can describe anyone ('I/he will probably do it'). Use 볼게요 when responding to someone; 볼 거예요 when just stating your plan.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -ㄹ게요 is pronounced [ㄹ께요]: the ㄱ is tensed to [ㄲ], so 볼게요 sounds like [볼께요].

drill.instruction: Answer each situation with a -(으)ㄹ게요 promise using the given verb.
drill.model: 친구가 영화를 추천했어요. (보다) → 그럼 제가 볼게요.
items: 게임 같이 하고 싶어요. (만들다 / 방을 만들다) → ___

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: -(으)ㄹ게요 is only for the speaker's own promise. To talk about what someone else will do, switch to -(으)ㄹ 거예요. You can't promise on another person's behalf with -ㄹ게요.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어 주세요 — Please do it (for me)
grammarNotes.func: Asks someone to do something for you, politely: 'please send it,' 'please recommend one.' The 주다 ('give') part adds the 'for me / for my benefit' nuance, making it warmer than a bare command. The everyday way to make digital-life requests.

examples.en: Please recommend a fun drama.
examples.note: 추천하다 → 추천해 주세요; 좀 softens the request even more.

examples.en: Please send me that video link.
examples.note: 보내다 → 보내 주세요; a typical chat request to do something for you.

examples.en: Please find the password for me.
examples.note: 찾다 has stem vowel ㅏ → 찾아 주세요.

examples.en: Please turn the music off for a moment.
examples.note: 끄다 → 꺼 주세요 (ㅡ drops before 어); asking someone to do it for your sake.

keyPoint.label: -아/어 주세요 (do it for me) vs. -(으)세요 (plain polite command)
keyPoint.body: -(으)세요 is a polite instruction with no 'for me' feeling: 여기 앉으세요 ('please sit here'). Adding 주다 → -아/어 주세요 frames it as a favor done for the speaker: 사진 보내 주세요 ('send me the photo, please'). For requests where someone helps you, use -아/어 주세요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 주세요 is said smoothly as [주세요]; keep the 아/어 and 주 as two clear beats (보내 주세요 = bo-nae ju-se-yo), not crushed together.

drill.instruction: Turn each verb into a polite '(do it) for me' request with -아/어 주세요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners drop the verb and attach 주세요 to a noun. 주세요 needs an -아/어 verb form in front: 추천하다 → 추천해 주세요. (주세요 by itself only works with a noun meaning 'please give me ~,' e.g. 물 주세요.)

grammarNotes.title: V/A-거든요 — you see, … (a reason or background)
grammarNotes.func: -거든요 ends a sentence to offer a reason or new background the listener doesn't know yet — like "you see" or "because…". It often answers a real or implied "why?"

formTable.ex: 보다 → 봤거든요 (I watched it, you see)
팬이다 → 팬이거든요 (I'm a fan, you see)

examples.ko: 이 드라마 꼭 보세요. 정말 재미있거든요.
examples.romanization: i deurama kkok boseyo. jeongmal jaemiitgeodeunyo.
examples.en: You should definitely watch this drama — it's really fun, you see.
examples.note: 거든요 gives the reason for the recommendation.

examples.ko: 그 노래 알아요. 제가 그 가수 팬이거든요.
examples.romanization: geu norae arayo. jega geu gasu paenigeodeunyo.
examples.en: I know that song — I'm a fan of that singer, you see.
examples.note: Noun + 이거든요 supplies background.

examples.ko: 어제 그 영화 봤거든요. 진짜 슬펐어요.
examples.romanization: eoje geu yeonghwa bwatgeodeunyo. jinjja seulpeosseoyo.
examples.en: I watched that movie yesterday, you see — it was really sad.
examples.note: Past 봤거든요 sets up the next comment.

examples.ko: 지금 통화 못 해요. 영화 보는 중이거든요.
examples.romanization: jigeum tonghwa mot haeyo. yeonghwa boneun jungigeodeunyo.
examples.en: I can't talk right now — I'm in the middle of a movie, you see.
examples.note: 거든요 explains the refusal.

keyPoint.label: 거든요 (new info) vs 잖아요 (shared info)
keyPoint.body: Both give a reason, but 거든요 tells the listener something NEW they didn't know (재미있거든요), while 잖아요 appeals to something you BOTH already know (재미있잖아요). Use 거든요 to introduce a reason, 잖아요 to remind.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 재미있거든요: the ㅆ+ㄱ tightens and the ending links — roughly [재미읻꺼든뇨].

drill.instruction: Add a reason with -거든요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 거든요 is not a question. Say it with a falling, confiding tone — it sets up a reason or a follow-up, not a yes/no question.

extendedDialogue.setting: Two friends chat about a drama and fix a streaming problem.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Have you watched this drama before?
lines.grammarNote: -ㄴ 적이 있어요 asks about experience.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네. 배우도 좋지만 댓글이 진짜 재미있거든요.
lines.romanization: ne. baeudo jojiman daetgeuri jinjja jaemiitgeodeunyo.
lines.en: Yes. The actor is good too, but the comments are really fun, you know.
lines.grammarNote: -지만 contrasts two good points; -거든요 gives the reason.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 친구가 자막이 좋다고 했어요. 영상도 공유했어요?
lines.romanization: chinguga jamagi jotago haesseoyo. yeongsangdo gongyuhaesseoyo?
lines.en: My friend said the subtitles are good. Did you share the video too?
lines.grammarNote: -다고 했어요 reports someone else's opinion.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: I shared it, but the video keeps cutting out.
lines.grammarNote: -는데요 raises a problem softly.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 와이파이를 다시 연결해 보세요. 좋아요도 눌렀어요?
lines.romanization: waipaireul dasi yeongyeolhae boseyo. joayodo nulleosseoyo?
lines.en: Try reconnecting the Wi-Fi. Did you hit like too?
lines.grammarNote: -아/어 보세요 gives troubleshooting advice.

readingText.title: 영상이 계속 끊기는데요
readingText.body: 민서는 친구에게 새 드라마를 추천했어요. 먼저 '이 드라마 본 적 있어요?'라고 물었어요. 친구는 배우도 좋지만 댓글이 진짜 재미있다고 했어요. 또 자막이 좋아서 한국어 공부에도 도움이 되는 것 같다고 했어요. 민서는 영상을 공유했지만, 친구는 영상이 계속 끊긴다고 했어요. 그래서 민서는 와이파이를 다시 연결해 보라고 했어요. 마지막에는 좋아요도 눌렀는지 물었어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo recommended a new drama to a friend. First, Minseo asked whether the friend had watched it before. The friend said the actor was good, but the comments were really fun. The friend also said the subtitles were good and seemed helpful for Korean study. Minseo shared the video, but the friend said the video kept cutting out. So Minseo told the friend to try reconnecting the Wi-Fi. At the end, Minseo asked whether the friend had also hit like.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 친구에게 무엇을 추천했어요?
친구는 무엇이 재미있다고 했어요?
영상이 끊길 때 민서는 무엇을 해 보라고 했어요?

culturalNote.title: Short reactions carry the mood
culturalNote.body: Korean entertainment chats often mix content words with quick reactions. A natural message may be short: 이 드라마 본 적 있어요? 댓글이 진짜 재미있거든요. ㅋㅋ, 헐, and 대박 can make a chat feel natural, but only when they respond to something specific.
culturalNote.tip: Keep digital verbs clear: 댓글을 달다, 좋아요를 누르다, 영상을 공유하다, 와이파이를 연결하다, 영상이 끊기다.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence asks about experience with a drama?
inlineExercises.explanation: -ㄴ 적이 있어요 asks whether someone has done something before.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence reports a friend's opinion?
inlineExercises.explanation: Adjectives use -다고 했어요 in reported speech.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence naturally describes buffering?
inlineExercises.explanation: 끊기다 describes the video or connection cutting out.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete: 와이파이를 다시 ___ 보세요. (use 연결하다)
inlineExercises.explanation: 연결해 보세요 means 'try connecting/reconnecting.'

inlineExercises.prompt: 그 드라마___ 본 적 있어요? (Have you ever watched that drama?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 보다 takes the thing watched as an object, so 드라마를 fits. 본 적 있어요 asks about experience.

inlineExercises.prompt: 그 배우를 ___ ? (보다 → have ever)
inlineExercises.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 asks about past experience. 보다 becomes 본 적 있어요?

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'The video keeps cutting out.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 끊기다 describes the stream or video cutting out. 계속 shows it keeps happening.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'Try reconnecting the Wi-Fi.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어 보세요 suggests trying an action. 다시 연결해 보세요 is natural troubleshooting Korean.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '그 드라마를 봤는 적 있어요?'
inlineExercises.explanation: Experience uses the past noun modifier before 적. 보다 becomes 본 적, not 봤는 적.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend said the subtitles are good. Which report fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: -다고 했어요 reports a statement. -냐고 would report a question.

bullets: Core flow: ask if someone has watched a drama, react to comments, report subtitle opinions, share a video, and fix buffering.
Use 본 적 있어요 for experience and -다고 했어요 to report someone else's opinion.
댓글을 달다, 좋아요를 누르다, 영상을 공유하다, and 와이파이를 연결하다 are the key digital action chunks.
영상이 끊기다 describes buffering or cutting out; do not use active 끊다 for that problem.

writingTask.prompt: Reply to a friend's drama recommendation: say whether you've seen it, give your impression, relay what someone said, and promise to watch.
writingTask.hint: Use V-(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 for experience, A/V-는 것 같아요 for impression, V-다고 했어요 for reported speech, A/V-지만 for contrast, and V-(으)ㄹ게요 to promise.
writingTask.model: 그 드라마는 본 적이 없어요. 친구가 배우들이 정말 좋다고 했어요. 자막은 없지만 재미있는 것 같아요. 오늘 밤에 볼게요.
writingTask.modelEn: I haven't seen that drama. My friend said the actors are really good. There are no subtitles, but it seems fun. I'll watch it tonight.

canDo: Say whether I have ever done something (본 적이 있어요/없어요)
Give a soft impression or guess (재미있는 것 같아요)
Relay what someone said (좋다고 했어요)
Make a clean contrast (자막은 없지만 재미있어요)
Promise to do something and give the background (볼게요, 보고 싶었거든요)

dialogue.ko: 네, 이번 학기 성적에 들어가니까 준비해야 해요.
dialogue.romanization: ne, ibeon hakgi seongjeoge deureoganikka junbihaeya haeyo.
dialogue.en: Yes, it counts toward this semester's grade, so we have to prepare.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 그럼 오늘부터 도서관에서 공부하기 시작하기로 했어요.
dialogue.romanization: geureom oneulbuteo doseogwaneseo gongbuhagi sijakagiro haesseoyo.
dialogue.en: Then I decided to start studying at the library from today.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 기말고사에서 좋은 성적을 받기 위해 시험 기간 동안 매일 공부해야 해요.
dialogue.romanization: gimalgosaeseo joeun seongjeogeul batgi wihae siheom gigan dongan maeil gongbuhaeya haeyo.
dialogue.en: In order to get a good grade on the final exam, we have to study every day during exam period.

chapters.guidedPractice: Build five school-life sentences: assignment obligation, class decision, study start, exam-period duration, and purpose for getting a good grade.
chapters.realLifeTask: Say what you need to study, by when, and what you will ask the teacher.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner gives a school deadline; answer with 과제, 중간고사, 기말고사, 도서관, or 공부해야 해요.
chapters.review: Can you connect 과제, 발표하다, 중간고사, 학기, 성적, 도서관, 공부하다, 받다, and 동안 in one school plan?

beginnerGuide.title: Assignments connect to exams
beginnerGuide.body: 과제, 발표, 중간고사, 기말고사 are not random school words. They form a deadline chain: 과제를 끝내야 해요, 중간고사 전에, 기말고사에서 좋은 성적을 받기 위해.

beginnerGuide.title: 동안 is a study-period word
beginnerGuide.body: 시험 기간 동안, 한 학기 동안, 방학 동안 all describe a stretch of time. Do not use 에 for this duration meaning.

beginnerGuide.title: Purpose sounds deliberate
beginnerGuide.body: 합격하기 위해 공부해요 sounds more planned than just 공부해요. Use it for serious goals like exams, scholarships, or graduation.

checkpoints: I can use 숙제, 시험, 수업, 발표, and 과제 in real sentences.
I can use -까지 for deadlines.
I can ask for explanation or feedback politely.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Talk about school life, assignments, and study plans.
exitTask.prompt: Say what you need to study, by when, and what you will ask the teacher.

sampleAnswer.ko: 금요일까지 발표를 준비해야 해요. 선생님께 피드백을 부탁드릴 거예요.
sampleAnswer.en: I have to prepare the presentation by Friday. I will ask the teacher for feedback.

checklist: I can use 숙제, 시험, 수업, 발표, and 과제 in real sentences.
I can use -까지 for deadlines.
I can ask for explanation or feedback politely.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You ask a classmate about a presentation assignment before midterms, plan when to start studying, talk about exam period, and explain why grades or scholarships matter.
objectives: Talk about assignments, presentations, midterms, finals, semesters, grades, and study plans.
Use V아/어야 해요, V기로 했어요, V기 시작하다, N 동안, and V기 위해서 in school-life sentences.
Separate class obligations, personal decisions, study periods, and exam goals.
hook.whyItMatters: Education Korean is deadline-heavy. Learners need more than 학교 and 시험: they need to say what must be finished, what was decided, when exam period lasts, and why they are studying.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어야 해요 — have to / must
grammarNotes.func: Expresses obligation or necessity: something you have to do. In school life it covers class rules, assignments, deadlines, and things teachers require of students.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in ㅏ or ㅗ
Verb stem ends in any other vowel

formTable.ex: 내다 → 내야 돼요 (have to hand it in)

examples.en: I have to hand in the homework by tomorrow.
examples.note: 내다 (to hand in) is the core homework verb; -까지 marks the deadline.

examples.en: During class you have to turn off your phone.
examples.note: 끄다 has a ㅡ stem; ㅡ drops before -어야, giving 꺼야 — a common spelling to notice.

examples.ko: 시험이 있어서 오늘 도서관에 가야 해요.
examples.romanization: siheomi isseoseo oneul doseogwane gaya haeyo.
examples.en: I have a test, so I have to go to the library today.
examples.note: 가다 ends in ㅏ, so it takes -아야; 도서관 keeps it in the school setting.

examples.en: In the classroom you have to speak in Korean.
examples.note: 말하다 is a 하다 verb → 해야; a typical classroom rule.

keyPoint.label: -아/어야 해요 vs. -아/어야 돼요
keyPoint.body: Both mean 'have to,' and in everyday speech they are interchangeable. -아/어야 돼요 sounds a touch more colloquial and is very common when talking; -아/어야 해요 is a little more neutral and shows up more in writing. Pick whichever you hear most — the meaning does not change.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 말해야 is pronounced [마래야]: the ㅎ weakens between vowels. 해야 해요 keeps two clear 해 syllables — don't blur them into one.

drill.instruction: Change each verb to the -아/어야 해요 form to state a school obligation.
items: 책을 읽다 → 책을 ___ (have to read the book)
교복을 입다 → 교복을 ___ (have to wear the uniform)
일찍 오다 → 일찍 ___ (have to come early)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'I need to / it's necessary' tempts learners to add 필요해요. Korean already builds the necessity into -아/어야 해요, so adding 필요하다 on top is redundant and unnatural.

grammarNotes.title: V-기로 했어요 — decided to V
grammarNotes.func: States a decision, plan, or promise that you (or a group) have already made. Common when classmates agree on a study plan or you resolve to do something for school.

formTable.when: Any verb, attach to the plain stem

formTable.ex: 지각 안 하기로 했어요 (decided not to be late)

formTable.when: A standing rule (let's make it a habit)
formTable.ex: 매일 복습하기로 해요 (let's review every day)

examples.en: I decided to study with my friends at the library.
examples.note: A shared decision; 하고 같이 marks who you made the plan with.

examples.en: This semester I decided not to be absent.
examples.note: Negative form uses -지 않기로; 결석하다 (to be absent) ties it to attendance.

examples.en: We decided to study for the test together on the weekend.
examples.note: A mutual promise between classmates — a very typical use.

examples.ko: 선생님이 다음 주에 시험을 보기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: seonsaengnimi daeum jue siheomeul bogiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: The teacher decided to give a test next week.
examples.note: The subject doesn't have to be 'I'; here the teacher made the decision.

keyPoint.label: -기로 했어요 vs. -(으)ㄹ 거예요
keyPoint.body: -기로 했어요 highlights that a decision was made (often jointly or as a resolution). -(으)ㄹ 거예요 just states a future plan or prediction. Use -기로 했어요 when the point is 'we agreed/decided,' not merely 'I will.'

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 했어요 is pronounced [해써요] with a tense ㅆ. 않기로 is read [안키로]: the ㅎ of 않 fuses with the following ㄱ into an aspirated [키].

drill.instruction: Turn each plan into a decision with -기로 했어요.
drill.model: 매일 단어를 외우다 → 매일 단어를 외우기로 했어요.
items: 동아리에 들다 → 동아리에 ___ (decided to join the club)
수업을 빠지지 않다 → 수업을 ___ (decided not to skip class)
도서관에서 만나다 → 도서관에서 ___ (decided to meet at the library)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners translate 'decided to study' literally with 결정하다 + a nominalized clause. Native speakers package the decision into -기로 하다 instead. Use the idiomatic pattern, not a word-for-word 'decide that.'

grammarNotes.title: V-기 시작하다 — start doing
grammarNotes.func: Says that an action begins or has begun. The verb is nominalized with -기 and followed by 시작하다 (to start). Useful for saying when you started studying, learning, or a new routine.

examples.en: I started learning Korean last year.
examples.note: -부터 marks the starting point in time, pairing naturally with -기 시작하다.

examples.en: After class ended, I started doing my homework.
examples.note: Marks a clear 'began the action' moment right after a school event.

examples.ko: 요즘 시험 때문에 도서관에 다니기 시작했어요.
examples.romanization: yojeum siheom ttaemune doseogwane danigi sijakaesseoyo.
examples.en: These days, because of exams, I've started going to the library.
examples.note: 다니다 (to go regularly) + 시작하다 = the start of a new routine.

examples.en: The teacher started explaining.
examples.note: Any subject works; here the teacher is the one beginning the action.

keyPoint.label: V-기 시작하다 vs. N을/를 시작하다
keyPoint.body: Use V-기 시작하다 to start an action (a verb): 공부하기 시작했어요. To start a thing (a noun), use N을/를 시작하다: 수업을 시작해요 (start the class). Don't say 수업하기 시작하다 when you simply mean 수업을 시작하다.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 시작했어요 is read [시자캐써요]: the ㄱ of 작 + the ㅎ of 했 fuse into an aspirated [ㅋ], and 했어요 becomes [캐써요].

drill.instruction: Combine into one sentence using -기 시작했어요.
items: 아침에 운동 / 하다 → 아침에 운동을 ___ (started exercising in the morning)
책 / 읽다 → 책을 ___ (started reading the book)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers reach for the heavier -는 것 nominalizer for 'started to learn.' With 시작하다, Korean prefers the lighter -기. -는 것을 시작하다 sounds clumsy and over-literal.

grammarNotes.title: N 동안 — for / during (a period)
grammarNotes.func: Marks a span of time over which something happens: 'for' a duration or 'during' a named period. Essential for saying how long you studied, or that something happened over vacation or a semester.

formTable.ex: 삼 년 동안 (for three years), not 삼 년에 동안

examples.en: I studied at the library for two hours.
examples.note: 두 시간 is a duration, so 동안 means 'for'; no particle between the number phrase and 동안.

examples.en: During vacation I went to a Korean language academy.
examples.note: 방학 (school vacation) is a named period, so 동안 means 'during.'

examples.ko: 시험을 보는 동안 휴대폰을 쓸 수 없어요.
examples.romanization: siheomeul boneun dongan hyudaeponeul sseul su eopseoyo.
examples.en: While taking the test, you can't use your phone.
examples.note: With a verb, use -는 동안 for 'while'; 시험을 보다 (to take a test) sets the school scene.

examples.en: I studied Korean for three years.
examples.note: 삼 년 (three years) is a duration → 'for'; again no particle before 동안.

keyPoint.label: N 동안 (a stretch) vs. N에 (a point)
keyPoint.body: Use 동안 for a span of time you do something over: 세 시간 동안 (for three hours). Use 에 for a single point in time: 세 시에 (at three o'clock). Don't mix them — 세 시간에 or 세 시간에 동안 are both wrong.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 동안 is two even syllables [동안]. 공부했어요 is [공부해써요], with the tense ㅆ in 했.

drill.instruction: Add 동안 (or -는 동안) to express the time span.
drill.model: 한 시간 / 공부하다 → 한 시간 동안 공부했어요.
items: 방학 / 학원에 다니다 → 방학 ___ 학원에 다녔어요
두 시간 / 숙제를 하다 → 두 시간 ___ 숙제를 했어요
수업을 듣다 / 졸다 → 수업을 ___ 졸았어요 (dozed off while in class)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'for three hours' makes learners insert a particle, but 동안 attaches straight to the time noun with nothing in between. No 에, no 을 before 동안.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-(으)니까 — because / so (reason before a plan)
grammarNotes.func: Gives a reason that leads into a request, suggestion, or plan: 'since A, (let's) B.' In school talk it links why something matters to what you should do next.

examples.en: Grades are important, so let's prepare in advance.
examples.note: Reason (중요하니까) leads into the suggestion.

examples.en: The exam is near, so I study at the library.
examples.note: 가깝다 is ㅂ-irregular: 가까우니까.

examples.en: There's a lot of homework, so let's start today.
examples.note: Consonant stem 많다 → 많으니까.

examples.ko: 수업이 끝났으니까 같이 밥 먹으러 가요.
examples.romanization: sueobi kkeunnasseunikka gachi bap meogeureo gayo.
examples.en: Class is over, so let's go eat together.
examples.note: Past 끝났 + -으니까; reason plus an invitation.

keyPoint.label: -(으)니까 vs. -아/어서 for 'because'
keyPoint.body: Both give reasons, but only -(으)니까 can lead into a command, suggestion, or 'let's' (시험이 가까우니까 공부해요). -아/어서 cannot: you can't say 시험이 가까워서 공부합시다. Use -(으)니까 when the next clause is a request or proposal.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 많으니까 is read [마느니까]: the ㅎ in 많 is silent before a vowel. 끝났으니까 is [끈나쓰니까].

drill.instruction: Join the reason and the plan with -(으)니까.
drill.model: 시험이 가깝다 + 도서관에 가요 → 시험이 가까우니까 도서관에 가요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: When the second clause is a command or suggestion ('take an umbrella'), Korean needs -(으)니까, not -아/어서. -아/어서 only works before a plain statement, not before an order or 'let's.'

grammarNotes.title: V-기 위해서 — in order to (purpose)
grammarNotes.func: Marks a deliberate goal: you do B in order to achieve A. Good for academic goals like passing, getting a scholarship, raising your grade, or getting into a program. Often shortened to -기 위해.

formTable.when: Any verb, attach to the stem
formTable.ex: 합격하다 → 합격하기 위해서 (in order to pass)
받다 → 받기 위해 (in order to get)
늦지 않기 위해서 (in order not to be late)

examples.ko: 좋은 성적을 받기 위해서 매일 공부해요.
examples.romanization: joeun seongjeogeul batgi wihaeseo maeil gongbuhaeyo.
examples.en: I study every day in order to get good grades.
examples.note: 받다 → 받기 위해서; purpose plus the daily habit.

examples.en: I studied hard in order to get a scholarship.
examples.note: Short form -기 위해; a very common academic goal.

examples.en: I go to an academy in order to pass the exam.
examples.note: 합격하다 (to pass) + -기 위해서; 학원 is a private academy.

examples.en: I get up early so as not to be late.
examples.note: Negative goal uses -지 않기 위해서; 지각하다 = to be late to school.

keyPoint.label: V-기 위해서 vs. V-(으)러
keyPoint.body: Both express purpose, but -(으)러 only attaches to motion verbs like 가다/오다 (공부하러 가요 = go to study). -기 위해서 has no such limit and works with any main verb (장학금을 받기 위해서 공부해요). For a goal that isn't 'going somewhere to do it,' use -기 위해서.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 받기 위해서 is read [받끼 위해서]: the ㄷ tenses the following ㄱ to [ㄲ]. 합격하기 is [합껴카기].

drill.instruction: State the goal with -기 위해서.
drill.model: 좋은 성적을 받다 / 매일 공부해요 → 좋은 성적을 받기 위해서 매일 공부해요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners mix two purpose patterns. Either use -(으)려고 (받으려고 공부해요) OR -기 위해서 (받기 위해서 공부해요), never both together. Don't stack 위해서 after a -(으)려고 ending.

extendedDialogue.setting: Classmates plan around a presentation assignment and upcoming exams.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 중간고사 전에 발표 과제를 끝내야 해요?
lines.romanization: junggangosa jeone balpyo gwajereul kkeutnaeya haeyo?
lines.en: Do we have to finish the presentation assignment before the midterm?
lines.grammarNote: -아/어야 해요 marks obligation.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네, 이번 학기 성적에 들어가니까 준비해야 해요.
lines.romanization: ne, ibeon hakgi seongjeoge deureoganikka junbihaeya haeyo.
lines.en: Yes, it counts toward this semester's grade, so we have to prepare.
lines.grammarNote: -니까 gives the reason for the obligation.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 그럼 오늘부터 도서관에서 공부하기 시작하기로 했어요.
lines.romanization: geureom oneulbuteo doseogwaneseo gongbuhagi sijakagiro haesseoyo.

lines.romanization: gimalgosaeseo joeun seongjeogeul batgi wihae siheom gigan dongan maeil gongbuhaeya haeyo.
lines.en: In order to get a good grade on the final exam, we have to study every day during exam period.
lines.grammarNote: -기 위해 and 동안 explain purpose and duration.

readingText.title: 중간고사 전에 발표 과제를 끝내야 해요
readingText.body: 민서는 이번 학기에 한국어 수업을 듣고 있어요. 중간고사 전에 발표 과제를 끝내야 해서 친구와 일정을 정했어요. 발표가 성적에 들어가니까 오늘부터 준비하기 시작하기로 했어요. 시험 기간 동안은 도서관에서 매일 공부할 거예요. 기말고사에서 좋은 성적을 받기 위해 복습도 하고, 모르는 것은 교수님께 질문하기로 했어요. 장학금을 받으려면 좋은 성적이 필요하니까 이번 학기에는 더 꾸준히 공부해야 해요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo is taking a Korean class this semester. Because the presentation assignment must be finished before the midterm, Minseo made a schedule with a friend. Since the presentation counts toward the grade, they decided to start preparing from today. During exam period, Minseo will study at the library every day. In order to pass the final, Minseo will review and ask the professor about things they do not know. Since good grades are needed for a scholarship, Minseo has to study more consistently this semester.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 언제까지 발표 과제를 끝내야 해요?
시험 기간 동안 어디에서 공부할 거예요?
무엇을 받으려면 좋은 성적이 필요해요?

culturalNote.title: Grades Shape The Schedule
culturalNote.body: Korean school conversations often connect assignments, exams, grades, and future goals. A student may talk about 과제 and 발표 first, then 중간고사 or 기말고사, then 성적, 장학금, or 전공. The natural language is practical: 끝내야 해요, 준비하기 시작했어요, 시험 기간 동안, 합격하기 위해.
culturalNote.tip: Use 선생님 for school or language teachers, and 교수님 for university professors.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence gives a school obligation?
options: 중간고사 전에 발표 과제를 끝내야 해요.
중간고사 전에 발표 과제를 끝낼 리가 없어요.
inlineExercises.correct: 중간고사 전에 발표 과제를 끝내야 해요.
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어야 해요 means have to.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence states a study decision?
inlineExercises.explanation: -기로 했어요 states what was decided.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence uses 동안 correctly?
inlineExercises.explanation: Put 동안 directly after the time span noun.

inlineExercises.prompt: 과제___ 해야 해요. (I have to do the assignment.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 하다 takes the assignment as an object, so 과제를 fits. 가 would make the assignment the subject.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 주에 ___ . (발표하다 → must)
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어야 해요 gives an obligation. 발표하다 becomes 발표해야 해요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I decided to study at the library during exam period.'
inlineExercises.correct: 시험 기간 동안 도서관에서 공부하기로 했어요
inlineExercises.explanation: 동안 gives the period, and 도서관에서 gives the study place. -기로 했어요 states the decision.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'I started studying for the midterm.'
inlineExercises.explanation: V-기 시작하다 means start doing. 준비하다 becomes 준비하기 before 시작했어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '시험 동안에 합격하기 위해서 공부해요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 합격하다 takes the exam target with 에. 동안 is for a time span, not the exam you pass.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence states a personal study decision?
inlineExercises.explanation: -기로 했어요 marks a decision. -아/어야 해요 marks obligation instead.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'I study for my grades.'
inlineExercises.explanation: N을 위해서 marks the goal or thing you are working for. 성적을 위해서 is natural for grade-related study.

bullets: Core flow: finish assignments before midterms, start preparing, study during exam period, and study for final goals.
V아/어야 해요 expresses school obligations; V기로 했어요 reports study decisions.
N 동안 marks a study period, while V기 위해서 marks a deliberate academic purpose.
과제, 발표, 중간고사, 기말고사, 성적, 장학금, 전공, and 교수님 should appear in real school sentences, not as isolated labels.

writingTask.prompt: Write a short note about your study plan: what you must do, what you decided, when you started, and why.
writingTask.hint: Use V-아/어야 해요 for obligation, V-기로 했어요 for a decision, V-기 시작하다 for starting, N 동안 for a period, V/A-(으)니까 for a reason, and V-기 위해서 for purpose.
writingTask.model: 다음 주에 중간고사가 있으니까 매일 도서관에서 공부해야 해요. 그래서 시험 기간 동안 친구하고 같이 공부하기로 했어요. 좋은 성적을 받기 위해서 지난주부터 공부하기 시작했어요.
writingTask.modelEn: Since there's a midterm next week, I have to study at the library every day. So I decided to study together with a friend during the exam period. To get good grades, I started studying last week.

canDo: Say what I have to do for school (과제를 내야 해요)
State a decision or study plan (같이 공부하기로 했어요)
Say when an action started (공부하기 시작했어요)
Give a reason that leads to a plan (시험이 있으니까 도서관에 가요)
State an academic purpose (장학금을 받기 위해서 공부해요)

chapters.title: Transportation in Depth
chapters.goal: Handle transport problems and route choices in more detail.
chapters.scenario: A bus is late, the subway is crowded, or you need to transfer.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: Where do I transfer if I want to get to Seoul Station?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.romanization: i hoseoneul tago sicheongyeogeseo il hoseoneuro garataseyo. seunggangjangeun ijjogiyeyo.
dialogue.en: Take Line 2 and transfer to Line 1 at City Hall Station. The platform is this way.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 부산 가는 KTX 표를 예매하려고 해요. 편도랑 왕복 중에 뭐가 나아요?
dialogue.romanization: busan ganeun KTX pyoreul yemaeharyeogo haeyo. pyeondorang wangbok junge mwoga naayo?
dialogue.en: I am trying to book a KTX ticket to Busan. Which is better, one-way or round-trip?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 돌아오는 시간이 정해지지 않았으면 편도로 예매하세요. 매진이면 다음 기차를 확인하세요.
dialogue.romanization: doraoneun sigani jeonghaejiji anasseumyeon pyeondoro yemaehaseyo. maejinimyeon daeum gichareul hwaginhaseyo.
dialogue.en: If the return time is not set, book it one-way. If it is sold out, check the next train.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 버스 지연 때문에 늦으면 택시로 갈게요.
dialogue.romanization: beoseu jiyeon ttaemune neujeumyeon taeksiro galgeyo.
dialogue.en: If I am late because of a bus delay, I will go by taxi.

chapters.guidedPractice: Write route, transfer, booking, and delay sentences: one with N(으)로, one with V(으)려고 해요, one with V면, one with N 때문에, and one with V(으)ㄹ 때.
chapters.realLifeTask: Explain one route, one problem, and one backup plan.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner asks how to get to Seoul Station or Busan; answer with transfer, platform, ticket, or delay vocabulary.
chapters.review: Can you separate 환승하다, 갈아타다, 예매하다, 매진, 지연, and N(으)로 in one travel plan?

beginnerGuide.title: Follow the trip order
beginnerGuide.body: Start with the subway route, then the transfer point, then the KTX ticket, then the delay plan. The vocabulary should match that order.

beginnerGuide.title: Use the right transport word
beginnerGuide.body: 환승 is the transfer event or system discount; 갈아타다 is the action of changing vehicles or lines. KTX tickets are usually 예매하다, and sold-out tickets are 매진.

beginnerGuide.title: Check particles
beginnerGuide.body: Use 에서 for the transfer place, 으로/로 for the line or means, 때문에 for the delay cause, and 때 for the moment you book or transfer.

checkpoints: I can use 갈아타다, 내리다, 타다, 막히다, and 늦다.
I can use 로/으로 for route and transport.
I can explain delays with -아서/어서 or -는 바람에.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Handle transport problems and route choices in more detail.
exitTask.prompt: Explain one route, one problem, and one backup plan.

sampleAnswer.ko: 버스가 막혀서 늦을 것 같아요. 지하철로 갈아탈게요.
sampleAnswer.en: I think I will be late because the bus is stuck in traffic. I will transfer to the subway.

checklist: I can use 갈아타다, 내리다, 타다, 막히다, and 늦다.
I can use 로/으로 for route and transport.
I can explain delays with -아서/어서 or -는 바람에.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You are starting at Hongik University Station, transferring to Seoul Station, booking a KTX ticket to Busan, and explaining a delay to a friend. Every word in this chapter should help with that trip.
objectives: Ask and answer subway transfer questions with 호선, 환승, 갈아타다, and 승강장.
Book a KTX ticket with 예매하다, 표, 편도, 왕복, and 매진.
Explain transport problems with 지연 때문에, V면, and 택시로.
hook.whyItMatters: Transportation Korean is built from small practical frames. Learners need to know which line to take, where to transfer, how to name a ticket type, and how to give a fallback plan when a bus or train is delayed.

grammarNotes.title: N(으)로 — by (a means of transport) / via (a route)
grammarNotes.func: Attach (으)로 to a noun to say what you travel by (버스로 = by bus) or which way you go (이 길로 = this way). In transportation talk it is the everyday particle for naming the vehicle, the subway line, or the road you take.

formTable.when: Noun ends in any other consonant
formTable.ex: 기차표 → 기차표로? No — for transport use 기차 → 기차로 (vowel). Consonant example: 비행기편 is rare; everyday case: 걸어서 is a verb. Use 버스 → 버스로 (vowel).

examples.en: I go to school by bus.
examples.note: 버스 ends in a vowel, so plain -로 marks the means of transport.

examples.en: It's faster if you go by subway.
examples.note: 지하철 ends in ㄹ, so it takes -로 (never -으로); the ㄹㄹ links smoothly as 'cheollo'.

examples.en: Go this way (via this road).
examples.note: Here (으)로 marks a route, not a vehicle. 길 ends in ㄹ, so -로.

examples.en: Shall we go to the airport by taxi?
examples.note: 택시 → -로 names the vehicle; 까지 marks the destination 'all the way to'.

keyPoint.label: (으)로 가다 vs 을/를 타고 가다
keyPoint.body: 버스로 가요 and 버스를 타고 가요 both mean 'go by bus.' (으)로 simply labels the means in one word; 을/를 타고 literally says 'ride and go,' picturing you boarding. Use (으)로 for the quick, neutral 'by ___,' and 을/를 타고 when you want to stress actually getting on.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After ㄹ the two ㄹ sounds link: 지하철로 is said [지하철로] as 'jihacheollo,' not 'jihacheoro.' Same for 이 길로 → 'gillo.'

drill.instruction: Add (으)로 to each word to mark the means or route of travel.
drill.model: 기차 → 기차로 가요. (I go by train.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'by bus' tempts learners to grab 에. But the means of transport always takes (으)로, never 에. 버스에 would point to the bus as a destination, like 'into the bus.'

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)러 가요 — go (somewhere) in order to do something
grammarNotes.func: Attach -(으)러 to a verb stem before a movement verb (가다 / 오다 / 다니다) to give the purpose of the trip: you go or come somewhere in order to do that action. Very common for travel errands like buying tickets or topping up a card.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a consonant
formTable.ex: 표를 받다 → 표를 받으러 가요 (go to pick up the ticket)

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel
formTable.ex: 타다 → 타러 가요 (go to catch/board it)
(표를) 팔다 → 팔러 가요 (go to sell the ticket)

examples.en: I'm going to the station to buy a train ticket.
examples.note: 사다 ends in a vowel → -러; the purpose (buying a ticket) comes before the movement verb 가요.

examples.en: I'm going to Busan to meet a friend.
examples.note: 만나다 → 만나러; the whole trip is for meeting the friend.

examples.en: I ran to the bus stop to catch the bus.
examples.note: 타다 → 타러; the destination keeps 에, the purpose clause stays separate.

examples.en: I'm going to the convenience store to top up my transit card.
examples.note: 충전하다 → 충전하러; a real pre-ride errand.

keyPoint.label: -(으)러 needs a 'go/come' verb
keyPoint.body: -(으)러 must be followed by a movement verb (가다, 오다, 다니다). You cannot say 표를 사러 공부해요 — the main verb has to involve going or coming. If your main verb is not movement, use -(으)려고 instead (Note 3).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 받으러 links the final ㄷ into the 으: say [바드러] 'badeureo,' not [받으러] with a hard stop.

drill.instruction: Join the task verb to -(으)러 and finish with 가요.
items: 기차를 타다 → ___ 가요. (go to catch the train)
카드를 충전하다 → ___ 가요. (go to top up the card)
표를 받다 → ___ 가요. (go to pick up the ticket)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners reach for -기 위해 because it maps onto English 'in order to.' But for a physical errand with go/come, -(으)러 is far more natural and shorter. Save -기 위해 for abstract or formal goals.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)려고 해요 — be planning / intending to do something
grammarNotes.func: Attach -(으)려고 하다 to a verb stem to say what you intend or plan to do. With travel it means 'I'm going to / I'm trying to' make the trip or booking. It states a decided intention, softer than the firm future -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a consonant
formTable.ex: 표를 찾다 → 찾으려고 해요 (I plan to pick up the ticket)

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel
formTable.ex: 타다 → 타려고 해요 (I intend to take it)
(표를) 팔다 → 팔려고 해요 (I plan to sell the ticket)

examples.ko: 이번 주말에는 기차로 부산에 가려고 해요.
examples.romanization: ibeon jumareneun gicharo busane garyeogo haeyo.
examples.en: This weekend I'm planning to go to Busan by train.
examples.note: 가다 → 가려고 해요; a decided personal plan, softer than 갈 거예요.

examples.en: Traffic is bad, so I'm going to take the subway.
examples.note: 타다 → 타려고 해요; an intention formed in reaction to the situation.

examples.ko: 부산 가는 KTX 표를 예매하려고 해요.
examples.romanization: busan ganeun KTX pyoreul yemaeharyeogo haeyo.
examples.en: I'm trying to book a KTX ticket to Busan.
examples.note: 예매하다 → 예매하려고 해요; the main verb is not a movement verb, which is fine for -(으)려고.

examples.en: I was going to check the last-train time.
examples.note: Past 했어요 signals an intention that may not have happened — a planned-but-changed nuance.

keyPoint.label: -(으)려고 vs -(으)러
keyPoint.body: -(으)러 needs a movement main verb and means 'go/come TO DO something' (표를 사러 가요). -(으)려고 (해요) states the intention itself and works with ANY main verb (표를 사려고 해요 = 'I plan to buy a ticket'). If you can drop 가요/와요 and still have a full sentence, you want -(으)려고 해요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: In casual speech people sometimes say 갈려고 with an extra ㄹ, but the standard form keeps one ㄹ: 가려고 'garyeogo,' not 갈려고.

drill.instruction: Turn each plan into a -(으)려고 해요 statement of intention.
items: 표를 예매하다 → ___. (plan to book the ticket)
지하철로 가다 → ___. (plan to go by subway)
표를 찾다 → ___. (plan to pick up the ticket)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 표를 사려고 가요. (meaning 'I plan to buy a ticket')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: To STATE the plan you need -(으)려고 해요 with 하다 at the end. 표를 사려고 가요 only works as 'I go in order to buy a ticket' (a purpose for going), overlapping with -(으)러. Decide: stating a plan → 해요; purpose for going → 가요/러.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-(으)면 — if / when (a travel condition happens)
grammarNotes.func: Attach -(으)면 to a verb or adjective stem to set up a condition: 'if/when ___, then ___.' In transportation it covers fallback plans: if the bus is delayed, if you miss the last train, if tickets are sold out.

formTable.ex: 놓치다 is a vowel stem; consonant example: 없다 → 없으면 (if there isn't)

examples.en: If the road is jammed, take the subway.
examples.note: 막히다 (vowel stem) → 막히면; the condition comes first, the advice second.

examples.ko: 버스를 놓치면 다음 버스를 기다려야 해요.
examples.romanization: beoseureul notchimyeon daeum beoseureul gidaryeoya haeyo.
examples.en: If you miss the bus, you have to wait for the next one.
examples.note: 놓치다 → 놓치면; a real cause-and-effect.

examples.en: If the tickets are sold out, check the next train.
examples.note: Noun state 매진 + 이면; for nouns use 이면 after a consonant.

examples.en: If the service interval is long, a taxi is better.
examples.note: Adjective stem 길- (ends in ㄹ) → 길면, ㄹ stays.

keyPoint.label: -(으)면 vs -(으)니까
keyPoint.body: -(으)면 is hypothetical 'if' (막히면 = if it gets jammed — may or may not happen). -(으)니까 gives a real, already-true reason 'since/because' (막히니까 = since it's jammed right now). Don't use -(으)면 for a present fact you can already see.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 없으면 links the ㅄ cluster: say [업쓰면] 'eopsseumyeon.' After a plain consonant the buffer 으 keeps the syllables clear: 놓치면 'notchimyeon.'

drill.instruction: Build an 'if' clause with -(으)면, then keep the given result.
drill.model: 길이 막히다 → 길이 막히면 지하철을 타세요.
items: 버스를 놓치다 → ___ 다음 버스를 기다려야 해요.
표가 없다 → ___ 입석으로 갈 수 있어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 지금 막히면 지하철을 타요. (meaning 'since it's jammed now')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: When the situation is already true right now, Korean uses -(으)니까 (since/because), not -(으)면. -(으)면 is for hypothetical or repeated conditions, not a fact you're looking at this moment.

grammarNotes.title: N 때문에 — because of (a transport cause)
grammarNotes.func: Use N 때문에 to name the noun reason that something happened or that a plan changed. In transportation it explains delays and disruptions: 지연 때문에 (because of a delay), 사고 때문에 (because of an accident).

formTable.ex: 지연 → 지연 때문에 (because of a delay)

formTable.when: Do NOT add 이/가 or 을/를

formTable.ex: 막혀서 늦었어요 (was late because it was jammed)

examples.en: I was late for the appointment because of a bus delay.
examples.note: 지연 is the noun cause; nothing goes between it and 때문에.

examples.en: The road is very jammed because of an accident.
examples.note: 사고 (accident) is a very common everyday traffic cause.

examples.en: Because of the rain, I can't catch a taxi.
examples.note: 비 (rain) + 때문에; a typical transport complaint.

examples.en: Because of the last train, we have to leave now.
examples.note: The last-train schedule is the reason for hurrying.

keyPoint.label: N 때문에 vs V/A-아서
keyPoint.body: Use N 때문에 when the reason is a NOUN (지연 때문에). When the reason is a verb or adjective, switch to -아/어서: 지하철이 늦어서 (because the subway was late). You cannot put a full verb directly before 때문에 — you'd need to nominalize it (늦었기 때문에).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 때문에 links the ㄴ into 에: say [때무네] 'ttaemune,' as one smooth phrase, not 'ttaemun-e' with a pause.

drill.instruction: Put the noun cause before 때문에 (no extra particle) and keep the result.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'because of the delay' has 'the,' which tempts learners to add a subject particle 이/가. But 때문에 attaches straight to the bare noun — no 이/가 and no 을/를 in front of it.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄹ 때 — when (the moment you do a travel action)
grammarNotes.func: Attach -(으)ㄹ 때 to a verb stem to name the moment an action happens: 'when transferring,' 'when booking,' 'when you ride.' It is the everyday way to give travel tips and warnings tied to a specific moment.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel
Verb stem ends in a consonant
formTable.ex: 갈아타다 → 갈아탈 때 (when you transfer); 받다 → 받을 때 (when you receive)

formTable.add: -ㄹ 때 (one ㄹ, the stem ㄹ drops into it)
formTable.ex: 놀다 → 놀 때; here use 만들다 → 만들 때

examples.en: When you transfer, check the exit number too.
examples.note: 환승하다 → 환승할 때; a real subway-navigation tip.

examples.ko: 표를 예매할 때 편도인지 왕복인지 확인하세요.
examples.romanization: pyoreul yemaehal ttae pyeondoinji wangboginji hwaginhaseyo.
examples.en: When booking a ticket, check whether it's one-way or round-trip.
examples.note: 예매하다 → 예매할 때; a useful ticket-buying check.

examples.en: When you get on the bus, tap your transit card.
examples.note: 타다 → 탈 때; an everyday boarding habit.

examples.ko: 막차를 탈 때는 시간을 꼭 확인해야 해요.
examples.romanization: makchareul tal ttaeneun siganeul kkok hwaginhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: When taking the last train, you really have to check the time.
examples.note: 때 can take 는 (탈 때는) for topic contrast.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄹ 때 (present/general) vs -았/었을 때 (completed)
keyPoint.body: Plain -(으)ㄹ 때 names the moment of an ongoing or general action: 탈 때 = 'when (in the act of) riding.' Add past -았/었을 때 for a moment after something finished: 내렸을 때 = 'when I had gotten off.' For habits and instructions you almost always want plain -(으)ㄹ 때.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: The 때 after -ㄹ tenses to a hard sound: 탈 때 is said [탈 떼] 'tal ttae,' and 할 때 is 'hal ttae,' with a tightened ㄸ.

drill.instruction: Make a -(으)ㄹ 때 clause and keep the given advice.
drill.model: 환승하다 → 환승할 때 출구 번호도 확인하세요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners often attach the present modifier -는 to 때, copying English 'the time when you transfer.' But 때 takes the -(으)ㄹ modifier, not -는: 환승할 때, never 환승하는 때.

exampleSentence.en: Where do I transfer if I want to get to Seoul Station?

extendedDialogue.setting: A Kakao-style travel chat while Minseo transfers to Seoul Station and books a KTX ticket.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 지금 홍대입구역인데 서울역 가려면 어디서 환승해?
lines.romanization: jigeum hongdaeipguyeoginde seouryeok garyeomyeon eodiseo hwanseunghae?
lines.en: I am at Hongik University Station now. Where do I transfer to get to Seoul Station?
lines.grammarNote: -려면 sets the route goal before the question.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.romanization: i hoseon tago sicheongyeogeseo il hoseoneuro garata. seunggangjangeun oreunjjogiya.
lines.en: Take Line 2 and transfer to Line 1 at City Hall. The platform is on the right.
lines.grammarNote: 에서 marks the transfer station; 으로 marks the line.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 고마워. 부산 가는 KTX 표를 예매하려고 하는데 편도면 돼?
lines.romanization: gomawo. busan ganeun KTX pyoreul yemaeharyeogo haneunde pyeondomyeon dwae?
lines.en: Thanks. I am trying to book a KTX ticket to Busan. Is one-way okay?
lines.grammarNote: -려고 해요 gives the intention before asking for advice.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 응, 돌아오는 시간 안 정했으면 편도로 해. 매진이면 다음 기차 확인하고.
lines.romanization: eung, doraoneun sigan an jeonghaesseumyeon pyeondoro hae. maejinimyeon daeum gicha hwaginhago.
lines.en: Yes, if you have not set the return time, book it one-way. If it is sold out, check the next train.
lines.grammarNote: 편도로 marks ticket type; 매진이면 sets a ticket-status condition.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 버스 지연 때문에 조금 늦으면 택시로 갈게.
lines.romanization: beoseu jiyeon ttaemune jogeum neujeumyeon taeksiro galge.
lines.en: If I am a little late because of the bus delay, I will go by taxi.
lines.grammarNote: N 때문에 gives the cause and V면 gives the condition.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 괜찮아. 환승할 때 출구 번호도 같이 확인해.
lines.romanization: gwaenchana. hwanseunghal ttae chulgu beonhodo gachi hwaginhae.
lines.en: No problem. When you transfer, check the exit number too.
lines.grammarNote: V(으)ㄹ 때 names the moment to check something.

readingText.title: 서울역에서 부산까지 가는 길
readingText.body: 민서는 홍대입구역에서 서울역으로 가려고 해요. 먼저 2호선을 타고 시청역에서 1호선으로 갈아타야 해요. 환승할 때는 승강장 방향과 출구 번호를 같이 확인하면 헷갈리지 않아요. 서울역에 도착하면 부산 가는 KTX 표를 예매할 거예요. 돌아오는 시간이 아직 정해지지 않아서 편도로 예매하려고 해요. 만약 표가 매진이면 다음 기차를 확인하면 돼요. 친구에게는 버스 지연 때문에 늦으면 택시로 가겠다고 메시지를 보냈어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo is planning to go from Hongik University Station to Seoul Station. First, Minseo takes Line 2 and transfers to Line 1 at City Hall Station. When transferring, checking both the platform direction and exit number helps avoid confusion. After arriving at Seoul Station, Minseo will book a KTX ticket to Busan. Since the return time is not set yet, Minseo plans to book one-way. If the tickets are sold out, Minseo can check the next train. Minseo also messaged a friend that if they are late because of a bus delay, they will go by taxi.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 어디에서 1호선으로 갈아타야 해요?
돌아오는 시간이 정해지지 않았으면 어떤 표로 예매해요?
버스 지연 때문에 늦으면 무엇으로 가겠다고 했어요?

culturalNote.title: Transfer Words People Actually Use
culturalNote.body: In subway directions, Koreans often say 환승 for the transfer event or transfer system and 갈아타다 for the physical action of changing lines or vehicles. Station signs may say 승강장 or 타는 곳; both point you to the platform area. For KTX, the natural verb is 예매하다 because tickets are usually booked with a seat and time. If tickets are gone, say 매진, not 품절. If a service is delayed, announcements and apps use 지연, while a person says 늦었어요.
culturalNote.tip: When you build a route sentence, check three particles first: 에서 for the transfer place, 으로/로 for the new line or means, and 때문에 for the cause of a delay.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence gives a natural subway transfer instruction?
inlineExercises.explanation: Use 에서 for the transfer station and 으로 for the line you change to.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which word is natural when KTX tickets are sold out?
inlineExercises.explanation: 매진 is for tickets and seats; 품절 is usually for store products.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence explains a delay cause correctly?
inlineExercises.explanation: Put the noun cause directly before 때문에 with no extra particle.

inlineExercises.prompt: KTX 표___ 예매했어요. (I booked a KTX ticket.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 예매하다 takes the ticket as an object, so 표를 fits. 가 would make the ticket the subject.

inlineExercises.prompt: 서울역에서 2호선으로 ___ . (갈아타다 → planning/intending)
inlineExercises.explanation: -려고 해요 expresses an intended plan. 갈아타다 becomes 갈아타려고 해요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Transfer to Line 2 at Seoul Station.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 에서 marks the transfer location, and (으)로 marks the line you transfer to. 갈아타세요 is the transit instruction.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'The tickets are sold out.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 표가 is the subject of being sold out. 매진됐어요 is the natural completed state.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '지연이 때문에 늦었어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: N 때문에 follows the noun directly. Do not put 이/가 before 때문에.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence says you will go by taxi?
inlineExercises.explanation: Transport method takes (으)로. 택시에 would mean to a taxi, which is not the intended meaning.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'I need to top up my transit card.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 충전하다 takes 교통카드 as the object. -해야 해요 marks the travel obligation.

bullets: Subway route: 어디서 환승해요? -> 시청역에서 1호선으로 갈아타세요.
Platform and route words: 호선 names subway lines, 노선 names routes, 승강장 is the platform area.
Ticket flow: KTX 표를 예매하다, 편도/왕복을 choose, 매진이면 다음 기차를 확인하다.
Delay flow: 지연 is for services; 늦다 is for people. 버스 지연 때문에 늦으면 택시로 갈게요.

writingTask.prompt: Message a friend explaining your route to meet them, including a fallback if something goes wrong.
writingTask.hint: Use N(으)로 for the means, V-(으)러 가다 for purpose, V-(으)려고 해요 for intention, A/V-(으)면 for a condition, N 때문에 for a cause, and V-(으)ㄹ 때 for timing.
writingTask.model: 지하철 2호선으로 가려고 해요. 표를 사러 매표소에 갈 거예요. 갈아탈 때 조심하세요. 사고 때문에 늦으면 버스로 갈게요.
writingTask.modelEn: I'm planning to go by subway line 2. I'll go to the ticket office to buy a ticket. Be careful when you transfer. If I'm late because of an accident, I'll go by bus.

canDo: Say what I travel by or which way I go (버스로, 2호선으로)
Give the purpose of a trip (표를 사러 가요)
State a travel intention (예매하려고 해요)
Make a fallback plan with a condition (늦으면 버스로 가요)
Explain a delay's cause and tie a tip to a moment (사고 때문에, 갈아탈 때 조심하세요)

chapters.title: Korean Social Customs
chapters.goal: Navigate Korean social habits without sounding rude or too casual.
chapters.scenario: You accept, decline, apologize, thank, or explain manners in a social setting.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.ko: 집들이에 갈 때 휴지랑 세제 중에 뭐가 나아요?
dialogue.romanization: jipdeurie gal ttae hyujirang seje junge mwoga naayo?
dialogue.en: When going to a housewarming, which is better, toilet paper or detergent?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 둘 다 괜찮아요. 집들이 선물로 많이 가져가잖아요.
dialogue.romanization: dul da gwaenchanayo. jipdeuri seonmullo manhi gajyeogajanhayo.
dialogue.en: Both are fine. People often bring them as housewarming gifts, you know.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: If we are about the same age, can I say we are the same age?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 그래도 처음엔 선배님 같은 호칭을 쓰는 편이에요.
dialogue.romanization: geuraedo cheoeumen seonbaenim gateun hochingeul sseuneun pyeonieyo.
dialogue.en: Even so, at first people tend to use a title like seonbaenim.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.en: If elders are there too, I will ask, 'May I help?'

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.ko: 좋아요. 눈치 있게 챙기면 분위기가 덜 어색해요.
dialogue.romanization: joayo. nunchi itge chaenggimyeon bunwigiga deol eosaekaeyo.
dialogue.en: Good. If you take care of things tactfully, the mood is less awkward.

chapters.guidedPractice: Write one sentence for a housewarming gift, one title/age sentence, one 눈치 sentence, one polite help offer, and one gratitude sentence with 덕분에.
chapters.realLifeTask: Write one polite acceptance, refusal, or apology for a real social situation.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner describes who is at the 집들이; choose a title, gift, and polite action that fits the atmosphere.
chapters.review: Can you explain why 나이, 호칭, 선배/후배, 어르신, 눈치, and 덕분에 belong together in this chapter?

beginnerGuide.title: Start from the room
beginnerGuide.body: At a 집들이, first notice who is there: coworkers, 선배, 후배, 동갑, or 어르신. That decides the 호칭 and speech level.

beginnerGuide.title: Gift words are practical
beginnerGuide.body: 휴지 and 세제 are common 집들이 선물 because they are useful household items. The point is not the object alone; it is showing consideration.

beginnerGuide.title: 눈치 is action
beginnerGuide.body: 눈치 is not only 'reading the room.' It becomes language through 도와드릴까요?, 먼저 하세요, 수고하셨습니다, and 덕분에.

checkpoints: I can use 죄송하지만 and 괜찮으시면 to soften a social sentence.
I can choose a polite expression for gifts, meals, or invitations.
I can explain a custom without overgeneralizing.

curriculumTrack.label: B1 Independent Korean
curriculumTrack.description: Discourse, reported speech, honorifics, observation, social domains, and longer explanations.

learningLayers.label: Core
learningLayers.purpose: Start here: these are the words and patterns you need for the main sentence.

learningLayers.label: Expand
learningLayers.purpose: Use these next so the same grammar works in more real situations.

learningLayers.label: Reference
learningLayers.purpose: Open these when a sentence feels confusing or you want to check the rule.

exitTask.canDo: Navigate Korean social habits without sounding rude or too casual.
exitTask.prompt: Write one polite acceptance, refusal, or apology for a real social situation.

sampleAnswer.ko: 초대해 주셔서 감사해요. 그런데 오늘은 일이 있어서 못 갈 것 같아요.
sampleAnswer.en: Thank you for inviting me. But I think I cannot go today because I have work.

checklist: I can use 죄송하지만 and 괜찮으시면 to soften a social sentence.
I can choose a polite expression for gifts, meals, or invitations.
I can explain a custom without overgeneralizing.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You are going to a Korean coworker's 집들이. You need to choose a practical gift, use a safe title, read the room, offer help politely, and thank people without sounding too casual.
objectives: Choose and explain housewarming gifts with 집들이, 선물, 휴지, and 세제.
Handle age and titles with 나이, 동갑, 선배/후배, 호칭, and 어르신.
Use 눈치, 도와드리다, 챙기다, 수고하셨습니다, and 덕분에 in socially careful sentences.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean social customs are not just facts about culture. They show up as sentence choices: what gift you bring, what title you use, when you offer help, and how you thank someone afterward.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-잖아요 — "you know (we both know this)"
grammarNotes.func: Reminds the listener of something you assume you both already know, or gently corrects them with a fact they should remember. It softens a reminder by framing it as shared knowledge rather than news — very common when explaining everyday manners and customs.

formTable.ex: 한국에서는 신발을 벗잖아요 (You take your shoes off in Korea, you know)
지난번에 제가 말했잖아요 (I told you last time, remember)
오늘 어버이날이잖아요 (It's Parents' Day today, you know)

examples.en: You hand things to elders with both hands, you know.
examples.note: Frames a manners rule as shared knowledge, so it sounds like a friendly reminder, not a lecture.

examples.ko: 집들이에는 보통 휴지나 세제를 사 가잖아요.
examples.romanization: jipdeurie-neun botong hyujina sejereul sa gajanhayo.
examples.en: You usually bring toilet paper or detergent to a housewarming, you know.
examples.note: Explains a custom the speaker assumes is familiar to both people.

examples.ko: 어제 같이 봤잖아요, 기억 안 나요?
examples.romanization: eoje gachi bwatjanhayo, gieok an nayo?
examples.en: We saw it together yesterday, remember? Don't you recall?
examples.note: Past form gently corrects the listener about a shared experience.

examples.en: You leave the priority seats empty on the subway, you know.
examples.note: Appeals to a publicly known norm to back up the speaker's point.

keyPoint.label: -잖아요 vs. -거든요
keyPoint.body: Use -잖아요 when you think the listener ALREADY knows it ('as you know'). Use -거든요 when it's NEW background the listener does not know yet ('the thing is…'). Same slot, opposite assumption about the listener.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -잖아요 is carefully [자나요]; the ㅎ-like sound is very light, and in fast speech it can flatten to [자아요]. Stick with [자나요].

drill.instruction: Complete each sentence with -잖아요 to remind the listener of a shared fact.
drill.model: 한국에서는 어른이 먼저 드시잖아요. (Elders eat first in Korea, you know.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: -잖아요 is a sentence ending attached straight to the stem (벗 + 잖아요). It is not a tag word you stick after a finished -아요/-어요 sentence the way English adds 'right?' at the end.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-거든요 — "the thing is… (here's the background)"
grammarNotes.func: Gives a reason or piece of background the listener does not yet know, often answering a real or expected 'why?'. It signals 'the thing is…' and is a soft, polite way to explain yourself in conversation.

formTable.ex: 제가 매운 걸 못 먹거든요 (The thing is, I can't eat spicy food)
어제 늦게 잤거든요 (I went to bed late yesterday, you see)
오늘이 제 생일이거든요 (Today's my birthday, you see)

examples.ko: 오늘은 일찍 가 볼게요. 시댁에 가야 하거든요.
examples.romanization: oneureun iljjik ga bolgeyo. sidaege gaya hageodeunyo.
examples.en: I'll head off early today. The thing is, I have to visit my in-laws.
examples.note: Gives an unknown reason for leaving early, softening the abruptness.

examples.ko: 꽃을 사 왔어요. 오늘 처음 인사 드리는 거거든요.
examples.romanization: kkocheul sa wasseoyo. oneul cheoeum insa deurineun geogeodeunyo.
examples.en: I brought flowers. It's the first time I'm greeting you properly, you see.
examples.note: Explains the gift by giving social context the host didn't know.

examples.ko: 술은 안 마실게요. 제가 운전해야 하거든요.
examples.romanization: sureun an masilgeyo. jega unjeonhaeya hageodeunyo.
examples.en: I won't drink. The thing is, I have to drive.
examples.note: Declines politely by offering a reason, which is socially expected.

examples.ko: 연락 못 드려서 죄송해요. 핸드폰이 고장 났거든요.
examples.romanization: yeollak mot deuryeoseo joesonghaeyo. haendeuponi gojang natgeodeunyo.
examples.en: Sorry I couldn't reach you. My phone broke, you see.
examples.note: Past form gives the unknown cause behind an apology.

keyPoint.label: -거든요 vs. -아서/어서
keyPoint.body: Both give reasons. -아서/어서 joins the reason to a clause in the SAME sentence ('Because A, B'). -거든요 ends its own sentence and offers the reason as new information the listener didn't have, so it usually stands alone as a reply.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -거든요 is [거드뇨] in quick speech, but the careful form is [거든뇨]→[거든요]. Keep the 든 clear.

drill.instruction: Finish each reply with -거든요 to give the listener new background.
drill.model: 저는 안 갈래요. 그날 약속이 있거든요. (I won't go — I have plans that day, you see.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers reach for -아서/어서 to answer 'why', but as a stand-alone reply -아서요 sounds clipped, while -거든요 is the natural, conversational choice. Don't force the reason into the same clause as the result.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-는데요 — "soften a careful statement or question"
grammarNotes.func: Ends a turn on an open, non-final note that leaves room for the listener to react. It softens statements, eases into careful questions, and sets up background before a request — essential for polite, indirect social talk.

formTable.ex: 좀 비싼데요 (It's a bit pricey, though…)
저는 처음인데요 (It's my first time, you see…)

examples.ko: 이거 집들이 선물로 드리려고 하는데요, 괜찮을까요?
examples.romanization: igeo jipdeuri seonmullo deuriryeogo haneundeyo, gwaenchaneulkkayo?
examples.en: I was thinking of giving this as a housewarming gift… would that be okay?
examples.note: Sets up the situation softly before a careful yes/no question.

examples.en: My outfit is a bit casual, though… is that still all right?
examples.note: Adjective form softens a worry instead of stating it bluntly.

examples.ko: 호칭을 잘 모르는데요, 뭐라고 부르면 될까요?
examples.romanization: hochingeul jal moreuneundeyo, mworago bureumyeon doelkkayo?
examples.en: I'm not really sure what to call you… what should I say?
examples.note: Trails off so the request for help feels hesitant, not pushy.

examples.ko: 예약은 했는데요, 시간이 좀 늦을 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: yeyageun haetneundeyo, sigani jom neujeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: I did make a reservation, but… we might be a little late.
examples.note: Past -는데요 concedes one point before adding a softer caveat.

keyPoint.label: Adjective -(으)ㄴ데요 vs. Verb -는데요
keyPoint.body: Verbs always take -는데요 (가는데요, 먹는데요). Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ데요 (비싼데요, 좋은데요). 있다/없다 act like verbs: 있는데요, 없는데요. Sorting verb from adjective is the part learners trip on most.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -는데요 is [는데요]. After ㄹ-final verb stems the ㄹ drops: 살다 → 사는데요 (not 살는데요).

drill.instruction: Add -는데요 / -(으)ㄴ데요 to soften each opener, then trail off.
drill.model: 이 자리 제 자린데요… (Um, this is my seat, though…)
items: 예약을 ___, 확인 좀 부탁드려요. (하다, past verb)
여기 사진 ___, 한 장만 부탁드려도 될까요? (찍다, verb)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners over-apply the verb pattern -는데요 to adjectives. Adjectives (비싸다, 좋다, 크다) must use -(으)ㄴ데요, so it's 비싼데요, not 비싸는데요.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 — "I tend to / I'm rather …"
grammarNotes.func: Describes a general tendency rather than a hard fact — 'on the … side', 'tends to be …'. It hedges a judgment, which sounds modest and natural when you comment on people, habits, or customs without being too absolute.

formTable.ex: 저는 일찍 가는 편이에요 (I tend to arrive early)
한국 사람들은 정이 많은 편이에요 (Koreans tend to be warm-hearted)
선물을 많이 받은 편이에요 (I got rather a lot of gifts)
술을 잘 안 마시는 편이에요 (I tend not to drink much)

examples.en: At first I tend to be careful with how I address people.
examples.note: Hedges a self-description so it sounds modest, not absolute.

examples.ko: 요즘 젊은 사람들은 명절에 한복을 잘 안 입는 편이에요.
examples.romanization: yojeum jeolmeun saramdeureun myeongjeore hanbogeul jal an imneun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: These days young people tend not to wear hanbok on the holidays.
examples.note: A soft generalization about a changing custom, leaving room for exceptions.

examples.ko: 그 선배님은 후배들을 잘 챙기는 편이에요.
examples.romanization: geu seonbaenimeun hubaedeureul jal chaenggineun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: That senior tends to look out for the juniors.
examples.note: Comments on someone's habit without stating it as a fixed rule.

examples.ko: 저는 분위기가 어색하면 먼저 말을 거는 편이에요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun bunwigiga eosaekamyeon meonjeo mareul geoneun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: When the mood is awkward, I tend to be the one who speaks up first.
examples.note: Describes a personal habit in a social setting, softly.

keyPoint.label: Verb 는 편 vs. Adjective (으)ㄴ 편
keyPoint.body: With a verb, use -는 편이다 for a habit (가는 편, 챙기는 편). With an adjective, use -(으)ㄴ 편이다 for a quality (많은 편, 비싼 편). 편이다 means 'leans that way', so never use it for a one-time event like '오늘 갔어요'.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 편이에요 is [펴니에요]; the ㄴ links into the next syllable. Keep 편 short, not 'pyeon-i'.

drill.instruction: Turn each fact into a softer tendency with -는/-(으)ㄴ 편이에요.
drill.model: 저는 / 일찍 자다 → 저는 일찍 자는 편이에요. (I tend to sleep early.)
items: 저는 / 술을 잘 안 마시다 (negative verb)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 많다 is an adjective, so it takes -(으)ㄴ 편이다 → 많은 편이에요, not the verb ending -는 편. Check whether the word is a verb or an adjective before you pick 는 or (으)ㄴ.

grammarNotes.title: V/A-(으)니까 — "since (so here's what to do)"
grammarNotes.func: Gives a reason that leads into advice, a request, or a decision: 'since X, (let's / please / I'll) …'. Unlike -아서/어서, it's the natural choice when the second clause is a suggestion or command — very common when explaining the reason behind a social custom.

formTable.when: Verb/Adjective stem ending in a vowel
formTable.ex: 집들이니까 선물을 챙기세요 (Since it's a housewarming, bring a gift)

formTable.when: Verb/Adjective stem ending in a consonant
formTable.ex: 어르신도 계시니까 조심하세요 (Since elders are here too, be careful)
덕분에 잘 됐으니까 감사 인사를 하세요 (Since it went well thanks to them, say thank you)
오늘이 첫날이니까 일찍 가요 (Since today's the first day, let's go early)

examples.en: Since it's a housewarming, take at least a small gift.
examples.note: Reason leading straight into advice — the classic -(으)니까 use.

examples.en: Since there are elders there too, be careful with your tone.
examples.note: 계시다 keeps it respectful; -(으)니까 ties the reason to the action.

examples.ko: 아직 잘 모르니까 호칭을 먼저 여쭤볼게요.
examples.romanization: ajik jal moreunikka hochingeul meonjeo yeojjwobolgeyo.
examples.en: Since I'm not sure yet, I'll ask first how to address them.
examples.note: Reason + the speaker's own decision (-ㄹ게요).

examples.ko: 분위기가 좀 어색하니까 제가 먼저 말을 걸어 볼게요.
examples.romanization: bunwigiga jom eosaekanikka jega meonjeo mareul georeo bolgeyo.
examples.en: Since the mood is a bit awkward, I'll be the one to break the ice.
examples.note: -(으)니까 supports a decision to act.

keyPoint.label: -(으)니까 vs. -아서/어서
keyPoint.body: Both mean 'because', but only -(으)니까 can lead into a command or suggestion: 늦었으니까 빨리 가세요 (O), 늦어서 빨리 가세요 (X). Use -아서/어서 for plain cause-and-result, -(으)니까 when you're telling someone what to do because of the reason.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -(으)니까 is [(으)니까] with a tense 까. Don't soften it to '니가'; the double ㄲ stays strong.

drill.instruction: Join the reason and the advice with -(으)니까.
drill.model: 집들이다 + 선물을 챙기세요 → 집들이니까 선물을 챙기세요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: When the second clause is a command or suggestion (가세요, 합시다, -ㄹ게요), Korean needs -(으)니까, not -아서/어서. -아서/어서 only works before a plain statement, so 'Since we're late, please hurry' must use 늦었으니까.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-지만 — "… but (I'll still do the polite thing)"
grammarNotes.func: Admits one fact, then turns to a contrasting choice: 'A, but B'. In social situations the second clause usually shows the careful or considerate option, so it's handy for explaining why you act politely even when you don't strictly have to.

formTable.ex: 바쁘지만 갈게요 (I'm busy, but I'll go)
늦었지만 인사는 드렸어요 (I was late, but I did greet them)
동갑이지만 존댓말을 써요 (We're the same age, but I use polite speech)

examples.en: We're the same age, but at first I use polite speech.
examples.note: Being the same age doesn't automatically mean casual speech.

examples.en: It's a little awkward, but I'll greet them first.
examples.note: Discomfort first, then the considerate action.

examples.en: I'm busy, but I prepared the housewarming gift ahead of time.
examples.note: Effort despite being busy shows consideration.

examples.ko: 친하지 않지만 선배님이라고 부르는 게 안전해요.
examples.romanization: chinhaji anchiman seonbaenimirago bureuneun ge anjeonhaeyo.
examples.en: We're not close, but calling them seonbaenim is the safe choice.
examples.note: Title before closeness — the careful option.

keyPoint.label: -지만 vs. 그렇지만 / 그런데
keyPoint.body: -지만 joins the two clauses inside one sentence (바쁘지만 갈게요). 그렇지만 / 그런데 do the same job but start a new sentence: 바빠요. 그렇지만 갈게요. Use -지만 to keep it as one smooth sentence.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -지만 is plain [지만]; no sound changes. After ㅂ-irregular adjectives the stem shifts: 어렵다 → 어렵지만 stays regular here (the ㅂ only changes before vowels).

drill.instruction: Connect the two ideas with -지만, putting the polite choice second.
drill.model: 동갑이다 + 존댓말을 써요 → 동갑이지만 존댓말을 써요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: -지만 attaches to the plain stem, not to a finished 해요/예요 form. With a noun it's 동갑 + 이지만 → 동갑이지만, never 동갑이에요 + 지만.
