extendedDialogue.setting: Minseo asks how to behave at a coworker's housewarming.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 집들이에 갈 때 휴지랑 세제 중에 뭐가 나아요?
lines.romanization: jipdeurie gal ttae hyujirang seje junge mwoga naayo?
lines.en: When going to a housewarming, which is better, toilet paper or detergent?
lines.grammarNote: V(으)ㄹ 때 sets the social situation.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 둘 다 괜찮아요. 집들이 선물로 많이 가져가잖아요.
lines.romanization: dul da gwaenchanayo. jipdeuri seonmullo manhi gajyeogajanhayo.
lines.en: Both are fine. People often bring them as housewarming gifts, you know.
lines.grammarNote: 잖아요 treats the custom as shared knowledge.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: If we are about the same age, can I say we are the same age?
lines.grammarNote: V면 asks about a condition.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 그래도 처음엔 선배님 같은 호칭을 쓰는 편이에요.
lines.romanization: geuraedo cheoeumen seonbaenim gateun hochingeul sseuneun pyeonieyo.
lines.en: Even so, at first people tend to use a title like seonbaenim.
lines.grammarNote: 편이에요 softens the social habit.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: If elders are there too, I will ask, 'May I help?'
lines.grammarNote: 계시다 and 도와드리다 keep the respectful tone.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 좋아요. 눈치 있게 챙기면 분위기가 덜 어색해요.
lines.romanization: joayo. nunchi itge chaenggimyeon bunwigiga deol eosaekaeyo.
lines.en: Good. If you take care of things tactfully, the mood is less awkward.
lines.grammarNote: 눈치 becomes action through 챙기다.

readingText.title: 집들이에서 호칭과 눈치 챙기기
readingText.body: 민서는 회사 선배 집들이에 가려고 해요. 집들이 선물로 휴지와 세제 중에서 고민하다가, 실용적인 세제를 사기로 했어요. 처음 만나는 사람들이 있을 수 있으니까 나이와 호칭도 조심하려고 해요. 나이가 비슷해 보여도 바로 반말하지 않고, 처음에는 선배님 같은 호칭을 쓰는 편이에요. 어르신도 계시면 먼저 도와드릴까요? 하고 물어볼 거예요. 분위기가 어색하면 눈치 있게 선물을 건네고, 마지막에는 초대해 주셔서 감사합니다, 덕분에 편했어요라고 말하려고 해요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo is going to a senior coworker's housewarming. After thinking between toilet paper and detergent as a housewarming gift, Minseo decided to buy practical detergent. Since there may be people Minseo is meeting for the first time, Minseo plans to be careful with age and titles too. Even if someone seems close in age, Minseo will not switch to casual speech right away and tends to use a title like seonbaenim at first. If elders are there, Minseo will ask first, 'May I help?' If the atmosphere feels awkward, Minseo will give the gift tactfully and at the end say, 'Thank you for inviting me. I felt comfortable thanks to you.'

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 집들이 선물로 무엇을 사기로 했어요?
나이가 비슷해 보여도 처음에는 어떻게 해요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 바로 반말하지 않고 선배님 같은 호칭을 쓰는 편이에요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 마지막에 어떤 감사 표현을 하려고 해요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 초대해 주셔서 감사합니다, 덕분에 편했어요라고 말하려고 해요.

culturalNote.title: 눈치는 말보다 타이밍
culturalNote.body: 눈치 is often translated as reading the room, but at a gathering it becomes timing: when to ask, when to help, when to stay quiet, and when to thank someone. At a 집들이, the safe pattern is simple. Bring a practical 선물, use a respectful 호칭 until the relationship is clear, ask before helping, and close with a warm 감사 expression such as 덕분에 편했어요.
culturalNote.tip: If you are unsure, combine a soft sentence ending with a respectful verb: 호칭을 잘 모르는데요, 어떻게 부르면 될까요?

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence naturally explains a housewarming gift custom?
options: 집들이 선물로 휴지나 세제를 많이 가져가잖아요.
inlineExercises.correct: 집들이 선물로 휴지나 세제를 많이 가져가잖아요.
inlineExercises.explanation: 선물로 marks the role, and 잖아요 points to a familiar custom.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence is safest when you do not know the title?
inlineExercises.explanation: Asking about 호칭 is safer than guessing too casually.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence thanks someone with a positive cause?
inlineExercises.explanation: 덕분에 is the warm positive-cause expression for gratitude.

inlineExercises.prompt: 어르신___ 도와드렸어요. (I helped the elder.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 도와드리다 still takes the person helped as an object. 드리다 adds respect toward the person receiving help.

inlineExercises.prompt: 제가 좀 ___ . (도와주다 → respectful help)
inlineExercises.explanation: 도와드리다 is the respectful form when helping someone senior or socially respected. -ㄹ게요 makes it your offered action.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Thanks to you, I had a good time.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 덕분에 credits the other person as the positive reason. 좋은 시간 보냈어요 is a natural thanks-after-visit phrase.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'I am bringing tissue as a housewarming gift.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 선물로 marks the role of the item as a gift. 휴지 is a common practical 집들이 gift.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the phrase for a senior host: '수고했어.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 수고했어 is casual and too low for a senior host. 수고하셨습니다 is safer and respectful.

inlineExercises.prompt: You do not know the safest title. Which strategy fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: When title is unclear, asking politely is safer than guessing casually. Korean social titles matter in first meetings.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'If we are the same age, we are 동갑.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 동갑 means the same age. -으면 sets the condition for using that word.

bullets: Housewarming set: 집들이, 선물, 휴지, 세제, 챙기다.
Title set: 나이, 동갑, 선배/후배, 호칭, 어르신.
Room-reading set: 눈치, 분위기, 어색하다, 도와드리다, 수고하셨습니다.
Gratitude set: 덕분에 is for positive causes; 때문에 can sound like blame.

writingTask.prompt: Advise a foreign friend on what gift to bring to a Korean housewarming and how to address people there.
writingTask.hint: Use V/A-잖아요 for shared knowledge, V/A-거든요 to explain background, V/A-는데요 to soften, V/A-(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 for a tendency, and V/A-(으)니까 for a reason leading to advice.
writingTask.model: 집들이에는 보통 휴지나 세제를 선물하잖아요. 그게 좋은 뜻이 있거든요. 그리고 선배는 나이가 많은 편이니까 호칭을 조심하는 게 좋은데요.
writingTask.modelEn: For a housewarming, people usually give toilet paper or detergent, you know. It carries a good meaning, you see. And since seniors tend to be older, it's good to be careful with how you address them.

canDo: Remind someone of shared knowledge (선물하잖아요)
Explain background or a reason (좋은 뜻이 있거든요)
Soften a statement or careful question (조심하는 게 좋은데요)
Describe a tendency modestly (나이가 많은 편이에요)
Give a reason that leads into advice (선배니까 호칭을 조심하세요)

chapters.scenario: A parent feeds a child, a teacher has students read, or a manager seats guests.

dialogue.en: Seen this way, you can tell who made someone do what.

chapters.guidedPractice: Write five pairs: base action first, causative action second. Example: 아이가 먹어요 -> 엄마가 아이에게 밥을 먹여요.
chapters.realLifeTask: Describe one scene with a causative verb, then rewrite it with -게 하다.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner gives a base verb; answer with a natural causative pair and one full sentence.
chapters.review: Can you tell who does the action and who causes it in 먹다/먹이다, 자다/재우다, 앉다/앉히다, 웃다/웃기다, and 울다/울리다?

beginnerGuide.title: Find the causer
beginnerGuide.body: In 사동 sentences, the subject is often not doing the base action. 엄마가 아이에게 밥을 먹였어요 means the child eats, but the mother causes or helps it happen.

beginnerGuide.title: Learn pairs, not suffix math
beginnerGuide.body: The suffix list is useful, but many causatives are memorized as pairs: 먹다/먹이다, 자다/재우다, 입다/입히다, 앉다/앉히다, 울다/울리다.

beginnerGuide.title: Separate causative and passive
beginnerGuide.body: Some forms look like passive forms, especially 읽히다. Read the whole sentence: 선생님이 학생들에게 본문을 읽혔어요 is causative; 책이 잘 읽혀요 is text-focused/passive-like.

checkpoints: I can find the person causing the action and the person doing it.
I can use common causatives like 먹이다, 입히다, 앉히다, 웃기다, and 울리다.
I can compare a built-in causative with V-게 하다.

sampleAnswer.en: The teacher had the students read the sentence. The teacher made the students read the sentence.

checklist: I can find the person causing the action and the person doing it.
I can use common causatives like 먹이다, 입히다, 앉히다, 웃기다, and 울리다.
I can compare a built-in causative with V-게 하다.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: You need to say that someone caused another person to eat, sleep, wear something, read aloud, sit down, laugh, cry, know something, or lower a level. The key is to separate the person doing the base action from the person or thing causing it.
objectives: Build natural causative pairs such as 먹다/먹이다, 자다/재우다, 입다/입히다, and 앉다/앉히다.
Choose between a lexical/morphological causative, V-게 하다, and V-게 만들다.
Avoid confusing causative forms with passive-looking forms such as 읽히다.
hook.whyItMatters: Causatives are not just grammar labels. They change the story: 아이가 먹었어요 means the child ate; 엄마가 아이에게 밥을 먹였어요 means the mother caused or helped the child eat.

grammarNotes.title: Lexical causatives: V + -이/히/리/기/우/구/추-
grammarNotes.func: A fixed, closed set of verbs that build a causative meaning ('make/get X to happen', or 'do the action to X') right into the verb stem by inserting -이-, -히-, -리-, -기-, -우-, -구-, or -추-. The doer of the plain verb becomes the object (usually -을/를), and a new causer becomes the subject. Because the set is fixed, you can't apply it to just any verb — each causative pair is learned as its own vocabulary item.

formTable.add: 먹다 → 먹이다 (feed), 죽다 → 죽이다 (kill), 끓다 → 끓이다 (boil sth)
formTable.ex: 엄마가 아기에게 밥을 먹여요. (Mom feeds the baby.)

formTable.add: 입다 → 입히다 (dress sb), 앉다 → 앉히다 (seat sb), 눕다 → 눕히다 (lay sb down)
formTable.ex: 아이에게 옷을 입혔어요. (I dressed the child.)

formTable.add: 살다 → 살리다 (save), 울다 → 울리다 (make cry), 알다 → 알리다 (let know)
formTable.ex: 동생이 형을 울렸어요. (The younger one made the older one cry.)

formTable.add: 웃다 → 웃기다 (make laugh), 벗다 → 벗기다 (take sth off sb), 남다 → 남기다 (leave sth)
formTable.ex: 그 영화가 저를 웃겼어요. (That movie made me laugh.)

formTable.add: 자다 → 재우다 (put to sleep), 깨다 → 깨우다 (wake sb), 타다 → 태우다 (give a ride)
formTable.ex: 아빠가 아기를 재웠어요. (Dad put the baby to sleep.)

formTable.add: 달다 → 달구다 (heat sth up), 낮다 → 낮추다 (lower), 맞다 → 맞추다 (set/adjust)
formTable.ex: 소리를 좀 낮춰 주세요. (Please turn the volume down.)

examples.en: I fed the puppy.
examples.note: 먹다 (eat) → 먹이다 (feed): the eater (강아지) takes -한테/에게, and the new causer (저) becomes the subject.

examples.en: Mom put the child to bed early.
examples.note: 자다 (sleep) → 재우다: the stem changes shape (자→재우), so memorize this pair — you can't just add a suffix.

examples.en: The nurse laid the patient down on the bed.
examples.note: 눕다 (lie down) → 눕히다: the causee (환자) takes -을/를 because the nurse is physically doing it to them.

examples.en: My friend always makes me laugh.
examples.note: 웃다 (laugh) → 웃기다: the causer doesn't have to be a person — a joke or a movie can be the subject too.

keyPoint.label: Same suffix, opposite job: causative vs. passive
keyPoint.body: The suffixes -이/히/리/기- also build passives, so one word can be either. 보이다 = 'be seen' (passive) or 'show' (causative); 잡히다 = 'be caught' (passive) or 'get sb to hold' (causative). Tell them apart by the arguments: a causative ADDS a causer-subject and keeps an object (친구가 저를 웃겨요 'my friend makes me laugh'), while a passive DROPS the agent and the old object becomes the subject (도둑이 잡혔어요 'the thief got caught'). If there's still a direct object being acted on, it's causative.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: Listen for the linking and aspiration the inserted consonant creates: 먹이다 is [머기다] (ㄱ links across), 입히다 is [이피다] (ㅂ+ㅎ → aspirated ㅍ), and 앉히다 is [안치다] (ㅈ+ㅎ → ㅊ). The suffix tends to fuse with the stem-final sound rather than staying separate.

drill.instruction: Turn the plain verb into its lexical causative and finish the sentence.
drill.model: 아기가 자다 → 엄마가 아기를 ____. → 엄마가 아기를 재워요. (Mom puts the baby to sleep.)
items: 아이가 옷을 입다 → 제가 아이에게 옷을 ____. (→ 입혀요)
모기가 죽다 → 이 약이 모기를 ____. (→ 죽여요)
아기가 깨다 → 시끄러운 소리가 아기를 ____. (→ 깨워요)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 엄마가 아기를 먹게 했어요. (to mean 'Mom fed the baby')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English has one verb 'feed', so learners grab the all-purpose V-게 하다 and say 먹게 했어요 — but that means 'made/let the baby eat (on its own)', not 'spoon-fed it'. When Korean has a dedicated lexical causative (먹이다, 재우다, 입히다), native speakers use it for the hands-on action. Save V-게 하다 for getting someone to do it themselves.

grammarNotes.title: V-게 하다 — make / have / let someone do something
grammarNotes.func: The productive, all-purpose causative: add -게 하다 to almost any verb or adjective stem to mean 'make/have/let someone do or become something.' Unlike the lexical causatives, this works with every verb, so it's the go-to whenever no special causative form exists. The causee is marked with -이/가, -을/를, or -에게/한테 depending on the nuance (letting vs. making vs. getting someone to do it).

formTable.add: 가다 → 가게 하다, 먹다 → 먹게 하다, 공부하다 → 공부하게 하다
formTable.ex: 선생님이 학생들을 일찍 가게 했어요. (The teacher made the students leave early.)

formTable.add: 행복하다 → 행복하게 하다, 깨끗하다 → 깨끗하게 하다
formTable.ex: 그 소식이 저를 행복하게 했어요. (That news made me happy.)
아이에게 채소를 먹게 했어요. (I got the child to eat vegetables.)
동생을 울게 하지 마. (Don't make your little sibling cry.)

examples.en: My mom makes me exercise every day.
examples.note: 운동하다 has no lexical causative, so -게 하다 is the only choice; -를 here signals fairly direct pressure.

examples.en: The teacher had the students read the book.
examples.note: -에게 marks the causee when you get someone to perform the action themselves.

examples.ko: 아이가 자고 싶어 해서 자게 했어요.
examples.romanization: Ai-ga jago sipeo haeseo jage haesseoyo.
examples.en: The child wanted to sleep, so I let him.
examples.note: With -이/가 and a permissive context, -게 하다 reads as 'let/allow', not 'force'.

examples.en: This song makes people dance.
examples.note: The causer can be an inanimate thing (노래); -게 하다 freely takes non-human subjects.

keyPoint.label: Lexical causative vs. V-게 하다 — how hands-on is the causer?
keyPoint.body: When both exist, they differ in directness. 재우다 / 먹이다 mean the causer DOES the action to the causee (physically putting to sleep, spoon-feeding). 자게 하다 / 먹게 하다 mean the causer gets the causee to do it THEMSELVES. So 아기를 재웠어요 = 'I put the baby to sleep,' but 아기를 자게 했어요 = 'I made the baby sleep (e.g., by turning off the lights).' Use -게 하다 whenever there's no lexical form, or when you specifically mean indirect causing / letting.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: -게 하다 is said as written, [게 하다]; in fast speech 하다 can weaken, but unlike some patterns it does NOT contract into one word — keep 게 and 하다 separate. Don't confuse the causative with plain adverbial -게 (e.g. 크게 'loudly'); the causative needs the following 하다.

drill.instruction: Rewrite using V-게 하다 to express 'make / have someone do it.'
drill.model: 학생들이 책을 읽어요. (causer: 선생님) → 선생님이 학생들에게 책을 읽게 해요.
items: 아이가 일찍 자요. (causer: 엄마) → 엄마가 아이를 일찍 ____. (→ 자게 해요)
동생이 방을 청소해요. (causer: 형) → 형이 동생에게 방을 ____. (→ 청소하게 해요)
학생들이 숙제를 내요. (causer: 선생님) → 선생님이 학생들에게 숙제를 ____. (→ 내게 해요)
아이가 채소를 먹어요. (causer: 아빠) → 아빠가 아이에게 채소를 ____. (→ 먹게 해요)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 선생님이 저를 공부하라고 했어요. (used loosely for 'made me study')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'make me do' covers everything, so learners reach for -라고 하다, which actually means 'told me to' (a reported spoken order), not 'made me'. For the neutral, everyday 'make/have someone do X,' the default is -게 하다. Use -라고 하다 only when there was a real spoken command, and save -게 만들다 (next note) for forceful or emotional results.

grammarNotes.title: V-게 만들다 — bring about a result (often emotional or forceful)
grammarNotes.func: Structurally just like V-게 하다 (add -게 만들다 to a verb or adjective stem), but with a stronger 'bring about / cause to become' flavor. Since 만들다 means 'make/create,' V-게 만들다 stresses that the causer actively PRODUCES the resulting state or behavior. It's especially common when the result is emotional (made me cry / angry / happy) or when the causing feels forceful, unintended, or hard to resist. The causer is very often an inanimate thing or a situation.

formTable.add: 울다 → 울게 만들다, 떠나다 → 떠나게 만들다, 포기하다 → 포기하게 만들다
formTable.ex: 그 영화가 저를 울게 만들었어요. (That movie made me cry.)

formTable.add: 화나다 → 화나게 만들다, 행복하다 → 행복하게 만들다
formTable.ex: 그 말이 저를 화나게 만들었어요. (Those words made me angry.)
스트레스가 저를 아프게 만들었어요. (Stress made me sick.)
분위기를 어색하게 만들지 마세요. (Don't make things awkward.)

examples.en: That drama made everyone cry.
examples.note: Emotional result + inanimate causer (드라마): the most typical use of -게 만들다.

examples.en: What you said made me angry.
examples.note: -게 만들다 fits strong feelings; here it sounds more loaded than the neutral 화나게 했어.

examples.en: The hot weather wears me out.
examples.note: A situation (날씨) as the causer is very natural with -게 만들다, often for an unwanted result.

examples.en: That accident made people anxious.
examples.note: With an adjective (불안하다), -게 만들다 means 'cause people to become anxious.'

keyPoint.label: -게 하다 vs. -게 만들다 — neutral instruction vs. strong/emotional result
keyPoint.body: -게 하다 is the neutral default: a person tells or gets someone to do something (엄마가 저를 운동하게 해요 'Mom makes me exercise'). -게 만들다 highlights a produced result, usually emotional or forceful, and very often with a thing/situation as the cause (그 영화가 저를 울게 만들었어요 'That movie made me cry'). You usually wouldn't say 엄마가 저를 운동하게 만들어요 for routine instructing — that sounds like she forced an unwilling you into it. Rule of thumb: choosing/instructing → -게 하다; an event or feeling that takes you over → -게 만들다.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 만들다 is [만들다]; in the past tense the ㄹ stays and you get 만들었어요 [만드러써요] — don't drop the ㄹ. -게 is light and unstressed, so the phrase often runs together as one breath group: 울게 만들었어요 → [울게 만드러써요].

drill.instruction: Use V-게 만들다 to say what the thing or situation caused (pick an emotion/result that fits).
drill.model: 그 영화 / 나 / 울다 → 그 영화가 나를 울게 만들었어. (That movie made me cry.)
items: 그 노래 / 사람들 / 춤추다 → ____. (→ 그 노래가 사람들을 춤추게 만들었어요)
네 말 / 나 / 화나다 → ____. (→ 네 말이 나를 화나게 만들었어)
시험 / 학생들 / 긴장하다 → ____. (→ 시험이 학생들을 긴장하게 만들었어요)
그 소식 / 우리 / 행복하다 → ____. (→ 그 소식이 우리를 행복하게 만들었어요)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 엄마가 저를 매일 청소하게 만들어요. (for routine 'Mom makes me clean every day')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'make me clean' is neutral, but -게 만들다 adds a forceful, almost resentful 'forced me into it' coloring, so it sounds off for an everyday instruction. For routine 'has me / makes me do X,' use -게 하다. Reserve -게 만들다 for genuinely strong or emotional results, and especially when a thing or situation is the cause (그 영화가 저를 울게 만들었어요).

extendedDialogue.setting: A learner practices causative pairs in caregiving, classroom, and emotion scenes.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 아이가 밥을 먹었어요와 엄마가 아이에게 밥을 먹였어요는 다르죠?
lines.romanization: aiga babeul meogeosseoyowa eommaga aiege babeul meogyeosseoyoneun dareujyo?
lines.en: The child ate and the mother fed the child are different, right?
lines.grammarNote: Base action versus caused action.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 네. 먹었어요는 아이가 한 행동이고, 먹였어요는 엄마가 하게 한 행동이에요.
lines.romanization: ne. meogeosseoyoneun aiga han haengdongigo, meogyeosseoyoneun eommaga hage han haengdongieyo.
lines.en: Yes. Ate is what the child did; fed is what the mother caused to happen.
lines.grammarNote: The causer and doer are different.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 그럼 선생님이 학생들에게 본문을 읽혔어요도 사동이에요?
lines.romanization: geureom seonsaengnimi haksaengdeurege bonmuneul ilkyeosseoyodo sadongieyo?
lines.en: Then is 'the teacher had the students read the passage' also causative?
lines.grammarNote: 읽히다 can be causative in the right sentence.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 맞아요. 하지만 책이 잘 읽혀요는 사동보다 피동처럼 느껴져요.
lines.romanization: majayo. hajiman chaegi jal ilkyeoyoneun sadongboda pidongcheoreom neukkyeojyeoyo.
lines.en: Right. But 'the book reads well' feels more passive-like than causative.
lines.grammarNote: Same-looking form, different sentence role.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 웃기다와 울리다는 감정이 바뀌는 사동으로 보면 되겠네요.
lines.romanization: utgidawa ullidaneun gamjeongi bakkwineun sadongeuro bomyeon doegenneyo.
lines.en: So I can see utgida and ullida as causatives where emotions change.
lines.grammarNote: Emotion causatives.

readingText.title: 누가 하게 만들었는지 보기
readingText.body: 사동사를 공부할 때는 접미사만 외우면 헷갈리기 쉬워요. 먼저 누가 실제 행동을 하는지 보고, 그다음 누가 그 행동을 하게 했는지 확인해야 해요. 아이가 밥을 먹으면 아이가 행동의 주체예요. 하지만 엄마가 아이에게 밥을 먹이면 엄마가 사동의 주체이고 아이가 먹는 사람이에요. 선생님이 학생들에게 본문을 읽혔어요는 학생들이 읽지만 선생님이 읽게 한 문장이에요. 반대로 책이 잘 읽혀요는 책이 쉽게 읽힌다는 뜻이라 사동보다 피동처럼 느껴져요. 그래서 먹이다, 재우다, 입히다, 앉히다 같은 단어는 기본형과 짝으로 외우는 것이 좋아요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: When studying causative verbs, memorizing only suffixes can be confusing. First check who actually performs the action, and then who causes that action to happen. If a child eats rice, the child is the doer. But if a mother feeds the child, the mother is the causative subject and the child is the one eating. In 'the teacher had the students read the passage,' the students read but the teacher caused it. By contrast, 'the book reads well' means the book is easy to read, so it feels more passive-like than causative. That is why words like 먹이다, 재우다, 입히다, and 앉히다 are best memorized as pairs with their base forms.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 사동사를 공부할 때 먼저 무엇을 확인해야 해요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 누가 실제 행동을 하는지 확인해야 해요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 엄마가 아이에게 밥을 먹이면 누가 밥을 먹어요?
책이 잘 읽혀요는 사동보다 무엇처럼 느껴져요?

culturalNote.title: Caregiving, Classroom, Workplace
culturalNote.body: Korean causatives appear most naturally in roles where someone guides another person's action: parents feed children, teachers have students read, staff seat guests, managers make employees work, and stories make people laugh or cry. If the sentence sounds too forceful with V-게 만들다, switch to V-게 하다 or a lexical causative such as 앉히다.
culturalNote.tip: Before choosing the form, name three roles in English: causer, person affected, base action. Then build the Korean sentence.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means the mother fed the child?
inlineExercises.explanation: 먹이다 means someone causes or helps another person eat.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence is causative 읽히다?
inlineExercises.explanation: The teacher causes the students to read. 책이 술술 읽혔어요 is passive-like/text-focused.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which form is better for a strong emotional result?
inlineExercises.explanation: V-게 만들다 fits emotional or resultative causation.

inlineExercises.prompt: 아이___ 자리에 앉혔어요. (I seated the child.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 앉히다 is causative, and 아이 is the person caused/helped to sit. That person takes 를.

inlineExercises.prompt: 아이에게 밥을 ___ . (먹다 → causative past)
inlineExercises.explanation: 먹이다 means feed or make someone eat. In polite past it becomes 먹였어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'The teacher made the student read the book.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 읽히다 can be causative: make someone read. 학생에게 marks who was made to read.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'I put the child to sleep.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 재우다 is the causative of 자다. 아이를 is the person you caused to sleep.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '아이가 밥을 먹였어요.' (intended: Mom fed the child.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 먹이다 needs a causer and the person fed. 엄마가 is the causer, and 아이에게 marks the child who receives the food.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means “The news made me cry”?
inlineExercises.explanation: 울리다 can mean make someone cry. 저를 marks the person affected by the news.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'Please let me know the result.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 알리다 means inform or let someone know. 결과를 is the information being given.

bullets: Base action: 먹다, 자다, 입다, 앉다, 웃다, 울다.
Lexical causative: 먹이다, 재우다, 입히다, 앉히다, 웃기다, 울리다, 알리다, 낮추다.
V-게 하다 is flexible and neutral; V-게 만들다 highlights a result or emotional force.
Always identify the causer, the affected person, and the base action before choosing the form.

writingTask.prompt: Describe an evening looking after a small child: what you made or had them do, and how a show affected them.
writingTask.hint: Use lexical causatives (먹이다, 재우다, 입히다, 앉히다) and the productive V-게 하다 / V-게 만들다 to say who made/had someone do something.
writingTask.model: 저녁에 아이에게 밥을 먹이고 따뜻한 옷을 입혔어요. 만화가 아이를 많이 웃게 했어요. 슬픈 장면은 아이를 울게 만들었어요. 그다음에 아이를 침대에 앉히고 재웠어요.
writingTask.modelEn: In the evening I fed the child and dressed them in warm clothes. The cartoon made the child laugh a lot. A sad scene made the child cry. After that I seated the child on the bed and put them to sleep.

canDo: Use lexical causatives for everyday care (밥을 먹이다, 옷을 입히다, 재우다)
Make or have someone do something with V-게 하다 (아이를 웃게 했어요)
Say something brought about a result with V-게 만들다 (영화가 울게 만들었어요)
Tell the causer from the doer in a causative sentence

chapters.title: 겠 — Volition, Inference, and Softened Speech
chapters.goal: Use 겠 for formal intention, careful guessing, or polite softening.
chapters.scenario: You promise to handle something, infer a result, or politely decline.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: Could you check my order, please?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Yes, I will check it right away.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: There are many people, so it looks like it will take some time.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Yes, it will take about ten minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.en: Then I will wait here.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: I will let you know as soon as it is ready.

chapters.guidedPractice: Write two service commitments with -겠습니다, two evidence-based inferences with -겠네요, and one softened refusal with 어렵겠습니다.
chapters.realLifeTask: Make one sentence with -겠습니다 and one guess with -겠네요.
chapters.friendPractice: A partner gives a context: service promise, inference, future plan, or soft refusal. Choose 겠, -(으)ㄹ 거예요, or -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요.
chapters.review: Can you explain why 확인하겠습니다, 피곤하시겠네요, and 참석하기 어렵겠습니다 use the same 겠 but do different jobs?

beginnerGuide.title: Separate three jobs
beginnerGuide.body: 겠 can mark a formal commitment, a confident inference, or softened formal speech. Do not translate every 겠 as simple future.

beginnerGuide.title: Service promise
beginnerGuide.body: In service or workplace speech, 확인하겠습니다 and 처리하겠습니다 sound like committed action. 확인할 거예요 sounds more like a plain future plan.

beginnerGuide.title: Inference and refusal
beginnerGuide.body: 피곤하시겠네요 infers from evidence. 참석하기 어렵겠습니다 softens a refusal instead of bluntly saying 못 가요.

checkpoints: I can use -겠습니다 for a formal promise or service action.
I can use -겠네요 when I infer from evidence.
I can choose between 겠, -(으)ㄹ 거예요, and 것 같아요.

curriculumTrack.label: B2 Advanced Control

exitTask.canDo: Use 겠 for formal intention, careful guessing, or polite softening.
exitTask.prompt: Make one sentence with -겠습니다 and one guess with -겠네요.

sampleAnswer.ko: 제가 확인하겠습니다. 자료를 보니 시간이 좀 걸리겠네요.
sampleAnswer.en: I will check it. Looking at the materials, it looks like it will take some time.

checklist: I can use -겠습니다 for a formal promise or service action.
I can use -겠네요 when I infer from evidence.
I can choose between 겠, -(으)ㄹ 거예요, and 것 같아요.
Make it about your real day: your name, place, time, or plan.
Keep the first version short before you make it longer.

hook.situation: The same 겠 appears in three very different moments: a staff member makes a formal promise, a researcher infers from data, and a colleague declines politely. You need to hear which job 겠 is doing before you translate it.
objectives: Use -겠습니다 for formal commitment and service speech.
Use -겠네요/-겠군요 for confident inference from evidence.
Separate 겠 from -(으)ㄹ 거예요 and -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 in future, inference, and softened refusal.
hook.whyItMatters: English often reduces 겠 to 'will,' but Korean uses it for register and stance. 확인하겠습니다, 피곤하시겠네요, and 참석하기 어렵겠습니다 all contain 겠, but they do different social work.

grammarNotes.title: V-겠어요 / V-겠습니다 — stating your own intention
grammarNotes.func: Attach 겠 to a verb stem to say what YOU are going to do, decided right now, as a will or promise. Because it carries the speaker's own will, it almost always has a first-person subject (저/제가). 겠어요 is polite-conversational; 겠습니다 is formal and sounds like a firm, clean promise — the kind you make to a boss, a teacher, or a customer.

formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹겠어요 (I'll eat / I'll have it)

examples.en: Let me do it first. I'll do it.
examples.note: First-person + 하겠습니다 = a firm offer to take something on; very common when volunteering.

examples.en: Today it's on me — I'll pay.
examples.note: 겠 here is a decision made on the spot, not a long-standing plan.

examples.en: Thank you for the food (lit. I'll eat well).
examples.note: A fixed mealtime phrase — 겠 signals you're about to start eating now.

examples.en: I'll get it done by tomorrow.
examples.note: A promise to someone you answer to; 겠습니다 sounds more responsible than a plain future.

keyPoint.label: 겠어요 vs 겠습니다
keyPoint.body: Same intention meaning, different register. 겠어요 is everyday polite ('제가 할게요'/'먹겠어요'); 겠습니다 is formal and weightier, so it's the default for promises, service speech, and announcements. Don't use either for someone ELSE's plan — for that you need -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (친구가 올 거예요).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 겠 ends in a [ㄷ] sound, so before 습니다 the ㅅ tenses and the batchim drops in: 겠습니다 → [게씀니다]. 겠어요 links smoothly as [게써요].

drill.instruction: Turn each verb into a first-person intention using -겠습니다.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'will' covers both my own decision and a guess about other people, so learners stretch 겠 to a third person. But volitional 겠 belongs to the speaker's own will — for what a friend is going to do, use -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-겠네요 / A/V-겠군요 — 'that must be…' (inference from evidence)
grammarNotes.func: This is the other big job of 겠: drawing a confident conclusion from what you can see, hear, or have just been told. Add 겠 to a verb or adjective stem, then 네요/군요 to react out loud. It means 'must be / I bet / I can tell.' 겠네요 is the everyday reaction; 겠군요 sounds a touch more reflective ('Ah, so it must be…').

examples.en: It's snowing outside? Then the roads must be jammed.
examples.note: Conclusion drawn from the snow you just heard about — classic 겠네요.

examples.ko: 이 집 줄이 기네요. 진짜 맛있겠어요.
examples.romanization: i jip ju-ri gi-ne-yo. jin-jja ma-sit-kket-sseo-yo.
examples.en: The line at this place is long. It must be really good.
examples.note: The long line is the evidence; 겠 turns it into a guess about the food.

examples.en: You worked all day? You must be really tired.
examples.note: Empathetic inference — Koreans use 겠네요 a lot to show they get how you feel.

examples.en: You passed the exam? Your parents must have been so happy.
examples.note: -셨겠어요 = past inference + honorific; 겠 works on past events too.

keyPoint.label: The two faces of 겠: will vs guess
keyPoint.body: With a first-person action verb, 겠 = intention (먹겠어요 = I'll eat). With an adjective, or a third-person situation plus 네요/군요, 겠 = inference (맛있겠네요 = that must be tasty). Adjectives can't 'intend' anything, so 춥겠어요 can only mean 'it must be cold,' never 'I will be cold.'

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 겠네요 → [겐네요] (the [ㄷ] of 겠 becomes ㄴ before ㄴ, by nasalization). 겠어요 links as [게써요], and 겠군요 → [겓꾼뇨] with the ㄱ tensing.

drill.instruction: React to each situation with an inference using -겠네요.
items: 다음 주에 시험이 세 개 있어요. → ___. (바쁘겠네요/힘들겠네요)
열 명 요리를 혼자 했어요. → ___. (정말 힘들었겠네요)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 맛있을 거예요. (reacting to food right in front of you)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'it'll be delicious' and 'it must be delicious' look similar, but Korean splits them: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is a neutral prediction, while 겠 is the on-the-spot reaction to evidence in front of you. Looking at a steaming dish, say 맛있겠어요, not 맛있을 거예요.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 — talking about a future plan
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 to state a plan or prediction about the future — yours OR someone else's. Unlike volitional 겠, it doesn't sound like an on-the-spot vow; it just reports what is going to happen. It's the everyday way to say 'I'm going to…' / 'X is going to…'.

formTable.ex: 가다 → 갈 거예요 (I'm going to go)
먹다 → 먹을 거예요 (I'm going to eat)

examples.en: I'm going to Busan this weekend.
examples.note: A settled plan, not a spur-of-the-moment decision — that's the difference from 겠.

examples.ko: 민수 씨는 안 올 거예요. 바쁘대요.
examples.romanization: min-su ssi-neun an ol kkeo-ye-yo. ba-ppeu-dae-yo.
examples.en: Minsu isn't going to come. He says he's busy.
examples.note: Third-person plan — perfectly fine here, unlike volitional 겠.

examples.en: I'm going to eat dinner at home.
examples.note: Stem 먹- ends in a consonant, so it takes 을 거예요.

examples.en: The weather will be clear tomorrow.
examples.note: A neutral forecast — the typical 'prediction' use, where 겠 would sound oddly personal.

keyPoint.label: 거예요 vs 겠
keyPoint.body: Both reach into the future, but the feel differs. -(으)ㄹ 거예요 = a settled plan or neutral prediction, and works for anyone (저도, 친구도). 겠 = a will/promise made right now, almost always first-person (제가 하겠습니다). So a server taking your order says 주문하시겠어요? (your intention), while you describe your trip with 갈 거예요 (it's planned).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: Standard spelling is 거예요 (you'll also see 거에요, but 거예요 is correct). The ㄹ of the -(으)ㄹ form tenses the next sound: 갈 거예요 → [갈 꺼예요], 먹을 거예요 → [머글 꺼예요].

drill.instruction: Make a future-plan sentence with -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
items: 내년 / 한국어를 배우다 → ___. (내년에 한국어를 배울 거예요)
오후 / 친구를 만나다 → ___. (오후에 친구를 만날 거예요)
점심 / 김밥을 먹다 → ___. (점심에 김밥을 먹을 거예요)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 제가 도와줄 거예요. (offering help on the spot)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: For a fresh offer or promise ('I'll help you with that'), -(으)ㄹ 거예요 sounds like a plan you already had and can feel flat. The willing, on-the-spot commitment calls for 겠 — 도와드리겠습니다.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 — a soft, tentative guess
grammarNotes.func: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 means 'I think / it seems / probably.' It softens a statement into a guess about the future or about something uncertain, so it sounds modest and polite. It pairs with this 겠 chapter as the gentler cousin of inference: where 겠네요 is a confident 'must be,' -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 is a hedged 'I think / probably.'

formTable.ex: 오다 → 올 것 같아요 (I think it'll come/rain)
비싸다 → 비쌀 것 같아요 (It looks expensive)
가다 → 간 것 같아요 (Seems they left)

examples.en: I think it's going to rain today.
examples.note: A hedged forecast — softer and more natural in conversation than 비가 오겠어요.

examples.ko: 이 옷은 저한테 좀 클 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i o-seun jeo-han-te jom keul geot ga-ta-yo.
examples.en: I think this shirt will be a bit big on me.
examples.note: Adjective 크다 + ㄹ 것 같아요; 좀 makes the guess even gentler.

examples.ko: 약속에 조금 늦을 것 같아요. 미안해요.
examples.romanization: yak-so-ge jo-geum neu-jeul geot ga-ta-yo. mi-an-hae-yo.
examples.en: I think I'll be a little late. Sorry.
examples.note: Used to soften bad news about yourself — much politer than a flat 늦어요.

examples.ko: 저 사람 한국 사람인 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: jeo sa-ram han-guk sa-ra-min geot ga-ta-yo.
examples.en: That person seems to be Korean.
examples.note: A guess about a present fact — gentler and less pushy than asserting it directly.

keyPoint.label: 겠네요 vs (으)ㄹ 것 같아요
keyPoint.body: Both are guesses, but the confidence differs. 겠네요 = a confident 'it must be…,' usually a quick reaction to evidence right there (춥겠네요). -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 = a softer 'I think / probably' that leaves room for doubt (추울 것 같아요). When you want to sound modest or unsure, reach for -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 것 같아요 → [걷 까타요]: the ㄱ of 같- tenses to [까] after the [ㄷ] of 것, and 같아요 links as [가타요]. The ㄹ form tenses too: 올 것 → [올 껃].

drill.instruction: Soften each guess with -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요.
drill.model: 비가 와요. → 비가 올 것 같아요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 맛있을 것 같아요. (reacting to a dish steaming in front of you)
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: When the evidence is right there and you're confident, -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 sounds oddly hesitant — like you're unsure about food you can clearly see is good. Use the confident 겠어요/겠네요 for that on-the-spot reaction, and save -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 for genuinely uncertain guesses.
