Two traps to remember: use 계세요 (not 있으세요) for a person who's present, and use 드리다 only when you're the one giving upward — when a senior gives to you, it's 주시다.

endingItems.title: Probably ... so (-ㄹ 텐데)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Expresses a strong guess or expectation, usually setting up a related comment, worry, or suggestion.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when you assume something is likely true and then add a thought based on it — concern, advice, or a contrast. Example: 길이 막힐 텐데 지하철로 갈까요? (It'll probably be jammed, so shall we take the subway?)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Built from -(으)ㄹ 터인데 (터 = expectation), almost always contracted to -(으)ㄹ 텐데. Vowel/ㄹ stem → -ㄹ 텐데 (바쁘다→바쁠 텐데, 오다→올 텐데, 멀다→멀 텐데), consonant stem → -을 텐데 (좋다→좋을 텐데, 먹다→먹을 텐데). PAST guess: -았/었을 텐데 (도착했을 텐데 = they've probably arrived). NOUN: -일 텐데 (학생일 텐데). It can end a sentence as a soft 'I'd expect... (but)': 맛있을 텐데. With 1st-person intention it can also mean '(I) intend to ..., so' (나는 집에 갈 텐데).
endingItems.contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ 텐데 vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요: 거예요 just states a plain prediction (비가 올 거예요 = it'll rain), while 텐데 wraps that prediction in a 'so / but / I'm worried' frame that leads into another clause (비가 올 텐데 우산 챙겨요 = it'll probably rain, so take an umbrella). Also vs -(으)니까 (definite reason): 텐데 is a GUESS-based lead-in, softer and less certain.
sentenceFrames: ___(으)ㄹ 텐데 괜찮을까요? (It'll probably ___, will it be okay?)

examples.ko: 지금쯤 도착했을 텐데 왜 연락이 없지?
examples.romanization: jigeumjjeum dochakaesseul tende wae yeollagi eopsji?
examples.en: They should've arrived by now — why haven't they texted?

examples.ko: 주말이라 사람 많을 텐데 좀 일찍 나갈까요?
examples.romanization: jumarira saram maneul tende jom iljjing nagalkkayo?
examples.en: It's the weekend so it'll probably be crowded — shall we head out a bit early?
You must be hungry, so please at least have some of this.

examples.ko: 비 올 텐데 우산 안 가져가요?
examples.romanization: bi ol tende usan an gajyeogayo?
examples.en: It's probably going to rain — you're not taking an umbrella?

commonMistakes: Spelling it 텐대 — it's 텐데 (from 터인데).
Confusing the consonant/vowel split: 먹다→먹을 텐데 (not 먹ㄹ 텐데), 오다→올 텐데 (not 오을 텐데).

practiceItems.prompt: Use 막히다: 'The road will probably be jammed, so let's leave early'
Use 배고프다 + honorific: 'You must be hungry, so eat this'
Past guess with 도착하다: 'They've probably arrived already'

studyOrder: Start with present guesses (바쁠 텐데, 좋을 텐데) and add a worry or suggestion after them.
Add the past form -았/었을 텐데 for 'they've probably already ...'.
Compare with -(으)ㄹ 거예요 so you reserve 텐데 for guesses that lead into another remark.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄹ 텐데 is how you make a confident guess and then lean into a follow-up thought — worry, advice, or a gentle 'but'. 길이 막힐 텐데 means it'll probably be jammed, and you'd add something like 일찍 나가요 (so let's leave early). It comes from 터(expectation) + 인데, and you'll almost always hear the squished form 텐데. Use -을 텐데 after a consonant (먹을 텐데) and -ㄹ 텐데 after a vowel (올 텐데); for a past guess, add 았/었을 (도착했을 텐데 = they've probably arrived). It's warmer and more thoughtful than a flat 거예요, because it shows you're guessing and caring at the same time.

endingItems.title: Get done / become (-아/어지다)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Makes a verb passive or shows a gradual change — something gets done, or a state comes about.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use for things that happen on their own or get done without a clear doer, and for adjectives that gradually change. Example: 글씨가 잘 안 써져요. (The writing just won't come out / the pen won't write.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Take the -아/어 connective and add 지다: ㅏ/ㅗ stems → -아지다 (작다→작아지다, 좋다→좋아지다), other vowels → -어지다 (만들다→만들어지다, 켜다→켜지다), 하다 → 해지다 (편하다→편해지다). With ADJECTIVES it means 'become/get more ~': 추워지다 (get colder), 많아지다 (increase). With some TRANSITIVE verbs it makes a passive of result: 켜다→켜지다 (get switched on), 깨다→깨지다 (get broken), 만들다→만들어지다 (get made), 쓰다→써지다 (get written). Conjugate 지다 normally (좋아졌어요, 깨졌어요).
endingItems.contrastWith: -아/어지다 vs 이/히/리/기 passive: -아/어지다 attaches very freely and often signals a CHANGE or a 'it just happens' feel (문이 잘 안 닫아져요... actually 닫히다 is preferred here), while the embedded-marker passive (닫히다, 열리다) is the lexical passive for a fixed verb set. For adjectives, only -아/어지다 works (날씨가 좋아졌어요 = the weather got better) — there's no 이/히/리/기 version.

examples.ko: 한국에 오래 살다 보니 한국말이 많이 편해졌어요.
examples.romanization: hanguge orae salda boni hangungmari mani pyeonhaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After living in Korea a while, Korean has gotten a lot more comfortable for me.
I dropped my phone and the screen got cracked.
The weather suddenly got cold.
The light keeps turning off, it's a bit weird.

commonMistakes: Using -아/어지다 where a fixed lexical passive is standard (the door 'gets closed' is 닫혀요, not 닫아져요).
Wrong connective vowel: 좋다→좋아지다 (not 좋어지다), 켜다→켜지다 (not 켜아지다).

practiceItems.prompt: Adjective change with 춥다: 'It got colder' (past)

studyOrder: Start with adjectives + 지다 to mean 'become more ~' (좋아지다, 추워지다, 많아지다).
Add the passive-of-result use on a few verbs (켜지다, 꺼지다, 깨지다, 써지다).
Compare with 이/히/리/기 so you know when the fixed lexical passive is the natural choice instead.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-아/어지다 has two everyday jobs. With adjectives it means 'get/become more ~': 추워지다 is to get colder, 좋아지다 is to get better — 날씨가 추워졌어요 means the weather turned cold. With certain verbs it makes a passive that focuses on the result: 깨지다 (get broken), 꺼지다 (turn off), 켜지다 (turn on) — 컵이 깨졌어요 means the cup got broken. You just take the -아/어 form and add 지다. One thing to watch: some verbs already have a fixed passive (the door 'gets closed' is 닫혀요, not 닫아져요), so 아/어지다 isn't a free pass for every verb — but for adjectives turning into changes, it's exactly right.

endingItems.title: Come to / end up (-게 되다)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Shows that something came about by circumstances rather than purely by your own choice.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when a situation leads to an outcome — you ended up doing something, came to feel a way, or things turned out so. Softens decisions so they don't sound boastful or blunt. Example: 회사 때문에 부산에서 살게 됐어요. (Because of work, I ended up living in Busan.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -게 되다 directly to the plain verb stem with no vowel harmony (가다→가게 되다, 먹다→먹게 되다, 알다→알게 되다, 하다→하게 되다). Then conjugate 되다: most often past 게 됐어요 (= came to / ended up), also future 게 될 거예요 and present 게 돼요. ㄹ-stems keep the ㄹ (살다→살게 되다). It pairs naturally with reasons like 덕분에, 때문에, 하다 보니까.
endingItems.contrastWith: V-게 되다 vs plain verb / -기로 하다: a plain 갔어요 just states you went; 가게 됐어요 frames it as 'it worked out that I went' (circumstances led there). And -기로 하다 is a deliberate decision YOU made (가기로 했어요 = I decided to go), whereas 가게 됐어요 downplays your agency. Korean often prefers 게 되다 to sound modest about good news (붙게 됐어요 = I ended up passing).
sentenceFrames: 덕분에 ___게 됐어요 (Thanks to that, I came to ___)
곧 ___게 될 거예요 (I'll come to ___ soon)

examples.ko: 원래 1년만 있으려고 했는데 한국에 계속 살게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: wollae 1nyeonman isseuryeogo haenneunde hanguge gyesok salge dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: I'd only planned to stay a year, but I ended up living in Korea for good.

examples.ko: 친구 소개로 그 회사에 들어가게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: chingu sogaero geu hoesae deureogage dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Through a friend's introduction, I ended up joining that company.

examples.ko: 한국 드라마를 보다 보니까 한국어에 관심을 가지게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: hanguk deuramareul boda bonikka hangugeoe gwansimeul gajige dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Watching Korean dramas, I came to take an interest in Korean.

examples.ko: 사정이 생겨서 모임에 못 가게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: sajeongi saenggyeoseo moime mot gage dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Something came up, so it turned out I can't make the gathering.

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before 게 — it's just 먹게 되다, 가게 되다, never 먹어게 / 가아게.
Using it for a firmly chosen plan when you mean a decision; for 'I decided to', use -기로 했어요 instead.

practiceItems.prompt: Use 살다: 'I ended up living in Korea' (past)
Use 알다: 'I came to know him' (past)
Use 못 가다: 'It turns out I can't go'

studyOrder: Learn the past 게 됐어요 first — it's the workhorse 'ended up / came to' form.
Pair it with reason phrases (때문에, 덕분에, -다 보니까) that explain how it came about.
Contrast with -기로 하다 so you separate 'it worked out' from 'I decided'.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-게 되다 says something came about because of circumstances, not just because you chose it. 한국에서 살게 됐어요 means I ended up living in Korea — maybe work or life pushed it that way. You attach -게 되다 straight to the stem (no vowel changes) and then usually use the past 게 됐어요. Koreans love this form for two reasons: it explains how a situation unfolded (덕분에 합격하게 됐어요 = thanks to you I ended up passing), and it sounds humble, since you're not bragging about your own decision. If you truly chose something on purpose, use 기로 했어요 instead; 게 됐어요 is for 'it turned out that...'.

endingItems.title: Resultant state (-아/어 있다)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Describes the ongoing state that remains after an action is completed.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use to say something stays in a finished condition — a door that's open, a person who's seated, a sign that's posted. The action already happened; you're describing the lingering result. Example: 의자에 앉아 있어요. (I'm (in a) seated (state).)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Take the -아/어 connective and add 있다: ㅏ/ㅗ stems → -아 있다 (앉다→앉아 있다, 남다→남아 있다), other vowels → -어 있다 (서다→서 있다, 열리다→열려 있다), 하다 verbs rarely use this. Works with INTRANSITIVE/result verbs and passives (가다→가 있다 = have gone and be there, 오다→와 있다, 죽다→죽어 있다, 켜지다→켜져 있다). For honor use 계시다 (앉아 계세요). NOTE: transitive 'be ~ing' is V-고 있다, not V-아/어 있다.
endingItems.contrastWith: V-아/어 있다 vs V-고 있다: 고 있다 = action in progress (문을 닫고 있어요 = I'm closing the door right now), while 아/어 있다 = the result-state after it's done (문이 닫혀 있어요 = the door is (already) closed). Also vs V-아/어 놓다: 놓다 stresses someone DID it and left it on purpose (문을 열어 놨어요), while 아/어 있다 just describes the existing state neutrally (문이 열려 있어요).

examples.en: A delivery has arrived (and is sitting) at the door.
It says 'under construction' on the wall.
Grandmother is (seated) on the sofa.

examples.ko: 불이 아직 켜져 있어요, 누가 있나 봐요.
examples.romanization: buri ajik kyeojyeo isseoyo, nuga inna bwayo.
examples.en: The light is still on — looks like someone's there.

commonMistakes: Using V-아/어 있다 with a plain transitive verb for 'be ~ing'. 'I'm reading' is 읽고 있어요, never 읽어 있어요.
Wrong connective vowel: 앉다→앉아 있다 (not 앉어 있다); 서다→서 있다 (the 어 + 어 contracts).

practiceItems.prompt: Use 앉다: 'I'm seated on the chair'
Use 오다: 'A package has arrived (and is here)'

studyOrder: Lock in the contrast with V-고 있다 first: progress vs. resulting state.
Practice with verbs that leave a state: 앉다, 서다, 눕다, 오다, 열리다, 켜지다.
Swap 있다 for 계시다 when the person in that state deserves respect (앉아 계세요).
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-아/어 있다 describes the state that's left over after an action finishes. 앉아 있어요 doesn't mean you're in the act of sitting down — it means you're already (in the state of) seated. 문이 열려 있어요 means the door is open (someone opened it earlier and it stayed that way). The big thing to remember: this is NOT how you say 'be doing' — that's V-고 있다. So 'I'm reading' is 읽고 있어요, but 'the package has arrived and is here' is 와 있어요. Use 아/어 있다 with verbs that naturally leave a result hanging around: arrived, seated, standing, open, turned on. It's everywhere in descriptions of how things currently are.

endingItems.hangul: 안 V / V-지 않다 / 못 V / V-지 못하다
endingItems.romanization: an V / -ji anta / mot V / -ji mothada
endingItems.title: Negation: don't vs can't
endingItems.plainEnglish: Two ways to say no — 안/-지 않다 for simple negation, and 못/-지 못하다 for inability.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use 안/-지 않다 when you simply don't or won't do something, and 못/-지 못하다 when you can't because of ability or circumstances. Example: 오늘은 술 안 마셔요. (I'm not drinking today.) vs 운전 못 해요. (I can't drive.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: SHORT form: put 안 or 못 right before the verb/adjective (안 가요, 못 가요, 안 비싸요). For 하다 ACTION verbs the negator splits the noun and 하다: 공부 안 해요 / 공부 못 해요 (not 안 공부해요). LONG form: attach -지 않다 / -지 못하다 to the plain stem (가지 않아요, 가지 못해요, 좋지 않아요). 못 is for verbs only (ability), not for adjectives — for adjectives use 안/-지 않다 (안 예뻐요). NOTE the pronunciation: 못 해요 sounds like [모태요], 못 가요 like [몯까요].
endingItems.contrastWith: 안 (안 가요) vs 못 (못 가요): 안 = choose not to / simply don't (안 먹어요 = I don't eat it / I'm not eating); 못 = unable to (못 먹어요 = I can't eat it — allergy, too full, etc.). Short vs long form is mostly the same meaning; -지 않다/못하다 is a touch more formal or emphatic and is required in longer written sentences.
sentenceFrames: 오늘은 ___ 못 가요 (I can't go ___ today)

examples.en: I don't eat meat — I'm vegetarian.
I worked late yesterday, so I couldn't work out.
This restaurant isn't that expensive.
It's so spicy I really can't eat it.

commonMistakes: Putting 안/못 before the whole 하다 verb: it's 공부 안 해요 / 청소 못 해요, not 안 공부해요 / 못 청소해요.
Using 못 with an adjective. For 'not pretty' say 안 예뻐요 / 예쁘지 않아요 — 못 only negates ability of verbs.

practiceItems.prompt: Say 'I don't drink (alcohol)' with short 안
Say 'I can't drive' with short 못 (운전하다)
Say 'It's not expensive' with long form (비싸다)

studyOrder: Master the short forms 안 V and 못 V first — they're what you'll say out loud most.
Practice the 하다 split (운동 안 해요, 운동 못 해요), the most common mistake spot.
Add the long forms -지 않다 / -지 못하다 for writing and emphasis, and remember 못 is verbs-only.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean has two flavors of 'no'. 안 (or the longer -지 않다) is plain negation: 안 가요 = I'm not going, 안 비싸요 = it's not expensive. 못 (or -지 못하다) means you CAN'T — you lack the ability or something blocks you: 못 가요 = I can't go, 운전 못 해요 = I can't drive. The classic trap is 하다 verbs: the 안/못 squeezes in between, so it's 공부 안 해요 and 운동 못 했어요, never 안 공부해요. One more rule: 못 is only for verbs (actions/ability), so 'not pretty' has to be 안 예뻐요, not 못 예뻐요. Get 안 vs 못 straight and your 'no' will sound natural right away.

endingItems.title: Almost happened (-ㄹ 뻔하다)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Says something nearly happened but didn't — a close call.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use for a near-miss, usually something bad you barely avoided: almost fell, almost forgot, almost late. Almost always in the past. Example: 길이 미끄러워서 넘어질 뻔했어요. (The road was slippery and I almost fell.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach to the verb stem: vowel/ㄹ stem → -ㄹ 뻔하다 (넘어지다→넘어질 뻔하다, 울다→울 뻔하다), consonant stem → -을 뻔하다 (죽다→죽을 뻔하다, 늦다→늦을 뻔하다). It almost always appears as past 뻔했어요 (= almost did, but didn't). Used with action verbs about events, not with adjectives. Often paired with 하마터면 ... -(으)ㄹ 뻔했다 (= 'I almost ...!'). 하다 verbs: 지각하다→지각할 뻔했어요.
endingItems.contrastWith: V-(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 vs V-(으)ㄹ 것 같았다: 뻔하다 means it genuinely ALMOST happened (and clearly did NOT) — a real close call, while -(으)ㄹ 것 같았다 is just 'it seemed like it would' (a guess/impression). 넘어질 뻔했어요 = I nearly fell; 넘어질 것 같았어요 = it felt like I was going to fall.
sentenceFrames: 큰일 ___(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 (That almost turned into a disaster)

examples.ko: 하마터면 지하철에 가방을 두고 내릴 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: hamateomyeon jihacheore gabangeul dugo naeril ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I almost left my bag on the subway and got off without it.

examples.ko: 차가 갑자기 튀어나와서 사고 날 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: chaga gapjagi twieonawaseo sago nal ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: A car suddenly darted out and there was almost an accident.

examples.ko: 알람을 못 들어서 회사에 지각할 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: allameul mot deureoseo hoesae jigakal ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't hear my alarm and almost got to work late.
It was so moving I almost cried.

commonMistakes: Using the present 뻔해요 — a near-miss is finished, so it's almost always past 뻔했어요.
Wrong consonant/vowel split: 죽다→죽을 뻔했어요 (not 죽ㄹ), 넘어지다→넘어질 뻔했어요 (not 넘어지을).

practiceItems.prompt: Use 지각하다: 'I almost was late (for work/school)'
Use 잊다 with 하마터면: 'I almost forgot!'

studyOrder: Learn it straight in the past as 'almost ...ed but didn't' — 넘어질 뻔했어요.
Add 하마터면 in front for the natural 'I almost ...!' exclamation.
Contrast with -(으)ㄹ 것 같았다 so 'it really almost happened' stays separate from 'it seemed it would'.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 is the 'I almost ___!' of Korean — a close call that, thankfully, didn't happen. 넘어질 뻔했어요 means I almost fell; 지각할 뻔했어요 means I almost got there late. Because a near-miss is already over, you'll basically always say it in the past as 뻔했어요. Pop 하마터면 in front to add drama: 하마터면 가방을 두고 내릴 뻔했어요 (I almost left my bag and got off!). Use -을 뻔했어요 after a consonant and -ㄹ 뻔했어요 after a vowel. It's super common in everyday storytelling about little disasters you dodged.

endingItems.title: Present Tense (Polite)
endingItems.plainEnglish: The everyday polite present tense — what is happening now or is generally true.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use V-아/어요 for almost everything in daily speech: current actions, habits, and general facts, e.g. 저는 커피를 마셔요 (I drink coffee). It is the safe default ending with most people.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Drop 다 from the stem. If the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 아요 (좋다→좋아요). Otherwise add 어요 (먹다→먹어요, 읽다→읽어요). 하다 verbs become 해요 (공부하다→공부해요). Watch contractions: 가다→가요, 오다→와요, 마시다→마셔요, 주다→줘요, 보내다→보내요.
endingItems.contrastWith: The same stem rule builds the past tense — present 먹어요 (I eat) vs past 먹었어요 (I ate). Also don't confuse polite 아/어요 with casual 반말, which simply drops 요 (먹어, 가).

examples.en: I go to school every day.
My sibling is eating now.
On weekends I usually meet friends.
I study Korean.

commonMistakes: Adding 아요 after a non-ㅏ/ㅗ vowel, e.g. saying 먹아요 instead of the correct 먹어요.
Forgetting the contraction: saying 가아요 instead of 가요, or 마시어요 instead of 마셔요.
studyOrder: Drop 다 to find the stem
Check the last stem vowel: ㅏ/ㅗ takes 아요, everything else takes 어요
Apply 하다 → 해요 and watch for contractions (가요, 와요, 마셔요)
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: The 아/어요 ending is the workhorse of Korean — the polite, everyday present tense you will use more than any other form. To build it, take the dictionary verb, drop 다, and look at the last vowel of what is left. If that vowel is the bright ㅏ or ㅗ you add 아요; for everything else you add 어요; and 하다 verbs turn into 해요. A few combinations squeeze together to be easier to say, so 가다 becomes 가요, not 가아요. Make 아/어요 your default and you will sound natural in almost any polite situation.

endingItems.title: Sino-Korean Numbers
endingItems.plainEnglish: The number set borrowed from Chinese — used for dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, and most measured amounts.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use Sino-Korean numbers for dates (삼월 오일), money (오천 원), minutes (십 분), phone numbers, floors, bus numbers, and counting above 100. Example: 1,234 = 천이백삼십사.
endingItems.attachmentRule: 0 영/공, 1 일, 2 이, 3 삼, 4 사, 5 오, 6 육, 7 칠, 8 팔, 9 구, 10 십, 100 백, 1,000 천, 10,000 만, 억 (100 million). Build by place value: 23 = 이십삼 (2·10 + 3), 405 = 사백오, 30,000 = 삼만. Korean groups large numbers by 10,000 (만), not 1,000.
endingItems.contrastWith: Do NOT mix with native numbers (하나, 둘…). Money, dates, and minutes are always Sino; hours and counting objects are native. So 7:07 is 일곱(native) 시 칠(Sino) 분.

examples.en: Today is March 15th.
How much is this? It's 4,000 won.
My phone number is 010-2345...
The exam is in November.

commonMistakes: Saying 십천 for 10,000 — it is 만 (or 일만).
Reading minutes with native numbers — minutes are Sino: 삼십 분, not 서른 분.
Forgetting that 6 (육) nasalizes after ㄴ/ㅁ and in 육월 → it becomes 유월 for June.
studyOrder: Memorize 일~십 plus 백·천·만
Build tens and hundreds by place value
Practice dates, money, and minutes
Watch 만-grouping for big numbers
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean has TWO number systems, and this is the 'Chinese-origin' one. You will use it constantly: every price, date, minute, and phone number is read with these. Learn 일 to 십 first, then 백 (100), 천 (1,000), 만 (10,000). To say bigger numbers you just stack place values: 이십삼 is literally 'two-ten-three' = 23. One surprise for English speakers: Korean counts big numbers in groups of 10,000 (만), so 30,000 is 삼만, not 'thirty-thousand'.

endingItems.title: Native Korean Numbers
endingItems.plainEnglish: The original Korean number set — used for counting things and people, ages, and the hour of the clock.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use native numbers to count objects (사과 세 개), people (두 명), animals (한 마리), age (스무 살), and hours (네 시). They are common from 1 to 99.
endingItems.attachmentRule: 하나 1, 둘 2, 셋 3, 넷 4, 다섯 5, 여섯 6, 일곱 7, 여덟 8, 아홉 9, 열 10; 스물 20, 서른 30, 마흔 40, 쉰 50, 예순 60, 일흔 70, 여든 80, 아흔 90. IMPORTANT: before a counter, 1–4 and 20 shorten: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무. So 한 개, 두 명, 세 시, 네 살, 스무 살.
endingItems.contrastWith: vs Sino numbers (일, 이…). Hours use native (다섯 시) but minutes use Sino (오 분). Age uses native (스무 살); a year/date uses Sino. Above ~100, Korean switches to Sino.

examples.en: Three apples, please.
I am twenty years old.
It's four o'clock now.
I have two cats.

commonMistakes: Not shortening before a counter: it's 한 개 (not 하나 개) and 세 시 (not 셋 시).
Using native numbers for minutes or money — those are Sino.
Using Sino numbers for age or the hour — those are native.
studyOrder: Memorize 하나~열 then the tens 스물~아흔
Learn the four shorteners 한·두·세·네 (+스무)
Use for things, people, age, and hours
Switch to Sino above ~100
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This is the 'home-grown' Korean number set, and the trickiest thing about it is that 1, 2, 3, 4 (and 20) change shape right before a counting word. You never say 하나 개 — you say 한 개. Memorize the four little shape-changers: 한, 두, 세, 네 (and 스무 for 20). You will use these for counting almost anything, for your age (스무 살), and for the hour on a clock (세 시 = three o'clock).

endingItems.title: Telling Time & Dates
endingItems.plainEnglish: How to read the clock and the calendar — which mixes BOTH number systems in one phrase.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use whenever you say a time or a date. The hour is a native number + 시; the minute is a Sino number + 분. Dates are Sino numbers + 년/월/일.
endingItems.attachmentRule: TIME: hour = NATIVE + 시, minute = SINO + 분. 7:07 = 일곱 시 칠 분. 3:30 = 세 시 삼십 분 (or 세 시 반, 'half'). DATE: year/month/day = SINO + 년/월/일. March 5 = 삼월 오일. Two month irregulars: June = 유월 (not 육월), October = 시월 (not 십월). Weekdays: 월·화·수·목·금·토·일 + 요일.
endingItems.contrastWith: The classic trap: in 일곱 시 칠 분, 시 takes a NATIVE number but 분 takes a SINO number — in the same breath. And 6월 = 유월, 10월 = 시월 each drop a sound.

examples.en: It's 7:07 now.
The meeting is at 2:30.
My birthday is June 10th.
Today is Friday.

commonMistakes: Saying 칠 시 — the hour must be native: 일곱 시.
Saying 육월 or 십월 — June is 유월, October is 시월.
Using native numbers for the minute (it's 칠 분, not 일곱 분).
studyOrder: Hour = native + 시
Minute = Sino + 분
Dates = Sino + 월/일
Memorize 유월 & 시월
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Reading a clock in Korean is famously confusing because ONE phrase uses both number systems. The hour is a native number (일곱 시 = seven o'clock) and the minute right after it is a Sino number (칠 분 = seven minutes). So 7:07 is 일곱 시 칠 분 — same digit, two different words! Dates are all Sino (삼월 오일 = March 5). Just memorize two odd months: June is 유월 and October is 시월.

endingItems.title: Counters (Measure Words)
endingItems.plainEnglish: To count a noun you add a 'counter' word, like 'two CUPS of coffee' — and each counter picks native or Sino numbers.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use whenever you count a noun: NOUN + NUMBER + COUNTER. 커피 두 잔 = two cups of coffee.
endingItems.attachmentRule: NATIVE-number counters: 개 (things), 명/분 (people; 분 is honorific), 마리 (animals), 살 (age), 시 (o'clock), 장 (sheets), 권 (books), 잔 (cups), 병 (bottles), 대 (cars/machines), 켤레 (pairs), 번 (times). SINO-number counters: 분 (minutes), 원 (money), 월/일/년 (date), 층 (floor), 호 (room), 인분 (food portions), 번 (number/order). Remember 1–4 shorten before native counters (한 개, 두 명, 세 잔).
endingItems.contrastWith: Watch the look-alikes: 분 = native 'people' (두 분) BUT Sino 'minutes' (이 분). 번 = native 'times' (세 번) BUT Sino 'order/number' (삼 번 버스).

examples.en: Two coffees, please.
I bought three tickets.
I have one puppy.
Three portions, please.

commonMistakes: Dropping the counter — Korean needs one: 사과 셋 → 사과 세 개.
Using the wrong number system for the counter (e.g., minutes are Sino).
Forgetting to shorten 하나/둘/셋/넷 before native counters.
studyOrder: Learn the pattern NOUN + NUMBER + COUNTER
Learn which counters take native vs Sino
Memorize the most common: 개·명·마리·잔·장·번
Always shorten 한·두·세·네 before native counters
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: In English you can just say 'two coffees,' but Korean almost always slips a 'counter' word in: 커피 두 잔 (coffee two cups). Different nouns use different counters — 개 for general things, 명 for people, 마리 for animals, 잔 for cups. The counter also decides whether the number is native or Sino. Start with the everyday ones (개, 명, 마리, 잔, 장) and remember the native numbers shrink in front: 한 개, 두 명, 세 잔.

endingItems.title: The (으) Rule: Consonant vs Vowel Stems
endingItems.plainEnglish: Dozens of endings add an extra 으 (or use 을/ㄹ) only when the stem ends in a consonant (받침).
endingItems.whenToUse: Apply it every time you attach an ending written with (으): -(으)면, -(으)세요, -(으)ㄹ 수 있다, -(으)ㄴ/ㄹ, -(으)니까, -(으)러, -(으)려고, -(으)ㄹ게요.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Look at the stem's last syllable. HAS a 받침 (consonant ending) → use the 으 form: 먹다 → 먹을 수 있다, 먹으면, 먹으세요, 먹은. NO 받침 (vowel ending) → drop the 으: 가다 → 갈 수 있다, 가면, 가세요, 간. The 으 is just a helper so two consonants don't crash together. Exception: ㄹ-stems (살다) drop their ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ endings (사세요, 사니까, 삽니다).
endingItems.contrastWith: This is exactly the 갈 수 있다 (vowel stem 가-) vs 먹을 수 있다 (consonant stem 먹-) difference. Same ending, but 먹- needs the 으/을 helper and 가- does not.

examples.en: come → can come (vowel stem, no 으)
receive → can receive (consonant stem, +을)
see → if (you) see (vowel stem)
sit → if (you) sit (consonant stem, +으)

commonMistakes: Adding 으 to a vowel stem: 가으면 is wrong → 가면.
Dropping 으 from a consonant stem: 먹면 is wrong → 먹으면.
Forgetting ㄹ-stems are special: 살다 → 사세요 (the ㄹ disappears).
studyOrder: Find the stem (drop 다)
Check: does it end in a 받침?
Yes → add 으/을; No → skip the 으
Remember ㄹ-stem exceptions
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This one rule answers your 갈 수 vs 먹을 수 question — and it controls dozens of endings. When an ending is written with (으) in parentheses, you only use that 으 if the verb stem ends in a consonant (a 받침). 먹- ends in ㄱ, so you say 먹을 수 있어요 and 먹으면. 가- ends in a vowel, so you just say 갈 수 있어요 and 가면. Think of 으 as a tiny cushion that keeps two consonants from colliding. Master this and half of Korean conjugation suddenly makes sense.

endingItems.title: Liaison: Linking 받침 to the Next Vowel
endingItems.plainEnglish: A final consonant (받침) slides over to start the next syllable when that syllable begins with a vowel.
endingItems.whenToUse: It happens automatically in pronunciation whenever a 받침 is followed by a syllable that starts with ㅇ (a vowel sound).
endingItems.attachmentRule: 받침 + ㅇ-vowel → the 받침 becomes the next syllable's first sound. 꽃이 sounds like 꼬치, 한국어 like 한구거, 음악 like 으막, 옷을 like 오슬. With a double 받침, only the SECOND consonant moves over: 읽어 sounds like 일거.
endingItems.contrastWith: The spelling never changes — only the sound links. This is why 읽어요 (written) is pronounced 일거요. Learners who read block-by-block sound robotic; linking makes you sound natural.

examples.en: Korean language — sounds like 한구거
The flower is pretty — 꽃이 sounds like 꼬치
I read a book — sounds like 채글 일거요
I go home — 집에 sounds like 지베

commonMistakes: Pronouncing each block separately (꽃#이) instead of linking to 꼬치.
Moving the wrong consonant in a double 받침 — only the second one links.
studyOrder: Spot a 받침 followed by a ㅇ-vowel syllable
Slide the 받침 into that syllable
For double 받침, move only the second one
Read whole words, not block-by-block
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean words flow together. When a syllable ends in a consonant and the next one starts with a vowel (the silent ㅇ), that consonant hops over and is pronounced at the start of the next syllable. So 한국어 is written in three blocks but sounds like 한구거, and 꽃이 sounds like 꼬치. The spelling stays put; only your mouth links them. This single habit is the biggest step from sounding like a textbook to sounding like a person.

endingItems.title: Nasalization
endingItems.plainEnglish: The stop sounds ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ turn into the nasal sounds ㅇ/ㄴ/ㅁ when followed by ㄴ or ㅁ.
endingItems.whenToUse: It happens automatically when a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ-type 받침 meets a following ㄴ or ㅁ — extremely common in -습니다/-ㅂ니다 verbs.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Before ㄴ or ㅁ: ㄱ(ㅋ,ㄲ) → ㅇ(ng); ㄷ(ㅅ,ㅆ,ㅈ,ㅊ,ㅌ) → ㄴ; ㅂ(ㅍ) → ㅁ. So 학년 → 항년, 입니다 → 임니다, 닫는 → 단는, 먹는 → 멍는, 끝나다 → 끈나다.
endingItems.contrastWith: Like liaison, it is a SOUND change only; spelling is unchanged. It's why polite 합니다 sounds like 함니다.

examples.en: Thank you — sounds like 감사함니다
Korean (language) — sounds like 한궁말
It ends — sounds like 끈나요
a person who eats — 먹는 sounds like 멍는

commonMistakes: Saying 학년 literally instead of 항년.
Missing it in -ㅂ니다/-습니다 endings (입니다 → 임니다).
studyOrder: Spot a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ 받침 before ㄴ or ㅁ
ㄱ→ㅇ, ㄷ→ㄴ, ㅂ→ㅁ
Apply it to every -습니다/-ㅂ니다
Trust your ears over the spelling
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: When a 'hard stop' consonant (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ) bumps into a nasal sound (ㄴ or ㅁ), it 'goes nasal' to match: ㄱ→ㅇ, ㄷ→ㄴ, ㅂ→ㅁ. The most useful place to notice this is the polite ending: 합니다 is pronounced 함니다, and 입니다 is 임니다. It's the same reason 학년 (school year) sounds like 항년. You don't change the spelling — your mouth just smooths the two sounds together.

endingItems.title: Palatalization
endingItems.plainEnglish: A 받침 ㄷ or ㅌ becomes a ㅈ/ㅊ sound when the next syllable is 이 (or 히).
endingItems.whenToUse: It happens when ㄷ/ㅌ at the end of a stem meets 이 or 히 — common in 같이, 굳이, 붙이다, and 닫히다.
endingItems.attachmentRule: ㄷ + 이 → 지 (ji): 굳이 → 구지, 해돋이 → 해도지. ㅌ + 이 → 치 (chi): 같이 → 가치, 붙이다 → 부치다. ㄷ + 히 → 치: 닫히다 → 다치다. It only triggers before 이/히 — not before other vowels.
endingItems.contrastWith: Only before 이/히. 같이 is 가치, but 같아 is just 가타 (no change). This is why romanizing 같이 as 'gati' is wrong — it's gachi.

examples.en: Let's go together — 같이 sounds like 가치
You don't have to bother — 굳이 sounds like 구지
to stick a sticker — 붙이다 sounds like 부치다
the door closes — 닫히다 sounds like 다치다

commonMistakes: Saying 가티 for 같이 — it's 가치.
Applying it before other vowels: 같아 stays 가타, not 가차.
studyOrder: Spot a ㄷ/ㅌ 받침 right before 이 or 히
ㄷ→ㅈ(지), ㅌ→ㅊ(치)
Only before 이/히, no other vowel
Apply to 같이, 굳이, 붙이다…
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: When a ㄷ or ㅌ at the end of a syllable runs into the vowel 이, your tongue is already near the roof of your mouth, so the sound shifts to ㅈ/ㅊ. That's why the very common word 같이 ('together') is pronounced 가치, not 'ga-ti.' Likewise 굳이 sounds like 구지. It only happens before 이 (or 히) — 같아 is still 가타. Once you know this, those 'why does it sound like that?' moments disappear.

endingItems.title: Aspiration
endingItems.plainEnglish: ㅎ merges with a neighboring ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ to form the breathy ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ.
endingItems.whenToUse: When a 받침 ㅎ meets ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅈ, or when a 받침 ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ meets ㅎ — common in 좋다, 축하, 못하다, 입학.
endingItems.attachmentRule: 받침 ㅎ + ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅈ → ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅊ: 좋다 → 조타, 놓고 → 노코, 많지 → 만치. 받침 ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ + ㅎ → aspirated: 축하 → 추카, 입학 → 이팍, 못하다 → 모타다, 백화점 → 배콰점.
endingItems.contrastWith: It's a merge, not a drop — the ㅎ doesn't vanish silently, it 'aspirates' the other consonant. So 좋다 is 조타 (with a strong t), not 조다.

examples.en: to be good — sounds like 조타
Congratulations — sounds like 추카해요
entrance exam — 입학 sounds like 이팍
I can't do it — 못해요 sounds like 모태요

commonMistakes: Saying 조다 for 좋다 — it's 조타.
Saying 축하 block-by-block instead of 추카.
studyOrder: Spot ㅎ next to ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ (either order)
They merge into ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ
Apply to 좋다, 축하, 못하다
Listen for the puff of air
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: The letter ㅎ is friendly — it merges with a neighbor instead of staying separate. When ㅎ touches ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ (in either order), the pair becomes one breathy consonant: ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ. So 좋다 is 조타, 축하 is 추카, and 못해요 is 모태요. The air 'puffs' out. This is why congratulations (축하) never sounds like 'chuk-ha' — it's 추카.

endingItems.title: Tensification
endingItems.plainEnglish: Plain consonants ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅅ/ㅈ become the tense ㄲ/ㄸ/ㅃ/ㅆ/ㅉ right after a stop 받침.
endingItems.whenToUse: After a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ-type 받침, a following plain consonant tightens — very common in everyday words like 학교, 식당, 숙제.
endingItems.attachmentRule: 받침 ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ (and family) + ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅅ/ㅈ → tense: 학교 → 학꾜, 먹다 → 먹따, 식당 → 식땅, 숙제 → 숙쩨, 입국 → 입꾹. It also appears after some ㄴ/ㄹ endings (갈게요 → 갈께요).
endingItems.contrastWith: Spelling shows the plain consonant, but you pronounce the tense one. 학교 is written with ㄱ but said with ㄲ (학꾜).

examples.en: I go to school — 학교 sounds like 학꾜
I eat at a restaurant — 식당 sounds like 식땅
Did you do the homework? — 숙제 sounds like 숙쩨
I'll go — 갈게요 sounds like 갈께요

commonMistakes: Saying a soft 학교 instead of the tense 학꾜.
Expecting the spelling to show ㄲ/ㄸ — it doesn't; only the sound is tense.
studyOrder: Spot a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ 받침 before a plain consonant
Tighten it: ㄱ→ㄲ, ㄷ→ㄸ, ㅂ→ㅃ, ㅅ→ㅆ, ㅈ→ㅉ
Apply to 학교, 식당, 숙제
Trust the sound, not the spelling
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: After a hard stop (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ at the end of a syllable), the next plain consonant gets 'squeezed' into a tense one. So 학교 sounds like 학꾜, 식당 like 식땅, and 숙제 like 숙쩨. The spelling still shows the soft consonant, but native speakers say the tense version automatically. You'll do it naturally once your ear gets used to it — for now, just know that 'school' is 학꾜, not a gentle 'hak-gyo.'

endingItems.title: Irregular Verb Types
endingItems.plainEnglish: Seven groups of verbs/adjectives whose stem changes before certain endings instead of staying fixed.
endingItems.whenToUse: Recognize the type from the stem's last letter, then apply its change when adding vowel endings like -아/어요 or -(으) endings.
endingItems.attachmentRule: ㅂ-irregular: 덥다 → 더워요, 돕다 → 도와요. ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 → 들어요, 걷다 → 걸어요. ㅅ-irregular: 짓다 → 지어요, 낫다 → 나아요. 르-irregular: 빠르다 → 빨라요, 모르다 → 몰라요. ㅡ-drop: 쓰다 → 써요, 바쁘다 → 바빠요. ㄹ-irregular: 살다 → 살아요 but 사세요/삽니다 (ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ). ㅎ-irregular (adjectives): 빨갛다 → 빨개요, 어떻다 → 어때요.
endingItems.contrastWith: Regular verbs keep the stem (먹다 → 먹어요). Irregulars change it (듣다 → 들어요, not 듣어요). The trigger is usually a vowel ending; before consonant endings many stay regular.

examples.en: The weather is so hot. (ㅂ: 덥다→더워요)
I listen to music. (ㄷ: 듣다→들어요)
He's fast. (르: 빠르다→빨라요)
I write a letter. (ㅡ: 쓰다→써요)

commonMistakes: Treating an irregular like a regular: 듣어요 → it's 들어요.
Over-applying: not every ㅂ/ㄷ/ㅅ verb is irregular (받다 → 받아요 is regular).
Forgetting ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ (살다 → 삽니다).
studyOrder: Identify the stem's last letter
Match it to one of the 7 irregular types
Apply the change before vowel endings
Memorize which common verbs are exceptions
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Most Korean verbs are predictable, but seven small groups bend their stem before certain endings. For example, ㄷ-verbs like 듣다 (to hear) turn the ㄷ into ㄹ before a vowel: 들어요, not 듣어요. ㅂ-verbs like 덥다 (hot) become 더워요. 르-verbs like 빠르다 (fast) become 빨라요. Don't try to memorize all at once — learn the type when you meet a common verb, and soon you'll feel the pattern. Watch out: not every verb that ends in ㅂ/ㄷ/ㅅ is irregular (받다 is regular: 받아요).

endingItems.title: Native Korean Numbers
endingItems.plainEnglish: The native number set (하나, 둘, 셋…) used to count things, people, animals, age, and the hour.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use native numbers to count objects, people, and animals, and to say age and o'clock: 사과 세 개 (three apples), 스무 살 (20 years old), 두 시 (two o'clock).
endingItems.attachmentRule: 1–4 and 20 change shape right before a counter: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무 (한 개, 두 명, 세 시, 네 마리, 스무 살). From 5 up there is no change: 다섯 개, 열 명. Tens are their own words: 열(10), 스물(20), 서른(30), 마흔(40), 쉰(50), 예순(60), 일흔(70), 여든(80), 아흔(90). Native counting normally stops at 99; from 100 you switch to Sino 백.
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with Sino numbers (일, 이, 삼…), used for minutes, money, and dates. The clock mixes them: the HOUR is native (세 시) but the MINUTE is Sino (삼십 분).

examples.en: Three apples, please.
My younger sibling is ten years old.
I keep two cats.
I ordered four cups of coffee.

commonMistakes: Using Sino numbers to count objects — 사과 삼 개 is wrong; say 사과 세 개.
Forgetting the shape change: it is 두 개 (not 둘 개) and 스무 살 (not 스물 살).
studyOrder: Memorize 하나~열 first
Learn the 1–4 + 20 shape changes (한·두·세·네·스무)
Practice with the counters 개·명·살·시
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean has two number systems, and this is the 'native' one. You use it to count things you can see and touch, plus age and the hour on a clock. The tricky part: 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷 and 스물 change to 한, 두, 세, 네, 스무 right before a counting word — so 'two cups' is 두 잔, not 둘 잔. From 다섯 (five) on, nothing changes.

endingItems.title: Sino-Korean Numbers
endingItems.plainEnglish: The Chinese-derived number set (일, 이, 삼…) used for minutes, money, dates, phone numbers, and large numbers.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use Sino numbers for minutes (삼십 분), money (천 원), dates (3월 5일), phone numbers, floors, and counting from the hundreds up.
endingItems.attachmentRule: 일(1) 이(2) 삼(3) 사(4) 오(5) 육(6) 칠(7) 팔(8) 구(9) 십(10), then 백(100), 천(1,000), 만(10,000), 억(100,000,000). Combine the digits: 23 = 이십삼, 105 = 백오, 2024 = 이천이십사. Zero is 영 or 공 (공 in phone numbers). Sino numbers never change shape before a counter.
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with native numbers (하나, 둘…). The classic trap is the clock: the HOUR is native (일곱 시) but the MINUTE is Sino (칠 분), so 7:07 = 일곱 시 칠 분.

examples.en: This is 3,000 won.
Please wait just ten minutes.
My birthday is May 10th.
Take bus number 105.

commonMistakes: Reading minutes with native numbers — 삼십 분 is right, 서른 분 is wrong.
Forgetting that 6월 and 10월 are read 유월 and 시월 (not 육월/십월).
studyOrder: Memorize 일~십
Learn 백·천·만 and how to combine digits
Apply to money, minutes, and dates
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This is the second number system, borrowed from Chinese. You use it for things you measure or label rather than count by hand: money, minutes, dates, phone numbers, and big numbers. Unlike native numbers, these never change shape. Watch the calendar: 6월 is 유월 and 10월 is 시월.

endingItems.hangul: 한 시 십 분 / 삼월 오일
endingItems.title: Telling Time & Dates
endingItems.plainEnglish: How to say clock times and calendar dates — which means mixing the two number systems.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when telling the time (두 시 삼십 분 = 2:30) or giving a date (오월 오일 = May 5th, 금요일 = Friday).
endingItems.attachmentRule: TIME — the hour is a NATIVE number + 시 (한 시, 두 시 … 열두 시); the minute is a SINO number + 분 (오 분, 삼십 분). So 7:15 = 일곱 시 십오 분, and 'half past' is 반 (두 시 반). DATE — year, month, and day all use SINO + 년/월/일: 2024년 3월 5일 = 이천이십사 년 삼 월 오 일. Days of the week use 요일 (월요일, 화요일…). Note the irregular months: 6월 = 유월, 10월 = 시월.
endingItems.contrastWith: The hour is the ONE everyday time word that uses native numbers; minutes, dates, and years all use Sino. Mixing them up (일곱 분, 칠 시) is the most common beginner mistake.

examples.en: It's 7:07 now.
Class ends at 3:30.
My birthday is October 9th.
Today is Friday.

commonMistakes: Saying 칠 시 (Sino) for 'seven o'clock' — the hour is native: 일곱 시.
Saying 일곱 분 (native) for minutes — minutes are Sino: 칠 분.
studyOrder: Hours = native number + 시
Minutes = Sino number + 분
Combine them: 일곱 시 칠 분
Dates = Sino + 월/일
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Telling time in Korean uses BOTH number systems at once, which surprises everyone. The hour is a native number + 시 (일곱 시 = seven o'clock), but the minute is a Sino number + 분 (칠 분 = seven minutes). So 7:07 is 일곱 시 칠 분. Dates are all Sino: 삼월 오일 (March 5). Just remember: hour = native, everything else = Sino.

endingItems.title: The (으) Insertion Rule
endingItems.plainEnglish: When a verb/adjective stem ends in a consonant, you add 으 before many endings; vowel-ending stems skip it.
endingItems.whenToUse: This runs through all of Korean. Whenever an ending is written with (으) — like (으)면, (으)세요, (으)ㄹ 수 있다, (으)러, (으)니까 — you choose the form by the stem's last sound: 먹으면 vs 가면, 먹을 수 있다 vs 갈 수 있다.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Drop 다 to get the stem. If the stem ends in a VOWEL (no 받침), use the short form: -면, -세요, -ㄹ, -러, -니까, -ㄴ (가면, 가세요, 갈, 가러, 가니까). If the stem ends in a CONSONANT (받침 있음), insert 으: -으면, -으세요, -을, -으러, -으니까, -은 (먹으면, 먹으세요, 먹을, 먹으러, 먹으니까). ㄹ-final stems are special: the ㄹ stays for most endings (살면, 살아요) but DROPS before ㄴ/ㅂ/(으)-endings (살다 → 사세요, 사니까, 산).
endingItems.contrastWith: It is the SAME choice across many endings, so learn it once instead of memorizing each ending: 갈 거예요 / 먹을 거예요, 가면 / 먹으면, 가세요 / 먹으세요, 가니까 / 먹으니까.
sentenceFrames: (vowel) 가 + 면 → 가면   ·   (consonant) 먹 + 으면 → 먹으면
갈 수 있어요  ·  먹을 수 있어요

examples.en: Can I eat this?
If you go over there, it's there.
Please read slowly.
Let's go eat (in order to eat).

commonMistakes: Adding 으 after a vowel stem — 가으면 is wrong; it is 가면.
Forgetting 으 after a consonant stem — 먹면/먹세요 are wrong; it is 먹으면/먹으세요.
studyOrder: Find the stem (drop 다)
Check for a final consonant (받침)
Consonant → add 으 (먹으면); vowel → skip it (가면)
Watch ㄹ-stems: 살다 → 사세요
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This is maybe THE most useful rule in Korean. Many endings are written with (으) in front — like (으)면 'if', (으)세요 'please', (으)ㄹ 수 있다 'can'. The 으 is just a little buffer vowel. If the verb stem ends in a consonant (먹-), add 으: 먹으면, 먹으세요, 먹을 수 있어요. If it ends in a vowel (가-), skip it: 가면, 가세요, 갈 수 있어요. Learn it once and it unlocks dozens of endings at the same time.

endingItems.title: Liaison — Linking Sounds (연음)
endingItems.plainEnglish: When a syllable ends in a consonant and the next starts with ㅇ (a vowel), that consonant slides over to begin the next syllable.
endingItems.whenToUse: This happens constantly in speech: 한국어 sounds like 한구거, 음악이 like 으마기, 꽃이 like 꼬치. The spelling never changes — only the sound links.
endingItems.attachmentRule: A final consonant (받침) before an ㅇ-initial syllable moves to become that syllable's onset: 꽃 + 이 → [꼬치], 음악 + 을 → [으마글], 옷 + 이 → [오시], 한국 + 어 → [한구거]. A double 받침 splits — one stays, one moves: 읽 + 어 → [일거], 앉 + 아 → [안자]. Liaison does not cross a clear pause between words.
endingItems.contrastWith: You still WRITE 꽃이, 음악을, 한국어 — only the pronunciation links. This is the #1 reason Korean sounds different from how it looks on the page.

examples.en: I study Korean. (sounds like 한구거)
The flowers are really pretty. (sounds like 꼬치)
I listen to music. (sounds like 으마글)
The clothes are too small. (sounds like 오시)

commonMistakes: Pronouncing each block separately (꼳-이 instead of 꼬치).
Forgetting a double 받침 splits: 읽어요 is [일거요], not [익어요].
studyOrder: Spot a 받침 followed by ㅇ
Slide the 받침 into the next syllable
For double 받침, keep one and move one
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean is written in neat syllable blocks, but in speech a final consonant 'jumps' onto the next block when that block starts with a vowel (the silent ㅇ). So 한국어 is read 한구거, and 꽃이 is read 꼬치. You keep spelling it the normal way — only the sound links up. Once you expect this, listening gets much easier.

endingItems.title: Nasalization (비음화)
endingItems.plainEnglish: A stop consonant (ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ) turns into a nasal (ㅇ/ㄴ/ㅁ) when the next syllable starts with ㄴ or ㅁ.
endingItems.whenToUse: Why 감사합니다 sounds like 감사함니다 and 학년 like 항년. It happens whenever a stop 받침 bumps into ㄴ or ㅁ.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Before ㄴ or ㅁ: a ㄱ-type 받침 (ㄱㄲㅋㄳㄺ) → ㅇ (학년 → [항년], 국물 → [궁물]); a ㄷ-type 받침 (ㄷㅅㅆㅈㅊㅌㅎ) → ㄴ (받는 → [반는], 옛날 → [옌날]); a ㅂ-type 받침 (ㅂㅍㄼㄿ) → ㅁ (입니다 → [임니다], 앞문 → [암문]).
endingItems.contrastWith: Spelling stays the same (입니다, 학년). This is different from liaison: nasalization happens before ㄴ/ㅁ, while liaison happens before a vowel (ㅇ).

examples.en: Thank you. (sounds like 감사함니다)
I'm in third grade. (학년 sounds like 항년)
The broth is hot. (국물 sounds like 궁물)
This is Korean food. (입니다 sounds like 임니다)

commonMistakes: Pronouncing the hard 합니다 as written instead of [함니다].
Missing it in -습니다/-ㅂ니다 endings, which always nasalize to [-슴니다]/[-ㅁ니다].
studyOrder: Find a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ 받침 before ㄴ or ㅁ
ㄱ→ㅇ, ㄷ→ㄴ, ㅂ→ㅁ
Apply it to every -ㅂ니다 ending
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Some 받침 sounds soften when they run into ㄴ or ㅁ. A ㄱ-sound becomes ㅇ (학년 → 항년), a ㄷ-sound becomes ㄴ (받는 → 반는), and a ㅂ-sound becomes ㅁ (입니다 → 임니다). That's why the polite -습니다 ending is pronounced -슴니다. You don't change the spelling — just the sound.

endingItems.title: Palatalization (구개음화)
endingItems.plainEnglish: A final ㄷ or ㅌ turns into ㅈ or ㅊ when the next sound is 이 (or 히).
endingItems.whenToUse: Why 같이 is pronounced 가치 and 굳이 is 구지. It only happens with ㄷ/ㅌ + 이.
endingItems.attachmentRule: When a 받침 ㄷ/ㅌ meets the vowel 이: ㄷ + 이 → 지 (굳이 → [구지], 해돋이 → [해도지], 맏이 → [마지]); ㅌ + 이 → 치 (같이 → [가치], 끝이 → [끄치], 붙이다 → [부치다]). With 히 it also applies: 닫히다 → [다치다].
endingItems.contrastWith: This is a special case of liaison: normally ㅌ + 이 would just link to [티], but before 이 the sound shifts forward in the mouth to [치]. Only ㄷ/ㅌ do this, and only before 이/히.

examples.en: Shall we go together? (같이 sounds like 가치)
You don't have to come (no need). (굳이 sounds like 구지)
I can't see the end. (끝이 sounds like 끄치)
I stick on a sticker. (붙여 area, 붙이- → 부치-)

commonMistakes: Reading 같이 as [가티] — before 이 it becomes [가치].
Over-applying it: it only affects ㄷ/ㅌ before 이/히, not other consonants or vowels.
studyOrder: Spot a ㄷ or ㅌ 받침 right before 이/히
ㄷ → 지, ㅌ → 치
Remember the common word 같이 → 가치
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: When ㄷ or ㅌ at the end of a syllable meets 이, the sound slides forward and becomes ㅈ or ㅊ. So 같이 ('together') is said 가치, and 굳이 is 구지. It's a small rule, but 같이 is such a common word that getting it right (가치, not 가티) makes you sound much more natural.

endingItems.title: Aspiration (격음화)
endingItems.plainEnglish: ㅎ merges with a neighboring ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ to make the strong, breathy ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ.
endingItems.whenToUse: Why 좋다 sounds like 조타 and 축하해요 like 추카해요. It works in either order (ㅎ before or after the stop).
endingItems.attachmentRule: ㅎ + ㄱ (or ㄱ + ㅎ) → ㅋ: 축하 → [추카], 그렇게 → [그러케]. ㅎ + ㄷ → ㅌ: 좋다 → [조타], 많다 → [만타]. ㅎ + ㅂ → ㅍ: 입학 → [이팍], 잡히다 → [자피다]. ㅎ + ㅈ → ㅊ: 좋지 → [조치], 맞히다 → [마치다]. ㅅ-type 받침 + 해 also works: 못해 → [모태].
endingItems.contrastWith: The two plain sounds fuse into ONE aspirated sound — you don't hear ㅎ separately. Compare plain 다 vs aspirated 타 in 좋다 → [조타].

examples.en: The weather is really nice. (좋다 sounds like 조타)
Happy birthday! (축하 sounds like 추카)
I can't do that. (못해 sounds like 모태)
I entered university. (입학 sounds like 이팍)

commonMistakes: Trying to pronounce ㅎ as a separate sound — 좋다 is one fused [조타], not [조ㅎ다].
Missing it in 못해/안 해도 — 못해 is [모태].
studyOrder: Find a ㅎ next to ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ (either order)
Fuse them into ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ
Practice 좋다 → 조타 and 축하 → 추카
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: The letter ㅎ is 'breathy', and when it touches ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, or ㅈ, the two fuse into one strong aspirated sound: ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, ㅊ. So 좋다 is said 조타, 축하 is 추카, and 못해 is 모태. You won't hear the ㅎ on its own — it gets absorbed into the harder sound.

endingItems.title: Question words
endingItems.plainEnglish: 누구, 어디, 언제, 뭐, 왜, 어떻게 turn a sentence into an open question.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use these when a yes/no answer is not enough and you need one missing detail.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Put the question word where the answer would normally appear: 누가 왔어요?, 어디에 가요?, 왜 못 가요?
endingItems.contrastWith: A plain rising tone makes a yes/no question. A question word asks for specific missing information.

examples.en: Who came?
Where are you going?
Why can't you go?

commonMistakes: Do not place every question word at the front as if it were English.
Do not answer 왜 with a place or 어디 with a reason.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean question words usually stay inside the normal sentence slot. If the missing answer is a person, use 누구/누가; if it is a place, use 어디; if it is a reason, use 왜.
studyOrder: Pick the missing information.
Choose the matching Korean question word.
Place it in the answer slot.
Keep the ending polite unless the context is casual.

endingItems.title: Speech levels
endingItems.plainEnglish: Korean endings change by situation: 해요체 for everyday politeness, 합쇼체 for formal settings, and 반말 only with close permission.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use 해요체 as the safe default for adult everyday speech. Use formal forms for announcements, service, interviews, and presentations.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Keep the same stem and change the ending/register: 가요, 갑니다, 가.
endingItems.contrastWith: Honorific 시 respects the person in the sentence; speech level manages your relationship with the listener.

examples.en: I'm going now.
I am going now. (formal)
I'm going now. (casual)

commonMistakes: Do not switch to 반말 just because the sentence is short.
Do not use formal 합쇼체 everywhere; it can sound stiff in close everyday talk.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Speech level is not just grammar decoration; it tells the listener how formal, close, or careful the situation is. When unsure, 해요체 is the safest spoken default.
studyOrder: Identify the listener.
Choose safe politeness first.
Add honorific 시 only when the subject needs respect.
Check whether the situation is casual, service, or formal.

endingItems.title: Possession / genitive
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use 의 to mark possession or a noun-to-noun relationship, especially in written or careful Korean.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use 의 for my/your/someone's things, institutional names, and careful noun phrases.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach 의 after the owner or first noun: 친구의 가방, 한국의 날씨.
endingItems.contrastWith: In fast spoken Korean, 의 is often dropped or pronounced like 에, but written Korean usually keeps it.

examples.en: My name is Hana.
It is my friend's bag.
Korea's weather is nice.

commonMistakes: Do not attach 의 after the possessed noun.
Do not overuse 의 in every spoken noun phrase when natural Korean would omit it.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: 의 links two nouns. The first noun owns, labels, or narrows the second noun. 제 is the common reduced form for 저의.
studyOrder: Find the owner or first noun.
Attach 의 to that noun.
Put the main noun after it.
Decide whether spoken Korean would naturally shorten it.

endingItems.title: The copula 이다
endingItems.plainEnglish: 이다 turns a noun into a sentence and changes shape in past, reason, background, and contrast clauses.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use 이다 when the predicate is a noun: student, doctor, plan, problem, reason.
endingItems.attachmentRule: After consonants use 이에요, after vowels often use 예요. In clauses it becomes 이라서, 이고, 이면, 이었어요/였어요.
endingItems.contrastWith: Adjectives and verbs do not need 이다. 학생이에요 is right, but 가다이에요 is not.

examples.en: I am a student.
I was a doctor.
Because they are my friend, I helped.

commonMistakes: Do not add 이다 after a verb stem.
Do not forget the noun-final consonant/vowel split for 이에요/예요.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: 이다 is the noun sentence-maker. If the last meaningful word is a noun, Korean needs a copula shape to finish the sentence.
studyOrder: Check whether the predicate is a noun.
Choose 이에요/예요 in polite speech.
Change 이다 when connecting clauses.
Do not attach it to action verbs.

endingItems.title: Volition, inference, and softening with 겠
endingItems.plainEnglish: 겠 can show the speaker will do something, infer something from evidence, or soften formal speech.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use 겠 for formal willingness, careful guesses, empathy, and service-style polite statements.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach 겠 to a verb or adjective stem before the final ending: 하겠습니다, 맛있겠어요, 힘드시겠어요.
endingItems.contrastWith: Plain future -(으)ㄹ 거예요 predicts or plans. 겠 often sounds more formal, inferential, or service-oriented.

examples.en: I will make the reservation.
It looks like it will rain.
That must be very hard for you.

commonMistakes: Do not treat 겠 as the only future tense.
Do not use service-style 겠 forms in every casual sentence.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: 겠 is a control knob for stance. It can mean 'I will', 'it looks like', or 'that must be', depending on who controls the action and what evidence the speaker has.
studyOrder: Decide whether this is will, guess, or empathy.
Attach 겠 to the stem.
Choose the right politeness ending.
Compare with -(으)ㄹ 거예요 before using it as future.

endingItems.title: Unreal conditionals
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use past conditional frames to talk about unreal results, regrets, and imagined alternatives.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use this when the condition did not happen and you are imagining a different result.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach 았/었더라면 to the past stem, then state the imagined result with -(으)ㄹ 텐데요 or -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
endingItems.contrastWith: Plain -(으)면 can be real or future. -았/었더라면 strongly points to an unreal past condition.

examples.en: If I had come early, I would have met them.
If I had had time, I would have gone.
It would have been good if I had studied.

commonMistakes: Do not use this for a simple future condition.
Do not forget that the condition is already unreal or regretted.

practiceItems.prompt: Say: If I had known, I would have gone.
Say: If I had time, I would have helped.

endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This form is for a path that did not happen. It often carries regret, relief, or reflection about a different possible outcome.
studyOrder: Confirm the condition did not happen.
Make the condition past.
Attach 더라면 or use 있었다면/이었다면.
Make the result imagined, not factual.

endingItems.title: Nominalisation contrast
endingItems.plainEnglish: 기 names an action as an abstract activity; 는 것 packages a more specific event or fact.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use 기 for general activities and evaluation. Use 는 것 when describing an event, fact, habit, or thing someone does.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach 기 directly to the verb stem. For 는 것, use the present modifier before 것.
endingItems.contrastWith: 기 is compact and activity-like; 는 것 is heavier and more event-like.

examples.en: Reading Korean is difficult.
Listening every day is important.
I didn't know that it was late.

commonMistakes: Do not use 기 for every English gerund.
Do not forget 것 when packaging a full clause as a noun.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Both forms let a verb behave like a noun. 기 feels like naming an activity; 는 것 feels like pointing to a specific thing, fact, or event.
studyOrder: Ask whether you mean an activity or a fact/event.
Use 기 for activity labels.
Use 는 것 for packaged clauses.
Check the particle after the nominalized phrase.

endingItems.title: Formal written connectors
endingItems.plainEnglish: Formal Korean writing uses connectors like 따라서, 그러나, 반면에, 즉, and 결국 to organise argument flow.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use these in essays, notices, reports, news-style writing, and structured explanations.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use them at the beginning of the next sentence or clause to show the relationship to the previous idea.
endingItems.contrastWith: Spoken connectors like 그래서 and 근데 are natural in conversation but often too casual for formal writing.

examples.en: It rained. Therefore, the game was canceled.
The price is high. However, the quality is good.
In other words, we need to check again.

commonMistakes: Do not mix very casual endings with formal written connectors.
Do not use 따라서 when the second sentence is not a result.

practiceItems.prompt: Connect: It snowed. Therefore, school is closed.
Start a contrast sentence with 그러나.

endingItems.beginnerExplanation: These words are road signs for written logic. They tell the reader whether the next sentence is a result, contrast, summary, or conclusion.
studyOrder: Name the logic relation.
Choose the connector.
Keep the sentence ending formal enough.
Check whether the previous sentence really supports the connector.

endingItems.title: Internet language and intensifiers
endingItems.plainEnglish: Korean digital language uses consonant emoticons, shortenings, and casual intensifiers that must stay in informal contexts.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use these in chats with friends, comments, memes, or casual texting, not in formal writing.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Place them like tone markers around short casual sentences: ㅋㅋ, ㅠㅠ, 진짜, 완전, 대박.
endingItems.contrastWith: Polite email, school writing, workplace notices, and customer messages need standard vocabulary instead.

examples.en: This is really amazing.
Today is so hard.
Haha, got it.

commonMistakes: Do not use ㅋㅋ or ㅠㅠ in formal assignments or business messages.
Do not assume every internet expression is safe with older or unfamiliar listeners.

practiceItems.prompt: Make a casual chat reaction: That's amazing.

endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Internet Korean is mostly about register. The words may be simple, but the social setting matters more than the literal meaning.
studyOrder: Identify the channel.
Check your relationship with the reader.
Choose casual or standard wording.
Remove internet markers before formal writing.

endingItems.title: Integrated production checklist
endingItems.plainEnglish: Before producing Korean, check purpose, listener, register, particles, verb shape, tense, connector, and closing.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use this before a final speaking or writing task, especially when combining several grammar points.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Run the checks in order: purpose, listener, register, sentence core, particles, tense, connector, ending.
endingItems.contrastWith: Do not only translate English word by word. Korean output needs sentence role, listener relationship, and ending choice.

examples.ko: 저는 내일 회의에 갈 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun naeil hoeuie gal su isseoyo.
examples.en: I can go to the meeting tomorrow.

examples.ko: 비가 와서 조금 늦을 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: biga waseo jogeum neujeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: I think I will be a little late because it is raining.
Thank you for checking.

commonMistakes: Do not stop checking after vocabulary is correct.
Do not mix casual slang with formal closings unless the task asks for register contrast.

practiceItems.prompt: Say one polite sentence about tomorrow's plan.

endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This card is a final quality gate. It helps you catch the things learners miss after they already know the words: particles, endings, tense, connectors, and social tone.
studyOrder: State the communicative purpose.
Choose the listener/register.
Build the Korean sentence core.
Check particles and endings.
Read it aloud once before submitting.

endingItems.title: Tensification
endingItems.plainEnglish: Some consonants become tense after blocked final consonants, so written Korean and spoken Korean may differ.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use this when a following consonant sounds stronger than its spelling after a 받침.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Notice the 받침 before ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ, or ㅈ; the next sound may tighten in pronunciation.
endingItems.contrastWith: Liaison carries a final consonant into a vowel. Tensification strengthens the next consonant instead.

examples.en: rice soup, often pronounced with a tense pp sound
school, often pronounced with a tense kk sound
to read, often pronounced with a tense tt sound

commonMistakes: Do not expect spelling and sound to match perfectly.
Do not add an extra vowel between the two consonants.

practiceItems.prompt: Read 국밥 with the common tense sound.
Read 학교 with the common tense sound.

endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean spelling keeps word history visible, but speech often tightens the next consonant after a final consonant. Recognising the pattern makes listening less surprising.
studyOrder: Find the 받침.
Look at the next consonant.
Listen for a tighter sound.
Keep the original spelling when writing.

items.prompt: Choose the Hangul word for “Hangul / Korean writing.”

items.hint: Break the syllable block into letters.

items.label: Syllable choice
items.prompt: 먹어요 has three written chunks: 먹 + ____ + 요.

items.hint: As for me, I am Hana.

items.prompt: Choose “I am busy, so I cannot go.”
Build: “If you have time, please call.”
Choose “It looks like it’s going to rain.”

items.hint: I found that it was really fun (recalling what you noticed).

items.prompt: Build: “I think this is a good idea.”

items.hint: said that he IS a student (이다 → 이라고).

items.prompt: Build: “She asked whether I had eaten.”
Choose “I decided to quit my job.”

items.hint: ended up working (it came about that I work).

items.prompt: Build: “I’m worried it might be too expensive.”
Build: “He seems to be angry (I guess).”
Choose “The more I learn, the more fun it gets.”

items.hint: since it was raining (the reason I noticed), I bought an umbrella.

items.prompt: Build: “I study hard in order to pass the exam.”

tracks.title: App Manual
tracks.summary: Start here before the course: what each tab is for, how a short study session flows, how to type Korean, and the big picture before Chapter 1.

units.title: How to use this app
units.situation: You opened Korean Core Starter and want a simple daily route instead of wandering through every tab.
units.goal: I can choose the right tab without guessing and understand how review, romanization, progress, and backup fit together.

beginnerGuide.title: The six tabs
beginnerGuide.body: Learn is the course path. Practice is review and short drills. Shadow is speaking imitation. Roleplay is guided conversation. Dictionary is the reference. Guide is practical help for Korea and for using this app.

beginnerGuide.title: The main rule
beginnerGuide.body: Do not treat the app like a dictionary database. Use Learn for the next small lesson, Practice for memory, and Dictionary only when a word keeps showing up and still feels unclear.

beginnerGuide.title: How review works
beginnerGuide.body: Items you miss can return through spaced review. The app brings them back after longer gaps so weak words stop disappearing instead of being forgotten after one chapter.

beginnerGuide.title: Romanization
beginnerGuide.body: Keep Romaja on at the very beginning. Around Chapter 3, try turning it off for short stretches so Hangul starts doing the work.

beginnerGuide.title: Progress and backup
beginnerGuide.body: Completion is stored in this browser. Use the backup card in Guide before changing devices, clearing browser data, or studying from another computer.

steps: Open App Manual once and read the study flow.
Open Learn when you want new material.
Open Practice when you want a short session or review.
Open Dictionary when you need a deeper explanation for a word, expression, or pattern.
Open Guide again for real-life Korea tasks, Korean typing, backup, and app setup.
Use Shadow or Roleplay briefly after a lesson when you want the sentence to become speakable.
checkpoints: I know what each tab is for.
I know Romaja is temporary support, not the final reading habit.
I know Practice is for memory, not random busywork.
I know progress lives in this browser unless I export a backup.

deepLinks.label: Open Learn
deepLinks.note: Start or continue the course path.

deepLinks.label: Open Practice
deepLinks.note: Clear review or run a short drill.

deepLinks.label: Open Dictionary
deepLinks.note: Search words, expressions, and patterns.

units.title: Study flow: short app sessions
units.situation: You want Korean to improve in small daily chunks, like a language app, without turning study into a long textbook sit-down.
units.goal: I can run a 10-15 minute session, finish one useful piece, and know what to ask a Korean friend or native helper later.

beginnerGuide.title: Think in small sessions
beginnerGuide.body: One good session is not a whole chapter. It can be one dialogue, one word chunk, one grammar note, one practice set, or one sentence you can actually say.

beginnerGuide.title: Daily route
beginnerGuide.body: Start with Practice for 3-5 minutes, then Learn for one new chunk, then end by saying or writing one sentence from memory. Stop while the next step still feels easy.

beginnerGuide.title: Chapter route
beginnerGuide.body: Read the warm-up dialogue first so you know the situation. Add only the words that belong to that chapter. Study the grammar note, then use Practice to prove you can choose the form without looking.

beginnerGuide.title: Native helper route
beginnerGuide.body: When a Korean native helps twice a week, bring three things: one sentence you made, one expression that felt weird, and one real-life situation you want to handle. Let the app explain the rule; let the native show what sounds natural.

beginnerGuide.title: When you feel stuck
beginnerGuide.body: Do not restart from Chapter 1. Clear due review, reread the last completed chapter, and try one focused Practice mode. If the same word keeps failing, open its Dictionary page and read the examples.

steps: Practice first: clear due review or run one short drill.
Learn next: continue the next unfinished screen, not necessarily the whole chapter.
Add review carefully: save useful words and expressions, not every item you see.
Produce one sentence: say it, type it, or use Roleplay if the chapter gives you enough pieces.
Mark complete only when the chapter goal feels usable without staring at the explanation.
On native-helper days, ask for naturalness and examples, not a full grammar lecture.
checkpoints: I can study for 10-15 minutes without choosing random tabs.
I know the order: review, new chunk, one output.
I know Dictionary supports learning but does not replace Learn.
I know how to use native help even when the helper is not a teacher.
units.notes: Pronunciation polish can wait until the core sentence habit is steady. For now, the strongest habit is to understand the sentence, recall it, and produce one small version yourself.

deepLinks.label: Run Practice first
deepLinks.note: A short memory warm-up before new content.

deepLinks.label: Continue Learn
deepLinks.note: Move one screen forward, then stop cleanly.

deepLinks.label: Open Roleplay
deepLinks.note: Use it after the chapter gives you enough language pieces.

units.title: Set up Korean typing
units.situation: You need to type Korean for drills, search, messages, delivery apps, maps, and daily life.
units.goal: I can install a Korean keyboard, switch to it, and use tap-input fallback when I do not have Korean typing ready.

beginnerGuide.title: Why this matters
beginnerGuide.body: Typing Korean lets you search Naver Map, text people, use delivery apps, and complete production drills. The app also gives tap-input fallback for typed answers so you are not blocked on day one.

beginnerGuide.title: iPhone or iPad
beginnerGuide.body: Open Settings > General > Keyboard > Keyboards > Add New Keyboard > Korean. Use the globe key to switch keyboards.

beginnerGuide.title: Android
beginnerGuide.body: In Gboard or Samsung Keyboard, open Languages, add Korean, and choose 2-set Korean. Use the globe or spacebar switcher to change languages.

beginnerGuide.title: Mac
beginnerGuide.body: Open System Settings > Keyboard > Input Sources, add Korean, and choose 2-Set Korean. Control-Space usually switches input sources.

beginnerGuide.title: Windows
beginnerGuide.body: Open Settings > Time & language > Language & region, add Korean, then switch with Win-Space. Choose the Korean Microsoft IME.

beginnerGuide.title: 2-set in 30 seconds
beginnerGuide.body: Consonants are on the left, vowels are on the right, and final consonants combine automatically. Type ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ and the keyboard builds 한.

steps: Install Korean input for your device.
Practice switching between English and Korean.
Type 한, 국, 어 slowly and watch the blocks combine.
Open Chapter 1 and use the Hangul trainer.
When a typing question appears before you are ready, use the tap-input fallback.
checkpoints: I can switch to Korean input.
I know 2-set Korean uses left-hand consonants and right-hand vowels.
I know the app has a tap-input fallback for typed drills.

deepLinks.label: Practice Hangul
deepLinks.note: Open Learn, then Start here — Hangul.

deepLinks.label: Try a typing drill
deepLinks.note: Use Write mode and turn on tap input if needed.

units.title: How Korean Works
units.situation: A quick map of Korean before grammar details start.
units.goal: I can explain the ten big ideas that make the first chapters less surprising.

beginnerGuide.title: A five-minute map
beginnerGuide.body: These ten cards explain Hangul, word order, particles, politeness, dropped subjects, numbers, and sound changes before you meet them one by one in the course.

checkpoints: I know Korean verbs usually come at the end.
I know particles show noun roles.
I know Romaja is temporary support.

tracks.title: Arrival & Connectivity
tracks.summary: Your first hours in Korea: clear the airport and immigration, plan your ARC, grab a SIM, and load a T-money card — with the survival Korean to do each one.

units.title: Clear immigration and plan your ARC
units.situation: At the airport arrivals hall, at the immigration desk and the help counter right after you land.
units.goal: I can answer basic immigration questions, ask for help in line, and know I must apply for my ARC within 90 days.

keyPhrases.note: Polite all-purpose greeting; say it as you step up to the immigration desk.
Simple reason for visit. For study or work, swap in 공부하러 왔어요 / 일하러 왔어요.
Uses the 'can' pattern. A polite way to check before continuing in English.
Your single most useful survival line when someone speaks too fast.

keyPhrases.en: I'm not sure / I don't understand.
keyPhrases.note: Say this instead of guessing; the officer will usually rephrase.

keyPhrases.en: Where do I apply for the Alien Registration Card?
keyPhrases.note: 외국인등록증 (ARC) is your key ID in Korea; you apply at an immigration office.
어디예요? = 'where is it?'. Swap 화장실 for any place you need.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.en: What is the purpose of your visit?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: I'm here to study. Please speak slowly.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.en: Okay, got it. How long will you stay?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: One year. Where do I apply for the ARC?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.en: You apply at the immigration office.

beginnerGuide.title: What the ARC is and the 90-day rule
beginnerGuide.body: The 외국인등록증 (Alien Registration Card, ARC) is the ID that lets you open a bank account, get a long-term phone plan, and more. If you're staying over 90 days, you must apply at an immigration office, generally within 90 days of arrival. Book your visit on HiKorea before you go — walk-in slots are scarce.

beginnerGuide.title: 해요체: the polite ending you'll hear most
beginnerGuide.body: Most phrases here end in -요 (왔어요, 신청해요, 모르겠어요). This 해요체 is polite but friendly — the right default with officials and strangers. You don't need the stiffer -습니다 form to be respectful.

beginnerGuide.title: Asking 'where' with 어디
beginnerGuide.body: 어디 means 'where'. 어디예요? asks 'where is it?' (화장실이 어디예요?), while 어디에서 marks where an action happens (어디에서 신청해요? = 'where do I apply?'). Hear the difference: 어디예요 = location of a thing, 어디에서 = location of an action.

checkpoints: I can greet the officer and state my reason for visiting (여행/공부하러/일하러 왔어요).
I can ask someone to slow down (천천히 말해 주세요) and say when I don't understand (잘 모르겠어요).
I can ask where to apply for my ARC (외국인등록증은 어디에서 신청해요?).
I know I must apply for the ARC at an immigration office within 90 days for a long stay.

drills.note: Swap 화장실 for 출구 (exit) or 택시 (taxi) to ask for other places.
Practice the V + ㄹ/을 수 있어요 'can' shape; try 도와줄 수 있어요? (can you help?).

steps: Have your passport, arrival card, and accommodation address ready at the immigration desk.
After immigration, collect baggage and pass through customs (declare items if asked).
If staying over 90 days, book an ARC appointment on HiKorea and gather documents (passport photo, application form, fee).

deepLinks.label: HiKorea (immigration & ARC)
deepLinks.note: Official portal to book immigration office visits and check ARC requirements.

units.costs: ARC application fee is typically around 30,000 KRW (pay at the immigration office); have a passport photo ready.
units.notes: Bring the exact documents listed on your visa type's HiKorea page; missing a photo or the fee is the most common reason for a wasted trip.

units.title: Buy a SIM or eSIM
units.situation: At an airport telecom booth or a neighborhood phone shop, choosing between prepaid and a plan.
units.goal: I can ask for a SIM, choose prepaid vs. a plan, ask the price, and confirm it will work in my phone.

keyPhrases.en: I'd like to buy a SIM.
keyPhrases.note: Uses the 'want' pattern V고 싶어요. 유심 = USIM, the standard word for a SIM card here.
N 주세요 = 'please give me N'. Add 데이터 for a data-focused SIM.
The essential price question. Works for anything you can point at.
Useful when comparing a monthly plan; 한 달 = one month.

keyPhrases.en: Do you have a prepaid SIM?
keyPhrases.note: 선불 = prepaid, 후불 = pay-later/plan. 있어요? = 'do you have?'

keyPhrases.en: Can I use it in my phone?
keyPhrases.note: Uses the 'can' pattern to confirm compatibility before paying. 폰 = phone.
V아/어 주세요 asks someone to do something for you; 개통 = activation.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Hello. I'd like to buy a SIM.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: Would you like prepaid or a plan?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: A prepaid SIM, please. How much is it?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.en: It's 30,000 won. Your passport, please.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Here you go. Please activate it here.

beginnerGuide.title: Prepaid (선불) vs. plan (후불)
beginnerGuide.body: 선불 (prepaid) is the easiest as a newcomer: pay up front, no contract, and usually only a passport is needed. 후불 (a monthly plan) is cheaper long-term but often requires your ARC and a Korean bank account, so most people start prepaid and switch after their ARC arrives.

beginnerGuide.title: Two ways to ask a price
beginnerGuide.body: 얼마예요? means 'how much is it?' for a one-time price. To compare monthly plans, add a time word: 한 달 얼마예요? ('how much per month?'). The pattern is just [time/thing] + 얼마예요?

beginnerGuide.title: 고 싶어요 vs. 주세요
beginnerGuide.body: Use V고 싶어요 to state what YOU want to do (사고 싶어요 = 'I want to buy'), and N 주세요 to ask the seller to hand you something (유심 주세요 = 'give me a SIM'). For an action done for you, use V아/어 주세요 (개통해 주세요 = 'please activate it for me').

checkpoints: I can say I want to buy a SIM (유심 사고 싶어요) and ask for a specific one (데이터 유심 주세요).
I can ask the price (얼마예요?) and the monthly price (한 달 얼마예요?).
I can tell prepaid from a plan (선불 / 후불) and ask if they have prepaid (선불 유심 있어요?).
I can confirm it works in my phone (제 폰에서 쓸 수 있어요?) and ask them to activate it (개통해 주세요).

drills.en: I'd like to buy a top-up card.
drills.note: Reuse V고 싶어요 with a new noun; swap 충전 카드 for 유심.

drills.ko: 이거 제 폰에서 쓸 수 있어요?
drills.romanization: igeo je poneseo sseul su isseoyo?
drills.en: Can I use this in my phone?
drills.note: 이거 = 'this one' (point at it). Practice the 'can' question form.

steps: Decide prepaid vs. plan: prepaid for the first weeks (passport only), a plan later once you have your ARC.
Check your phone is unlocked and supports Korean bands or eSIM before you buy.
Hand over your passport for registration and ask the staff to activate the SIM on the spot.

deepLinks.label: Naver Map (find a phone shop)
deepLinks.note: Search a carrier name to find a nearby shop and its hours.

units.costs: Airport prepaid SIMs commonly run ~25,000–50,000 KRW depending on data and days; monthly plans vary by carrier.
units.notes: eSIM works only on supported phones — confirm 제 폰에서 쓸 수 있어요? before paying, since prepaid SIMs are often non-refundable once opened.

units.title: Buy and charge a T-money card
units.situation: At a convenience store or a subway station machine, getting the transit card you'll tap on every bus and train.
units.goal: I can buy a T-money card, load cash onto it, check whether card payment works, and ask for my balance.

keyPhrases.note: N 주세요. 티머니 is the standard rechargeable transit card sold at convenience stores.
V아/어 주세요 + amount. 만 원 = 10,000 won; 충전 = top-up/charge.

keyPhrases.en: Can I charge it with a card?
keyPhrases.note: 카드로 uses the -로/으로 'by means of' particle. Many stores only top up T-money with cash.
잔액 = remaining balance; 확인해 주세요 = 'please check (for me)'.
현금으로 = 'with cash' (-으로 after a consonant). Use this if card top-up isn't available.
오천 원 = 5,000 won; -만 = 'just/only' that amount.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Hello. A T-money card, please.

dialogue.ko: 네, 사천 원이에요. 충전도 해 드릴까요?
dialogue.romanization: ne, sacheon wonieyo. chungjeondo hae deurilkkayo?
dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.en: Sure, it's 4,000 won. Shall I charge it too?

dialogue.ko: 네, 만 원 충전해 주세요. 카드로 충전돼요?
dialogue.romanization: ne, man won chungjeonhae juseyo. kadeuro chungjeondwaeyo?
dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Yes, please charge 10,000 won. Can I charge it with a card?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.en: Top-ups are cash only.

dialogue.ko: 그럼 현금으로 충전할게요. 잔액 확인해 주세요.
dialogue.romanization: geureom hyeongeumeuro chungjeonhalgeyo. janae kwaginhae juseyo.
dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.en: Then I'll charge with cash. Please check the balance.

beginnerGuide.title: Why T-money first
beginnerGuide.body: 티머니 is a prepaid card you tap on buses, the subway, and even many taxis and convenience stores. Buy the card once (about 2,500–4,000 KRW, non-refundable) at any convenience store, then top it up with cash as you go — no app or registration needed to start.

beginnerGuide.title: The -로/으로 particle ('by means of')
beginnerGuide.body: Attach -로 after a vowel and -으로 after a consonant to say HOW you do something: 카드 → 카드로 ('by card'), 현금 → 현금으로 ('by cash'). So 카드로 충전돼요? literally asks 'does it charge by card?' Keep cash handy — store top-ups are usually cash only.

beginnerGuide.title: 충전해 주세요 = asking for the favor
beginnerGuide.body: 충전 ('charge/top-up') becomes a request with 해 주세요: 만 원 충전해 주세요 = 'please charge 10,000 won (for me)'. Put the amount first, then the verb. The same 확인해 주세요 ('please check') works for your balance: 잔액 확인해 주세요.

checkpoints: I can buy a T-money card (티머니 카드 주세요).
I can ask to load a specific amount (만 원 충전해 주세요 / 오천 원만 충전해 주세요).
I can ask if card payment works (카드로 충전돼요?) and say I'll pay cash instead (현금으로 충전할게요).
I can ask the clerk to check my balance (잔액 확인해 주세요).

drills.note: Swap the amount: 오천 원 (5,000) or 이만 원 (20,000) + 충전해 주세요.

drills.en: Can I charge it with a card?
drills.note: Change the means: 현금으로 충전돼요? ('can I charge with cash?').

steps: Buy the T-money card at any convenience store (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven) or a subway vending machine.
Top up with cash at the counter or a station machine; tell the clerk the amount (e.g. 만 원).
Tap on entry (and exit on the subway/some buses); recharge before the balance runs low.

deepLinks.label: T-money official site
deepLinks.note: Card types, balance/refund info, and where T-money is accepted.

deepLinks.label: Naver Map (find a store/station)
deepLinks.note: Locate a nearby convenience store or subway station to buy and recharge.

units.costs: Card itself ~2,500–4,000 KRW (non-refundable); top up any amount in cash. Card top-ups at stores are usually cash only.
