私 private + 物 object + 函 box

hanjaRoots.note: 體 = body or form. It appears in PE, body temperature, and writing style.

hanjaRoots.note: 心 = heart or mind. It helps with feelings, attention, caution, and psychology words.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 티머니 means "T-money (transit card)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 티머니 (timeoni) means "T-money (transit card)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 티머니 주세요 ("A T-money card, please."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 티머니 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: Do you have a T-money card?

examples.en: I bought a T-money card at the convenience store.
examples.note: Past purchase.

examples.en: I ride the bus with T-money.
examples.note: Method.

examples.en: There is no balance on my T-money.
examples.note: Problem.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 티머니 (T-money) is the most common rechargeable transit card. You buy and recharge it at convenience stores and stations, and use it on subways, buses, and many taxis.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not say 티머니를 충전돼요; say 티머니를 충전해요 or 충전해 주세요.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 충전 means "charge / top-up" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: "charge / top-up" is 충전 (chungjeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 충전해 주세요 ("Please charge it / top it up."). Watch the particle attached to 충전 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Please charge it / top it up.
Can I top up by card?

examples.en: I topped up at the subway station.
examples.note: Past.

examples.en: You can only top up with cash.
examples.note: Limitation.

examples.en: Please charge 5,000 won.
examples.note: Amount.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 충전 means recharging value onto a card or topping up a balance (transit cards, prepaid SIMs, gift cards). The verb is 충전하다, and the request 충전해 주세요 is essential.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
충전 adds balance; do not confuse it with 결제, which means making a payment.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 유심 means "SIM / USIM card" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 유심 (yusim) = "SIM / USIM card". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 유심 주세요 ("A SIM card, please.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 유심, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I want to buy a SIM card.
Do you have a prepaid SIM?

examples.en: I bought a SIM card at the airport.
examples.note: Past.

examples.en: I want to change my SIM.
examples.note: Desire.

examples.ko: 이 유심은 한 달 동안 써요.
examples.romanization: i yusimeun han dal dongan sseoyo.
examples.en: I use this SIM for one month.
examples.note: Duration.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 유심 (USIM/SIM) is the small card that gives your phone a Korean number and data. Travelers often choose 선불 유심 (prepaid SIM) or an eSIM at the airport or a phone shop.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
유심 is the physical card; the plan or number service is 요금제, which is related but different.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 외국인등록증 means "Alien Registration Card (ARC)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 외국인등록증 (oegugindeungnokjeung) means "Alien Registration Card (ARC)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 외국인등록증이 있어요 ("I have an ARC."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 외국인등록증 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help, then change a single part.

examples.en: You need an ARC at the bank.
examples.note: Requirement.

examples.en: I have to apply for an ARC.
examples.note: Obligation.

examples.en: Do you have your ARC?
examples.note: Question.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 외국인등록증 (ARC) is the ID card for foreign residents. You usually apply within 90 days at an immigration office, and you need it for banking, phone contracts, and many services.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Carry the actual 외국인등록증 card; a passport alone is often not enough for resident services.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 공항 means "airport" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: "airport" is 공항 (gonghang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 공항에 가요 ("I go to the airport."). Watch the particle attached to 공항 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I buy a SIM at the airport.

examples.en: I arrived at Incheon Airport.
examples.note: Arrival.

examples.en: I took a taxi at the airport.
examples.note: Action place.

examples.en: How do I get to the airport?
examples.note: Directions.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 공항 is airport. From the airport you can reach the city by 공항철도 (airport railroad), 공항버스 (airport limousine bus), or taxi.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For going to the airport use 공항에 가요; for actions done there use 공항에서.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 환승 means "transfer (transit)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 환승 (hwanseung) = "transfer (transit)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 어디서 환승해요? ("Where do I transfer?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 환승, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

examples.en: I transfer at City Hall Station.
examples.note: Place.

examples.en: I transferred from bus to subway.
examples.note: Route.

examples.en: It is cheaper if you transfer with one card.
examples.note: Condition.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 환승 means transferring between buses and subways. If you tap the same transit card, transfers within a time limit are usually discounted or free.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Tap your card when getting off too, or you may lose the 환승 transfer discount.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 정류장 means "bus stop" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 정류장 (jeongnyujang) means "bus stop". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 버스 정류장 어디예요? ("Where is the bus stop?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 정류장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I get off at the next stop.

examples.en: I get off at the next stop.
examples.note: Travel.

examples.en: I wait for the bus at the stop.
examples.note: Action place.

examples.en: Where is the bus stop?
examples.note: Question.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 정류장 is a bus stop. For the subway you say 역 (station) instead. Knowing 다음 정류장 (next stop) helps you get off at the right place.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Use 정류장 for buses and 역 for subway or train stations.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 표 means "ticket" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: "ticket" is 표 (pyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 표 한 장 주세요 ("One ticket, please."). Watch the particle attached to 표 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: I want to buy a ticket.

examples.en: I booked a KTX ticket.
examples.note: Past booking.

examples.en: Two tickets, please.
examples.note: Counter.

examples.en: The tickets are sold out.
examples.note: Status.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 표 is a ticket for a train, bus, or movie. For trains like KTX and SRT you often 예매 (book in advance) online or at the station; tickets are counted with 장.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Count tickets with 장: 표 한 장, 표 두 장, not 표 하나 in formal counting.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 택시 means "taxi" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 택시 (taeksi) = "taxi". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 택시 타요 ("I take a taxi.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 택시, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.

examples.en: I took a taxi from the airport.
examples.note: Past.

examples.en: Please go to this address.
examples.note: Direction.

examples.en: I cannot catch a taxi.
examples.note: Problem.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 택시 is taxi. Apps like Kakao T are common; if you show the address in Korean and say 여기로 가 주세요, the driver can take you there.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Show the destination in Korean as an address or in an app; English place names may not be understood.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 월세 means "monthly rent" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 월세 (wolse) means "monthly rent". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 월세가 얼마예요? ("How much is the monthly rent?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 월세 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: How much is the monthly rent?

examples.en: The monthly rent is 500,000 won.
examples.note: Price.

examples.en: I have to pay rent every month.
examples.note: Obligation.

examples.en: The rent is too expensive.
examples.note: Complaint.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 월세 is monthly rent, usually paired with a smaller deposit (보증금). It contrasts with 전세, a large lump-sum deposit with little or no monthly rent.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
월세 (monthly rent) and 전세 (lump-sum deposit lease) are different contracts; do not mix them up.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 보증금 means "deposit (housing)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: "deposit (housing)" is 보증금 (bojeunggeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 보증금이 얼마예요? ("How much is the deposit?"). Watch the particle attached to 보증금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

examples.en: The deposit is 10 million won.
examples.note: Price.

examples.en: You pay the deposit when you sign the contract.
examples.note: Timing.

examples.en: You get the deposit back when you move out.
examples.note: Return.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 보증금 is the deposit a tenant pays the landlord. With 월세 it is usually returned when you move out, minus any unpaid rent or damage.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Keep the contract (계약서); you need it to get your 보증금 back.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 계좌 means "bank account" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 계좌 (gyejwa) = "bank account". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 계좌를 만들고 싶어요 ("I want to open a bank account.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 계좌, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: I want to open a bank account.
I send money to the account.

examples.en: I opened an account at the bank.
examples.note: Past.

examples.en: I open an account with my ARC.
examples.note: Requirement.

examples.en: Please transfer to the account.
examples.note: Transfer.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 계좌 is a bank account. To open one (계좌를 만들다) you usually need your 외국인등록증 (ARC) and a phone number; the passbook is 통장.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Opening an account often requires an ARC (외국인등록증); a passport alone may not be accepted.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 분리수거 means "separated recycling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 분리수거 (bullisugeo) means "separated recycling". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 분리수거를 해요 ("I sort the recycling."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 분리수거 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.

usagePhrases.en: I have to sort the recycling.
May I throw it away here?

examples.en: Plastic is separated for recycling.
examples.note: Rule.

examples.en: Food waste is thrown out separately.
examples.note: Rule.

examples.en: When is the recycling day?
examples.note: Schedule.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 분리수거 is the strict trash sorting used in Korea: plastic, paper, glass, cans, and food waste go separately, often on set days. Rules vary by district (구).
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
General trash must go in a 종량제봉투 (volume-rate bag); recyclables are sorted separately.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 종량제봉투 means "volume-rate trash bag" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: "volume-rate trash bag" is 종량제봉투 (jongnyangjebongtu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 종량제봉투 주세요 ("A volume-rate trash bag, please."). Watch the particle attached to 종량제봉투 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Where do I buy the trash bags?
I throw it in the official bag.

examples.en: I buy trash bags at the convenience store.
examples.note: Place.

examples.en: I put general trash in the official bag.
examples.note: Use.

examples.en: There are several bag sizes.
examples.note: Info.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 종량제봉투 is the official, district-specific bag you must use for general trash; you buy it at convenience stores and marts. Using the wrong bag can mean it is not collected.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Buy the bag for your district (구); bags from another district may not be collected.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 약국 means "pharmacy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 약국 (yakguk) = "pharmacy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 약국이 어디예요? ("Where is the pharmacy?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 약국, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

examples.en: I bought cold medicine at the pharmacy.
examples.note: Past.

examples.en: There is a pharmacy next to the hospital.
examples.note: Location.

examples.en: The pharmacy is closed.
examples.note: Status.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 약국 is a pharmacy. For prescription medicine you bring a 처방전 from a clinic; for minor issues, pharmacists can recommend over-the-counter medicine.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
For prescription drugs you need a 처방전; not everything is available without one.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 처방전 means "prescription" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 처방전 (cheobangjeon) means "prescription". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 처방전 주세요 ("The prescription, please."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 처방전 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.

examples.en: I got a prescription at the clinic.
examples.note: Past.

examples.en: I gave the prescription to the pharmacy.
examples.note: Action.

examples.en: This medicine needs a prescription.
examples.note: Requirement.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 처방전 is a prescription written by a doctor. You receive it at a 병원 or clinic and take it to a 약국 to get the medicine; many drugs require it.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
처방전 (prescription) is from the clinic; you fill it at the 약국 (pharmacy), which is a different place.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 택배 means "parcel delivery" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: "parcel delivery" is 택배 (taekbae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 택배가 왔어요 ("A package arrived."). Watch the particle attached to 택배 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.

usagePhrases.en: Please leave it at the door.

examples.en: The package has not arrived yet.
examples.note: Status.

examples.en: I sent the parcel at the convenience store.
examples.note: Place.

examples.en: What is the tracking number?
examples.note: Tracking.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 택배 is courier parcel delivery (for example CJ대한통운 or 우체국). You track it with a 송장 번호 (tracking number); convenience-store drop-off and pickup are common.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
택배 is parcel courier service; 배달 usually means food delivery, which is a different service.

newcomerVocab.shortExplanation: 미세먼지 means "fine dust (air pollution)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
newcomerVocab.explanation: 미세먼지 (misemeonji) = "fine dust (air pollution)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 미세먼지가 많아요 ("There is a lot of fine dust.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 미세먼지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.

usagePhrases.en: There is a lot of fine dust.
How is the fine dust today?

examples.en: The fine dust is bad today.
examples.note: Condition.

examples.en: I wear a mask because of the fine dust.
examples.note: Reason.

examples.en: The fine dust level is bad.
examples.note: Index.

newcomerVocab.nuance: 미세먼지 is fine dust or air pollution, reported daily as 좋음(good), 보통(normal), 나쁨(bad), and 매우 나쁨(very bad). On bad days people wear masks and limit outdoor time.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
미세먼지 (PM10) and 초미세먼지 (PM2.5) are reported separately; check both.

patterns.shortExplanation: N이에요 / 예요 means "to be / am / is / are" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: N이에요 / 예요 (N-ieyo / yeyo) means "to be / am / is / are" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 학생이에요 ("I am a student."). Use 이에요 after a final consonant and 예요 after a vowel.

examples.en: I am a student.
examples.note: Introduction.

examples.en: This place is a school.
examples.note: Place.

examples.en: My name is Hana.
examples.note: Formal.

patterns.nuance: Use 이에요 after a final consonant and 예요 after a vowel.
commonMistakes: Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.
Check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective before using it.

patterns.shortExplanation: N이/가 있어요 means "there is / have" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "there is / have" uses the pattern N이/가 있어요 (N-i/ga isseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 시간이 있어요 ("I have time."). Use for existence or possession. 이 follows consonants; 가 follows vowels.

examples.en: I have time.
examples.note: Possession.

examples.en: Is there a bathroom here?
examples.note: Question.

examples.en: I have a reservation.
examples.note: Formal.

patterns.nuance: Use for existence or possession. 이 follows consonants; 가 follows vowels.
commonMistakes: Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.
Check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective before using it.

patterns.english: there is not / do not have
patterns.shortExplanation: N이/가 없어요 means "there is not / do not have" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: N이/가 없어요 (N-i/ga eopseoyo) = "there is not / do not have". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 시간이 없어요 ("I do not have time."). Use for absence or not having something.

usagePhrases.en: I do not have a reservation.

examples.en: I do not have time.
examples.note: Common.

examples.en: There is no water here.
examples.note: Existence.

examples.en: There is no problem.
examples.note: Formal.

patterns.nuance: Use for absence or not having something.
commonMistakes: Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.
Check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective before using it.

patterns.shortExplanation: N 주세요 means "please give me N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: N 주세요 (N juseyo) means "please give me N" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 물 주세요 ("Water, please."). Use for ordering or asking for an item. Add 좀 when you want the request to sound a little softer.

examples.en: Water, please.
examples.note: Basic.

examples.en: One of these, please.
examples.note: Quantity.

examples.en: Receipt, please.
examples.note: Shopping.

patterns.nuance: Use for ordering or asking for an item. Add 좀 when you want the request to sound a little softer.
commonMistakes: Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.
Check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective before using it.

patterns.shortExplanation: V고 싶어요 means "want to do" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "want to do" uses the pattern V고 싶어요 (V-go sipeoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 먹고 싶어요 ("I want to eat."). Attach 고 싶어요 to a verb stem to say what you want to do.

examples.en: I want to drink coffee.
examples.note: Desire.

examples.en: I want to go home.
examples.note: Travel.

examples.en: I want to rest today.
examples.note: Health.

patterns.nuance: Attach 고 싶어요 to a verb stem to say what you want to do.
commonMistakes: Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.
Check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective before using it.

patterns.shortExplanation: V고 싶지 않아요 means "do not want to do" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V고 싶지 않아요 (V-go sipji anayo) = "do not want to do". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 먹고 싶지 않아요 ("I do not want to eat."). Negative desire. Softer than saying 싫어요 in many situations.

usagePhrases.en: I do not want to eat.
I do not want to go.
I do not want to speak.
I do not want to wait.

examples.en: I do not want to eat right now.
examples.note: Soft refusal.

examples.en: I do not want to go today.
examples.note: Feeling.

examples.en: I do not want to talk about that.

patterns.shortExplanation: V/A-잖아요 means "you know (shared/obvious reason)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V/A-잖아요 (-janayo) = "you know (shared/obvious reason)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 내가 어제 말했잖아. ("I told you yesterday, remember."). Attach 잖아(요) straight onto a plain verb or adjective stem; there is no 으 buffer, so a final consonant changes nothing (많다 to 많잖아요). For past events use 았/었잖아요 (말했잖아요), and a noun adds 이잖아요 / 잖아요 (주말이잖아요, 친구잖아요). The core job is to remind the listener of a fact you both already share, almost like saying 'come on, you know this' — it flags the reason as common ground rather than new news. Because it presumes the other person should already know, leaning on it too hard sounds mildly accusatory ('I already TOLD you'), which is why it is a friends-and-close-coworkers ending with no true 합니다 form. The classic English-speaker trap is reaching for it to deliver fresh information ('나 어제 이사했잖아요' to someone who never knew you moved) — that lands as a passive-aggressive scold; for genuinely new background you want 거든요 instead.

usagePhrases.note: 았/었잖아 for a past event you both witnessed

patterns.nuance: Attach 잖아(요) straight onto a plain verb or adjective stem; there is no 으 buffer, so a final consonant changes nothing (많다 to 많잖아요). For past events use 았/었잖아요 (말했잖아요), and a noun adds 이잖아요 / 잖아요 (주말이잖아요, 친구잖아요). Because it presumes the other person should already know, leaning on it too hard sounds mildly accusatory ('I already TOLD you'), which is why it is a friends-and-close-coworkers ending with no true 합니다 form. The classic English-speaker trap is reaching for it to deliver fresh information ('나 어제 이사했잖아요' to someone who never knew you moved) — that lands as a passive-aggressive scold; for genuinely new background you want 거든요 instead.
commonMistakes: English speakers use 잖아요 to break news ('우리 헤어졌잖아요' to someone who didn't know) — but it presumes shared knowledge, so it sounds like a scolding 'as you should know.' For info the listener lacks, switch to 거든요 (헤어졌거든요).
Don't aim it at elders or strangers; even with 요 the 'you already know this' flavor reads as naggy or rude. Reserve it for friends and close colleagues, and soften with a gentle, not falling, tone.
It is not a yes/no question marker. 비싸잖아요? to ask 'isn't it expensive?' is unnatural — for confirmation use 비싸지 않아요? or 비싸죠?.

patterns.shortExplanation: V/A-거든요 means "(it's) because / here's the thing" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V/A-거든요 (-geodeunyo) means "(it's) because / here's the thing" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 저 오늘 못 가요. 약속이 있거든요. ("I can't come today. I have plans, see."). Add 거든(요) to a plain verb or adjective stem with no 으 buffer (작다 to 작거든요); past uses 았/었거든요 (잤거든요), and a noun adds 이거든요 (학생이거든요). It supplies a reason or piece of background the listener does NOT yet have — think of it as verbally opening a parenthesis: '(the thing is...)'. It frequently answers a 왜? or sets up the next sentence of a story, and the rising-then-settling intonation invites the listener to keep listening. The single most useful contrast for learners is 거든요 vs 잖아요: 거든요 delivers NEW information ('약속이 있거든요' = you didn't know I have plans), while 잖아요 recalls SHARED information ('약속 있다고 했잖아요' = I already told you). Said with a flat, clipped falling tone to a stranger it can sound a touch defensive or self-justifying, so let the pitch stay light.

It supplies a reason or piece of background the listener does NOT yet have — think of it as verbally opening a parenthesis: '(the thing is...)'. It frequently answers a 왜? or sets up the next sentence of a story, and the rising-then-settling intonation invites the listener to keep listening. The single most useful contrast for learners is 거든요 vs 잖아요: 거든요 delivers NEW information ('약속이 있거든요' = you didn't know I have plans), while 잖아요 recalls SHARED information ('약속 있다고 했잖아요' = I already told you). Said with a flat, clipped falling tone to a stranger it can sound a touch defensive or self-justifying, so let the pitch stay light.
commonMistakes: The number-one error is swapping 거든요 and 잖아요. 거든요 = the listener does NOT know yet; 잖아요 = you both already know. Telling a friend who already heard the news '나 차였거든' is fine as fresh disclosure, but if they witnessed it, 차였잖아 fits.
Don't use 거든요 as a neutral connector mid-sentence the way 아서/니까 work. It is sentence-final ('비싸거든요.'), not 'O 비싸거든 안 사요' — for a reason clause inside one sentence use 비싸서/비싸니까.
Avoid a hard, falling, clipped tone with strangers; '바쁘거든요!' snapped out sounds defensive, like 'because I'm busy, obviously.' Keep the pitch soft and informative.

patterns.shortExplanation: V/A-더라고요 means "I noticed / it turned out (firsthand)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "I noticed / it turned out (firsthand)" uses the pattern V/A-더라고요 (-deoragoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 가 보니까 생각보다 좋더라고요. ("When I went, it was better than I thought."). Attach 더라고(요) to a plain verb or adjective stem to report something you personally witnessed, felt, or realized at an earlier moment and are now relaying — the 더 carries the meaning 'I retrieved this from my own past observation.' Crucially it marks firsthand evidence: you must have seen, heard, or directly experienced it, never merely been told. Because the discovery belongs to you, you normally avoid it for your OWN deliberate actions or feelings you already knew about (X 나 학생이더라고요), though it works beautifully for self-realizations you stumbled onto (혼자 살아 보니까 외롭더라고요 = I found out, to my surprise, that I'm lonely). Compare it with plain past 았/었어요, which just states a finished fact flatly; 더라고요 adds 'and this is what I noticed about it,' a reporter's color. The 고 is routinely dropped in speech, leaving the very casual 더라.

commonMistakes: Don't use 더라고요 for secondhand news you only heard. '친구가 시험 떨어졌더라고요' is odd if you weren't there — for hearsay use 떨어졌대요 (-대요). 더라고요 demands your own eyes/ears.
Avoid it for your own settled, already-known feelings or intentions: '나 너 좋아하더라고요' is wrong because you already knew. It only fits feelings you newly discovered in yourself (살아 보니 외롭더라고요).

It is past-leaning observation, so don't pair it with a clearly present-and-ongoing 'right now.' For what you see this second, use 보여요/네요 (비 와요 / 비 오네요), not 비 오더라고요, which implies you noticed it earlier.
Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.
Check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective before using it.

patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ래요? means "shall we? / wanna? / will you?" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ래요? (-(eu)llaeyo) = "shall we? / wanna? / will you?". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 커피 마실래? ("Wanna grab coffee?"). Add ㄹ래요 after a vowel stem (가다 to 갈래요) and 을래요 after a consonant stem (먹다 to 먹을래요); ㄹ-final stems keep their single ㄹ and just add 래요 with no 으 buffer (놀다 to 놀래요, 만들다 to 만들래요). As a question it casually proposes doing something together or probes the listener's own will/preference; as a statement it declares your intention (저 갈래요 = I'll go / I feel like going). The sharp contrast to learn is ㄹ래요? vs ㄹ까요?: ㄹ까요? consults the other person's opinion on a shared plan ('shall we?', 같이 갈까요?), whereas ㄹ래요? asks what THEY personally want to do (같이 갈래요? = do you feel like going?), so it can sound a bit direct or even presumptuous to a superior. Because it centers the listener's raw will, polite as it is with 요, it is not deferential enough for a clear senior — there you upgrade to 가실래요? or 가시겠어요?.

examples.en: If you're free this weekend, wanna catch a movie?
examples.note: soft 반말 ask-out probing their willingness

examples.en: Wanna order delivery for lunch together?
examples.note: consonant stem 먹을래요 in an office invite

examples.en: Wanna grab a drink today? Just one round, light.
examples.note: 한 잔 하다 collocation for casual drinking

ㄹ-final stems take only 래요 with no 으: 놀다 to 놀래요 (never 놀을래요), 만들다 to 만들래요 (never 만들을래요).

Don't confuse it with ㄹ까요?. 갈까요? consults a shared decision ('shall we go?'), while 갈래요? asks the listener's personal want. Using 갈래요? when you mean a joint 'shall we' can sound like you're pushing your plan onto them.

patterns.shortExplanation: V/A-는데요 means "soft contrast / leading-on ending" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V/A-는데요 (-neundeyo) means "soft contrast / leading-on ending" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 지금 좀 바쁜데요. ("I'm kind of busy right now, though."). Verbs take 는데요 (가다 to 가는데요); adjectives take ㄴ데요 after a vowel (예쁘다 to 예쁜데요) and 은데요 after a consonant (좋다 to 좋은데요); 있다/없다 behave like verbs (재밌는데요) and the past for both is 았/었는데요 (재밌었는데요). Ending a sentence on 는데요 leaves the thought hanging open — it softens a statement, plants an unspoken 'but...,' or hands the conversational floor to the other person to react. Think of it as a half-finished bridge: you build the first span and let the listener walk across it. The crucial split for learners is the adjective rule: descriptive words must NOT take 는 (바쁜데요, not 바쁘는데요), because only action verbs and 있다/없다 use 는. Tonally, a trailing 는데요...? can convey surprise, mild pushback, or a polite hedge all at once depending on pitch, which is why it rarely stands fully alone with strangers without surrounding context.

usagePhrases.en: I'm kind of busy right now, though.
usagePhrases.note: adjective 바쁘다 to 바쁜데요, soft refusal

usagePhrases.en: I don't really know about that, though.
usagePhrases.note: verb 모르다 to 모르는데요, polite hedge

examples.ko: 그 사람 나쁘진 않은데요, 좀 제 스타일은 아니에요.
examples.romanization: geu saram nappeujin aneundeyo, jom je seutaireun anieyo.
examples.en: He's not bad, but he's just not my type.
examples.note: 는데요 sets up the gentle 'but' before the real point

examples.ko: 디자인은 괜찮은데요, 마감일은 좀 무리일 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: dijaineun gwaenchaneundeyo, magamireun jom muriil geot gatayo.
examples.en: The design's fine, but the deadline seems tight.
examples.note: softens office pushback by half-agreeing first

examples.ko: 저 지금 카페에 있는데, 너 어디야?
examples.romanization: jeo jigeum kapee inneunde, neo eodiya?
examples.en: I'm at the cafe right now, where are you?
examples.note: 는데 as a lead-in that invites a response

patterns.nuance: Verbs take 는데요 (가다 to 가는데요); adjectives take ㄴ데요 after a vowel (예쁘다 to 예쁜데요) and 은데요 after a consonant (좋다 to 좋은데요); 있다/없다 behave like verbs (재밌는데요) and the past for both is 았/었는데요 (재밌었는데요). commonMistakes: Never put 는 on a plain adjective: it's 바쁜데요 / 좋은데요, not 바쁘는데요 / 좋는데요. Only verbs and 있다/없다 take the 는 form.

Don't mistake sentence-final 는데요 for the mid-sentence connector -는데. Here it deliberately trails off to imply more; '날씨가 좋은데요.' standing alone hints 'so shall we go out?' and needs context or a follow-up to land.

Watch the contrast 는데 vs 지만. Both mean 'but,' but 는데 sets a soft, open backdrop that invites continuation (좋은데 비싸요 = it's nice, and well, it's pricey...), while 지만 states a flatter, more clear-cut contrast (좋지만 비싸요 = it's nice but it's expensive). Overusing 지만 in chat sounds stiff.

patterns.english: I'm planning to / I intend to
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)려고요 means "I'm planning to / I intend to" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "I'm planning to / I intend to" uses the pattern V-(으)려고요 (-(eu)ryeogoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 저 일찍 자려고요. ("I'm planning to sleep early."). Add 려고요 after a vowel stem (자다 to 자려고요) and 으려고요 after a consonant stem (모으다 to 모으려고요, 찾다 to 찾으려고요) to announce your own pre-formed intention, very often as a reply to '뭐 할 거예요?'. It is the relaxed, conversational clipping of 려고 해요, with the 해요 simply left implied. The contrast you must nail is 려고 vs 으러: both involve purpose, but 으러 attaches only to a movement verb to mark the goal of going/coming (사러 가요 = I go in order to buy), while 려고 states a standalone plan/aim and pairs with any verb (사려고요 = I'm planning to buy). A second caution: 려고요 reports the speaker's intention, so it is awkward to assert flatly about someone else's plan — for a third person's apparent intent you soften to 려나 봐요 or simply ask them.

usagePhrases.en: I'm just gonna rest at home today.
I'm trying to save up some money.
I'm planning to switch jobs next year.

examples.ko: 이번 주말엔 소개팅 한번 나가 보려고요.
examples.romanization: ibeon jumaren sogaeting hanbeon naga boryeogoyo.
examples.en: I'm thinking of trying a blind date this weekend.
examples.note: 나가 보다 + 려고요 softens to 'thinking of trying'

examples.ko: 월세 너무 비싸서 좀 더 싼 데로 이사 가려고요.
examples.romanization: wolse neomu bissaseo jom deo ssan dero isa garyeogoyo.
examples.en: Rent's too high, so I'm planning to move somewhere cheaper.
examples.note: reason clause + intended action

examples.en: I'm planning to leave after the first round of the work dinner.
examples.note: sequences plans with 가고 ... 빠지려고요

patterns.nuance: Add 려고요 after a vowel stem (자다 to 자려고요) and 으려고요 after a consonant stem (모으다 to 모으려고요, 찾다 to 찾으려고요) to announce your own pre-formed intention, very often as a reply to '뭐 할 거예요?'. A second caution: 려고요 reports the speaker's intention, so it is awkward to assert flatly about someone else's plan — for a third person's apparent intent you soften to 려나 봐요 or simply ask them.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse 으려고 with 으러. Use 으러 only with go/come for the purpose of an errand (밥 먹으러 가요 = I go to eat); use 려고 for a standalone intention with any verb (밥 먹으려고요 = I'm planning to eat). '밥 먹으러요' as a full answer is wrong.
State it only about your own plans. For someone else's intention, '친구가 오려고요' sounds off — say 친구가 오려나 봐요 ('seems like my friend intends to come') or just report 온대요.
Don't graft a future ending on top: it's already forward-looking, so 자려고 할 거예요 is redundant. Say 자려고요 or, more fully, 자려고 해요.

patterns.shortExplanation: V-는 중이에요 means "in the middle of doing" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-는 중이에요 (-neun jung-ieyo) = "in the middle of doing". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 지금 가는 중이에요. ("I'm on my way right now."). Attach 는 중이에요 to a plain verb stem to stress that an action is actively unfolding at this very moment; ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ before 는 (만들다 to 만드는 중이에요, 살다 to 사는 중이에요). The Sino-Korean noun 中 (중) literally means 'the middle/midst,' so 가는 중 paints 'in the very midst of going.' With a bare noun you skip the verb form and say N 중이에요 (회의 중이에요 = mid-meeting, 공사 중 = under construction). The contrast to internalize is 는 중이에요 vs plain 고 있어요: 고 있어요 broadly marks ongoing or even habitual action (요즘 한국어 배우고 있어요 = I'm learning Korean these days), while 는 중이에요 zooms in on this single moment of being mid-task and resists habitual or stretched readings. Because it needs a real unfolding action, it rejects adjectives and stative verbs like 알다/있다 — there is no 아는 중이에요.

usagePhrases.en: I'm on my way right now.
I'm in the middle of eating.
I'm in the middle of working.
usagePhrases.note: single ongoing task, not a habit

examples.ko: 미안, 지금 일하는 중이라 이따 톡할게.
examples.romanization: mian, jigeum ilhaneun jungira itta tokalge.
examples.en: Sorry, I'm working right now, I'll text you later.
examples.note: 는 중이라 = 'because I'm mid-task' giving a reason

examples.ko: 거의 다 왔어요, 지금 엘리베이터 타는 중이에요.
examples.romanization: geoui da wasseoyo, jigeum ellibeiteo taneun jungieyo.
examples.en: I'm almost there, getting in the elevator now.
examples.note: pinpoints the action happening this second

examples.en: I'm on a diet, so I'll pass on the chicken today.
examples.note: noun 다이어트 + 중이라 for an ongoing state

patterns.nuance: Attach 는 중이에요 to a plain verb stem to stress that an action is actively unfolding at this very moment; ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ before 는 (만들다 to 만드는 중이에요, 살다 to 사는 중이에요). commonMistakes: Don't attach it to adjectives or stative verbs: 아는 중이에요 / 예쁜 중이에요 are wrong because there's no unfolding action. For knowing a state, just say 알아요.
It marks the present midst, not the near future. 가는 중이에요 means 'I'm already en route,' NOT 'I'm about to leave.' For 'about to,' use 가려고요 or 곧 갈게요.
Don't overuse it for long-term, habitual things. 'These days I'm learning Korean' is 한국어 배우고 있어요, not 배우는 중이에요, which would oddly imply you're mid-lesson at this instant.
Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.
Check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective before using it.

patterns.shortExplanation: V/A-나 봐요 means "seems like / I guess (from evidence)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V/A-나 봐요 (-na bwayo) means "seems like / I guess (from evidence)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 비 오나 봐요. ("Looks like it's raining."). Verbs and 있다/없다 take 나 봐요 (오다 to 오나 봐요, 있다 to 있나 봐요); descriptive adjectives instead take ㄴ가/은가 봐요 (바쁘다 to 바쁜가 봐요, 좋다 to 좋은가 봐요), and nouns take 인가 봐요 (신입인가 봐요). The literal sense — 'I look (봐요) at whether (나)...' — captures that you are inferring from visible evidence, drawing a careful conclusion from something you observed rather than asserting it outright. The contrast learners need is 나 봐요 vs 겠어요/것 같아요: 겠어요 leans on gut feeling or general assumption (춥겠어요 = it must be cold, I imagine), and 것 같아요 is the all-purpose 'I think/seems,' while 나 봐요 specifically signals 'based on this clue in front of me, I gather...'. Since it is an outside guess, you don't apply it to your own clear feelings — 나 슬픈가 봐 (I guess I'm sad) only works as wry self-observation, never as a plain statement of how you feel.

usagePhrases.note: verb 오다 to 오나 봐요, inferring from a clue

usagePhrases.en: Seems like those two are dating.
usagePhrases.note: 반말 나 봐, guessing from what you saw
adjective takes ㄴ가/은가 봐요, not 나 봐요

examples.ko: 걔가 읽씹하네. 나한테 관심 없나 봐.
examples.romanization: gyaega ilkssipane. nahante gwansim eopsna bwa.
examples.en: He left my message on read. Guess he's not into me.
examples.note: 없다 takes 없나 봐, conclusion from evidence

examples.ko: 팀장님 아직 안 가셨네요. 마감 때문에 바쁜가 봐요.
examples.romanization: timjangnim ajik an gasyeonneyo. magam ttaemune bappeunga bwayo.
examples.en: The team lead hasn't left yet. Must be busy with the deadline.
examples.note: adjective 바쁜가 봐요 inferred from an observed fact

examples.ko: 다들 그 집 올리던데, 거기 핫플인가 봐요.
examples.romanization: dadeul geu jip ollideonde, geogi hatpeuringa bwayo.
examples.en: Everyone's posting that place; must be the new hotspot.
examples.note: noun 핫플 + 인가 봐요 from social-media evidence

patterns.nuance: Verbs and 있다/없다 take 나 봐요 (오다 to 오나 봐요, 있다 to 있나 봐요); descriptive adjectives instead take ㄴ가/은가 봐요 (바쁘다 to 바쁜가 봐요, 좋다 to 좋은가 봐요), and nouns take 인가 봐요 (신입인가 봐요). The contrast learners need is 나 봐요 vs 겠어요/것 같아요: 겠어요 leans on gut feeling or general assumption (춥겠어요 = it must be cold, I imagine), and 것 같아요 is the all-purpose 'I think/seems,' while 나 봐요 specifically signals 'based on this clue in front of me, I gather...'. Since it is an outside guess, you don't apply it to your own clear feelings — 나 슬픈가 봐 (I guess I'm sad) only works as wry self-observation, never as a plain statement of how you feel.
commonMistakes: Use ㄴ가/은가 봐요 for plain adjectives, not 나 봐요: 좋은가 봐요 / 바쁜가 봐요 (never 좋나 봐요 / 바쁘나 봐요). Verbs and 있다/없다 are the ones that take 나 봐요.
Don't use it about your own feelings you plainly know. '나 화났나 봐요' to report your own clear anger is odd; 나 봐요 is an outside-looking-in guess, fine only as ironic self-discovery.

Don't blur it with 겠어요. 비 오겠어요 is a forecast-style assumption ('it'll probably rain'); 비 오나 봐요 means you see a clue right now (wet ground, dark sky) and infer it's raining. Pick by whether you have present evidence.

patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 means "almost (did but didn't)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "almost (did but didn't)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 (-(eu)l ppeonhaesseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 늦을 뻔했어요. ("I almost ran late."). Add ㄹ 뻔했어요 after a vowel stem (늦다... wait, 늦다 is consonant — 넘어지다 to 넘어질 뻔했어요) and 을 뻔했어요 after a consonant stem (늦다 to 늦을 뻔했어요); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (울다 to 울 뻔했어요). It describes an event that very nearly occurred but ultimately did NOT — a near-miss or close call — and it is locked in the past tense 했어요 because the moment of almost-happening is already over. The defining nuance is the relief or alarm baked in: you escaped the outcome, so it usually pairs with a 살았다-style payoff (덕분에 살았어요, 겨우 피했어요) or a hair-raising setup. Don't confuse it with 을 것 같았어요 ('it seemed like it would'), which is a guess about likelihood; 뻔했어요 asserts the thing was a whisker away from really happening. The English trap is using it for things that DID happen — 'I almost finished' meaning you nearly completed it is NOT 끝낼 뻔했어요 (which would mean you came close but failed); for that, use 거의 끝냈어요.

usagePhrases.note: consonant stem 늦다 to 늦을 뻔했어요
반말 vowel stem 넘어지다 to 넘어질 뻔했어
ㄹ-stem 울다 drops ㄹ to 울 뻔했어요

examples.note: 겨우 underscores the narrow escape

examples.en: I almost forgot the deadline; the reminder saved me.

patterns.nuance: Add ㄹ 뻔했어요 after a vowel stem (늦다... wait, 늦다 is consonant — 넘어지다 to 넘어질 뻔했어요) and 을 뻔했어요 after a consonant stem (늦다 to 늦을 뻔했어요); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ (울다 to 울 뻔했어요). It describes an event that very nearly occurred but ultimately did NOT — a near-miss or close call — and it is locked in the past tense 했어요 because the moment of almost-happening is already over. The defining nuance is the relief or alarm baked in: you escaped the outcome, so it usually pairs with a 살았다-style payoff (덕분에 살았어요, 겨우 피했어요) or a hair-raising setup. patterns.shortExplanation: V/A-는 척하다 means "to pretend / act as if" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V/A-는 척하다 (-neun cheokada) = "to pretend / act as if". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 자는 척했어. ("I pretended to be asleep."). Present-tense verbs take 는 척하다 (자다 to 자는 척해요); descriptive adjectives take ㄴ/은 척하다 (예쁘다 to 예쁜 척해요, 괜찮다 to 괜찮은 척해요); and a completed past action takes 은/ㄴ 척하다 (듣다 to 들은 척하다 → 안 들은 척해요). The bound noun 척 means 'a put-on pose,' so the construction literally stages an act you don't truly feel or do — you perform the outside of a state without the inside. It carries a clear undertone of falseness or insincerity, which is why it pairs naturally with 그냥, 일부러, or 안 (그냥 못 본 척했어요). The near-twin 체 (못 본 체했어요) means the same thing with a slightly bookish, old-fashioned flavor; in everyday speech 척 dominates. patterns.english: I think / it seems / it looks like (a softened guess or opinion)
patterns.shortExplanation: A/V-는 것 같아요 means "I think / it seems / it looks like (a softened guess or opinion)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: A/V-는 것 같아요 (-neun geot gatayo) means "I think / it seems / it looks like (a softened guess or opinion)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 맛있는 것 같아요 ("I think it's tasty"). Literally 'it is like the thing that...' (것 = thing/fact, 같다 = to be like/same), so you are framing your statement as a resemblance to truth rather than a flat fact — that hedge is the whole point and is why Koreans reach for it constantly. The form tracks tense on the modifier: present verb takes -는 (가는 것 같아요), adjective and past verb take -(으)ㄴ (추운 것 같아요, 먹은 것 같아요), and a future/probability guess takes -(으)ㄹ (올 것 같아요). Contrast it with the blunter guess word 같다 used as -겠- (오겠어요 'it'll surely come') and with -나 보다/-(으)ㄴ가 보다, which infer from outside evidence ('looks like, judging by what I see'); -는 것 같다 is your own soft impression, even about your own feelings (저 그 사람 좋아하는 것 같아요 = I think I like him). Register: neutral-polite and very safe, so people even soften their own opinions with it to avoid sounding pushy. The English-speaker trap is treating it as 'I think THAT (a clause)' and trying to keep a full sentence + 라고 생각해요; here the clause must be squeezed into a modifier before 것. In speech 것 almost always shrinks to 거: -는 거 같아요.

patterns.english: decided to / made up my mind to (often a plan or promise)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-기로 했어요 means "decided to / made up my mind to (often a plan or promise)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "decided to / made up my mind to (often a plan or promise)" uses the pattern V-기로 했어요 (-giro haesseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 담배 끊기로 했어요 ("I decided to quit smoking"). Here -기 turns the verb into a noun ('the doing of X') and -로 marks it as the direction/terms you settled on, so the literal feel is 'I set things toward doing X' — a resolution or an arrangement. Attach -기로 하다 straight onto any verb stem with zero sound change (운동하다 → 운동하기로, 끊다 → 끊기로), then report it in the past, 했어요, because the deciding is already done; the present 하다 (-기로 해요) reads as 'let's decide to / it's agreed that we'll', a softer proposal, which is the key contrast learners miss. Compare -(으)ㄹ게요 'I'll (promise to you, here and now)' and -(으)려고 해요 'I intend/plan to': -기로 했어요 is the firmest — a concluded decision or a mutual pact, often a New Year's resolution or a plan made with others (같이 가기로 했어요). It also commonly pairs with 약속하다 and 마음먹다. Negative puts the negation INSIDE the embedded clause — 안 V-기로 했어요 (안 가기로 했어요) or the smoother V-지 않기로 했어요 (가지 않기로 했어요); don't move 안 outside as V-기로 안 했어요, which flips the meaning to 'didn't decide to V'. English-speaker pitfall: don't translate 'decided' with 결정했어요 every time — 결정하다 is heavy/formal (a board decides a policy); everyday personal resolutions overwhelmingly use -기로 했어요.

patterns.english: ended up (completely) doing it — finished it off, often with regret or relief
patterns.shortExplanation: V-아/어 버렸어요 means "ended up (completely) doing it — finished it off, often with regret or relief" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-아/어 버렸어요 (-a/eo beoryeosseoyo) = "ended up (completely) doing it — finished it off, often with regret or relief". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 다 먹어 버렸어요 ("I ended up eating it all"). 버리다 on its own means 'to throw away', and as an auxiliary it keeps that flavor: the action is done all the way, finished off, gone past the point of return — and that completeness carries emotion, either regret ('darn, I went and did it') or relief ('there, it's finally off my plate'). Build it by taking the verb's -아/어 connector and adding 버리다: stems with ㅏ/ㅗ take -아 버리다 (가다 → 가 버리다, 오다 → 와 버리다), other stems take -어 버리다 (먹다 → 먹어 버리다, 잊다 → 잊어 버리다), and 하다 → 해 버리다. Contrast its sibling -아/어 두다/놓다, which means doing something and leaving it ready ('do it in advance and keep it'), the opposite mood from 버리다's 'do it and be rid of it'; and note that 버리다 colors the feeling, while -았/었어요 alone just reports the fact. It loves 다, 그냥, 벌써 (다 먹어 버렸어요, 그냥 가 버렸어요). English-speaker pitfall: there is no English auxiliary for this, so learners drop it — but plain 다 썼어요 'I spent it all' loses the rueful punch of 다 써 버렸어요 'I went and blew it all'. Spacing matters too: write 버리다 as a separate word from the -아/어 form.

patterns.english: I'm worried that... / in case... (anxiety about something happening)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ까 봐요 means "I'm worried that... / in case... (anxiety about something happening)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ까 봐요 (-(eu)lkka bwayo) means "I'm worried that... / in case... (anxiety about something happening)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 늦을까 봐요 ("I'm worried I'll be late"). This is the wondering ending -(으)ㄹ까 ('I wonder if...') frozen in front of 보다 ('to see/consider'), so the literal nuance is 'considering that maybe X might happen' — and what falls out is anxiety: you are bracing for an unwanted possibility. Attach -ㄹ까 봐(요) to vowel-ending stems (가다 → 갈까 봐, 오다 → 올까 봐) and -을까 봐(요) to consonant stems (늦다 → 늦을까 봐, 밀리다 → 밀릴까 봐); for a worry about something already over use -았/었을까 봐요 (놓쳤을까 봐요 = worried I missed it). The sharp contrast to memorize is with the look-alike question -(으)ㄹ까요? 'shall we? / I wonder, do you think?' (갈까요? = shall we go?) — same syllables, totally different job: -ㄹ까 봐요 is never a question, it states a fear. Mid-sentence it becomes -(으)ㄹ까 봐(서) + the precaution you take because of the fear (비 올까 봐 우산 챙겼어요). It also pairs naturally with 걱정하다/불안하다. English-speaker pitfall: don't render 'in case' with 만약 + a conditional; 'in case it rains' is 비 올까 봐, and crucially the worry clause must describe a bad/unwanted outcome — you wouldn't use it for something you hope for.

I don't eat it because I'm afraid of gaining weight
I didn't say it for fear of getting scolded

patterns.english: (someone) said that... — reporting a statement someone made
patterns.shortExplanation: V-다고 했어요 means "(someone) said that... — reporting a statement someone made" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "(someone) said that... — reporting a statement someone made" uses the pattern V-다고 했어요 (-dago haesseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 바쁘다고 했어요 ("He said he's busy"). The endings split by word class, which is the heart of the pattern: present-tense VERBS take -ㄴ다고/-는다고 (가다 → 간다고 했어요, 먹다 → 먹는다고 했어요), but ADJECTIVES and 이다 attach plain -다고 (춥다 → 춥다고 했어요), and the past is -았/었다고 했어요 for both. Nouns use N(이)라고 했어요. The contrast that trips learners is the question version -냐고 했어요 ('asked whether...') — statements report with -다고, questions with -냐고, and mixing them is the classic reported-speech error. In casual speech everything contracts to -대(요): 간대요 (= 간다고 해요), 바쁘대 (= 바쁘다고 해), a form you'll hear far more than the full one. patterns.english: it's worth doing / good enough to / can be done (reasonably)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 만해요 means "it's worth doing / good enough to / can be done (reasonably)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 만해요 (-(eu)l manhaeyo) means "it's worth doing / good enough to / can be done (reasonably)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 볼 만해요 ("It's worth watching"). 만하다 here means 'to be worth / be of a level that justifies it', so V-(으)ㄹ 만하다 says the action is worth the effort, or at least decent and tolerable — note that 'decent' often means faint praise, not glowing. Attach -ㄹ 만하다 to vowel-ending stems (보다 → 볼 만하다, 가다 → 갈 만하다) and -을 만하다 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 만하다, 참다 → 참을 만하다); the past is -(으)ㄹ 만했어요. Two contrasts sharpen it: don't confuse this 만하다 (one word, 'worth doing', after -(으)ㄹ) with the size-comparison 만하다 ('as big as', as in 손바닥만 하다); and weigh it against the stronger -(으)ㄹ 가치가 있다 'has real value/merit' — -(으)ㄹ 만하다 is lighter, the register of 'eh, it's worth a look' or 'edible enough'. It leans on the future-potential modifier -(으)ㄹ precisely because you're judging whether doing it would pay off. patterns.english: (it) ended up / came to be that... — a change of state, often not fully by your own choice
patterns.shortExplanation: V-게 됐어요 means "(it) ended up / came to be that... — a change of state, often not fully by your own choice" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "(it) ended up / came to be that... — a change of state, often not fully by your own choice" uses the pattern V-게 됐어요 (-ge dwaesseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 한국에 살게 됐어요 ("I ended up living in Korea"). 되다 means 'to become / come about', so V-게 되다 frames an outcome as something that turned out that way through circumstances, not pure personal will — which is exactly why it sounds humble and is the polite default for explaining how your life changed. It often appears with 우연히, 결국, 어쩌다 보니. English-speaker pitfall: learners translate it as plain 'became' and drop 되다, collapsing 알게 됐어요 'I came to know' into 알았어요 'I knew/found out' — and they overuse the willful 결정했어요 where a modest 게 됐어요 is the socially smoother choice.

patterns.english: while you're at it / since you're already doing it anyway
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 김에 means "while you're at it / since you're already doing it anyway" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ 김에 (-(eu)n gime) = "while you're at it / since you're already doing it anyway". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 나온 김에 ("while I'm out anyway"). 김 here is the noun 'occasion/opportunity created by an action', so -(으)ㄴ 김에 means 'taking advantage of the fact that you've (already) done X, also do Y' — the second clause is the real point, riding for free on the first. Attach -ㄴ 김에 to vowel-ending stems (나오다 → 나온 김에) and -은 김에 to consonant stems (씻다 → 씻은 김에); a present, ongoing action takes -는 김에 (청소하는 김에 'while I'm cleaning anyway'). The set phrase 말 나온 김에 ('since it's come up in conversation') is worth memorizing whole. Contrast it with two near-misses: -(으)면서 means doing two things simultaneously and equally ('while/as'), whereas 김에 is opportunistic and tilts toward the add-on; and -(으)니까 just gives a reason ('since/because'), without the 'might as well piggyback' flavor. English-speaker pitfall: the literal logic 'since you WILL go anyway' tempts learners to use the future -(으)ㄹ 김에, but 김에 attaches to the completed/initiated action with -(으)ㄴ (or ongoing -는) — say 가는 김에 / 나온 김에, never 갈 김에. It also pairs naturally with 이왕 ('seeing as you're at it') for extra emphasis.

patterns.english: to the extent/point that... / so much that...
patterns.shortExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄹ 정도로 means "to the extent/point that... / so much that..." as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: A/V-(으)ㄹ 정도로 (-(eu)l jeongdoro) means "to the extent/point that... / so much that..." — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 죽을 정도로 피곤해요 ("I'm dead tired (tired to the point of dying)"). 정도 is the Sino-Korean noun 程度 (程 'degree' + 度 'measure'), literally 'degree/measure', so A/V-(으)ㄹ 정도로 sets a vivid 'enough-to' benchmark that conveys how intense something is — you describe a degree by naming what it could reach. Attach -ㄹ 정도로 to vowel-ending stems (아프다 → 아플 정도로) and -을 정도로 to consonant stems (죽다 → 죽을 정도로); the benchmark clause comes first and the thing being measured follows (죽을 정도로 피곤해요 = tired to the point of dying). You can also close a sentence with -(으)ㄹ 정도예요 'it's to that extent'. Contrast it with -(으)ㄹ 만큼, which is very close ('as much as / to the degree that') but more neutral/quantitative and often interchangeable, whereas -(으)ㄹ 정도로 leans expressive and is the go-to for hyperbole (죽을 정도로, 미칠 정도로); and don't confuse 정도 here with 정도 meaning 'about/approximately' (한 시간 정도 'about an hour'). It rides the future-potential modifier -(으)ㄹ because the benchmark is a hypothetical reach, not a real event. English-speaker pitfall: learners drop in the present -는 (아프는 정도로) by habit, but the slot needs -(으)ㄹ (아플 정도로); and they try to map it onto 'so ... that' word order — in Korean the 'that' clause (the degree) goes FIRST, before the predicate it modifies.

usagePhrases.note: Stock hyperbole; benchmark 죽을 정도로 precedes 피곤해요

patterns.english: as much as / to the same degree as (N)
patterns.shortExplanation: N만큼 means "as much as / to the same degree as (N)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "as much as / to the same degree as (N)" uses the pattern N만큼 (-mankeum). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 너만큼 잘하고 싶어요 ("I want to be as good as you"). 만큼 attaches straight onto a noun with no space and no sound change (너→너만큼, 형→형만큼, 돈→돈만큼) and sets that noun as the yardstick: 'as Adj as N.' It also rides on a verb/adjective modifier — 먹은 만큼 (as much as you ate), 노력한 만큼 (as much as you tried) — but THERE 만큼 is spaced and means 'in proportion to,' which is the dividing line learners blur: glued to a bare noun = equal degree, spaced after -은/는/을 = proportional payoff. Compare it with 처럼: 만큼 measures AMOUNT/degree ('as much as'), while 처럼 measures MANNER/likeness ('like, in the way of'), so 너처럼 means 'like you (in style)' but 너만큼 means 'to the same level as you.' The big English-speaker trap is that 만큼 has no separate word for 'as'; you do NOT add a second 'as,' and the adjective comes LAST: 너만큼 잘해 (literally 'you-as-much do-well'), never 만큼 잘해 너.

usagePhrases.note: Bare noun as the standard of comparison

patterns.english: considering it's (an) N / for an N (it's surprisingly...)
patterns.shortExplanation: N치고 means "considering it's (an) N / for an N (it's surprisingly...)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: N치고 (-chigo) = "considering it's (an) N / for an N (it's surprisingly...)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 초보치고 잘하네요 ("You're good for a beginner"). 치고 glues to a noun with no space (초보→초보치고, 겨울→겨울치고) and means 'measured against the norm for an N, this defies that norm' — i.e. better/worse/different than an N usually is. Add 는 → 치고는 to lean harder into the contrast (주말치고는 한산해요). The closest cousin is N에 비해 ('compared to'), but the line is sharp: 에 비해 lines up two separate things ('A에 비해 B' = relative to A, B is...), whereas 치고 stays inside ONE category and plays the member off its own stereotype ('for a beginner, surprisingly good'). There's also a flipped use — N치고 + a negative = 'there's no N that isn't...': 한국 사람치고 김치 안 먹는 사람 없어요 ('no Korean doesn't eat kimchi'); context separates the two instantly. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 치다 (to hit) — this 치고 is a fixed comparative particle, and learners wrongly try to translate 'for' with 위해 (which means 'for the sake of,' a totally different 'for').

usagePhrases.note: Core 'better than the norm for an N'
치고 + a description that breaks the stereotype
치고는 stresses the contrast more strongly

patterns.english: looks / seems (a certain way) — judging by appearance
patterns.shortExplanation: A-아/어 보이다 means "looks / seems (a certain way) — judging by appearance" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: A-아/어 보이다 (-a/eo boida) means "looks / seems (a certain way) — judging by appearance" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 피곤해 보여요 ("You look tired"). Take an adjective's -아/어 form and add 보이다 (spaced): ㅏ/ㅗ stems take -아 보이다 (좋다→좋아 보이다, 작다→작아 보이다), others take -어 보이다 (힘들다→힘들어 보이다), 하다 adjectives → 해 보이다 (피곤하다→피곤해 보이다), and ㅡ-stems drop the ㅡ (예쁘다→예뻐 보이다, 바쁘다→바빠 보이다). The whole point is JUDGING BY SIGHT — 보이다 is the passive/intransitive of 보다 ('to see'), so it literally says 'X shows up as Adj to the eye.' The crucial contrast is with -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다 ('seems'): 것 같다 covers ANY evidence — texts, tone, a hunch — while 아/어 보이다 is reserved for what you actually SEE, which is the exact pitfall: 'he seems busy (from his messages)' must be 바쁜 것 같아요, not 바빠 보여요. Also keep -아/어 보이다 (looks) apart from the identical-looking -아/어 보다 ('try doing'); only adjectives + 보이다 give the 'appears' meaning, while verbs + 보다 give 'attempt.'

usagePhrases.note: Reading someone's face — the everyday use

commonMistakes: Using it for non-visual guesses: 'It seems he's busy (judging by his texts)' is 바쁜 것 같아요, not 바빠 보여요 — 보이다 needs something you can literally SEE.

Forgetting the ㅡ-drop: 예쁘다 becomes 예뻐 보여요, not 예쁘어 보여요, and 바쁘다 → 바빠 보여요, not 바쁘어 보여요.

patterns.shortExplanation: N에 비해 means "compared to / in comparison with (N)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "compared to / in comparison with (N)" uses the pattern N에 비해 (-e bihae). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 작년에 비해 비싸요 ("It's expensive compared to last year"). 에 비해 attaches to a noun (작년→작년에 비해, 가격→가격에 비해) and frames 'relative to N, this is more/less...' 비해 is the -아/어 form of the Sino-Korean verb 비하다 (比하다, 比 'compare'); fuller variants are 에 비해서 (서 added, conversational) and the written/formal 에 비하여. To compare against a clause, nominalize first: V-는 것에 비해 (사는 것에 비해 = compared to living...). It overlaps with N치고 but differs sharply: 에 비해 lines up TWO separate items as a measuring stick ('A에 비해 B'), while 치고 keeps one item inside its own category ('for an N'). English-speaker pitfalls cluster here: (1) the particle is 에, not 와/하고, so 'compared TO last year' is 작년에 비해, never 작년과 비해 or 작년 비해; (2) don't substitute the everyday verb 비교하다 (比較하다, 'to compare') — the set adverbial phrase is locked as 비하다→비해, so 가격과 비교해서 is grammatical as a full verb but is NOT this fixed pattern.

To compare against a clause, nominalize first: V-는 것에 비해 (사는 것에 비해 = compared to living...). It overlaps with N치고 but differs sharply: 에 비해 lines up TWO separate items as a measuring stick ('A에 비해 B'), while 치고 keeps one item inside its own category ('for an N'). English-speaker pitfalls cluster here: (1) the particle is 에, not 와/하고, so 'compared TO last year' is 작년에 비해, never 작년과 비해 or 작년 비해; (2) don't substitute the everyday verb 비교하다 (比較하다, 'to compare') — the set adverbial phrase is locked as 비하다→비해, so 가격과 비교해서 is grammatical as a full verb but is NOT this fixed pattern.
commonMistakes: Using the wrong particle: it's N에 비해, not N과/와 비해 or bare N 비해. 'Compared to last year' = 작년에 비해.
Swapping in 비교해(서): the fixed phrase is 비하다 → 비해. 비교하다 is a normal verb ('가격을 비교해 봤어요' = I compared the prices), but it is not this set 에 비해 pattern.
Trying to attach it straight to a verb: you can't say 사는 에 비해. Nominalize first — 사는 것에 비해 (compared to living/buying).

patterns.english: even though / despite the fact that
patterns.shortExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 means "even though / despite the fact that" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 (-(eu)nde-do) = "even though / despite the fact that". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 열심히 했는데도 떨어졌어요 ("Even though I worked hard, I failed"). This is the -는데/-(으)ㄴ데 background ending plus 도 ('even'), literally 'even given the situation that...' Present verbs take -는데도 (먹다→먹는데도, 하다→하는데도); adjectives take -(으)ㄴ데도 (춥다→추운데도, 바쁘다→바쁜데도); the past for both is -았/었는데도 (잤는데도 = even though I slept); nouns take N인데도. It means 'even though X (which I'd expect to lead elsewhere), surprisingly Y.' The sharp contrast is with plain -지만 ('but'): -지만 is a flat, neutral 'but' that just joins two facts, whereas -는데도 carries the speaker's surprise or frustration that the expected consequence FAILED to follow (열심히 했지만 떨어졌어요 = 'I worked hard but failed,' a calm statement; 열심히 했는데도 떨어졌어요 = 'I worked hard and STILL failed?!', with felt letdown). English-speaker pitfall: the 'still/anyway' that English often adds in the second clause is already baked into -는데도, and the most common error is picking the wrong modifier — adjectives never take -는데도.

Even though it's cold, I (still) go out

Even though I'm broke, I bought it again

patterns.english: only / merely (do) — nothing more than that
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 means "only / merely (do) — nothing more than that" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 (-(eu)l ppun-ida) means "only / merely (do) — nothing more than that" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 할 뿐이에요 ("I'm just doing it (that's all)"). Attach -ㄹ 뿐이다 to vowel-ending stems (하다→할 뿐이다) and -을 뿐이다 to consonant stems (믿다→믿을 뿐이다); 뿐 is a bound noun, so it is spaced from the modifier. The past is -았/었을 뿐이다 (도와줬을 뿐이에요 = I only helped), and a noun takes N일 뿐이다 (친구일 뿐이에요). It pins the situation down to exactly ONE thing — 'that's all there is to it' — and is frequently defensive or modest. Watch the close rival 만 ('only'): 만 narrows the noun/object ('나만 = only ME'), but -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 narrows the whole PREDICATE/action ('I only DID, nothing else'), and the two even team up as -(으)ㄹ 뿐 (just) for emphasis. The flagship English-speaker pitfall is confusing -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 with -(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라: the first CLOSES a statement off ('merely that and no more'), while the second OPENS it up ('not only that, but also'). They look almost identical but point in opposite directions.

usagePhrases.note: Limiting your action to one thing
Modest set phrase, very common in interviews
Noun → N일 뿐이에요; clearing up assumptions

examples.en: I'm just listening, that's all.
examples.note: Simple 'nothing more than this one action' with 있을 뿐이에요

patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 means "not only... (but also)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "not only... (but also)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 (-(eu)l ppunman anira). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 맛있을 뿐만 아니라 싸요 ("It's not only tasty but also cheap"). Attach -ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 to vowel stems (싸다→쌀 뿐만 아니라) and -을 뿐만 아니라 to consonant stems (좋다→좋을 뿐만 아니라); the past is -았/었을 뿐만 아니라. Literally it's 뿐 ('only') + 만 ('just') + 아니라 ('and not'), i.e. 'it isn't JUST that...,' so the second clause piles on something MORE, typically marked with 도 ('also'): 'not only A, but B too.' The handiest shape is the noun form N뿐만 아니라 (돈뿐만 아니라 = not only money), where 뿐만 glues onto the noun. The near-twin is -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다, which does the OPPOSITE — it shuts a statement down to one thing, while 뿐만 아니라 adds a second; one closes, one opens. A second useful contrast is N뿐만 아니라 vs N도 ('also'): 도 just tags one extra item, whereas 뿐만 아니라 explicitly says 'even beyond the obvious first thing.' English-speaker pitfall: don't separate the noun with a space (it's 돈뿐만, not 돈 뿐만), and remember the pairing 'not only A but also B' is realized with a trailing 도 in clause two, not a fronted word for 'also.'

usagePhrases.en: It's not only tasty but also cheap
usagePhrases.note: Two pluses stacked on a verb/adjective stem

usagePhrases.en: Not just me — everyone's like that

patterns.english: in order to / for the sake of (doing)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-기 위해(서) means "in order to / for the sake of (doing)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-기 위해(서) (-gi wihae(seo)) = "in order to / for the sake of (doing)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 돈을 모으기 위해 알바해요 ("I work part-time to save money"). Attach -기 위해(서) to a verb stem (모으다→모으기 위해, 합격하다→합격하기 위해); 위해서 (with 서) is conversational, 위하여 is the formal/written form. 위해 comes from the Sino-Korean verb 위하다 (爲하다, 爲 'for the sake of'). After a noun, use N을/를 위해(서) (가족→가족을 위해 = for my family). It marks a DELIBERATE, planned goal, so it reads a touch more formal and purposeful than casual -(으)려고 ('intending to'); that's the sharp contrast — -(으)려고 is everyday spoken intention and dislikes formal endings (-(으)려고 합니다 is fine, but goals on signs/resolutions prefer 위해), while -기 위해 suits written aims, mission statements, and earnest explanations. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) a NOUN needs 을/를 — 건강을 위해, never 건강 위해; (2) a VERB uses the -기 nominalizer, never the dictionary form — 모으기 위해, never 모으다 위해; (3) the subject of both clauses should match (you can't easily use 위해 to say 'so that SOMEONE ELSE does X' — for that, switch to -도록 or -게).

usagePhrases.note: The goal, then the action taken toward it

Using the dictionary form with a verb: it's the -기 nominalizer — 모으기 위해, not 모으다 위해 or 모아 위해.

patterns.english: as long as / so long as (a condition holds)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-는 한 means "as long as / so long as (a condition holds)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-는 한 (-neun han) means "as long as / so long as (a condition holds)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 내가 사는 한 ("as long as I live"). Attach -는 한 to a verb stem (살다→사는 한, with ㄹ dropping before ㄴ; 있다→있는 한). This 한 is the Sino-Korean noun 限 ('limit, boundary'), so the clause literally sets 'the boundary/extent within which' the main clause stays true. It very often appears negative — V-지 않는 한 (포기하지 않는 한 = as long as you don't give up) = 'unless.' The sharp contrast is with plain -(으)면 ('if'): -(으)면 is a loose, common 'if/when' that just triggers a result, whereas -는 한 draws a firm CONDITION-BOUNDARY that must hold the whole time ('for as long as / only within the limit that'), so it feels stronger and more absolute — 비가 오면 안 가요 ('if it rains, I won't go') vs 비가 오지 않는 한 가요 ('I'll go unless it rains,' i.e. rain is the one boundary that stops me). English-speaker pitfall: this is a TIME/condition 'as long as,' not the QUANTITY 'as much as' (that's 만큼), and the literary set phrase 가능한 한 ('as far as possible') is fixed — don't read 한 as the number 'one.'

usagePhrases.note: 살다 → 사는 한 (ㄹ drops before ㄴ)

I'll help as much as I can

commonMistakes: Forgetting the ㄹ-drop: 살다/알다 become 사는 한 / 아는 한 before -는, not 살는 한 / 알는 한.

Swapping in -(으)면 when you need a firm boundary: '비가 오면 안 가요' (if it rains) is softer than '비가 오지 않는 한 가요' (unless it rains). Use -는 한 for a condition that must hold throughout, especially the 'unless' sense.

patterns.english: so much that... / as a result of being so... (and then something happened)
patterns.shortExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄴ 나머지 means "so much that... / as a result of being so... (and then something happened)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "so much that... / as a result of being so... (and then something happened)" uses the pattern A/V-(으)ㄴ 나머지 (-(eu)n nameoji). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 놀란 나머지 소리쳤어요 ("I was so startled that I screamed"). Attach the past modifier -(으)ㄴ + 나머지 to verbs and adjectives (놀라다→놀란 나머지, 긴장하다→긴장한 나머지, 기쁘다→기쁜 나머지); consonant stems take -은 나머지 (참다→참은 나머지). 나머지 normally means 'the remainder/leftover,' and here it figuratively names 'what spilled over from an extreme state' — i.e. the first clause was SO intense that it overflowed into the (usually negative or startling) result in the second. The natural rival is -아/어서 ('because'): -아/어서 states a plain, calm cause-and-effect, whereas -(으)ㄴ 나머지 dramatizes an EXTREME degree whose overflow produced an unintended result (긴장해서 실수했어요 = 'I was nervous so I slipped,' neutral; 긴장한 나머지 이름까지 까먹었어요 = 'I was SO nervous I even forgot my name,' vivid and excessive). It's somewhat literary/dramatic, shining in storytelling, news, and lively retellings rather than flat chit-chat. English-speaker pitfall: it ALWAYS takes the past modifier -(으)ㄴ even for a present feeling — never -는 나머지 — and the result clause should be a real, often unwanted consequence, not just any factual statement.

usagePhrases.en: I was so startled that I screamed
usagePhrases.note: Extreme cause overflowing into a result

usagePhrases.en: I was so nervous I stammered
He was so angry he just stormed out
usagePhrases.note: Strong emotion drives an impulsive result

patterns.nuance: Attach the past modifier -(으)ㄴ + 나머지 to verbs and adjectives (놀라다→놀란 나머지, 긴장하다→긴장한 나머지, 기쁘다→기쁜 나머지); consonant stems take -은 나머지 (참다→참은 나머지). 나머지 normally means 'the remainder/leftover,' and here it figuratively names 'what spilled over from an extreme state' — i.e. the first clause was SO intense that it overflowed into the (usually negative or startling) result in the second. The natural rival is -아/어서 ('because'): -아/어서 states a plain, calm cause-and-effect, whereas -(으)ㄴ 나머지 dramatizes an EXTREME degree whose overflow produced an unintended result (긴장해서 실수했어요 = 'I was nervous so I slipped,' neutral; 긴장한 나머지 이름까지 까먹었어요 = 'I was SO nervous I even forgot my name,' vivid and excessive). It's somewhat literary/dramatic, shining in storytelling, news, and lively retellings rather than flat chit-chat. English-speaker pitfall: it ALWAYS takes the past modifier -(으)ㄴ even for a present feeling — never -는 나머지 — and the result clause should be a real, often unwanted consequence, not just any factual statement.
commonMistakes: Using the present -는 나머지: this pattern ALWAYS takes the past modifier -(으)ㄴ even for a current feeling — 놀란 나머지, not 놀라는 나머지; 긴장한 나머지, not 긴장하는 나머지.
Choosing it for an everyday, calm cause: for plain 'because' use -아/어서 (긴장해서 실수했어요). Reserve -(으)ㄴ 나머지 for an EXTREME degree that overflows into an unintended/dramatic result.

Pairing it with a neutral, expected outcome: the second clause should be a striking or unwanted consequence (so-much-that...), not a flat fact — 'I was so nervous I forgot my name' fits; 'I was so nervous I prepared well' does not.
