patterns.english: doing one thing and then switching mid-action (and in the middle...)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-다가 means "doing one thing and then switching mid-action (and in the middle...)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-다가 (-daga) = "doing one thing and then switching mid-action (and in the middle...)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 가다가 ("on the way (while going, then...)"). Attach -다가 straight onto any verb stem with no sound change (가다 → 가다가, 먹다 → 먹다가, 일하다 → 일하다가). The picture is: you were in the middle of action 1, and before finishing it you stopped, switched, or something else happened — so action 1 is left unfinished, often interrupted by surprise. In casual speech the 가 is dropped to just -다 (집에 가다 길 잃었어). CONTRAST with -고 나서: -다가 means the first action was cut short partway (밥 먹다가 나갔어 = stopped eating, left), whereas -고 나서 means it fully finished first (밥 먹고 나서 나갔어 = ate, then left). Also note 같은 주어 — the doer of action 1 and action 2 is normally the same person. Pitfall for English speakers: 'while' in English covers both simultaneous and interrupted action, but if two things truly happen AT THE SAME TIME with no switch (listen to music while studying), that is -(으)면서, not -다가.

usagePhrases.note: Frozen adverbial: a switch or event happens mid-trip

usagePhrases.en: I woke up in the middle of sleeping
at this rate / if this keeps up
usagePhrases.note: Set phrase warning of a bad outcome ahead

examples.en: On my way home I stopped by the convenience store.
examples.note: Simple: 가다가 = en route, then a detour. 들르다 = drop by

examples.en: I was watching Netflix and just ended up falling asleep.
examples.note: Casual; pairs naturally with -아/어 버리다 for an unintended result

examples.en: I ran into an old work colleague while walking.
examples.note: Real situation: an unexpected event cuts into the ongoing action; 동료 = coworker

Using -다가 for two genuinely simultaneous actions with no switch — 'I study while listening to music' is 음악 들으면서 공부해요 (-(으)면서), because nothing is interrupted or switched; -다가 needs a mid-action change.

patterns.english: after finishing (and then, once that's done)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-고 나서 means "after finishing (and then, once that's done)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-고 나서 (-go naseo) means "after finishing (and then, once that's done)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 밥 먹고 나서 ("after eating (it's all done)"). Attach -고 나서 to any verb stem with no sound change (먹다 → 먹고 나서, 끝나다 → 끝나고 나서, 운동하다 → 운동하고 나서). The 나다 part ('to come out / be completed') adds the feeling that action 1 is thoroughly DONE and over before action 2 starts — it stresses completion more strongly than plain -고. CONTRAST with plain -고: 손 씻고 먹어요 just lists two actions in order, but 손 씻고 나서 먹어요 spotlights 'only after the washing is fully finished do I eat.' CONTRAST with -은 후에/-은 다음에: those are interchangeable in meaning ('after'), but -고 나서 sounds more spoken and a touch more emphatic about finishing. You can swap to -고 나면 for a conditional 'once you've done X, then...' (운동하고 나면 개운해요). Pitfall: only the FINAL verb carries tense — never put -았/었 on the first clause (밥 먹고 나서, not 밥 먹었고 나서), and the subject of both clauses is normally the same person.

usagePhrases.note: First action fully completed before the next

usagePhrases.en: I work out after I get off work

usagePhrases.note: Common with 보다 'try'; decide only once you've mulled it

examples.en: Wash your hands and then eat.
examples.note: Simple and emphatic: eat only once the washing is done

examples.en: Once I get my paycheck, I'll treat you.

examples.en: Let's have lunch together after the meeting wraps up.
examples.note: Office sequence; tense sits only on the final verb 먹어요, not on 끝나다

patterns.english: while still in that state / leaving it as it is (without changing it)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 채로 means "while still in that state / leaving it as it is (without changing it)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "while still in that state / leaving it as it is (without changing it)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄴ 채로 (-(eu)n chaero). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 불 켠 채로 잤어요 ("I slept with the light left on"). Add -ㄴ 채로 to vowel-ending stems (켜다 → 켠 채로) and -은 채로 to consonant-ending stems (입다 → 입은 채로, 앉다 → 앉은 채로). 채 is a noun meaning 'the state as it stands,' so the structure literally says 'in the state of having done X.' It describes doing the main action while a PRIOR state is left unchanged — you turned the light on, then left it that way and slept. The 로 is often dropped to just -(으)ㄴ 채. CONTRAST with -(으)면서: -(으)면서 is two ACTIONS at once (먹으면서 봐요 = eat while watching, both ongoing), but -(으)ㄴ 채로 freezes a finished state that simply persists (불 켠 채로 잤어요 = the turning-on already happened, the lit state just remains). CONTRAST with -(으)ㄴ 상태로, which is almost identical but a touch more neutral/written; -채로 carries a faint nuance of 'and you weren't supposed to.' Pitfall: pick verbs that leave a lasting result-state (켜다, 신다, 앉다, 누르다, 열다), never an ongoing motion — 'while running' is not 뛴 채로 but 뛰면서.

usagePhrases.en: I slept with the light left on
usagePhrases.note: A finished state (lit) held during sleeping

usagePhrases.en: He came in with his shoes still on
usagePhrases.note: 신다 → 신은 채로; a big faux pas in Korean homes
서다 → 선 채로; the standing state held during eating
감다 → 감은 채로; common set image

examples.en: I put slippers on over my socks (with my socks still on).
examples.note: Simple result-state: the socks were already on and stayed on. 신다 → 신은 채로

Using the wrong tense ending — it's always -(으)ㄴ 채로 (the result-state form), never 켜는 채로 or 켤 채로; the state must already exist before the main clause happens.
Negating in the wrong spot — to say 'without taking it off,' put 안 before the verb: 안 벗은 채로, not 벗지 않은 채로 ... 안. The 안 ... -(으)ㄴ 채로 frame is the natural one.

patterns.english: because of (an unexpected, usually bad thing that messed things up)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-는 바람에 means "because of (an unexpected, usually bad thing that messed things up)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-는 바람에 (-neun barame) = "because of (an unexpected, usually bad thing that messed things up)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 늦잠 자는 바람에 ("because I overslept"). Attach -는 바람에 to any verb stem (늦다 → 늦는 바람에, 놓치다 → 놓치는 바람에, 막히다 → 막히는 바람에). 바람 here is not 'wind' the weather but a noun meaning 'a sudden gust of cause/consequence,' so it frames an abrupt, unintended reason that led to a negative or surprising result. Despite the present-looking -는, it always points to a PAST cause, and the result clause sits in past tense. Because the cause is outside your control, it commonly comes off as an excuse. CONTRAST with -아서/어서: -아서 is the neutral all-purpose 'because' (good or bad, 길이 막혀서 늦었어요 just states it), while -는 바람에 adds the flavor 'and that unwelcome thing ruined it' (길이 막히는 바람에 = traffic, of all things, jammed me up). CONTRAST sharply with -덕분에 'thanks to,' which is the POSITIVE cause for a good result. Pitfall: it takes verbs only, never adjectives (no 추운 바람에), and you cannot use it for a command or suggestion in the result clause.

usagePhrases.note: The classic 'it wasn't my fault' excuse setup

usagePhrases.en: I was late because of traffic
usagePhrases.note: 막히다 = get jammed; cause beyond your control
Unintended cause leading to a bad result
갑자기 pairs well; an out-of-the-blue disruption

examples.note: Simple cause→bad result; the result clause 놓쳤어요 is past

Attaching it to an adjective — there is no 추운 바람에 or 바쁜 바람에; the cause must be a verb (an event), so rephrase as 날씨가 추워서 or use a verb like 추워지는 바람에.

patterns.english: it's probably the case that... (but) / I'd guess... so (worry or contrast)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 텐데 means "it's probably the case that... (but) / I'd guess... so (worry or contrast)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 텐데 (-(eu)l tende) means "it's probably the case that... (but) / I'd guess... so (worry or contrast)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 바쁠 텐데 ("you must be busy, but..."). Add -ㄹ 텐데 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 올 텐데, 바쁘다 → 바쁠 텐데) and -을 텐데 to consonant-ending stems (좋다 → 좋을 텐데; 힘들다 drops ㄹ → 힘들 텐데). It comes from 터(예정·추측의 의존명사, 'the expected case') + -ㄴ데, so it means 'it must/should be the case that...' followed by a contrast, worry, or gentle suggestion. For a PAST guess use -았/었을 텐데 (피곤했을 텐데 = you must have been tired). It often trails off softly as a caring -ㄹ 텐데(요). CONTRAST with -ㄹ 건데, which sounds nearly the same but means 'I'm GOING to (my own plan), but' (저는 갈 건데 = I intend to go) — 텐데 is a GUESS about someone/something, not your own intention. CONTRAST with -겠지만: that is a drier 'probably... but,' while -ㄹ 텐데 leans warm and considerate, anticipating the listener's situation. Pitfall: English 'would' is ambiguous; here it is conjecture about a likely state, so don't use it for plans or promises.

usagePhrases.note: Considerate lead-in before asking a favor

usagePhrases.en: you must be worn out, so rest a bit
you must be hungry, so eat something
they should be here soon, but...

CONTRAST with -겠지만: that is a drier 'probably... but,' while -ㄹ 텐데 leans warm and considerate, anticipating the listener's situation. Pitfall: English 'would' is ambiguous; here it is conjecture about a likely state, so don't use it for plans or promises.
commonMistakes: Confusing it with -ㄹ 건데 (a plan: 'I'm going to, but') — 내일 비가 올 텐데 is a GUESS about the weather, while 내일 갈 건데 is YOUR intention to go. Mixing them flips a forecast into a plan.
Using it for a fact you already know for certain — if you've confirmed they arrived, say 도착했는데, not 도착했을 텐데; 텐데 is specifically for an unconfirmed conjecture.
Forgetting the past form for a past guess — 'you must have been tired yesterday' is 어제 피곤했을 텐데, not 어제 피곤할 텐데, which would point the guess at the wrong time.

patterns.english: (I observed X) and then... / used to..., but now... (firsthand change)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-더니 means "(I observed X) and then... / used to..., but now... (firsthand change)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "(I observed X) and then... / used to..., but now... (firsthand change)" uses the pattern V-더니 (-deoni). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 그러더니 ("and then (after doing that)"). Attach -더니 directly to a verb or adjective stem (그러다 → 그러더니, 아프다 → 아프더니, 기침하다 → 기침하더니). The 더 is the 'I personally witnessed it' retrospective marker, so -더니 links something you SAW/HEARD firsthand in the past to the result or change that followed — 'he kept coughing (I watched it), and then he got sick.' The subject of plain -더니 is normally someone/something OTHER than 'I,' because you're reporting an outside observation. CONTRAST with -았/었더니: that combined form flips the subject to 'I' and means 'because I did/experienced X, this resulted' (많이 먹었더니 배불러 = I ate a lot, so now I'm full); use 었더니 for your own cause, plain 더니 for what you observed in others. CONTRAST with -니까: -니까 is a neutral logical 'because/since,' while -더니 always carries that eyewitness, watched-it-unfold flavor and a sense of change. Pitfall: don't narrate your own neutral actions with plain -더니 — it sounds odd to say 내가 가더니.

usagePhrases.note: Links an observed action to what followed next

usagePhrases.en: he kept coughing and then caught a cold
it was cold this morning but now it's warm
I ate a lot so now I'm sleepy

examples.en: The sky got dark and now it's raining.
examples.note: Simple observed cause→change; 더니 reports what you watched happen

examples.ko: 걔 어제 야식 먹더니 오늘 속이 안 좋대.
examples.romanization: gyae eoje yasing meokdeoni oneul sogi an jotae.
examples.en: She had a late-night snack yesterday and now says her stomach's off.
examples.note: Casual; subject is 걔 (someone else), 야식 = late-night food

examples.en: I starved all day so now I feel dizzy.
examples.note: Here -았더니 = MY own action led to this state; 굶다 = skip meals

commonMistakes: Using plain -더니 about your OWN action — for 'I overdid it, so...' say 내가 무리했더니, not 내가 무리하더니. Plain -더니 is for what you observed in someone/something else.

Mistaking -더니 for a neutral 'because' like -니까 — 비가 오니까 우산 챙겨 (since it's raining, take an umbrella) is logical reasoning, but 비가 오더니 길이 막히네 means 'it started raining and then, sure enough, the road jammed' — eyewitness change, not a request.
Pairing -더니 with a command or suggestion in the second clause — say what RESULTED (감기 걸렸어요), not an instruction; 기침하더니 약 먹어 is wrong.
Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.

patterns.english: since / seeing as (I saw or heard X, so I did Y)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-길래 means "since / seeing as (I saw or heard X, so I did Y)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-길래 (-gillae) = "since / seeing as (I saw or heard X, so I did Y)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 싸길래 샀어요 ("it was cheap so I bought it"). Attach -길래 directly to a verb or adjective stem (싸다 → 싸길래, 울다 → 울길래, 맛있다 → 맛있길래); for nouns use N(이)길래. It gives a reason rooted in something you personally NOTICED or were told, which then prompted your own response — so the second clause is almost always YOUR own choice, usually past tense (싸길래 샀어요 = it was cheap, so I bought it). CONTRAST with -아서/어서: -아서 states a general or objective cause for any result (싸서 잘 팔려요 = it's cheap so it sells well, a fact about the world), but -길래 ties an observed reason specifically to what YOU then did in reaction. CONTRAST with -기에: same meaning, but -기에 is the more formal/written twin, while -길래 is conversational and warmer. Pitfall: the result clause cannot be a general truth or someone else's action — 'it's cheap so everyone buys it' is 싸서 다들 사요, not -길래; -길래 must lead to your own reactive deed. It also doesn't fit commands ('since it's cheap, buy it' uses 싸니까, not 싸길래).

usagePhrases.en: it was cheap so I bought it
it looked good so I ordered it
there was no reply so I called
everyone was going so I went too

examples.en: It looked tasty so I bought one.
examples.note: Simple: observed reason (looked good) → my action (bought)

examples.ko: 편의점에서 1+1 하길래 두 개 사 왔어요.
examples.romanization: pyeonuijeomeseo 1+1 hagillae du gae sa wasseoyo.
examples.en: It was buy-one-get-one at the convenience store so I grabbed two.
examples.note: Everyday deal; 1+1 (원 플러스 원) = BOGO; reason I saw → what I did

examples.en: The reviews were good so I booked that restaurant.
examples.note: Real decision based on info; 리뷰가 좋다 = reviews are good → my booking

Using -길래 in a command or request — 'since it's cheap, buy it' is 싸니까 사 or 싸길래 사긴 어렵다... no; use 싸니까 사세요. The result of -길래 is a past deed you already did, not an order to someone.

Putting it with your own internal reason rather than an observed one — 'I was hungry so I ate' is best as 배가 고파서 먹었어요; -길래 wants an external trigger you noticed (others, a sign, a price), not your own feeling.

patterns.english: (it's been some time) since... (how long since an action)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 지 means "(it's been some time) since... (how long since an action)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ 지 (-(eu)n ji) means "(it's been some time) since... (how long since an action)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 온 지 얼마 안 됐어요 ("it hasn't been long since I came"). Add -ㄴ 지 to vowel-ending stems (오다 → 온 지, 만나다 → 만난 지) and -은 지 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹은 지; 살다 drops ㄹ → 산 지). It measures the time ELAPSED since an action happened, and is normally followed by a duration plus 됐어요/지났어요 (한국에 온 지 1년 됐어요 = it's been a year since I came to Korea). Crucially, write 지 with a SPACE — this time-elapsed 지 is a separate noun-like word. CONTRAST sharply with the negative-ish -지 in 안/-지 않다: 온 지 1년 됐어요 (space; time since) vs 오지 않았어요 (no space; 'didn't come') are completely different 지. CONTRAST also with -(으)ㄴ 후에 'after': 온 후에 = once you've arrived (sequence), but 온 지 = how much time has passed since arriving (measurement) — they are not interchangeable. Pitfall: only works with verbs (an action that started the clock), never adjectives; ask elapsed time with 얼마나 됐어요? ('how long has it been?').

usagePhrases.en: it hasn't been long since I came
it's been a year since we met
usagePhrases.note: Duration + 되다 to clock the gap

usagePhrases.en: it's been a while since I ate
how long since you bought it?
usagePhrases.note: 사다 → 산 지; asking elapsed time

examples.ko: 밥 먹은 지 한 시간밖에 안 됐어요.
examples.romanization: bam meogeun ji han siganbakke an dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: It's only been an hour since I ate.
examples.note: Simple measurement; 밖에 + 안 = 'only.' Note 먹다 → 먹은 지

examples.ko: 한국에 산 지 이제 막 6개월 됐어요.
examples.romanization: hanguge san ji ije mak 6gaewol dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: I've only just hit six months living in Korea.
examples.note: Newcomer self-intro; the ㄹ-drop 살다 → 산 지 is the tricky part

examples.ko: 걔랑 연락 끊은 지 진짜 오래됐어.
examples.romanization: gyaerang yeollak kkeuneun ji jinjja oraedwaesseo.
examples.en: It's been ages since I cut off contact with them.
examples.note: Casual; 연락(을) 끊다 = stop contact → 끊은 지 measures the gap

It measures the time ELAPSED since an action happened, and is normally followed by a duration plus 됐어요/지났어요 (한국에 온 지 1년 됐어요 = it's been a year since I came to Korea). CONTRAST also with -(으)ㄴ 후에 'after': 온 후에 = once you've arrived (sequence), but 온 지 = how much time has passed since arriving (measurement) — they are not interchangeable. Using the present or future form of the verb — it must be the past-attributive -(으)ㄴ (온 지, 산 지), never 오는 지 or 올 지, because the action that started the clock is already done.
Mixing it up with -(으)ㄴ 후에 'after' — 졸업한 후에 취직했어요 (after graduating I got a job, a sequence) is not 졸업한 지 취직했어요; use 지 only to count how long it's been (졸업한 지 3년 됐어요).
Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.

patterns.english: the more (you do/it is) X, the more Y
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ수록 means "the more (you do/it is) X, the more Y" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "the more (you do/it is) X, the more Y" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ수록 (-(eu)l-surok). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 갈수록 ("more and more (as time goes on)"). Add -ㄹ수록 to vowel-ending stems (가다 → 갈수록, 보다 → 볼수록) and -을수록 to consonant-ending stems (먹다 → 먹을수록; 알다 drops ㄹ → 알수록). It expresses proportional change: as one thing increases, another shifts along with it ('the more X, the more Y'). It is very commonly reinforced by putting -(으)면 on the front of the same verb — 보면 볼수록 (the more I look), 알면 알수록 (the more I learn) — a fixed, natural-sounding doubling. Write 수록 ATTACHED to the stem with no space. CONTRAST with -(으)니까/-아서 'because': those give a single cause→effect, but -ㄹ수록 sets up a sliding scale where Y keeps moving as X keeps growing. Pitfall: don't write a space (-ㄹ 수록 is wrong) and don't confuse it with the ability pattern -ㄹ 수 있다 — 갈수록 (more and more, one chunk) has nothing to do with 갈 수 있다 (can go). English 'the more... the more' uses two clauses with 'the'; Korean folds it into one suffix, so resist translating word for word.

usagePhrases.en: more and more (as time goes on)
usagePhrases.note: Frozen adverbial; things intensify over time

usagePhrases.en: the more I look, the prettier it is
usagePhrases.note: 면 + 수록 doubling for natural emphasis

usagePhrases.en: the more I eat, the sleepier I get
the more I learn, the harder it gets

examples.en: The more I see it, the more I like it.
examples.note: Simple set phrase; the 면+수록 doubling is how natives say it

examples.ko: 한국어는 하면 할수록 재밌는 거 같아요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoneun hamyeon halsurok jaeminneun geo gatayo.
examples.en: The more I do Korean, the more fun it seems to get.
examples.note: Encouraging learner line; 하다 → 할수록

examples.en: Seoul is a city you grow more attached to the longer you live there.
examples.note: 정(이) 들다 = grow attached; 살다 → 살수록 (ㄹ-drop)

Dropping the helpful -(으)면 lead-in where natives expect it — 'the more I look' sounds bare as just 볼수록; the idiomatic form is 보면 볼수록 with the verb repeated.
Forgetting the ㄹ-irregular drop — 알다 becomes 알수록 (not 알을수록) and 살다 becomes 살수록 (not 살을수록); the stem ㄹ stays and you add just 수록.

patterns.english: even if / even though (hypothetically, no matter what)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-더라도 means "even if / even though (hypothetically, no matter what)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-더라도 (-deorado) = "even if / even though (hypothetically, no matter what)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 힘들더라도 ("even if it's hard"). Attach -더라도 directly to a verb or adjective stem (가다 → 가더라도, 힘들다 → 힘들더라도, 늦다 → 늦더라도); for nouns N(이)더라도. It concedes a strong or even unlikely hypothetical — 'even supposing that happens, the result still holds.' For a past supposition use -았/었더라도 (알았더라도 = even if I had known). It very often pairs with 아무리 ('no matter how') up front for extra force. CONTRAST with -아도/어도: both translate as 'even if,' but -아도 is the everyday, can-be-real concession (비가 와도 가요 = even if it rains I'll go, quite plausible), while -더라도 is stronger and more hypothetical, used for emphatic or less likely cases (비가 오더라도 = even supposing it rains). CONTRAST with -(으)ㄴ/는데도 'even though,' which concedes a REAL current fact (비가 오는데도 = even though it IS raining), not a hypothetical. Pitfall: don't reach for -더라도 to describe something already happening — that's -는데도; reserve -더라도 for suppositions, especially after 아무리.

usagePhrases.en: no matter how busy, eat your meals
I'll go even if it rains
come for sure even if you're late

examples.en: Even if it's a bit pricey, I'll buy the good one.
examples.note: Simple concession; 더라도 grants the price point and holds the choice

examples.en: No matter how tired you are, don't skip your workout.
examples.note: Casual firm advice; 아무리...더라도 is the natural pairing

examples.en: Even if the terms look good, read the contract carefully.
examples.note: Practical living advice; 계약서 = contract, 꼼꼼히 = thoroughly

patterns.nuance: Attach -더라도 directly to a verb or adjective stem (가다 → 가더라도, 힘들다 → 힘들더라도, 늦다 → 늦더라도); for nouns N(이)더라도. It concedes a strong or even unlikely hypothetical — 'even supposing that happens, the result still holds.' For a past supposition use -았/었더라도 (알았더라도 = even if I had known). It very often pairs with 아무리 ('no matter how') up front for extra force. CONTRAST with -(으)ㄴ/는데도 'even though,' which concedes a REAL current fact (비가 오는데도 = even though it IS raining), not a hypothetical. commonMistakes: Treating it as identical to -아도/어도 — both mean 'even if,' but -더라도 is more hypothetical and emphatic, used for stronger or less likely suppositions, while -아도 fits ordinary, plausible cases.
Using -더라도 for a fact that is actually true right now — 'even though it's raining (and it is)' is 비가 오는데도, not 비가 오더라도, which only supposes the rain.
Forgetting the past form for a past hypothetical — 'even if I had known' is 알았더라도, not 알더라도, which would wrongly point the supposition at the present.
Do not say the study symbol V or N out loud; replace it with a real verb stem or noun.
Check whether the pattern attaches to a noun, verb, or adjective before using it.

patterns.english: have no choice but to / can't help but (it's the only option)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 means "have no choice but to / can't help but (it's the only option)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 (-(eu)l subakke eopda) means "have no choice but to / can't help but (it's the only option)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 기다릴 수밖에 없어요 ("I have no choice but to wait"). Built from 수 ('way, possibility') + 밖에 ('except, outside of') + 없다 ('not exist'), so it literally says 'there is no way except doing it' — i.e. that one action is the sole remaining option, and you're resigned to it. Attach -ㄹ 수밖에 없다 to vowel stems (가다 → 갈 수밖에 없다), -을 수밖에 없다 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 수밖에 없다); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (살다 → 살 수밖에 없다). Past: -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없었어요. CONTRAST: don't confuse it with the plain ability/possibility -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다. 갈 수 없어요 = 'I can't go (it's impossible)'; 갈 수밖에 없어요 = 'I have no choice but to go (going is the only option left).' The 밖에 flips the meaning from impossibility to inevitability. Note 밖에 always pairs with a negative (없다), and here it grammatically requires no 안 — 없다 already carries the negation. With adjectives it means 'is bound to be ~' (비싸다 → 비쌀 수밖에 없다 = it can't help but be expensive). PITFALL: English speakers reach for '~할 수 없다' when they mean 'I'm forced to'; that backfires into 'I cannot.' Also resist a space inside 수밖에.

usagePhrases.en: I have no choice but to wait
usagePhrases.note: Resigned to the only option; 없어요 carries the negation, no 안 needed

usagePhrases.en: I had no choice but to put up with it
Of course it's expensive (it can't help but be)
usagePhrases.note: Adjective 비싸다 + 죠 = 'naturally, as you'd expect'

usagePhrases.en: I had no choice but to go
usagePhrases.note: Casual 반말; forced by circumstances, not by desire

examples.ko: 막차 끊겨서 택시 탈 수밖에 없었어요.
examples.romanization: makcha kkeunkyeoseo taeksi tal subakke eopseosseoyo.
examples.en: The last train was gone, so I had no choice but to take a taxi.
examples.note: 막차 끊기다 = miss the last train; -아서 gives the cause that forced the only option

examples.ko: 월급은 그대론데 물가는 오르니까 아낄 수밖에 없죠.
examples.romanization: wolgeubeun geudaeronde mulganeun oreunikka akkil subakke eopsjyo.
examples.en: My salary's the same but prices keep rising, so of course I have to save.
examples.note: -(으)니까 supplies the reason; 죠 invites agreement that this is the obvious result

examples.en: The boss tells me to, so I've got no choice but to work overtime.
examples.note: -잖아 frames it as something the listener already knows; status (사장님) makes refusal impossible

patterns.nuance: Built from 수 ('way, possibility') + 밖에 ('except, outside of') + 없다 ('not exist'), so it literally says 'there is no way except doing it' — i.e. that one action is the sole remaining option, and you're resigned to it. Attach -ㄹ 수밖에 없다 to vowel stems (가다 → 갈 수밖에 없다), -을 수밖에 없다 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 수밖에 없다); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (살다 → 살 수밖에 없다). Past: -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없었어요. CONTRAST: don't confuse it with the plain ability/possibility -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다. 갈 수 없어요 = 'I can't go (it's impossible)'; 갈 수밖에 없어요 = 'I have no choice but to go (going is the only option left).' The 밖에 flips the meaning from impossibility to inevitability. Note 밖에 always pairs with a negative (없다), and here it grammatically requires no 안 — 없다 already carries the negation. With adjectives it means 'is bound to be ~' (비싸다 → 비쌀 수밖에 없다 = it can't help but be expensive). PITFALL: English speakers reach for '~할 수 없다' when they mean 'I'm forced to'; that backfires into 'I cannot.' Also resist a space inside 수밖에.
commonMistakes: Writing a space inside the chunk (수 밖에) — 수밖에 is one unit (modifier + 수 + 밖에), then 없다 stands alone: 갈 수밖에 없어요.
Using the present modifier 가는 수밖에 — the form is the future/irrealis modifier -(으)ㄹ + 수밖에 없다 (갈 수밖에 없다), never 가는 수밖에.
Confusing it with 갈 수 없다 ('cannot go'). Adding 밖에 reverses the sense to 'have no choice but to go,' so don't treat them as the same negative.

patterns.english: there's no way that / it can't possibly be that
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 means "there's no way that / it can't possibly be that" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "there's no way that / it can't possibly be that" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 (-(eu)l riga eopda). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 그럴 리가 없어요 ("There's no way that's the case"). 리 here is the dependent noun 理 (Sino-Korean 'reason, principle'), so the phrase literally says 'there is no reason/grounds for it to be so' — a confident logical denial, not a wishy-washy guess. Attach -ㄹ 리가 없다 to vowel stems (오다 → 올 리가 없다), -을 리가 없다 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 리가 없다). For a past doubt use -았/었을 리가 없다 (갔을 리가 없다 = no way they went); for nouns, N + 일 리가 없다 (사실 → 사실일 리가 없다). The 가 is routinely dropped in speech: -(으)ㄹ 리 없어요. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 vs -(으)ㄹ 리 만무하다 — both mean 'no way,' but 만무하다 (萬無, 'utterly absent') is bookish/written (올 리 만무하다 reads like an essay), while 리가 없다 is everyday spoken. Also distinguish it from the soft hedge -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 ('might'): 리가 없다 is the opposite pole — strong disbelief, 'surely not.' REGISTER: it carries emotional conviction (often surprise or indignation), so it lands naturally with -잖아/-는데. PITFALL: English speakers map 'there's no way' to time/possibility and grope for 방법(method) or 가능성(possibility); the idiomatic word is 리, and it must follow the -(으)ㄹ modifier, never stand alone.

usagePhrases.en: There's no way that's the case
usagePhrases.note: Set phrase of disbelief; 그럴 = 그렇다's -(으)ㄹ form
Past doubt → -았을 리가 없다, denying a completed action

usagePhrases.en: There's no way they've arrived already
usagePhrases.note: 가 dropped (리 없어요) — very natural in speech

usagePhrases.en: There's no way this is free

patterns.english: it's basically / it amounts to / you could say (when you do the math)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 means "it's basically / it amounts to / you could say (when you do the math)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 (-(eu)n/neun semida) = "it's basically / it amounts to / you could say (when you do the math)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 거의 다 한 셈이에요 ("It's basically all done"). 셈 is a native Korean noun meaning 'a count, a reckoning' (from 세다 'to count'), so this pattern frames a situation as 'when you tally it up, it effectively equals X' — reality isn't literally X, but practically counts as X. Present verbs take -는 셈이다 (사는 → 사는 셈이다), past/completed verbs -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (끝나다 → 끝난 셈이다), adjectives -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (싸다 → 싼 셈이다). Often paired with 거의 ('almost') or 다 ('all'). CONTRAST: -는 셈이다 vs -(으)ㄴ/는 셈 치다 — 셈이다 states a calculated fact ('it amounts to ~'), whereas 셈 치다 means 'let's pretend/treat it as' a deliberate choice to regard something a certain way (속은 셈 치자 = 'let's just consider ourselves cheated and move on'). Also distinguish from -나 마나 (next door in this set): 셈이다 says 'it practically counts AS done,' not 'doing it is pointless.' REGISTER: neutral, very common in casual reasoning and explanations. PITFALL: English 'basically' is also a filler; here 셈이다 is a genuine equivalence claim, so don't tack it on to a literally-true statement (다 한 셈이에요 = 'practically done,' NOT '100% finished'). Match the modifier to tense — 끝난 셈 for a finished thing, not 끝나는 셈.

usagePhrases.note: Completed action → -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (한 셈); 거의 다 = 'almost entirely'

usagePhrases.en: It's basically like I got it for free
usagePhrases.note: When a discount is so huge it tallies up to free

usagePhrases.note: 셈 치다 = deliberately 'consider it as' (a choice), vs 셈이다 = it amounts to

examples.ko: 이번 달 회식이 다섯 번이면 거의 매주 모인 셈이네.

examples.note: 회식 = team dinner; 모인 셈 (completed); -네 marks a fresh realization while doing the math

Also distinguish from -나 마나 (next door in this set): 셈이다 says 'it practically counts AS done,' not 'doing it is pointless.' REGISTER: neutral, very common in casual reasoning and explanations. PITFALL: English 'basically' is also a filler; here 셈이다 is a genuine equivalence claim, so don't tack it on to a literally-true statement (다 한 셈이에요 = 'practically done,' NOT '100% finished'). Match the modifier to tense — 끝난 셈 for a finished thing, not 끝나는 셈.
commonMistakes: Mismatching the modifier: a finished thing is 끝난 셈, an ongoing one is 하는 셈, an adjective is 싼 셈 — don't say 끝나는 셈 for something already over.
Treating it as a literal '100%' claim. 다 한 셈이에요 means 'practically done,' so don't use it when the task is truly, fully complete.
Confusing 셈이다 (it amounts to) with 셈 치다 (let's pretend it is). 없던 일로 한 셈 치자 = 'let's just treat it as if it never happened' — a chosen stance, not a calculated fact.

patterns.english: might / may / it's possible that (I'm not sure)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 means "might / may / it's possible that (I'm not sure)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 (-(eu)ljido moreuda) means "might / may / it's possible that (I'm not sure)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 비 올지도 몰라요 ("It might rain"). Composed of the indirect-question modifier -(으)ㄹ지 ('whether ~') + 도 ('even') + 모르다 ('not know'), so it literally means 'I don't even know whether it'll happen' = there's a genuine chance. Attach -ㄹ지도 모르다 to vowel stems (오다 → 올지도 모르다), -을지도 모르다 to consonant stems (늦다 → 늦을지도 모르다). Past possibility: -았/었을지도 몰라요 (갔을지도 몰라요 = might have gone). 도 can drop for a slightly firmer hunch: -(으)ㄹ지 몰라요. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 vs -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 — both render 'might/probably,' but -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 is an impression from evidence ('looks like it will,' 비 올 것 같아요 watching dark clouds), while -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 flags an uncertain possibility you want the listener to brace for ('it might rain, just so you know'). It also sits opposite -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 in this set: 리가 없다 = strong denial, -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 = open uncertainty. REGISTER: neutral; frequently used to soften warnings or hedge plans. PITFALL: 모르다 normally means 'don't know,' so beginners read 올지도 몰라요 as 'I don't know if it comes' — but as a fixed pattern it means 'might come.' Keep the -(으)ㄹ지 modifier intact; -는지/-(으)ㄴ지 would shift the time reference.

usagePhrases.note: Hedged weather guess; vowel stem 오다 → 올지도
Warning a friend in advance; consonant stem 늦다 → 늦을지도

usagePhrases.en: He might be busy, so ask ahead

commonMistakes: Reading 모르다 as 'don't know' here — 올지도 몰라요 is the fixed pattern 'might come,' not 'I don't know whether it comes.'
Using 올지도 몰랐어요 when you mean 'it might have come.' Past possibility lives in the verb stem (왔을지도 몰라요); 몰랐어요 only describes a past state of not knowing.
Reaching for -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 when you specifically want to warn of an unsure risk. 늦을 것 같아요 = 'I think I'll be late (impression)'; 늦을지도 몰라요 = 'I might be late (brace yourself).'

patterns.english: is bound to / naturally tends to (it's only natural that)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-기 마련이다 means "is bound to / naturally tends to (it's only natural that)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "is bound to / naturally tends to (it's only natural that)" uses the pattern V-기 마련이다 (-gi maryeonida). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 사람은 누구나 실수하기 마련이에요 ("Everyone is bound to make mistakes"). 마련 is a native noun meaning 'a settled arrangement / the way things are set up,' so '-기 마련이다' states that an outcome is built into the nature of things — it's bound to happen, by default. Attach -기 마련이다 straight to any verb or adjective stem with no sound change (늙다 → 늙기 마련이다, 바쁘다 → 바쁘기 마련이다, 실수하다 → 실수하기 마련이다); nouns take N(이)기 마련이다. A fully synonymous variant is -게 마련이다 (실수하게 마련이다) — same meaning, freely interchangeable. CONTRAST: -기 마련이다 vs -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 — both touch 'inevitability,' but 마련이다 is a calm general truth about how the world tends to work ('people are bound to age'), while 수밖에 없다 is one person's forced choice in a specific situation ('I had no choice but to take a taxi'). REGISTER: neutral-to-reflective, the voice of proverbs and life lessons; it carries a soothing, philosophical tone, great for reassuring someone. PITFALL: English speakers borrow 'I'm bound to be late today' and try 마련이다 for a one-off — wrong; it's strictly for repeating, general truths, not a single scheduled event. Also attach to the bare stem, never the present modifier (실수하기/실수하게 마련, never 실수하는 마련).

patterns.english: no point doing it / whether you do it or not (the result's the same)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)나 마나 means "no point doing it / whether you do it or not (the result's the same)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)나 마나 (-(eu)na mana) = "no point doing it / whether you do it or not (the result's the same)". This sets the connective -(으)나 ('whether one does') against 마나 (a contracted -(으)나 of 말다, 'to not do'), so it weighs 'doing it' against 'not doing it' and concludes the two come out identical — hence 'no point.' patterns.english: half-heartedly / barely (do something in a half-done, distracted way)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-는 둥 마는 둥 means "half-heartedly / barely (do something in a half-done, distracted way)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-는 둥 마는 둥 (-neun dung maneun dung) means "half-heartedly / barely (do something in a half-done, distracted way)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 밥을 먹는 둥 마는 둥 했어요 ("I barely picked at my food"). 둥 is a dependent noun meaning roughly 'in such a manner,' and the pattern juxtaposes 'doing (-는 둥)' with 'not doing (마는 둥, from 말다),' painting an action performed so half-heartedly it's barely happening — distracted, rushed, going through the motions. Attach -는 둥 마는 둥 to a verb stem (먹다 → 먹는 둥 마는 둥, 듣다 → 듣는 둥 마는 둥); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (놀다 → 노는 둥 마는 둥). It's usually capped with 하다 or another verb describing what you did instead. CONTRAST: -는 둥 마는 둥 vs -(으)나 마나 — they look like cousins (both pair a verb with 말다) but mean opposite things. -는 둥 마는 둥 describes HOW you did it (sloppily, half-done — 밥을 먹는 둥 마는 둥 = 'picked at the food'); -(으)나 마나 judges that doing it is POINTLESS because the result won't change (먹으나 마나 = 'no point eating'). Don't swap them. REGISTER: casual and vivid, slightly critical — it usually conveys distraction or lack of sincerity, so it's for describing behavior you found half-baked. PITFALL: the modifier of 말다 here is 마는 (the ㄹ drops before -는), so never write 말는. And it always takes present -는 둥; 먹은 둥 마는 둥 is wrong for this 'half-heartedly' meaning.

patterns.english: also for the purpose of / partly to (doing two things at once)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 겸 means "also for the purpose of / partly to (doing two things at once)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "also for the purpose of / partly to (doing two things at once)" uses the pattern V-(으)ㄹ 겸 (-(eu)l gyeom). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 바람도 쐴 겸 산책해요 ("I take a walk partly to get some air"). 겸 is the Sino-Korean dependent noun 兼 ('combine, hold concurrently'), so -(으)ㄹ 겸 frames one action as serving two aims at once — 'partly in order to ~ (and partly for something else).' Attach -ㄹ 겸 to vowel stems (보다 → 볼 겸), -을 겸 to consonant stems (먹다 → 먹을 겸); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (놀다 → 놀 겸). It very often comes doubled: A-(으)ㄹ 겸 B-(으)ㄹ 겸 ('partly to A, partly to B'), and a main action follows. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄹ 겸 vs -(으)러 (purpose 'in order to') — -(으)러 names the single main reason for going/coming (밥 먹으러 가다 = 'go in order to eat'), while -(으)ㄹ 겸 adds a SECONDARY purpose riding along ('while I'm at it, also to ~'), implying there's already another reason. So 산책할 겸 나왔어요 = 'I came out, and a walk was one of the reasons too.' REGISTER: neutral, everyday; great for casually justifying outings and two-birds-one-stone plans. PITFALL #1: use the future modifier -(으)ㄹ, never -는 겸 (볼 겸, not 보는 겸). PITFALL #2: 겸 cannot end a sentence by itself like a finite verb — it needs a following main action (볼 겸 왔어요), so don't stop at 볼 겸이에요.

usagePhrases.note: Two-in-one rationale; the walking serves the exercise aim on the side

patterns.english: tends to be / is on the ... side (rather than strongly)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 means "tends to be / is on the ... side (rather than strongly)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 (-(eu)n/neun pyeonida) = "tends to be / is on the ... side (rather than strongly)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 저는 매운 거 잘 먹는 편이에요 ("I'm on the side of handling spicy food well"). 편 is the Sino-Korean noun 便 ('side, group, leaning'), so '-(으)ㄴ/는 편이다' literally places something 'on the ~ side,' softening a claim from 'very' to 'rather/relatively.' Verbs take -는 편이다 (먹다 → 먹는 편이다), adjectives -(으)ㄴ 편이다 (크다 → 큰 편이다, 작다 → 작은 편이다); past habits use -(으)ㄴ 편이었다. CONTRAST: -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 vs the bare adjective — 키가 커요 asserts 'I am tall' flatly, while 키가 큰 편이에요 hedges to 'I'm on the taller side,' relative to others, sounding modest and non-absolute. It also differs from -(으)ㄴ/는 척하다 ('pretend to be') despite both using a 편/척 + 이다/하다 frame — 편이다 is an honest mild judgment, not a pretense. REGISTER: neutral and very polite-friendly; Koreans use it constantly for self-description and comparisons to avoid sounding boastful or blunt (술은 약한 편이에요 is gentler than 술 못 마셔요). PITFALL #1: match the modifier to word type — verbs -는 편 (먹는 편), adjectives -(으)ㄴ 편 (큰 편), so never 크는 편. PITFALL #2: because it means 'relatively,' don't pair it with intensifiers like 아주/완전 ('totally'); that contradicts the very softening it provides.

patterns.english: do (it), but... / it's true that ~, though (conceding then qualifying)
patterns.shortExplanation: V-기는 하다 means "do (it), but... / it's true that ~, though (conceding then qualifying)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-기는 하다 (-gineun hada) means "do (it), but... / it's true that ~, though (conceding then qualifying)" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 먹기는 했어요 ("I did eat it (but...)"). Built from the nominalizer -기 + the contrast topic particle 는 + a dummy 하다 that echoes the verb's meaning, so it isolates and concedes one point ('as for doing it, yes') while signaling a 'but' is coming. Attach -기는 하다 to a verb or adjective stem (먹다 → 먹기는 하다, 좋다 → 좋기는 하다); in speech 기는 almost always contracts to 긴 (먹긴 해요). For tense, conjugate the final 하다 (먹기는 했어요 = 'I did eat, but...'); you can also fully repeat the verb instead of using 하다 (가긴 가다, 좋긴 좋다). CONTRAST: -기는 하다 vs -지만 — both pivot to a contrast, but -지만 is a neutral 'but' joining two clauses (좋지만 비싸요 = 'it's good but expensive'), whereas -기는 하다 first GRANTS/concedes the point with extra emphasis ('it IS good, I'll give you that... but'), carrying a reluctant, qualifying tone. So 좋긴 한데 비싸요 admits the merit before pushing back. It's usually followed by 그런데/근데 or -지만/-(으)ㄴ데. REGISTER: conversational and very common for soft disagreement, polite hedging, or a gentle 'no.' PITFALL: don't drop the verb's meaning into a bare 하다 — 가긴 하다 keeps 'go' via the repeated stem (or you say 가긴 가다); 가는 하다 is wrong. And since it sets up a contrast, 좋긴 해요 left alone feels unfinished unless the 'but' is understood.

patterns.nuance: Built from the nominalizer -기 + the contrast topic particle 는 + a dummy 하다 that echoes the verb's meaning, so it isolates and concedes one point ('as for doing it, yes') while signaling a 'but' is coming. Attach -기는 하다 to a verb or adjective stem (먹다 → 먹기는 하다, 좋다 → 좋기는 하다); in speech 기는 almost always contracts to 긴 (먹긴 해요). For tense, conjugate the final 하다 (먹기는 했어요 = 'I did eat, but...'); you can also fully repeat the verb instead of using 하다 (가긴 가다, 좋긴 좋다). CONTRAST: -기는 하다 vs -지만 — both pivot to a contrast, but -지만 is a neutral 'but' joining two clauses (좋지만 비싸요 = 'it's good but expensive'), whereas -기는 하다 first GRANTS/concedes the point with extra emphasis ('it IS good, I'll give you that... but'), carrying a reluctant, qualifying tone. So 좋긴 한데 비싸요 admits the merit before pushing back. It's usually followed by 그런데/근데 or -지만/-(으)ㄴ데. REGISTER: conversational and very common for soft disagreement, polite hedging, or a gentle 'no.' commonMistakes: Collapsing the verb into a bare 하다 (가는 하다) — you must repeat the action's meaning: 가긴 하다, or fully 가긴 가다.
Leaving it hanging without the contrast. It exists to set up a 'but,' so 좋긴 해요 by itself feels incomplete unless the qualifier is clearly implied.
Reaching for plain -지만 when you want to first concede with emphasis. -지만 is a neutral 'but'; -기는 하다 grants the point ('it IS good, granted...') before pushing back.

patterns.shortExplanation: N을/를 좋아해요 means "to like N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "to like N" uses the pattern N을/를 좋아해요 (N-eul/reul joahaeyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 김치를 좋아해요 ("I like kimchi."). 좋아하다 is the VERB 'to like (something)', so the thing you like takes the object marker 을/를, not the subject marker 이/가. Add 을 after a consonant (음악을), 를 after a vowel (커피를). The huge English-speaker trap is its adjective cousin 좋다, which means 'is good/likeable' and takes 이/가: 커피가 좋아요 literally says 'coffee is good (to me)', while 커피를 좋아해요 says 'I like coffee' as an action with you as the doer — both translate to English 'I like coffee', but mixing the particles (커피가 좋아해요) is wrong. 좋아하다 conjugates as a regular 하다-style verb: stem 좋아하 + 여요 contracts to 좋아해요 in the 요-form, 좋아합니다 in formal speech. For people, 좋아하다 carries a romantic 'have a crush on' tone (그 사람을 좋아해요 = I have feelings for that person), so to say you merely enjoy someone's company use a softer phrasing. It pairs naturally with hobbies, food, music, and seasons.

patterns.english: to go by N / toward N
patterns.shortExplanation: N(으)로 가요 means "to go by N / toward N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: N(으)로 가요 (N-(eu)ro gayo) = "to go by N / toward N". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 버스로 가요 ("I go by bus."). The particle (으)로 marks either the MEANS (by what / how) or the DIRECTION (toward which way) of a motion, so 버스로 가요 = 'go by bus' and 오른쪽으로 가요 = 'go to the right'. Attach 로 after a vowel or after the consonant ㄹ (지하철로, 서울로, 사무실로 — 사무실 ends in ㄹ), and 으로 after every other consonant (집으로, 부엌으로). The key contrast for English speakers is 에 vs (으)로: 에 marks a fixed DESTINATION you arrive at (서울에 가요 = go to Seoul, full stop), while (으)로 stresses the ROUTE or HEADING ('toward/in the direction of Seoul', not necessarily stopping there). For transport, English 'by bus' must become 버스로, never 버스에 — 버스에 가요 would weirdly mean 'go onto the bus'. With direction nouns (왼쪽, 이쪽, 위), only (으)로 works. It also collocates with 갈아타다 (지하철로 갈아타요 = transfer to the subway) and means/material more broadly (한국어로 말해요 = speak in Korean).

patterns.english: to go in order to V
patterns.shortExplanation: V(으)러 가요 means "to go in order to V" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V(으)러 가요 (V-(eu)reo gayo) means "to go in order to V" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 밥 먹으러 가요 ("I go to eat."). (으)러 attaches to a verb stem to state the PURPOSE of moving, and it is locked to motion verbs only — 가다, 오다, 다니다, 나가다 and the like. Add 러 to a vowel stem (만나러), 으러 to a consonant stem (먹으러); ㄹ stems keep the ㄹ and take 러 (놀러 가요 = go to hang out). The classic English-speaker confusion is (으)러 vs (으)려고: both mean 'in order to', but (으)러 must end in a going/coming verb and names only the errand of that trip (밥 먹으러 가요), whereas (으)려고 works with ANY main verb and expresses broader intention (밥 먹으려고 일찍 왔어요 = 'I came early intending to eat'). Word order matters: the place comes first with 에, then the purpose, then the motion verb — 도서관에 공부하러 가요, not '공부하러 도서관에 가요'-style English ordering. It frequently pairs with everyday errands: 사러(go to buy), 만나러(go to meet), 보러(go to watch a movie), 배우러(go to learn).

patterns.shortExplanation: V아/어 보세요 means "try doing V (please)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "try doing V (please)" uses the pattern V아/어 보세요 (V-a/eo boseyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 먹어 보세요 ("Please try eating it."). V아/어 보다 means 'do V and see / give V a try', and in the imperative 보세요 it becomes a warm, polite suggestion — exactly what a shopkeeper, host, or friend says when recommending. Build the 아/어 form first: 아 after a stem vowel ㅏ or ㅗ (가 → 가 봐요), 어 otherwise (먹어 봐요), and 해 for 하다 verbs (해 보세요). The biggest pitfall is treating it as a literal command 'try!': it is softer and more inviting than the bare imperative 드세요/가세요, so 먹어 보세요 = 'why don't you give it a taste' rather than a blunt order. Don't confuse the suggestion 보세요 with the past 봤어요, which reports EXPERIENCE ('have you tried/done it before?': 한국 음식 먹어 봤어요?). Note also the homophone trap: 보다 here is the auxiliary 'try', not the main verb 'see/look'. It collocates with food (먹어/마셔 보세요), clothes (입어/신어 보세요), and gentle encouragement (한번 해 보세요 = give it a shot).

patterns.shortExplanation: A-ㄴ/은 N means "an adjective describing a noun" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: A-ㄴ/은 N (A-n/eun N) = "an adjective describing a noun". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 예쁜 가방 ("a pretty bag"). This is how a Korean ADJECTIVE attaches to a noun in front of it (the modifier always precedes the noun). Add ㄴ to a vowel stem (예쁘다 → 예쁜 가방) and 은 to a consonant stem (작다 → 작은 집); irregulars shift: ㅂ-adjectives like 춥다 become 추운 날씨, ㄹ stems drop ㄹ (길다 → 긴 머리). A core English-speaker trap is that 있다/없다-type 'adjectives' (맛있다, 재미없다) use the VERB-style ending 는, not 은: it's 맛있는 음식, never '맛있은'. Another is mixing this adjective-modifier with the verb-modifier: descriptive states take A-ㄴ/은 (작은 = 'small'), but ongoing actions take V-는 (먹는 = 'eating'). Don't carry over English word order — Korean never says 'a bag pretty'; the adjective sits before the noun with no copula. These modifiers pile up naturally: 작고 예쁜 집 ('a small, pretty house').

patterns.english: a noun that does the verb
patterns.shortExplanation: V-는 N means "a noun that does the verb" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-는 N (V-neun N) means "a noun that does the verb" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 먹는 사람 ("a person who eats"). Attach 는 to a verb stem to turn the verb into a present-tense modifier describing the noun behind it: 먹는 사람 = 'a person who is eating / who eats'. This is Korean's equivalent of an English relative clause ('the person WHO eats'), but it sits in FRONT of the noun, so the whole clause is read right-to-left into English. ㄹ stems drop the ㄹ before 는: 살다 → 사는 곳 ('the place where I live'), 알다 → 아는 사람 ('someone I know'). The key tense contrast English speakers must learn: V-는 = present/habitual action (가는 버스 = 'the bus that goes'), V-(으)ㄴ = completed/past (간 사람 = 'the person who went'), V-(으)ㄹ = future/prospective (갈 사람 = 'the person who will go'). Don't confuse this verb 는 with the adjective modifier A-ㄴ/은; only 있다/없다 adjectives borrow the 는 form. Common partners: 사는 곳, 아는 사람, 좋아하는 음식, 자주 가는 가게.

Don't confuse this verb 는 with the adjective modifier A-ㄴ/은; only 있다/없다 adjectives borrow the 는 form. Common partners: 사는 곳, 아는 사람, 좋아하는 음식, 자주 가는 가게.

patterns.english: it seems like N / looks like N
patterns.shortExplanation: N 같아요 means "it seems like N / looks like N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "it seems like N / looks like N" uses the pattern N 같아요 (N gatayo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 학생 같아요 ("He seems like a student."). N 같다 means 'is like N / seems to be N', expressing a resemblance or a soft guess, and the noun sits directly before 같아요 with NO object or subject marker (학생 같아요, never '학생을 같아요'). The adjective 같다 conjugates as a regular ㅏ-stem: 같 + 아요 → 같아요. Two contrasts matter for English speakers. First, 같다 ('same/like') vs 비슷하다 ('similar'): 같다 leans toward 'practically identical / seems to BE it' (쌍둥이 같아요 = 'they're like twins'), while 비슷하다 just means 'roughly alike'. Second, this NOUN-pattern (N 같아요) is a guess about identity or likeness, whereas the VERB/ADJECTIVE pattern V/A-(으)ㄴ/는 것 같아요 expresses a tentative judgment about a situation (비가 오는 것 같아요 = 'it seems to be raining'). A frequent trap is forcing 처럼 here: 처럼 ('like, as') modifies a following verb (천사처럼 웃어요 = 'smiles like an angel'), but to predicate 'it seems like an angel' you need 천사 같아요. Collocates with impressions: 꿈 같아요, 거짓말 같아요, 진짜 같아요.

usagePhrases.note: A soft guess about someone's identity.

patterns.shortExplanation: N보다 더 A means "more A than N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: N보다 더 A (N-boda deo A) = "more A than N". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 저보다 더 커요 ("taller than me"). 보다 is the comparison particle 'than', and it attaches to the STANDARD you measure against (the thing being beaten), then 더 ('more') plus the adjective: 저보다 더 커요 = 'taller than me'. A frequent English-speaker error is attaching 보다 to the wrong side — in '오늘은 어제보다 더 추워요', the topic 오늘 is what's colder and 어제 (yesterday) is the baseline with 보다, mirroring English 'today is colder THAN yesterday'. 더 is often optional and idiomatic (어제보다 추워요 already implies 'colder'), but adding 더 sounds natural and emphatic; its opposite 덜 means 'less' (어제보다 덜 추워요 = 'less cold than yesterday'). For the superlative 'the most', switch to 제일/가장 (제일 커요 = 'the biggest'). Don't use 보다 with a 'than' clause the English way before a verb — Korean keeps it as 'N보다'. It collocates with size, speed, weather, and quantity: 키가 커요, 빨라요, 더워요, 많아요.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 attaches to the baseline 저 (me).
Swap 더 for 덜 to mean 'less'.

examples.en: I'm taller than my sibling.
examples.note: Simple: 보다 marks the person you outdo.

examples.en: Today is colder than yesterday.
examples.note: Everyday: 더 emphasizes the bigger degree.

examples.en: The subway is much faster than the bus, so I'll go by subway.
examples.note: Real situation: 훨씬 ('much') intensifies the comparison.

patterns.shortExplanation: V기로 했어요 means "decided to V" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V기로 했어요 (V-giro haesseoyo) means "decided to V" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 가기로 했어요 ("I decided to go."). V기로 하다 reports a DECISION or resolution to do something; 기 nominalizes the verb, 로 marks it as the chosen course, and 하다 ('to do/decide') is kept in the past 했어요 because the deciding already happened — even when the action itself is future (내일 가기로 했어요 = 'I('ve) decided to go tomorrow'). Attach 기로 했어요 straight to the plain stem (가기로, 배우기로, 운동하기로); for the negative, put 안 before the verb (안 먹기로 했어요 = 'decided not to eat'). The main English-speaker pitfall is conjugating 하다 to the future (가기로 할 거예요 is a different nuance: 'I'm going to decide') or to the present (가기로 해요 sounds like a soft proposal 'let's decide to go'); for an already-settled plan, lock it in the past: 했어요. Contrast with V(으)ㄹ게요, which is an on-the-spot promise/volition ('I'll do it', 제가 갈게요), whereas 기로 했어요 reports a decision reached beforehand, often a mutual or deliberate one. It collocates with resolutions and arrangements: 같이 가기로 했어요, 끊기로 했어요, 매일 운동하기로 했어요.

usagePhrases.note: 하다 verb; a New Year's-style resolution.
Negative: 안 goes before the verb.

examples.en: I've decided to learn Korean.
examples.note: Simple: announcing a personal decision.

examples.en: I've decided to go to Korea next year.
examples.note: Everyday: a future plan kept in past 했어요.

examples.romanization: geongangeul wihaeseo oneulbuteo keopireul kkeunkiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: For my health, I've decided to quit coffee starting today.
examples.note: Real situation: a resolution with a reason and a start point.

patterns.shortExplanation: N 동안 means "during N / for N (duration)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "during N / for N (duration)" uses the pattern N 동안 (N dongan). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 한 시간 동안 ("for one hour"). 동안 is a duration noun meaning 'the span / while', placed after a time-length noun to say how long something lasts: 한 시간 동안 = 'for one hour', 방학 동안 = 'during the vacation'. No particle goes between the noun and 동안 (한 시간 동안, never '한 시간에 동안'). The crucial English-speaker contrast is 동안 vs 에: 에 pins an action to a POINT in time ('AT 3 o'clock', 세 시에 갔어요), while 동안 stretches it over a STRETCH of time ('FOR three hours'). So 'I studied for three hours' is 세 시간 동안 공부했어요, but 'I studied at three' is 세 시에 공부했어요. With a verb clause it becomes V-는 동안 ('while ~ing': 제가 자는 동안 = 'while I sleep'). Also distinguish 동안 (a duration) from 까지 (a deadline 'until'): 'until 3' is 세 시까지, 'for 3 hours' is 세 시간 동안 — English 'for' here is NOT 위해(서). It collocates with study, travel, waiting, and stays: 공부했어요, 여행했어요, 기다렸어요, 살았어요.

usagePhrases.note: A period of time as the span.

examples.en: I waited for one hour.
examples.note: Simple: stating how long an action lasted.

examples.en: I went to Korea (and came back) during the vacation.

examples.romanization: jega janeun dongan chinguga jeonhwareul haetdeoragoyo.
examples.en: While I was sleeping, my friend (apparently) called.

patterns.english: intend to V / plan to V
patterns.shortExplanation: V(으)려고 해요 means "intend to V / plan to V" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V(으)려고 해요 (V-(eu)ryeogo haeyo) = "intend to V / plan to V". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 가려고 해요 ("I plan to go."). Use this to announce your own intention or a not-yet-fixed plan: the verb 하다 at the end literally means you are 'trying to / setting out to' do the verb. Form it by adding 려고 after a vowel stem (가다 -> 가려고 해요) and 으려고 after a consonant stem (먹다 -> 먹으려고 해요), then attach 해요. Sharp contrast: -(으)려고 해요 is a leaning or wish, softer and less committed than -(으)ㄹ 거예요, which is a settled decision; '내일 자려고 해요' = 'I'm thinking of sleeping early' whereas '내일 잘 거예요' = 'I will sleep early.' English-speaker pitfall: this is for the speaker's mind, so do not use it to report what someone else firmly will do, and never bolt a noun onto it — say '공부하려고 해요', not '공부 하려고 해요'.

usagePhrases.note: Future leaning, softer than 배울 거예요.
Stem 쉬- ends in a vowel, so no 으.

examples.en: I'm planning to sleep.

examples.en: I intend to meet a friend this weekend.

patterns.shortExplanation: V아/어 주시겠어요? means "could you please V?" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V아/어 주시겠어요? (V-a/eo jusigesseoyo) means "could you please V?" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 도와주시겠어요? ("Could you please help me?"). This is the gentlest everyday way to ask a favor of someone you don't know well: 주다 ('do it for me') becomes honorific 주시다, and the -겠- adds a tentative 'would you mind' softness that a flat 주세요 lacks. Build the 아/어 form (도와 from 돕다, 열어 from 열다, 말해 from 말하다), then add 주시겠어요. Contrast: 주세요 is a clear polite request ('please do X'), while 주시겠어요? is a deferential question ('might I ask you to X?') — perfect for staff, strangers, or anyone senior; 줄래? in the casual tab is only for close friends. Pitfall: English speakers often forget the 아/어 link and say '돕아 주시겠어요' — the verb 돕다 is ㅂ-irregular, so it must be 도와 주시겠어요.

patterns.english: it is good to V / you should V
patterns.shortExplanation: V는 게 좋아요 means "it is good to V / you should V" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "it is good to V / you should V" uses the pattern V는 게 좋아요 (V-neun ge joayo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 가는 게 좋아요 ("It's good to go."). This gives gentle, non-pushy advice — literally 'doing V is good' — so it lands much softer than a direct order. Attach 는 게 좋아요 to the dictionary stem (가다 -> 가는 게 좋아요); ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ before 는, so 만들다 -> 만드는 게 좋아요 and 살다 -> 사는 게 좋아요. The 게 here is a contraction of 것이 ('the thing of doing X'). Sharp contrast: 는 게 좋아요 is a friendly recommendation, whereas -아/어야 해요 is an obligation you cannot skip; '쉬는 게 좋아요' = 'you'd be better off resting' but '쉬어야 해요' = 'you have to rest.' Pitfall: don't write the past 'V은 게 좋아요' for advice — advice about an action you should take always uses the present 는 게, since you're recommending it now.

usagePhrases.note: ㄹ-stem 만들다 drops ㄹ before 는.

patterns.english: I think it will / it seems
patterns.shortExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 means "I think it will / it seems" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: A/V-(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 (A/V-(eu)l geot gatayo) = "I think it will / it seems". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 비가 올 것 같아요 ("I think it'll rain."). Use this to make a soft prediction or guess about something not yet certain — literally 'it seems like the thing that will happen.' Add ㄹ 것 같아요 after a vowel stem (오다 -> 올 것 같아요) and 을 것 같아요 after a consonant stem (늦다 -> 늦을 것 같아요); 같다 means 'to be like / seem.' Important contrast inside this same pattern: the -(으)ㄹ form is a guess about the future or the uncertain ('비가 올 것 같아요' = 'it looks like it'll rain'), while -는 것 같아요 guesses about right now ('비가 오는 것 같아요' = 'it seems to be raining') and -(으)ㄴ 것 같아요 guesses about the past ('비가 온 것 같아요' = 'it seems it rained'). Pitfall: English 'I think' is often a firm opinion, but -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 is deliberately tentative and polite, so don't use it when you actually know — for certainty use -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

usagePhrases.en: It looks like it'll be tasty.

usagePhrases.note: Soft opinion, not a firm claim.

examples.en: I think it'll rain.
examples.note: Bare weather guess.

examples.romanization: giri makyeoseo jom neujeul geot gatayo.
examples.en: Traffic's heavy, so I'll be a bit late.
examples.note: Reason clause + 좀 to soften.

examples.romanization: i yeonghwa pyeongi joteonde jaemiisseul geot gatayo.
examples.en: The reviews were good, so I think this movie will be fun.
examples.note: Evidence + tentative judgment.

patterns.shortExplanation: V(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 means "have done V before" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 (V-(eu)n jeogi isseoyo) means "have done V before" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 가 본 적이 있어요 ("I've been there before."). This is the 'have you ever...' experience pattern: 적 is a bound noun meaning 'a (past) occasion,' so the whole thing literally says 'there exists an occasion on which I did V.' Add ㄴ 적이 있어요 after a vowel stem (가다 -> 간 적이 있어요) and 은 적이 있어요 after a consonant stem (먹다 -> 먹은 적이 있어요); swap 있어요 for 없어요 to say you never have. Sharp contrast with plain past tense: -았/었어요 just reports that something happened ('어제 갔어요' = 'I went yesterday'), while -(으)ㄴ 적이 있어요 highlights it as a life experience worth noting ('가 본 적이 있어요' = 'I've had the experience of going'), so it pairs naturally with -아/어 보다 ('try'). Pitfall: don't use it for a recent or one-time event you'd describe with a date — 'I ate breakfast this morning' is 아침을 먹었어요, not 먹은 적이 있어요.

usagePhrases.note: Pairs with 보다 'try': 가 보다 -> 가 본.

examples.en: I've been there before.
examples.note: Bare experience statement.

examples.en: Have you ever watched a Korean movie?
examples.note: Question form with 을 object.

examples.note: Contrastive 은 marks experience vs none.

patterns.shortExplanation: N 때문에 means "because of N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "because of N" uses the pattern N 때문에 (N ttaemune). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 비 때문에 ("because of the rain"). Use this to name a noun as the cause of something, usually a result you didn't choose — it leans toward blame or unwanted consequences. Place the noun directly before 때문에 with no particle (비 때문에, 일 때문에). Sharp contrast: 때문에 most often introduces a negative cause ('비 때문에 취소했어요' = 'I canceled because of the rain'), whereas 덕분에 ('thanks to') introduces a positive cause you're grateful for ('친구 덕분에 잘 끝났어요'), so swapping them changes the whole tone. Also note 때문에 takes a NOUN; to give a verb/adjective reason you must say -기 때문에 (바쁘기 때문에). Pitfall: English 'because' is one word that handles both, but Korean splits noun-cause (때문에) from clause-cause (-아서 / -니까 / -기 때문에), and learners wrongly insert a particle — it's 비 때문에, never 비가 때문에.

examples.en: I canceled the plan because of the rain.
examples.note: Bare noun cause.

examples.en: These days I'm so busy because of work.
examples.note: Adds time word 요즘.

examples.en: I couldn't go to school yesterday because of a cold.
examples.note: Cause + 못 (couldn't) result.

patterns.english: because / since V (reason for a request)
patterns.shortExplanation: V(으)니까 means "because / since V (reason for a request)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V(으)니까 (V-(eu)nikka) = "because / since V (reason for a request)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 비가 오니까 ("since it's raining"). This gives a reason that the speaker is presenting as grounds for what comes next — a request, a suggestion, or a command — so it's the 'since...' that leads into 'so let's / so please.' Add 니까 after a vowel stem (오다 -> 오니까) and 으니까 after a consonant stem (없다 -> 없으니까). Crucial contrast: -(으)니까 vs -아/어서. Use -니까 before an order, request, or suggestion ('비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요'), but -아/어서 before a plain statement of result and never before a command ('비가 와서 못 갔어요' = 'I couldn't go because it rained'). Also, -아/어서 cannot carry a past-tense marker on its clause, but -니까 can (갔으니까). Pitfall: English speakers default to one 'because' everywhere — saying '늦어서 미안해요' is right, but '늦으니까 미안해요' sounds like you're justifying yourself rather than apologizing, so for apologies and pure cause use -아/어서.

usagePhrases.note: Vowel stem 오다 -> 오니까, leads to a request.

examples.en: Since it's raining, take an umbrella.
examples.note: Reason + command (the 니까 home turf).

examples.en: Since I'm busy today, let's meet tomorrow.

examples.en: Since I've already read it all, you may take this book.
examples.note: Past-tense 봤으니까 + offer.

patterns.shortExplanation: N처럼 means "like N / as N" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: N처럼 (N-cheoreom) means "like N / as N" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 가수처럼 ("like a singer"). Use this to say one thing resembles or behaves the same way as a noun — 'like / just as.' Attach 처럼 directly to the noun with no particle (가수처럼, 꿈처럼). Sharp contrast: 처럼 expresses likeness or equal degree ('가수처럼 노래해요' = 'sings like a singer'), but 보다 expresses inequality / comparison ('가수보다 잘해요' = 'sings better than a singer'), so they are opposites — one means 'similar to,' the other 'more/less than.' 처럼 also overlaps with 같이 in this sense (가수같이 노래해요 ≈ 가수처럼 노래해요), though 처럼 is the more neutral default. Pitfall: English 'like' doubles as 'such as' for examples, but Korean 처럼 only means 'resembling'; to list examples ('fruits like apples') you'd use 같은 (사과 같은 과일), not 사과처럼 과일.

examples.note: Bare likeness frame.

patterns.english: even if V / even though V
patterns.shortExplanation: V아/어도 means "even if V / even though V" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "even if V / even though V" uses the pattern V아/어도 (V-a/eodo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 비가 와도 ("even if it rains"). This concedes a condition that doesn't change the outcome — 'even if / even though.' Build the 아/어 form, then add 도 ('also/even'): use 아 after a bright vowel ㅏ or ㅗ (가다 -> 가도, 오다 -> 와도), 어 otherwise (먹다 -> 먹어도), and 해 for 하다 verbs (공부해도). Contrast with -(으)면 ('if'): -(으)면 says the result depends on the condition ('비가 오면 안 가요' = 'if it rains I won't go'), while -아/어도 says the result holds in spite of it ('비가 와도 가요' = 'even if it rains, I'll go') — so they point in opposite directions. It also overlaps with -지만 ('but'), but -아/어도 is hypothetical ('even if it were') whereas -지만 reports an actual fact ('비싸지만 샀어요' = 'it was expensive but I bought it'). Pitfall: pick the vowel by sound, not by spelling out the stem — 오다 contracts to 와도, never 오아도.

examples.en: Even if it's a bit pricey, if the quality's good I'll buy this.
examples.note: Concession combined with a 면 condition.

patterns.english: while doing V (at the same time)
patterns.shortExplanation: V(으)면서 means "while doing V (at the same time)" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V(으)면서 (V-(eu)myeonseo) = "while doing V (at the same time)". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 걸으면서 ("while walking"). Use this when one person does two actions at the same moment — the action in the 면서 clause runs concurrently with the main verb. Add 면서 after a vowel stem (보다 -> 보면서) and 으면서 after a consonant stem (먹다 -> 먹으면서); for ㄷ-irregular verbs the ㄷ becomes ㄹ (듣다 -> 들으면서). Key rule and contrast: the subject of both actions must be the SAME person, which is exactly how -(으)면서 differs from -(으)ㄹ 때 ('when,' which just sets a time and allows different subjects) and from -고 ('and then,' which lets actions be sequential rather than overlapping). 'TV를 보면서 밥을 먹어요' = doing both at once; 'TV를 보고 밥을 먹어요' = watch first, then eat. Pitfall: English 'while' can cover two different people ('while I cooked, he cleaned'), but Korean -(으)면서 cannot — for two separate subjects acting at once use -는 동안 (동안 = 'during') instead.

usagePhrases.note: Stem 마시- ends in a vowel, no 으.

examples.en: I study while listening to music.
examples.note: Bare simultaneous frame, one subject.

examples.en: I watch TV while eating.
examples.note: Two objects, both done by 'I'.

examples.romanization: jeoneun keopireul masimyeonseo chinguhago cheoncheonhi iyagihaesseoyo.
examples.en: I chatted slowly with a friend while drinking coffee.

patterns.shortExplanation: V기 시작하다 means "start doing" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V기 시작하다 (-gi sijakada) means "start doing" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 저는 한국어를 배우기 시작했어요. ("I started learning Korean."). This pattern turns a verb into a noun with 기 and then feeds it to 시작하다 (始作하다, Sino-Korean 始 'begin' + 作 'make/do'), so literally you are 'doing the beginning of the action'. Use it when you want to spotlight the very moment an action gets underway: 비가 오기 시작했어요 ('it started to rain'). The close rival is plain 시작하다 with a noun object, 공부를 시작하다 ('start studying'): use that when the activity is already a noun, but use V기 시작하다 when you have a verb and want to keep its verb meaning. English speakers carry over 'start to' versus 'start -ing' as if Korean had two forms, but Korean only has this one, so do not say 오게 시작하다 or 와서 시작하다. The other trap is attaching 기 to a noun: 비기 시작하다 is wrong because 비 is already a noun; you need a verb stem like 오- before 기.

usagePhrases.note: past 했어요 is the default; the start already happened
weather verbs like 오다 take this pattern naturally
marks a true first time, a milestone

usagePhrases.en: Once I start exercising I feel good.
usagePhrases.note: stack 면 on the whole pattern for 'once you start'

examples.note: 언제 + past asks for the starting point

examples.en: These days I've started reading books.
examples.note: 요즘 frames a newly begun habit

patterns.shortExplanation: V게 되다 means "come to / end up" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "come to / end up" uses the pattern V게 되다 (-ge doeda). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 한국에 살게 됐어요. ("I ended up living in Korea."). V게 되다 frames a result as something that happened TO you rather than something you chose: 되다 means 'become', so the whole thing says 'it came to be that...'. Reach for it when outside circumstances, fate, or other people produced the outcome — 한국에 살게 됐어요 quietly signals 'it worked out that I live in Korea', softer and more humble than 한국에 살아요 ('I live in Korea', a flat fact). Contrast it sharply with V기로 하다, which marks a firm personal decision: 회사를 그만두기로 했어요 = 'I decided to quit' (my will), whereas 회사를 그만두게 됐어요 = 'I ended up quitting' (circumstances pushed me). Koreans love this pattern precisely because it downplays personal agency, which sounds modest and polite. The English-speaker pitfall is overusing it for plain decisions — if you clearly chose something, 게 되다 sounds evasive, as if you are dodging responsibility. Also note the spelling: 되다 contracts to 돼요 (되 + 어요), not 되요, in casual and polite speech.

usagePhrases.note: result of circumstances, not a stated choice

usagePhrases.en: I came to like that person.
usagePhrases.note: a gradual, unplanned change of feeling

usagePhrases.en: I ended up quitting the company.
usagePhrases.note: implies it was not fully my decision

usagePhrases.en: I've come to eat spicy food now.
usagePhrases.note: 이제 + pattern shows a new state you grew into

examples.en: How did you come to learn Korean?
examples.note: 어떻게...게 됐어요 politely asks 'what led you to'

examples.en: I suddenly ended up moving.
examples.note: great for unexpected life changes

patterns.shortExplanation: V아/어 있다 means "state continues" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V아/어 있다 (-a/eo itda) = "state continues". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 문이 열려 있어요. ("The door is open."). V아/어 있다 describes the lingering STATE left behind after an action finishes: the door was opened and stays open, so 문이 열려 있어요 ('the door is open'). Pick 아 있다 when the stem's last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ (앉아 있다) and 어 있다 otherwise (열려 있다, 서 있다). The notorious confusion is with V고 있다, the progressive: 고 있다 is the action still happening, 아/어 있다 is the result still in place. So 앉고 있어요 = 'I am (in the act of) sitting down', while 앉아 있어요 = 'I am seated'; 문을 열고 있어요 = 'I am opening the door', 문이 열려 있어요 = 'the door is (already) open'. Notice 아/어 있다 takes mostly intransitive or passive verbs (오다, 가다, 서다, 열리다, 켜지다) and the noun gets 이/가, not 을/를. The English-speaker trap is using it with transitive action verbs like 먹다 or 읽다: 밥을 먹어 있어요 is wrong; an action you keep doing needs 고 있다 (밥을 먹고 있어요).

usagePhrases.note: passive 열리다 + the door takes 이/가, not 을/를
the result of turning it on still holds

usagePhrases.en: I am sitting on a chair.
usagePhrases.note: 앉- ends in ㅏ so it takes 아 있다

examples.note: state after 피다 (to bloom) completes

patterns.shortExplanation: V(으)ㄹ 때 means "when" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V(으)ㄹ 때 (-(eu)l ttae) means "when" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 밥을 먹을 때 물을 마셔요. ("When I eat, I drink water."). 때 is the noun 'time/occasion', so V(으)ㄹ 때 literally means 'the time when V', naming the moment an action or state holds: 밥을 먹을 때 = 'when (I) eat'. Attach ㄹ 때 after a vowel-final stem (갈 때) and 을 때 after a consonant-final stem (먹을 때, 좋을 때). This works with adjectives too — 피곤할 때 ('when tired') — which sets it apart from time markers reserved for verbs. The key contrast is with the connective -(으)면 ('if/whenever'): -(으)ㄹ 때 pins down a specific occasion or duration ('during the time when'), while -(으)면 states a condition ('if it happens'). So 비가 올 때 우산을 써요 = 'when it rains (at that time) I use an umbrella', whereas 비가 오면 = 'if/whenever it rains'. For a completed past moment, switch to V았/었을 때: 어렸을 때 ('when I was young'). The English-speaker pitfall is dropping the 으: consonant stems need it (좋을 때, not 좋ㄹ 때), and learners often forget that 때 is a real noun that can take particles like 에 or 부터.

usagePhrases.note: 먹- ends in a consonant, so 을 때

usagePhrases.en: When I head home, I call.

patterns.shortExplanation: V는 동안 means "while / during" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "while / during" uses the pattern V는 동안 (-neun dongan). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 제가 요리하는 동안 기다려 주세요. ("Please wait while I cook."). 동안 is the noun 'a stretch of time/duration', so V는 동안 means 'during the whole time that V is going on', framing two events that share the same span: 제가 요리하는 동안 기다려 주세요 ('please wait while I cook'). Because 동안 is a present-tense duration noun, the verb takes the 는 modifier ending, never 은. Contrast it with V(으)ㄹ 때: 때 points at the moment or occasion ('at the time when'), while 동안 stresses the continuous span throughout which something runs in parallel. So 자는 동안 = 'all the while I sleep (the whole duration)', whereas 잘 때 = 'when I sleep / at sleeping time'. 동안 can also stand alone after a plain noun of duration: 방학 동안 ('during the vacation'), 한 시간 동안 ('for one hour'). The English-speaker pitfall is attaching 은 instead of 는 (자은 동안 is wrong; it must be 자는 동안), and translating 'while' too loosely — if you mean contrast ('while X, Y is different'), Korean uses -는데 or -지만, not 동안, which is purely about overlapping time.

usagePhrases.note: two actions run over one shared span

usagePhrases.en: While I study, I keep my phone off.
usagePhrases.note: main clause holds throughout the studying

usagePhrases.en: It rained while I was sleeping.
usagePhrases.note: a background event filling the same period

examples.en: While I wait, I read a book.

examples.en: While the baby slept, I cleaned.
examples.note: two events overlapping in real time

patterns.shortExplanation: A/V-지만 means "but" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: A/V-지만 (-jiman) = "but". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 한국어는 어렵지만 재미있어요. ("Korean is hard but fun."). -지만 clips straight onto a verb or adjective stem to join two clauses that pull against each other: 한국어는 어렵지만 재미있어요 ('Korean is hard but fun'). It is the everyday, neutral 'but', equally at home in writing and speech. The sharp contrast to learn is -지만 versus -는데: -지만 states a clean, head-on opposition (A, but the opposite B), while -는데 gives softer background or contrast that sets up the next remark — 비싸지만 샀어요 simply says 'expensive but I bought it', whereas 비싼데 살까요? leans into 'it's pricey, so... should I buy it?'. After a noun you need the copula: 학생이지만 ('though I'm a student'), not 학생지만. Tense usually sits on the final clause, not before 지만, so 'I was tired but studied' is 피곤하지만 공부했어요, with 했 carrying the past. The English-speaker pitfall is starting a brand-new sentence with 'But...' as in English; Korean prefers to fold the contrast into one sentence with 지만, or to use 하지만/그렇지만 as a sentence-opener instead of bare 지만.

usagePhrases.note: contrasts two adjectives in one breath

usagePhrases.en: It's raining but I'm going out.
usagePhrases.note: verb stem + 지만, no tense before it

usagePhrases.en: I'm hungry but I'm holding out.
usagePhrases.note: sets two opposing states side by side

usagePhrases.en: I'm a student, but I work too.
usagePhrases.note: after a noun use 이지만, not bare 지만

examples.en: These clothes are pricey but pretty.
examples.note: trade-off between price and looks

examples.en: I ate a lot but I'm hungry again.
examples.note: to stress the past, 었지만 is allowed

examples.en: I'm tired but I study anyway.
examples.note: tense stays on the second verb, 공부해요

The English-speaker pitfall is starting a brand-new sentence with 'But...' as in English; Korean prefers to fold the contrast into one sentence with 지만, or to use 하지만/그렇지만 as a sentence-opener instead of bare 지만.
