Beginning a sentence with a lone 지만 the way English starts with 'But...'. 지만 must attach to a stem; to open a sentence use 하지만 or 그렇지만.

patterns.shortExplanation: V거나 means "or" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V거나 (-geona) means "or" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 주말에 자거나 영화를 봐요. ("On weekends I sleep or watch movies."). -거나 attaches to a verb (or adjective) stem to offer alternative ACTIONS — 'do this or do that' — when either option is fine: 주말에 자거나 영화를 봐요 ('on weekends I sleep or watch a movie'). The crucial split for English speakers is that Korean splits 'or' by part of speech: -거나 joins verbs/adjectives, while (이)나 joins nouns. So 'coffee or tea' (two nouns) is 커피나 차, but 'drink coffee or drink tea' (two verbs) is 커피를 마시거나 차를 마셔요. A second rival is -든지, which adds a 'whichever, no matter which' nuance ('do whatever, sleep or watch a movie, I don't care'), while plain -거나 just lists open options neutrally. You can chain more than two: 자거나 먹거나 쉬어요. The English-speaker pitfall is using 거나 to connect nouns (커피거나 차 is wrong — use 커피나 차) and confusing it with 아니면 ('or else / otherwise'), which links whole sentences rather than gluing two verbs inside one clause.

patterns.shortExplanation: N마다 means "every" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "every" uses the pattern N마다 (-mada). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 저는 아침마다 운동해요. ("I work out every morning."). 마다 is a particle you stick onto a noun to mean 'each / every one without exception', and it carries two flavors: with a time noun it means 'every time' (아침마다 = 'every morning'), and with a countable noun it means 'each individual one' (사람마다 = 'each person'). It often pairs with 다르다 to say things differ case by case: 나라마다 문화가 달라요 ('every country has a different culture'). Compare it with the standalone 매 (every) and 모든 (all): 매일 and 날마다 both mean 'every day', but 매 attaches to specific time words (매일, 매주, 매년) while 마다 is freer and can ride any noun (가게마다, 집집마다). And 모든 사람 ('all people') views the group as a whole, whereas 사람마다 zooms in on each member one by one. The English-speaker pitfall is attaching 마다 to a verb (자마다 is wrong) — for 'every time you do X' you need V(으)ㄹ 때마다 (잘 때마다) — and reaching for 매 with nouns it doesn't take, where 마다 is the safe, productive choice.

patterns.shortExplanation: V자마자 means "as soon as" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V자마자 (-jamaja) = "as soon as". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 집에 오자마자 손을 씻어요. ("The moment I get home, I wash my hands."). -자마자 fuses onto a verb stem to say the second action follows the first with zero gap: 집에 오자마자 손을 씻어요 ('the moment I get home, I wash my hands'). It is the tightest 'right after' connector. Compare it with V은/ㄴ 후에 ('after'), which only says B happens later, allowing any delay, while 자마자 insists on immediacy and often a touch of surprise — 도착한 후에 전화해요 = 'I'll call sometime after arriving', but 도착하자마자 전화해요 = 'I'll call the instant I arrive'. Two grammar facts trip learners up: never put a tense marker before 자마자 (write 끝나자마자, not 끝났자마자) even when the whole sentence is past, because the final verb carries the tense — 보자마자 웃었어요 ('I laughed the moment I saw it'). The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like 'as soon as' clauses that take their own tense in English ('as soon as I arrived'), and confusing it with the time noun phrase V는 대로, which is more formal and planning-oriented ('as soon as it's done, per arrangement').

usagePhrases.note: B follows A with no gap at all

patterns.shortExplanation: V(으)려면 means "if you intend to" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V(으)려면 (-(eu)ryeomyeon) means "if you intend to" — a sentence frame, not a single word. Keep the frame and swap the marked V or N for your own, e.g. 한국어를 잘하려면 매일 연습해요. ("To get good at Korean, practice daily."). V(으)려면 is a contraction of 려고 하면 ('if you intend/plan to'), so it sets up a goal and then states what you must do to reach it: 한국어를 잘하려면 매일 연습해요 ('if you mean to get good at Korean, practice daily'). Use 려면 after a vowel-final stem (가려면, 잘하려면) and 으려면 after a consonant-final stem (읽으려면, 먹으려면). It naturally leads into advice or requirements, so it loves to pair with 야 하다/돼요, 세요, or 필요하다: 건강하려면 잘 자야 해요. Contrast it with the plain conditional -(으)면, which states a neutral 'if/when' about facts, while -(으)려면 specifically frames a deliberate goal or intention you are aiming at: 비가 오면 = 'if it rains' (a circumstance), but 살을 빼려면 = 'if you intend to lose weight' (your aim). The English-speaker pitfalls are dropping the 으 on consonant stems (읽려면 is wrong — say 읽으려면) and using 려면 for things outside your control; since it implies intention, you would not say 비가 오려면 for 'if it rains', because rain is not something you intend.

patterns.shortExplanation: V았/었어요 means "polite past tense" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: "polite past tense" uses the pattern V았/었어요 (Vat/eosseoyo). Plug a real verb stem or noun into the slot: 어제 밥을 먹었어요. ("I ate rice yesterday."). Take the verb stem. If the last vowel of the stem is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 았어요; all other vowels add 었어요. Contracted stems: 하다 → 했어요; 오다 → 왔어요; 보다 → 봤어요. Irregular ㅂ stems drop ㅂ and add 웠어요 (춥다 → 추웠어요). Irregular ㄷ stems change ㄷ to ㄹ before 었어요 (듣다 → 들었어요). Irregular ㅅ stems drop ㅅ (낫다 → 나았어요). Irregular 르 stems: 모르다 → 몰랐어요, 다르다 → 달랐어요. Contrast with V-고 있었어요 (past progressive) and V았/었었어요 (remote past / past-perfect nuance). The doubled past 았/었었어요 signals an action that was true in the past but is no longer true: 살았었어요 = 'I used to live there (but no longer do)'. Avoid confusing the ㅂ-irregular past 웠어요 with the future -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

patterns.shortExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 means "future tense / strong intention" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 (V-(eu)r geoyeyo) = "future tense / strong intention". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 내일 친구를 만날 거예요. ("I will meet a friend tomorrow."). Take the verb stem. After a vowel-final stem add -ㄹ 거예요 (가다 → 갈 거예요, 하다 → 할 거예요). Contrast with V-(으)ㄹ게요 (first-person promise/commitment only) and A/V-겠- (volition or inference based on sensory evidence). Four suffixes attach to specific verb stems to create passive verbs: -이- (보다 → 보이다, 쓰다 → 쓰이다), -히- (읽다 → 읽히다, 잡다 → 잡히다), -리- (팔다 → 팔리다, 듣다 → 들리다), -기- (안다 → 안기다, 막다 → 막히다).

patterns.shortExplanation: N에게 / 한테 / 께 means "to / from a person" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: N에게 / 한테 / 께 (Nege / hante / kke) = "to / from a person". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 친구에게 문자를 보냈어요. ("I sent a text to a friend."). Attach directly to a noun. 에게 is written/formal; 한테 is colloquial; 께 is honorific. Direction 'to': 친구에게 편지를 써요. Direction 'from': add 서 to the dative — 에게서 / 한테서 / 께서. For non-person recipients use N에 not N에게. Distinguish N에게서 (from a person) from N에서 (from a place). The particle 한테 is identical in function to 에게 but is conversational — do not use in formal writing.

patterns.shortExplanation: N밖에 + 부정 means "nothing but / only with negation" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.

Attach 밖에 directly to a noun. The predicate MUST be negative: 없다, 안 V, 못 V, V지 않다. N밖에 없어요 = 'there is only N / nothing but N'. Using 밖에 with a positive predicate is ungrammatical. Contrast with N만 (only N, takes a positive predicate). N밖에 emphasizes scarcity or restriction — the speaker feels the amount is insufficient. 밖에 없다 is very common and should be memorized as a chunk.

patterns.shortExplanation: -군요 / -구나 means "realization / exclamation ending" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
patterns.explanation: -군요 / -구나 (-gunyo / -guna) = "realization / exclamation ending". It is a reusable structure — change one word at a time and the grammar stays correct: 그렇군요. 몰랐어요. ("Oh, I see. I didn't know that."). Polite form: verb/adjective stem + 군요. For action verbs in present tense add 는 before 군요: V-는군요. For descriptive verbs attach directly: A-군요. Casual/intimate form: -구나. Contrast with -네요 (pattern-113): -네요 is more common in everyday speech and implies direct sensory discovery; -군요 is slightly more literary/formal. -구나 is used in casual speech or when talking to oneself / to a child. 그렇군요 is a very common filler meaning 'I see / is that so?'.

patterns.shortExplanation: N만 means "only / just" as a reusable Korean sentence pattern.
